They were largest on tasks that ask for abstract classification and for the detection of patterns in unfamiliar material, and much smaller on tasks that draw on stored knowledge, such as vocabulary and arithmetic. Consider a person asked what a spade and a pair of shears have in common. She can answer that both are tools, or that one is used to dig the flower bed and the other to trim the hedge around it. The first answer earns credit; the second does not. Yet the second is not stupid. It reflects a habit of thinking about things in terms of their practical relations, a habit well suited to a life in which what matters about a spade is whether it will break the ground before the rain comes.

On this reading, the twentieth century did not make people more intelligent in some general sense; it trained a particular style of thought. Mass schooling, work that deals in symbols rather than objects, and a culture saturated with categories and hypotheticals rewarded the habit of setting aside what things are for and attending to what kind of thing they are. The tests, built by people who had that habit, measured it well. Nor is the spread of the habit a trivial change, since it is precisely the habit that a world of written rules, formal classifications and hypothetical planning keeps demanding of the people who live in it. The gains are therefore real, since the habit genuinely spread, but they are not gains in a single underlying power that would make the average person of today a match for the most gifted minds of a century ago.

This resolution is attractive, but it has a price that is not always acknowledged. If scores on the most abstract tests reflect habits cultivated by a particular kind of society, then the tests cannot be quite what they were often taken to be, a culture-free measure of raw capacity. They remain good predictors of success in schools and workplaces, but partly because those institutions demand the very habits the tests detect. It does not follow that the tests are worthless, or that differences in scores within a generation mean nothing; among people educated in broadly similar ways, scores can still capture real differences in how well they reason. What does follow is that comparisons across generations, and across societies with very different patterns of schooling and work, need to be interpreted with far more caution than a single number invites.

The picture of the ageing mind that most people carry is one of steady decline. Memory falters, thinking slows, and the sharpness of youth gives way, from some point in early adulthood, to a long and gentle slide. The picture is not invented. On tasks that require rapid processing of unfamiliar information, such as spotting a target among distractors or holding several new items in mind while manipulating them, performance does fall with age, and the fall can be detected well before what anyone would call old age. But the picture has been assembled in a way that makes the decline look both steeper and more uniform than it is.

Much of the early evidence came from comparing people of different ages at a single moment, a method that is quick and cheap and was therefore used widely. A group of seventy-year-olds tested alongside a group of twenty-five-year-olds differs from it in more than age: the older group grew up with less schooling, different work and less familiarity with the kind of test being given. Studies that follow the same people over decades tend to show later and gentler declines than such snapshots suggest, though they carry biases of their own, since those who stay in a long study are often healthier and more able than those who drop out. Neither method gives a clean view, and the honest summary is that some decline is real, while its timing and size are less certain than the familiar picture implies.

More important, the familiar picture attends to only half of what changes. Knowledge of words, of facts, of how things usually go and how people usually behave, goes on accumulating well into later life, and on tests that draw on it older adults often outperform younger ones. Some researchers have gone further, proposing that part of the measured slowing reflects not failing machinery but a larger store: a mind that knows more words takes longer to find any one of them, much as a large library takes longer to search than a small one. The proposal is contested, and it cannot explain away every loss. It does, however, show that the same observation, a slower response, can be read as a symptom of deterioration or as a cost of accumulation, depending on what one assumes about the mind producing it.

It would be a mistake to replace the narrative of decline with an equally simple narrative of wisdom, in which age brings a serenity and judgement that compensate for everything else. Older people are not uniformly wise, and losses in speed and working memory have real consequences, for learning a new technology, for instance, or for following a fast conversation in a noisy room. The more defensible view is that ageing changes the mix of a person's capacities rather than lowering a single level, and that whether the change amounts to a loss depends on the task. In a setting that rewards speed with novel material, the young will usually have the advantage; in one that rewards the recognition of familiar patterns, a wide vocabulary or an accurate sense of how situations tend to unfold, the advantage may lie the other way. A good deal of everyday competence, from running a household to reading the mood of a tense meeting, belongs to the second kind. A society that judges older minds only by the first kind of task will find decline wherever it looks.

The line-judgement experiments of the 1950s are among the most retold stories in psychology, and the moral usually drawn from them is a gloomy one. A participant sits among strangers who, one after another, give an obviously wrong answer about which of several lines matches a standard; when the participant's turn comes, he often repeats their error. The lesson, we are told, is that ordinary people will deny the evidence of their own eyes rather than stand apart from a crowd. This reading has become so familiar that it is easy to forget how much interpretation it smuggles in.

Begin with the numbers that the gloomy version tends to leave out. On the critical trials, most of the answers participants gave were correct, and a sizeable share of people never yielded at all. A study that is remembered as a demonstration of conformity could as easily be remembered as a demonstration of independence under strange and uncomfortable conditions. Which of these stories gets told says more about the teller than about the data.

More important is the question of what yielding meant. Outside the laboratory, when several people who seem competent and sincere all report the same thing, the rational response is to give their reports considerable weight, even against one's own impression. Our senses err, and other people are among the best instruments we have for catching their errors. A participant who reasoned, 'I cannot see why they are all saying this, but it is unlikely that every one of them is mistaken,' was not abandoning reason; he was applying a rule that serves well almost everywhere except in a room deliberately arranged to defeat it. On this view much of what looks like spineless deference is better described as informational influence: treating others as evidence.

None of this means that the pressure in the room was imaginary. Variations in which participants wrote their answers privately, rather than announcing them aloud, produced far less agreement with the majority, which suggests that some yielding was about avoiding embarrassment rather than about belief. Participants interviewed afterwards also described acute discomfort, and some admitted that they had answered against what they saw. Normative pressure, the wish to fit in, was real. The point is not that it was absent but that it was only part of the picture, and that collapsing everything into it produces a caricature.

The caricature matters because it shapes the remedies we prescribe. If people conform because they are weak, the cure is to exhort them to be brave. If they conform partly because they are sensibly using others as sources of information, the cure is better information: making dissent visible, so that a single honest voice breaks the appearance of unanimity, and designing institutions in which the reasons behind a majority view can be inspected rather than merely counted.

Few findings in social psychology have escaped the laboratory as completely as the bystander effect. In its popular form it says that the more people witness an emergency, the less likely the victim is to receive help, and it is usually offered as evidence of modern apathy: crowds of onlookers, each waiting for someone else to act. The idea owes much of its fame to a newspaper account of a murder in a city street in the 1960s, in which dozens of neighbours were said to have watched and done nothing. Later investigation suggested that the account greatly exaggerated both the number of witnesses and their indifference, but by then the story had become a parable.

The experiments that followed were more careful than the parable. Their central claim was not that people are callous but that responsibility, when shared, is diluted. A person who believes that she alone has heard a cry for help knows that if she does not act, no one will; a person who knows that others have heard it can reasonably suppose that someone better placed is already responding. Ambiguity compounds the effect. In a group, each witness looks to the others to work out whether anything is really wrong, and the calm faces of people who are themselves only watching can persuade everyone that nothing is.

Yet there is a gap between what these studies measured and what the popular version claims. They showed that a given individual is less likely to help when others are present. They did not show that a victim is less likely to be helped. The two come apart because a crowd contains many potential helpers: even if each one is somewhat less willing, the chance that at least one of them steps forward can remain high, and may rise as the crowd grows. Some recent studies of recorded conflicts in public places have reported that in most of them at least one bystander intervened, a pattern hard to reconcile with the image of the paralysed crowd.

None of this makes the original research worthless. The mechanisms it identified are real, and they help explain why emergencies in which no one is sure what is happening, or whose job it is to act, can go unanswered. What it does not support is a sweeping verdict on human nature. The practical advice that follows from the research is modest and useful: if you need help, single out one person and tell that person what to do, so that responsibility is no longer shared and the situation is no longer ambiguous.

Imagine being told, after a brief task in which you estimated the number of dots flashed on a screen, that you belong to the group of 'overestimators'. You never meet another member of your group; you do not know who they are; nothing hangs on the label. You are then asked to divide small sums of money between two anonymous people, one described as an overestimator and the other as an underestimator. Experiments built on this design, which came to be called the minimal group paradigm, found that people reliably gave a little more to members of their own arbitrary category. Some even preferred allocations that maximised the gap between the groups over allocations that would have given their own group more in absolute terms.

The result has often been read as a revelation about human nature. If a meaningless label is enough to produce favouritism, the argument runs, then tribalism must be wired into us, waiting for any pretext, and the deeper divisions of nation, religion and ethnicity are only this primitive tendency writ large. The reading is dramatic, but it outruns the evidence in two ways.

First, what the experiments mostly showed was favouritism, not hostility. Participants tilted rewards towards their own side, but they were generally reluctant to impose costs on the other side when the task was framed as distributing penalties rather than rewards. Giving one's own a little more is not the same as wishing the others harm, and a theory of intergroup conflict that treats the two as interchangeable will misunderstand both. Second, the favouritism itself may be less mindless than it looks. Several later studies suggested that it shrinks when participants are told that members of their group will not know how they allocated, as though people were partly acting on an expectation that their own side would reciprocate. On that account the label is not a trigger for blind loyalty but a cue about whom one is in a cooperative relationship with.

None of this makes the original finding trivial. It remains striking that so thin a basis for belonging should shape behaviour at all, and the speed with which people adopt a category as their own deserves to be taken seriously. But the lesson that follows is not the fatalistic one. If group membership can be conjured from a coin toss or a dot-counting task, then it can also be redrawn: categories that are learned so easily are not fixed, and identities that cut across existing divisions can be built by the same mechanism that builds divisions in the first place.

What the laboratory cannot tell us is why particular divisions in the world become bitter. Real groups have histories, grievances and competing claims on land, jobs and power, and a five-minute label carries none of these. The minimal group paradigm shows where the raw material of loyalty comes from; it does not show what turns that material into enmity.

Empathy enjoys a reputation that few other psychological capacities can match. To be told that one lacks it is an accusation; to call for more of it is to sound wise. Yet if empathy is understood in its strict sense, as the capacity to feel what another person feels, to be distressed by their distress and buoyed by their relief, there are reasons to doubt that it is a dependable guide to how we ought to act, however much it enriches how we live.

The trouble lies in its shape. Empathy works like a narrow beam: it illuminates whatever it is pointed at with great intensity and leaves everything else in darkness. It is most easily directed at people who are near us, who resemble us and who can be seen as individuals with faces and names. It is notoriously insensitive to number; the plight of one child described in detail can move us more than a report of thousands suffering in the same way, because thousands cannot be felt, only counted. A capacity with these properties will reliably favour the identifiable over the statistical, the familiar over the strange and the present over the future, and those are precisely the biases that moral reasoning is supposed to correct.

There is a darker possibility as well. Because empathy is felt for particular victims, it can be recruited against other people. An account of a single person wronged by a member of some group can stir a fierce sympathy that is then turned into demands for punishment of the whole group. The emotion in such cases is genuine; what is wrong is its range.

The obvious objection is that without empathy we would not care at all, and that a morality built only on principle would be bloodless. But this assumes that empathy is the only route to concern. Many people help strangers without imagining their way into the strangers' experience, out of a settled wish that others fare well, a sense of fairness, or the plain recognition that suffering is bad wherever it occurs. Psychologists sometimes distinguish empathy from compassion along these lines: the first means sharing another's feeling, the second means caring about another's good without necessarily sharing the feeling. Compassion, unlike empathic distress, does not exhaust the carer, and it can be extended to people one will never see.

None of this is an argument for coldness. In friendship, in parenting and in the consulting room, the ability to feel with another person is part of what makes the relationship what it is, and nobody would wish it away. The claim is narrower: that when we must decide how to allocate help across many people, or how to treat those we do not know, a feeling that shines only where it is pointed should be checked by judgement rather than trusted as the measure of what is right.

Why should anyone help a stranger they will never meet again? Kindness between relatives can be explained by shared interests, and kindness between neighbours by the expectation that favours will be returned. But much of human cooperation takes place between people who are neither kin nor repeat partners: the traveller who returns a lost wallet, the customer who corrects an undercharge. One influential answer is that such acts are paid for not by the person helped but by everyone who comes to hear of them. If people prefer to help those who have a record of helping others, then a good reputation is an asset, and an act of generosity towards a stranger is an investment in it. Biologists call this arrangement indirect reciprocity.

The idea has an obvious weakness, and its defenders have had to work hard to answer it. Reputation is only as useful as the information that carries it. In a small band where everyone watches everyone, deeds are seen and remembered; in a large society most of them go unwitnessed. Here language does decisive work. Gossip, often dismissed as idle, is the channel through which a person's conduct becomes known to people who never saw it, and a great deal of everyday conversation consists of exactly this exchange of judgements about absent third parties. Without such talk, indirect reciprocity could hardly operate beyond the scale of a village.

A subtler problem concerns the judgements themselves. Suppose I refuse to help someone who is known to cheat. Should observers count my refusal against me? If they do, anyone who withholds help from cheats will be punished for it, and cheating becomes safer. If they do not, observers must keep track not only of what people did but of whom they did it to and why. Models of indirect reciprocity suggest that cooperation is far more stable under the second, more demanding standard, which may help explain why people care so much about motives and context when they assess one another's behaviour.

It would be too much to say that reputation explains all cooperation among strangers. People sometimes behave generously in conditions of genuine anonymity, and laboratory attempts to show that subtle cues of being watched, such as pictures of eyes, make people more generous have produced mixed results. A defender of the reputational account can reply that habits formed in a world where anonymity was rare are not switched off merely because a particular situation happens to be unobserved. That reply is plausible, but it shifts the explanation from calculation to disposition, and it should be acknowledged as a shift. What survives is a narrower and more defensible claim: that the expectation of being talked about is one of the main forces that make large-scale cooperation possible, and that it works only as well as the talk is accurate.

For a time it was widely believed, among journalists and fact-checkers as much as among researchers, that correcting a false belief could make matters worse. The idea, which came to be called the backfire effect, held that people confronted with evidence against a cherished belief would not merely resist it but cling to the belief more tightly, as though the correction were an attack to be repelled. It had an intuitive appeal: most of us have argued with someone who seemed to grow more certain with every fact we offered. And it carried a discouraging moral. If correction backfires, perhaps it is better not to correct at all.

Subsequent research has been considerably kinder to correction. Larger studies, with more varied topics and more diverse participants, have generally found that people who receive a factual correction move, on average, towards the accurate view, even when the correction cuts against their political loyalties. Reversal of the kind the early findings described appears to be rare, and some of the original results have proved difficult to reproduce. The more careful conclusion is not that people are perfectly responsive to evidence but that they are responsive to it in the ordinary, imperfect way: they update, though often less than they should.

It is worth asking why the backfire idea spread so far on so slender a basis. Part of the answer is that it flattered a certain cynicism about the public, and part is that it confused resistance with reversal. Someone who hears a correction and does not change his mind has resisted it; someone who becomes more convinced of the falsehood has reversed. The first is common and unremarkable, since people rarely abandon a belief after a single encounter with contrary evidence. Only the second would justify the conclusion that correcting is counterproductive, and it is the second that the evidence has failed to find with any regularity.

This does not mean that correction is a cure. Its effects often fade over weeks, so that people drift back towards the belief they were talked out of, and accepting that a particular claim is false does not necessarily change the attitudes the claim was used to support. A voter may concede that a politician's statistic was wrong and still admire the politician exactly as much. These are serious limits, but they are limits of a different kind. They call for corrections that are repeated, that offer an alternative explanation rather than a bare denial, and that are not expected to carry more weight than a single fact can bear. They do not call for silence.

The history of the backfire effect is thus a small lesson about the life of findings as well as about belief. A striking result, especially one that confirms what people already suspect, can travel much faster than the slower work of checking it, and the effort to correct a mistaken finding meets the same ordinary resistance, though not reversal, that greets any correction.

In most human groups some people are listened to more than others, get their way more often and receive a larger share of whatever the group values. Students of status have long suspected that this single word conceals two different arrangements. In one, a person rises because others fear him: he can hurt them, withhold what they need or make their lives difficult, and they defer in order to avoid those costs. In the other, a person rises because others want something from him that he gives freely, usually knowledge or skill, and they defer in order to stay close enough to learn. The first route is commonly called dominance and the second prestige, and an influential line of thought in evolutionary anthropology holds that the second is a distinctively human addition to an older primate inheritance.

The argument for that view rests on the peculiar importance of cultural learning in our species. A creature that acquires most of its survival skills by copying others faces a constant problem of whom to copy, and a strong incentive to secure access to the best models. Deference, on this account, is a kind of payment: the learner offers attention, praise, small services and a willingness to yield in disputes, and in return is tolerated at the elbow of the skilled. If the account is right, it explains why prestige is freely conferred rather than extracted, why prestigious people are approached rather than avoided, and why we find ourselves imitating not only what admired people do well but much else about them besides.

That last consequence deserves more attention than it usually receives, because it shows that prestige is not simply the benign twin of dominance. Imitation guided by prestige is broad and indiscriminate. A learner cannot always tell which of a successful person's habits are responsible for the success, and so tends to copy a bundle of them: the method, but also the dress, the opinions and the manner of speech. In a small community this overspill is cheap and may even be useful, since the bundle often travels together for good reasons. In a large society with mass media, it allows people who are prestigious in one domain to exert influence far outside it, and the deference they receive bears no relation to any competence they have in the matters on which they are now heeded.

There is a further complication. The two routes are clean in theory and tangled in practice. A person who gains prestige acquires allies, resources and a following, and these are exactly the instruments with which dominance is exercised; prestige can thus be converted into the power to coerce, and the conversion is not always visible to those who continue to admire. Conversely, a dominant figure may cultivate the outward marks of prestige, surrounding himself with displays of learning or generosity that make submission feel like admiration. Observers who ask simply whether a leader is feared or respected will often find that the honest answer is both.

None of this undermines the distinction; it is precisely because the two routes can be told apart in principle that their mixture in practice becomes something to look for. What it undermines is the comfortable assumption that a society which replaces dominance with prestige has thereby solved the problem of status. Prestige allocates influence according to perceived excellence, and perception can be managed. The practical question for any institution is therefore not whether it rewards prestige rather than force, which most modern institutions at least claim to do, but whether it keeps the deference people receive tied to the domain in which they have actually earned it.

Few episodes have shaken social psychology as much as the attempts, over roughly the past decade and a half, to repeat some of its best-known experiments. Among the findings that fared worst were studies of so-called behavioural priming, which reported that subtle exposure to an idea could shift what people did shortly afterwards: that reading words associated with old age made people walk more slowly down a corridor, for instance, or that being reminded of money made them less helpful. Such results were taught in lecture halls and retold in popular books. When larger and more carefully controlled attempts to reproduce several of them found effects much smaller than those first reported, or none that could be detected, the reaction within the field was bitter, and the debate quickly took on the character of a trial.

That framing has not served anyone well. It invites the question of who was dishonest, when the more troubling lesson is that dishonesty was largely unnecessary. A literature can come to look robust through practices that most of the people using them regarded as normal: running small studies, trying several reasonable ways of analysing the data and reporting the one that worked, and publishing successes while filing failures away. Each practice, taken alone, seems a minor licence. Together they make it likely that a field will accumulate striking positive results whether or not the underlying effects are real, and that the most surprising results, which are the most likely to be false, will also be the most celebrated.

It is important to be clear about what the failed replications do and do not show. They do not show that priming in general is an illusion. That encountering one word makes a related word easier to recognise a moment later is among the most reliable findings in the study of cognition, and nothing in the recent debate casts doubt on it. Nor does a failed repetition of a single study prove that the effect it sought is exactly zero; it shows that the effect, if it exists, is smaller or less dependable than the original report implied. The questions under dispute concern a particular, ambitious claim: that brief and incidental cues reliably steer complex social behaviour.

Defenders of that claim have often replied that social behaviour is sensitive to context, so that an effect obtained with one population, in one decade, with one set of materials, need not appear when any of these is changed. There is something to this. Human beings are not inert objects, and it would be strange if the meaning of a word list were identical across cultures and generations. But the reply has a cost that its proponents do not always acknowledge. The original studies were presented as revealing general features of human minds, not as local facts about particular groups of students. If the effects are so delicate that unknown features of a setting can abolish them, then those general claims were overstated, and an appeal to hidden moderators that is made only after a failure, and never specified in advance so that it could be tested, explains everything and therefore nothing.

The reforms that the episode prompted, such as registering hypotheses and analyses before collecting data and running studies large enough to detect modest effects, have costs of their own. Research becomes slower and more expensive, and fewer dazzling results will appear. That is the right trade. A science of social behaviour that publishes fewer surprises, each of which can bear weight, is worth more than one whose surprises must all be taken on trust.

Ask someone to describe the route from their home to the nearest railway station and watch their hands. Before they have finished the first sentence, the hands will usually be tracing turns, marking distances and pointing at landmarks that are nowhere in the room. The common explanation is that gesture is a kind of visual aid for the listener, a way of adding pictures to words. On this view the hands are an accessory to communication, useful when they help an audience and idle otherwise. The explanation is not wrong, but it is incomplete, and the part it leaves out is the more interesting one.

If gesture existed only for listeners, people would stop gesturing when nobody could see them, and yet they do not: speakers on the telephone continue to move their hands, if somewhat less than they would face to face, and people who have been blind from birth gesture when they talk, even to listeners they know to be blind. A habit that persists when it can no longer inform anyone is unlikely to be explained entirely by what it does for others. The more economical conclusion is that gesture also does something for the person who produces it.

What it seems to do is lighten the work of thinking, for when people are asked to explain a problem while keeping their hands still, many speak more haltingly and struggle to find the words they want, particularly words for shapes, directions and positions. Children explaining how they solved a sum sometimes show with their hands a strategy that their words have not yet reached, pointing to two numbers together while describing a different procedure aloud. Such children are often found to be on the verge of learning the correct method, as if the hands had arrived at an idea before speech could carry it. Gesture, on this account, is not a translation of finished thought into movement; it is one of the places where thought is still being worked out.

It would be easy to overstate the case, since not every flourish of the hands is cognitive labour; some gestures are plainly social, like a wave or a shrug, and some speakers gesture little without thinking any worse for it. Nor does the evidence show that thought depends on the body in some mysterious way that rules out abstract reasoning. The claim is more modest: that for many people, much of the time, moving the hands is part of how a difficult idea gets held in mind. Even that modest claim has practical consequences, because a teacher who attends only to what a pupil says may miss what the pupil is close to understanding, and a classroom that rewards stillness may be quietly removing a tool that some children use to think.

When people imagine an intelligent animal, they usually imagine something built on the plan of their own bodies: a large brain in the head that gathers information, makes decisions and issues commands to obedient limbs. The octopus is a standing challenge to that picture. Its evolutionary line separated from ours more than half a billion years ago, long before either lineage had anything resembling a complex brain, so whatever intelligence it now has was assembled independently. And it was assembled on a strikingly different plan, for more of the octopus's neurons lie in its arms than in its central brain.

The arrangement has consequences that can be observed. An octopus arm can carry out a sequence of movements, such as reaching towards an object and bending to draw it in, with little apparent direction from the centre, and an arm separated from the body will for a time continue to respond to touch and to grasp what it meets. Each arm, it seems, handles much of the detail of its own movement, while the central brain sets broader goals. Instead of a commander and its troops, the better image might be a coordinator working with partners that each know their own business.

Popular writing has been quick to turn this into a slogan, describing the octopus as an animal with nine brains, or as a colony of minds sharing one body. The slogan goes too far. The arms are not independent agents with purposes of their own; they share a body, a nervous system and, in ordinary life, a single course of action, and the animal behaves as one creature pursuing one end at a time. What the anatomy shows is not that the octopus is many minds but that one mind can be organised so that much of its work is done at the edges.

That is the real lesson, and it reaches beyond octopuses. Much thinking about intelligence, in animals and in machines alike, has assumed that it must be centralised: that there must be some single place where everything comes together and is decided. The octopus suggests that centralisation is one solution among several, suited to some bodies and not to others. An animal with eight flexible arms and no skeleton faces a control problem that no single centre could easily solve, since each arm can bend at any point along its length and in any direction. Handing much of the work to the arms may be less an evolutionary curiosity than a sensible answer to the body the animal actually has.

The mirror test has an appealing simplicity: an animal is given a mark it cannot see directly, perhaps a spot of odourless dye on the forehead, and is then shown a mirror. If it uses the reflection to inspect or rub at the mark on its own body, it is said to recognise itself. Great apes generally pass, most monkeys generally fail, and over the decades a handful of other species have been reported to pass or nearly pass. Because the result is so easy to state, it has come to be treated as a kind of membership test: those who pass belong among the self-aware, and those who fail are presumed to lack a self worth the name.

The test does measure something real. To pass, an animal must grasp that the moving figure in the glass is not another individual and that what it sees there corresponds to its own body. That is not a trivial achievement, and it is reasonable to think that animals capable of it have some representation of their own bodies as objects among others. The difficulty lies in what is inferred from failure, and in how much is read into success.

Consider failure first, since the test presupposes an animal that relies heavily on vision, that attends to its own appearance, and that is bothered enough by an odd mark to investigate it. Many animals meet none of these conditions. A dog, which navigates its world largely by smell, may simply have no interest in a silent image that gives off no scent; an animal whose species does not groom may see no reason to touch a spot on its skin. Failing a test designed around one animal's priorities is weak evidence that another animal lacks the capacity being tested, in the way that a person's failure to answer a question asked in an unfamiliar language reveals little about her knowledge.

Success is open to over-reading too. Recognising one's body in a mirror shows an understanding of the body as one's own; it does not show, by itself, that the animal reflects on its past, imagines its future or thinks of itself as a person with a history. These are richer capacities, and the leap from the mirror to them is a leap of interpretation, not of evidence. None of this makes the test worthless. It makes it one probe among many, informative within its range and silent outside it. The error is not in running the test but in letting a single, visually biased procedure decide which minds are admitted to the category of the self-aware.

It has become a commonplace that every age describes the brain in the image of its most impressive machine. When ornamental gardens were fitted with water-driven statues that moved as visitors stepped on hidden plates, nerves were pictured as pipes and the animal spirits as fluid pressed through them. When the telegraph and then the telephone exchange spread across cities, the nervous system became a network of wires, with the brain as the central office where calls were connected. In our own time it is a computer, processing information, storing memories and running programs. The pattern is real, and critics have drawn a sharp lesson from it: the metaphors are fashions, each as quaint as the last will soon appear, and the computer image will go the way of the fountain.

The lesson is half right. It is true that none of these images was the whole truth, and that each looks dated once the technology behind it is familiar. But to call them mere fashions is to miss what each one got right. The hydraulic picture captured the idea that something must travel from the senses to the centre and back to the muscles. The switchboard captured the importance of connections, of which signal is routed to which destination. The computer captured the idea that what matters about these signals is the information they carry and the transformations performed on it, rather than the stuff that carries them. Each metaphor, in other words, was adopted because it made some feature of the nervous system thinkable, and each left behind a contribution that survived its own retirement.

The real danger lies elsewhere, because a metaphor brings with it not only the features that fit but a whole set of features that come along unexamined. The computer image invites us to think of memory as storage, a place where a record sits unchanged until retrieved, when remembering appears to be closer to reconstruction, the record altered a little each time it is used. It invites a sharp division between hardware and software, when in the brain the program and the machine are hard to tell apart, since use reshapes the very structures that do the work. These are not reasons to abandon the metaphor but reasons to keep asking which of its features we are actually entitled to.

The sensible course, then, is neither to treat the current metaphor as a literal description nor to dismiss it as a passing fashion, but to use it while keeping an account of where it fails. Metaphors are tools for thinking about something that cannot be seen directly, and the history of brain science suggests that thinking without any of them is not an available option. What can be avoided is the habit of mistaking the tool for the thing.

Among the people who first tried to build thinking machines, a surprise emerged that has never quite been absorbed. The tasks that seemed to demand the most intelligence, such as proving theorems, playing chess or solving problems in algebra, turned out to be comparatively tractable for computers, while tasks that any small child performs without effort, such as recognising a face across a room, picking up an unfamiliar object or walking over uneven ground, proved stubbornly hard. The observation is often associated with the roboticist Hans Moravec, and it is usually called a paradox. Whether it deserves the name depends on what we took difficulty to be in the first place.

The most common explanation is evolutionary. Seeing, grasping and moving have been refined over hundreds of millions of years of animal life, and the machinery that performs them is vast, ancient and almost entirely hidden from awareness. Abstract reasoning, by contrast, is a recent arrival, practised deliberately and with effort. We notice the effort and conclude that reasoning is hard; we notice nothing when we recognise a friend's face, and conclude that perception is easy. On this account the paradox is an artefact of introspection: our sense of difficulty tracks how much of a skill reaches consciousness, not how much computation it requires.

This explanation is persuasive, but it should not be stretched into the claim that every skill we find effortless is computationally deep, or that every skill we find laborious is shallow. Some effortless skills may be easy for machines too, and some laborious ones, like long division, are trivial for any pocket calculator while others remain hard. The evolutionary story explains a general tendency; it does not supply a rule. Nor has the gap stood still. Machines have become far better at recognising images and speech than early researchers expected, though a robot that can fold an unfamiliar garment or clear an untidy table remains much harder to build than a program that plays chess at a master's level.

The deeper lesson concerns our idea of intelligence itself. For a long time intelligence was identified with the activities that educated adults found hardest and prized most: calculation, logic, formal games. The paradox suggests that this identification was parochial. What humans find hard is a measure of human limitations, not a measure of how much intelligence a task needs, and the competences we share with other animals may contain more of what is difficult about minds than the competences that distinguish us. A cat crossing a cluttered shelf without disturbing anything is solving problems that our best machines still find formidable, and it would be odd to call that achievement unintelligent merely because no cat could sit an examination.

The claim that language shapes thought has had an unusual career. In its strong form, the view that the categories of one's language set the limits of what one can perceive or conceive, it was once fashionable, then thoroughly discredited, and it is now defended by almost nobody. The objections are familiar. Speakers of languages that lack a word for some distinction can usually learn to make it when they need to; translation, though imperfect, is possible; and people routinely think thoughts for which they struggle to find words. If a language were a prison, its inmates would not so regularly be found outside the walls.

From the ruins of the strong view a weaker one has been rebuilt, and the evidence for it is more respectable. Colour has been the favoured test case, because the spectrum is continuous while languages divide it differently: some have only a few basic colour terms, others a dozen. In one well-known kind of experiment, speakers of a language that has separate basic words for lighter and darker blue were found to be slightly quicker at telling apart two blues that fell on opposite sides of that boundary than two blues on the same side, while speakers of a language with a single basic word for blue showed no such advantage. The effect was modest, but it was there, and it seemed to show that words reach down into perception.

What the same line of work also found, however, is more revealing than the effect itself. When participants performed the colour task while silently rehearsing a string of digits, which occupies the verbal system, the advantage largely disappeared, whereas a comparable task that occupied spatial memory instead left it intact. The words, it seems, were not permanently altering how the visual system sorted colours. They were being used, there and then, as an aid to the task, recruited on the spot and set aside when the verbal system was busy elsewhere.

Defenders and critics of linguistic relativity have both tended to miss what this implies. The defenders read such results as vindication: language shapes thought after all. The critics read the smallness of the effects as deflation: language barely matters. But the finding fits neither reading well. It suggests that language does not so much reshape a mind that would otherwise be neutral as serve as one of the instruments a mind reaches for while it works. On this picture the interesting question is not whether a speaker's language has engraved its categories on her perception, but how often, and in which tasks, thinking proceeds by borrowing words as tools. That question is in one respect more modest than the relativists' and in another more radical, since it implies that much ordinary thought is partly carried out in language even where we take it to be wordless.

In the 1890s the British psychologist Conwy Lloyd Morgan proposed a rule for interpreting animal behaviour that has shaped the study of animal minds ever since. In paraphrase, it says that we should not explain an animal's action as the product of a higher mental faculty if it can be explained as the product of a lower one. The rule was a response to a real problem. Much of what then passed for evidence about animal intelligence consisted of anecdotes sent in by pet owners and naturalists, in which dogs reasoned, cats planned and birds grieved, and in which the observer's own feelings were read into whatever the animal happened to do. Against this habit, Morgan's canon was a discipline: before crediting a creature with insight, ask whether trial and error, habit or simple association would account for what you saw.

As a corrective, the canon did its work well. It pushed the field towards controlled observation and towards explanations that could be tested, and it is partly responsible for the expectation that claims about animal cognition must now survive experiments designed to rule out simpler accounts. But a rule that is useful against one error can become an error of its own when it is applied without thought. Over the following century the canon hardened, in many hands, into a presumption that the lowest available explanation is always to be preferred, whatever the animal and whatever the evidence.

The trouble with that presumption is that it is not as neutral as it looks. It treats 'lower' as if it meant 'simpler' and 'simpler' as if it meant 'more probably true', and neither equation holds in general. An explanation in terms of association may require positing a long and improbable history of exactly the right rewards, while an explanation in terms of a modest capacity to represent what another animal can see may be the more economical of the two. Evolution complicates the picture further. If a chimpanzee and a human behave alike in similar circumstances, the assumption that the behaviour rests on similar mechanisms is, given their close kinship, arguably the simpler hypothesis; to insist on a different and lower mechanism for the chimpanzee alone is to multiply explanations, not to reduce them.

There is also a question of cost. The canon guards against one kind of mistake, crediting animals with capacities they lack, and is silent about the opposite mistake, denying them capacities they have. Both mistakes are real, and the second is not obviously the less harmful, especially where the capacities in question include the ability to suffer. An investigator who refuses on principle to credit a dog with fear until every leaner account has been excluded will seldom be caught overstating anything, but she may spend a career understating what is in front of her. A principle that treats one error as serious and the other as negligible is not a principle of caution; it is a bias that happens to look like one.

None of this is a case for returning to the anecdote. Morgan himself appears to have intended his rule as a guard against careless inference rather than as a ban on crediting animals with higher faculties when there is independent evidence for them. The better successor to the canon is not its opposite but a symmetrical standard: state the rival hypotheses, rich and lean alike, and design observations that would tell them apart. Simplicity then becomes something to be argued for in each case, rather than a verdict delivered in advance.

Any science of consciousness faces an awkward fact at its foundation. The thing it studies is, by most accounts, directly available only to the person who has it, and the scientist learns about it chiefly through what that person says or otherwise signals: I saw the flash, or I did not; the face looked angry; the tone seemed to come from the left. Two opposite attitudes to this fact have been common. One holds that reports are so unreliable, so shaped by expectation, vocabulary and the wish to please, that a science resting on them is no science at all. The other treats a sincere report as the last word, since no one, it is said, is better placed than the subject to know what she experiences.

Neither attitude survives inspection, and the second is the easier to dismiss. People are often wrong about their own experience in ways that can be demonstrated: they confidently describe detail at the edges of their visual field that is not available to them, and they misjudge the order or timing of events they claim to have perceived. A report is a response produced by the subject, shaped by the question asked and the categories available, and it can misdescribe the experience it is about. But the first attitude draws the wrong conclusion from this. Every scientific instrument can misreport what it measures; the usual response is to study its errors, not to throw it away. A report is best treated as evidence about experience, fallible but informative, to be calibrated against other evidence rather than either revered or ignored.

The most productive methods have used reports in exactly this spirit. In masking experiments, the same image is shown on many trials, sometimes followed so quickly by a second image that the first is not reported as seen. Because the physical stimulus is held constant, differences in brain activity between seen and unseen trials can be attributed, at least tentatively, to the difference in experience rather than to the stimulus. The approach is powerful, but it carries a hidden complication. On seen trials the subject not only experiences the image but also prepares and makes a report about it, so some of the activity that distinguishes the two kinds of trial may belong to reporting rather than to experiencing.

To get around this, researchers have designed experiments in which subjects make no report at all, and conscious states are inferred from other signs, such as involuntary eye movements that track which of two competing images is being experienced. Critics point out a circle here: those signs were themselves validated by showing that they agree with reports. If reports are suspect, so, it seems, are the signs that stand in for them. The objection is clever, but it proves less than it appears to. The history of measurement is full of such circles. Early thermometers were checked against the sensation of warmth and then against one another, and in time they came to correct the very sensations against which they had first been checked. A circle of mutual calibration is vicious only if it never widens; when independent methods, each imperfect, are tested against one another and turn out to agree, confidence in all of them can rise together.

None of this guarantees that a science of consciousness will answer every question asked of it, and some philosophers doubt that any amount of correlating brain activity with reports could explain why experience exists at all. That doubt may be justified. But it is a doubt about the reach of the science, not about whether reports can serve as its data, and running the two together has done more to obscure the field than either the sceptics or the enthusiasts have usually admitted.

For much of the last century, the standard official response to an informal settlement was to remove it. Planners looked at a hillside of self-built houses, narrow lanes and improvised water connections and saw a problem of housing quality, to be solved by demolition and the construction of orderly blocks elsewhere, usually on cheaper land at the edge of the city. The logic seemed humane as well as tidy: people living without drains or secure walls would be given drains and secure walls. That the residents frequently resisted, and that many of the new blocks were half empty within a few years, was read as ingratitude, or as evidence that the poor did not know their own interests.

A different reading is now more common, and it is more persuasive. An informal settlement is not simply a stock of poor dwellings; it is a working arrangement of livelihoods, and its location is usually its chief asset. A family that sells cooked food near a bus depot, a tailor who takes in work from a nearby market, a mother whose children attend a school within walking distance: all of them chose the site because of what it is close to. Relocation to a distant estate improves the walls while destroying the arrangement. The household may gain a toilet and lose two hours a day to travel, or lose the income that made the new rent payable at all. Seen this way, the empty blocks were not a puzzle but a verdict.

Upgrading in place starts from this recognition. Instead of replacing the settlement, it adds what is missing: paved lanes, drainage, water and sewer lines, street lighting and, crucially, some form of secure tenure, so that residents can invest in their houses without fearing that the next official survey will mark them for demolition. Because the residents remain where they are, the networks that sustain them survive, and the public money spent goes into infrastructure rather than into reproducing, at great cost and in the wrong place, a community that already existed.

None of this makes upgrading a universal remedy. Some settlements stand on land that floods every monsoon or slides in heavy rain, and to improve them in place is to invest in a future disaster. Nor is upgrading automatically benign: lanes widened for drainage can require the demolition of some houses, and a programme that installs pipes but withholds tenure leaves residents improved and still insecure. The case for upgrading is therefore not that informal settlements are good as they are, a romantic view their residents rarely share. It is that the people who built them understood something about the city that the planners who wished to clear them did not.

Few words in urban debate do as much damage as 'density', largely because it is used, often by the same speaker within a single argument, to mean two quite different things. In its technical sense density is a ratio: the number of people, or of dwellings, on a given area of land. In ordinary speech it usually means something closer to crowding, the experience of too many people in too little room: a family of six in a single room, a queue that spills into the road, a train in which nobody can turn round. The two can occur together, but they need not, and treating them as one has shaped a century of planning.

Consider two districts with the same number of residents per hectare. In the first, people live in tall apartment buildings with generous flats, set among parks and wide streets. In the second, the same population is packed into low houses, several households to a building, with lanes too narrow for a cart. On a map of density the districts are identical; to anyone who lives in them they could hardly be more different. Conversely, a scattered agricultural village, where extended families share a single dwelling, can be acutely crowded indoors while being nearly empty by the hectare. Density, in short, describes land; crowding describes the conditions of daily life.

The confusion has a history. The diseases that ravaged industrial cities in the nineteenth century were widely blamed on density, and reformers responded by trying to spread people out. Yet what made those cities so lethal was a combination of overcrowded rooms, contaminated water and absent sewers, and where water and drains were improved, death rates in dense districts fell even though the districts often remained dense. The reformers were right that something was wrong; they were imprecise about what it was, and the imprecision outlived them, surviving in zoning codes and building regulations long after the sanitary conditions that had justified it had disappeared.

This is not to say that density is costless. Many people living close together compete for parks, school places and quiet, and a district can feel oppressive even when no room in it is overcrowded. Perception counts, and planners who dismiss it will find their schemes resented. But the remedies differ. Crowding is relieved by more floor space per person and by services; the costs of density are managed by design, by open space and by the quality of the street. A policy that caps density in the name of relieving crowding may achieve neither, pushing people into fewer and more crowded rooms, or out to the edge of the city.

In the last two decades the walkable neighbourhood has become one of the few planning ideals on which almost everyone claims to agree, and with agreement has come measurement. Composite indices now rate districts by the number of shops, schools and stops within a short radius, the density of street intersections and the share of homes near public transport. Estate agents quote such figures; municipal plans set targets for raising them. It would be churlish to deny the good these indices have done. They gave walking, long treated as what people did when they could not drive, a place in the arithmetic of planning, and they made visible how many districts had been designed as if nobody would ever arrive on foot.

Yet what the indices measure is proximity, and proximity is not the same as walkability. A street can lie within five minutes of a pharmacy, a school and a bus stop and still be miserable to walk along: a narrow pavement beside four lanes of fast traffic, no shade under a summer sun, the blank walls of parking structures on either side, crossings that demand a long detour. Two districts with identical scores can therefore offer entirely different experiences, and the index has no way of registering the difference, because it counts what lies at the end of the walk and ignores the walk itself.

This blindness is not accidental; it reflects an assumption that walking is chiefly a means of reaching places. For many people it is that, but it is also something more: the way a child learns a neighbourhood, the way an elderly resident keeps in contact with the world, the occasion for the chance encounters on which local life depends. These goods are produced en route, by the quality of the street, its pace, its frontages, its benches and its shade, not by the count of destinations. A measure built around destinations will systematically undervalue them.

The danger is sharpest when the index ceases to be a description and becomes a target. A city told to raise its score can do so cheaply by permitting a few more shops near existing homes, while the hostile road that separates residents from those shops remains untouched. The number improves; the walk does not. None of this argues for abandoning measurement. It argues for remembering what the measurement leaves out, and for treating a high score as the beginning of an inquiry into a street rather than its conclusion.

In many large cities, a good part of the open space created in recent decades does not belong to the public at all. Developers are permitted to build taller or larger than the rules would otherwise allow on condition that they provide a plaza, an arcade or a garden that anyone may enter. The arrangement looks like an elegant bargain: the city gains open space without paying for it, and the developer gains floor area worth far more than the ground surrendered. Critics have long complained that the resulting spaces are often bleak, hidden or quietly discouraging, with benches too narrow to sit on and guards who appear the moment anyone lingers.

The usual form of the complaint is that these spaces are private, and that private space can never be truly public. This puts the matter in the wrong place. Ownership, by itself, settles very little. Many publicly owned squares are fenced at night, patrolled against skateboarders and stripped of seating to deter people who might sleep there, while some privately owned courtyards are generous, well kept and genuinely welcoming. If the test of publicness were the name on the title deed, we would have to call the first kind more public than the second, which is absurd.

What makes a space public is better described as a set of permissions: the right to be there without a reason, to stay without buying anything, to gather with others, to hand out a leaflet or to hold a placard. These permissions are exactly what private management is tempted to withdraw, not out of malice but because each of them is a small risk to the owner and none of them earns anything. A plaza can be open to all in the formal sense while being governed by rules, often unpublished, that make it public only for the well dressed and the briefly passing. The question to ask is therefore not who owns a space but who writes its rules, and to whom the writers must answer.

Seen this way, the bargain need not be abandoned; it needs to be completed. A city that trades floor area for open space is entitled to specify not only the dimensions of the plaza but the permissions that come with it, to publish them at the entrance, and to enforce them against owners as firmly as it enforces its building codes. Where it fails to do so, it has not acquired public space at all. It has paid, in floor area, for something that looks like a square and behaves like a lobby.

Few settlement forms have been as consistently disparaged by writers as the suburb. For the better part of a century, novelists, critics and social scientists have described it in a nearly fixed vocabulary: monotonous rows of identical houses, lawns tended out of anxiety rather than pleasure, a life of commuting, shopping and television in which neighbours are near but never known. The suburb, in this account, is where individuality goes to be smoothed away. The striking thing about the indictment is not its severity but its uniformity, which ought to make us suspicious. A form of life chosen by many millions of households can hardly be as simple as the language used to dismiss it.

Part of the indictment is sound. A district built around the car leaves those who cannot drive, the young, the old and the poor, stranded in a landscape in which nothing is within reach on foot. Zoning that separates homes from shops and workplaces by law multiplies journeys and empties the streets of the casual traffic through which neighbours become familiar. These are real costs, and they fall unevenly. But they are the costs of particular design decisions, and the critique of the suburb has rarely been content to remain at that level.

Its deeper charge is cultural, and here it is weakest. It reads sameness of form as sameness of life, as if a street of similar houses must contain similar people living similar days; anyone who has knocked on the doors of such a street knows otherwise. It also tends to treat the wish for a garden, a quiet bedroom and a door one can close as a failure of imagination, when for families leaving cramped flats these were precisely the goods that city life had denied them. The critics, many of whom lived by choice in the centres of large cities, were often describing a preference they did not share as a pathology from which others suffered.

None of this requires us to admire the suburb, or to ignore the costs of a pattern of building that consumes land and fuel at a great rate. It requires only that criticism be aimed at what can be changed. The desire for privacy and space is not a defect to be corrected; the absence of a shop within walking distance is. A suburb with a small centre, mixed uses and streets that a child can safely cross would answer most of the sound objections without asking anyone to want a different life.

Arguments about gentrification tend to collapse into a single question: are the people who lived in a neighbourhood forced out when wealthier newcomers arrive? The question has the merit of being answerable, at least in principle. One can follow households over time, count how many leave, and compare the rate with that in neighbourhoods that have not changed. Suppose such a count found that long-standing residents of a gentrifying district left no faster than residents of similar districts elsewhere. Many would conclude that the harm of gentrification had been exaggerated, and that what remained of the complaint was mere nostalgia.

That conclusion would be premature, because it assumes that the only way to lose a neighbourhood is to leave it. Consider the resident who stays. The grocer who extended credit has been replaced by a shop whose prices assume another income; the bench outside it, once a place to sit for an afternoon, now draws the attention of a security guard; the park is the same park, but the conduct expected in it has quietly changed, and complaints to the police now come from people she does not know, about behaviour that was ordinary a decade ago. She has not moved, and no count of departures will register her, yet the place in which she lives has been withdrawn from her as surely as if she had. To call this nostalgia is to mistake a loss of standing for a loss of scenery.

The difficulty is that the language best suited to describing this loss, the language of a neighbourhood's 'character', is also the language most readily turned to the opposite purpose. Affluent districts invoke their character to resist new housing, to keep out flats that might bring poorer residents, to preserve a streetscape that functions, whatever its owners intend, as a barrier. If character means the look of the buildings and the tone of the streets, then the long-standing resident and the exclusionary homeowner are making the same argument, and it is not one that deserves much sympathy.

The way out is to locate character not in the fabric of a place but in the relations it sustains: who is able to use it, on what terms, and with what claim to be heard. On this view, what the staying resident has lost is not a familiar shopfront but the practical standing she once had in her own street, and what the exclusionary homeowner defends is not a set of relations at all but the absence of people who might form new ones. The distinction will not settle every case, and it asks more of planners than a count of departures does. But it allows us to take the quieter harms of gentrification seriously without lending our sympathy to every resident who would prefer that nothing near them ever changed.

The familiar story of urbanisation runs in one direction. People leave the countryside for the city, struggle for a generation in its least desirable quarters, and are eventually absorbed, their children speaking the city's idiom and regarding the village as a place of grandparents and holidays. Migration, on this account, is a passage with a beginning and an end, and the only question worth asking about a migrant is how far along it he has come. The story is not false; it describes what happened to many families in many countries. But it has acquired the status of a norm, against which other patterns are measured and found wanting, and this has made it difficult to see a pattern that is, in much of the world, at least as common.

A large number of those who work in cities never complete the journey the story describes. They come for a season of construction or a few years in a factory, return for the harvest, a wedding or an illness in the family, and come back again, sometimes to the same city and sometimes to another. Their earnings pay school fees and debts in the village; the village holds their land, their elders and, often, their spouses and children. A household can live this way for decades, and many do. Seen through the one-way story, such people are migrants who have not yet settled, a transitional population whose double life is a symptom of incomplete integration. Seen on its own terms, the pattern looks rather different: a way of spreading risk across two places, so that a lost job in the city or a failed crop in the village need not be ruinous, because the other place remains.

The distinction matters because city governments have tended to act on the first reading. A resident whose household is registered elsewhere, whose stay is irregular, and whose address is a worksite or a shared rented room is easily treated as a visitor: excluded from subsidised housing, from schools for the children who come along, from the electoral roll, and from the attention of politicians who answer to those who are on it. The exclusion then produces the very evidence that justifies it. Denied a secure foothold in the city, the circular migrant has every reason to keep the village in reserve, and the persistence of his village ties is then cited as proof that he never really belonged.

It would be a mistake to romanticise circulation in its turn. Some who move back and forth would settle in the city if they could, and return to the village only because the city offers them nothing to stay for; for them, circularity is less a strategy than a sentence. Others genuinely prefer a life lived in two places and would keep it even if the city were more welcoming. The difficulty is that from the outside the two groups look identical, and a policy designed for one will misjudge the other.

What follows is not a single programme but a change in the condition attached to belonging. A city that made its entitlements portable, that allowed a worker to enrol his children in school without proving permanent residence, and that encouraged cheap rental housing suited to stays of months rather than decades would serve both groups at once. It would allow those who wish to settle to do so, and those who wish to circulate to circulate without penalty. What it would cease to do is demand that a person surrender one home as the price of being recognised in another.

In the language of property, home and ownership have become almost interchangeable. To own the place one lives in is to 'have a home'; to rent is to be on the way to one, or to have failed to arrive. The equation is so familiar that it seems less a claim than a definition, and policies built on it, from subsidised mortgages to the sale of public housing to its tenants, present themselves not as choices among ways of housing people but as the extension of home itself to those who lack it.

Yet if one asks what people mean when they say that a place feels like home, the answers rarely mention title. They mention routines that have settled into the rooms, objects arranged by one's own hand, the confidence that one will be there next year, the freedom to decide who comes in, the ability to paint a wall or plant a window box or keep a dog. Home, in this sense, is less a thing one possesses than something one does, a practice of shaping a space and being shaped by it over time. And a practice of this kind needs two conditions: enough control over the space to shape it, and enough security of tenure to make the shaping worthwhile.

Neither condition is the same as ownership, though ownership has usually supplied both. A tenant on a twelve-month lease who may be asked to leave at short notice, who must seek permission to hang a picture, and whose rent can rise without limit, has good reason not to invest himself in his rooms; he is camping, however long he stays. But the cause of his condition is not that he rents. It is that his tenancy is short, revocable and hedged with prohibitions. Where tenancies are long, rents predictable and tenants free to alter their surroundings within reason, renters make homes much as owners do, while an owner whose mortgage payments consume most of his income, and who fears that a lost job means a lost house, may know the very precariousness that the equation reserves for tenants.

None of this means that ownership confers nothing distinctive. The owner can knock down a wall, not merely paint it; he can leave the house to his children; he answers to no landlord. A tenant, however secure, lives in a space whose final shape is decided by someone else. These are real goods, and it would be odd to deny that many people want them for good reasons. The objection is not to ownership but to the assumption that it is the only door into home, an assumption that directs public effort towards turning tenants into owners while leaving the conditions of tenancy, under which a large and often growing share of urban households live, largely untouched.

The cost of that assumption is not only sentimental. A household that expects to move at a landlord's word does not join the school committee, does not plant a tree it will not see grow, does not learn the names of neighbours it may lose within the year. Schools, associations and local shops all depend on residents who expect to stay long enough for their efforts to bear fruit. The practices through which people make a home are continuous with those through which they make a neighbourhood, so that insecurity inside the door becomes thinness of attachment outside it. To treat home as a matter of title is therefore to misunderstand not only what renters lack but what cities lose when they lack it.

Most people in the modern West assume that a name is a fixed possession, given once at birth and carried, with perhaps one change at marriage, until death. The assumption is so deep that we rarely notice it is an assumption at all, yet in a wide range of societies a person's name has been expected to change over a lifetime, and one of the commonest occasions for the change is the birth of a child. When a man becomes known as the father of his first child, or a woman as the mother of hers, anthropologists speak of teknonymy: naming a parent through the offspring. The Arabic custom of addressing a man as Abu, 'father of', followed by the name of his eldest son, is perhaps the most familiar instance, but the practice in various forms has been recorded on several continents.

It is tempting to read teknonymy as a simple sign that children are prized, and there is something in this. But the more interesting point is what the custom reveals about how such societies understand a person. In a system of fixed names, identity is treated as something an individual owns from the start, and relationships are added to it later, like rooms built onto a house. In a teknonymous system the order is reversed: a person becomes fully visible in social life only by standing in a relationship; the new name announces not that the individual has changed but that their position in a web of kin has changed. One is addressed less as a self than as a point where generations meet.

This also explains a feature that puzzles outsiders. In some communities it becomes mildly rude to use the old personal name of an adult who has a child, much as it would be odd for us to call a judge by a childhood nickname in court. The personal name has not been forbidden; it has simply been outranked by a title that carries more social information. Where the practice extends further, so that a grandparent is named after a grandchild, a person's name can track their rise through the generations, and the most senior people come to be known almost entirely through their descendants.

None of this should be romanticised, for a system that names people through their children can be hard on those who have none, who may remain, in the language of address, permanently junior. Nor is the Western fixed name as individualistic as it looks, since a surname itself announces a lineage. The contrast is one of emphasis rather than of kind, but the emphasis matters. To change a person's name at the birth of a child is to state, every time that person is greeted, that adulthood is not a private achievement but a place in a sequence.

National accounts were designed to measure what passes through markets, and for most of their history they have counted the meal bought in a restaurant but not the meal cooked at home, the hour a paid nurse spends with an elderly patient but not the hour a daughter spends with her mother. The omission was never a secret: early statisticians acknowledged it and set it aside as a practical matter, since household work was hard to observe and there was no price at which to record it. The result, however, was a picture of the economy in which a large share of the work that keeps people alive appeared to be no work at all.

In recent decades, time-use surveys, in which people record how they spend each part of a day, have made it possible to estimate how many hours households devote to cooking, cleaning and care. Turning those hours into money, however, requires a choice between methods that rest on different assumptions. One method, replacement cost, asks what it would cost to hire someone to do the same tasks. Another, opportunity cost, asks what the person doing the work could have earned in paid employment during those hours. The two methods can produce very different totals, and they can rank the same work differently: an hour of childcare by a surgeon is worth a great deal on the second method and rather little on the first.

Critics sometimes take this disagreement as proof that the whole exercise is arbitrary, but that conclusion is too quick. Every figure in national accounts rests on conventions, and the fact that a convention must be chosen does not make zero, the convention long in use, the neutral one. Recording household care at zero is also a valuation, and almost certainly the least accurate available. Estimates, even rough ones, have changed how policy debates can be conducted: they make it harder to describe cuts to public care services as savings when the work has simply moved into homes.

There is, nonetheless, a limit to what a price can capture. Both methods treat care as a bundle of tasks that could in principle be handed to someone else. Much of it can be. But part of what a family member provides is the fact that it is they who provide it, and that element has no market equivalent because it cannot be bought. A figure for unpaid care is therefore best understood as a floor rather than a measure: it shows that the work is not nothing, without claiming to say what it is worth.

When European travellers and administrators first described marriages in which the groom's family transferred cattle, cloth or other goods to the bride's family, many of them reached for the language of the market.
