The bride, they concluded, was being bought. The description had the appeal of simplicity, and it fitted a ready-made story in which other peoples' customs were cruder versions of the observers' own commercial habits. Words such as 'price' and 'purchase' entered official reports, and they shaped how the custom was seen long after closer study had cast doubt on them. The description also misread, in nearly every important respect, what the transfer did.

Consider first where the goods go. In many systems they are not kept by the bride's father as profit but are distributed among a wide circle of her kin, each of whom thereby acquires an interest in the marriage succeeding. Consider next where they go afterwards. Often the cattle received when a daughter marries are the very cattle used to secure a wife for her brother, so that a herd travels from family to family and the transfers form a chain linking households that may never meet. A purchase ends a relationship between buyer and seller; this transfer begins several. Consider, finally, what the transfer secures. In a number of societies what passes with the goods is not the woman herself but the affiliation of her future children to the husband's lineage, which is why, in some of them, the goods must be returned if the marriage ends before any children are born.

On this reading, bridewealth is less a price than a contract between groups, and one that gives the bride's family a continuing stake in how she is treated. A family that has shared the goods out among its members, and may have to gather them again in order to return them, has reason both to support the marriage and to intervene when it goes badly. The goods, in other words, work less like a payment than like a pledge, and a pledge held by many hands is harder to ignore than one held by a single man.

It would be naive, however, to treat this as the whole story. Where cash has replaced cattle and the sums demanded have risen with the incomes of urban grooms, the transfer can begin to behave much more like a price: it is negotiated against the bride's education or earning power, it is kept by a narrower set of relatives, and young men may delay marriage for years in order to raise it. Critics who see a market in such arrangements are not simply repeating the old error. The lesson is not that the travellers were wrong and the custom is innocent, but that the meaning of a transfer depends on the web of obligations around it, and that when the web thins, the meaning changes.

Few claims in social history have travelled as far as the idea that childhood was invented. In its best-known form, put forward in the middle of the twentieth century, it held that medieval Europe had no notion of childhood as a distinct stage of life. Children, on this account, passed almost directly from infancy into the company of adults, working, drinking and dressing as they did; painters showed them as miniature men and women; and parents, facing high infant mortality, refrained from investing much feeling in creatures who might not survive. Childhood as we know it, protected, sentimentalised and set apart, was a discovery of the early modern centuries.

The thesis was a brilliant provocation, and much of it has not survived. Later historians, reading letters, court records, sermons and the evidence of excavated objects, assembled a large body of material showing that medieval parents grieved for dead children, bought or made toys for living ones, and recognised that the young needed particular kinds of care. The argument from paintings proved especially weak. Artistic conventions are not photographs, and an age that painted saints with golden discs around their heads was not simply reporting what it saw. To infer an absence of feeling from an absence of naturalistic portraiture is to mistake a style for a sentiment.

Yet it would be a mistake to conclude that nothing changed. The critics established that medieval people knew children were different and loved them; they did not establish that childhood occupied the same place in social life. What the early modern period did see was the gradual spread of institutions that sorted the young by age and held them apart from adult work: schools divided into classes, a growing literature addressed specifically to children, and eventually laws fixing the ages below which a person could not be employed or married. None of these changes was sudden, and none reached every class or region at once; the children of the poor worked beside adults long after the children of the prosperous had been sent to school. Childhood as a feeling may be ancient. Childhood as a segregated, age-graded stage, organised by institutions, is far more recent.

Seen this way, the original thesis and its critics were partly talking past each other. One side asked whether people recognised and cared for children; the other, without always saying so, asked how societies arranged the passage from birth to adult status. This is why the debate could run for so long without resolution: each side could cite evidence the other did not dispute, because each was answering a different question. The second question is the more fruitful, because it leaves room for the observation that every society has children but not every society has childhood in the same form.

Discussions of population ageing tend to begin with a single number. The old-age dependency ratio divides the number of people above a fixed age, usually sixty-five, by the number of people of working age, conventionally fifteen to sixty-four. As birth rates fall and lives lengthen the ratio rises, and a rising ratio is read as a growing burden: fewer shoulders, it is said, bearing the weight of more pensioners. The image is vivid and the arithmetic is simple, which is precisely why the measure deserves more suspicion than it usually receives.

The ratio rests on two equations that are rarely stated. The first is that everyone between fifteen and sixty-four supports others and everyone above sixty-five is supported by them. Neither half is true. Large numbers of people of working age are in education, unemployed, caring full-time for relatives or otherwise outside paid work, while many people beyond the threshold continue to earn, to pay taxes and, perhaps most importantly, to provide unpaid care. In many families it is grandparents whose looking after small children allows both parents to hold jobs; on the ratio's accounting, those grandparents appear only as a cost. The same error runs in the other direction for the many people in their fifties who have left paid work early through illness or redundancy, and who depend on others well before the line is reached.

The second equation is that a given age means the same thing in every generation. A sixty-five-year-old today in most countries can expect to live considerably longer, and in better health, than a sixty-five-year-old of the generation in which the threshold was fixed. To keep the line at sixty-five as life expectancy rises is to classify as old an ever larger share of people who are, by the standards that originally justified the line, not old at all. Some demographers have proposed measuring age prospectively, by the years a person can expect still to live rather than the years already lived; on such measures, populations age considerably more slowly than the headline ratio suggests.

None of this means that ageing is costless. The final years of a long life often bring a need for intensive medical and personal care, and as more people reach advanced old age that need grows in ways no redefinition can wish away. The objection is not to concern but to calibration. A measure that counts heads by birthday rather than activity by circumstance will tend to exaggerate the problem in its general form and to obscure it in the specific form, very late life, in which it is most acute.

For much of the twentieth century, anthropologists sorted the ties they recorded into two kinds. Some were 'real', resting on birth and descent; others were 'fictive', a convenient label for godparents, sworn brothers, adopted children and the many other relations that people treated as kinship but that did not, so the observer thought, rest on blood. The distinction seemed merely descriptive, and it took some time to see that it carried a theory with it: that the true foundation of kinship is biological, and that everything else is imitation.

The difficulty is that many of the people being described did not share the theory. In a number of societies, people become kin by eating food grown on the same land, by living in the same house, or by being nursed at the same breast. Under Islamic law, for instance, children nursed by the same woman are barred from marrying one another, much as siblings by birth would be; the tie created by milk is not a metaphor for kinship but a form of it. In such places, ties made in these ways may carry the same obligations of help, hospitality and mourning as ties of birth. Where relatedness is understood to accumulate through feeding and sharing over years, to call such ties fictive is not to describe them but to overrule the people who live them.

This is not an argument that biology is irrelevant. Birth is, almost everywhere, one of the most powerful ways of reckoning who belongs to whom, and an attempt to dissolve it entirely into choice would be its own kind of distortion. The point is narrower: biology is one idiom of relatedness among several, and which idioms count, and how much, varies from place to place. Nor is the West an exception that proves the biological rule. Adoption, the blended families formed by remarriage, and the arrangements made possible by donated eggs and sperm all require people to decide, often painfully, whether a tie of birth or a tie of care should prevail when the two come apart.

Seen this way, kinship is something people do as well as something they are born into. The older vocabulary was not useless, since it pointed to real differences in the ways ties are formed and maintained. Its error lay in treating one culture's answer to the question of what makes people kin as the standard against which every other answer was to be measured, and in mistaking that answer for a fact of nature rather than a choice that other peoples had made differently.

Every few years a new generation is given a name, and with the name comes a character. One cohort is said to be idealistic and later complacent, another cynical, another anxious, entitled or unusually attached to its telephones. The labels are used by marketers, journalists and employers with a confidence that would be remarkable in any other classification of human beings. We would hesitate to say that everyone born under a given star sign shares a temperament; we say something not very different, and with far less hesitation, about everyone born within a given span of fifteen years. The labels are also remarkably durable: once a cohort has been named and described, the description tends to follow it into middle age, revised only when a newer cohort arrives to take its place as the subject of worry.

The trouble begins with a problem of method that social scientists have long recognised. When one group of people differs from another, the difference may reflect their age (the young almost everywhere change jobs more often than the middle-aged), the period in which they are observed (everyone, of whatever age, was affected by a recession or a new technology), or the cohort into which they were born, meaning a lasting imprint left by the conditions of their early years. Only the last is a generational effect in the strict sense. But the three are bound together by arithmetic: a person's age is simply the current year minus the year of birth, so that once any two are known the third is fixed. No set of observations can by itself pull them apart; some assumption from outside the data is always required. Much of what is confidently attributed to a generation turns out, on inspection, to be what people of that age have always done, or what people of every age were doing at the time.

A second difficulty concerns boundaries. The years at which one generation is said to end and the next to begin are chosen by convention, and different sources disagree about them by several years. A person born on the last day of one span and a person born on the first day of the next are assigned different characters, while two people born fourteen years apart within one span are assigned the same. Differences within a labelled cohort, by class, region, education and much else, are typically far larger than the differences between cohorts, which is to say that the label groups people along the axis on which they least differ.

None of this shows that generations are a fiction. There is a serious idea buried under the marketing: that people who come of age during a war, a depression or a political upheaval may carry its mark for life, and may differ in lasting ways from those who met the same events earlier or later in their lives. Such effects have been found, and they are not trivial. But they are anchored to events rather than to calendars; they mark some members of a cohort far more deeply than others, depending on where and how the event touched them; and they rarely produce a single character that an entire cohort shares.

Why, then, do the calendar labels persist? Part of the answer is that they are convenient, turning a tangle of causes into a story with protagonists. Part of it is that they flatter, inviting each cohort to see itself as distinctive and its elders or juniors as the problem. The cost of the story is easy to miss. When young adults find housing unaffordable or work insecure, attributing their situation to a generational temperament converts a question about economic arrangements into a question about character, and a question about character has no obvious policy answer.

There is a familiar story about the family in South Asia. Once, it runs, people lived in large joint households: an elderly couple, their married sons with wives and children, perhaps unmarried daughters and a widowed aunt, all sharing one roof, one kitchen and one purse under the authority of the eldest man. Then came cities, salaried jobs and the ideal of the companionate couple, and the joint family began to break up into small units of parents and children. The story is told with pride by those who see the old household as a school of duty and with relief by those who see it as a school of obedience, but both versions agree about the direction of travel. It is repeated by planners, preachers and novelists alike, and it is so familiar that it is rarely asked for its evidence.

The evidence for the story is weaker than its popularity suggests. Much of it comes from counting households at a single moment, and a single moment is a poor guide to a process that unfolds over decades. A joint household is not a permanent structure but a phase. A young couple may live alone for some years; the household becomes joint when a son marries and brings his wife home; it may grow when a second son does the same; and it often divides when the father dies and the brothers set up separate hearths, each of which may in turn become joint a generation later. In a population in which every family followed this cycle exactly, a count taken on any given day would find a great many nuclear households, even though nearly everyone would spend part of life in a joint one. A high proportion of nuclear households, then, is not by itself evidence that the joint family is disappearing.

The wider theory behind the story fares little better. It was long assumed that industry produced the nuclear family, by moving work out of the home and rewarding people who could move to wherever the jobs were. Yet historians of north-western Europe found that small households of parents and children were already common there long before the factories arrived; if anything, the causation may have run partly the other way. A society's household form, it seems, is not simply read off its economy.

This is not to say that nothing has changed. Migration for work has scattered many families across cities and countries, so that brothers who would once have shared a courtyard now live hundreds of kilometres apart. But dispersal is not the same thing as dissolution. Money flows back to parents; decisions about marriages, property and the education of children are still taken together; a son abroad may be more bound by his family's expectations than a son next door. Some families keep a common fund into which brothers in different cities pay, and from which the costs of weddings and illnesses are met. A census that defines the joint family by shared residence will record such a family as several nuclear ones, and will miss the jointness that matters most to its members.

It would be equally mistaken to swing to the opposite view and declare the joint family unchanged. What is being renegotiated, often bitterly, is less the size of the household than the authority within it: whether a daughter-in-law must defer to her mother-in-law, whether elders decide whom the young marry, whether property passes to sons alone. The quarrels are often sharpest where the household is still shared, because shared space turns every question of precedence into a daily one. These are real changes, and they are better described as a transformation of jointness than as its end.

passages.topic: Ritual and belief as social practice
paragraphs: It is tempting to treat superstition as a residue of ignorance, a set of mistaken beliefs that education will eventually wash away. The difficulty with this view is that superstition does not distribute itself the way ignorance does. Highly trained surgeons, pilots, stage actors and professional athletes, people who know a great deal about the causal workings of their craft, are often among the most attached to private rituals: a particular pair of socks, a fixed sequence of gestures before a performance, a refusal to say certain words aloud. If superstition were merely a gap in knowledge, these would be the last people we would expect to keep it.

A more useful observation is that superstition gathers where two conditions meet: the outcome matters a great deal, and a significant part of it lies beyond the actor's control. Ethnographers have described fishing communities that use no protective magic when they work in a sheltered lagoon, where skill reliably brings a catch, yet surround voyages into the open sea with elaborate rites. The same people hold the same beliefs about the world; what changes is their exposure to chance. Examinations, sporting finals and opening nights share this structure. Preparation counts, but on the day itself something unaccountable remains, and the ritual fills the space that preparation cannot reach.

What the ritual supplies, on this account, is not a causal lever over the outcome but a way of acting when no further useful action is available. Anxiety in the face of uncertainty tends to seek an outlet, and an outlet that is fixed, brief and familiar is better than one that is improvised, such as a last-minute change to a plan that was sound. A tennis player who bounces the ball exactly the same number of times before every serve is not, in any serious sense, trying to bend the laws of physics. She is marking a boundary between deliberation and execution, and the routine protects the execution from second thoughts.

None of this makes superstition harmless. The same disposition that steadies a performer can lead a patient to choose a charm over a treatment that works, or a trader to mistake a lucky streak for a method. The line falls roughly where the ritual stops occupying the residue of chance and begins to displace action that would genuinely improve the odds. Understood this way, superstition is neither a quaint error to be laughed at nor a hidden wisdom to be celebrated, but a predictable human response to exposure that deserves to be judged by what it crowds out.

passages.topic: Ritual and belief as social practice
paragraphs: A common modern objection to traditional mourning customs is that they put grief on a timetable. Many traditions mark fixed days after a death, often a gathering within the first two weeks, another around the fortieth day and a final observance at the first anniversary, and for centuries some communities prescribed the clothes a widow might wear and the months during which she should not appear at celebrations. To a sensibility that prizes authentic feeling, this looks like an intrusion: grief, it is said, is personal, it follows no calendar, and nobody has the right to tell a bereaved person when to stop.

The objection contains a truth, but it misreads what the calendar was for. The fixed days rarely claimed to measure how long sorrow lasts. What they did was settle a set of practical questions that otherwise fall, at the worst possible moment, on the people least able to answer them. When should relatives visit, and when should they leave? What is it acceptable to say? When may the household resume ordinary work without seeming callous? A prescribed sequence answers all of these in advance, so that the bereaved are spared the labour of inventing their own conduct while they are exhausted, and so that neighbours know when their presence is expected.

In this sense the timetable was addressed less to the mourner than to everyone around the mourner, translating an event that isolates one household into a sequence of obligations that the wider community could recognise and discharge. Its main work was coordination. Where such scripts have weakened, the result has not obviously been freer grief. Friends hesitate, unsure whether a call would comfort or intrude; colleagues say nothing for fear of saying the wrong thing; and the bereaved, told that they may grieve in their own way, often find that their own way is a lonely one, because nobody else knows what part to play in it.

This is not an argument for restoring every old rule, nor for pretending that the old forms were uniformly benign. Some customs plainly bore down hardest on those with least power, and a widow who was obliged to wear mourning for years was being policed as much as consoled. The lesson is narrower. A society that abandons shared forms for mourning does not thereby hand grief back to the individual; it removes the cues that let others accompany it. Any replacement worth having would keep that coordinating function while dropping the demand that inner feeling match an outward schedule.

passages.topic: Ritual and belief as social practice
paragraphs: Anthropologists have long described rites of passage as moving in three phases. The person undergoing the rite is first separated from an existing status, then passes through a transitional period in which he or she belongs to neither the old condition nor the new, and is finally incorporated into the community in a new role: adult, married, initiated, ordained. Of these phases the middle one, often called liminal, from the Latin word for a threshold, has attracted by far the most attention, and for good reason. It is there that most of the strange features of such rites are concentrated: seclusion in the forest or a special hut, the shaving of heads, the wearing of identical plain garments, the suspension of names, the imposition of hardship and silence.

A simple reading treats these features as a waiting room, a pause while the real change, the conferral of new status, is prepared offstage. This misses their function. Stripping novices of names, clothing and possessions removes the markers by which they were previously ranked, so that for a time sons of important families and sons of poor ones are indistinguishable. Shared hardship then does two things at once. It makes the novices receptive to instruction, since people deprived of their usual footing listen differently, and it binds them to one another in a way that often outlasts the ritual, creating cohorts whose loyalty cuts across lineage and wealth.

In recent decades, however, the idea has travelled far from its origins, and something has been lost on the way. The liminal phase is now often celebrated as a zone of freedom, creativity and play, and the word is applied to almost any in-between experience: the years after school, a period of unemployment, a long journey abroad. This enthusiasm overlooks how tightly the traditional threshold was managed. Elders set its length, prescribed what novices could eat and say, and decided when it was over. Its ambiguity was real, but it was ambiguity held inside a firm frame, and its whole point was the return.

That frame is what most modern transitions lack. A young person who drifts between education and employment may experience the disorientation of the threshold without its discipline, its companions or, above all, its exit. There is no moment at which the community declares the passage complete and receives the person in a new capacity. None of this implies that the old rites should be revived, since their authority rested on forms of social life that no longer exist. But the comparison suggests that what made liminality productive was not the openness that its modern admirers praise. It was the certainty that the openness would end.

passages.topic: Ritual and belief as social practice
paragraphs: There are two familiar ways of misunderstanding pilgrimage, and they are mirror images of each other. The first treats the journey as mere transport: what matters is arrival at the shrine, the sight of the image or the relic, the bath in the river, and the road is simply the price paid to get there. The second, popular among those who walk old pilgrim routes for reasons they would not call religious, reverses the emphasis. The destination, on this view, is almost a pretext; the real value lies in the walking itself, the days of effort, the strangers met on the way, the slow emptying of the mind.

Each view captures something that pilgrims genuinely report, but both detach two elements that draw their meaning from each other, and neither can be made intelligible without the other. The hardships of the road are not valuable in the abstract. Blistered feet on a hiking holiday are an inconvenience; the same blisters on the way to a sacred place become an offering, a sign of seriousness, a story to be told on return. What converts them is the fixed point towards which they are directed. Equally, the shrine does not possess its full weight for the pilgrim independently of the effort spent reaching it. A visitor who arrives by car on a whim may see exactly what the pilgrim sees and still not have had the pilgrim's experience.

The history of easier travel bears this interdependence out in an unexpected way, and it is worth dwelling on because it runs against a natural expectation. One might have predicted that when roads, railways and buses made distant shrines accessible within hours, the effortful element would simply vanish. In many places it has instead been reintroduced by choice. Pilgrims who have covered most of the distance in comfort often leave the vehicle to walk the final stretch, sometimes barefoot, sometimes on their knees. The effort has been condensed rather than abandoned, as though people sense that arrival without cost would not count as arrival at all.

None of this means that the walker who sets out with no particular reverence is deceived about what he finds. Long days on foot do change people, and the change can be real without being religious. But it is worth noticing what such a walker relinquishes, perhaps without realising it, when the destination becomes optional rather than obligatory. The pilgrim cannot decide halfway that another town would do just as well, and that inability is part of what lends the road its gravity. A journey that could end anywhere is a fine thing; it is simply a different thing from one that must end in a particular place.

passages.topic: Ritual and belief as social practice
paragraphs: Visitors to shrines that are frequented by people of more than one religion tend to come away with one of two stories. In the first, the shrine is evidence of a deep harmony beneath official differences: here, at the tomb of a holy figure or a spring credited with healing powers, ordinary believers ignore the boundaries their clergy insist on and share a common devotion. In the second, the arrangement is a fragile truce, a curiosity that survives only until politics catches up with it. Both stories are told about sites around the Mediterranean, in the Balkans and across South Asia, and both, I think, misdescribe what sharing usually involves.

Close observation of such places rarely finds a single, blended faith. More often it finds parallel use. One community lights lamps in the evening, another comes on a particular weekday; one group knows the saint by one name and story, another by a different name and a different story, and neither is much troubled by the discrepancy. Custodians, frequently from one community, accept offerings from all and refrain from asking visitors what they believe. The sharing is real, but it consists in a set of practical accommodations rather than in agreement, and it works partly because certain questions are never posed: above all, the question of whose shrine it really is.

This is why the harmony story, attractive as it is, puts the emphasis in the wrong place. The arrangement does not depend on people believing the same thing; it depends on their not being required to settle what they believe about this particular place. Nor does the truce story fare better. Many such sites have been shared for generations, through periods of considerable tension elsewhere, which is hard to square with the idea that their peace is merely a pause. What usually threatens them is not the slow pressure of difference but a sudden demand for definition, when some authority, a government department, a heritage body or a movement seeking to purify practice, insists that the site be registered, restored or claimed as belonging to one tradition alone.

It would be romantic to pretend that these places were free of friction. Custodians could favour their own community, quarrels over offerings were common, and the vagueness that allowed sharing also allowed one side to quietly enlarge its claim. Still, the lesson they offer is more interesting than either of the usual stories. Coexistence, they suggest, need not wait for agreement about ultimate questions. It can rest on a carefully maintained ambiguity, which is a social achievement in its own right and, like most achievements, easier to destroy than to build.

passages.topic: Ritual and belief as social practice
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, social scientists took it nearly for granted that modernisation and religion were locked in a zero-sum relationship. As societies industrialised, urbanised and educated their populations, faith would retreat, first from public life and then from private conviction. When the last decades of the century brought vigorous religious movements on several continents, and when religion returned to the centre of political argument in places where it had supposedly been tamed, many concluded that the secularisation thesis had simply been refuted. Some of its former defenders said as much.

Both the confidence and the recantation, however, rested on treating as one hypothesis what was really a bundle of several. One strand concerns differentiation: the process by which law, medicine, education, science and the economy come to operate by their own criteria, no longer answerable to religious authority. A second concerns decline: a fall in belief, membership and practice among individuals. A third concerns privatisation: the withdrawal of religion from public argument into the domain of personal choice. These claims are logically independent. A society could see religious practice flourish while its hospitals, courts and universities remain entirely outside clerical control, and that combination is in fact common.

Once the strands are separated, the evidence looks different. The decline thesis has fared poorly as a universal law; patterns of belief vary too widely between societies at similar levels of wealth to support it. The privatisation thesis has fared worse still, since religious voices are plainly present in public debate. But differentiation has held up remarkably well, and the point most often missed is that the religious resurgence itself tends to presuppose it. Movements that seek public influence organise as voluntary associations, compete for members, lobby legislatures, commission surveys and appeal to rights. They act, that is, as one set of claimants among many within institutions they do not control, which is precisely the condition that differentiation describes.

It would be too quick to declare the older thesis vindicated by this route. A theory that predicted the fading of faith and got that prediction wrong in much of the world cannot be rescued by pointing to the part that survived, and some of its proponents did expect the strands to move together. The more modest conclusion is that the debate has been conducted at the wrong level of generality. To ask whether the world is becoming secular is to ask a question with no single answer; to ask which institutions have slipped free of religious authority, and on what terms religion now competes for influence within them, is to ask questions that the evidence can actually settle.

passages.topic: Ritual and belief as social practice
paragraphs: Many societies have set aside days on which the ordinary order is turned upside down. In the Roman Saturnalia, masters are said to have waited on their slaves at table; in parts of medieval Europe, junior clergy elected a mock bishop and parodied the liturgy; in countless village festivals men dress as women, children give orders to adults, and the powerful are mocked in songs that would be punished at any other time of year. Such festivals of inversion have long puzzled those who study them, because they seem to put the most fundamental arrangements of a society at risk for the sake of a few days of licence.

Two explanations have dominated. The first, often called the safety valve theory, holds that inversion protects the order it mocks. Resentments that accumulate under hierarchy are released in a bounded, harmless form, and when the festival ends everyone returns to their place, relieved and more willing to stay there. The second reverses the judgement. On this view, the festival gives people a glimpse of a world arranged otherwise, keeps alive the memory that rank is not natural, and so contains the seed of real defiance. Supporters of each view can point to cases. Rulers have tolerated and even funded such festivals, which suggests they found them useful; they have also banned them, which suggests they found them dangerous, and on a few occasions a carnival has indeed turned into a riot.

What both explanations share is the assumption that the meaning of inversion is fixed by its form, so that one need only decide, once and for all, whether turning the world upside down conserves it or threatens it. The historical record does not support so tidy a choice, since the same festival, with the same masks and the same songs, has been a harmless frolic in one decade and the occasion of an uprising in the next. The difference lay not in the ritual but in its circumstances: a bad harvest, a disputed tax, a quarrel between factions of the elite that made the mockery of one of them useful to the other. Inversion, in other words, does not carry its own political charge; it takes one from the situation into which it is performed.

The safety valve theory has a further weakness that is easy to overlook because its central image is so vivid. It pictures discontent as a kind of pressure that builds up in a closed vessel and can be let off in measured bursts. There is little reason to think that resentment, which is attached to particular injuries and particular persons, behaves like steam that can be vented without residue; people who have mocked their masters for a day do not obviously feel less aggrieved afterwards, and they may feel more entitled to their grievance for having heard it voiced aloud by a crowd. The image persuades because it is mechanical, not because anyone has observed the mechanism.

A more promising account starts from a simpler observation. To turn a world upside down, one must first show which way up it is. The mock bishop presupposes a real one; the servant who gives orders for a day makes plain who gives them on every other day. Inversion is thus a vivid lesson in hierarchy, and in that sense it does teach the order it reverses. But the lesson cuts both ways, since a ranking that can be so easily reversed in play is shown to be a convention rather than a fact of nature. Which of these lessons is learned depends, again, on what else is happening. That is an unsatisfying conclusion only for those who wanted the festival to have a single meaning.

passages.topic: Ritual and belief as social practice
paragraphs: Why do so many religious and quasi-religious groups ask their members to do things that are difficult, uncomfortable or expensive? Long fasts, pre-dawn prayers, restrictive diets, distinctive dress that invites ridicule, vows that forgo income or marriage: from a narrowly economic point of view these look like pure loss. An influential answer, borrowed from the study of animal behaviour, is that the costs are the point. A signal that is cheap to send can be sent by anyone, and so tells an observer little. A signal that is costly to send, and costlier still for someone who does not mean it, is credible precisely because it is hard to fake.

Applied to ritual, the idea runs as follows. Groups that depend on mutual aid, sharing harvests, lending money or protecting one another, are vulnerable to people who take the benefits of membership without bearing its burdens. Demanding rituals screen such people out. Someone who is willing to rise before dawn for years, or to give up foods that everyone else enjoys, is unlikely to be only nominally attached, and the others can extend trust accordingly. The theory also explains a pattern that has often been remarked upon: groups that lower their demands in the hope of attracting members sometimes find that they lose them instead, as the value of belonging falls along with its cost.

This is a genuinely illuminating account, and it captures something that purely symbolic interpretations of ritual tend to miss: that rituals are not only statements of meaning but also transactions with consequences for who can rely on whom, and that their cost is part of how they work rather than an unfortunate by-product. But it is incomplete in at least three ways. First, it explains why a ritual should be costly, not why it should take the particular form it does. Any sufficiently burdensome act would serve as a signal, yet communities care intensely about the precise words, gestures and times of their observances, and would not accept a different hardship of equal cost as a substitute. Second, many of the most demanding practices are imposed on children long before they could choose them. A rite performed on an infant may say something about the commitment of the parents, but it cannot be a signal of the child's own.

The third gap is the most important. The signalling theory treats ritual as a message addressed to observers, as though the performer were already fully committed and merely needed to prove it. Yet people who undertake demanding practices commonly report that the practice changes them: that the fast or the vigil produces the conviction it was supposed to display. If that is so, cost does not only reveal commitment but helps to manufacture it. A person who has sacrificed much for a group has reasons to value it that did not exist before the sacrifice, and the observer who reads his devotion as a signal is reading something that the ritual itself helped to create.

None of these objections overturns the signalling account. They suggest instead that it describes one function among several, the one most visible to an outsider calculating whom to trust. A fuller theory would ask what ritual does to the people who perform it as well as what it tells the people who watch, and would treat the form of a rite as something that matters in its own right rather than as an arbitrary carrier of cost.

When a job that was once filled by school leavers begins to advertise for graduates, the usual explanation is that the work has become more demanding. Machines have taken over the routine tasks, the story goes, and what remains calls for the analytical habits that only a university can supply. There is something to this. Some occupations really have changed beyond recognition, and an office clerk today handles systems that would have baffled a clerk of fifty years ago. But the explanation is offered far more often than it is checked, and when one looks at what people in many of these jobs actually do, the change in the work is often modest beside the change in the paperwork required to get it.

A more economical account treats the degree less as a certificate of skill than as a ticket in a queue. When few people held degrees, an employer who asked for one was selecting a small group who were, on average, more persistent and better connected than the rest. As degrees became common, the same requirement no longer separated anyone, and employers who wanted to keep selecting raised the bar again, asking for a master's where a bachelor's had once sufficed. Each employer is behaving sensibly; it is merely using the cheapest filter available. Yet the sum of these sensible choices resembles a crowd at a parade in which everyone stands on tiptoe: no one sees better than before, and everyone is more tired.

The costs of this arrangement are not evenly spread. Students from families that can afford several years of fees and forgone earnings keep pace with the rising bar; those who cannot are shut out of work they could perfectly well perform. A requirement introduced in the name of competence thus ends up rewarding the capacity to pay for time. Meanwhile the graduates themselves often discover that much of what they studied is barely used in the job, and that what the employer valued was the signal rather than the substance.

None of this is an argument against education, which has goods that no labour market can measure. It is an argument against confusing two things that the word 'qualification' runs together: what a person can do, and how long a person has been able to stay in school. Some employers have begun to test applicants directly on the tasks the job involves. Where this is done, an awkward question comes into view, namely whether the degree requirement it replaces was ever a guarantee of quality or merely a habit that nobody had thought to examine.

We tend to think of the weekend as a natural feature of the calendar, as if two days of rest had always followed five of work. In fact the arrangement is fairly recent, and its history suggests that free time is not simply the absence of work but something that has to be made, defended and shaped. Before the factory, many artisans worked in bursts, labouring late into the night to finish an order and then taking a day or two off whenever it suited them; in parts of England the habit of stretching Sunday's rest into Monday was common enough to be given a mock saint's name, 'Saint Monday'.

Factory production could not tolerate this irregularity. Machines were expensive and had to run whenever the hands were present, and an employer could not plan production around workers who might drift in on Tuesday, so the long struggle over hours was therefore also a struggle over the shape of time. Workers wanted fewer hours; employers wanted predictable ones. The compromise that eventually emerged, first a half-day on Saturday and later the whole of it, gave each side part of what it sought. Workers won rest that was guaranteed rather than snatched, and employers won a workforce that turned up, sober, on Monday morning.

It would be wrong to see the outcome merely as a defeat dressed up as a victory. For most working people, guaranteed free time was a real gain, and it was won against resistance. But the weekend also changed what free time was. Leisure that had once been taken at the worker's discretion became a fixed block, the same for everyone, and a block that was the same for everyone could be sold to. Football matches, excursion trains and seaside resorts arranged themselves around Saturday afternoon and Sunday, and leisure came increasingly to mean something one went out and paid for at a scheduled time.

The lesson is not that the old irregular rhythm was better; it was often tied to poverty, to insecurity and to binges of overwork that left people exhausted. It is that arguments about working hours are never only about quantity. When people today argue over flexible schedules or a four-day week, they are reopening a question that the industrial age settled in one particular way: not merely how much time should be free, but who decides when it falls and what it is for.

In the large households of the nineteenth century, the best servant was the one who was least noticed. Grand houses were built with back staircases so that maids carrying coal or slops need never meet the family on the main stairs, and bells rang in a basement corridor so that a summons could be issued without anyone having to see who answered it. In some houses servants were expected to turn aside, even to face the wall, when a member of the family passed. It is tempting to read all this as snobbery, a taste for keeping inferiors out of sight, but snobbery explains less than it seems to. The invisibility of servants was not a by-product of the genteel household; it was one of the things the household was for.

What a gentleman's house displayed, above all, was ease: meals that appeared, fires that were lit, linen that was clean, all without visible effort. The ease was manufactured by a great deal of labour, and the labour had to be hidden for the ease to be believed. A servant glimpsed scrubbing a step was a reminder that comfort had a cost and a source; a servant unseen allowed the family to experience comfort as a natural condition of their kind of life. In this sense the architecture of concealment did not merely reflect a social hierarchy but helped to produce one, by allowing one class to appear exempt from necessity.

Large-scale domestic service of this kind has largely disappeared, and it is easy to assume that its logic went with it. Yet much of the modern service economy seems designed to recreate the same experience by other means. Food arrives at the door from a kitchen the customer never sees, carried by a courier who is a first name on a screen. Offices are cleaned at night, after the staff have gone home. Apps promise that groceries, laundry and repairs will simply happen, and their designers speak, revealingly, of removing friction, as though the friction in question were not, very often, the encounter with another person who is doing the work.

The comparison must not be pressed too far. The modern courier or cleaner is not bound to a single household, keeps hours that end, and has legal protections that a Victorian scullery maid lacked; to call such workers servants is to erase real gains. But the aspiration that the old houses expressed in brick and bells, the wish to receive service without meeting the server, has proved remarkably durable. What has changed is less the wish than the means of satisfying it, and the means are now available to far more people than ever owned a back staircase.

The idea that some jobs require workers to manage their own feelings, and not merely their hands or their minds, has travelled a long way from its origins in the study of flight attendants and debt collectors. It now turns up in discussions of nursing, teaching, retail and call centres, and even of the unpaid work of keeping a family cheerful. This expansion has drawn a predictable objection: if every job involves some management of emotion, the critics say, then the concept marks out nothing in particular. A surgeon must stay calm, a lawyer must appear confident, and a builder who loses his temper with clients will not keep them; are these, too, emotional labourers?

The objection is fair against the loose use of the term, but it misses what the original idea was pointing at. The distinction was never between jobs that involve feeling and jobs that do not. It was between feeling that a worker manages according to her own judgement and feeling whose display is specified, monitored and sold by someone else. The surgeon's calm serves the operation and is left to her; nobody scripts it. The call-centre agent, by contrast, may be told how often to use the customer's name, scored on the warmth of her voice, and disciplined for a sigh. The emotion is part of the product, and the employer, not the worker, sets its terms.

Seen this way, the concept is narrower than its popular use suggests, but also sharper. It directs attention not to the presence of emotion at work but to its ownership, and it suggests where the cost of such work lies. Most people can smile at a stranger without harm; the difficulty arises when the smile must be produced on demand, for hours, regardless of how the worker is treated, and when failing to produce it is a disciplinary matter. One would expect work of this kind to produce a fatigue unlike ordinary tiredness, and perhaps an uncertainty about which friendly feelings are one's own.

None of this implies that friendliness in service is a sham, or that customers who enjoy it are dupes. Many workers take pride in easing a stranger's day, and a scripted greeting can be delivered with real goodwill. The point is that goodwill freely given and goodwill required by contract are different things, even when they look identical from the other side of the counter, and a concept that cannot tell them apart has lost the very thing that made it worth having.

For a long time the sociology of taste worked with a simple map. At the top of the social order sat a refined culture of opera, poetry and the old masters, at the bottom sat popular entertainments, and a person's place in society could be read, with fair accuracy, from the position of their preferences on this ladder. Elites, on this picture, distinguished themselves by what they refused. Liking the wrong music was not merely a private failing but a mark of origin.

Surveys of cultural consumption in a number of wealthy countries have since complicated the map. The most educated and affluent groups, it turns out, are no longer best described as snobs who like only high culture. They are more often omnivores: they go to the opera and to the cinema, read literary fiction and crime novels, and are happy to discuss both a string quartet and a pop album. Some observers have greeted this as the end of cultural hierarchy, a sign that the old boundaries between high and low have dissolved and that taste has become a matter of individual preference rather than of class.

That conclusion is premature. Breadth of taste is itself unevenly distributed, because it requires money, time, travel and, above all, the confidence to move between worlds without feeling out of place. The person who can talk knowledgeably about both a symphony and a street-food stall has accumulated a cultural range that is far harder to acquire than a liking for either alone. Moreover, omnivores rarely consume popular forms in the same way as their usual audiences. They tend to approach them with a knowing, curatorial attitude, prizing a song for its place in the history of a genre or enjoying a film with a touch of irony, and this manner of liking can mark distance as effectively as refusal once did.

Nor is the omnivore's appetite unlimited. Research on what people say they dislike has suggested that the forms most often rejected by the highly educated tend to be those most associated with the least educated, so that the boundary has moved rather than vanished. None of this means that the loosening of old hierarchies is an illusion; it is a genuine change that the opera house must now compete for prestige with a well-chosen food truck. But distinction has not disappeared with the decline of snobbery. It has learned to express itself through openness, and openness is harder to criticise than exclusion because it looks so much like a virtue.

Two accounts of the professions have long competed for our assent, and each is right about something. The first, which professionals themselves favour, holds that a profession is defined by esoteric knowledge put at the service of clients who cannot judge it. Because a patient cannot assess a diagnosis or a litigant a legal argument, the state licenses practitioners, and the licence is a guarantee of competence that protects the public from charlatans. The second account, favoured by economists of a sceptical turn, treats the same licence as a barrier to entry: by limiting the number who may practise, a profession raises its fees, and its talk of public protection is simply the language in which a cartel describes itself.

What the two accounts share is more interesting than what divides them. Both look at one profession at a time, as if each stood alone facing its clients, and both assume that the work a profession does is simply given: there are diseases, so there are doctors; there are disputes, so there are lawyers. Yet the boundaries of professional work are anything but given. Whether persistent unhappiness is a medical condition, a psychological difficulty, a spiritual crisis or a social problem is not settled by the nature of unhappiness. It is settled, provisionally and repeatedly, by contests among psychiatrists, psychologists, clergy and social workers, each of whom claims that the problem properly belongs to it.

Seen from this angle, a profession is less a guild guarding a fixed territory than one party in a system of rival claims, and its history is a history of conquests and retreats. Licensing remains important, but as a weapon in a jurisdictional struggle rather than as either a certificate or a mere device for fixing prices. Knowledge, too, matters in a different way. What wins a contested problem is often not superior skill in treating it but a more abstract body of theory, one that allows a profession to redefine the problem in its own terms and so to argue that its rivals were treating the symptoms rather than the thing itself. A profession whose knowledge is purely practical can be displaced by one that can explain why that practice works.

This does not mean that competence is irrelevant or that the cartel theorist is merely cynical. Clients are protected by licensing, and fees are raised by it. But neither effect explains why some professions grow while others shrink, or why a body of practitioners who are perfectly good at their work can find that work quietly reassigned to others. The fate of a profession, on this view, depends less on how well it does what it does than on its ability to persuade others, including the state and the public, that the problems of the moment are its problems.

The phrase 'conspicuous consumption', coined by Thorstein Veblen in the 1890s, named a habit of the wealthy of his day: the purchase of goods whose chief use was to show that one could afford them. The mansion, the carriage and the idle household were, on this account, less comforts than advertisements. The idea proved so useful that it outlived the society that prompted it, and it still shapes how we picture status spending: the logo on the handbag, the oversized car, the watch that costs more than a year's rent.

The picture now misleads more than it reveals, at least at the top. As mass production and global supply chains have made once-rare goods cheap, the handbag and the car have become available, in passable imitations, to almost anyone with a credit card. Display of this kind has lost much of its power to separate, and many of the most advantaged households have turned away from it. Their spending flows instead into things that are hard to see and harder to copy: private tuition and a house in the right school catchment, retirement savings, organic groceries, exercise classes, domestic help that frees time for reading, and clothing whose quality is recognised only by those who know what to look for. The signal, where there is one, is addressed to a narrow audience of peers rather than to the street. The pattern has come to be called inconspicuous consumption.

It would be easy to treat the change as an improvement in taste, a retreat from vulgar display into quieter and more sensible habits. In part it is. Much of this spending yields real benefits in health, in learning and in security, and few would wish the rich to return to buying gold-plated taps. But the shift has two consequences that the language of good taste conceals. The first is that inconspicuous goods are more effective at reproducing advantage than conspicuous ones ever were. A diamond can be sold; a childhood spent in good schools, with books at home and parents who have time, becomes part of a person and can neither be taken away nor easily acquired later. Spending of this kind does not merely display a position; it passes it on.

The second consequence is moral. Conspicuous consumption invited criticism precisely because it was conspicuous. The flashy car was an obvious target for the satirist and the moralist, and its owner could be accused of vanity. Inconspicuous consumption is much harder to criticise, because it presents itself not as display but as virtue: one is not showing off, one is merely eating well, looking after one's health and investing in one's children. The vocabulary that surrounds it, of wellness, sensible choices and doing the best for one's family, offers the satirist nothing obviously vulgar to mock. Those who cannot afford to do the same are not envied so much as quietly judged, as though their diets and their children's results were failures of character rather than of income.

None of this is an accusation of bad faith. It does not require us to think the affluent hypocritical, or the parent paying for tuition secretly bent on buying status; most such choices are made sincerely, for the reasons people give. The point is structural rather than personal. A society in which advantage is transmitted through the visible accumulation of objects at least makes its inequalities legible. One in which advantage flows through habits, schooling and time has made them harder to see, and inequalities that are hard to see are also harder to argue about.

Few political promises are as widely shared as the promise of social mobility. Parties that agree on little else agree that a child's prospects should not be fixed by the circumstances of her birth, and the claim that mobility has stalled is one of the most damaging charges that can be laid against a government. Yet the word covers two quite different things, and much public argument about it goes astray because the two are run together.

The first is absolute mobility: the share of people who end up better off than their parents, whether by income or by the kind of work they do. The second is relative mobility: the extent to which a person's position in the distribution, as opposed to their standard of living, differs from their parents' position. The two can move independently. In a period of rapid growth and expanding professional employment, most children may outearn their parents and many may enter occupations their parents never held, even if the chance of a child born near the bottom reaching the top, compared with that of a child born near the top, has not changed at all. Everyone rides the escalator up, but the order of people on it stays the same.

This distinction explains a puzzle. When growth slows and the expansion of professional jobs levels off, absolute mobility falls, and people who do no better than their parents feel, reasonably enough, that something has closed. They often conclude that society has become less fair. Imagine a town where a mill employed one generation and new offices employed the next. The children did better than their parents without anyone being pushed aside, and the town experienced this as openness. When the offices stop hiring, the grandchildren find that the climb has ended. Yet on the measures that track their position against the children of the office managers, the chances may be much as they were: what has disappeared is not openness but the rising tide that once let a whole generation move up without anyone having to move down. The sense of closure is real; its diagnosis is frequently mistaken.

The distinction also exposes an awkwardness that politicians prefer to leave unspoken. Absolute mobility can, in principle, be enjoyed by everyone at once. Relative mobility cannot. If positions are ranked, then for one family to climb another must fall, and a serious commitment to relative mobility is therefore a commitment to downward mobility for some children of the comfortable. It is not surprising that the comfortable resist it, often without any sense of doing so, through the ordinary devices of private tuition, a well-placed word, or the purchase of a house near the right school. Each of these looks like ordinary care for one's own children; together they amount to a defence of position.

None of this makes one kind of mobility the real one. Absolute mobility answers a question about material progress: are people living better than their parents did? Relative mobility answers a question about fairness: does birth still decide where one ends up? Both questions matter, and neither is easy to answer with confidence, since incomes fluctuate and occupations change their meaning across generations. But a society that wants more of the second kind should be honest that it cannot be had at no one's expense, and a society that mourns the loss of the first should not mistake a slower economy for a more rigid one.

Ask a collector why she keeps buying stamps, coins or toy cars long after there is any room left to display them, and the answer is rarely about the objects themselves. More often it concerns a gap: the one issue missing from a run, the single variant that would finish a set. Collecting, on this view, is less a love of things than a love of completion. The individual stamp matters because of the place it occupies in a series, and its value to the collector rises sharply as the series nears its end, often far beyond anything a buyer outside the hobby would think of paying.

Manufacturers learned long ago to exploit this. A cereal box that contains one of twelve plastic figures, a sticker album with a few deliberately scarce pages, a line of trading cards issued in waves: each turns an ordinary purchase into a step towards a whole that the buyer did not know he wanted until he was shown its outline. The empty album is the real product. Once its spaces are printed, every blank becomes a small reproach, and the purchase that fills it brings a satisfaction out of all proportion to what was bought.

It would be easy to conclude that collecting is simply a manufactured compulsion, a weakness that the market has learned to farm. That conclusion goes too far. Many of the most devoted collectors pursue series that no company ever designed: the railway timetables of a vanished line, the matchboxes of hotels that have since closed, the scattered editions of a minor poet. Here it is the collector who defines the set, deciding what counts as belonging to it and therefore what counts as missing. Such collecting is a way of ordering the world, of drawing a boundary around a scattered field and making it intelligible. Many museums began, in part, as exactly this kind of private project.

The difference between the two kinds of collecting is not the passion involved, which can be equally intense, but who holds the map. When the series is invented by a seller, completion is a target set by someone else, and the finish line is often moved just as it comes into view, with a new wave or a special edition. When the collector draws the map, completion is a judgement she makes for herself, and the pleasure lies as much in the defining as in the finding. The danger of the commercial version is not that it creates desire, since all collecting does that, but that it quietly takes the act of definition away from the person doing the collecting.

A curious feature of the market for retro goods is how many of their buyers are too young to remember the originals. Record players styled like those of the nineteen-sixties, cameras that imitate the look of early film models, soft drinks reissued in the bottles of half a century ago: these sell briskly to people for whom the period they evoke is something seen in old films rather than lived. Whatever such buyers are nostalgic for, it cannot be their own past, and any explanation of the trade has to begin from that awkward fact.

The usual explanation is that they are being fooled, that advertisers have invented a golden age and sold it back to a generation with no means of checking. There is something in this, but it misreads what the buyer is after. Nostalgia has always been less a memory than a mood, a way of expressing dissatisfaction with the present by furnishing it with an imagined contrast against which its deficiencies become visible. The retro object does not claim to restore the past; it offers a small, ownable piece of a world that seems slower, sturdier and easier to understand than the one its owner actually lives in. That such a world never quite existed matters less than the fact that the feeling it answers is real.

What is striking is how carefully the past is edited in the process. The reissued record player has a socket for a phone; the vintage-look camera stores its pictures on a memory card and adds the scratches digitally. The inconveniences that made the originals what they were, the waiting, the expense, the fragility, are removed, and only the surface is kept. Retro design is in this sense the opposite of preservation: it keeps the look of an earlier time while discarding the conditions that gave the look its meaning.

None of this need be a cause for scorn. Some revived products are genuinely better made than the disposable goods they replaced, and a taste for the durable, in an economy organised around rapid obsolescence, is not foolish. But it is worth being clear about what is being bought. The buyer of a retro radio is not recovering a lost way of life; he is purchasing a token of his unease with his own, and the market is happy to supply as many such tokens as that unease will bear.

Few words are used more freely by restaurant reviewers than 'authentic', and few are applied more selectively. A dish is praised as authentic when it is served in a cramped room, by a cook who speaks the diner's language haltingly, at a price that suggests nobody is getting rich. The same dish, served with tablecloths and a wine list, is suspected of having been tamed. Authenticity, in this usage, is less a property of the food than of the scene around it, and the scene is one that the visiting diner has come to consume.

Consider a hypothetical family that opens a restaurant serving the cooking of its home region in a city several thousand kilometres away. From the start, the cooks make changes. Some ingredients cannot be found and are replaced with local ones; some dishes are too laborious for a kitchen that must turn out fifty plates a night; others are sweetened or softened because the first customers sent them back. Within a generation the menu has become something that exists nowhere else: neither the food of the home region nor the food of the new city, but the food of the people who moved between them.

Purists treat this history as a decline, and they reward the restaurants that seem to have resisted it, the ones with a second menu in the home language that outsiders must know to ask for. Yet even that second menu has passed through the same kitchen, the same suppliers and the same compromises. To call it the real food and the first menu a betrayal is to take one stage of a continuous adaptation and freeze it as the original. More troubling, the judgement is usually made by people with no stake in the tradition, who are in effect asking immigrant cooks to perform their own foreignness for an audience's satisfaction.

None of this means that every adaptation is innocent. Cooks under commercial pressure sometimes strip a cuisine of everything difficult until it is recognisable only by name, and something real is lost when that happens. But the loss is better described as a narrowing of what the cooks themselves are free to make than as a departure from a fixed original. The more useful question to ask of a restaurant is not whether its food matches some imagined source, but whether the people cooking it have the room to cook what they think is good.

An old explanation of fashion holds that it trickles down. Those at the top of a society adopt a new style to mark themselves off; those just below copy it, hoping to borrow some of the prestige; and once the style has spread far enough to lose its power to distinguish, the people at the top abandon it for something else. Fashion, on this account, is a chase that can never end, because the very success of imitation destroys the value of what is imitated.

The obvious objection is that much of what is worn today did not begin at the top. Jeans were work clothes; the hooded sweatshirt was athletic gear; a great many styles that now appear on expensive runways were first worn by the young, the poor or the marginal, and were adopted by designers only later. If fashion so often bubbles up rather than trickling down, the old theory seems simply mistaken about the direction in which influence travels, and with it, one might suppose, about everything that followed from that direction.

But direction was never the heart of the theory. Its real claim was that fashion is driven by a double motive, the wish to belong and the wish to stand apart, and that the two cannot both be satisfied for long. That claim survives the reversal untouched. When a luxury house borrows the clothing of a street subculture, it is not abandoning distinction but finding a new source of it: the style carries a borrowed credibility that a conventional luxury garment lacks, and wearing it signals a knowingness that cannot be acquired simply by paying more. The members of the subculture, for their part, frequently drop the style once it appears in expensive shops, for precisely the reason the old theory would predict.

What has changed is the speed. When copies of a new look can reach inexpensive shops within weeks, visible novelty becomes a weak marker of status, since it is available to almost anyone almost at once. Increasingly, those who most wish to stand apart do so not by wearing what is new but by having had it first: by access to small releases that sell out in minutes, by acquaintance with designers before they are celebrated, by knowing what is coming rather than displaying what has arrived. The chase continues; it has simply moved to ground where the pursuers find it harder to follow.

When a global fast-food chain enters a new country, the first thing commentators examine is its menu. If the chain serves the same burger it serves at home, critics see cultural flattening, the erosion of local tastes by a single corporate palate. If it introduces a spiced vegetable patty or a rice dish for the local market, its defenders announce that globalisation, far from erasing difference, accommodates it. Both sides agree, without ever saying so, that the menu is where the question of cultural influence will be settled.

That assumption deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives. A menu is the part of a chain that is easiest to change and, for that very reason, the part that tells us least. What the chain actually exports is a format: a way of organising food, labour and time. The counter at which one orders without a waiter, the fixed price displayed in advance, the promise that the meal will taste the same today as it did last month, the kitchen run like an assembly line by staff who can be trained in days: these travel intact, and they carry assumptions about efficiency and predictability that are far more foreign to many food cultures than any particular ingredient. A spiced patty served through such a system is a local flavour in a global grammar.

Yet it would be wrong to infer that the format simply imposes its meanings wherever it goes, for customers bring meanings of their own. In some places a visit to a chain restaurant has been, at least for a time, a special occasion rather than a convenience: a clean, cool and respectable room in which a family can celebrate a birthday, or two young people can meet without attracting comment. The format was designed for speed, but the customers linger. They take a system built to minimise the time spent at the table and turn it into a place for spending time.

The interesting story, then, has three layers rather than one. The format is global and changes slowly; the meanings attached to it are local and can diverge sharply from what its designers intended; the menu sits between them, adjusted constantly in response to both. To read cultural influence from the menu alone is like judging the spread of a language by the loanwords it has picked up, while ignoring both its grammar and the uses to which its new speakers put it.

It has become common to describe the fashion for owning less, the bare room, the small wardrobe of good clothes, the ritual of discarding whatever does not earn its place, as a revolt against consumer society. Its advocates present it as a turn from having to being; its critics, when they bother, dismiss it as one more passing style. Both responses take the movement at its word, as a stance towards consumption. Neither asks what owning little communicates, which is a different question from what it intends.

At the end of the nineteenth century the economist Thorstein Veblen described how the wealthy display their standing through conspicuous consumption, spending visibly on what serves display rather than use. The sparse interior seems at first to invert his picture. Yet emptiness has its own costs, and they are not evenly distributed. A bare floor in a crowded city is a quantity of expensive space left deliberately unfilled. A wardrobe of a dozen garments presupposes that each is durable enough, and the owner's life predictable enough, to require no more. Above all, the confident discarding of objects depends on the assurance that they can be replaced when needed. Households that live close to scarcity keep things, the spare part, the old jar, the coat a size too large, because they cannot count on being able to buy them again; for them, accumulation is a form of insurance. To throw away freely is to display that one has no need of such insurance.

It does not follow that those who embrace minimalism are hypocrites whose real aim is to impress. That objection confuses motive with function. A practice can be sincerely chosen for its own reasons, calm, order, a dislike of waste, and still operate socially as a signal that its practitioners neither chose nor want. Many who pare down their possessions are doing exactly what they say. The point is rather that the meaning of a pattern of consumption is not fixed by the consumer's intention; it is fixed by what the pattern makes legible to others, and what restraint makes legible, in a society where most people cannot afford its preconditions, is security.

The more consequential lesson concerns the hope of opting out. If even refusal can be read as a position within the system of display, then consuming less is not, by itself, an exit from that system; it is a move within it, and often one available only to those already well placed. This is not an argument for consuming more. It is an argument for suspicion towards any claim that a change in private taste can amount to a social critique, since the field of taste has repeatedly proved able to absorb its own refusals and return them as distinctions.

Marketers like to say that the strongest brands have communities rather than customers. They point to the owners of a particular make of motorcycle who ride together on weekends and have its emblem tattooed on their arms, to the users of a computer maker's products who queue overnight for a new model and argue online with the users of its rivals, and to the enthusiasts who restore and exhibit a discontinued car long after its manufacturer has stopped caring about it. Some commentators go further and call such groups tribes, or even congregations, complete with rituals, myths and heretics, as though buying a product were the first step in a conversion.

The comparison is not empty. Members of these groups share a body of lore, the founding story, the legendary models, the right and wrong ways to use the product, and newcomers learn it much as initiates learn a tradition. They define themselves partly against outsiders, often the owners of a rival brand, and they police their own boundaries, distinguishing the real enthusiast from the person who has merely bought the thing. Most strikingly, they develop a sense of ownership over the brand that is not legal but moral. When a company alters a celebrated design or moves production to another country, its most loyal customers frequently respond not as disappointed consumers but as betrayed members, as though something that belonged to them had been taken without their consent.

Yet the tribal analogy conceals as much as it reveals. Membership of a tribe is not usually something one buys, and leaving it is not usually as easy as buying something else. A brand community, by contrast, is entered through a purchase and can be abandoned at the price of another. More important, the symbols around which it gathers are the legal property of a firm whose interests are not the members' interests. The firm can redesign the emblem, discontinue the product or sell the brand to a competitor, and the members, however devoted, have no formal say in any of it. A tribe whose totem could be sold at auction would be a strange tribe indeed.

It is tempting to resolve the tension by declaring one side the truth: either the community is an illusion manufactured by advertising, or the commercial setting is incidental and the solidarity is all that matters. Neither will do. The solidarity is real; people form friendships, give one another practical help and find meaning in these groups, and much of this happens without the company's involvement or even against its wishes. But the solidarity is organised around something its members do not control, and that fact shapes it. The anger that follows an unpopular redesign is the anger of people discovering, often for the first time, the limits of an ownership they had felt but never possessed.
