The partner, uncertain whether reckless conduct will be supported, has reason to be careful; the adversary, uncertain whether aggression will be resisted, has reason to be careful too. Consider a hypothetical great power that promises to defend an island partner but declines to say whether the promise covers a dispute the partner itself might start. The silence is not an oversight. It is the policy.

The balance between the two fears is rarely the same for both members. A small state facing a powerful neighbour usually fears abandonment far more than entrapment, since it has few other places to turn, while its larger protector, with interests elsewhere and wars it would prefer not to fight, tends to fear entrapment more. Much of the friction within alliances that look harmonious from outside comes from this asymmetry: the junior partner asks for firmer pledges, the senior partner resists giving them, and each suspects the other of bad faith when each is in fact responding sensibly to its own position.

Ambiguity is not free, however. Its value depends on each party reading the uncertainty in the way the protecting power intends, and there is no guarantee that they will. An adversary may conclude that a vague commitment is a hollow one and test it, discovering too late that it was real. A partner may conclude that it will be supported whatever it does, because it cannot imagine its patron allowing it to fall. Deliberate vagueness thus trades the visible risks of a firm commitment for the hidden risk of miscalculation, which is the more dangerous for being invisible until a crisis reveals it. The strategy rewards a protecting power that understands both its partner and its adversary well, and punishes one that merely hopes it does.

It is tempting to picture the great periodic fair of the pre-modern world as a market that happened to be very large. Merchants arrived with bales of cloth, casks and livestock; buyers came from the surrounding districts; for a few weeks a meadow outside a town became a crowded street of stalls, and then it emptied again until the following year. On this view the fair existed because trade was too thin to support permanent shops, and it faded once towns grew large enough to sustain them. The account is not wrong, but it describes the visible part of the fair and mistakes it for the whole.

Much of what happened at a fair left no bales behind. Merchants who met there once or twice a year used the occasion to settle accounts that had been running since the previous meeting, cancelling what one owed another against what a third owed the first, so that relatively little coin had to change hands. Promises to pay at the next fair circulated as a kind of credit, and their value rested on the expectation that everyone would return. A fair, in this sense, was a calendar as much as a place: it fixed the dates on which obligations fell due and gave distant traders a reason to keep faith with one another. A merchant who failed to appear risked more than a season's sales; he risked his standing with every partner who had expected to meet him.

It was also a clearing house for news. Prices in distant regions, the solvency of a trading house, a harvest failure, rumours of war: all of this travelled with the people who came, and a merchant who stayed at home was not only missing customers but trading blind. The gossip of the fair was not idle. It was the means by which a scattered commercial world kept a rough common picture of itself. A thinly attended fair was therefore a loss twice over, since the absence of buyers was also an absence of reports, and those who controlled the best information often profited more than those who carried the most goods.

Seen this way, the decline of the great fairs looks different. Permanent shops certainly took over much of the retail business, but the deeper loss was of the fair's other functions, which passed to institutions that did not depend on bodily presence: banks that kept accounts all year round, regular postal services and, later, printed lists of prices. None of this means that fairs ceased to matter as markets; many survived for centuries as places to buy animals or household goods. What they lost was their role as the hinge on which a whole year of commerce turned, and that role had never been visible in the stalls.

Few ideas feel more natural than the distinction between home and work. We leave one for the other in the morning and return in the evening, and much of our moral vocabulary depends on the contrast: home is where we are valued for who we are, work where we are valued for what we produce. Yet for most of recorded history, in most agrarian and artisan societies, the distinction would have puzzled the people who lived in households. The house was where the work was done.

Consider a weaver's dwelling in a pre-industrial town, or a farmstead in the countryside. The looms or the dairy stood beside the hearth, and the people who ate at the table included not only parents and children but apprentices, servants and labourers who lived under the same roof and the same authority. The head of the household was at once father, employer and, in a limited sense, magistrate, answerable to the wider community for the conduct of everyone in his charge. Records of such households often used the word family to mean this whole working unit, and a reader who assumes that it meant blood relatives alone will misread them badly. Children worked as soon as they were able, carding wool or minding animals, and learning a trade was part of growing up in the house rather than something that began when a child left it.

None of this should be romanticised. The working household was a hierarchy, often a harsh one, in which servants could be beaten and wives had little legal standing apart from their husbands. Nor was it universal: the poorest labourers, who owned no tools and rented a single room, had little to bring home but their wages. The point is not that the old arrangement was better, but that it was different in kind, and that the difference matters for how we read later history.

When production moved into workshops, mills and offices, the household did not simply lose its economic role; it acquired a new meaning. Freed of the loom and the dairy, it could be imagined as a private refuge, governed by affection rather than discipline, and this ideal was then projected backwards as if it had always existed. The ideal was real enough for those who could afford it, but it was an ideal, not a description of the past. Laments about the decline of the family often rest on that projection. What changed over these centuries was less the strength of family feeling than the range of tasks the household was expected to perform, and a history that confuses the two will find decline where there was mainly transformation.

Before the railways, every town kept its own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over the local meridian, and because the sun appears to move westward, a town some distance to the west of another reached its noon a few minutes later. Nobody minded, because nothing travelled fast enough for the difference to matter; a coach journey of several days absorbed a quarter of an hour's discrepancy without anyone noticing it. The railway changed this, and the standard account of what followed is a story of practical necessity. Timetables drawn up in dozens of local times produced confusion and, on single-track lines, danger, so the companies adopted a single reference time and governments eventually followed.

The account is true as far as it goes, but it treats the change as a technical adjustment, like agreeing on a common gauge for the rails. It was more than that. Local time had been public in a literal sense: anyone could see the sun, and the clock on the church or the town hall was set by an observation that a curious citizen could, in principle, check. Standard time was set somewhere else, by astronomers in a distant observatory, and reached the town along a telegraph wire. The hour on the station clock was no longer a fact about the place where one stood but a decision taken elsewhere and transmitted to it.

This helps to explain a resistance that is usually remembered only as quaint. Some towns kept two clocks running side by side, or fitted a public dial with an extra hand so that the sun's reckoning and the railway's could be read together, and some local worthies denounced the new hour as an imposition. It is easy to read them as people clinging to habit in the face of progress. But they had grasped something that the language of convenience obscures: a shared standard is also a centre of authority, and agreeing to it means accepting that the definition of an everyday reality will henceforth be made by people one will never meet.

None of this is a case against standard time, whose benefits were real and soon taken for granted. Few people today would wish to return to a world in which the hour changed as one rode across a county. The argument is rather that the history of timekeeping is also a history of who is entitled to say what time it is, and that this question did not disappear when it was settled. Each later standard, from time signals broadcast by radio to the clocks that now synchronise themselves silently over networks, has extended the same arrangement, and each has made it a little harder to notice.

A familiar story about the history of reading holds that, for most of antiquity and much of the Middle Ages, people could read only aloud, and that silent reading was a late discovery which transformed the inner life of the West. The story is usually supported by a much-cited anecdote in which an ancient writer records his surprise at finding a learned man reading without voicing the words. It is a vivid story, and like many vivid stories it has been asked to carry more weight than it can bear.

Scholars who have examined the evidence more closely have found a fair number of ancient readers who read silently, and they point out that surprise at a practice is not evidence that it was unknown, only that it was unusual where it was observed. The more defensible claim is not that silent reading was impossible but that it was not the default. Texts were frequently written without spaces between words, which made voicing them a useful aid, and, more importantly, reading was often a social act. A household, a monastery or a circle of friends would gather while one person read to the others; a book was something one heard as often as something one saw.

What changed, then, was less the technique than the setting. As books became cheaper and more numerous, as spaces between words and other aids to the eye became standard, and as people of moderate means came to have rooms, or at least corners, to themselves, reading moved from the common table to the private chair. Freed from the pace of the voice, the eye could also move faster, and a reader alone could get through more books, and more kinds of book, than a listener ever could. The shift was gradual and uneven, and reading aloud never vanished. Families read novels to one another well into the age of print, and workers in some trades paid a colleague to read to them while they laboured.

Even corrected in this way, the history matters. A text that is heard together is interpreted together: listeners react, object and argue, and the meaning of a passage is settled, if it is settled at all, in company. A text read alone is answerable only to its reader, who may skip, reread or linger over a sentence that no one else will ever know about. It would be too much to say that private reading created the private self. It would be too little to say that it changed nothing about how people came to think of their thoughts as their own.

It is easy to write the history of urban smell as a simple story of progress. Pre-modern cities stank of sewage, tanneries, slaughterhouses and unwashed bodies; reformers built drains and water supplies; the stench retreated. Every part of this is true, and anyone inclined to romanticise the crowded streets of earlier centuries should be reminded of it. But the story assumes that the nose is a constant instrument, registering the same smells with the same disgust in every age, and that assumption does not survive a reading of the sources.

Residents of older towns certainly complained about smells, but their complaints were selective. Odours that later generations would find unbearable, such as the smell of a dung heap beside a house, were often accepted as part of ordinary life, while others, associated with particular trades or with neighbours who were disliked, drew sustained protest. What made a smell intolerable depended less on its strength than on what it was thought to mean. And from the late eighteenth century onwards, in much of Europe, smells came to carry a very specific meaning with new urgency. Under the old theory that disease spread through foul air, now taken up by physicians and reformers, a bad smell was not merely unpleasant; it was a warning, perhaps even the danger itself.

The theory was wrong, but it was productive. Because it identified smell with sickness, it gave reformers a reason, and a sense of urgency, to remove the sources of smell, and many of the measures they took, from covered sewers to the regular removal of refuse, did reduce disease, though for reasons they did not understand. A mistaken idea about how illness spread thus helped to justify works whose real benefit lay elsewhere. When the germ theory displaced it, smell lost its medical authority; it did not lose its power.

Freed from medicine, the vocabulary of smell attached itself more firmly to persons. Middle-class households that had learned to fear foul air now learned to fear the odour of the poor, the newcomer and the manual worker, and the judgement passed easily from bodies to character. The cleaner cities became, the more a lingering smell could serve as a mark of social distance. This is why a history of smell cannot be only a history of drains; it must also be a history of who was allowed to call whom offensive, and of how a sense that seems the most immediate of all has always been schooled.

The phrase most people use for the overland trade between China and the Mediterranean is a nineteenth-century coinage, and it carries a picture with it: a single road, and on it long caravans of camels carrying silk from one end of Asia to the other. The picture is attractive and largely misleading, for very few goods, and fewer merchants, made the whole journey. What existed instead was a chain of overlapping regional circuits, each worked by traders who knew their own stretch of desert, mountain and oasis intimately and knew little of what lay beyond it.

In such a system a bale of silk might change hands many times between the place where it was woven and the place where it was worn. Each exchange added a margin, which is one reason why goods from the far end of the chain were so costly, and each was made between people who had reason to trust one another because they met repeatedly. The merchant in an oasis town did not need to know the distant market where the silk would end up; he needed to know the caravan leader who would buy it from him and the one who had sold it to him. Long-distance trade, on this view, was an accumulation of short-distance relationships.

This has consequences that the romantic image hides. First, the system was more resilient than a single road would have been: when war or banditry closed one segment, goods could often find a way round it through neighbouring circuits, and trade slowed rather than stopped. Second, knowledge travelled poorly along the chain even when goods travelled well, and buyers at one end often held fanciful beliefs about where their luxuries came from, because no one they dealt with had seen the source. Third, those who profited most were frequently neither the producers nor the final buyers but the middlemen at the junctions where circuits met, whose cities grew rich on the margin.

It would be wrong to conclude that no one crossed the whole distance. Pilgrims, envoys and a few adventurous traders made extraordinary journeys, and some left accounts that are still read. But these travellers are remembered precisely because they were exceptional, and their fame has shaped our picture of the ordinary trade far more than the ordinary trade itself, which left few memoirs. A history built on the exceptional journey will see a road; a history built on the routine exchange will see a web, and it is the web that explains how the trade actually worked.

Two stories are commonly told about the measures that late medieval and early modern cities took against plague. In the first, the health boards of the Italian city-states, with their isolation hospitals, their passes for travellers and their periods of enforced seclusion for ships and households, are the ancestors of modern public health: rational officials confronting an epidemic with the tools of an emerging state. In the second, the same measures are a chapter in the history of coercion, in which the sick and the poor were locked away, their goods burned and their livelihoods destroyed by authorities who feared contagion more than they valued the people who might carry it. Each story can be furnished with abundant evidence. What both tend to overlook is that the measures could work only with a degree of cooperation that neither officials nor force could guarantee.

Quarantine depends, at its most basic, on information. A household must be shut up before the disease spreads from it, which means that someone must report the first case, and the people best placed to report it are the members of the household themselves, together with their neighbours. Every one of them had reasons to stay silent. A shut household lost its income; its members might be removed to an isolation hospital from which many did not return; its bedding and clothing might be burned. Families that concealed a death, bribed an inspector or slipped out of the city before the doors were sealed were not simply defying authority. They were responding sensibly to the costs that reporting imposed on them, and neighbours who might have informed on them faced, in their turn, the prospect of being shut up beside them.

Where the measures had any success, it seems to have been because authorities, sometimes reluctantly, took on obligations in return. Some cities fed shut-up households at public expense, paid compensation for goods that had been destroyed, or relied on clergy and charitable brotherhoods to bring food, relief and reassurance to the confined. Such provisions were expensive and often inadequate, and the surviving records do not allow us to say with any confidence how much difference they made to mortality. But they changed the calculation facing a family that suspected illness, and the complaints of officials who lacked the means to provide them suggest that concealment rose when relief failed.

It might be objected that this underrates force. Cities did post guards, punish concealment severely and, on occasion, execute those who broke quarantine. Yet harshness had a cost that its advocates rarely counted: the more frightening the consequences of discovery, the stronger the incentive not to be discovered, and an epidemic that goes underground is harder, not easier, to contain. A household that expected to be sealed in with its sick, guarded and fined had every reason to wait, to hide the first symptoms and to hope, and each day of waiting was a day in which the disease could travel. Severity could secure compliance from those already known to the authorities; it could not make the unknown come forward.

The lesson is not that plague regulations were humane, for many plainly were not, nor that they were futile. It is that measures which depend on people revealing something about themselves are bargains, whether or not those who impose them think of them in that way, and the point is not confined to plague. Their success is limited by what disclosure costs the person who discloses, and an authority that wishes to know must first make knowing bearable.

The usual history of artificial light is a history of liberation. For most of human existence the coming of darkness set a hard limit on what people could do: work stopped, travel became dangerous, and the town shrank to the circle of the hearth. Oil lamps, then gas, then electricity pushed that limit back, until the night became little more than a dimmer continuation of the day, available for labour, commerce and pleasure. The story is not false. But it treats the night as an absence, a gap waiting to be filled, and in doing so it forgets that the pre-industrial night was a time with its own rules, its own inhabitants and its own uses.

In many European towns before public lighting, the night was governed differently from the day. Gates were shut, curfew bells were rung, and anyone abroad after dark without a lantern and a good reason might be stopped and questioned by the watch. The respectable stayed indoors; the streets belonged to watchmen, to those whose trades required darkness, to lovers, thieves and the young. This was not freedom in any simple sense, for the dark was also where violence went unpunished. It was, however, a separate jurisdiction, a time in which the authority of the day ran only weakly and in which much that could not be done openly was done.

The first systematic street lighting was installed less to lengthen the working day than to bring this jurisdiction under control. Its sponsors spoke of safety, and they meant it, but safety meant visibility, and visibility meant that the street at midnight could be watched and policed by the same standards as the street at noon. Accounts from several cities describe crowds breaking lamps in moments of unrest, and it is tempting to dismiss this as mere vandalism. It is more plausibly read as a recognition, however inarticulate, that the lamps were an extension of an authority that the crowd had reason to resist. The lamp, in this sense, was an instrument of the day carried into the night.

Yet to replace the story of liberation with a story of discipline would be to make the opposite mistake. Lighting did extend surveillance, but it also opened the night to people who had been effectively shut out of it. Respectable women, families, the elderly and the cautious could now walk to a theatre or a shop after dark, and whole new forms of sociability, from evening promenades to late markets, grew up in the lit streets. For many people the expansion of the policed night was, quite simply, an expansion of their world. The same lamp that exposed the thief to the watch made the street usable for the seamstress walking home.

What lighting did, then, was neither simply to free the night nor simply to conquer it, but to abolish it as a distinct social time. The day's rules, the day's people and the day's activities spread into hours that had once belonged to others. Those who had held the dark, the watchmen, the night trades and the young, lost not their lives but their hours, and the newcomers to the lit street rarely noticed what had been displaced. Whether we count this as a gain or a loss depends largely on whom we imagine walking the street, and it is precisely the habit of imagining only one kind of walker that has made the history of light so easy to tell and so hard to tell well.

Imagine a cinema that sells popcorn in two sizes: a small tub at a modest price and a large tub at nearly twice that. Most customers buy the small one, until the cinema adds a third option, a medium tub priced only slightly below the large. Hardly anyone buys the medium, yet sales of the large tub rise sharply, so that the new option has done its work without ever being chosen. It exists to make the large tub look like a bargain, and in many such cases it succeeds; marketers call such an option a decoy, and the pattern it produces turns up often enough, with magazine subscriptions, holiday packages and software plans as well as snacks, to deserve a more careful explanation than the claim that customers are easily fooled.

The standard account of choice in economics assumes that a person arrives at a shop with a ranking of the available goods already settled, and that the shop merely reveals it. On that account the decoy should be inert: if I prefer the small tub to the large one, the arrival of a medium tub that I do not want should leave my ranking of the other two untouched. What the decoy suggests instead is that many preferences are not retrieved but assembled on the spot, from the comparisons the menu makes easy. The medium tub is easy to compare with the large, being the same product at almost the same price with visibly less popcorn, whereas the comparison between the small and the large, which requires trading money against quantity, is considerably harder. Consequently, people lean on the easy comparison and let it settle the hard one.

It would be a mistake to conclude that preferences are endlessly pliable, for the effect is strongest when buyers are unsure what they want and have little experience of the product; a regular who knows exactly how much popcorn she can eat is rarely moved. It also weakens when the decoy is so plainly inferior that customers notice the trick, and resentment at being steered can push them the other way. These limits matter, because they show that the decoy exploits a gap in knowledge rather than a defect of reason: constructing a preference out of whatever comparisons are available is a perfectly sensible strategy for someone who lacks better information.

The more interesting lesson concerns the menu itself. We usually treat the set of options as neutral background and the decision as the thing to be explained, but the decoy shows that the background is part of the decision. Whoever arranges the options, whether a cinema, a software firm setting its subscription tiers or a restaurant pricing its wine list, is not merely displaying choices but helping to form them. This does not make every arrangement sinister, since some arrangement is unavoidable, but it does mean that the question of what people chose cannot be separated from the question of what they were shown.

Suppose a dozen firms bid for the right to drill in a tract of seabed whose reserves nobody knows, and that each firm commissions its own survey, and the surveys, being estimates, scatter around the true figure, some too high and some too low. If each firm bids what its own survey says the tract is worth, the contract will go to the firm whose survey was most optimistic, so that winning, in other words, is itself evidence of having overestimated. The firm that celebrates its victory has been selected for its error, and it will on average pay more than the tract is worth. This phenomenon is the winner's curse, and the striking thing about it is that no bidder needs to be foolish for it to occur, since each estimate may be honest and, taken alone, unbiased.

The remedy, in principle, is simple: a bidder should ask not what the tract is worth given its survey, but what it is worth given its survey and given that it has won. The second question yields a lower number, and a bidder who answers it will shade its bid below the raw estimate, more sharply the more rivals there are, since the highest of many estimates is more likely to be inflated than the highest of a few. Shading of this kind is not timidity but the correct response to a feature of the situation that the unconditioned estimate ignores.

A natural objection is that the curse should vanish with experience, because firms that overpay will lose money, notice and adjust, while those that do not will be driven from the market. There is truth in this, and seasoned bidders in many settings do shade their bids, but the learning is slower than the objection supposes. The outcome of any single auction is noisy, since a tract that disappoints may simply have been unlucky. Worse, the firms that lose never discover what the prize was really worth, so the information that would correct everyone's estimates is gathered only by the winners, and slowly. A lesson that must be extracted from a few expensive and ambiguous victories is not quickly learned.

For this reason the design of an auction matters as much as the wisdom of its participants. Formats in which bids are revealed as they rise allow each bidder to watch rivals drop out and to infer something about their estimates, and a bidder who can see how far others are willing to go has less reason to fear that its own enthusiasm is an error. Sealed bids, by contrast, leave each participant alone with a single survey and its uncorrected optimism. The point is not that one format is always superior, since open bidding has weaknesses of its own, among them the ease with which rivals can signal to one another, but that the curse is a property of the information structure, and so can be eased by changing that structure rather than by exhorting bidders to be cleverer.

A great deal of advertising tells the viewer almost nothing. A television spot in which a famous athlete drinks a soft drink on a beach conveys no fact about the drink's price, ingredients or taste that a sceptical viewer could check, and critics of advertising have long drawn what seems the obvious conclusion: if the message carries no information, the money spent on it is either wasted or devoted to manipulation, persuading people to want things by associating them with glamour. The conclusion is natural, but it rests on the assumption that whatever an advertisement communicates must be contained in what it says or shows, and that assumption is open to question.

Consider the matter from the firm's side. A company launching a product that is cheap to try, such as a breakfast cereal or a shampoo, makes its money not from the first purchase but from the repeat purchases of customers who liked it. A firm confident that its product is good therefore expects a long stream of returns from anyone it persuades to try it once, whereas a firm that knows its product is mediocre expects most of those who try it never to return. Lavish advertising is accordingly worth far more to the first firm than to the second, and a consumer who sees a product advertised extravagantly may reasonably infer that its maker is wagering on repeat business. On this view the expense of the advertisement is itself the message, and the athlete and the beach matter chiefly because everyone can see that they cost a fortune.

The argument has real force, but its reach is limited. It applies most clearly to what economists call experience goods, whose quality can be judged only after use, and only where repeat purchase is likely; a firm selling something that people buy once in a lifetime gains little from the signal, because satisfied customers will not return in any case. For goods whose qualities can be inspected before purchase, such as the dimensions of a table or the fare for a train journey, advertising informs directly and requires no signalling story at all. Nor does the argument show that every extravagant campaign is a reliable signal, since a firm may overspend from vanity or miscalculation, and imitators may learn to mimic the outward appearance of expense more cheaply than it seems.

A familiar objection is that ordinary consumers do not reason in this way, since nobody watching a soft drink advertisement contemplates the economics of repeat purchase. The objection misunderstands what the argument requires. Consumers need not reconstruct the logic; it is enough that they follow a rule of thumb, such as trusting brands they have heard of, and that the rule tends, on the whole, to reward them. The signalling account does not vindicate advertising, and it leaves the question of manipulation entirely open. What it does establish is that an advertisement without content is not, for that reason alone, an advertisement without meaning.

Defenders of nudging, the practice of steering choices by altering how options are presented rather than by forbidding or taxing any of them, have a ready answer to the charge that it is manipulative. Someone, they point out, must decide which option on a form is pre-selected, which dish stands at eye level in a canteen and which paragraph of a letter comes first; since there is no presentation without some arrangement, the choice is not between influencing people and leaving them alone but between influencing them thoughtfully and influencing them carelessly. The argument is sound as far as it goes, and critics who speak as though an unarranged menu were available are attacking a position nobody holds.

Yet the argument from inevitability answers a weaker objection than the one that matters. What troubles the more careful critics is not that choice architects influence us, which is unavoidable, but that many of the most effective nudges work precisely to the extent that they go unnoticed. A default enrolment in a savings scheme succeeds partly because inertia keeps people where they were placed, but also because many never register that a decision was made on their behalf; a smaller plate reduces consumption chiefly when diners do not reflect that they have been served less. Influence of this sort does not engage the faculties by which people govern themselves, but routes around them.

One way to sharpen the worry is to ask whether a given nudge would survive disclosure. Suppose a canteen posted a notice explaining that fruit had been placed at the front because the management wanted employees to eat more of it. If the arrangement continues to work, its power did not depend on concealment, and it begins to look less like manipulation than like a reminder. If it stops working once explained, that is evidence that it relied on a gap between what people were doing and what they understood themselves to be doing, and an institution that relies on such gaps owes its public a justification that it cannot easily give in public.

The test is not decisive in every case, and it should not be mistaken for a general condemnation. Some nudges would plainly survive disclosure: a letter telling people that most of their neighbours pay their taxes on time would plausibly work whether or not recipients knew why it had been sent, since the information is itself the influence. Others might fail it for innocent reasons, because a disclosure can itself distract, or can provoke a reflexive contrariness that has nothing to do with the merits of the option. What the test accomplishes is to shift the debate from an unanswerable question, whether influence is present, to an answerable one, whether the influence could be avowed. That shift concedes to the defenders everything their best argument actually establishes, and withholds from them only what it never established.

When information was scarce, the economic problem it posed was one of supply: how to print, carry and store enough of it for the people who wanted it. That problem has largely been solved, and its solution has exposed another. The abundance of material has made scarce the one resource that every piece of it requires, namely the attention of those who are meant to receive it. Every article, message and video competes for the same limited hours of the same limited minds, and while the cost of producing one more piece of content has fallen almost to nothing, the supply of attention has not grown at all.

This shift explains a feature of modern commerce that once seemed puzzling, the enormous number of services offered at no charge. A search engine, a social network or a mobile game that costs its user nothing is not a gift; it is paid for with attention, which the provider gathers and resells to advertisers, so that the user is less a customer than a supplier of the commodity being traded. Described in this way, the arrangement is not obviously unfair. Many people would gladly exchange a few seconds of distraction for a useful map or a convenient way of keeping in touch with distant friends, and for them the bargain may be a good one.

The difficulty lies elsewhere, in the fact that the price is never stated. When a product is sold for money, its price is a number that buyers can compare across sellers, and the comparison disciplines firms, since a shop that charges too much loses its customers to a cheaper rival. Attention has no such number attached to it. A user cannot easily tell whether one free application takes ten minutes of her day or two hours, still less whether a rival would take less, and so the competitive pressure that keeps money prices in check operates feebly, if at all. Firms competing for attention are therefore rewarded not for charging less of it but for extracting more, and the design of their products follows accordingly, towards endless feeds, automatic playback and notifications timed to recapture a wandering mind.

It does not follow that free services should be prohibited or that their users are dupes. What follows is narrower and, in a way, more practical: a market in which one side cannot see the price it pays will not protect that side as markets ordinarily do, and remedies should therefore aim at making the price visible. A service that reported to each user, plainly and regularly, how much time it had absorbed would not end the trade in attention, but it would give its users what every functioning market requires, a figure to compare.

In most markets the price does the work of allocation. If more people want a good than there are units of it, the price rises until the excess disappears, and whoever is willing to pay the new price obtains the good. But there is a family of markets in which this mechanism cannot operate, because each side must choose the other. A university cannot simply admit whoever is willing to pay the most, nor can an applicant simply buy a place; a hospital hiring junior doctors cares which doctors it gets, and the doctors care which hospital they join. In such markets, sometimes called matching markets, a transaction requires mutual acceptance, and no single number can bring about a match that both sides want.

Left to themselves, matching markets tend to fail in characteristic ways. One is unravelling: because the strongest candidates are in demand, employers try to secure them by making offers earlier than their rivals, and the competition for earliness can push offers so far forward that they are made before anyone knows how good the candidates are. Another is congestion: when offers must be accepted or refused quickly, a candidate holding one offer may not learn in time of a better one, and the market clears without having considered all its possibilities. A third is strategic misrepresentation, in which participants conceal their true preferences, ranking a likely option first rather than the one they actually want, because they fear that revealing their real wishes will cost them.

The remedy that has often been adopted is not deregulation but construction: a clearinghouse to which both sides submit ranked lists, and which computes an assignment by a procedure known to have certain properties. The property most often sought is stability, meaning that there is no applicant and employer, not matched to each other, who would both prefer to be. A stable assignment removes the motive to break ranks, since no such pair can do better by striking a private deal, and with a suitable procedure at least one side can be given no reason to misreport its preferences. Such clearinghouses show that a market is not always a spontaneous order arising wherever people are free to trade; it can be an artefact, built to solve problems that freedom alone creates.

None of this means that design can substitute for the willingness of participants. A clearinghouse works only if enough of both sides join it, and an elegant procedure is useless if the most sought-after employers find it more profitable to recruit privately. Nor can a procedure deliver every desirable property at once: no procedure, for instance, can give both sides complete reason to report honestly while always producing stable outcomes. The designer chooses among imperfect options, and the choice reflects judgements about whose interests deserve protection. The engineering of markets is thus a political as well as a technical art, but it is an art that can be practised well or badly, and the difference matters to the people whose lives it arranges.

For a long time economists were embarrassed by a simple question. Water is essential to life and diamonds are not, yet water is cheap and diamonds are dear; how could prices, which were supposed to reflect value, so plainly invert the order of importance? Eighteenth-century writers posed the puzzle as a contrast between value in use and value in exchange, and many concluded that exchange value must therefore have some source other than usefulness. The most influential answer located that source in the costs of production, and above all in labour: diamonds are dear because finding and cutting them takes enormous effort, while water, in most places, merely has to be collected.

The cost theory had obvious merits, since goods that are hard to produce are frequently expensive, but it struggled with cases in which effort and price come apart. A pearl found by chance in an oyster served at dinner fetches no less than one obtained by days of diving, and a wine from a celebrated year commands its price long after the labour that made it has been forgotten. The resolution that eventually prevailed, worked out independently by several writers in the later nineteenth century, abandoned the attempt to attach value to goods as such. What matters, it held, is not the usefulness of water in general but the usefulness of one more unit of it to someone who already has a certain amount. A person with enough water to drink, cook and wash would gain little from an extra bucket, while a person with few diamonds, or none, would prize one more highly. Price tracks this marginal usefulness, not the total.

The resolution is genuine, and its elegance is rightly admired. But it achieved both more than it is usually credited with and less. It achieved more because it moved value from things to situations: the same bucket of water is nearly worthless in a town beside a river and beyond price to a traveller lost in a desert, although nothing about the water has changed. It achieved less because it was never a theory of importance. To say that water is cheap is to say that, where it is plentiful, nobody would give much for one more unit of it; it is not to say that water matters little. The marginal account explains why prices may be low on goods that are indispensable, and in doing so it warns us against reading prices as a ranking of what matters.

That warning is regularly forgotten. Public argument often treats the market price of something as the measure of its contribution, so that an activity commanding high prices is assumed to be more valuable to society than one commanding low ones, and resources that cost nothing, such as clean air, are treated as though they were of no account until they become scarce. The marginal theory does not license this inference; if anything it predicts the error, since it shows that abundance alone can drive a price towards zero whatever the total importance of the good. Abundance, moreover, is not always permanent, and a price set while a resource was plentiful says little about what it will be worth once it is not.

None of this is a case against prices, which remain an unrivalled means of coordinating what millions of people do with information that no single mind possesses. It is a case for remembering what question a price answers. A price tells us what one more unit of something is worth to those at the margin, here and now. It does not tell us what the whole of it is worth, or what it would be worth to people who are not in the market at all, and a society that forgets the difference may discover the value of its cheapest goods only when it is too late to pay for them.

Give a group of people an ordinary object, a coffee mug, say, or a pen, and then ask them how much they would accept to sell it; ask another group, who were not given the object, how much they would pay to acquire one. In experiments of this kind the sellers' prices have repeatedly been found to exceed the buyers' by a wide margin, even though the two groups were formed at random and there is no reason to think that the owners care more for mugs. Merely owning a thing, it seems, makes it more valuable to its owner. The finding has come to be known as the endowment effect, and it has become one of the best-known results in behavioural economics.

The standard interpretation explains it by loss aversion. People, on this view, evaluate outcomes not in absolute terms but as gains and losses relative to a reference point, and losses loom larger than equivalent gains. Once the mug is mine, giving it up registers as a loss, whereas acquiring it, for someone who does not own it, registers only as a gain, and since the loss weighs more heavily, the owner demands more in compensation than the non-owner will pay. The account is economical, and it connects the mug experiments with a wide range of other behaviour, from the reluctance of investors to sell shares that have fallen in value to the stubbornness with which people defend entitlements they have only recently acquired.

A rival interpretation treats the gap as, at least in part, an artefact of the way such experiments are conducted. Participants who have never sold anything in a laboratory may be unsure what is being asked, may suspect that the experimenter knows the object's true value, or may simply apply a rule from everyday life, never to sell for less than it would cost to replace the thing. When procedures are altered so that participants practise the bidding mechanism and understand that misstating their values cannot help them, some studies have found the gap to shrink considerably. Supporters of this view also point out that professional traders, who buy and sell as a matter of routine, appear to show much less of the effect in the goods they deal in.

Each interpretation captures something real, and the dispute is less sharp than it is sometimes made to appear. The traders' case is telling not because it refutes loss aversion but because it suggests where loss aversion applies. A dealer who holds a stock of mugs holds them in order to sell them; parting with one is the purpose of having it, and so it does not register as a loss. A person who has been given a mug to use is in a different position, because the mug has already become, in a small way, part of her possessions, and parting with it means giving something up rather than completing a transaction. On this reading, what matters is not ownership as such but the frame in which a thing is held, as something to use or as something to exchange.

That reading has consequences beyond the laboratory. It implies that the gap between buying and selling prices is not a fixed constant of human nature, to be entered into economic models as a permanent correction, but a variable that depends on how people come to think of what they have. Markets that encourage people to regard their possessions as stock, as resale platforms arguably do, may weaken the effect; arrangements that encourage people to regard what they hold as their own, as long trial periods for products arguably do, may strengthen it. Whether either tendency is desirable is a separate question. The point is that the endowment effect, properly understood, is less a fact about objects or owners than a fact about the relation between them.

A common complaint about relative poverty lines is that they confuse poverty with inequality. If a household counts as poor whenever its income falls below, say, half of the median, then a country in which everyone became twice as rich would have exactly as many poor people as before. Critics take this as a decisive objection: a measure that cannot register a general rise in living standards, they say, is measuring the spread of incomes and calling it hardship. The objection is tidy, and it is not wrong about the arithmetic. It is wrong, I think, about what poverty is.

Being poor has never meant only lacking the calories and shelter needed to stay alive. It has meant being unable to do what one's neighbours take for granted: to send a child to school in clothes that will not draw mockery, to return a dinner invitation, to keep a telephone so that an employer can call. These requirements are set by the society one lives in, and they rise as that society grows richer. A family that could once manage without a refrigerator or a bank account cannot easily do so when shops, schools and employers assume that it has both. Relative lines track this moving threshold of participation, and that is exactly why their indifference to a uniform rise in incomes is not a defect. If everyone's income doubled, the cost of taking part in ordinary life would roughly double too.

This does not mean that relative measures can stand alone. Their weakness shows most plainly in a recession. When median income falls, the line falls with it, and a household whose income has not changed may be counted as having escaped poverty while its circumstances are no better, and its anxieties perhaps worse. A measure that reports falling poverty in the middle of a slump will strike most people as perverse, and they will be right. Absolute lines, fixed in real terms at some past standard, have the opposite virtue: they register whether the poorest are gaining or losing ground in purchasing power, whatever is happening to everyone else.

The sensible conclusion is not to choose between the two but to read them together, as answers to different questions. An absolute line asks whether the poor can buy more than they could before; a relative line asks whether they can still live as members of the society around them. A government that improves the first while the second worsens has achieved something real, but it has not abolished poverty, and it should not be allowed to claim that it has.

Few proposals in development policy provoke as reliable a reaction as giving poor households money with no strings attached. The objection usually arrives before the argument has been heard: the money will be drunk, gambled or otherwise wasted. It is worth noticing how rarely this suspicion is applied to other recipients of public money: pensioners are not asked to show receipts, and a tax refund arrives without an accompanying lecture on how it ought to be spent. The worry is reserved for people whose poverty is taken, often without anyone saying so, as evidence that they cannot be trusted with choices.

The suspicion has been tested more often than its persistence would suggest. Evaluations of cash programmes in a range of poor countries have generally found little sign that recipients increase their spending on alcohol or tobacco, and many have found the money going to food, school costs, livestock, tools and the repair of homes. This should not be surprising, since a household living close to the margin knows its own most pressing constraint far better than an official in a distant ministry, and the constraint differs from one family to the next: a roof for one, a debt for another, a sewing machine for a third. A transfer in kind, or one tied to a particular use, has to guess, and it guesses the same thing for everyone.

None of this makes conditions pointless. Where the aim is a specific behaviour whose benefits fall partly on others, or arrive too late to weigh heavily with a hard-pressed parent, such as keeping a daughter in school or bringing an infant for vaccination, a condition can do work that cash alone may not. And in remote places where markets are thin, a sudden injection of money can push up the prices of the few goods available rather than raising what people can actually buy. These are genuine qualifications, and a careful designer of programmes will take them seriously; but they are reasons for attaching conditions in particular cases, argued on their merits, not grounds for a general presumption that the poor will misuse what they are given.

The practical upshot is a reversal of the burden of proof. The default should be cash, and anyone proposing to restrict its use should have to show what the restriction achieves and what it costs, including the cost of monitoring and the quieter cost of telling adults that they are not trusted. Paternalism is sometimes justified, and there will be programmes in which the case for it can be made convincingly; it should not, however, be the starting assumption.

For a period, small loans to the poor were spoken of as something close to a cure. The story was compelling: a woman borrows a modest sum, buys a second sewing machine or a stock of vegetables to sell, repays from her profits, borrows again, and climbs by degrees out of poverty. Lenders who reported repayment rates that conventional banks could only envy seemed to prove that the poor were creditworthy, and from creditworthiness it seemed a short step to prosperity. The step proved longer than advertised.

When careful evaluations compared similar communities with and without access to microcredit, they tended to find effects that were real but modest. Some households started or expanded businesses; average incomes and consumption rose little, if at all; and the transformation of lives promised in the brochures was hard to find in the data. It would be easy to read this as a verdict that microcredit failed. That reading, I think, mistakes what was being tested. The original story assumed that most poor people are frustrated entrepreneurs held back only by a lack of capital. Many are not. They run tiny enterprises because steady wage work is unavailable, and given the choice many would take a factory job at a fixed wage over the uncertainties of a market stall.

Seen in this light, the more interesting finding is how borrowers actually used their loans. A good deal of the money went not into enterprises but into managing life's lumpy expenses: a wedding, a hospital bill, school fees due all at once, a new roof before the rains. For households whose incomes arrive irregularly, the ability to turn a stream of small repayments into a single usable sum is genuinely valuable, even if it never shows up as a rise in average income. Microcredit, on this view, is less an engine of growth than a financial service, comparable to the savings and insurance that the better-off take for granted.

This reframing is not a licence for complacency. Where lenders multiply and compete for the same clients, households can take one loan to repay another, and a service that smooths hardship can become a source of it. Nor should the modest average conceal a minority of borrowers, usually those who already ran established businesses, for whom credit made a larger difference. The lesson is not that small loans are worthless but that they should be judged as what they are, and regulated with that in mind, rather than against a promise they were never likely to keep.

Among the ideas that have shaped thinking about growth and fairness, few have travelled as far as the proposal, first advanced in the middle of the twentieth century, that inequality traces an inverted U as an economy develops. In the early stages, the argument ran, inequality rises as some workers move from a poor and fairly equal agricultural sector into a richer and more unequal industrial one; later, as most of the workforce has made the move and the new urban classes gain education and political voice, inequality falls again. The idea was offered tentatively, on the strength of a handful of national histories, but it hardened over the following decades into something closer to a law.

The mechanism at its core is sound as far as it goes. If a population is divided between two sectors with different average incomes, moving people from the lower to the higher will, by simple arithmetic, widen overall inequality for a time and then narrow it once the shift is largely complete. What does not follow is that this arithmetic governs the course of inequality in real economies, where it competes with many other forces. As data accumulated for more countries and longer periods, the curve proved elusive. Some economies grew rapidly while inequality stayed flat or fell; others saw inequality rise again after a long decline, a second upswing for which the original story had no room.

The damage done by treating the curve as a law was not mainly to economic theory. It was to policy. If rising inequality is a natural stage of development that growth will itself reverse, then governments in poor countries can be told to tolerate it, and governments in rich ones can be assured that any widening is a passing disturbance. Both lessons encourage waiting. Yet in the historical episodes that did show a decline, the fall rarely arrived on its own. It came alongside the spread of public schooling, the growth of organised labour, progressive taxation and, in several cases, the destruction of concentrated wealth by war and inflation.

A better reading treats the inverted U not as a path that development follows but as a record of what happened in some places when particular structural shifts met particular political choices. Read that way, the curve still teaches something, chiefly that the movement of people between sectors matters for how incomes are distributed. What it cannot do is assure a government that inequality will take care of itself.

Debates about the informal economy, the vast realm of unregistered firms and unprotected work that employs a majority of workers in many poorer countries, tend to divide into two camps. One sees informality as exclusion. On this account, people sell vegetables on pavements or take casual work on building sites because the formal economy has too few jobs to absorb them; informality is a waiting room, and its occupants would leave if a door opened. The other camp sees informality as a choice. Registering a business, paying taxes and complying with labour law are costly, and for many firms the benefits of formality, such as access to the courts and to bank credit, are not worth the price. Informality, on this account, is a rational response to a state that asks much and offers little.

Each camp marshals real evidence, and each tends to generalise from the cases that suit it. The exclusion view draws on the lives of the poorest informal workers, whose earnings are low, whose hours are long and who report that they would gladly take a salaried job. The choice view draws on a different population: owners of small but established workshops and trading firms who could register, who know what registration would involve and who have decided against it. Both groups are informal. They are not otherwise much alike, and an argument about which of them represents the informal economy is rather like an argument about whether the typical resident of a city is a banker or a street sweeper.

The distinction matters most when governments decide to act. Programmes that cut the cost of registration, by reducing fees, merging permits or allowing firms to register online, are well designed for the second group and largely irrelevant to the first. A woman frying snacks at a bus stand is not informal because the registration form is long; she is informal because what she earns would not cover the obligations that formality brings, and because no employer has offered her anything better. For her, simplification changes nothing. Campaigns that instead treat informality as evasion and respond with fines and evictions fall hardest on precisely those who had the least choice.

It would be wrong to conclude that the informal economy is merely a collection of unrelated cases. The groups are linked, since established informal firms often employ, supply or buy from the poorest workers, and conditions in one tier affect the other. But the links are a reason to design policy for each tier with the others in view, not a reason to pretend that one diagnosis fits all. The question to ask about any informal worker is not whether informality is chosen or imposed in general, but which of the two it is for that worker.

A donor that pays for a new clinic likes to believe that it has paid for a clinic. Often it has not, or not in the sense it imagines. Suppose a government had already planned to build the clinic from its own revenue. When a donor offers to fund it, the government can accept, release the money it had set aside and spend it on something else entirely: a road, a pay rise for civil servants, an extra battalion. The clinic gets built either way. What the aid has really financed is whatever the government would otherwise have gone without, and the donor, which may never learn what that was, has had no say in choosing it.

Economists call this fungibility, and once it has been seen it is hard to unsee. It implies that the earmark on a grant, the label saying that the money is for health or for schools, may tell us little about what the grant actually changes. Studies comparing donors' allocations with recipients' overall spending have often found that aid labelled for a sector raises spending in that sector by less than the amount given, though rarely by nothing. The lesson many have drawn is that donors are funding governments, not projects, whether or not they admit it.

The lesson is right, but it is easy to overstate. Fungibility depends on the government having planned to do the thing anyway. Where a donor funds something the government would not have undertaken, a programme against a neglected disease, say, or a school in a district whose population carries no political weight, the money cannot be redirected in the same way, because there was no planned expenditure to release. Fungibility is also weaker when a government's budget is so stretched or so rigid that there is little slack to shift. And aid often brings more than money: technical staff, systems for buying supplies, and a degree of scrutiny that can change how a sector is run, effects that no accounting of shifted budget lines will capture.

Nor is fungibility in itself a scandal. If a recipient government has sound priorities, the freedom to move money to where it is most needed is an advantage, and donors who insist on rigid earmarks may simply be paying for the comfort of a plaque. The difficulty arises where priorities are poor, because there the earmark offers protection only on paper. What follows is not that earmarking is useless but that donors cannot rely on it to do their thinking for them. The question that matters is less what a grant is labelled for than what kind of government receives it.

Why are some countries rich and others poor? For several decades the question has been staged as a contest between two answers. One points to geography: to climate, soils, disease and distance from the sea, which shape what can be grown, how healthy workers are and how cheaply goods can be moved. The other points to institutions: to whether property is secure, contracts are enforced and rulers are constrained, which shape whether people find it worth their while to invest, innovate and trade. Each side has its favourite evidence, and each has scored points against the other.

The institutional camp's strongest card is the observation that geography changes slowly while fortunes can change fast. Two halves of a peninsula with the same climate, the same soils and, until the middle of the twentieth century, a shared history can diverge dramatically within a couple of generations once they are placed under different political systems. Institutionalists have also pointed to a pattern among formerly colonised regions: some of those that were relatively densely settled and prosperous five centuries ago are relatively poor today, while some that were thinly populated then are rich now. Geography did not flip in the interval. What changed, the argument goes, were the institutions that colonisers imposed, extractive where there was wealth and labour to seize, more inclusive where settlers came to live.

The geographers' reply is that these comparisons, however striking, do not dispose of their case. A landlocked country far from major markets pays more to export every tonne it produces, whatever its laws say, and a tropical region where malaria is endemic carries a burden of illness that good government can reduce but not abolish overnight. These are direct effects, and no amount of constitutional reform makes a mountain range easier to cross. Geographers add that the peninsula, however vivid, is a single case, and that a single case can show that institutions are capable of mattering without showing how much they usually matter across the wide run of countries.

What both camps tend to overlook is how much of their contest is artificial. The reversal story itself, read carefully, is a story about geography working through institutions. Colonisers chose to settle or to extract partly according to how likely they were to survive the local diseases, and the soils of some regions suited crops that were profitable to grow with coerced labour on large estates. The institutions that resulted were, in this sense, partly geographical in origin, even if they later took on a life of their own. To ask, as statistical exercises often do, how much of the variation in income is due to geography and how much to institutions is to treat as rival causes what are frequently links in a single chain. The exercise can produce a number, but the number answers a question that the history does not pose.

None of this restores geography as destiny. The institutionalists are right that the same land can support very different outcomes, and that a country is not condemned by its latitude. The point is rather that the question 'which matters more?' should give way to the question 'how did they combine here?', which has a different answer in different places and cannot be settled by a single coefficient. For one country the answer may lie largely in a coastline that made trade cheap long before anyone drafted a constitution; for another, in rules imposed by outsiders that outlived the conditions which first made them profitable.

Income is the most convenient measure of how well people are doing, and convenience has a way of turning into authority. A figure for income per head can be compared across countries and decades, added up and divided, and reported to a decimal place. Yet what it measures is a means. People do not value income for its own sake but for what it allows them to do and to be: to be adequately nourished, to move about without danger, to read, to take part in the life of a community, to have some say in the decisions that shape their lives. The capability approach, as it has come to be called, proposes that development should be judged by these freedoms directly rather than by the resources that are supposed to produce them.

The case for the shift rests on a simple observation with large consequences. The same income does not yield the same freedoms to everyone. A person who uses a wheelchair needs more resources than a neighbour to reach the same workplace; a pregnant woman needs more food than a man of the same age to be equally well nourished; a household in a cold climate must spend on heating what a household elsewhere can spend on anything it likes. Social arrangements matter as much as bodies and climates. Where custom keeps women from travelling alone, a rise in household income may leave a daughter's freedom to attend a distant college exactly where it was. Measures of income, by construction, are blind to these differences in the rate at which resources become lives.

The standard objection is that the approach, whatever its philosophical appeal, cannot be made to work. Which capabilities count? How should being literate be weighed against being healthy, or political voice against freedom from hunger? Any answer, critics say, is either so vague as to be useless or, once written down as a definite list with definite weights, an imposition of some theorist's values on people who might rank their lives differently. A list drawn up in a university, they add, need not be the list that a farmer or a factory worker would draw up, and a framework that began by taking people's own lives seriously would then end by overruling their judgments about those lives.

The objection is weaker than it looks, because it applies with equal force to the measure it is meant to defend. Income per head also aggregates very different things, and it also weights them. It weights them by market prices, which record what people with money are willing to pay, so that a luxury bought by the rich can count for more than a staple that the poor cannot afford. These are value judgments as well; they are simply made silently, by the market, rather than openly, by someone who must defend them. A framework that forces its users to state and argue for their weights has not introduced a new difficulty. It has exposed an old one.

This does not mean that every attempt to turn capabilities into a single index succeeds. Composite scores that average a few indicators can reproduce the very problem the approach set out to solve, burying under one number the differences in conversion that made income misleading in the first place. The approach is at its strongest not as a rival ranking but as a discipline of attention: a way of asking, in any given place, which freedoms people lack and why, and of noticing when a rising average conceals a stagnant life.

An economy organised entirely by prices would have no need of firms. Every task, from sweeping a floor to designing a circuit, could be bought from whoever offered it most cheaply, and each worker would be a small business selling services by the hour. That actual economies look nothing like this is so familiar that it rarely seems to require explanation. Yet it does. Inside a firm, resources move not because a price has changed but because someone has been told to move them, and the coexistence of these two methods of coordination, the market outside and the hierarchy within, is one of the quieter puzzles of economic life.

The standard answer is that using the market is not free. Before anything can be bought, a buyer must find sellers, compare their terms, write a contract and then check that the contract has been honoured. When a task recurs daily and its details cannot be specified in advance, these costs multiply, and it becomes cheaper to hire someone on open-ended terms and direct the work as it arises. On this view the firm is a device for economising on bargaining: it grows until the cost of organising one more activity internally equals the cost of buying it outside. The account has real explanatory power. It predicts, correctly, that firms tend to bring in-house the activities that are specific to their own operations, where a supplier who knew it was indispensable could hold them to ransom.

What the account leaves out is suggested by its own vocabulary. It describes the firm almost entirely in terms of costs avoided, as if the best a firm could do were to match what an ideal market would have delivered at no expense. But a group of people who work together for years does not merely save on contracts; it produces something that no contract could have bought. Such a group learns which of its members can be trusted with ambiguity, how to divide a problem that none of them fully understands, and which shortcuts are safe. This knowledge is rarely written down and often cannot be, because it lives in habits and in the expectations people hold of one another. It cannot be purchased from outside because it does not exist outside; it is a product of the firm's continued existence.

None of this overturns the bargaining view, which remains the best guide to where the boundary of a firm will fall in any particular case. A carmaker deciding whether to make its own seats is weighing exactly the costs that view describes. The difficulty arises only when the account is taken as a complete theory of what firms are for. Then it makes the firm look like a regrettable necessity, a patch over the imperfections of exchange, and it renders the most valuable thing a firm possesses, the shared competence of people who have learned to work together, invisible to the very analysis that claims to explain it.

A piece of folk wisdom, repeated in many places, holds that a family business rarely survives the founder's grandchildren. The founder builds it through hard work, the children keep it going out of duty, and the grandchildren, raised in comfort, let it slip away. The story is usually told as a lesson about character: wealth softens those who inherit it, and the hunger that built the firm cannot be handed down along with the shares. It is a satisfying story, and like most satisfying stories it is only partly true.

Consider first the plain arithmetic of inheritance. A founder typically owns the whole firm and answers to no one. If the shares are divided among three children, and each of them divides theirs among three more, the third generation may consist of nine or more owners, some of whom work in the business and some of whom have never set foot in it. Those who draw a salary want the profits reinvested; those who live elsewhere want dividends; those who need cash want to sell, and there may be no agreed price at which the others can buy them out. Quarrels follow, but they follow from the structure, and the most energetic cousin in the world could not make them disappear.

A second difficulty lies in how leaders are chosen. A firm that insists the chief executive must be a member of the family has narrowed its field of candidates to a handful of people who happen to share a surname. Even if every one of them is capable, the chance that the best available manager is among them is small. The founder often makes matters worse by postponing the question altogether, because the business is so bound up with his sense of who he is that planning for his own departure feels like planning for his death. When the moment can no longer be avoided, it tends to arrive suddenly, through illness or a quarrel, and the successor is whoever is standing nearest.

None of this means that character is irrelevant; some heirs are indeed less driven than their parents, and some fortunes really are spent rather than lost. But the family firms that last for many generations tend to have one thing in common, and it is not a lucky supply of hard-working grandchildren. They separate the role of owner from the role of manager, write down rules for how shares may be sold within the family, and are willing to hire an outsider to run the business when no relative is suited to it. Their survival is less a triumph of virtue than of design.

When a dominant company is overtaken by a newcomer, the explanation usually offered is some version of complacency: its managers, the story goes, grew comfortable, stopped listening to the market and failed to perceive what was approaching. The story has the appeal of a fable, and it permits the rest of us to believe that an identical fate could be avoided simply by remaining vigilant. Its difficulty is that, in many of the best known cases, the incumbent's managers were neither lazy nor blind. They were doing, carefully and well, exactly what they had been trained to do.

The pattern runs roughly as follows. A new technology appears that is, at first, worse than the existing one by the measures that the incumbent's best customers care about. It is slower, or less precise, or less durable, but it is cheaper and simpler, and it finds a small market among buyers who were never well served by the established product. The incumbent asks its customers whether they want the new thing, and they say no. It examines the margins, and they are thin. It looks at the size of the market, and it is too small to move a company of its scale. Every one of these judgements is correct, and together they lead the firm to put its money where its profits are. Meanwhile the new technology improves, year by year, until it is good enough for the mainstream, and the incumbent discovers that its careful attention to its best customers has left it with nothing to offer the rest.

It may be objected that this account is written with the convenient clarity of hindsight, since for every cheap technology that grew up to displace its betters, many others remained toys and disappeared, and an incumbent that chased all of them would have squandered its resources. The objection is fair, but it strengthens rather than weakens the point. If good managers cannot tell in advance which small markets will matter, then vigilance alone cannot be the remedy, because the problem is not a failure to look but a set of rules for deciding what is worth looking at.

What seems to help is therefore structural rather than psychological: firms that have survived such transitions have often placed the new venture in a separate unit, with its own costs and its own measures of success, small enough that a small market can still excite it. This is no guarantee, since separate units can be starved or smothered by the parent organisation, but the arrangement at least removes the new business from the scrutiny of the rules that would have judged it, correctly by their own lights, not worth the trouble.

Business journalism has a favourite kind of hero: the chief executive who arrives at a struggling company, takes bold decisions and turns it around. Magazine profiles, admiring biographies and conference speeches all tell the story in the same way, with the leader at the centre and everything else as scenery. The habit is understandable, since a firm is an abstraction and it is far easier to praise or blame a person than a set of market conditions. But the habit also produces a systematic error about how much any one leader actually controls.

Consider what else moves a company's results. Demand for its products rises and falls with the economy and with the fortunes of its industry; the price of its raw materials is set in markets it cannot influence; many of the products it sells were conceived years earlier, under managers who have since left. A new chief executive who takes over at the bottom of a downturn will, in the ordinary course of things, preside over a recovery, and the recovery will be credited to him. His successor, arriving at the peak, will be blamed for the decline that follows. Neither may have done much to cause what happened while he was in charge.

Imagine two firms in the same industry, with similar products and similar costs. One appoints a celebrated leader just as the market begins to recover; the other keeps an unremarkable manager who has run it for years. Both firms prosper over the next three years, but only one of them is written about, and the story of its revival will attribute to leadership what was largely a rising market carrying both firms upward. Such comparisons are rarely made, because the second firm has no story to tell.

None of this means that leaders are irrelevant.
