In moments of genuine crisis, or when a firm must choose between strategies that will shape it for decades, the judgement of the person at the top can matter a great deal. The error lies in degree, not in kind. Yet the error has consequences, for boards that believe in saviours go looking for them outside the firm, pay them accordingly, and dismiss them when results return to the ordinary, only to begin the search again. An organisation that understood how much of its fate lay beyond any individual might spend less on heroes and more on the people and systems that carry it through every leader's tenure.

Few management practices divide opinion as sharply as forced ranking, the system in which managers must place a fixed share of their staff in each band of a performance scale, so that some employees are always rated outstanding, most are rated adequate and a few are always rated poor, often with the expectation that the last group will leave. Its defenders make a reasonable case. Left to themselves, managers tend to rate almost everyone above average, partly out of kindness and partly to avoid difficult conversations, and a scale on which everyone scores highly conveys no information at all. A forced distribution, on this view, simply obliges managers to say what they already know.

The difficulty is that the system assumes far more than it appears to. It assumes, first, that performance within each team is spread along a curve, so that any group of a dozen people must contain its stars and its laggards. In a large population this may be roughly true, but a small team may have been assembled precisely because all its members are good, and forcing a distribution upon it manufactures distinctions that the work itself does not support. It assumes, second, that performance belongs to individuals, when in most organisations the results that matter are produced by people working together, and the contribution of any one of them is hard to separate from that of the rest.

The second assumption matters most, because of what the system teaches. If my rating depends on being ranked above my colleagues, then helping a colleague is a cost to me, and sharing an idea is a gift to a rival. The employees who learn this lesson fastest are not necessarily the most capable; they are the most attentive to how they appear. Over time, able people may also learn to avoid strong teams, since a good performer is safer among weaker colleagues than among excellent ones. A system introduced to reward merit ends by rewarding position.

It would be too strong to say that forced ranking never does any good. In an organisation where years of inflated ratings have left no way of distinguishing good work from bad, a single round of hard comparison may expose problems that polite evaluation had concealed. The harm comes when a jolt is turned into a permanent regime, and the habits of comparison it encourages become the ordinary way in which colleagues regard one another.

Inquiries into industrial disasters have a way of finding a culprit. An operator ignored a warning, an inspector signed a form he had not read, a manager overruled an engineer whose objections were inconvenient. Such findings are rarely false, but they are often beside the point, because they treat as a single failure of judgement what was in fact the end of a long and orderly process. Many organisations do not stumble into catastrophe; they walk towards it by steps that each seemed reasonable at the time.

Consider a hypothetical chemical plant whose procedures say that a certain vessel must be shut down if its pressure exceeds a stated limit. One night the gauge registers a reading marginally above the permitted limit. Shutting down would be expensive, the excess is small, and the engineers on duty judge, correctly as it turns out, that the vessel is in no danger. Nothing untoward happens, and the next time the reading creeps over the limit there is a precedent, which makes the decision considerably easier. After a dozen such nights the limit has quietly moved: the written figure still stands in the manual, but the working figure, the one people actually act on, is higher. No one decided to change it. The change was made by the accumulated absence of harm.

This is what makes the process so difficult to detect from within the organisation itself. Each step is defended by evidence, and the evidence is genuine, for the vessel really did not fail. What is mistaken is the inference drawn from it, that a risk which has not yet produced harm has thereby been shown to be small. Success becomes a reason for confidence, and confidence a reason to look less closely, so that the organisation's sense of its own safety grows at the same rate as its actual exposure to danger. By the time an outsider asks why the plant routinely runs above its limit, the question sounds naive, because everyone inside knows that it always has.

It does not follow that every departure from the rules is a step towards disaster. Written procedures are drafted in advance by people who cannot foresee every situation, and an organisation whose staff never deviated from them would be unable to adapt; much good practice begins as a sensible exception. The danger lies not in deviation itself but in deviation that is never recognised as such. A departure that is noticed, argued over and formally adopted is a decision; one that simply accumulates is drift, and drift answers to no one.

Few words in the vocabulary of management carry as much reproach as slack. Idle machines, unfilled hours, inventory sitting in warehouses and staff whose days are not fully booked all appear, to the analyst armed with a spreadsheet, as resources that are paid for and not used. The programmes that set out to remove them, under whatever name is fashionable at the time, can usually point to impressive savings in their first year, and the savings are real. What such programmes measure less well is what the slack had been doing before it was removed, because its work was done in circumstances that the measurements were not designed to capture.

The first of those circumstances is the shock. A supply chain that holds no spare stock is cheaper to run on every ordinary day, and on the day a single supplier fails it halts entirely, because there is nothing between the failure and the factory floor. A hospital ward staffed exactly to its average occupancy works smoothly in most weeks and is overwhelmed in the week that an infection spreads. In each case the margin that looked like waste was a store of capacity held against an event whose timing could not be known, and its value appears only in the period that the efficiency audit treats as an exception. To judge slack by ordinary days is to judge an umbrella by the weather on days when it did not rain.

The second circumstance is less dramatic and perhaps more important. Organisations do not only respond to events; they also change themselves, and change requires time that is not already claimed. An engineer who has an afternoon free may try out an idea that no plan had scheduled; a manager with some unallocated budget can fund a small experiment without first writing a case for it that no one yet knows how to write. Most of these experiments come to nothing, which is exactly why a system that requires every hour and every rupee to be justified in advance will not permit them. The new products and methods that later look inevitable often began in precisely the margins that a thorough efficiency drive would have closed.

It would be naive to conclude that slack is always benign. Spare resources can shelter inefficiency as easily as invention, and a department with more staff than it needs may use the surplus not to experiment but to protect its own comfort or to fight for its standing within the firm. Some slack is indeed waste, and some of the people who defend it are defending their privileges. The critics of slack are therefore not simply wrong; they are answering a question that is badly posed. Asking how much slack an organisation has, and how quickly it can be reduced, treats a heterogeneous quantity as if it were uniform.

The more useful question is what the slack is for and who can see it. A reserve whose purpose is understood, whose size is reviewed and whose use is reported can be defended on the days when it seems idle, and trimmed when it has outlived its purpose. A reserve that exists only because no one has looked at it will be either preserved for the wrong reasons or eliminated by the first auditor who does. The aim is neither to maximise slack nor to abolish it, but to hold it deliberately, as an organisation holds any other asset whose returns arrive irregularly.

A durable genre of business writing proceeds by a method that looks, at first sight, impeccably empirical. The author selects a number of companies that have performed outstandingly over a long period, studies them closely, and identifies the practices they share: a strong culture, perhaps, or a fierce attention to customers, or a willingness to abandon unprofitable lines. These practices are then offered as the causes of greatness, and the reader who adopts them is invited to expect something of the same result. The books sell well, partly because the companies are vivid and partly because the method appears to replace opinion with evidence.

The first difficulty is one of selection. By studying only the companies that succeeded, the method has no way of knowing how many companies followed the same practices and failed. If a great many firms had strong cultures and attended closely to their customers, and most of them disappeared, then these traits are not what separated the winners from the rest; they were simply common, and the winners, being a subset of the many, happened to possess them as well. The graveyard of failed firms is not consulted because it cannot easily be visited: failed companies leave few records, attract no researchers and give no interviews.

A second difficulty is subtler. Many of the traits that the method identifies are not observed independently of performance but described after the fact, by people who already know the result. A company that is doing well is said to have a bold strategy and a confident leadership; the same company, a few years later and in decline, is said to have been reckless and arrogant, though nothing in its conduct may have changed. The observers are not being dishonest when they do this; they are reading the same conduct in the light of what it later led to. Where descriptions of this kind are the raw material, the correlation between good practices and good results is partly manufactured by the way in which the practices were recognised.

Defenders of the genre have an answer to the first point: compare the successful firms with a matched set of less successful ones, drawn from the same industries and periods. This is a real improvement and should be acknowledged as such. But it does not remove the second difficulty, since the comparison firms are still described by people who know how they fared, nor does it settle a third, which emerges only with time. Several of the companies held up as models in such studies later stumbled badly, and the explanation usually offered is that they abandoned the principles that had made them great. That explanation can be given whatever happens. A theory that accounts for success by the presence of certain practices, and for failure by their supposed absence, has arranged never to be wrong.

None of this shows that the study of successful firms is worthless. Close accounts of how particular companies work can suggest hypotheses worth testing, and some of the practices they describe may well be beneficial. What the genre cannot do is what it most often claims to do: to identify, from the records of the winners, the reasons they won. A reader who wishes to learn from such books would do better to treat their lists of principles as questions rather than answers, and to remember that in a competitive market a large part of any outcome may be owed to timing and circumstance, which no one can copy.

Every wave of labour-saving machinery revives an old piece of arithmetic. If a factory needs a fixed quantity of work done, and a new machine does a third of it, then a third of the workers must go. Extend the sum across a whole economy and the conclusion seems inescapable: the more productive we become, the fewer of us will be needed. Economists have a name for the premise hidden in this calculation. They call it the lump of labour fallacy, the assumption that there is a set amount of work to be shared out, so that any work done by a machine, a newcomer or a pensioner who stays on is necessarily work taken from someone else.

The premise fails because the quantity of work is not fixed; it depends on what people want and can afford. When a machine makes cloth cheaper, households that once owned two shirts buy five, and the money they no longer spend on clothing goes on furniture, travel or schooling, each of which employs someone. The jobs created in this way are rarely the jobs that were lost, and they often appear in places and trades that nobody at the time thought to connect with the original invention. That is precisely why the destruction is so visible and the creation so easy to overlook. A closed mill is a single event with an address; the thousand small expansions that follow are scattered across an economy and are reported, if at all, as ordinary growth.

The same error appears in proposals that look generous. Schemes to push older workers into early retirement so that the young can find work, or to cap weekly hours so that employment is spread more thinly, assume that the jobs given up by one group pass intact to another. There is little reason to expect this. A worker who retires early also stops earning and spending at the old rate, and a firm that loses an experienced employee may simply produce less rather than hire a novice to take her place.

None of this means that the anxiety is foolish. The fallacy concerns the total amount of work, not its distribution, and a correct argument about totals is cold comfort to a fifty-year-old weaver whose skills no longer have a buyer. Transitions can take a generation, and the people who bear their cost are seldom the people who collect the gains. The proper conclusion is narrower than either side usually admits: technology does not abolish work in aggregate, but it can ruin particular lives and places, and policy ought to be judged by what it does for them rather than by whether it rescues a fixed stock of jobs that never existed.

Labour law in most countries rests on a binary. A worker is either an employee, who accepts direction in exchange for a wage and a bundle of protections, or an independent contractor, who sells a result, chooses her own methods and bears her own risks. The line was drawn for a world in which the difference was usually obvious: the clerk at a desk was one, the plumber who came to fix the office pipes was the other. Platform work has made the line hard to find. A driver who logs into an app chooses when to work and may refuse any job, which looks like independence; the same driver cannot set the fare, does not know which passenger comes next, and can be removed by an algorithm whose criteria she never sees, which looks very much like direction.

Two responses dominate the debate. One holds that platform workers are employees in all but name and that courts should simply say so. The other holds that flexibility is the whole attraction of such work, that many who do it also study or hold other jobs, and that imposing fixed shifts, minimum hours and the rest of the employment bundle would destroy the thing they value. Each side is right about what the other ignores. The first is right that the platform exercises a control over the terms of work that no genuine contractor would accept; the second is right that the employment bundle was designed around a fixed schedule and a single employer, and fits awkwardly onto someone who works eleven hours one week for three different apps and none the next.

What both share is the assumption that protections must come as a package attached to a status. That assumption is a historical accident rather than a principle. Some protections, such as a minimum rate for time actually worked, insurance against injury on the job or a right to be told why an account was suspended, depend on nothing that a flexible schedule makes impossible. Others, such as paid holidays calculated over a working year, are harder to translate, though not obviously impossible if entitlements accrue by the hour and follow the worker rather than the firm.

Unbundling has dangers of its own. A menu of separable protections invites firms to lobby for the cheapest selection, and a third category of worker, introduced to accommodate the platforms, could become a convenient place to move people who are at present employees. The case for unbundling is therefore not that it is free of risk, but that the binary has already failed: forcing a new form of work into one of two old boxes guarantees that, whichever box is chosen, a large part of the reality will be misdescribed.

Why does a string quartet cost so much more to hear today, relative to a shirt or a radio, than it did a century ago? Not because the musicians have become greedy or the concert halls inefficient. Performing a quartet required four players and roughly forty minutes then, and it requires the same now; no innovation has allowed three musicians to play it in half the time without destroying the thing being bought. Meanwhile workers in manufacturing have become many times more productive, and their wages have risen accordingly. The musicians' pay must rise too, or they would drift into other work. So the price of the quartet climbs relative to goods whose production has been transformed, even though nothing about the quartet has changed.

Economists sometimes call this the cost disease, and its reach goes far beyond concert halls. Teaching, nursing, care of the elderly and much legal and administrative work share the quartet's structure: the service largely consists of a person's time and attention, and attempts to compress that time often degrade what is delivered. A class of sixty is cheaper per pupil than a class of thirty, but it is not the same product at a lower price. Where productivity in such sectors lags, their share of national spending rises, and with it a persistent suspicion that schools and hospitals are squandering money, since nearly everything else seems to be getting cheaper.

The diagnosis contains a consolation that is often missed. If the relative cost of services rises because the rest of the economy has become more productive, then society as a whole is richer, and can afford those services even at their higher relative price. A family that spends a larger share of its income on its children's schooling than its grandparents did may also own far more and work fewer hours. What feels like a crisis of affordability is, on this view, partly a change in the composition of a growing budget.

The argument should not be stretched into a blanket excuse. That some cost growth in services is unavoidable does not mean that all of it is; administrative layers can multiply in a hospital as easily as in any other organisation, and the cost disease offers them no defence. Nor is the consolation automatic. The higher relative price of care falls hardest on those whose incomes have not shared in the general gain, and public budgets that depend on taxes voters resist may cut services long before the arithmetic says they must. The cost disease explains a pattern; it does not settle who should pay for it.

Arguments about working from home usually turn on a single question: are people as productive at the kitchen table as they are at the office desk? For many experienced professionals the honest answer appears to be yes, or close enough. They know their jobs, they know whom to ask, and they gain hours that once disappeared into commuting. But the question is framed around the output of a worker who is already competent, and it says little about how anyone becomes competent in the first place.

Consider a hypothetical accounting firm that sends everyone home. Its partners notice no fall in billable work during the first year, and the move looks like a clear success. What they cannot see is what their newest recruits are missing. In an office, a junior accountant overhears a senior colleague talking a nervous client through a bad result, watches how a disputed figure is checked, and asks a quick question that would feel too trivial to put in an email. None of this appears in any measure of output, and almost none of it is deliberately taught. It is absorbed, in the way apprentices have always absorbed a trade, by being near people who practise it.

Remote arrangements tend to remove exactly this kind of learning, because it depends on unplanned exposure and remote work is organised around planned contact. A video call is scheduled, has an agenda and ends when the agenda is done. The junior who would have learnt by watching instead learns only what someone remembered to explain. The cost is real but delayed: it shows up years later, as a cohort of mid-career staff who are slower to exercise judgement than their predecessors were at the same stage, by which time the decision that caused it has long been forgotten.

This is not an argument for ordering everyone back to their desks. Offices have never guaranteed this kind of learning; a junior placed among seniors who keep their doors shut learns little more than one at home. Firms can also try to replace accidental exposure with deliberate arrangements, such as pairing juniors with seniors on live work or inviting them to sit in on difficult calls. The point is that such arrangements must be built on purpose, and a firm that judges remote work only by the output of its experienced staff will not notice that it needs them until the damage is done.

Early researchers in artificial intelligence made a natural assumption about which problems would yield first. They took easy to mean what people find easy and hard to mean what people find hard, and so they assumed that a machine which could play respectable chess or prove theorems in logic would soon be able to fold laundry or cross a cluttered room. Matters turned out almost the other way round. Programs that could beat strong players at board games arrived long before machines that could reliably pick up an unfamiliar object without crushing or dropping it. The observation that the faculties we think of as higher are the cheap ones to mechanise, while those we take for granted are expensive, has come to be described by roboticists as a paradox.

It is a paradox only if our sense of difficulty is a good guide to the difficulty of a task, and a plausible explanation is that it is not. Perception and movement have been refined over an immense evolutionary history, and they run beneath awareness, so they feel like nothing at all. Explicit reasoning is recent and effortful, and its effortfulness is precisely what we notice. The feeling of difficulty, on this account, measures how new a skill is to our species rather than how much computation it requires.

The implication for work is uncomfortable for a familiar way of ranking jobs. We tend to treat the skills of the hospital cleaner, the gardener and the care worker as basic and those of the clerk who reconciles accounts as advanced. Yet the cleaner moves through rooms that are never arranged twice in the same way and handles objects of every shape and texture, while the reconciliation follows rules that can be written down. A machine finds the second job far easier to take over than the first. Forecasts that expect automation to climb steadily upward from the bottom of the wage scale may therefore have the direction partly backwards.

Two cautions are in order. First, the paradox describes a stage of technology, not a law of nature; methods that learn from vast numbers of examples have already eroded some of the advantage that perception once enjoyed, and it would be rash to assume the boundary will stay where it is. Second, being hard to automate is not the same as being well rewarded. The skills that resist machines are often widely shared among people, and abundance keeps wages low whatever a robot can or cannot do. The paradox tells us which tasks machines will struggle with; it does not tell us that the people who perform them will prosper.

The economist's textbook treats a trade union as a cartel of sellers. By bargaining collectively, workers withhold their labour unless paid more than a competitive market would offer, and the familiar consequences follow: fewer people employed in the unionised firm, more crowding into the sectors that remain open, and an output somewhat smaller than it might have been. On this view the only interesting question about a union is how large a premium it extracts and how much inefficiency that premium causes. Whatever else unions do, their grievance committees, their disputes over safety rules, their elected stewards on the shop floor, is incidental to the price they set.

That picture leaves out a choice every dissatisfied worker faces. She can leave, taking her skills to another employer, or she can stay and try to change what troubles her. Without a union, leaving is often the only safe course, because an individual who complains about a dangerous machine or an arbitrary supervisor marks herself as troublesome, and whatever she might have told the firm is lost when she walks out. A union changes the calculation. It allows complaints to be made collectively, through procedures, by people who cannot easily be singled out, and so it converts a stream of quiet departures into a stream of information that management would otherwise have had to buy, if it could buy it at all. Firms that hear this information may lose fewer trained workers and correct faults they did not know they had.

Seen this way, a union has two faces, and the question is not which of them is real but which predominates in a given setting. Where management treats the grievance procedure as an adversary to be outmanoeuvred, voice tends to harden into obstruction, and the cartel face is what remains. Where management treats the same procedure as an early warning, voice can make the firm more productive than a non-union rival, enough in some cases to offset the higher wage bill. The evidence on unions and productivity is accordingly mixed, and it ought to be; a single average effect conceals the very variation that matters.

This is why measuring unions only by their wage premium is a category error rather than a harmless simplification. It judges an institution that partly exists to carry information by the one effect, the price it sets, that carries no information about what is going wrong on the shop floor. It also hides the fact that the value of voice depends on whether anyone is listening, so that the same union under a different management can be a burden or an asset. None of this establishes that unions are good for firms, still less that they always raise productivity. It establishes only that the question cannot be answered by looking at the price of labour alone.

For about a century after industrialisation, the working week in the richer economies shrank steadily, from something like sixty hours or more to around forty. Many observers assumed the trend would continue. If each generation could produce more in an hour than the last, it seemed natural that part of the gain would be taken as leisure, and confident predictions were made in the early twentieth century that the grandchildren of that era might work perhaps fifteen hours a week. In much of the rich world the decline instead slowed sharply after the middle of the century, and for many full-time professionals it appears to have reversed. The puzzle is not that people work at all, but that productivity kept rising while the hours of so many stopped falling.

The simplest explanation is that people chose income over time. Higher pay makes an hour of leisure more expensive, since each hour off now forgoes more, and it also makes people richer, so that they can afford more leisure. Which of these pulls is stronger is an empirical matter, and for a long period the second seemed to win. Perhaps, the argument runs, it simply stopped winning: people discovered new things to want faster than their incomes satisfied the old wants. A related account adds that much of what people buy matters to them chiefly in relation to what others have, so that a general rise in income buys no one a better position and the race to earn resumes at a higher level.

Both accounts treat hours as something workers choose, as they might choose how much bread to buy. That premise deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives. For most employees hours come attached to a job, and the menu of jobs is set largely by employers. A firm that pays a fixed cost for each person it hires, in recruitment, training, benefits and supervision, has good reason to prefer fewer people working longer to more people working less. In many professions, moreover, long hours have become a signal of commitment, and promotion goes to those who send it; a lawyer who would gladly trade a fifth of her salary for a fifth of her week may find that the trade is not on offer at all, or that it costs her far more than a fifth of her career. Under such conditions the hours we observe tell us what jobs offer, not what workers want.

The institutional account has a limitation of its own. It cannot easily explain why some people, given a genuine choice, still work very long hours, and it would be a mistake to deny that for many of them the work itself is the attraction. Nor are the averages uniform. In some economies the same decades that lengthened the week for well-paid professionals left many lower-paid workers with fewer hours than they wanted, pieced together from part-time or irregular shifts. An average that holds steady can conceal one group working too much and another too little.

What follows is that the old prediction failed less because of a mistake about human desire than because of a mistake about how labour markets work. The forecasters assumed that rising productivity would be divided between income and leisure by the free choices of workers. The division has in fact been made largely by the structure of jobs, and that structure can be altered: by rules on hours, by the way benefits are financed, by what firms choose to reward. Whether people would then work less is an open question, but it is one that the present arrangement prevents us from answering.

For a long time the standard story about technology and pay was a story about skill. New machines, and computers above all, were thought to complement educated workers and to substitute for the rest, so that demand for the educated rose faster than their supply and the gap between their wages and everyone else's widened. Inequality, in this account, was the outcome of a contest in which schooling had to keep pace with machines, and the remedy was plain: produce more graduates. The story had the virtue of simplicity and the defect of predicting a smooth gradient, with the prospects of jobs improving in proportion to the schooling they required.

What many studies of rich economies in the closing decades of the twentieth century found instead was a hollowing out. Employment grew at the top of the wage distribution and, more surprisingly, at the bottom, while the middle shrank. The explanation that has largely displaced the skill story looks not at workers but at tasks. A computer, on this view, is good at carrying out any procedure that can be fully specified in advance, and the jobs made up mostly of such procedures, keeping ledgers, typing correspondence, inspecting items on a production line, happened to sit in the middle of the wage scale. Jobs at the top require judgement and the framing of problems; many jobs at the bottom, guarding a building, preparing food, helping an elderly person to bathe, require adaptability in physical settings that no program could specify. Neither kind of task was routine, and so both survived.

The task view is a real advance. It explains a pattern the skill view could not, and it shifts attention from the credentials of workers to the content of work. But its central category is less solid than it appears. Whether a task counts as routine is usually settled by asking whether it has in fact been automated, and a classification fixed by results cannot then be used to predict them without circularity. Tasks once thought to demand judgement, such as reading medical images or drafting standard contracts, are now discussed as candidates for automation, and if they are automated they will be relabelled routine after the event. The line between routine and non-routine describes the frontier of a particular technology; it is not a fact about the tasks themselves.

A second difficulty is subtler. Both the skill story and the task story treat technology as an external force that arrives and to which labour markets adjust. Yet which tasks are automated is a decision made by firms, and it depends on what machines cost relative to people, on how the tax system treats investment in equipment compared with spending on wages, and on whether managers regard workers as a cost to be reduced or a capacity to be developed. The same software can be deployed to remove a clerk or to let her handle cases that once needed a specialist. Polarisation, from this angle, is not simply what computers do to jobs; it is partly what a given set of incentives led firms to do with computers.

None of this makes the task view wrong, and it would be careless to replace one tidy determinism with another in which every outcome is a choice. Some tasks really are cheaper to mechanise than others, and no tax code will make a typing pool competitive again. The claim is narrower: that the shape of the wage distribution reflects technology filtered through institutions, and that a theory which treats the filter as fixed will mistake a policy question for a law of nature.

A recurring complaint about modern money holds that it lost its integrity when it ceased to be tied to gold. On this view, a currency backed by metal disciplines governments: they cannot issue what they do not hold, and so savers are protected from the slow erosion of their wealth by inflation. The appeal is easy to understand, since gold is tangible, scarce and ancient, while paper notes and electronic balances seem by comparison to be mere promises, and promises can be broken.

Yet the discipline the gold standard imposed was less a protection than a transfer of risk. Under a metallic standard, the quantity of money depended on the pace of mining and on the flow of metal between countries, neither of which had much to do with the needs of trade. When output grew faster than the stock of gold, prices had to fall, and falling prices are hard on anyone who owes money. A farmer who borrowed against next year's harvest found that the harvest fetched less while the sum he owed stayed exactly the same. Long stretches of gold discipline were therefore stretches in which debtors, who were usually the less wealthy, bore much of the cost of keeping money sound for their creditors.

Nor did the standard remove discretion from governments as completely as its admirers suggest. Countries suspended convertibility during wars and crises, altered the official price of gold, and managed their reserves with a good deal of judgement. The rule held while it was convenient and was set aside when it was not; what it chiefly removed was the ability to respond to a slump without first abandoning the rule itself, and many economic historians have observed that, in the depression of the 1930s, the countries that left gold earlier tended to recover earlier.

None of this means that the nostalgia is groundless. Its real object is not the metal but trust: people want assurance that whoever controls money will not debase it for short-term ends. That is a legitimate demand, and governments have given it plenty of justification, but it is better met by institutions whose conduct can be observed, questioned and corrected than by tying the supply of money to the accidents of geology. Gold offers the comfort of a rule that no one made; the difficulty is that a rule no one made is also a rule that no one can sensibly adjust when circumstances change.

Insurance works by pooling: many people each pay a modest premium so that the few who suffer a loss can be compensated, and the arrangement rests on a fact that is easy to overlook: no one in the pool knows in advance who the unlucky will be. If the pool holds a mixture of people whose risks differ but cannot be told apart, a single price can cover everyone, and the careful and the careless alike buy protection they value.

The trouble begins when buyers know more about their own risk than the insurer does. Those who expect to claim find a uniform premium a bargain; those who expect not to find it expensive, and some of them leave. The insurer, seeing claims rise relative to premiums, raises the price, which drives out the next group of relatively safe customers. In the extreme case the pool shrinks until only the riskiest remain, and a product that many people would have wanted cannot be sold at a price that anyone else will pay. Economists call this unravelling adverse selection, and it can happen even though no one has lied to anyone.

Two remedies are available, and neither is free. The first is for insurers to close the gap in information through medical examinations, questionnaires and records of past claims. Each of these helps, yet each also wears away the pooling that made insurance worth having, because a pool sorted precisely by risk is no longer sharing much risk at all. A person found to have a costly condition before buying cover will be quoted a premium close to the expected cost of treating it, which is to say no insurance in any useful sense. The second remedy is to make membership compulsory or nearly universal, so that the low-risk cannot walk away. This keeps the pool mixed, but it asks the healthy to subsidise the sick on terms that some of them did not choose and regard as unfair.

The choice between these remedies is often presented as a technical matter for actuaries, but it is better understood as a choice about how much of life's bad luck a society wishes to share. For risks that people largely take on by choice, such as a dangerous hobby, pricing by risk seems fair enough. For risks that arrive at birth or by pure chance, sorting begins to look like penalising people twice: once through fate, and again through the price.

Imagine a small-town bank that is entirely sound: its loans are prudent and its borrowers will repay, although those loans run for years while its deposits can be withdrawn on any day. Suppose a rumour spreads that this institution is in trouble. Each depositor now faces a simple calculation: if others withdraw and I do not, my bank may have to sell its loans in a hurry and at a loss, leaving me with little, whereas if I withdraw first, I lose nothing. It is therefore rational to run whether or not the rumour is true, and once enough people run, the rumour becomes true. Such a bank fails not because it was unsound but because it was believed to be.

Deposit insurance is the classic answer, because a guarantee from the state, up to some limit, alters the calculation entirely. A depositor who stays put loses nothing even if her bank collapses, so she has no reason to join a run, and because no one runs, the guarantee is seldom called upon. Seen in this light, insurance looks almost like a free lunch: a promise that, by being believed, makes its own fulfilment unnecessary.

The objection is familiar. Insured depositors have no reason to ask what their bank does with their money, and a bank whose depositors do not ask can take risks that it would otherwise have to justify to them. The guarantee that ends panics may thus encourage the very recklessness that makes failures likely. Critics conclude that deposit insurance trades a visible problem for a hidden one, and some would scale it back so that depositors once again have a reason to pay attention.

The objection is sound as far as it goes, but it rests on a curious picture of who disciplined banks before guarantees existed. Ordinary depositors were never skilled readers of loan books; what they were skilled at was panic. The discipline they supplied was indiscriminate, striking prudent and imprudent banks without distinction once fear took hold, as the town bank illustrates. If insured depositors stop watching, little genuine scrutiny is lost, and the task passes to those equipped for it: supervisors with the power to inspect, and the large uninsured creditors whose money remains at stake. The lesson of the objection is not that guarantees are a mistake but that they must be paired with oversight, and that the limit on cover matters a great deal, since it decides who still has a reason to care.

Long before there were central banks, people understood that a ruler who clipped the edges of coins, or mixed base metal into silver, was taking a share of his subjects' wealth without asking them. The modern version of the idea holds that a government which finances its spending by creating money imposes an inflation tax on everyone who holds that money. No law is passed and no collector calls; the price of bread simply rises, and the real value of the cash in people's pockets falls in proportion. In one respect the analogy with taxation is exact: resources move from the public to the issuer of money, who has spent the new money before its effect on prices is felt.

Critics of this practice argue that it is worse than ordinary taxation precisely because it is hidden: a tax on incomes must be proposed, debated and voted upon; an inflation tax requires only that the issuing authority do nothing to stop it. It also tends to fall heavily on those least able to protect themselves, such as households that keep their savings in cash or depend on incomes fixed in money terms, while it benefits anyone whose debts shrink in real value as prices rise. Among the largest such debtors, of course, is often the state itself.

The analogy misleads, however, when it is pressed too far. A tax is a deliberate choice, whereas much inflation arises from events that no government chose, such as a failed harvest, a war in a distant region or a sudden jump in the price of fuel. Moreover, where most money takes the form of bank deposits that pay interest, and where that interest rises when inflation rises, the revenue a state gains from mild inflation is modest. To describe every increase in prices as a tax is to attribute intention and gain in cases where there may be neither.

What the old idea gets right is the question it trains us to ask: who gains? When inflation is high and persistent and the state is a heavy debtor, the answer frequently points to the treasury, and the language of taxation is then not rhetoric but accurate description. When inflation is mild, or arrives from abroad through the price of imports, the same language obscures more than it reveals. The concept of an inflation tax is best treated as a tool of diagnosis rather than as a verdict reached in advance.

The case for an independent central bank is usually made in terms of temptation. Elected governments face voters at regular intervals, and before an election they are tempted to loosen money, buying a brief rise in output and employment at the price of higher inflation later. Because the public comes to anticipate this, it builds the expected inflation into wages and prices in advance, so that the boost to output never materialises and only the inflation remains. Handing monetary policy to an appointed body with a mandate for stable prices removes the temptation and makes promises of low inflation believable. The gain, on this account, lies in credibility rather than in any superior cleverness on the part of the officials.

Against this stands a democratic objection that is easy to underrate. Decisions about interest rates have large effects on the distribution of income and wealth, between borrowers and savers, between the owners of assets and those who live on wages, and between one region and another. In a democracy, choices with consequences of that kind are supposed to be made by people who can be removed at the ballot box. To delegate them, the objection runs, is to take out of public contest exactly the decisions that most need it.

Both positions are partly right, and the distance between them narrows once we ask what, precisely, has been delegated. Independence in the choice of instruments is not the same as independence in the choice of goals. A legislature can fix the target, an inflation rate for instance, and require the central bank to explain in public whenever it misses; that body then decides how to reach the target, and it alone sets the interest rate. This arrangement preserves the commitment that defeats electoral temptation while leaving the ends of policy with elected representatives, and it answers much of the democratic objection without surrendering the gain in credibility.

The settlement is stable, however, only while the mandate remains narrow. When central banks are asked in addition to secure financial stability, support employment, steer credit towards favoured sectors or manage the risks of a changing climate, the claim that they merely apply technical means to democratically chosen ends begins to wear thin, because deciding how to trade these goals off against one another is itself a political judgement. The more a central bank is asked to do, the weaker its claim to be left alone while doing it.

Debt is described, almost everywhere, in moral vocabulary. We speak of honouring our debts and of meeting our obligations, while default is treated as a failure of character and the borrower who cannot pay is presumed to have been improvident. These words are old, and they carry the experience of every society that has had to persuade strangers to trust one another across time. The language is not wholly misplaced, since a promise to repay is a promise, and a society in which such promises were lightly broken would soon find that no one would lend at all.

The moral framing, however, assigns the whole of the responsibility to one side of what is a two-sided contract. A loan is made by a lender who chose to lend, who estimated the chance of not being repaid and built that chance into the rate of interest, and who has been paid, in that higher rate, for bearing exactly the risk that sometimes comes to pass. When a borrower defaults, the risk for which the lender was compensated has simply materialised. To treat default as a sin rather than as an outcome the contract foresaw is to let lenders collect the premium for risk while disowning the risk itself.

This asymmetry has practical consequences. Where the moral framing is strong, lenders come under less pressure to judge carefully whether a borrower can repay, since any failure will be laid at the borrower's door, and borrowers in difficulty may conceal their distress out of shame instead of seeking to renegotiate early, when a settlement would cost both parties least. A lender that knows blame will travel in only one direction has in effect been relieved of part of the cost of its own mistakes, and an institution relieved of that cost can be expected to make more of them. The bankruptcy law of many countries embodies a different view: it treats a fresh start for an honest debtor as a social good, partly on the practical ground that a person crushed by debts that can never be paid produces little for anyone, creditors included.

None of this licenses casual default, and a borrower who spends money he never meant to return has done wrong in the plainest sense. The point is that obligation runs in both directions: the borrower owes repayment, and the lender owes care in deciding to lend. A moral language that recognised both duties would not be softer than the one we have; it would simply be more accurate about where responsibility lies when a loan goes bad.

When a market collapses, the verdict arrives quickly: it was a bubble, and those who bought near the top were caught up in a collective madness. The diagnosis is comforting, because it implies that the error was obvious and that sober people would have avoided it. It is also, in a great many cases, a judgement that could have been made only afterwards. A price that later falls by three quarters was not necessarily irrational when it was paid; it may have been a reasonable wager on an outcome that simply did not occur.

Consider the shares of firms built around a genuinely new technology. No one knows at the outset which of them will dominate, how large the market will become, or how long any dominance will last. A high price for the whole group can reflect the small chance of an enormous success for one or two of its members, and when most of them then fail, the collapse in prices is consistent with the original bet having been a sensible one. Hindsight converts uncertainty into folly by forgetting that the winners were not known in advance. The same consideration explains why confident announcements that a bubble is under way have such a mixed record, since prices have sometimes gone on rising for years after the warning was issued.

None of this shows that bubbles are a myth. Something does distinguish a bubble from a failed bet, but it is not the size of the eventual fall; it is the reason for which the asset was bought. A buyer who pays a high price because she believes the asset will yield returns that justify it is making a wager that may be mistaken but is not speculative in the narrow sense. A buyer who pays the price only because he expects someone else to pay more, and who would not hold the asset on its own merits for a day, is taking part in something of a different kind: a chain whose value depends on recruiting a next buyer, and which must at some point break.

The difficulty is that this distinguishing mark lies in motives, and prices do not record motives. Two buyers paying the same price on the same day may be doing quite different things, and an observer who sees only the price cannot tell how much of a market consists of believers and how much of passers-on. That is why proposals that regulators should identify bubbles as they form and deflate them, by raising interest rates or restricting purchases, ask for a judgement that is rarely available in time, and why such measures, if applied, are likely to fall on sound and unsound investments alike.

A more modest aim is within reach. What turns the collapse of a price into a wider calamity is usually not the fall itself but the borrowing that financed the purchases, because losses on borrowed money pass from the buyer to the lender, and from the lender to everyone who depends on it. Limits on leverage do not require anyone to know whether a price is justified; they require only that whoever turns out to be wrong should be wrong mainly with his own money. This is less dramatic than a promise to prick bubbles before they grow, and it will disappoint those who want the next crash prevented rather than contained, but a rule that works without foresight has the considerable merit of not depending on a capacity that no one possesses. Such a policy does not aim to prevent bubbles. It aims to make them survivable.

The textbook account of banking runs roughly as follows. Savers deposit money; a bank keeps a fraction of each deposit as reserves and lends out the rest; the borrower spends the loan, the recipient deposits it at another bank, which in turn lends out most of it, and so on, until the original deposit has been multiplied by a factor that depends on the fraction held back. On this account banks are intermediaries, passing the savings of some people on to the projects of others, and the quantity of money in an economy is ultimately governed by the central bank's control over the quantity of reserves.

As a description of what actually happens when a loan is made, this has the sequence backwards. A bank that approves a loan does not hand over notes taken from a vault of accumulated deposits; it credits the borrower's account with a new deposit, and the money the borrower then spends did not exist a moment earlier. Lending creates deposits rather than the reverse. What limits a lender is therefore not a pool of prior savings but its judgement of whether a loan will be repaid at a profit, the capital it must hold against possible losses, the demand from creditworthy borrowers, and the price at which it can obtain the reserves needed to settle payments with other banks, a price that the central bank sets through the rate of interest rather than through the quantity of reserves.

The textbook is not simply wrong. A single bank that lends freely will soon find its new deposits draining away as borrowers pay people who bank elsewhere, and it must then attract deposits or borrow reserves to cover the outflow; from the standpoint of one institution, lending does seem to require funding. The error lies in generalising from the single bank to the system. What is a drain for one bank is an inflow for another, and the system as a whole is constrained less by the deposits it has gathered than by the willingness of banks to lend and of borrowers to borrow.

The difference matters for policy. If the multiplier story were right, a central bank that supplied banks with abundant reserves would set off a roughly proportionate expansion of lending. On the alternative account, when borrowers are cautious and banks are worried about losses, additional reserves may simply sit unused, because nothing in the decision to lend was waiting for them. Arguments about why lending has stalled are then better directed at the demand for credit and the condition of banks' balance sheets than at the quantity of reserves.

A further implication is drawn less often. If banks merely passed on existing savings, the direction of their lending would be a secondary matter, a question of how efficiently funds that already exist are placed. If instead banks create money when they lend, then their decisions about whom to lend to determine what new purchasing power enters the economy, and where. A boom in lending against existing houses and a boom in lending to firms that build new things both enlarge the supply of money, yet they do very different things with it: the first mainly raises the price of what is already there, while the second adds to what there is. Banking, on this view, is not a neutral pipe between savers and borrowers but one of the principal means by which a society decides what its new money will be used for.

Few ideas in economics are cited as often, or misunderstood as thoroughly, as comparative advantage. In everyday commentary trade is described as a contest: a country wins when it is better at making things than its rivals and loses when they overtake it. On this view a nation that is less productive than its neighbours in every industry would have nothing to sell and would be wise to close its borders. The principle of comparative advantage was formulated precisely to show why this conclusion does not follow, and the fact that the conclusion is still drawn suggests that the principle is more often invoked than understood.

The core insight concerns opportunity cost rather than absolute ability. Consider a hypothetical lawyer who types faster than any secretary she could hire. It does not follow that she should do her own typing, because every hour spent at the keyboard is an hour withdrawn from legal work that earns far more. The secretary, though slower at typing, gives up much less by doing it. Both are better off when each concentrates on the task in which his or her relative sacrifice is smallest and they exchange the results. The same reasoning applies to countries. What determines the pattern of trade is not which country is best at producing a good, but which country forgoes the least of other goods in producing it, and every country, however unproductive overall, has some activity in which that sacrifice is comparatively low.

Two consequences follow that sit uneasily with the language of contest. First, gains from trade do not require one party to lose: the lawyer and the secretary both gain, and so do a rich and a poor economy that trade on the basis of their differing costs. Second, a country cannot have a comparative advantage in everything, since being relatively better at one activity means, by definition, being relatively worse at another. A government that promises to make its nation competitive in every industry is therefore promising something that is not merely difficult but incoherent.

None of this implies that the critics of open trade have nothing to say. The textbook argument compares two settled states and is silent about the passage between them; workers who lose their jobs when an industry contracts do not costlessly reappear in the industry that expands, and the losses can be concentrated in particular towns for a generation. Comparative advantage can also shift over time as skills and capital accumulate, which is why some economists defend temporary support for new industries. These are serious objections, but they are objections to the timing and distribution of the gains, not to the logic of opportunity cost. They do not restore the image of trade as a race in which one runner's progress is another's defeat.

Special economic zones are usually defended with a simple argument. Where a country's regulations, infrastructure or courts are too poor to attract investors, it may be impossible to repair them everywhere at once; it is easier to draw a boundary around a small area, supply it with reliable power, quick customs clearance and predictable rules, and invite firms to set up inside. The zone becomes a place where the business environment the country cannot yet afford for itself is provided in miniature. Inside the fence, so the thinking goes, investors will find conditions that would take a generation to create outside it.

The reasoning is persuasive within its limits, and it explains why so many governments have tried the experiment. But it also contains the seed of a common failure. A zone designed to protect investors from the surrounding economy can succeed too well. Firms import their components free of duty, assemble them with local labour and export the finished product, while buying almost nothing from domestic suppliers and teaching them nothing. Export figures rise, and an observer counting shipments would call the zone a triumph. Yet the economy outside the fence may be little changed, apart from the wages paid to workers who commute in, and those wages often reflect the kind of routine assembly that is easiest to move elsewhere when costs rise.

What distinguishes the zones that have mattered is not the generosity of their tax holidays but the degree to which they leak. In the more instructive cases, local firms learned to supply the foreign plants, managers trained inside the zone left to start businesses outside it, and, most important, rules first tried within the boundary were later extended across the country once they had shown that they worked. The zone, on this view, is less an enclave than a laboratory, and a laboratory whose findings never leave the building has failed at its central task, whatever it produces.

It would be naive to conclude that governments should simply abolish the boundary and expect the benefits to spread. The isolation of a zone is often what makes it politically possible in the first place, since it lets reformers try new rules without confronting at once every interest that benefits from the old ones. The point is that isolation should be treated as a starting condition to be outgrown, not as the design itself. A zone that is still, after decades, an island of efficiency in an unchanged sea is evidence less of success than of a reform that stalled.

As tariffs have fallen over the past several decades, attention in trade disputes has shifted to a less visible kind of obstacle: the technical standards a product must meet before it can be sold. Rules on labelling, safety testing, permitted additives and packaging are written for reasons that sound unimpeachable, and many of them are exactly what they claim to be. But a rule can protect consumers and domestic producers at the same time, and it is not always easy to say which purpose is doing the work.

The usual complaint is that standards are protectionism by other means, and examples are easy to imagine. Suppose a country requires that cheese be aged in wooden barrels of a particular kind, a method its own dairies have used for generations, while foreign producers age theirs in steel vessels that yield a product no less safe. The rule says nothing explicit about origin, and its authors need never mention foreign cheese at all, yet its effect is almost that of a ban on imports. A tariff of this severity would be denounced at once; dressed as a quality rule, it may pass unnoticed for years.

It does not follow, however, that every standard which burdens importers is suspect. Almost any rule imposes costs on foreign firms, if only because they must learn it, and societies differ honestly in the risks they will tolerate. One country may accept a pesticide residue that another refuses, not because its farmers lobbied but because its citizens weigh the balance between price and caution differently. To treat all such divergence as disguised protection would be to deny countries the right to set their own levels of acceptable risk, which is a large part of what self-government means.

The more useful test is therefore not whether a standard falls harder on foreigners, but whether its burden is necessary to the purpose it states. A rule that specifies an outcome, such as a maximum level of bacteria, leaves producers free to reach it by any method and so admits anyone who can meet it. A rule that specifies a method, when other methods would achieve the same outcome, deserves closer scrutiny, because the extra cost it imposes buys no additional safety. The distinction will not settle every dispute; outcomes can be hard to measure, and a method is sometimes prescribed precisely because checking the outcome is impractical. But it shifts the argument from motives, which are hard to prove, to fit, which can at least be examined.

For a generation, the managers of manufacturing firms were taught to regard inventory as waste. Parts sitting in a warehouse tie up money, take up space and conceal problems that a tighter system would expose, so the ideal was to have each component arrive just as it was needed, often from a single supplier chosen because it was the cheapest or the best. Applied across borders, this logic produced supply chains of remarkable length and precision, in which a product might cross several frontiers as it was assembled, with little stock held at any stage.

The gains were real, and it would be a mistake to dismiss them in hindsight. Lower costs reached consumers as lower prices, and firms in poorer countries gained access to markets they could not otherwise have entered. But a system tuned to perform well under normal conditions can perform very badly under abnormal ones. When a single factory, port or region on which many chains depend is shut by a fire, a flood or a closed border, there is no slack anywhere to absorb the shock, and the shortage of one cheap part can halt the assembly of goods worth thousands of times as much.

A popular response is to call for production to be brought home. The instinct is understandable, but as a remedy for fragility it is oddly chosen. A chain that depends on one domestic plant is no less exposed to a single fire or flood than one that depends on a single foreign plant; it has merely moved its point of failure to a place that feels more familiar. What protects against disruption is not proximity but redundancy: more than one supplier for critical parts, suppliers in places unlikely to suffer the same shock at the same time, and stocks large enough to bridge an interruption.

Redundancy, however, costs money, which is precisely why lean systems eliminated it. A firm deciding how much spare capacity to keep weighs the expense against its own expected losses from a disruption, but some of the losses fall on others: on patients who cannot obtain a medicine, on other firms whose lines stop, on workers sent home without pay. Because these costs do not appear in the firm's accounts, it will tend to hold less insurance than would be sensible for the economy as a whole. The real question, then, is not where things are made but who pays for the resilience that markets left to themselves will tend to supply too sparingly.

When a country lowers its barriers to imports, the gains and the losses arrive in very different forms. The gains are spread thinly across millions of households, each of which pays a little less for clothing, appliances or food, usually without noticing why. The losses fall heavily on a few: the workers of a particular mill, the shops that depended on their wages, the town whose tax base was the mill. A small saving that nobody notices is politically weightless; a closed factory is a photograph on the front page. Those who lose know exactly what they have lost and whom to blame, while those who gain rarely connect their small savings to a decision taken in a distant ministry. It is not surprising that the politics of trade so often seems out of proportion to its economics.

Economists have a standard reply. Because the total gains exceed the total losses, the winners could in principle compensate the losers and still come out ahead, so that everyone ends up better off. The argument is correct as arithmetic, and it is the foundation of the case that open trade raises national welfare. But the word that carries the weight is 'could'. A compensation that is possible but never paid is no comfort to the people who bore the losses, and to present it as though it settled the matter is to confuse a hypothetical with a policy.

Where governments have tried to pay, the record is unimpressive, though the reasons are instructive. Programmes reserved for workers who could prove that their jobs were lost to imports required them to establish a cause that is often impossible to isolate, since a plant may close because of foreign competition, new machinery and poor management all at once. Many eligible workers never applied; many who applied were retrained for occupations that were themselves shrinking. The failure lay less in the idea of compensation than in tying it to a cause that could not be reliably identified.

This suggests that the better course is not a trade-specific remedy at all but support that follows the worker regardless of why the job disappeared: insurance against lost earnings, help with moving to where work exists, and training linked to employers who are actually hiring. Such measures cannot be justified as payment for trade alone, and they will cost more than narrow programmes did. Yet the case for open trade has always rested on the claim that its benefits are broadly shared. If that claim is to be more than an assertion, the sharing has to be done by someone, and it will not happen by itself.

Trade statistics were designed for a world in which goods were made in one place and sold in another. A customs officer records the full value of a shipment as it crosses the border and attributes it to the country from which it was sent. When a product is made from start to finish in a single country, this convention is harmless. When it is assembled from parts made in a dozen, the convention produces a curious distortion: the country where the last screw is turned is credited with the entire value of the product, including the much larger share that was created elsewhere and merely passed through.

Consider a hypothetical tablet computer assembled in one country from a display made in a second, chips designed in a third and fabricated in a fourth, and software written in a fifth. When the finished tablet is shipped to a sixth country, the statistics record an export of its full factory price from the assembling country, though the work done there may account for only a small fraction of that price. The bilateral balance between the assembler and the buyer swells accordingly, while the suppliers of the costlier components, whose contribution travels unseen inside the assembler's shipment, appear in the bilateral figures as having sold nothing to the final market at all.

Statisticians have responded by trying to trace value added: to ask, for each product, how much of its value was created in each country, and to tally trade on that basis. The striking feature of the results is not that a country's overall position changes, for it largely does not. Its balance with the world as a whole is much the same however one counts, since the value of each imported component is recorded once as an import and again inside the export, and the two entries cancel. What changes is the map: the bilateral balances that attract political attention are redistributed, often substantially, from assemblers towards the countries that supply the most valuable parts.

This matters because bilateral balances are routinely read as a scorecard of who is gaining at whose expense, and policy is sometimes made on that reading. A tariff aimed at the country with which a large deficit is recorded may, on the value-added view, fall chiefly on workers who contributed a modest share of what was bought, while leaving untouched the countries that contributed the most. The value-added figures are not beyond dispute. They depend on tables of who buys inputs from whom that are compiled infrequently and filled out with estimates, and they cannot replace the gross figures that customs administrations need for their own purposes. But one need not regard them as precise to see that they expose a habit of reading the gross bilateral figures as though they measured something they were never built to measure.

The argument for protecting infant industries is older than most of the arguments now made against it, and it is more respectable than its critics often allow. Its premise is that productivity in many industries is learned rather than given. A new steelworks or shipyard in a country without one begins with inexperienced workers, untested managers and suppliers who do not yet know what it needs; it will make costly mistakes for years before it reaches the efficiency of established foreign rivals. If it must meet those rivals at once, it may never survive long enough to learn. A period of protection, on this view, is not a subsidy to inefficiency but an investment in the learning that will eventually remove it.

The argument gains force from a further point. Much of what a pioneering firm learns does not stay inside it. Workers it trains move to competitors, suppliers it develops go on to serve other customers, and the mere demonstration that an industry can work in a given place lowers the risk for those who follow. Over time a cluster of related firms may form around the pioneer, each drawing on skills that the pioneer paid to create. Because the pioneer bears the cost of this learning but captures only part of its benefit, an unaided market will produce too little of it, and there is a case in principle for public support.

The difficulty lies not in the logic but in the ending. Protection is granted on the promise that it is temporary, yet every year it lasts it builds a constituency for its continuation: owners whose profits depend on it, workers whose jobs appear to, and officials whose standing is tied to the industry's survival. Worse, the protection itself weakens the motive to learn. A firm that knows its shelter will be extended whenever it fails to become competitive has little reason to bear the pain of becoming so, and the infant can remain an infant indefinitely, growing larger without growing up. The many cases in which protection outlived any plausible learning period are not accidents of bad administration; they are what the incentives predict.

It follows that the argument stands or falls on whether the exit can be made credible in advance. Protection whose duration is fixed and public, whose renewal depends on measurable progress, and whose beneficiaries are required to compete in some market where the shelter does not reach them, such as export markets, is a different policy from protection granted open-endedly. Export performance is especially revealing, because a firm cannot fake competitiveness in a market it does not control. A protected firm that must also sell abroad, at prices set by rivals it cannot shut out, learns quickly whether it has improved, and so does the government that shelters it. The interesting historical question is therefore not whether successful industrialisers protected their industries, since many did, but whether they attached conditions that forced the protected firms to improve.

None of this makes the conditions easy to impose. Withdrawing support from a large employer that has missed its targets requires a government able to bear the political cost, and the very constituency that protection creates is what makes that cost high. Protection also has victims who are easy to overlook: the firms that must buy the sheltered product at a higher price, and whose own competitiveness suffers as a result. The infant-industry case, then, is best understood not as a general licence but as a demanding bargain, sound in theory and available in practice only to states that can enforce its terms.

The most familiar objection to industrial policy is that governments cannot pick winners. Officials, the objection runs, have neither the information nor the incentives to know which industries will flourish; investors risking their own money are better placed to judge, and when the state substitutes its judgement for theirs it will usually back the wrong horses and keep feeding them long after the race is lost. The objection has history on its side, in the sense that the record of state-backed ventures includes many expensive failures. But it rests on a picture of the problem that deserves closer inspection.

The picture is one in which the menu of possible industries is known and the only question is which item to choose. Investors, in this picture, already know what a country could produce profitably, and the government's error is to overrule them. Yet for an economy trying to move into activities it has never undertaken, no one possesses this knowledge. Whether a particular region can grow cut flowers for export, assemble electronic components or write software for foreign clients depends on a mass of local particulars, from the reliability of the roads to the habits of the workforce, that can be learned only by trying. An investor asked in advance would have no better basis for a forecast than an official; both would be guessing. The relevant knowledge is not hidden in investors' heads waiting to be consulted; it does not yet exist.

Producing it is costly, and here the market's usual advantages turn against it. The first entrepreneur to discover that a product can be made profitably in a given place bears the full cost of the experiment if it fails, but if it succeeds, others can copy the discovery cheaply, entering the industry once its viability has been shown. The pioneer thus bears the losses of failure while sharing the rewards of success, and rational investors will undertake fewer such experiments than the economy as a whole would want. The case for public involvement follows not from officials knowing more than investors, but from no one knowing enough and the cost of finding out being borne unevenly.

If this is right, the objection about picking winners is aimed at the wrong target. A policy of supporting discovery will back many ventures that fail; that is what experiment means, and a programme that never failed would be one that was taking no risks. Measured by the share of its bets that pay off, a sound programme of discovery may look worse than a timid one. The genuine danger lies elsewhere: support, once given, may become impossible to withdraw, so that the losers are kept alive at public expense. What matters is less the ability to pick winners than the ability to let losers go, and the second ability, though rarely discussed, is at least as hard to acquire as the first.

The approach has a cost of its own, and it would be dishonest to minimise it. Discovering what local firms could do requires officials to work closely with them, to learn what obstacles they face and what help would remove them. The same closeness that yields information also invites capture, in which those meant to be overseen come to set the terms. Officials who meet the same managers every month will find it hard to tell them, when a review date arrives, that support is ending. There is no formula that separates collaboration from collusion, only practices, such as public criteria and fixed review dates, that make the difference easier to see. That is a weaker guarantee than the advocates of industrial policy would like, but it is a stronger one than its critics usually assume.

A familiar way of thinking about pollution treats it as a simple wrong: one party harms another, and the law should stop the harm or make the harmer pay. An influential argument in economics asks us to look at the situation differently. Suppose the smoke from a small factory soils the washing of a few households nearby. The harm, on this view, is reciprocal: to protect the washing is to restrict the factory, and to protect the factory is to burden the households. If the parties could bargain freely and cheaply, the argument runs, they would arrive at the efficient outcome whoever held the legal right. If the households had the right to clean air, the factory would pay them to tolerate some smoke whenever its gains exceeded their losses; if the factory had the right to emit, the households would pay it to fit a filter whenever the filter cost less than the damage it prevented.

The conclusion is often summarised as a reason for governments to stand aside: define property rights clearly, and private bargaining will do the rest. That reading takes the conditional for the claim. The striking result holds only when bargaining is nearly costless, and the more interesting lesson lies in how rarely that condition is met. A few households and one factory can meet around a table. A city of several million people breathing the exhaust of a million vehicles cannot. Each resident's share of the harm is small, working out who caused how much of it is difficult, and every resident has a reason to let others negotiate and pay while enjoying the cleaner air for nothing. The costs of finding the parties, measuring the damage and enforcing an agreement swamp whatever gains the bargain might bring.
