Any account that treats the present climate as wholly unprecedented must therefore explain why the appetite it deplores appears so reliably in the commercial history of every earlier medium of mass communication.

But the second story trades on an ambiguity in the word 'want'. A feed ranked by engagement learns what people react to: what they click, what they pause over, what they reply to in anger. Reaction is not the same as endorsement. A person may linger over a provocative post in the way a driver slows to look at an accident, and may say, if asked afterwards, that she wishes she had seen less of such material. A system that learns only from the lingering will give her more of it, and will describe the result as giving her what she wants. It is giving her what she wanted in the moment of reaction, which may be the opposite of what she wants on reflection.

The older media of indignation differed in a further way that the mirror story overlooks. A newspaper editor chose what to print, but the feedback that reached him was slow and coarse, a matter of sales figures and letters to the editor. A feed reports, to every person who publishes in it, exactly how each post performed, often within minutes. Those who write for such an audience learn quickly which tone is rewarded, and many adjust accordingly, not because they are cynical but because they would like to be read. The ranking system therefore does not merely distribute a fixed supply of anger; it shapes the supply, by teaching producers what pays. A mirror that trains the face in front of it is not a mirror.

It does not follow that the remedy is simply to rank posts by what people say, on reflection, that they value. Reflective preferences are harder to measure, easier to misreport and, when a platform infers them, open to the charge that the platform has substituted its own judgement for the user's. These are real objections, and they counsel modesty about any redesign. But they cut both ways. A system that optimises for momentary reaction has also made a judgement about what its users really want; it has simply made that judgement silently, and in favour of the version of the user that is easiest to count. Neutrality, in this domain, is not an available option; the only choice is between an explicit conception of the user's interests and an implicit one.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: showing that testimony is as reliable as perception and reasoning, so that what we are told should be accepted unless it is proved false.
options.B: defending a defeasible default of trust in what others tell us against the demand that every source be verified before it is believed.
options.C: explaining how con artists exploit the trust that ordinary hearers extend to speakers, and how hearers might learn to resist them.
options.D: defending the self-reliant thinker who believes nothing on another's say-so against the charge that such a thinker would know very little.

questions.question: The example of the child who refuses to believe her teachers (paragraph 2) serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that children are more credulous than adults and therefore acquire false beliefs more readily than adults do.
options.B: argue that schools should place less weight on the formal qualifications of the teachers they employ.
options.C: give an instance of testimony that a hearer ought to reject because the speaker has an evident motive to deceive.
options.D: show that the checking the stricter picture demands would itself depend on having first accepted what one was told.

questions.question: A traveller asks a stranger for directions to the railway station and follows them, although she has noticed the stranger winking at his companions as if playing a prank. On the view the author defends, the traveller is best described as

options.A: acting reasonably, because trust is the default and the stranger had given her no proof that his directions were false.
options.B: acting as the stricter picture requires, since she ought first to have checked the stranger's record of giving accurate directions.
options.C: failing to use her entitlement to trust properly, because a plain sign of deceit should have overridden the default.
options.D: acting unreasonably only if the directions turn out to be wrong, since the outcome shows whether her trust was warranted.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 4 that the author locates the main weakness of a default of trust in

options.A: the uneven and exploitable ability of hearers to notice the signals that ought to override it.
options.B: its tendency to make a community poorer in what that community can collectively know.
options.C: the lack of any principled way to tell such trust apart from mere credulity in a hearer.
options.D: the burden it places on every speaker to prove her honesty before anyone believes her.

questions.question: According to the passage, the birdwatcher would properly be asked whether she had ruled out a mechanical decoy if

options.A: someone in a position to know had just announced that decoys were placed along that part of the river.
options.B: she could not tell from the inside whether she was dreaming the scene she reported to others.
options.C: a philosopher pointed out that a decoy indistinguishable at that distance is perfectly conceivable.
options.D: her view of the riverbank had been partly blocked by trees or by the light on the water.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the author says the sceptic 'changes the subject'. This most nearly means that the sceptic

options.A: introduces a new topic, dreaming, that has no bearing on whether someone is really sitting in a room reading.
options.B: uncovers a hidden flaw in ordinary claims to know that the people making those claims had failed to notice.
options.C: replaces the standard that governs ordinary claims to know with a far stricter one and then judges those claims by it.
options.D: abandons the question of what we know and turns instead to the practical question of how we ought to act.

questions.question: The author's attitude to the response that would 'concede the argument and shrug' (paragraph 2) is best described as

options.A: approving, because the response rightly sees that the sceptic's conclusion leaves practical life entirely untouched.
options.B: critical, because the response grants the sceptic's standard a correctness that it has never been shown to have.
options.C: dismissive, because the response overlooks the real possibility that we are in fact dreaming at this moment.
options.D: ambivalent, because the response is generous to the sceptic in one respect but unfair to him in another.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's account of which alternatives a knower must exclude?

options.A: Experienced birdwatchers misidentify herons far less often than beginners do, even when they view the birds from a considerable distance in poor light.
options.B: Many trained philosophers find the sceptic's argument very hard to refute, and some of them regard every refutation proposed so far as unsuccessful.
options.C: On rivers where decoys are known to be common, careful observers routinely check for them before they report a sighting of any wading bird.
options.D: In everyday conversation, people readily withdraw a claim to know as soon as an unlikely alternative is merely mentioned, even with no reason to think it obtains.

questions.question: According to the passage, a majority of experts counts for more when

options.A: its members were all trained by the most eminent teacher working in that particular field.
options.B: it outnumbers the dissenting minority by a wide margin and has done so for a long time.
options.C: its members defend their position more fluently and confidently than the dissenters can.
options.D: its members arrived at their views independently of one another rather than from one common source.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as evidence a layperson can use in judging between disagreeing experts EXCEPT

options.A: whether either expert has made checkable predictions, and how those predictions turned out.
options.B: the number of years each expert has spent working in the field concerned.
options.C: how the other members of the field divide on the question in dispute between them.
options.D: whether either expert stands to gain money or reputation from being believed by the public.

questions.question: The contrast between the careful scientist and the confident charlatan in paragraph 3 serves to

options.A: argue that experts ought to hedge their claims and admit uncertainty more often than they now do.
options.B: illustrate how an expert's financial or institutional interests can be hidden from the public.
options.C: explain why an expert's fluency and ease are poor guides to whether that expert is right.
options.D: suggest that scientists are, on the whole, less trustworthy than other kinds of experts on most questions.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the indirect methods described in paragraph 2

options.A: can make some lay beliefs about an expert dispute more reasonable than others without guaranteeing a correct choice.
options.B: allow a layperson to become as certain about the dispute as the experts themselves are about it.
options.C: are of no use when the question in dispute is among the questions that matter most to the public.
options.D: are most useful to a layperson who can also follow the technical arguments that each expert puts forward.

questions.question: According to the passage, discounting a dissenter because she dissents is faulty reasoning because

options.A: it shows disrespect towards a colleague whose competence and care one has already acknowledged.
options.B: it uses the disputed conclusion itself as the only evidence that the dissenter has gone wrong.
options.C: it ignores information that the dissenter possesses and that the person discounting her lacks.
options.D: it gives the dissenter's view more weight than one's own view on the question under dispute.

questions.question: The example of the two auditors in paragraph 3 functions in the argument primarily to

options.A: show that auditors and similar specialists are seldom true peers, because one of them is usually more careful than the other.
options.B: show that the equal-weight principle must be given up, since some disagreements between equals call for no change of view.
options.C: show that one may hold firm against a peer whenever one is confident that one's own conclusion is correct.
options.D: show that the equal-weight principle applies only where one lacks dispute-independent grounds for thinking the other party erred.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's view of the objection that the equal-weight principle undermines itself?

options.A: It is decisive, because a principle that recommends doubting itself cannot coherently be held by anyone at all.
options.B: It succeeds only if the principle's critics outnumber its defenders among the thoughtful people who have considered it with care.
options.C: It does not show that the principle is false, though it does show that conciliation cannot be all there is to rational belief.
options.D: It is beside the point, because the principle governs disagreements about particular bodies of evidence and not disagreements about principles themselves.

questions.question: In which of the following situations would the author most clearly hold that a person ought to move towards a disagreeing colleague's view?

options.A: Two equally careful historians, working from the same documents, date the same undated letter to different decades, and neither can fault the other's reasoning except by its conclusion.
options.B: Two equally careful chemists disagree about a reaction, but one of them knows that the other's sample was contaminated in a way the other has not noticed.
options.C: Two equally able judges disagree about a verdict, and one of them maintains that the accused was in two different cities at the same moment.
options.D: Two students disagree about a proof, one of whom has studied the topic for years while the other first met it in yesterday's lecture.

questions.question: According to the passage, the shopper's explanation of her choice cannot be true because

options.A: she was not paying attention to the scarves at the moment she made her choice.
options.B: the scarves she chose among did not differ in the respects that she cited.
options.C: an onlooker would have given a quite different explanation of the very same choice.
options.D: she gave it without hesitation, which shows that she had rehearsed it in advance.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the onlooker mentioned in paragraph 2 as

options.A: unable to explain the choice at all, since he has no access to the inner states that caused it.
options.B: likely to explain her choice more accurately if he had first watched her shopping on other occasions.
options.C: better placed than the shopper to explain her choice, since he is free of the biases that distort her view of herself.
options.D: no worse placed than the shopper herself to say why she chose the scarf she did.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: First-person authority is genuine but lies in settling our own commitments, not in discerning the causes of our past actions.
options.B: People ought to be far more sceptical than they are about their own reports of bodily sensations such as pain.
options.C: We know our sensations with certainty, but we can know our beliefs and intentions only by inference from what we do.
options.D: Our sincere explanations of our own choices are usually false, and so self-knowledge is for the most part an illusion.

questions.question: Which of the following questions would a person answer with the kind of authority the passage describes in paragraph 3?

options.A: Whether the ache she has been feeling in her shoulder since the morning is still there now.
options.B: Why she chose ten years ago to study law rather than medicine when she left school.
options.C: Whether she will accept the post she has just been offered, now that she has had time to think it over.
options.D: Whether her irritability over the past week has been caused by her lack of sleep.

questions.question: The examples of the pharmacist and the traveller in paragraph 1 are used to

options.A: show that whether someone deserves blame depends on how her action turns out rather than on what she intended.
options.B: illustrate cases in which a person's ignorance properly excuses her from blame for what she did.
options.C: suggest that most appeals to ignorance are counterfeit and should be met with suspicion by those who hear them.
options.D: show that people who handle goods on behalf of others ought to inspect those goods far more carefully.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the manager in paragraph 2 is responsible because he

options.A: deliberately kept himself from learning facts that he foresaw he might be obliged to act on.
options.B: lied when he later claimed that he had not known how the results were being achieved.
options.C: personally instructed his staff to falsify the safety records in order to meet their targets.
options.D: failed to check every record that his staff produced, as any responsible manager must.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the phrase 'counterfeit form' of the excuse refers to

options.A: a version of the excuse that is used chiefly by people who hold positions of power over others.
options.B: a version of the excuse that courts and other authorities almost never accept in practice.
options.C: a version in which the person lies about what he knew at the time he acted.
options.D: a version that looks like the genuine excuse but lacks any title to the force the genuine one has.

questions.question: Which of the following people would the author most likely regard as guilty of cultivated ignorance?

options.A: A tourist who dines at a popular restaurant without knowing that its kitchen recently failed a hygiene inspection carried out by the local authorities.
options.B: A shopper who buys a cheap shirt at a busy market without first researching the conditions in the distant factory where it happens to have been made.
options.C: A landlord who, after a tenant reports a smell of gas, decides against having the boiler inspected because a fault would oblige him to pay for repairs.
options.D: A clerk who routinely files a forged contract whose forgery an expert examiner later needed specialised laboratory equipment to detect at all.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as things with which intellectual humility is sometimes confused EXCEPT

options.A: an indifference to receiving public credit or recognition for one's own intellectual achievements.
options.B: a habit of introducing one's claims with an acknowledgement that one might be mistaken.
options.C: a tendency to hold every one of one's opinions with only a low degree of confidence.
options.D: a readiness to yield on questions of fact to those people who know more than oneself.

questions.question: When the author says that 'I may be wrong' is 'cheap to say' (paragraph 2), the point is that

options.A: it is a vulgar or careless form of words that thoughtful and well-educated speakers usually take care to avoid.
options.B: saying it costs the speaker nothing and so is no evidence that she really holds her views open to correction.
options.C: it is now said so often in ordinary discussion that it has quite lost the meaning it once had for speakers.
options.D: it undervalues what the speaker knows and so misrepresents how much confidence her evidence actually warrants.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, on the account the author favours, a person who is highly confident about many matters

options.A: ought to defer to recognised experts on every one of the matters about which she happens to feel confident.
options.B: is unlikely to be intellectually humble, since humility consists largely in holding most of one's opinions loosely.
options.C: can be intellectually humble only if she expresses her opinions to others in a suitably modest and tentative manner.
options.D: may still be intellectually humble, if her confidence rests on good grounds and she attends to where her grounds are weak.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the objection raised at the start of paragraph 4?

options.A: Most people find it considerably easier to detect errors in the reasoning of others than to detect errors in their own reasoning.
options.B: Some thinkers who are paralysed by self-scrutiny are nonetheless excellent judges of the arguments that other people put forward in their fields.
options.C: Whenever people fail to notice how their ambitions colour their judgements, their weighing of evidence about the world is distorted to the same degree.
options.D: Many people whom their colleagues regard as intellectually humble are no better than average at weighing evidence about the world.

questions.question: The author's remark that humility 'can be overdone' (paragraph 5) implies that

options.A: humility is valuable only in moderation, and so it matters less to a thinker than the capacity for good reasoning does.
options.B: a thinker who ignores her own limitations is less at fault than one who is paralysed by attention to them.
options.C: the right relation to one's limitations requires judging their extent accurately, not merely attending to them as much as possible.
options.D: the account set out in paragraph 3 must finally be abandoned in favour of the view that humility is a kind of low confidence.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: showing that scientific models are false, and that science therefore yields understanding of the world but never knowledge of it.
options.B: criticising educational systems for testing how well students remember statements rather than how well they can apply them.
options.C: defending the view that understanding is knowledge of causes against the objection that some causes cannot be known.
options.D: arguing that understanding differs from knowledge both in requiring a usable grasp of dependencies and in its more selective relation to truth.

questions.question: The student who has memorised the explanation of the seasons (paragraph 2) serves primarily to

options.A: present someone who seems to know why something happens without understanding it, against the view stated in paragraph 1.
options.B: show that the student does not really know why the seasons change, since an answer that is merely memorised is not knowledge.
options.C: illustrate how idealised models allow students to reason about cases for which their explanations were never originally stated.
options.D: show that what is learned from textbooks and teachers is less reliable than what a student works out through her own reasoning.

questions.question: The passage suggests that part of understanding the simple model of a gas consists in

options.A: knowing a more accurate description of gases that the simple model was introduced to replace in teaching.
options.B: recognising the conditions under which its simplifications stop being harmless and the model begins to mislead.
options.C: being able to state the model correctly in the words used by a reliable textbook or a reliable teacher.
options.D: believing, as the model assumes, that actual gas molecules occupy no space and exert no forces on one another.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author be most likely to accept?

options.A: Knowledge, like understanding, can tolerate falsehood in respects that are irrelevant to the question being answered.
options.B: A person who understands a phenomenon must hold at least some false beliefs about that phenomenon.
options.C: Any explanation that can be applied fluently to new cases yields understanding, whether or not it gets the dependencies right.
options.D: A person can come to understand a phenomenon partly by means of a representation that she knows is not literally true.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards educational systems that measure success by the reproduction of correct statements is best described as

options.A: neutral, because the passage describes how such systems operate without passing any judgement on them.
options.B: contemptuous, because the reproduction of correct statements has no educational value of any kind.
options.C: critical, because such measures cannot detect the gap between possessing an explanation and understanding it.
options.D: approving, because such measures reliably identify the students who know why the things they study happen.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: accept that tools can do memory's work while arguing that this reveals a new reliance on trust, not a larger mind.
options.B: show that biological memory is more trustworthy than notebooks and phones because it cannot be distorted by anyone.
options.C: defend the claim that the mind includes every device its owner consults, against critics who would confine it to the brain.
options.D: warn people who keep their appointments in phones that strangers are likely to tamper with what they have stored.

questions.question: According to the passage, devices differ from biological memory in that

options.A: they store information more accurately, whereas memory steadily loses and distorts what it holds over time.
options.B: others can routinely change what they hold, whereas memory is not open to such revision in the same way.
options.C: they let a person retrieve stored facts with no effort at all, whereas memory always requires some work to search.
options.D: they influence what a person does only when consulted, whereas memory guides action without being consulted.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'authority' refers to

options.A: the degree of confidence a person places in her own recollections.
options.B: the legal ownership of a device and of the data that are stored in it.
options.C: who is entitled to revise the information on which a person's beliefs rest.
options.D: the expertise that makes a particular source of information worth trusting.

questions.question: Based on the passage, the author would most likely describe the case of a woman whose diary has been secretly rewritten by a colleague as

options.A: a real injury to what she knows, best understood as a betrayal of the trust on which her beliefs had come to depend.
options.B: evidence that the diary had become part of her mind, which is the full explanation of why the change feels so harmful.
options.C: proof that the diary was never part of her mind, since nothing belonging to a mind can be altered by someone else.
options.D: an inconvenience no worse than mislaying a shopping list, since the true entries in her diary can usually be reconstructed later from other records.

questions.question: The example of the man and the cake in paragraph 1 serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate how tiredness at the end of a day corrupts a person's judgement of what is good for him.
options.B: present an ordinary lapse whose puzzling features the rest of the passage sets out to explain.
options.C: establish the old view that nobody ever knowingly chooses the worse of two courses.
options.D: show that most people lack the willpower needed to keep their resolutions about food.

questions.question: According to the passage, the muscle picture of the will has the merit of

options.A: treating a lapse as something internal to the person rather than as something imposed on her.
options.B: showing that people who give in to temptation have, for the moment, changed their minds about what is best.
options.C: explaining why putting temptations out of sight helps people keep their resolutions.
options.D: fitting the way lapses feel and accounting for why they are more frequent late in tiring days.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, according to the attentional account, the man who eats the cake

options.A: still holds that refusing is better but has, in the moment, stopped keeping that reason vividly before him.
options.B: has temporarily concluded that eating the cake is the better course after all.
options.C: lacks the strength to act on a judgement that remains clear and vivid to him as he reaches out.
options.D: will certainly give in again unless someone else removes the cake from his sight.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the practical advantage the author claims for the attentional account?

options.A: Lapses of resolution are considerably more frequent in the evening than in the morning, especially after demanding work.
options.B: People who give in to temptation usually report afterwards that they felt overcome at the time by a desire that seemed stronger than they were.
options.C: People who kept tempting food out of view and planned their responses in advance lapsed as often as people who did neither.
options.D: Some temptations prove strong enough to defeat even people who have planned carefully how they will respond.

questions.question: According to the passage, the argument from analogy concludes that another person is in pain on the basis of

options.A: a direct perception of the person's distress in the expression on her face.
options.B: a link between pain and behaviour that one has observed in one's own case.
options.C: what the other person reports, in words, about the feelings she is having.
options.D: a large number of observations of many different people who were in pain.

questions.question: The example of the seeds in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: argue that inductive reasoning in general cannot be trusted when it is applied to living things.
options.B: suggest that the minds of other people differ from one another as much as seeds in a sack do.
options.C: show that the conclusion about other minds can never be confirmed by any further observation.
options.D: illustrate why a conclusion drawn from one instance would be rejected in ordinary reasoning.

questions.question: The author's comparison between seeing that the mother is upset and seeing 'that the cup is full' suggests that

options.A: recognising another person's feeling can be as direct as perceiving an ordinary fact about an object.
options.B: children learn to read emotions by first reasoning carefully about the behaviour of physical objects.
options.C: children understand other people's emotions before they understand facts about physical objects.
options.D: feelings, like the contents of a cup, can be measured precisely by a sufficiently careful observer.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the author's reply to the sceptic?

options.A: People frequently misjudge what strangers from unfamiliar backgrounds are feeling, even when they try hard to understand them.
options.B: Some people can keep a calm and composed face while concealing intense grief or anger from those around them.
options.C: Young children recognise their own mothers' feelings much more quickly than they recognise the feelings of strangers.
options.D: Adults turn out to identify what others feel only by consciously working from observed movements to conclusions about hidden states.

questions.question: The passage presents the judgement view of emotions as explaining each of the following EXCEPT

options.A: why an emotion can be appropriate or inappropriate to its circumstances.
options.B: why a friend can sometimes be argued out of her jealousy by being shown a misreading.
options.C: why a fear can persist after the person has concluded that there is no danger.
options.D: why emotions are directed at objects instead of being mere sensations about nothing.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, if the judgement theory were correct, the frightened traveller would have to be described as

options.A: perceiving the aircraft as dangerous while judging that it is in fact quite safe.
options.B: both believing and denying, at one and the same time, that flying is dangerous.
options.C: simply ignorant of how safe air travel is compared with the drive to the airport.
options.D: undergoing a mere sensation, like an itch, that is not directed at anything.

questions.question: The illusion of the two lines in paragraph 3 serves primarily to

options.A: suggest that emotional conflicts can be ended by a decisive measurement, as the ruler ends doubt about the lines.
options.B: prove that emotions and perceptions are mental states of exactly the same kind in every respect.
options.C: show that a state can present things one way while the person believes otherwise, without contradiction.
options.D: demonstrate that emotions are usually unreliable guides to what is actually valuable in the world.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the perceptual model of emotion can best be described as

options.A: endorsement, qualified by the recognition that the model leaves part of emotional life unexplained.
options.B: neutrality, since the passage sets out the two models side by side without preferring either of them.
options.C: unqualified enthusiasm, since the model removes every difficulty that faced the judgement view.
options.D: scepticism, since emotions are answerable to the person who has them in a way that perceptions are not.

questions.question: According to the passage, the second difficulty for the memory theory is that

options.A: most people forget their early childhood, so memory cannot reach the first years of anyone's life.
options.B: memories might be transferred into another body, which would make two quite different people one and the same person.
options.C: identity must hold from one end of a chain to the other, whereas direct memory need not.
options.D: telling a genuine memory from a convincing false one seems to require knowing already who the rememberer is.

questions.question: It can be inferred that allowing 'overlapping chains of memory' (paragraph 3) to carry identity would let the memory theorist say that

options.A: a vivid but false impression of an examination can now be told apart from a genuine memory of it.
options.B: the old woman is the child, because the teacher links the two even though the old woman recalls nothing of the child.
options.C: the old woman is not the child, since only a direct memory of an earlier stage of life can establish identity with it.
options.D: the teacher and the child are two different people, since the old woman remembers only the teacher.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Personal identity consists in memory, provided memory is understood as overlapping chains rather than direct recall.
options.B: Memory cannot settle who a person is, but it does measure how closely she is tied to her own past.
options.C: Personal identity is ultimately a matter of the body, since memory presupposes the very identity it was originally meant to explain.
options.D: Because memories fade over time, a person gradually ceases to be the same person she once was.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates the distinction the author draws in paragraph 4?

options.A: A man who has forgotten his early years is identified by fingerprints, showing that bodily continuity is what personal identity consists in.
options.B: Two people both claim to remember winning the same prize as children, and the dispute is settled by checking records of which of them was actually present.
options.C: A woman who has lost all memory of her past is told by her doctors that she is now a different person from the one who was admitted.
options.D: A man accepts that he made a promise decades ago but feels it binds him only weakly, having lost almost every link to the life in which he made it.

questions.question: The example of the manager in paragraph 2 is used to show that

options.A: a person can decide each case fairly while the pattern of what she notices remains unfair.
options.B: assertive employees receive better treatment because they complain more often and more loudly.
options.C: managers in general are much less fair than they believe themselves to be.
options.D: applying identical rules to everyone leads, sooner or later, to unjust outcomes for some of the people affected.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the word 'upstream' refers to

options.A: the earlier policy decisions that fixed the rules she now applies to every request for leave.
options.B: the pressure that more senior managers exert on the way she treats her own team.
options.C: the shaping of what a person perceives before she weighs any of the options before her.
options.D: the reserved employee's failure to tell anyone that he was anxious and withdrawn.

questions.question: The objection stated at the start of paragraph 3 depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Attention is formed over time by habits and stories that a person is able to influence.
options.B: Moral life is located chiefly in what a person notices rather than in what she decides.
options.C: Every lapse of attention is, when examined closely, really a deliberate choice of some kind.
options.D: A person can rightly be blamed only for what lies within her voluntary control.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Moral improvement consists solely in learning to see better and never in learning to choose better.
options.B: Since changes in attention are invisible from outside, they cannot be judged morally by other people.
options.C: Someone may be answerable for a failure to notice even if that particular failure was not something she chose.
options.D: Because attention is shaped by habit, each single lapse of attention deserves the same blame as a deliberately bad decision.

questions.question: According to the alternative view described in paragraph 2, attitudes such as resentment and gratitude are

options.A: feelings that a careful moral philosopher should try to exclude from judgements of blame.
options.B: part of living among persons, not conclusions drawn from a theory of causation.
options.C: suspended whenever it can be shown that a person's choice had antecedent causes.
options.D: justified only after the question of whether every choice is determined has been settled.

questions.question: The reference to compulsions, illnesses and conditions of upbringing in paragraph 4 serves to

options.A: show that the practice of blame has been revised by applying its own excusing principles to new cases.
options.B: illustrate how metaphysical arguments eventually forced societies to soften their harsh moral judgements.
options.C: establish that most societies have gradually come to accept the thesis that every human choice is causally determined.
options.D: suggest that people affected by such conditions should no longer be held responsible for anything they do.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the most sweeping sceptical arguments overreach because

options.A: reactive attitudes are natural to human beings and so can never be shown to be mistaken in any case.
options.B: the evidence that every choice has antecedent causes is considerably weaker than sceptics usually suppose.
options.C: the general fact that choices have causes does not show that any particular excusing condition applies.
options.D: people outside philosophy continue resenting and forgiving whatever the latest argument happens to conclude.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main argument of the passage?

options.A: The free will debate is unreal, and findings about self-control are therefore irrelevant to the question of when people deserve blame for what they do.
options.B: Whether anyone is responsible depends on whether determinism is true, a question that the sciences of the mind will eventually settle.
options.C: Because responsibility is a shared practice answerable only to itself, its present standards of blame and excuse are beyond rational criticism.
options.D: Responsibility rests on a shared practice rather than on metaphysics, yet that practice can be corrected, partly with help from the study of the mind.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim in paragraph 5?

options.A: A rigorous philosophical proof that every human choice is determined leaves most people's feelings of resentment entirely unchanged.
options.B: Findings that a condition once dismissed as laziness impairs planning led schools to stop punishing pupils who have it.
options.C: Judges who were taught the general philosophical arguments for determinism became noticeably more lenient toward every kind of offender.
options.D: Societies have differed widely, across history and across regions, in which conditions they treat as diminishing responsibility.

questions.question: According to the passage, the normative form of the narrative view holds that

options.A: a life that cannot be gathered into a coherent story is in some way deficient.
options.B: stories should be used only for making promises, recovering from loss and understanding others.
options.C: a person is a thing that persists unchanged beneath the experiences she has over a lifetime.
options.D: human beings do in fact come to understand themselves through stories about their lives.

questions.question: The reference to a novelist at the end of paragraph 3 serves to

options.A: contrast fiction, in which leaving out what does not fit is harmless, with a life, in which it can be costly.
options.B: recommend that people model their understanding of themselves on the methods of skilled writers of fiction.
options.C: show that novels give a more truthful picture of human experience than the stories that people tell about their own lives.
options.D: argue that people who tell stories about their lives are deliberately deceiving those who listen to them.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard a person who does not experience her life as a plot as

options.A: evidence that the descriptive claim about narrative is false of most human beings.
options.B: having a different way of being a self rather than a defective one.
options.C: probably concealing a story about herself that she would prefer not to acknowledge.
options.D: unreflective about her own past in a way that limits what she can know about herself.

questions.question: In the final paragraph, the claim that the narrative view 'turns a difference in temperament into a deficiency' means that the view

options.A: shows that temperament rather than narrative is what a person's self really consists in.
options.B: regards living by stories and living in the present as mere differences of temperament, neither better than the other.
options.C: explains differences of temperament between people as the outcome of the better or worse life stories they have told.
options.D: treats people who do not live by stories as lacking something when they merely differ in disposition.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's position on the two forms of the narrative view?

options.A: The descriptive form is false, but the normative form remains valuable as an ideal toward which to work.
options.B: The descriptive form is true of everyone, but the normative form wrongly places value on coherence.
options.C: The descriptive form fits many people but probably not all, and the normative form is the more troubling of the two.
options.D: Both forms are false, since narrative has no genuine part to play in a life that is lived well and truthfully.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that blame rightly responds in part to outcomes, while granting that the control principle captures one strand of moral judgement.
options.B: show that the second driver deserves greater blame because he drove more recklessly than the first driver did on the same road.
options.C: defend the principle that people should be blamed only for what lies within their control against our emotional reactions to outcomes.
options.D: argue that the driver who arrived home safely should be treated as blameless because his careless drive harmed no one.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, if the principle that we should be blamed only for what lies within our control is correct, the two drivers

options.A: should each be judged by the harm that their careless driving might have caused on some other night.
options.B: deserve different penalties in law but should feel exactly the same degree of guilt about the drive afterwards.
options.C: deserve exactly the same blame, because their choices, states of mind and recklessness did not differ.
options.D: deserve no blame at all, because neither of them could control whether a child would be on the road.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the driver who arrived home without incident

options.A: ought to feel the same guilt as the second driver, since the two of them drove with equal recklessness.
options.B: owes an apology to the family of the child, since he imposed the same risk that led to the child's death.
options.C: deserves no criticism, because the control principle captures only one strand of our thinking about blame.
options.D: has no ground for taking credit for the fact that his careless drive happened to end without harm.

questions.question: In the last sentence of the passage, the claim that a certain theory has 'impoverished' our moral concepts means that the theory

options.A: makes our moral concepts harder for ordinary people to apply, because it depends on abstract principles about control.
options.B: strips out features of moral life, such as owing an apology for harm actually done, that those concepts rightly contain.
options.C: removes from our moral judgements the emotional confusion about outcomes that had previously distorted them.
options.D: gives too much weight to the outcomes of actions and too little weight to the character of the agent.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the simple form of consequentialism described in paragraph 2 would regard a bystander who declined a rescue that was the best act available to him as

options.A: having acted wrongly, since on that view the best available act is always the one required.
options.B: having performed a supererogatory act of his own by choosing to stay on the riverbank and call for help.
options.C: having done nothing open to criticism, since on that view heroic rescues are never required of anyone.
options.D: having acted permissibly, as long as he did nothing to obstruct anyone else who attempted the rescue.

questions.question: The remark that rescuers 'rarely say that those who held back did wrong' (paragraph 3) serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that rescuers who say that they 'had no choice' are mistaken about the real nature of what they did.
options.B: confirm the defenders' point that people are reluctant to blame others for practical reasons such as usefulness.
options.C: establish that the simple consequentialist is right about what the rescuer ought to have done in the river.
options.D: show that the rescuer's sense of obligation is personal rather than general, which the defenders' reply does not account for.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best fits the author's description in paragraph 4 of the region beyond duty?

options.A: A citizen pays his taxes in full, although he could probably have evaded part of them without ever being detected.
options.B: A doctor feels that she must volunteer in an epidemic zone, though she does not think that colleagues who stay at home are at fault.
options.C: A lawyer handles a case without charging a fee because the court has assigned the case to him under its standing rules.
options.D: A shopper chooses one brand of soap over another for no reason except habit, and would be equally content with either.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the defenders' reply in paragraph 3 is best described as

options.A: neutral, since the author reports the reply without offering any judgement on whether it succeeds.
options.B: wholly persuaded, since the author thinks it reconciles consequentialism with the experience of rescuers.
options.C: appreciative of its ingenuity but convinced that it leaves something important unexplained.
options.D: dismissive, since the author treats it as a confusion that captures nothing of how we actually blame.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: When a promise conflicts with a stronger duty, the stronger duty prevails and the promiser owes compensation for the breach.
options.B: The firmness of promises is an illusion, since a promiser can always claim that his situation was not foreseen.
options.C: Promises bind only within limits set by a shared, reasonable understanding of the circumstances in which they were made.
options.D: A promise must always be kept, because the person who made it freely chose to create the obligation.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, on the author's account, a person who misses a promised lunch in order to take an injured cyclist to hospital

options.A: has committed a minor wrong against the friend, which is excused by the greater urgency of the cyclist's need.
options.B: owes the friend compensation for the lunch, though the friend should not think less of him for missing it.
options.C: need offer the friend no explanation, since both parties already understand that emergencies fall outside promises.
options.D: has not violated any right that the friend acquired when the promise was accepted.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply in paragraph 4 to the worry that promises lose their firmness?

options.A: Some promisers privately intend, at the very moment of promising, to break their promise if it becomes inconvenient.
options.B: For most promises, reasonable people in the promisee's position disagree sharply about which emergencies would excuse the promiser.
options.C: Many people readily forgive a broken promise when the reason they are given for it is a genuine emergency.
options.D: In a few unusual cases, even careful observers cannot agree whether a promise was meant to cover a particular emergency.

questions.question: The passage supports each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: The duty to help the cyclist overrides a right to the promiser's presence at lunch that the friend had acquired.
options.B: A promise gives the person to whom it is made a kind of authority over part of the promiser's future conduct.
options.C: Missing a promised lunch may call for an apology for the friend's wasted time even when missing it was right.
options.D: Letting the promisee's reasonable understanding fix the limits of a promise keeps those limits open to public view.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards a wholesale dismissal of moral intuitions as

options.A: self-undermining, since the dismissal itself appears to depend on judgements of the kind it rejects.
options.B: sound for intuitions about harm, but mistaken for intuitions about which features of a case matter.
options.C: decisive, since it shows that every moral intuition has causes that are unrelated to moral truth.
options.D: irrelevant, because the empirical sciences face no comparable difficulty about the judgements they start from.

questions.question: The reference to the empirical sciences in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: show that moral intuitions can be checked against perception in the same way that scientific reports can.
options.B: suggest that relying on starting judgements that are not questioned at the outset is not a defect peculiar to moral inquiry.
options.C: illustrate how an intuition about harm can come to ignore the quantity of harm that is actually done.
options.D: concede that moral philosophy is less rigorous than science, because its starting judgements can never be checked at all.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about the debunker in paragraph 4?

options.A: Intuitions about the same cases differ considerably between cultures and between historical periods.
options.B: Moral theories have in the past overturned several reactions to cases that were once very widely shared.
options.C: A debunker could justify discarding all moral intuitions from purely non-moral premises, with no judgement about which features of cases matter.
options.D: Philosophers who reject intuitions in their writing still rely on them when making their everyday decisions.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the remark that 'the circle is wide' is best understood to mean that

options.A: the method takes a long time to arrive at a state of balance, although it does arrive there in the end.
options.B: the method admits so many intuitions that it is able to endorse almost any moral theory whatever.
options.C: critics have exaggerated the circularity, because in the end principles hold final authority over judgements about cases.
options.D: the adjustment ranges over a great many judgements and principles, so its circularity does not leave it empty.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: explaining how a victim can stop thinking about a wrong once the person who committed it has died.
options.B: arguing that forgiveness remains possible without an apology, although an apology often makes it easier and more apt.
options.C: showing that genuine forgiveness requires the wrongdoer to acknowledge the wrong, express remorse and make amends.
options.D: criticising people who forgive quickly on the ground that they lack both self-respect and moral seriousness.

questions.question: According to the account the author favours, to forgive is to

options.A: excuse the wrongdoer, on the ground that he could not in the circumstances have acted otherwise.
options.B: accept the wrongdoer's apology and restore the relationship to what it had been before the wrong.
options.C: decide that the wrong no longer matters, so that it need no longer be judged as a wrong at all.
options.D: give up resentment and the claim to repayment while still judging that the act was wrong.

questions.question: If the woman described in paragraph 2 forgave her former friend although he refused to admit anything, the author would most likely regard her forgiveness as

options.A: genuine, though offered as a gift and for reasons of her own rather than in answer to his remorse.
options.B: a sign that she lacks self-respect, since anyone who forgives without receiving an apology lacks it.
options.C: impossible, since on any sound account the conditions for forgiving depend on the friend's change of heart.
options.D: a way of excusing the wrong, since nothing in the friend's conduct has changed to make forgiving him fitting.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the view that forgiveness must be earned is best described as

options.A: approving, since the author holds that wrongs rightly make demands on wrongdoers.
options.B: contemptuous, since the author holds that it confuses forgiveness with forgetting.
options.C: respectful of its moral seriousness but critical of what it implies for victims.
options.D: indifferent, since the author's real concern is the danger of forgiving too readily.

questions.question: The author suggests that, if relativism is true, a tolerant culture faced with a culture that prizes conquest could

options.A: persuade the conquering culture to stop by showing that its own standards in fact forbid conquest.
options.B: do no more than report that tolerance is valued in its own culture, without giving the other a reason.
options.C: justify intervening by force to protect the peoples that the conquering culture threatens.
options.D: condemn conquest as wrong by appealing to a moral standard that both cultures are bound to accept.

questions.question: The author makes or accepts each of the following points EXCEPT that

options.A: the argument of paragraph 2 establishes that moral relativism is false.
options.B: doubt about moral matters can leave people unable to object to anything at all.
options.C: the case against intervention can rest in part on the poor record of forced conversion.
options.D: certainty that one's own customs embody universal truth has been used historically to justify coercion.

questions.question: Which of the following positions is closest to the view the author describes in paragraph 4?

options.A: A visitor declines to judge her hosts' customs at all, believing that their rightness depends only on the standards of her hosts.
options.B: A visitor judges her hosts' custom to be unjust and supports forcing them to give it up, since moral truths bind everyone alike.
options.C: A visitor praises her hosts' customs in public to avoid giving offence, while privately condemning them as barbaric.
options.D: A visitor judges one of her hosts' customs to be unjust, says so when asked, and still opposes any attempt to abolish it by force.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 3 in the author's argument?

options.A: It concedes that the objection of paragraph 2 fails, since believing relativism does in practice make people more tolerant.
options.B: It presents historical evidence that cultures holding relativist beliefs have been more tolerant than other cultures.
options.C: It considers a revised version of the relativist's case and argues that this version abandons the claim that relativism grounds tolerance.
options.D: It shows that relativism is false by demonstrating that doubt always leaves people unable to object to anything.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Moral progress is best pictured as a single line along which every society advances in the same direction.
options.B: Moral progress is real but is better understood as a series of corrections than as the widening of a circle of concern.
options.C: Moral progress consists in extending moral concern to those beings who were previously left outside its boundary.
options.D: Talk of moral progress is largely the self-congratulation of each age as it looks back on the ages before it.

questions.question: The author's discussion of the beating of wives in paragraph 3 suggests that

options.A: the reform of such practices came about by extending moral concern to people who stood outside the circle.
options.B: attitudes to wives have changed far less over time than attitudes to the treatment of children have.
options.C: a practice can be gravely wrong even when those it harms are fully recognised as objects of moral concern.
options.D: in the societies that permitted such beating, wives were not regarded as being morally considerable at all.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Any extension of moral concern to new beings is an advance, whatever form the extension takes.
options.B: Changes in moral attitudes, like changes in fashion, are neither better nor worse than what they replace.
options.C: The inclusion of animals within moral concern is the clearest case of moral progress in recent times.
options.D: An age may rightly judge some earlier practices mistaken without being able to state a complete moral theory.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's criticism of the circle image in paragraph 4?

options.A: Some movements that extended concern to distant peoples used that concern chiefly as grounds for ruling them against their wishes.
options.B: Many people who doubt the idea of moral progress in theory still accept it when they consider particular cases.
options.C: Concern for the welfare of animals has grown steadily in many countries over the course of the last century.
options.D: Several societies that once excluded foreigners from moral concern later came to include them fully and fairly.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures what the author means by 'the vanity of the present' in paragraph 5?

options.A: the preference of each generation for its own fashions, such as the length of coats, over older ones
options.B: the belief of present societies that they are more prosperous and comfortable than those of the past
options.C: a society's pride in how wide its own circle of concern is compared with the circles of its neighbours
options.D: an age's habit of treating its own standards as the measure by which earlier ages are found wanting

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 1 that, on the conception of virtue described there, a person who is generous to her friends but consistently mean to strangers

options.A: lacks the virtue of generosity, since her good conduct does not extend across circumstances.
options.B: should be assessed by the outcomes that her generous acts produce for the friends who receive them.
options.C: possesses the virtue of generosity, though only in a partial form that is genuine as far as it goes.
options.D: has a virtue rather than a mere habit, provided that her generosity to her friends is entirely sincere.

questions.question: The reference in paragraph 3 to advice about avoiding temptation and choosing companions serves to

options.A: suggest that full virtue can be acquired quickly by anyone who follows a few simple practical rules.
options.B: illustrate the breadth across circumstances that distinguishes a genuine virtue from a mere habit.
options.C: show that the classical tradition already treated ordinary character as easily swayed by circumstance.
options.D: show that the experimental findings on which the situationists rely are unreliable and should be set aside.

questions.question: Which of the following is most analogous to the dilemma that paragraph 5 says virtue ethics now faces?

options.A: A rulebook for a game can be replaced without loss by a description of how skilled players actually behave in matches.
options.B: A map can be drawn to show the route an expert ought to take or to record the paths walkers actually use, but hardly to do both at once.
options.C: A recipe that usually fails when beginners attempt it must have been written incorrectly by the cook who devised it.
options.D: A training programme grows more effective the more often its trainees repeat each of the exercises it prescribes.

questions.question: The passage provides support for each of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Some of the experimental work on which the situationists draw has since been called into question.
options.B: If virtue ethics claimed that most people have the virtues, the experimental evidence would count heavily against it.
options.C: Making virtue very rare in order to answer the critics weakens the theory's claim to describe moral life as it is lived.
options.D: The situationist evidence, if accepted, shows that the classical account of full virtue is mistaken.

questions.question: The author's stance towards the debate between the situationists and the defenders of virtue ethics is best described as

options.A: partisan in favour of the situationists, whose experimental evidence is said to refute the theory of virtue.
options.B: balanced: each side is granted a real point, and the defenders' reply is shown to carry a price.
options.C: partisan in favour of the defenders, whose reply is said to meet the challenge without any cost to the theory.
options.D: detached and sceptical, holding that nothing either side has said bears on the truth of virtue ethics.

questions.question: The central argument of the passage is that

options.A: citizens owe obedience to their state only if they have signed an explicit agreement to obey its laws and accept its courts.
options.B: the right to leave a country is the most important test of whether a state's authority over its citizens is legitimate.
options.C: merely living in a country cannot supply the consent that would legitimise its authority, though the freedom to leave still matters.
options.D: tacit consent is a sound basis for political authority provided that emigration is made cheap and easy for every citizen.

questions.question: According to the passage, emigrating does not free a person from political authority because

options.A: nearly every habitable part of the earth already falls under the claim of one state or another.
options.B: the costs of abandoning one's language, family and work are far too high for most people to bear.
options.C: the country of origin continues to make legal claims on its citizens even after they have settled abroad.
options.D: most states refuse to admit newcomers who are unable to bring their savings with them from the country they left.

questions.question: Which one of the following best captures the meaning of 'the choice of a ruler' as used in paragraph 2?

options.A: Each citizen may decide for herself which of the state's laws she is willing to accept.
options.B: A person who leaves can decide which state will govern her, but not whether any state does.
options.C: Citizens of every state are entitled to elect, at regular intervals, the government under which they live.
options.D: Those who leave a country usually end up living under a stricter government than the one they left.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following about a state that allows its citizens to emigrate freely?

options.A: It has no stronger claim on its citizens' loyalty than a state that seals its borders against them.
options.B: It is legitimate so long as the cost of leaving remains low enough for most of its citizens to bear.
options.C: It passes one test of legitimacy, but its right to govern those who stay depends on how it treats them.
options.D: Its citizens who choose to remain have, by staying, given it a valid if tacit form of consent to its laws.

questions.question: According to the passage, what distinguishes toleration from indifference?

options.A: Toleration requires that one first come to approve of the practice that others follow.
options.B: Toleration is a feeling of mild dislike, whereas indifference is the absence of any feeling.
options.C: Toleration concerns matters of public law, whereas indifference concerns private habits like diet.
options.D: Toleration involves refraining from acting against something that one still regards as wrong.

questions.question: The example of the mother in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: illustrate how a person can keep an objection while ranking it below other reasons for not interfering.
options.B: show that disagreements within a family are much harder to tolerate than disagreements between strangers who meet only rarely.
options.C: demonstrate that an objection to another person's choices usually fades once it has been spoken aloud.
options.D: suggest that toleration comes most easily when the person tolerated depends on the tolerator for money.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the critics who find toleration condescending is best described as

options.A: dismissive, since the author treats their complaint as a simple misunderstanding of what toleration really means.
options.B: persuaded, since the author concedes that a just society should move beyond toleration towards affirmation.
options.C: neutral, since the author sets out the critics' view without indicating whether it has any merit at all.
options.D: qualified disagreement: their complaint is granted some force, but toleration is defended as fitting a deeply divided society.

questions.question: Which of the following is the clearest case of toleration in the sense the passage defines?

options.A: A shopkeeper who has no opinion either way about his customers' diets stocks whatever foods they ask for.
options.B: A club secretary who thinks a member's taste in clothes absurd tells him so, but votes against a stricter dress code.
options.C: A man who once disapproved of his brother's marriage comes to admire the couple and stops objecting.
options.D: A resident who objects to a neighbour's new fence complains to the council and has the fence removed.

questions.question: The case of punishing an innocent person whom the public believed guilty (paragraph 1) is used to

options.A: suggest that justifying punishment only by its effects would permit something most people find unacceptable.
options.B: establish that swift punishment deters more effectively than slow and careful punishment of offenders.
options.C: show that forward-looking theories are mistaken in assuming that punishment actually deters people from committing crime.
options.D: argue that public opinion is an unreliable guide to whether accused persons are guilty or innocent.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, on the expressive view, a fine for parking in a forbidden place differs from an equal charge for using a toll road in that

options.A: the first is felt as a heavier burden, since a fine is normally larger than a charge for a service.
options.B: the first is meant to discourage future offences, whereas the second only raises money for the road.
options.C: only the first conveys that the driver has done something wrong for which he is answerable.
options.D: only the second is a declaration by the community, since the toll is fixed in advance by public authority.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the expressive theorist's reply in paragraph 3?

options.A: Long prison sentences do less to reduce reoffending than shorter sentences combined with close supervision after release.
options.B: Judges in different countries tend to deliver their verdicts in quite different styles and in very different forms of language.
options.C: Fines that are very small relative to an offender's wealth tend to be treated by offenders as a routine cost of doing business.
options.D: Where courts declare offenders guilty but impose no penalty, the public judges those offences as serious as ones punished by imprisonment.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT

options.A: a principle of proportion is the only constraint that could set limits on how severe punishment becomes.
options.B: the same prison sentence may be heard as lenient in one society and as harsh in another.
options.C: the expressive theory, though it needs supplementing, captures something that forward-looking theories overlook.
options.D: a theory that justifies punishment solely by its effects faces a serious difficulty about the innocent.

questions.question: As used in the last sentence of the passage, 'hold it more lightly' most nearly means

options.A: cut the rewards attached to achievement until the inequalities between people become small.
options.B: keep rewarding achievement while giving up the belief that rewards show what people morally deserve.
options.C: stop using tests of talent and effort to decide who receives positions and rewards in a society.
options.D: treat success as a matter of pure chance that has nothing whatever to do with a person's effort.

questions.question: The author's distinction between desert and entitlement implies that a person who won a prize in a competition whose rules had been rigged in her favour

options.A: would deserve the prize in a deep moral sense, since no competitor chooses the rules under which a contest is run.
options.B: would be entitled to the prize, provided that her talent was the product of her own effort rather than luck.
options.C: would not be entitled to the prize, even if she were in fact the most talented competitor.
options.D: would be wronged if the prize were taken away, because she competed on the understanding that winning would bring it.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates entitlement without desert, in the author's sense?

options.A: A lottery winner has a valid claim to the jackpot under the rules of the draw, though nobody thinks she earned it.
options.B: A firm abolishes all bonuses because its managers conclude that performance is mostly a matter of good luck.
options.C: A worker paid less than a colleague for the same work complains that the firm's pay scale is unfair to her.
options.D: A runner who finished second insists that she deserved the prize more than the winner because she trained harder.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Meritocracy is superior to aristocratic privilege because it rewards people for qualities that they have freely created in themselves.
options.B: A fair society should keep reducing inequalities of reward until they no longer reflect any differences in people's talent or effort.
options.C: Because talent and effort depend so heavily on luck, no one is truly entitled to any of the rewards that a meritocratic society distributes.
options.D: Luck in talent and effort defeats the idea that rewards track moral worth, not the case for honouring rewards earned under fair rules.

questions.question: According to the critics described in paragraph 2, the ideal of public reason falls unevenly because

options.A: laws justified by shared reasons tend in practice to serve the interests of the largest groups in society.
options.B: citizens whose convictions already resemble the shared vocabulary lose nothing by observing it.
options.C: citizens with religious convictions are forbidden from voting on any laws that touch on those convictions.
options.D: legislators and judges are held to a much stricter standard of justification than ordinary citizens.

questions.question: On the reading of the ideal that the author defends in paragraph 3, the ideal of public reason would be violated if

options.A: a judge supported a decision with shared reasons that some citizens nevertheless found unconvincing.
options.B: a citizen explained to her neighbours that she voted for a law because of her religious convictions.
options.C: a coercive law were enacted that could be defended only by appeal to a doctrine many citizens reject.
options.D: most supporters of a law had been moved by considerations other than the shared reasons offered for it.

questions.question: The comparison with a bridge at the end of the passage serves to

options.A: show that ordinary citizens lack the competence to judge laws and should defer to the officials who draft them.
options.B: support the claim that whether a law is justified does not depend on why each of its supporters backed it.
options.C: concede that insincere advocacy weakens the legitimacy of any law that is passed with its help.
options.D: illustrate the critics' complaint that the ideal demands technical expertise that most citizens do not possess.

questions.question: The author's reply to the critics in paragraph 3 depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Most citizens' political views are in fact independent of their wider philosophical or religious outlooks.
options.B: Legislators and judges, unlike ordinary citizens, hold no comprehensive convictions of their own about value.
options.C: Whether a law could be supported by shared reasons can be judged apart from the reasons its supporters actually gave.
options.D: Citizens who argue from their own outlooks will usually go on to supply shared reasons for their positions as well.

questions.question: According to the passage, the second, 'less often stated' part of the case for majority rule is that

options.A: those outvoted on one question can expect to win on others, because coalitions shift as issues change.
options.B: majorities are more likely than minorities to reach the correct answer on most questions of public policy.
options.C: counting every vote equally is the only procedure that can treat each voter as the equal of every other.
options.D: minorities can always appeal to independent courts to protect the interests that matter most to them.

questions.question: The passage suggests that encouraging 'cross-cutting associations' would help a persistent minority chiefly because such associations

options.A: persuade members of the majority that decisions reached by counting votes are very often mistaken.
options.B: guarantee smaller groups a fixed share of the seats in the national legislature and in regional bodies.
options.C: move decisions about the most contested questions out of elected bodies and into independent courts.
options.D: make it less likely that the same people end up on the losing side of every vote that matters to them.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as a cost of a proposed remedy EXCEPT that

options.A: rules requiring supermajorities make it harder to change whatever injustices the existing arrangement contains.
options.B: rights that no majority may override transfer power to courts that the minority cannot hold to account.
options.C: electoral systems giving smaller groups a share of seats tend to make stable governments harder to form.
options.D: giving regions power over their own affairs can produce new minorities inside those very regions.

questions.question: In a country whose politics are dominated by a single linguistic division that could, with effort, be loosened, which policy would the author most likely favour first?

options.A: Granting the region where the linguistic minority is concentrated full control over its own internal affairs.
options.B: Replacing elections with an arrangement under which the two language communities take turns to hold office.
options.C: Requiring a two-thirds majority for all legislation that affects the interests of the linguistic minority in any way.
options.D: Supporting national bodies, such as trade associations and sports leagues, whose members are drawn from both language communities.

questions.question: According to the passage, why might the tenant's life contain little interference even though she is not free?

options.A: The law prevents landlords from evicting tenants who have complained to them about necessary repairs.
options.B: She shapes her own conduct to stay in the landlord's good graces, so he rarely has any reason to intervene.
options.C: Her lease forbids the landlord from interfering with the choices she makes about how to live in the flat.
options.D: She is able to contest the landlord's decisions in court whenever he acts against her interests.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 5, 'the structures that make some things unthinkable to attempt' refers to

options.A: arrangements of power under which people do not even try certain things because of how others could respond.
options.B: social customs that make certain choices look irrational to every member of a society, whatever their position.
options.C: laws that explicitly forbid certain actions and punish those who are caught attempting them.
options.D: institutions that guarantee rights of exit, of appeal and of collective voice to those subject to power.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the benevolent ruler described in paragraph 3?

options.A: His rule is legitimate in the rival tradition's sense provided his subjects remain free to leave his territory.
options.B: His subjects would become free in the rival tradition's sense if he publicly promised never to interfere with them.
options.C: On the non-interference view, his subjects could count as freer than citizens restrained by laws they are able to contest.
options.D: He dominates his subjects only on those occasions when he actually chooses to interfere with their choices.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the critics' objection in paragraph 4?

options.A: Some relationships, such as long friendships, contain no capacity at all for either party to make the other's life worse.
options.B: Efforts to decide which forms of power over others are arbitrary have repeatedly turned on how much each form lets its holder interfere.
options.C: Tenants whose leases permit eviction at will report far more anxiety than tenants whose leases are secure.
options.D: Granting workers rights of appeal and collective voice has, in several firms, reduced how often they defer to managers.

questions.question: The author's overall attitude towards the view of freedom as non-domination is best described as

options.A: appreciative of its diagnostic insight, while doubting that it can serve as a precise measure of freedom.
options.B: convinced that it should replace the non-interference view as the single correct account of political freedom.
options.C: sceptical, regarding it as an elastic notion that in the end collapses back into the non-interference view.
