options.D: neutral, presenting the two traditions side by side without venturing any judgement on their relative merits.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the two views described in paragraph 2 escape the levelling-down objection because they

options.A: require that every inequality above a minimum standard of living be removed, whatever the cost to the better off.
options.B: deny that people who are badly off have any special claim on the resources that a society has to distribute.
options.C: treat inequality as bad in itself, but as much less bad than the suffering of people who lack enough to live on.
options.D: attach no value to narrowing a gap between people when that narrowing raises no one's well-being.

questions.question: The example of a promise kept at terrible cost (paragraph 3) is offered to show that

options.A: something can be good in one respect even when it is not the right choice overall.
options.B: promises ought to be kept even when keeping them causes great harm to the person who made them.
options.C: equality and the keeping of promises are two values that usually come into conflict with each other.
options.D: egalitarians, like people who keep costly promises, are often admired chiefly for their consistency.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, calling equality, on the defence just given, 'a strangely impersonal' value means that it

options.A: can be assessed only by impartial officials who have no personal stake in how goods are distributed.
options.B: could make a situation better even though the situation was better for no particular person.
options.C: applies to the design of public institutions rather than to private relationships between individuals.
options.D: is held in a detached and unemotional way, as a matter of principle rather than of feeling for others.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that a relational egalitarian, considering a society that has abolished titles but retains very large differences in wealth, should

options.A: set aside questions of income entirely, since the relational view is concerned with standing and not distribution.
options.B: regard that society as fully equal in the relevant sense, since no one in it holds any formal rank.
options.C: favour reducing everyone's wealth to the level of the poorest, since this would make all the citizens equal.
options.D: ask whether those differences have become large enough to give some people standing over others.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Equality cannot be a genuine value in its own right, because every genuine value must make situations better for some person.
options.B: The levelling-down objection shows that egalitarians should give priority to benefits for the worse off rather than value equality as such.
options.C: The levelling-down objection can be answered, but the answer makes equality impersonal, which favours a relational account despite its open questions.
options.D: The levelling-down objection is decisive against every form of egalitarianism except one concerned with relations of rank between persons.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that employees never genuinely consent to the terms on which they are hired, whatever their contracts say.
options.B: challenge the standard defences of watching employees and suggest a narrower basis on which watching can be justified.
options.C: argue that every form of workplace monitoring is unjustified and that employers should stop watching their staff altogether.
options.D: explain how the timing of calls has damaged the quality of the help that customers receive from support workers.

questions.question: The example of the carpenter in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: indicate that workers paid by the day are entitled to more privacy than workers who are paid a monthly salary.
options.B: illustrate the claim that consent given by someone who badly needs a job cannot make its terms fair.
options.C: show that buying someone's labour does not give the buyer a right to observe all that the person does.
options.D: suggest that employers should judge the quality of finished work rather than count the hours spent on it.

questions.question: According to paragraph 3, the information produced by monitoring grows less useful as more of it is collected because

options.A: what is recorded increasingly reflects behaviour staged for the observer, not the work.
options.B: managers who receive very large quantities of data cannot interpret it with any accuracy.
options.C: customers complain when support workers end their calls before problems have been fully solved.
options.D: employees learn to disable or evade the software that records their keystrokes and pauses.

questions.question: Which of the following practices would the author be most likely to regard as justified?

options.A: A call centre times every call and ranks its staff each week by average call length in order to encourage greater efficiency.
options.B: A firm records every employee's screen throughout the working day, having explained the policy in each contract and obtained every employee's signed agreement to it.
options.C: An office installs software that logs idle minutes on all computers so that managers can see which employees are working hardest.
options.D: A hospital logs which staff open patient files and reviews a log only when a file appears to have been opened without a clinical reason.

questions.question: According to the passage, what makes a lie harmful is chiefly that

options.A: the listener is likely to act on the false belief and suffer some material loss as a direct consequence.
options.B: the liar's own character is corrupted, so that his later statements gradually become less believable to everyone.
options.C: the lie, once discovered, damages the relationship between the speaker and listener beyond repair.
options.D: the listener is left with an unchosen false belief, and the trust he placed in the speaker is misused.

questions.question: The used car negotiation in paragraph 3 is introduced in order to

options.A: suggest that competent buyers are better at detecting falsehoods than most managers are.
options.B: demonstrate that misleading is just as bad as lying even when both parties are on their guard.
options.C: identify a kind of situation in which misleading is genuinely less objectionable than lying.
options.D: show that deceiving people is acceptable in commercial dealings because buyers expect to be deceived.

questions.question: A doctor knows that a patient's prognosis is poor. Asked about it, she says, truthfully, that most people with the condition live for many years, intending the patient to infer that her own outlook is good. On the passage's argument, the doctor has

options.A: done something worse than lying, because a misleading truth is much harder for a trusting listener to detect.
options.B: wronged the patient in much the same way as she would have if she had simply told her a lie.
options.C: acted acceptably, because the patient remained entirely free to ask directly about her own case and to draw her own conclusions.
options.D: wronged the patient only if the patient later learns the truth and is distressed by what she discovers.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the widely shared intuition described in paragraph 1 as

options.A: tracking a real difference, though one that matters only in certain kinds of relationship.
options.B: correct in its ordinary moral form but mistaken in the form that legal systems have given it.
options.C: a rationalisation invented by people who want to deceive others without feeling guilty about it.
options.D: a reliable guide in every setting, although people like the employee sometimes misapply it.

questions.question: According to the passage, the appeal of substituted judgement lies mainly in the fact that it

options.A: spares relatives the need to discuss treatment decisions with doctors and with other members of the family.
options.B: tends to produce outcomes that are medically better for patients than the outcomes of the best-interests standard.
options.C: lets the patient's own values keep governing her care after she has lost the ability to decide.
options.D: gives doctors, rather than relatives, the final responsibility for decisions about an unconscious patient's treatment.

questions.question: The example of the trial of dialysis in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: demonstrate that the best-interests standard leads to kinder outcomes than substituted judgement does.
options.B: illustrate a decision on which a patient's known views give the surrogate no real guidance.
options.C: show that patients who wish to die at home generally refuse treatments that may prolong their discomfort.
options.D: illustrate a clear prior instruction that a surrogate who respects the patient's autonomy is bound to follow.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about the second cost of substituted judgement?

options.A: Relatives who later doubted their reading of a patient's wishes were, on the whole, no more distressed than relatives asked from the start to decide what was best for her.
options.B: Patients who left written instructions were more likely to have their wishes followed than those who expressed them only in conversation.
options.C: Many relatives say that they found substituted judgement a real comfort when they were required to make difficult treatment decisions on behalf of patients who had lost the capacity to decide.
options.D: Doctors and relatives frequently disagree about what an unconscious patient would have wanted, and such disputes are seldom openly resolved.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that a surrogate who has no reliable knowledge of a patient's wishes on the matter at hand should

options.A: reconstruct her wishes as carefully as possible from scraps of earlier conversation and follow that reconstruction.
options.B: abandon substituted judgement in this case and also in cases where her wishes are clearly known, for the sake of consistency.
options.C: refuse to take part in the decision, leaving it to doctors who can judge the patient's interests more objectively.
options.D: acknowledge openly that he is choosing what seems best for the patient rather than what she would have chosen.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'directed wrongs' are best understood as wrongs that

options.A: consist in what is done to some particular person, so that benefiting someone else cannot repair them.
options.B: are committed deliberately and with full knowledge, as opposed to harms that are caused by accident or neglect.
options.C: are ordered by one person but carried out by another, as when the unfaithful man pays his friend.
options.D: cause damage only through the total amount of similar harm that everyone together has committed.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would describe a scheme that credits travellers for planting trees that would have been planted anyway as one that

options.A: is morally no different from buying a pardon, which confirms the critics' charge against offsetting in general.
options.B: still partly undoes the harm of the flight, since the traveller paid in good faith for what she was promised.
options.C: shows that offsetting is incoherent even for aggregate harms once it is actually put into practice.
options.D: leaves the harm unrepaired, a failing to be exposed by checking the scheme rather than by condemning offsetting.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the worries described in paragraph 4 is best described as one of

options.A: full endorsement: the worries show that offsetting ought to be discouraged until conduct has changed.
options.B: qualified acceptance: the worries are genuine, but they do not show that offset harms remain unrepaired.
options.C: detached neutrality: the worries are reported without any judgement of their weight or of their relevance.
options.D: dismissive contempt: the worries are rhetorical tricks that do not deserve a serious reply from anyone.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's claim that offsetting emissions is, in principle, a genuine undoing?

options.A: Investigations of several offset schemes have found that the forests they credited to their buyers were later cut down to make way for timber and farmland.
options.B: Most people who hear both the fidelity case and the author's reply to it continue to find the original objection to offsetting by far the more persuasive of the two.
options.C: The damage done by a tonne of emissions depends on how long it stays in the air, so carbon absorbed decades later cannot cancel the harm done meanwhile.
options.D: Travellers who regularly buy offsets tend to fly more often than they did before they began buying them, and say they feel less guilty about it.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a possible source of special obligations EXCEPT

options.A: being the parent of the child whose needs are in question.
options.B: living within the same municipal boundary as the people one might help.
options.C: having harmed the people who are now in need of help.
options.D: sharing with others an institution that one sustains and benefits from.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that the resident in paragraph 3 who gives to a shelter in his own city

options.A: can be justified only if he has personally harmed some of the people whom the shelter helps.
options.B: acts wrongly, because all money given to charity ought to go wherever it will do the most good.
options.C: fulfils a special obligation, because he shares the institutions of his city with the people in the shelter.
options.D: is moved mainly by nearness, which does not create the kind of duty he may believe it does.

questions.question: The final paragraph of the passage functions mainly to

options.A: weigh the strongest remaining case for local giving and show that its force depends on circumstances.
options.B: establish that donors should always give where they are able to watch the results of their giving.
options.C: introduce a further reason why the first camp's arithmetic would dissolve the bonds that make moral life recognisable.
options.D: restate the author's earlier conclusion that special obligations arise from dependence, history and reciprocity.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the author's position on the dispute described in paragraph 1?

options.A: The local camp is right about loyalty but wrong about knowledge, since distant programmes can now always be assessed more reliably than local ones.
options.B: Both camps are equally mistaken, because how much one should give locally depends solely on how well donors can verify what their money achieves.
options.C: Partiality in giving can be justified by genuine relationships, but the local camp tends to mistake mere nearness for such relationships.
options.D: The camp that favours giving wherever money does the most good is right, because special obligations are sentiment that a rigorous ethics should discard.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the usual response to uncertainty about insect suffering is mistaken chiefly because it

options.A: relies on outdated evidence about how the nervous systems of insects are organised.
options.B: assumes that insects feel pain in exactly the way that dogs and birds feel it.
options.C: treats not knowing whether insects suffer as though it were knowing that they do not.
options.D: ignores the economic importance of the industry that farms insects for animal feed.

questions.question: Paragraph 3 contributes to the argument of the passage mainly by

options.A: conceding that the weighing in paragraph 2 proves too much, and then replacing it with a quite different argument from shared physiology.
options.B: showing that bacteria and plants deserve moral consideration for the same reasons that insects do.
options.C: demonstrating that insects possess the same capacity for pain as the animals whose suffering we already accept.
options.D: defending the weighing in paragraph 2 against a charge of proving too much, by setting insects apart from bare possibility.

questions.question: Which of the following would best fit the practical conclusion of the passage?

options.A: A government bans the use of all agricultural pesticides until scientists have shown that insects are unable to feel pain.
options.B: An insect farm adopts, at little extra cost, a quicker killing method that would cause less suffering if its insects can suffer.
options.C: A campaign urges households to take care never to step on ants because each ant killed is a serious moral loss.
options.D: An insect farm keeps its present methods unchanged until research establishes beyond doubt that insects feel pain.

questions.question: The author's reply to the objection in paragraph 3 depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: How likely an organism is to be sentient can be judged, at least roughly, by which pain-related features it shares with animals known to feel pain.
options.B: Bacteria and plants certainly cannot feel pain, so any argument that assigns them moral weight must rest on a premise that is simply mistaken.
options.C: Expected suffering ought to be the only consideration in deciding how any kind of organism, large or small, may be treated by human beings.
options.D: Insects possess every behavioural and physiological feature that is found in the animals whose capacity for pain we already accept without hesitation.

questions.question: According to the passage, the growth argument for discounting holds that

options.A: continued economic growth will in time repair whatever harm present policies impose on later generations.
options.B: outcomes in the distant future are less certain to happen and should therefore weigh less in present decisions.
options.C: the same resources will do less good for future people if they turn out to be richer than we are.
options.D: the well-being of future people matters less than ours simply because it will occur at a later date.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the statement that each component of a discount rate 'encodes a substantive view' is best understood to mean that the rate

options.A: states its moral assumptions openly before arriving at a figure that can be applied to any decision.
options.B: carries a moral judgement inside what appears to be a neutral technical setting.
options.C: reflects the private opinions of the economists who first proposed using discount rates in policy.
options.D: turns a moral view into a precise figure that experts can then check against the evidence.

questions.question: The comparison in paragraph 3 between discounting by time and discounting by distance implies that, in the author's view,

options.A: when a person lives is no more relevant than where a person lives to how much that person's suffering counts.
options.B: people living in distant countries today have a stronger claim on us than people who will be born in later centuries.
options.C: discounting the suffering of distant people is acceptable in practice, though discounting the suffering of future people is not.
options.D: a person's preference for a pleasure today over a larger one next year is as indefensible as discounting future generations.

questions.question: Suppose analysts assess a policy that would prevent the permanent loss of a stretch of inhabited coastline two centuries from now, and they discount that loss at the expected rate of growth in consumption. On the passage's reasoning, the most fitting objection is that

options.A: the loss lies too far in the future for its size to be estimated with enough confidence for it to enter any calculation at all.
options.B: the growth rate hides a pure time preference within it, and such a preference has no defence across generations.
options.C: any discount at all is forbidden for harms this far ahead, including the small discount the passage allows for the chance that no future people will exist.
options.D: a loss of this kind is not made good by greater wealth, so discounting it at the growth rate treats it as repurchasable.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Someone who rejects pure time preference entirely could still defend applying a low discount rate to some future outcomes.
options.B: A discount rate of zero is the only rate consistent with treating future people as having the same moral standing as ourselves.
options.C: Once pure time preference has been set aside, nothing remains that could justify discounting future harms at all.
options.D: The rates commonly used are too low, because they give too little weight to the chance that there will be no future people.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, the identified lives that communities rush to save are often

options.A: those of people living close to the engineers and machines that are needed to rescue them.
options.B: those of victims whose danger happens to be reported, not all who face similar danger.
options.C: those of people who are already personally known to the rescuers or to their communities.
options.D: those whose rescue costs less per life than the measures that would prevent similar deaths.

questions.question: Paragraph 4 serves mainly to

options.A: concede that, from that standpoint, prevention is always to be chosen over rescue whatever the cost of either.
options.B: show that the assurance rescue provides is worth more than all the lives that prevention could save.
options.C: argue that the standpoint used to favour prevention can also make room for the value of rescue.
options.D: explain why advocates of prevention are wrong to reason from the position of someone not knowing his fate.

questions.question: The remark that statistical accounting 'has no column for' assurance (paragraph 3) suggests that such accounting

options.A: is right to ignore assurance, because a benefit of that kind cannot be given any value at all.
options.B: shows that the value of assurance is greater than the value of the lives that each rescue saves.
options.C: has been designed by economists deliberately to conceal the value of rescue and favour prevention.
options.D: omits a benefit of rescue that is enjoyed even by people who are never themselves in danger.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument in paragraph 3?

options.A: Residents feel equally sure of being helped in an emergency whether their town spares no expense on rescues or strictly caps what any rescue may cost.
options.B: Most people greatly overestimate the chance that they themselves will ever be trapped, lost or stranded in a disaster that requires a costly rescue.
options.C: Some rescues fail despite enormous expense and effort, and the people who were trapped die long before the rescuers are able to reach them.
options.D: Measures such as guardrails, better lighting and screening save many more lives for each rupee spent than even the best-run rescues do.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author's overall position?

options.A: Communities spend too much on rescue and should move that money into prevention until the spending per life saved is equal.
options.B: Rescue and prevention serve such different values that neither can sensibly be judged by the standard that is used to judge the other.
options.C: Rescuing identified people has a real value that its critics miss, but that value offers no excuse for how little is spent on prevention.
options.D: The preference for identified lives is a costly bias that consistent accounting should remove, though the assurance that it brings to everyone deserves a little weight.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that models in economics and biology idealise more heavily, and therefore less reliably, than the models used in physics.
options.B: recast the falsehoods in scientific models as claims about which factors matter, claims that can be checked by relaxing them.
options.C: defend the familiar view that idealised models are convenient fictions whose missing details ought to be restored once better methods allow it.
options.D: show that every idealisation is eventually exposed as harmful once a model is carried into conditions it was not built for.

questions.question: The examples of the feather and the parachutist in paragraph 3 serve to

options.A: suggest that the motion of falling objects can never be modelled usefully without including the effect of the air.
options.B: demonstrate that air resistance is the most common source of error in the models that physicists actually use.
options.C: illustrate the earlier claim that adding missing factors to a model buries the very pattern it was built to display.
options.D: show that an assumption that some factor does not matter can hold in one setting yet fail in another.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, the phrase 'an artefact of the simplification' refers to a result that

options.A: survives unchanged when the population is treated as very large rather than as infinitely large.
options.B: owes its existence to the model's simplifying assumption rather than to any feature of the world being modelled.
options.C: was first reached through a simplified model and was later confirmed by more detailed observation of the world itself.
options.D: is valuable chiefly as a historical record of the way in which an earlier model was put together.

questions.question: A traffic model treats all drivers as having identical reaction times, which is plainly false. On the passage's reasoning, which of the following would best show that this idealisation is harmless for the model's prediction of where queues form?

options.A: Every traffic engineer consulted agrees that no real population of drivers has identical reaction times.
options.B: Treating drivers as identical lets the model's equations be solved far more quickly than any more realistic formulation would allow.
options.C: The model's predictions about where queues form have been presented to city planners for many years without any complaint.
options.D: Rerun with a realistic spread of reaction times among drivers, the model still places the queues in the same spots.

questions.question: According to the passage, the barometer reading is able to predict the storm because

options.A: the reading and the storm are both produced by the same fall in atmospheric pressure.
options.B: a falling reading is the only reliable sign that the weather is about to deteriorate.
options.C: forecasters have learned to adjust their barometers so that the readings anticipate the storm.
options.D: the fall in the reading brings about a change in the air that causes the storm a short time later.

questions.question: The example of the hillside in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: show that something can be a reliable predictor of an event without explaining that event at all.
options.B: suggest that geological events are too irregular for any scientific account of them to be given with confidence.
options.C: show that an event can be adequately explained even when it could not have been forecast beforehand.
options.D: illustrate the claim that a theory which explains everything and forbids nothing deserves suspicion.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that, in the author's view, a factor helps to explain an outcome when

options.A: the factor and the outcome are both effects of some deeper cause acting on them both.
options.B: knowing the factor in advance would have allowed someone to forecast the outcome before it occurred.
options.C: the factor has been observed, reliably and in many cases, to occur shortly before the outcome.
options.D: a different value of that factor would have led to a different outcome.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's case against the view described in paragraph 1?

options.A: Had the soil and clay been fully measured in advance, the relevant laws would have fixed the very week the slope failed.
options.B: Geologists frequently revise their published accounts of particular landslides as new information about the slope comes to light later.
options.C: Barometer readings quite often fall without any storm following, so their forecasts are rather less reliable than is commonly claimed.
options.D: Working scientists routinely test a proposed explanation by checking whether the predictions it implies about other conditions are actually borne out in practice.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the investigator who measured one adult's height drew no general conclusion because

options.A: a single measurement of any quantity, however carefully it is taken, is never enough to support a general conclusion.
options.B: the investigator knew that adults vary in height, so one case could not stand in for the rest.
options.C: human height is too difficult to measure with the precision that a melting point allows.
options.D: the investigator lacked the principle of uniformity that the other investigator had managed to find.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Because every inductive step depends on earlier inductions, scientific knowledge rests in the end on nothing more than habit.
options.B: A single careful trial is more trustworthy than a large sample whenever the substance under study is chemically pure.
options.C: Inductive steps are licensed by knowledge of particular domains, and the regress this creates does not make scientific practice irrational.
options.D: The sceptical argument about induction fails, since a principle of uniformity can be supported by the record of past successful inferences.

questions.question: Which of the following reasoners proceeds in the way the passage regards as sound?

options.A: A pollster who simply assumes that nature is uniform concludes that every future election will go the way the last one did.
options.B: A botanist, knowing that a certain trait hardly varies within a plant species, judges a new population's trait from a handful of specimens.
options.C: A physician who tests a new drug on one patient and, finding it effective, prescribes it to all patients alike.
options.D: A geologist who refuses to generalise from any finite set of rock samples, on the ground that induction can never be justified.

questions.question: The author would accept each of the following EXCEPT the claim that

options.A: any single item of background knowledge can be questioned while the rest of it is held fixed.
options.B: two investigators may both reason well while drawing very different conclusions from a single observation.
options.C: the background knowledge that licenses an inductive step was itself acquired by inductive means.
options.D: a domain-based account of induction makes the regress that the sceptic describes disappear altogether.

questions.question: According to the passage, a curve that passes exactly through every measured point is usually a poor guide to the next measurement because

options.A: in fitting every point it has also reproduced the errors that the measurements happen to contain.
options.B: complicated curves are harder to calculate with, so that mistakes creep in when they are used to predict.
options.C: nature is simple, so a complicated curve cannot correspond to the way things really are.
options.D: such a curve can be drawn only when the measurements are entirely free of error.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a preference for the simpler of two well-fitting models is most clearly justified when

options.A: the more complex model has already been tested against new data and has predicted them better.
options.B: the data are abundant and precise enough to reveal fine structure in whatever is being measured.
options.C: the data available are few in number and each measurement carries a substantial margin of error.
options.D: the simpler model is the one that scientists find easier to state, to teach and to calculate with.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the statistical justification of simplicity is best described as one of

options.A: studied neutrality, laying out its strengths and its costs without ever indicating which way the balance falls.
options.B: polite scepticism, because in the end it leaves simplicity a matter of taste, like a preference for a tidy desk.
options.C: qualified endorsement: it is more promising than the alternatives, but it supports less than is often claimed for it.
options.D: enthusiastic acceptance, because it finally demonstrates that the simpler hypotheses are the ones more likely to be true.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that simplicity is 'a discount applied in proportion to our ignorance'?

options.A: With small and noisy samples, models with fewer adjustable parameters predict new data better than models that have many.
options.B: Even where data are vast and highly precise, simpler well-fitting models keep predicting new measurements better than complex ones.
options.C: Scientists in many fields report that they choose simpler models chiefly because these are easier to teach to students.
options.D: Whether one model has more parameters than another sometimes depends on the variables in which both of them happen to be written.

questions.question: According to the passage, when a prediction derived from a theory fails, logic alone establishes that

options.A: at least one element of the theory and its accompanying assumptions is mistaken, though not which one.
options.B: the theory itself is false, whatever assumptions were made about the instruments and the conditions of the experiment.
options.C: the instruments used in the experiment were faulty or had been wrongly calibrated.
options.D: the theory must be replaced by another one that also explains its earlier successes.

questions.question: The case of Mercury in paragraph 3 is introduced mainly to

options.A: prove that Newtonian mechanics was mistaken whenever it postulated an unseen planet to explain an irregular orbit.
options.B: demonstrate that astronomers of the period clung to Newton's theory out of a dogmatic reluctance to abandon it.
options.C: suggest that the general theory of relativity was devised chiefly in order to explain the orbit of Mercury.
options.D: show that the strategy that worked for Uranus does not always work and so carries no guarantee.

questions.question: The author's remark that, at the time, the two anomalies 'looked much the same' suggests that

options.A: the anomalies of Uranus and of Mercury had the same underlying cause, though this was not yet recognised.
options.B: astronomers of the period lacked the instruments they needed to tell a real planet from an imagined one.
options.C: the discovery of Neptune owed more to luck than to the soundness of the calculations that preceded it.
options.D: the astronomers who looked for a planet near Mercury cannot fairly be faulted for reasoning as they did.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards scientists who keep a theory despite an anomaly is best described as

options.A: conditional approval, since such tenacity is reasonable but becomes dogma when it rests on assumptions invented only to save the theory.
options.B: firm disapproval, since a theory that has met a clear anomaly ought to be given up rather than protected further.
options.C: unreserved admiration, since holding on to a theory in the face of anomalies is always what good science requires.
options.D: detached indifference, since whether to keep or abandon a theory is a question the author leaves entirely to historians.

questions.question: The solvent example implies that a laboratory which judged harm to workers to be far worse than lost revenue should

options.A: report only the cost of withdrawing the solvent and leave every judgement about harm to the firm's managers.
options.B: demand more evidence of harm than usual before declaring the solvent dangerous to the workers who use it.
options.C: be prepared to declare the solvent harmful on less evidence than it would require if both errors seemed equally serious.
options.D: refuse to reach any conclusion until the evidence about the solvent leaves no room for any doubt at all.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's response in paragraph 3 to the suggestion that scientists simply report probabilities?

options.A: Probabilities reported by scientists are now usually accompanied by a full statement of the statistical model that was used to obtain them.
options.B: Teams analysing the same borderline samples classified them differently according to which error they most wanted to avoid, changing the probabilities they reported.
options.C: Most of the laboratories that test industrial chemicals are funded, directly or indirectly, by the firms that manufacture those chemicals.
options.D: Officials who receive probability estimates from scientists often misread them and, as a result, make poorer decisions than they otherwise would.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of the final paragraph?

options.A: It limits the conclusion of the argument by separating a proper role for values from an improper one.
options.B: It concedes that the argument built on the solvent example fails, and restores the picture of objectivity in paragraph 1.
options.C: It answers the reply in paragraph 3 by showing that probabilities can after all be reported without any judgement of value.
options.D: It introduces a new example in order to show that researchers often discount results that they find unwelcome.

questions.question: In the final paragraph, 'moving the evidence' refers to

options.A: raising or lowering the amount of evidence required in the light of what is at stake if one errs.
options.B: transferring the weighing of errors to an earlier stage of the research where it is harder to see.
options.C: presenting the evidence to the people who must act instead of accepting or rejecting the hypothesis oneself.
options.D: allowing a preference for one conclusion to alter what the results are taken to be, for instance by setting aside an unwelcome finding.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Thought experiments are arguments in disguise, whose vivid imagery adds persuasive force but nothing to the logical content of their conclusions.
options.B: The best thought experiments give direct insight into the necessary laws of nature, as Galileo's case of the falling bodies shows.
options.C: Thought experiments inform by bringing unstated expectations into conflict with explicit theory, and are only as reliable as those expectations.
options.D: Thought experiments should not be trusted in modern physics, since its subject matter lies far outside everyday experience.

questions.question: According to paragraph 3, the supposition that heavier bodies fall faster contradicts itself because the two bodies tied together should fall

options.A: more slowly than the light body alone, since the air around them drags the heavier of the two bodies back.
options.B: more slowly than the heavy body alone, since the light one holds it back, and yet faster, since the pair is heavier.
options.C: at exactly the speed of the heavy body alone, since the light body, being so much lighter, adds nothing to the pair.
options.D: faster than either body alone in the imagined case, while in actual trials the pair is observed to fall more slowly.

questions.question: On the passage's account, which of the following imagined scenarios would produce a conviction that deserves the least confidence?

options.A: Imagining what a traveller moving at nearly the speed of light would see in a mirror held at arm's length.
options.B: Imagining whether a tall stack of books would topple over if the bottom book were pulled out very quickly.
options.C: Imagining whether a ladder leaning against a wall would slip if a heavy person climbed all the way to its top.
options.D: Imagining how two carts of equal weight would move after rolling into each other at walking pace.

questions.question: The passage supports each of the following claims EXCEPT that

options.A: a thought experiment collects no new data, so what it teaches cannot come from fresh observation.
options.B: the premises of a successful thought experiment may be discovered only in the course of running it.
options.C: the tacit expectations on which thought experiments draw were formed among objects of moderate size and speed.
options.D: the argument reading is unable to reconstruct Galileo's scenario as a set of premises and a conclusion.

questions.question: The author's criticism of the insight reading in paragraph 3 implies that an adequate account of Galileo's result must

options.A: show that the result could have been set out as a complete argument before the scenario was ever imagined.
options.B: trace the result to what Galileo and his readers already believed rather than to a newly perceived law.
options.C: establish that the result holds for all bodies, including those moving through a resisting medium.
options.D: explain why the scenario had to be carried out with real bodies before its conclusion could be trusted.

questions.question: According to the passage, one merit of the frequency view is that it

options.A: identifies chance with a physical tendency that each particular set-up possesses on its own.
options.B: assigns a definite chance to a single toss even when no long run of tosses ever takes place.
options.C: ties chance to something countable and so explains why observed frequencies serve as evidence about chances.
options.D: removes the need to decide which class of similar cases a particular event belongs to.

questions.question: The example of the toss 'described down to the exact force and angle of the flick' (paragraph 3) serves to

options.A: illustrate how a physicist with suitable equipment can measure the propensity of any set-up directly.
options.B: show that the propensity view meets its own form of the problem that the choice of class raised for frequencies.
options.C: show that a coin toss is really deterministic, so that its chance of heads is not truly one half.
options.D: explain why the frequency view cannot assign any chance to a coin that is tossed only once.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the account of chance given in paragraphs 4 and 5?

options.A: The beauty of a painting depends on the taste of whoever happens to be looking at it.
options.B: The age of a fossil can be estimated, but never exactly, because every dating method carries some error.
options.C: A hill's height is definite once one says whether it is measured from sea level or from the plain below.
options.D: The colour of an object is the one it shows under the single lighting that best reveals its true nature.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard two doctors who state different chances of recovery for the same patient as

options.A: both mistaken, since no chance can properly be assigned to the recovery of a single patient.
options.B: certainly in conflict, since the patient has a single chance of recovery that at most one of them has identified.
options.C: both merely expressing their own degrees of confidence, since chance is in the end a matter of perspective.
options.D: possibly both correct, if each is relying on a different specification of the patient's circumstances.

questions.question: On the author's account, the choice of which specification of the circumstances to use, unlike the chance given a specification,

options.A: is settled by the purposes of whoever needs the chance rather than by facts about the world.
options.B: can be settled only by gathering longer runs of observed frequencies for the event in question.
options.C: is left wholly open, so that any figure anyone proposes for the chance is as good as any other.
options.D: is fixed by nature, which singles out one description of each event as the correct one.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: establish that whenever a population's expectations rise, the satisfaction it reports will fall regardless of its conditions.
options.B: urge governments to abandon measures of wellbeing and return to judging their success by economic output and income.
options.C: argue that life-satisfaction scores record expectation-dependent judgements and so should supplement, not replace, other measures of wellbeing.
options.D: show that life-satisfaction surveys are unreliable because respondents cannot accurately report how they feel from moment to moment.

questions.question: According to the passage, two people whose days contain the same mixture of pleasure, worry and boredom may report different scores because

options.A: one of them misunderstands the scale on which the answer is meant to be given.
options.B: they bring different expectations to the judgement of their lives.
options.C: one of them earns more and therefore has more of the means to living well.
options.D: one of them remembers the worrying parts of recent days more vividly than the other does.

questions.question: The warning that a government 'could succeed by teaching its citizens to want less' (paragraph 4) implies that

options.A: governments that adopt satisfaction scores usually set out to lower their citizens' expectations on purpose.
options.B: people who have learned to want less are genuinely better off than those whose expectations remain high.
options.C: lowering expectations is the only reliable way for any government to raise the scores it reports.
options.D: average reported satisfaction could rise without any improvement in how people actually live.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the phrase 'cut out the middleman' refers to

options.A: asking people about their lives directly instead of judging how well they live through income, which is only a means.
options.B: removing the cost of commissioning economic statistics by replacing them with cheaper surveys of opinion.
options.C: ignoring the standards that respondents use and recording only the sensations they feel during the day.
options.D: allowing citizens to report their satisfaction to researchers without any government official being involved in the process.

questions.question: The example of a friend's illness in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: illustrate the popular claim that worry comes from caring about outcomes that one is quite unable to change.
options.B: prove that a person's goodness depends partly on whether the people he helps actually recover.
options.C: suggest that the Stoics regarded the recovery of friends as a matter of no importance whatever.
options.D: show that judging an outcome to be not up to us is compatible with caring about it.

questions.question: Which of the following lawyers acts most fully in the spirit of the doctrine as the author interprets it in paragraphs 2 and 3?

options.A: One who stops taking difficult cases, reasoning that since verdicts are not up to her she has no reason to expose herself to them.
options.B: One who prepares every case thoroughly, argues it as well as she can, and judges her own conduct by the quality of that work rather than by the verdict.
options.C: One who works on each case with great intensity and full seriousness because she believes her worth as a lawyer is measured by how many of her cases she wins.
options.D: One who stays calm in court by deciding that her clients' fates are no concern of hers, since she cannot control how judges rule.

questions.question: The remark about someone who uses the doctrine 'to stop voting because elections are not up to him' suggests that the author regards the popular version of the doctrine as

options.A: open to being used as a justification for disengagement that the original doctrine does not allow.
options.B: an accurate account of how the ancient Stoics themselves behaved in public life.
options.C: mistaken in claiming that the outcome of an election is not up to any single voter.
options.D: more demanding than the original, because it requires a person to give up caring about results.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude toward the Stoic doctrine when it is read in the careful way the passage recommends?

options.A: Dismissive, since the author regards it as a recipe for withdrawing from public life and private obligations.
options.B: Approving without reservation, since the author accepts the Stoic decision to treat partly controllable outcomes as indifferent.
options.C: Respectful of its coherence and its demands, but doubtful that sorting outcomes into two classes fits how they actually matter to us.
options.D: Admiring of its demands, and confident that its main difficulty disappears once the popular misreading of it is corrected.

questions.question: According to the passage, the usual moral drawn from the story of the tree is that

options.A: every question about what a thing is good for is unreasonable and should be dropped altogether.
options.B: things that are of no use to anyone have no value and are rightly passed by without a second glance.
options.C: people with conspicuous gifts are likely to be exploited, so wise people avoid drawing attention to themselves.
options.D: craftsmen should learn to find uses even for timber that seems useless at first sight.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'the carpenter's glance' refers to

options.A: a refusal to attend to anything that does not bear fruit or produce food.
options.B: a careful study of an object that eventually reveals its hidden and unexpected value.
options.C: the skill of quickly judging the quality of timber that comes from long practice in a trade.
options.D: a habit of looking at things only for what they can contribute to some purpose beyond themselves.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the author's main claim about the story of the tree?

options.A: It is mainly practical advice that talented people should hide their gifts in order to survive in a dangerous world.
options.B: Its chief target is a way of seeing that reduces things to their usefulness to someone, not usefulness itself.
options.C: It shows that things are valuable in proportion to how little they can be used by people.
options.D: It demonstrates that modern institutions are wrong to ask what subjects of study or land are good for.

questions.question: Which of the following, if it were added to the end of the story, would most weaken the author's reading of it?

options.A: The tree admits it would gladly have become timber had that been safe, and values its uselessness only as a way of staying alive.
options.B: On waking, the carpenter tells his dream to the apprentice, who doubts whether a tree could ever really speak to anyone.
options.C: The carpenter, waking from his dream, refuses to let his apprentice cut the tree down and reflects at length that he had misjudged it from the start.
options.D: Travellers continue to rest in the shade of the great tree for many generations after the carpenter's death.

questions.question: According to the passage, the mirror argument is most effective against

options.A: the dread of the physical pain that people expect to suffer in the course of dying.
options.B: the fear of missing the future events and achievements that a longer life would have brought.
options.C: the fear of death imagined as a condition in which one will somehow find oneself.
options.D: the regret people feel about the many centuries of history that passed before they were born.

questions.question: The final sentence of paragraph 3, contrasting being born earlier with dying later, is used to support the claim that

options.A: the fear of death as a dark and silent condition is a confusion that the mirror argument exposes.
options.B: the goods lost by dying would have belonged to this very life, whereas the goods of earlier centuries could never have been ours.
options.C: our attitudes in ordinary life to the pleasures that are still to come differ from our attitudes to pleasures that are already over.
options.D: people are inconsistent when they dread the time after their death but feel nothing at all about the time before their birth.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's objection to the symmetry argument in paragraph 3?

options.A: Many people who say they fear death admit, when questioned closely, that they picture it as a dark and silent condition they will endure.
options.B: Epicurus and Lucretius both wrote in the hope of freeing their readers from fears they considered groundless.
options.C: Some people who are dying report that they fear the process of dying far more than they fear being dead.
options.D: On reflection, people regret the goods they missed by being born late as much as the goods they will lose by dying.

questions.question: The last sentence of the passage implies that

options.A: any argument that wholly removed the fear of losing one's future would also weaken a concern that the author regards as legitimate.
options.B: no argument about death can offer any genuine consolation, since every fear of death reflects care for the future.
options.C: Lucretius intended his argument to teach readers to care less about the future, and the author shares that aim.
options.D: grief in advance for a life cut short is a confusion that a better argument than Lucretius' could dispel.

questions.question: It can be inferred that those who accuse the teaching of 'moral recklessness' understand it to recommend

options.A: meeting success with pride and failure with an equally strong sense of shame.
options.B: refusing to act at all whenever the outcome of an action is uncertain.
options.C: acting without weighing what one's actions are likely to bring about.
options.D: choosing whatever action will be most visibly successful and most widely praised.

questions.question: Which of the following teachers best shows the relation to results that paragraph 4 says the teaching can sensibly ask for?

options.A: One who gives up teaching a difficult class altogether once her first method fails, concluding from the failure that she simply lacks the talent for the work.
options.B: One who keeps using a method she believes is right without checking whether her pupils are learning anything from it.
options.C: One who chooses whichever methods will produce the most impressive results for visiting inspectors, whether or not her pupils actually benefit from them.
options.D: One who sees that a new method is not helping her class, changes it, and does not take the failure as proof she is a poor teacher.

questions.question: Paragraph 3 contributes to the argument chiefly by

options.A: restating the objection of paragraph 1 in a stronger form before the author's final reply in paragraph 4.
options.B: going beyond showing that detachment is compatible with good action to claim that it actually helps action go well.
options.C: conceding that anxiety about results is sometimes useful because it keeps agents attentive to what they do.
options.D: introducing the difficulty that most actions unfold over time and so must be adjusted as their effects gradually appear.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's stance toward the teaching by the end of the passage?

options.A: Sympathetic, having rejected the charge of recklessness, yet unwilling to claim that the teaching removes every difficulty.
options.B: Neutral, since the author declines to say whether the objection that the teaching is reckless succeeds or fails.
options.C: Sceptical, since the author ends by doubting that anyone could actually live by the teaching under real pressure.
options.D: Dismissive, since the physician example shows that the teaching cannot be followed by anyone whose work has consequences.

questions.question: According to the passage, loneliness differs from solitude in that loneliness

options.A: is a painful sense of having too little connection, which can be felt even in the company of others.
options.B: is always chosen by the person who suffers it, while solitude is always imposed by others.
options.C: is a circumstance of being physically alone, whereas solitude is a feeling about the state of one's relationships with others.
options.D: arises only when a person lives alone for a long period with no prospect of company returning.

questions.question: The claim that 'Friendship is richer between people who could survive without it' (paragraph 3) suggests that

options.A: the best friendships are those in which the friends spend long periods apart from each other.
options.B: people who are capable of solitude have comparatively little need of friends and seldom go out of their way to seek them.
options.C: people who depend on others for company cannot form friendships of any kind.
options.D: a relationship held together partly by an inability to bear one's own company is, to that extent, less freely chosen.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: The value of an evening spent alone depends partly on the state of the person who spends it.
options.B: Solitude remains valuable however long it continues, provided the person chose it at the outset.
options.C: Programmes that tackle loneliness should aim to improve people's connections with one another.
options.D: A person can be lonely while spending most of each day in the company of others.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's warning in paragraph 4 about policies and technologies that aim to reduce time spent alone?

options.A: Programmes against loneliness substantially reduce the suffering of those who take part in them, as their organisers had hoped.
options.B: Some contemplatives in the past found their early periods of retreat painful before they came to value them.
options.C: People who spend less time alone because of such measures keep as much chosen, undivided time as before, since the hours they give up were mostly unwanted ones.
options.D: Many people who are lonely remain so even after they have begun to spend much more time in company.

questions.question: According to the passage, Aristotle placed amusement with work rather than with leisure because amusement

options.A: is pursued in modern societies mainly for the skills and stamina that it helps people to build.
options.B: provides the relaxation that we need because we cannot labour without a break, and so serves further activity.
options.C: was available only to citizens who were supported by the labour of slaves and artisans.
options.D: is an activity chosen for its own sake and is therefore the highest use of a person's free time.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the statement that free time is 'colonised by the logic it was supposed to interrupt' means that

options.A: activities once done for their own sake have been abandoned in favour of rest and sleep.
options.B: people have so little time off that work fills almost every hour of the day.
options.C: employers increasingly demand that their staff remain available for work during evenings and holidays.
options.D: standards drawn from work come to govern how free time is judged and spent.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 4 in the passage?

options.A: It accepts the objection that Aristotle's leisure depended on others' labour and concludes that his account of leisure must be revised for modern use.
options.B: It shows that Aristotle's exclusion of most people from leisure discredits his account of what leisure is, along with his picture of the good life.
options.C: It accepts a serious objection to Aristotle in full while arguing that it applies to who had leisure, not to what leisure is.
options.D: It argues that the objection to Aristotle is unjust, since modern societies have extended to nearly everyone the leisure he reserved for a few.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as leisure in Aristotle's sense?

options.A: A retired engineer who spends his evenings studying the music of a tradition he loves, though he will never perform or write about it.
options.B: A musician practising scales for several hours each evening to prepare for a paid audition with an orchestra.
options.C: A factory hand who spends his weekends watching comedies to unwind before the start of the next working week.
options.D: An office worker who reads philosophy before bed because it helps her sleep and work more sharply the next day.

questions.question: The author's claim that 'the language of rest and productivity has no words to state' the demand in paragraph 5 suggests that this language

options.A: was invented by employers to persuade workers that long hours are good for them and their families.
options.B: values free time only by its relation to work, so it cannot express the worth of activities done for their own sake.
options.C: is too imprecise to measure how much free time the people of a society actually have each week.
options.D: is used mostly by schools and cities, which ought instead to leave free time to the choices of individuals.

questions.question: In the exercise described in paragraph 2, each component of a person is examined to determine whether it

options.A: is permanent, whether it is reliably satisfying and whether it lies under one's control.
options.B: can be perceived directly, whether it can be described in words and whether others share it.
options.C: existed before the person's birth and whether it will continue after the person dies.
options.D: is a cause of suffering, whether it can be removed and whether it is a form of craving.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'an unchanging owner standing behind it' refers to

options.A: the teacher in the early discourses who leads listeners through the components of a person.
options.B: the person regarded as a stream of experiences that has a history, makes choices and bears consequences.
options.C: the bodily form, which stays the same throughout a life while feelings and perceptions change.
options.D: a self thought of as something over and above the stream of experiences, to which those experiences belong.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that the no-self teaching contradicts itself, since someone must exist to entertain the doctrine and to be disappointed by it.
options.B: defend the no-self teaching as a practical therapy that, because it aims only at reducing craving, stands beyond the reach of philosophical criticism.
options.C: show that the no-self teaching escapes a common refutation because it is chiefly practical, yet still rests on a contestable claim that deserves argument.
options.D: establish that the chariot analogy settles the question whether a person is anything more than an organised stream of experiences.

questions.question: Suppose it were shown that a person is, after all, something more than the organised stream of experiences. Based on the passage, the author would most likely hold that

options.A: the tradition would also have to abandon its claims that the stream of experiences has a history, makes choices and bears consequences.
options.B: the easy refutation described in paragraph 1 would at last be vindicated as an objection to the teaching as the tradition states it.
options.C: the exercise of paragraph 2 would then lack the authority the tradition claims for it, since that authority depends on revealing how things are.
options.D: the exercise would remain fully justified, since it would still reduce craving whether or not the belief it induces is true.

questions.question: The chariot example in paragraph 3 serves to

options.A: show that the tradition regards persons as fictions, since the word 'chariot' names nothing that really exists in the world.
options.B: illustrate how a name can pick out an organised whole without there being any further thing over and above its parts.
options.C: prove that the components of a person are permanent, since the parts of a chariot survive when it is taken apart.
options.D: settle the metaphysical question that paragraph 4 raises about whether a person is more than an organised stream.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain how the defects of the retinal image, such as its blind spot, are corrected by the beliefs a viewer holds about the world.
options.B: defend the view that seeing is a form of conscious reasoning in which the brain, like a careful clerk, weighs the evidence.
options.C: show that visual illusions reveal how unreliable perception is, so that what we see should be checked against measurement.
options.D: argue that seeing actively interprets ambiguous evidence, while denying that this makes the senses untrustworthy.

questions.question: According to the passage, the retinal image is ambiguous in the sense that

options.A: eye movements make it change from moment to moment, so that no single image can ever be relied on.
options.B: it is upside down and flat, so the brain has to turn it the right way up before anything can be seen at all.
options.C: the same pattern on the retina is consistent with more than one arrangement of things in the world.
options.D: the blind spot removes part of every image, leaving gaps that the viewer's expectations must fill in.

questions.question: The author explains that perceptual assumptions rarely mislead us outside the laboratory because they are mostly true of the environments in which they were formed. Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this explanation?

options.A: People who move into surroundings that violate their perceptual assumptions are, from the start, misled no more often than people who grew up there.
options.B: Laboratory illusions are deliberately constructed by researchers so as to exploit the assumptions that ordinary vision relies on.
options.C: Viewers who are told exactly how an illusion works go on seeing it just as strongly as they did before being told.
options.D: Some perceptual assumptions, such as the assumption that light comes from above, turn out to be shared by people raised in very different places and cultures.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the statement that 'the guess is tightly disciplined by the evidence' most nearly means that

options.A: repeated correction trains the brain, over time, to stop guessing and simply register the signal as it is.
options.B: the interpretation perception settles on is held in check by what the incoming signal actually contains.
options.C: perception refuses to adopt any expectation that the viewer has not personally confirmed by experience.
options.D: the viewer consciously tests each perceptual guess against careful measurement before accepting it as true.

questions.question: According to the passage, viewers fail to see the unexpected figure because

options.A: attention lets only part of what reaches the eye into conscious experience.
options.B: they do notice the figure faintly but forget the impression before they are questioned about the video.
options.C: the figure appears too briefly and too indistinctly to register clearly on a short recording.
options.D: the light from an unexpected object does not reach the retina while the eyes are busy tracking a moving ball.

questions.question: The remark that the driver's 'honesty is not in question; his access to his own lapse is' implies that

options.A: he is probably concealing his inattention at the junction in order to avoid being blamed for what happened.
options.B: cyclists who appear suddenly at junctions are among the most common causes of collisions with careful drivers.
options.C: he glimpsed the cyclist dimly at the junction but has since lost the memory of that fleeting impression.
options.D: his account is sincere yet mistaken, since a cyclist he never consciously saw left nothing in his experience to report.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the selectivity of attention is best described as

options.A: alarmed, regarding it as a serious defect of the mind that ought to be corrected through training.
options.B: accepting, treating it as the price of focus while warning against trusting it where misses are costly.
options.C: dismissive, treating the experiments as amusing curiosities with little bearing on ordinary life.
options.D: admiring, holding that attention can be relied on to admit whatever genuinely matters in a scene.

questions.question: Which of the following design decisions best reflects the lesson drawn in the final paragraph?

options.A: Asking pilots how confident they are that they would spot an unexpected obstacle, and grounding those who report low confidence.
options.B: Training drivers to widen their attention so that they take in the whole visual field at once rather than one part of it.
options.C: Fitting a machine with an alarm that halts the task in progress, so that an operator is not relied on to glance at a light.
options.D: Placing a warning light directly in the operator's line of sight, on the grounds that anything plainly in view will be noticed.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the phrase 'conviction and correctness have come apart' means that

options.A: how sure people feel about these memories no longer tracks how accurate the memories are.
options.B: people remember the shocking event correctly but feel unsure about the details surrounding it.
options.C: people grow steadily less confident in these memories as the memories become less accurate over the years.
options.D: each memory splits into a true core and an invented portion, which the person can readily tell apart.

questions.question: The example of the woman who concedes that she wrote the earlier account suggests that

options.A: people readily give up a vivid memory once they are shown a written record that contradicts what they now recall.
options.B: evidence that a memory has changed need not shake the feeling that its present version is the authentic one.
options.C: she has knowingly revised her story over the years so as to make it more dramatic when telling it to others.
options.D: accounts written in the shock of the moment are less reliable than those formed after a period of calm reflection.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the final paragraph in the passage?

options.A: It turns to a separate subject, the use of memory as evidence in courts, for which the earlier paragraphs have not prepared the reader.
options.B: It withdraws the earlier claim that flashbulb memories are often inaccurate, in the light of evidence that emotion strengthens memory.
options.C: It grants a real effect of emotion on memory and shows that the grant leaves the main argument standing.
options.D: It offers readers a reliable technique for telling their accurate flashbulb memories apart from their inaccurate ones.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: Emotion may improve memory for the features of an experience that were central to it.
options.B: Repeated retelling of an event can make a reconstructed version of it feel like the original memory.
options.C: A person can accept that her earlier account differs from her present one without ceasing to trust the present one.
options.D: How vivid a memory is and how certain its owner feels give no indication at all of whether it is true.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: describing the biological processes through which memories that are seldom used gradually decay in the brain.
options.B: recommending that people give up memory aids so that their minds can edit stored information more efficiently.
options.C: questioning the belief that an ideal memory would keep everything, by showing how forgetting helps memory work.
options.D: arguing that the fear of forgetting in old age is unfounded, since most memory loss turns out to be beneficial.

questions.question: The example of recalling every parking space one has ever used serves to

options.A: show that people with very complete recall are unusually good at everyday tasks such as finding their cars.
options.B: demonstrate that most forgetting is caused by the brain running short of room in which to store information.
options.C: suggest that memories of places are forgotten more readily than memories of faces.
options.D: illustrate how holding every memory with equal force would bury the one that is needed.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the account of forgetting given in paragraph 3?

options.A: A library that withdraws books from its shelves once readers report that they contain factual errors.
options.B: A library that sends rarely borrowed books to a distant store, keeping much-borrowed titles on the open shelves.
options.C: A library that shelves every book it has ever owned in the main hall, arranged strictly in order of arrival.
options.D: A library that destroys a share of its old books at random each year to free space for new acquisitions.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Failing to recall a name at an important moment can be a genuine loss even when the forgetting comes from a sound design.
options.B: The memory losses caused by dementia are best understood as an extreme form of the useful editing that all memories perform.
options.C: A memory that held on to everything would be more useful, though less comfortable to live with, than the one we have.
options.D: Because forgetting is the price of a sensible policy, the cost of any particular memory lapse is more apparent than real.

questions.question: According to the passage, when chess pieces are arranged at random,

options.A: strong players recall them more accurately than real positions, since no familiar habits mislead them.
options.B: strong players reconstruct the positions little better than beginners do.
options.C: neither group can reconstruct a single piece of the position after it has been removed.
options.D: beginners outperform masters, because the masters try to force the pieces into familiar patterns.

questions.question: The author calls the random-position result 'more instructive' than the first result most probably because it

options.A: shows that beginners could become strong players more quickly by studying random positions instead of real games.
options.B: proves that skill at chess depends entirely on perception and not at all on calculation.
options.C: reveals that the memory of strong players fails when they are given only a few seconds to look at a board.
options.D: rules out the explanation that masters simply have a greater capacity to store pieces in memory.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, 'knowledge that has been absorbed into perception' refers to

options.A: learning that now shapes what the specialist sees, without having to be called up step by step.
options.B: facts the specialist has forgotten that resurface without warning when she is under pressure.
options.C: a mysterious faculty that works independently of anything the specialist has studied or practised.
options.D: rules that the specialist silently recites to herself while she looks over an image or a board.

questions.question: On the passage's account, an experienced radiologist shown an image of a rare condition unlike any she has studied would be most at risk of

options.A: recognising the condition at once, because trained perception carries over to every image in her field.
options.B: performing exactly as a novice would, since her skill rests only on a larger memory for images.
options.C: forming a quick and confident first impression that turns out to be wrong.
options.D: failing to form any impression of the image until she had worked through written diagnostic rules.

questions.question: According to the passage, while an interval is passing, the sense of how long it is lasting depends largely on

options.A: how pleasant or unpleasant the person finds the activity that fills the interval.
options.B: how much attention is being paid to the passing of time itself.
options.C: how many distinct memories the events of the interval are laying down.
options.D: how old the person is and how routine the rest of his life has become.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the middle-aged complaint that the years go faster

options.A: shows that the felt passage of a single afternoon speeds up steadily as people grow older.
options.B: is mistaken, because older people in fact keep more distinct memories of each year than young people do.
options.C: concerns how a past year looks as a whole, not how its hours feel while they are being lived.
options.D: arises because adults pay closer attention to clocks and calendars than young people usually do.

questions.question: In the last sentence, the quotation marks around 'really' serve to

options.A: cast doubt on the idea that there is one true fact about how long an experience felt.
options.B: express scorn for people who believe that novelty can be used to lengthen their lives.
options.C: signal the author's view that remembered duration is truer than the duration felt at the time.
options.D: show that the word is quoted from the cheerful advice that the author criticises earlier in the paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the explanation offered in paragraph 3 for why the years seem to pass faster in middle age?

options.A: Middle-aged adults habitually plan further ahead than adolescents do, and many of them say that they spend more of their time thinking about the future.
options.B: Middle-aged adults report that individual afternoons pass at much the same rate as they did when they were adolescents.
options.C: Travellers returning from a varied holiday judge it to have lasted longer than a routine week at work of the same length.
options.D: Adults whose lives remain as full of first experiences as in youth report the same speeding up of the years as adults with routine lives.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Mind wandering is better understood as a symptom of unhappiness than as its cause, contrary to what researchers at first believed.
options.B: Training in attention should be abandoned, since every attempt to suppress the wandering mind is futile and does real harm.
options.C: The opposed verdicts on mind wandering largely reflect the different occasions studied; its worth depends on when it occurs and whether it is noticed.
