options.D: Mind wandering is chiefly productive work on plans and unfinished problems, and its costs have been exaggerated by narrowly designed experiments.

questions.question: According to the passage, researchers began to study mind wandering directly by

options.A: asking people at the end of each day to estimate how often their minds had drifted.
options.B: measuring the errors people made while reading or driving under laboratory conditions.
options.C: recording the solutions that came to people unbidden while they were in the shower or out walking.
options.D: interrupting people at random moments and asking what they had been thinking about.

questions.question: The author's remark about a person who is worried implies that

options.A: a link between mind wandering and low mood does not by itself show that wandering makes people unhappy.
options.B: the studies that linked wandering with low mood were badly conducted and ought to be set aside.
options.C: worried people perform better than others on tasks that demand continuous attention.
options.D: mind wandering is always produced by unhappiness and never contributes to it in any way.

questions.question: Which of the following outcomes of a course in attention training would the author regard as most successful?

options.A: A trainee now lets her thoughts roam freely during important meetings, on the chance that unbidden solutions may come to her there.
options.B: A trainee still lets her thoughts drift while gardening but now notices quickly when they drift in a meeting she needs to follow.
options.C: A trainee no longer lets her thoughts drift on any occasion, whether at work, at lectures or at home.
options.D: A trainee feels happier than before because she now spends more of her waking time thinking about her future plans.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the two bodies of research 'are, for the most part, looking at different occasions'?

options.A: Errors made while driving are more dangerous than errors made while reading, so lapses at the wheel matter more.
options.B: Studies reporting costs were run mainly in laboratories, while studies reporting benefits were often run in everyday settings.
options.C: People report that their minds wander more often when they are worried than when they are content.
options.D: A survey of the research finds that studies reporting costs and studies reporting benefits mostly used tasks of very similar difficulty.

questions.question: The comparison of a test to a thermometer in paragraph 1 serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that tests, like thermometers, are precise instruments that schools ought to use more often.
options.B: show that the effects of a test can be measured accurately only when a week has passed since it was taken.
options.C: capture the common assumption that testing records learning without changing it, which the passage goes on to reject.
options.D: illustrate how a student's anxiety rises during an examination much as a temperature rises during a fever.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the advantage of retrieval practice was long overlooked partly because

options.A: measurements taken soon after study could make rereading look at least as effective as recall.
options.B: students who practised recall concealed their gains from researchers because they were anxious about being tested.
options.C: rereading produces stronger memories in the short run, which later decay into confidently held errors.
options.D: researchers regarded tests as too unpleasant to be worth studying as a method of learning.

questions.question: Which of the following study routines best matches the practice the author recommends?

options.A: A student sits one long, formally graded examination at the end of term, whose marked scripts are never returned to her.
options.B: After each chapter, a student shuts the book, writes out what she remembers and then checks her account against the text.
options.C: A student reads each chapter three times over, until every sentence feels familiar and slides past without effort.
options.D: A student answers practice questions from memory every evening but never looks up whether her answers were right.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that what strengthens memory is 'the effort of retrieval, not the apparatus of examination'?

options.A: Students who reread a passage felt more confident about a coming test than those who practised recall, although a week later they remembered less of it.
options.B: Students who sat a formal, high-stakes examination reported feeling far more anxious than students who practised recall at home with their books closed.
options.C: Students who received feedback after each attempt at recall remembered more a week later than students who attempted the same recall without any feedback.
options.D: Answering recall questions improved memory a week later only when done under formal examination conditions, and not when done in an informal, ungraded session.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: The benefit of retrieval practice may fail to appear in a test given only a few minutes after study.
options.B: Attempting to recall material benefits memory only when the learner succeeds in producing the right answer.
options.C: A learner's confidence at the end of a study session can be a misleading guide to what the session achieved.
options.D: Students who are left to choose their own method of study will seldom choose to practise recall.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain how vivid news reporting manufactures public fear of dramatic accidents that are in fact very unlikely to happen.
options.B: argue that resources for safety should be allocated strictly in proportion to the number of deaths each hazard is expected to cause.
options.C: argue that public fear of some hazards partly expresses defensible values, while warning that such fear still needs to be examined.
options.D: show that expert rankings of hazards are mistaken and that policy should defer to the rankings the public prefers.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following makes a hazard feel more frightening?

options.A: Its being placed on people by others rather than accepted by them through their own choice.
options.B: Its being so familiar from everyday life, like driving, that people rarely stop to think about it.
options.C: Its producing deaths a few at a time, spread out over many years, rather than all at once.
options.D: Its having been studied for a long time by experts who publish their estimates of the danger.

questions.question: The example of the rock climber who objects to a factory's chemical release serves mainly to

options.A: support the claim that legal systems ought to prohibit factories from releasing any untested chemicals into rivers.
options.B: show that a preference which ignores expected deaths can rest on a coherent distinction between risks that are chosen and risks that are imposed.
options.C: illustrate the kind of error in arithmetic that leads ordinary people to rank hazards differently from experts.
options.D: demonstrate that recreational activities such as climbing are in fact more dangerous than most forms of industrial pollution.

questions.question: A town council meets strong local opposition to a planned waste incinerator whose expected effect on health is small. Which course of action is most consistent with the author's recommendation?

options.A: Sort the objections into those about consent, fairness or control, which deserve weight, and those that stem only from a recent alarming story.
options.B: Proceed as planned, since the expected toll is small and residents' fear is a problem of perception to be corrected with figures.
options.C: Abandon the incinerator, since strong public dread is itself a verdict that a council has a duty to accept without question.
options.D: Show residents vivid images of road accidents in the town, so that their fears are redirected toward the hazards that really matter.

questions.question: According to the passage, later attempts to reproduce the early findings on choice overload

options.A: revealed that the early experiments had been badly designed and that their reported results could not be trusted at all.
options.B: consistently confirmed the early findings, although the effects they found were somewhat smaller than those first reported.
options.C: showed that larger assortments always made people more likely to buy, so that the early findings were simply reversed.
options.D: found the effect in some cases, found nothing in others, and sometimes found that larger assortments increased buying.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the description of the novice as 'drowning' suggests that the novice

options.A: is enjoying the large selection even more than the wine enthusiast who is merely browsing.
options.B: cannot find a suitable fund because most of the forty funds on offer are poor choices.
options.C: is overwhelmed because he has no way of sorting the options in front of him.
options.D: is taking a dangerous financial risk by choosing a pension fund without professional advice.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the author would regard shortening a restaurant's menu as most clearly justified when

options.A: diners take longer to order than the staff would like, even though they are satisfied with what they choose.
options.B: most diners are regular customers who know the kitchen well and have firm preferences among its dishes.
options.C: the dishes differ along many dimensions, such as price, cuisine and spice, that diners find hard to compare.
options.D: most of the dishes on it are mediocre or are barely distinguishable from one another.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's account of choice overload?

options.A: Several shops that trimmed their product lines in the hope of raising sales found that their sales fell instead.
options.B: Shoppers faced with many nearly identical products were more satisfied after the range was reduced to a few.
options.C: Novices given forty pension funds sorted by risk level, with a default marked, were as reluctant to choose as novices given the same funds unsorted.
options.D: Wine enthusiasts reported enjoying a shop with forty bottles on offer more than a shop that offered only eight.

questions.question: According to the passage, the pull of an anchor on people's estimates persists even when

options.A: the quantity being estimated is one that participants deal with every day and know well.
options.B: participants have seen for themselves that the number was produced at random.
options.C: participants have been told the correct answer to the question before giving their estimate.
options.D: the anchor is mentioned only after participants have already written down their estimates.

questions.question: The image of 'a reluctant traveller who halts at the nearest acceptable station' serves to

options.A: convey the older account's claim that anchoring results from adjustment that stops early for want of effort.
options.B: show that people resist arbitrary numbers until they are given a financial reason to care about being accurate.
options.C: express the author's own preferred explanation of how numbers supplied by negotiators and sellers distort judgement.
options.D: suggest that anchors work by making certain recollections more readily available than others to the person judging.

questions.question: On the selective account described in paragraph 3, a person given an anchor and asked to deliberate longer before estimating would most likely

options.A: give the same estimate but feel less confident in it, because the extra search would raise doubts about the anchor.
options.B: disregard the anchor entirely, because longer reflection would reveal that the number was arbitrary and irrelevant.
options.C: stay close to the anchor, because the extra search would mostly turn up more evidence consistent with it.
options.D: move further from the anchor, because the extra time would let adjustment continue beyond its usual stopping point.

questions.question: A buyer receives an opening price from a seller. Which piece of advice best follows from the author's conclusion?

options.A: Before responding, ask the seller to explain in detail how the figure was reached, so that its basis becomes clear.
options.B: Before responding, take time to reflect carefully on the figure offered and decide calmly how far to move away from it.
options.C: Treat the figure as an obviously self-interested number that cannot influence the judgement of an experienced buyer.
options.D: Before responding, set out the reasons that might make the figure a poor guide to what the item is worth.

questions.question: According to the passage, on tasks that are very hard, many people

options.A: rate themselves below average compared with others while still overestimating their own scores.
options.B: judge both their own scores and their standing relative to others accurately, because poor results are obvious.
options.C: rate themselves above average compared with others while underestimating how well they have actually done.
options.D: give much wider ranges for their estimates than they do on easy tasks, so that their overprecision disappears.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that if people knew as much about others' performance as about their own, then

options.A: the tendency to give ranges that are too narrow when forecasting uncertain quantities would largely disappear.
options.B: the reversals between easy and hard tasks in how people rank themselves against others should become smaller.
options.C: people would place themselves above others on every kind of task, whatever its level of difficulty.
options.D: people would stop overestimating their own scores on very hard tasks such as juggling or composing verse.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the claim that overconfidence is 'the most pervasive of the biases' is best described as

options.A: sceptical, because the claim treats as a single tendency several that behave quite differently.
options.B: dismissive, because the author holds that people are not in fact overconfident in any systematic way.
options.C: neutral, because the author only reports competing definitions of the term without judging any of them.
options.D: approving, because the author goes on to show how overconfidence underlies most of the other biases.

questions.question: The passage makes each of the following claims about overprecision EXCEPT that it

options.A: appears among specialists in a field as well as among novices who know little about it.
options.B: reverses on very hard tasks in much the same way as the tendency to rank oneself above others.
options.C: is reduced only a little when forecasters are simply urged to be more humble about their estimates.
options.D: does particular harm when projects are budgeted against ranges too narrow to include the outcome.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, a problem 'dressed in unfamiliar clothes' is one that

options.A: is described in technical language that the participants were not taught to understand.
options.B: involves colleagues from a professional background different from that of the participants.
options.C: demands a decision far more urgent than any of the cases that were discussed in the session.
options.D: takes a form unlike the examples through which the biases were taught in the workshop.

questions.question: The contrast between a textbook problem about sunk costs and a real decision about a struggling project serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate the tendency of people to see biases in their colleagues while believing their own reasoning to be sound.
options.B: argue that textbooks on decision-making ought to replace their tidy examples with problems drawn from real work.
options.C: explain why skill at recognising a bias in labelled examples does not readily carry over to actual decisions.
options.D: show that real decisions carry higher stakes than textbook problems and therefore produce stronger biases.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a manager who has just attended a typical workshop on biases is most likely to

options.A: become more doubtful of their own conclusions than of the conclusions their colleagues reach.
options.B: make noticeably fewer errors on new problems that arise in the course of their own work.
options.C: become better at naming biases in colleagues' reasoning while remaining confident in their own judgement.
options.D: lose the ability to recognise biases even in the textbook examples used during the session.

questions.question: The author's claim that redesigning procedures has 'the practical merit of not depending on each person's ability to catch themselves in the act' rests on which assumption?

options.A: That training built around practice and feedback never produces improvements that outlast the session in which it is given.
options.B: That procedures such as collecting independent estimates can still work as intended when the people following them are as biased as before.
options.C: That people who follow such procedures for long enough will gradually learn to recognise their own biases without help.
options.D: That biases are a form of ignorance which a well-designed procedure can cure by supplying the people involved with the knowledge they lack.

questions.question: According to the passage, intuitive expertise can be learned only where

options.A: cues in the environment are linked to outcomes and practice comes with quick, clear feedback.
options.B: judgements are made rapidly and without the interference of slow and deliberate reasoning.
options.C: experts are able afterwards to explain step by step how they reached each of their judgements.
options.D: the person has received formal instruction in the theory that underlies the judgements of the field.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Intuitions in medicine generally merit trust, whereas the intuitions of those who forecast markets generally do not.
options.B: Experienced professionals' intuitions are usually right and should be preferred to formulas whenever the two disagree.
options.C: The confidence an expert feels in a judgement is a useful, though imperfect, sign of whether the judgement is correct.
options.D: Whether an intuition merits trust depends on whether the setting in which it was formed allowed valid patterns to be learned.

questions.question: A weather forecaster has spent many years issuing next-day forecasts for a region whose weather follows recognisable patterns, checking each forecast against the next morning's weather. On the passage's account, this forecaster

options.A: deserves trust in a given forecast only if he feels highly confident that this particular forecast is correct.
options.B: cannot be trusted unless he is able to explain the reasoning by which he arrived at each of his forecasts.
options.C: has had the conditions needed to develop intuitions about next-day weather that deserve a measure of trust.
options.D: can be trusted to the same degree when making long-range predictions about the region's climate over the next decade.

questions.question: The claim that subjective certainty 'tells us almost nothing about whether to trust a judgement' implies which of the following?

options.A: Confidence in a judgement grows only in environments that lack regular links between cues and outcomes.
options.B: Experts who feel certain of a judgement are usually less accurate than experts who feel some doubt about it.
options.C: Wherever experts feel confident, their intuitive judgements should be replaced by simple statistical formulas.
options.D: Two experts who are equally sure of their judgements may nonetheless deserve very different degrees of trust.

questions.question: The remark that 'descriptions do not fall from the sky' (paragraph 2) means that

options.A: descriptions are imposed by people in authority, so that listeners seldom feel able to question the way they are put.
options.B: descriptions are chosen by speakers, and the choice often reveals something about what the speaker knows or believes.
options.C: descriptions used in experiments are carefully designed by researchers so that each pair is exactly equivalent.
options.D: descriptions take on their meaning only once the listener already knows the numbers that they are describing.

questions.question: On the account given in paragraph 2, a listener told that a glass is 'half empty' could reasonably infer that

options.A: the glass probably held more at some earlier point and has since been partly emptied.
options.B: the glass now holds noticeably less than half of what it could hold when full.
options.C: the speaker would like the listener to refill the glass before anyone else drinks from it.
options.D: the speaker is gloomy by temperament and tends to see the worst side of most situations.

questions.question: Paragraph 4 functions in the argument chiefly to

options.A: defend the principle that logically equivalent descriptions must produce the same choice in every situation.
options.B: show that the classic demonstration was badly designed and that its findings should not be relied upon.
options.C: refute the information account by showing that framing effects persist even when the frame is plainly arbitrary.
options.D: limit the information account by showing that it explains framing effects only in part.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the account of framing given in paragraph 2?

options.A: Participants who read the word 'die' reported stronger unease than those who read the word 'live', even when told the figures matched.
options.B: Framing effects were just as large when the descriptions were assigned by a visible coin toss as when a speaker chose them.
options.C: Speakers who favoured a treatment mostly cited survival figures, and listeners hearing survival figures more often guessed the speaker favoured it.
options.D: Speakers describing a quantity rarely chose their words according to whether the quantity had recently risen or fallen.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the author's position on the principle that logically equivalent descriptions should produce the same choice?

options.A: It is a fair standard only where the choice of description carries no information about the speaker or the situation.
options.B: It is a sound requirement of rationality that ordinary people violate whenever they respond differently to equivalent descriptions.
options.C: It is irrelevant to real choices, because framing effects in the end reflect only the emotional pull of particular words.
options.D: It is mistaken, because two descriptions that seem equivalent never really express the same proposition at all.

questions.question: According to the passage, the first research tradition infers the shortcuts the mind uses from

options.A: comparisons of how well simple and complex rules predict cases that have not yet been seen.
options.B: the pattern in which people's answers depart from answers fixed by logic or probability.
options.C: people's own reports, given after the task, of the rules they believe they followed.
options.D: studies of the environments in which human judgement first developed and is now exercised.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the 'frame' to which the rival tradition objects is best understood as

options.A: the statistical techniques that researchers in the first tradition use to analyse their experimental results.
options.B: the theory that human judgement developed in environments quite unlike those of the modern laboratory.
options.C: the wording in which experimental problems are put to participants, which shapes the answers they give.
options.D: the practice of judging responses against logical and probabilistic norms on problems built in the laboratory.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, in a small and noisy sample, a model that weighs many cues will predict new cases worse than a simple rule because it

options.A: neglects the one or two strong cues on which the simple rule relies for its predictions.
options.B: contains more systematic error than the simple rule, which it trades for a gain in flexibility.
options.C: fits accidental features of the sample at hand that will not recur in the new cases.
options.D: requires more computation than people with limited capacity are able to carry out reliably.

questions.question: Paragraph 3 serves chiefly to

options.A: argue that the case for simple rules appeals to a different normative standard rather than discarding normative standards.
options.B: concede that the first tradition was right to judge responses by their agreement with a probabilistic calculation.
options.C: establish that simple rules are superior to elaborate models in every environment in which decisions are made.
options.D: show that the rival tradition, by praising heuristics that ignore information, rejects the authority of statistical theory.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the rival tradition is best described as

options.A: endorsement of its main claims, including its further claim that minds reliably select whichever rules best suit the task at hand.
options.B: acceptance of its critique of how errors are judged, with doubt that people have been shown to fit their rules to their tasks.
options.C: approval of its success in refuting the first tradition's findings about the systematic errors people make.
options.D: rejection of its argument, on the ground that ignoring information is in the end a symptom of limited mental capacity.

questions.question: The central argument of the passage is that boredom

options.A: is a state of the same kind as hunger, since both are unpleasant and both disappear once they are satisfied.
options.B: is harmless in most settings, because people can nearly always find some more engaging activity to turn to.
options.C: has become harder for people to tolerate because a constant supply of entertainment is now available to them.
options.D: is better understood as a prompt to change an unengaging activity than as a mere absence of feeling.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the statement that boredom 'curdles into frustration or something close to despair' means that boredom

options.A: turns into a more painful state when the person has no means of responding to it.
options.B: slowly disappears once the person accepts that nothing else can be done.
options.C: is hidden from the person feeling it, who mistakes it for some other emotion entirely.
options.D: becomes a more useful signal the longer a person is prevented from acting on it.

questions.question: The reference to hunger in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: argue that people should be less worried about boredom than about the physical needs of their bodies.
options.B: suggest that boredom, like hunger, is a bodily need that must be met at regular intervals through the day.
options.C: show that a state can be unpleasant and still have a purpose, as the author claims boredom does.
options.D: illustrate that boredom is a more disagreeable experience than most of the other unpleasant states people know.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a person who never feels bored because every pause is filled with small distractions as

options.A: more likely than other people to fall into frustration and despair whenever they cannot act on the signal.
options.B: possibly missing information about parts of their life, such as work or routine, that no longer suit them.
options.C: confirming the common view that boredom is an empty space which can be filled with anything at hand.
options.D: having solved the problem that boredom poses, since the unpleasant feeling no longer arises for them.

questions.question: The passage implies that the commuter in paragraph 2 now takes out her phone mainly because

options.A: the familiar features of the journey set off the action without any present decision by her.
options.B: she decided long ago that the journey was the right time for checking her messages.
options.C: she lacks the firmness of resolve that would allow her to keep the phone in her pocket.
options.D: she has a strong wish to look at it each time she sits down in the carriage.

questions.question: According to the passage, people often find it easier to change their routines after moving house because

options.A: a new home usually brings with it a fresh set of goals and daily reminders of them.
options.B: people who choose to move are generally less attached to their old habits than others are.
options.C: moving house tends to strengthen a person's resolve to make a fresh start in life.
options.D: the cues that used to set off their old behaviour are no longer present in the new setting.

questions.question: Someone habitually eats snacks while watching television each evening and wants to stop. Which approach would the author regard as most promising?

options.A: Writing down each evening the health reasons for cutting back on snacks before switching on the set.
options.B: Promising a friend to resist the snacks and reporting every lapse to that friend the next day.
options.C: Watching in a different room, where no food is kept and the usual armchair is absent.
options.D: Allowing snacks on the weekend only after a full week of successfully resisting them on weekdays.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the author's account of what a habit is?

options.A: Habits that people form during childhood are much harder to break than the habits they form as adults.
options.B: Strong intentions to stop a routine barely reduce it while its usual setting persists, but a changed setting reduces it sharply.
options.C: Many people who move to a new city report feeling more anxious during their first year in the new place.
options.D: People who write down specific goals are more likely than others to begin and keep up a programme of exercise.

questions.question: According to the passage, conditions such as persistent noise resist adaptation probably because they

options.A: tend to arrive suddenly in a person's life rather than building up by degrees.
options.B: are usually more severe in their effects than the gains to which people adjust.
options.C: cannot be compared with any earlier state in the life of the person affected.
options.D: keep demanding attention instead of settling into the background of experience.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the remark that the flat line 'describes almost nobody in it' implies that

options.A: the average wellbeing of such groups has usually been misreported in the studies that measure it.
options.B: individuals who return to their earlier level after a major life event are very rare in such studies.
options.C: an average showing no change can coexist with large changes, in both directions, for nearly everyone in a group of that kind.
options.D: most people in such studies are unwilling to report honestly how their wellbeing has changed.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a person considering a move to escape a persistently noisy flat

options.A: should base the decision mainly on temperament, since it is temperament that fixes how content a person can be.
options.B: has good reason to expect a lasting improvement, since noise is among the conditions people fail to adapt to.
options.C: will find that the benefit of the quieter home fades about as quickly as the pleasure of a higher salary.
options.D: should expect to adapt to the noise in time, so that the trouble and cost of moving are probably not worthwhile.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 3?

options.A: When the individual paths in such studies are examined, nearly everyone's wellbeing turns out to return close to its earlier level.
options.B: People adjust more slowly to living in a larger house than they do to receiving a substantial rise in salary.
options.C: Average wellbeing tends to rise in the year before a wedding and to fall back gradually in the years that follow it.
options.D: In most groups studied, average wellbeing returns almost exactly to its earlier level within a few years of a major event.

questions.question: According to the information gap account as the passage presents it, people are rarely curious about subjects they know nothing about because

options.A: they hold no earlier beliefs about such subjects that new information might overturn or correct.
options.B: such subjects seem too difficult to them to be worth the effort that learning would require.
options.C: curiosity needs a general appetite for novelty, which wholly unfamiliar subjects fail to satisfy.
options.D: they cannot notice what is missing in a field they are unable to see at all.

questions.question: The author's objection to the reply described in paragraph 3 implies that a good account of curiosity should

options.A: draw its evidence from observing classrooms rather than from studying puzzles, riddles and mysteries.
options.B: describe curiosity in terms of many small gaps closed in succession rather than one large gap.
options.C: be capable of ruling out some patterns of behaviour instead of fitting any pattern after the event.
options.D: treat the wandering kind of curiosity as more important than the kind that seeks a single answer.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of the kind of curiosity that, in the author's view, the information gap account fits poorly?

options.A: Reading on in a detective novel to learn which of the suspects actually committed the crime.
options.B: Leafing through an old atlas in a second-hand bookshop with no particular place in mind.
options.C: Walking through a museum to find a painting a friend recommended, whose gallery has been forgotten.
options.D: Working steadily through a crossword in order to fill in the answer to the one clue that remains.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the information gap account is best described as

options.A: appreciative of what it explains but doubtful that it accounts for every form of curiosity.
options.B: dismissive, because the account turns curiosity into a vocabulary instead of a genuine hypothesis.
options.C: neutral, setting out the account and the objections of its critics without taking any side between them.
options.D: wholly approving, since it explains both the stimulating effect of partial knowledge and the end of curiosity.

questions.question: Paragraph 1 mainly serves to

options.A: explain why the experience of grief is much harder to study systematically than the experience of dying.
options.B: trace the familiar sequence back to an origin that differs from the use now made of it.
options.C: argue that the stages of grief have never been observed in any patient or in any bereaved person.
options.D: present evidence that the sequence accurately describes how terminally ill patients respond to their diagnosis.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a bereaved person who feels deep sadness that eases over some months, without anger or bargaining,

options.A: is probably in a state of denial, which the model treats as the first of the five stages of grief.
options.B: is unusual, because most bereaved people report experiencing every one of the named feelings at some point.
options.C: may well be grieving in a way that is common and is not a sign of feelings being avoided.
options.D: will pass through the missing stages later, once the full reality of the loss has finally been faced.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as a consequence of treating the stage model as a standard EXCEPT that

options.A: researchers stopped studying grief because the model appeared to have settled the important questions.
options.B: friends or professionals may urge a grieving person to move on to the next stage of the sequence.
options.C: a bereaved person may come to believe that something is wrong with his own reactions to the death.
options.D: a grieving person who does not feel an expected emotion may be told she has not faced her loss.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's overall attitude towards the stage model of grief?

options.A: Hostile, regarding the model's popularity chiefly as evidence of how readily the public accepts unsupported ideas.
options.B: Ambivalent, unable to decide whether the research on bereavement supports the model or tells against it.
options.C: Sympathetic, holding that the model's inaccuracy matters little when set against the comfort it has given to many.
options.D: Critical of its use as a norm for how people should grieve, while granting that it once met a genuine need.

questions.question: According to the passage, praise that tells a child about the quality of the work may strengthen interest because it

options.A: feeds the child's sense of competence, which is what made the activity enjoyable.
options.B: removes the child's expectation that drawing will be rewarded again in the future.
options.C: comes unexpectedly and so cannot have been the child's reason for drawing.
options.D: is less tangible than a prize and so is harder for the child to treat as a payment.

questions.question: A pupil already loves playing the piano. Based on the passage, which of the following is most likely to reduce the pupil's interest in playing?

options.A: Telling the pupil after a recital which passages were played with particular skill and feeling.
options.B: Giving the pupil an unannounced treat in a week when the practice had been especially long.
options.C: Announcing that the pupil will receive a small gift for every hour of practice completed.
options.D: Offering a reward only for practising scales, which the pupil finds tedious, and not for playing pieces.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that rewards for a task that is dull at the outset

options.A: will always produce a lasting interest in the task once the necessary skill has been developed.
options.B: can sometimes keep a person at it until growing skill makes the task itself enjoyable.
options.C: work better when they are given for doing the task well than when they are given merely for doing it.
options.D: will reduce interest in the task as soon as the rewards are withdrawn, just as they do for enjoyed tasks.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the phrase 'converted from play into work and then left unpaid' suggests that the child

options.A: has been made to draw harder and longer than before, so that the activity itself has become tiring.
options.B: comes to enjoy drawing only when other children are drawing too and there is a prize to compete for.
options.C: resents the adults for withdrawing a payment that the child had been led to believe would continue.
options.D: now sees drawing as a job done for the prize, so that without the prize it no longer seems worth doing.

questions.question: According to the passage, in engineering the term 'strain' refers to

options.A: the relation between a load and the capacity of a body to withstand it.
options.B: the load itself, considered apart from the body that has to bear its weight.
options.C: the deformation that a load produces in the body that is subjected to it.
options.D: the internal force per unit area within a body that is subjected to a load.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that borrowing the word 'stress' from engineering was a mistake that the sciences of living things should now correct.
options.B: demonstrate that claims about 'good stress' are false and are promoted mainly by people who have advice to sell.
options.C: explain how the breadth of the term 'stress' allowed researchers in several separate disciplines to discover connections.
options.D: argue that 'stress' is worth keeping but that claims using it must be clear about which sense they rely on.

questions.question: The remark in paragraph 2 that popular discussion 'acquires the authority of the first reading and the scope of the second' implies that such discussion

options.A: gets the effects of reactions right but goes wrong by leaving out the part played by how people interpret their situation.
options.B: borrows a certainty available only when the claim is nearly true by definition and applies it to demanding situations generally.
options.C: is more trustworthy when it concerns people's reactions to demands than when it concerns the demands themselves.
options.D: relies on the standing of experts to support claims that hold good only for the small number of people they have studied.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's criticism, in paragraph 3, of advice built on the phrase 'good stress'?

options.A: Most such advice states plainly that it concerns how people interpret their reactions, and it cites studies that test this claim.
options.B: Some demanding situations, such as training for a long race, are widely regarded as experiences worth seeking out.
options.C: Researchers in different disciplines use the phrase 'good stress' in noticeably different ways from one another.
options.D: Physiological reactions to demand improve performance only up to a moderate level and impair it beyond that point.

questions.question: Paragraph 4 functions in the passage chiefly to

options.A: show that ordinary language cannot be reformed, so the word must simply be accepted as people use it.
options.B: concede that the confusions described in the earlier paragraphs have in practice done very little harm.
options.C: head off an apparently natural conclusion by pointing to a benefit of the word's looseness.
options.D: give an example of a substantive hypothesis about stress that research has since gone on to confirm.

questions.question: According to the passage, the blood sugar version of the resource theory faced the particular difficulty that

options.A: the coordinated replications could not include any measures of blood sugar.
options.B: people who thought willpower was plentiful consumed fewer sweet drinks.
options.C: sweet drinks were found to weaken rather than restore people's self-control.
options.D: effortful thinking seems to alter the brain's total energy use only slightly.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the findings about people's beliefs regarding willpower are 'awkward' for the resource theory because

options.A: they prove that the experience of mental fatigue after effort is an illusion created by people's expectations.
options.B: a physical store ought to run down with use whatever a person happens to believe about it.
options.C: they show that people who hold strong beliefs about willpower have larger stores of the resource to draw on.
options.D: they came from the same laboratories that had earlier failed to reproduce the basic depletion effect.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the account of mental fatigue set out in paragraphs 3 and 4 EXCEPT:

options.A: A person's persistence at a dull task recovers only after rest, however the task is framed or rewarded.
options.B: A volunteer stays absorbed in demanding work for longer when he can see clearly how it helps the people he serves.
options.C: Two equally demanding tasks leave people differently tired, depending on how rewarding each of the tasks feels to them.
options.D: Someone who has worked hard on a report all afternoon feels a growing pull towards a film she has been looking forward to.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to what happens, on the account the author favours, when mental fatigue sets in?

options.A: A student stops revising for an examination because she has now covered everything that the syllabus requires.
options.B: A shopper who has spent an hour in one store grows restless as the other stores nearby seem ever more worth the time.
options.C: A car slows to a halt on the motorway because the petrol in its tank has finally run out after a long journey.
options.D: A runner's leg muscles weaken over the course of a long race and need several days of rest before regaining strength.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the 'evening collapse' mentioned in paragraph 1 as

options.A: something best prevented by rationing effort through the day, as the failure of the resource model now shows.
options.B: an illusion that came to seem real largely because the resource model became so widely accepted.
options.C: evidence that everyday wisdom about tiredness has been refuted by the replication studies described in paragraph 2.
options.D: a real experience that the resource model described vividly but explained wrongly.

questions.question: According to the passage, what must the child serving imaginary tea do?

options.A: Keep the cup from toppling over at any point, since a spill would break the rules that the game has set up for everyone taking part.
options.B: Copy the way she has seen adults receive guests, so that she gradually learns the social role of a host.
options.C: Treat the cup as full inside the game while knowing it is empty, and let events in the game have their fitting effects.
options.D: Believe for the length of the game that the cup really holds tea, so that the pretence feels convincing to her.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'double bookkeeping' refers to

options.A: keeping track of how things actually are and how they are within the pretence, both at the same time.
options.B: recording a child's play twice over, once in the child's own memory and once in the notes of a watching adult.
options.C: moving back and forth between pretending and ordinary activity several times during a single afternoon.
options.D: a child's habit of counting imaginary objects alongside real ones, such as the cups, the tea and the animals.

questions.question: The third paragraph primarily serves to

options.A: reject the suggestion, made in paragraph 2, that pretend play and counterfactual thought share a capacity.
options.B: argue that most make-believe is too repetitive and loose to be of any real value to a child's development.
options.C: narrow the author's claim by conceding what the link between pretence and reasoning does not establish.
options.D: present evidence that children who spend more time pretending go on to become better at reasoning about causes.

questions.question: The author's reservation about turning free play into guided activities with stated learning outcomes rests chiefly on the concern that

options.A: guided activities take time away from the reading and counting that young children need to master well before their schooling begins.
options.B: any adult involvement in a child's game interferes with the reasoning about suppositions that pretence exercises.
options.C: stated learning outcomes cannot be measured reliably in children as young as the ones who play such games.
options.D: a child who senses that a particular answer is expected will stop exploring suppositions and try to read the adult instead.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: The best form for a lesson depends on its subject matter, which is why maps are the natural way to teach geography.
options.B: The belief that matching lessons to a learner's style improves learning lacks support, and labelling learners by style can do harm.
options.C: Teachers should present every lesson in visual, spoken and active forms so that learners of every style are reached.
options.D: People do not really have preferences about how they take in information, so the idea of learning styles is a myth.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, which pattern of results is the learning styles theory committed to predicting?

options.A: The advantage of one teaching method over another reverses depending on which style a group of learners has been assigned.
options.B: Learners who state a clear preference for one form of instruction learn faster than learners who state none at all.
options.C: Learners classed as visual outperform learners classed as auditory whatever form the lesson is delivered in.
options.D: Learners of every style do better when a lesson combines visual, spoken and practical elements in a single session.

questions.question: The passage gives each of the following as a reason the learning styles idea is appealing EXCEPT that it

options.A: fits the ordinary, everyday experience that people favour some ways of receiving information over others.
options.B: gives teachers something practical and concrete to do with their respect for individual difference among pupils.
options.C: has been borne out by studies teaching learners both in their own style and in another.
options.D: seems to show proper respect for the many differences between individual learners in a class.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 2?

options.A: Teachers who accept the theory of learning styles report feeling noticeably more confident when they plan lessons for mixed classes.
options.B: Students taught a stretch of coastline from maps remembered it better than students given only a spoken description of it.
options.C: Most learners, when asked, can readily name a way of receiving information that they prefer over the others available.
options.D: Learners sorted by style and taught in both formats showed a reversal: visual learners gained more from diagrams, auditory learners more from talk.

questions.question: According to the passage, practising one type of problem at a time falls short because it

options.A: spares the learner the decision about which procedure a problem needs, a decision a mixed examination requires.
options.B: produces more errors during study than mixed practice does, and the errors discourage learners from continuing.
options.C: prevents the learner from becoming fluent in any one procedure before the examination arrives.
options.D: takes much longer than rereading the chapter, and so leaves the student too little time for review.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a quiz given to students on a topic they have never been taught as

options.A: useful chiefly because it shows students how much of the topic still remains for them to learn later.
options.B: an unhelpful difficulty, since there is nothing learned for the effort of retrieval to consolidate.
options.C: a useful difficulty, because any effortful test is preferable to the familiarity produced by rereading.
options.D: no less valuable than spacing study sessions apart, provided that the quiz is followed by careful rereading.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward learners who prefer rereading and blocked practice is best described as

options.A: sympathetic to the reasons for their choice while holding that the choice is mistaken.
options.B: approving, since the fluency these methods produce is usually a reliable sign of real competence.
options.C: scornful, since they keep using poor methods despite clear information about which methods work.
options.D: indifferent, since the passage is concerned with how teachers judge lessons rather than with students.

questions.question: Which of the following practices best fits the passage's account of a useful difficulty?

options.A: A student copies out key passages with her non-dominant hand during revision, so that each line takes longer to finish.
options.B: A student attempts problems from next year's syllabus before learning this year's methods, so as to struggle as much as possible.
options.C: A student works through problems grouped by type, raising the difficulty steadily within each group as her confidence grows over the weeks.
options.D: A student revising for a mixed examination shuffles problems from last month's topics, so that each must first be identified before it is solved.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the phrase 'confidence without accuracy' describes

options.A: a violinist who keeps playing wrong notes boldly because no teacher is present to correct the mistakes.
options.B: practitioners whom long experience has made sure of their judgements, although those judgements are not reliably right.
options.C: the excessive faith that researchers have placed in counting hours of practice as a measure of skill.
options.D: beginners who feel sure of themselves before they have done enough practice to justify that feeling.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the popular rule that a fixed number of hours will make anyone an expert as

options.A: a fair summary of what the research on practice has shown about how experts are made.
options.B: accurate for fields where feedback is slow and noisy, though misleading for games and sports.
options.C: an overstatement that stretches sound findings about practice into a promise they cannot keep.
options.D: evidence that talent, rather than practice, is what finally separates the great from the good.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's explanation in paragraph 3 of why practice accounts for less in some fields?

options.A: In sports with stable rules and quick feedback, some athletes who practise a great deal still fail to reach the elite level.
options.B: Top chess players began playing at an earlier age, on average, than the many chess players who never managed to reach the top level of the game.
options.C: In one profession, members who learn quickly whether they erred improve more with experience than colleagues who learn the results only years later.
options.D: Financial analysts with long careers earn considerably more, on average, than analysts with shorter careers.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of the final paragraph?

options.A: It grants that practice builds expertise but denies that equal hours bring equal results, without making talent decisive.
options.B: It introduces new evidence that talent is a fixed endowment that settles in advance who can become an expert.
options.C: It recommends that people who want to become experts should choose fields in which feedback on their efforts is quick and reliable.
options.D: It reverses the argument of paragraph 3 by conceding that hours of practice do in the end determine expertise.

questions.question: According to the passage, when adolescents estimate the dangers of various activities in a calm setting, their estimates

options.A: improve noticeably once they have received formal instruction about the risks involved in them.
options.B: are often not far from the estimates that adults give for the same activities.
options.C: are markedly less accurate than the estimates they give when they are in the company of friends.
options.D: show that most of them believe harm happens only to other people and never to themselves.

questions.question: The passage suggests that an important reason information campaigns about risk have had limited success is that they

options.A: have usually given adolescents information about risks that is inaccurate or deliberately exaggerated.
options.B: come from schools and governments, sources whose advice adolescents are inclined to distrust and ignore.
options.C: assume a capacity to apply general facts to one's own conduct that most adolescents do not yet possess.
options.D: try to supply missing knowledge, when the difficulty lies largely in how knowledge is used in certain situations.

questions.question: Which of the following measures is most in keeping with the approach the author favours in paragraph 4?

options.A: A course trains teenagers to calculate the statistical risks of common activities, so that they can weigh dangers as carefully as adults do.
options.B: A programme asks each teenager to sign a private pledge never to ride with a reckless driver, so that the promise guides later choices.
options.C: A campaign shows teenagers vivid images of injuries caused by careless driving, so that the dangers of speeding are kept firmly in their minds.
options.D: A school arranges for evening events to end with a supervised bus home, so that riding with a newly licensed classmate becomes the awkward option.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the account of adolescent development given in paragraph 3 EXCEPT:

options.A: Some teenagers who spend most of their time among friends take fewer risks than many adults do.
options.B: The gap between sensitivity to reward and the capacity for restraint narrows as people move through their twenties.
options.C: The heightened response to reward in adolescence is limited to non-social rewards such as money or prizes.
options.D: A risky choice made by an adolescent among friends may reflect the circumstances as well as the state of the brain.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: explaining why adults learn the early stages of a new language faster than young children usually manage to do.
options.B: replacing the image of a language window that shuts at a fixed age with a picture of gradual age effects that differ by component.
options.C: arguing that adult immigrants fall short in a new language chiefly because they are not immersed in it as children are.
options.D: showing that age has no real effect on how well a second language is eventually learned, once exposure is held equal.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that a simple comparison between the final attainment of child and adult immigrants

options.A: cannot by itself show how much of the gap between them is due to age rather than to conditions of learning.
options.B: proves that adults who are immersed in a language learn it every bit as well as children who are immersed.
options.C: shows that differences in exposure, not age, account for the whole of the gap between the two groups.
options.D: tends to overstate the advantage that adult learners hold over child learners in vocabulary and memory.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'a set of different sensitivities' most nearly means

options.A: the varying degrees to which a learner's first and second languages influence each other over many years.
options.B: several distinct stages of childhood, each of them especially suited to the learning of a different language.
options.C: different learners, each of whom responds to a new language with a different level of anxiety or confidence.
options.D: separate parts of language ability, each affected to a different degree by the age at which learning starts.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's position?

options.A: Adults beginning a language progressed faster over their first year of study than children beginning the same language.
options.B: Among learners matched for the amount and kind of daily exposure, attainment fell sharply at one particular age, with little decline before or after it.
options.C: Late learners who were immersed as fully as children still differed from them in fine judgements about word endings.
options.D: Some adults who began a language late reached native-like command of it after many years of intensive immersion.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, the gains in test scores were

options.A: far larger on abstract classification and pattern detection than on vocabulary and arithmetic.
options.B: confined to the countries that had introduced mass schooling earlier than their neighbours had.
options.C: roughly equal across the different kinds of task that together make up a standard intelligence test.
options.D: largest on the tasks that draw most heavily on stored knowledge, such as vocabulary and arithmetic.

questions.question: The discussion of the two answers about the spade and the shears suggests that

options.A: test makers once gave credit for practical answers of this kind but stopped doing so as mass schooling spread.
options.B: intelligence tests ought in fairness to award credit for practical answers as well as for abstract classifications.
options.C: an answer can earn no credit on a test while still reflecting a sensible way of thinking about the world.
options.D: people who give practical answers are less able than others to reason abstractly when a task requires it.

questions.question: Paragraph 1 functions mainly to

options.A: establish that the Flynn effect is merely an artefact of the way intelligence tests were renormed at intervals over time.
options.B: pose a dilemma whose two obvious resolutions both look unacceptable, which the rest of the passage tries to escape.
options.C: describe the methods by which researchers in many countries first detected the rise in raw scores and confirmed it.
options.D: argue that earlier generations were less intelligent than is usually supposed by those who remember them.

questions.question: The author's position on the twentieth-century rise in scores is best characterised as holding that the gains

options.A: mark a genuine spread of one style of thinking, without amounting to a rise in general intellectual power.
options.B: are real, and this shows that the tests were never good predictors of how people would fare at school or work.
options.C: are an artefact of the way tests were constructed and reveal nothing about how people's thinking has actually changed.
options.D: show that people today have greater general intelligence than earlier generations, though the tests exaggerate the size of the difference.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the explanation of the gains offered in paragraphs 2 and 3?

options.A: Throughout the whole period of rising scores, the tests went on predicting quite accurately how well people would perform at school and at work.
options.B: People of average ability today do no better than the most gifted people of a century ago when set wholly unfamiliar practical problems.
options.C: Scores on abstract tasks rose as fast among people with little schooling and manual jobs as among people whose education and work centred on symbols.
options.D: During the same decades, average scores on vocabulary tests also rose, though by a much smaller amount than scores on abstract tasks did.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Older adults are on the whole wiser than younger adults, and their wisdom makes up for their slower processing.
options.B: Studies that follow the same people for decades give a more reliable picture of ageing than one-time comparisons.
options.C: Mental decline with age is largely an illusion produced by flawed comparisons between people from different generations.
options.D: Ageing alters the balance among mental capacities, so whether it counts as decline depends on what a task demands.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the proposal that part of the slowing reflects a larger store of knowledge is best described as

options.A: strict neutrality, reporting the proposal without offering any judgement about its worth or its limits.
options.B: dismissive scepticism, on the ground that the proposal is contested and cannot account for every loss.
options.C: qualified interest: doubtful that it accounts for every loss, but valuing what it shows about interpretation.
options.D: firm endorsement, on the ground that it shows apparent decline to be simply the cost of accumulated knowledge.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that studies following the same people over decades

options.A: may understate the decline that occurs in the population at large, because those who remain in them tend to be healthier and more able.
options.B: give the more accurate estimate of when decline begins, because they remove the effect of differences in schooling between generations.
options.C: confirm that the decline in rapid processing begins in early adulthood and continues steadily, just as the familiar picture holds.
options.D: overstate decline, because the people who take part become less interested in performing well as the years go by.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the proposal described in paragraph 3?

options.A: Slowing in older adults is just as marked on tasks that call on no stored knowledge as on tasks requiring the retrieval of words.
options.B: A computer model of word retrieval, given ever larger vocabularies with its processing unchanged, slowed down in the way that older adults do.
options.C: Younger adults who know two languages well name pictured objects as quickly as younger adults who know only one language.
options.D: Older adults score higher than younger adults on tests of vocabulary and general knowledge drawn from everyday life.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a shortcoming of the familiar picture of the ageing mind EXCEPT that it

options.A: treats a slower response as necessarily a sign of deterioration, when it might be a cost of accumulation.
options.B: rests heavily on comparisons that mix the effects of age with differences between generations.
options.C: overlooks the knowledge that goes on accumulating well into later life and on which older adults often excel.
options.D: fails to recognise the serenity and sound judgement that age reliably brings to those who reach it.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: dispute the usual gloomy moral of the experiments, arguing that much yielding was sensible reliance on others as evidence, though pressure also played a part.
options.B: argue that participants in the experiments yielded almost entirely because they feared embarrassment, and that their reasoning about the majority played no real part.
options.C: recommend that institutions train their members to trust their own perceptions and to resist the views of a majority whenever those views conflict with their own.
options.D: show that the line-judgement experiments were badly designed, since a room arranged to mislead participants cannot reveal anything about behaviour in everyday life.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the variations in which participants wrote down their answers privately are significant because they

options.A: reveal that the original experiments had exaggerated the number of participants who never yielded to the majority.
options.B: show that participants answering in private no longer gave the majority's reports any weight at all as evidence.
options.C: indicate that some agreement with the majority reflected a wish to avoid embarrassment, not a change of belief.
options.D: prove that participants who answered aloud had been persuaded that the majority's wrong answer was in fact correct.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'informational influence' refers to

options.A: giving way to a group's opinion publicly in order to avoid the discomfort of standing alone.
options.B: allowing what other people report to count as evidence about how things actually are.
options.C: the tendency of confident individuals to spread their views to a crowd that listens to them.
options.D: the effect of an experimenter's instructions on how participants interpret an ambiguous task.

questions.question: Which of the following practices is most in keeping with the remedy the author proposes in the final paragraph?

options.A: A committee announces the majority's preliminary view before discussion begins, so that members can see quickly where opinion lies.
options.B: A company runs workshops urging staff to have the courage of their convictions and to trust their own judgement over that of colleagues.
options.C: A board requires all its decisions to be unanimous, so that no member is ever left in the uncomfortable position of a lone dissenter.
options.D: A review panel publishes the reasoning behind each member's vote and records every dissenting opinion alongside the final decision.

questions.question: According to the passage, ambiguity strengthens the bystander effect because

options.A: witnesses who are unsure what is happening assume that the authorities have already been called.
options.B: people are reluctant to help strangers whose situation they cannot fully understand or explain.
options.C: onlookers in a large crowd find it physically harder to see clearly what is happening to the victim.
options.D: each witness reads the calm of the other onlookers as a sign that nothing serious is happening.

questions.question: The distinction drawn in paragraph 3 implies which of the following?

options.A: Victims are always more likely to be helped in a large crowd than when only a single witness happens to be present.
options.B: Showing that each person helps less in a group does not by itself settle how likely a victim is to be helped.
options.C: The laboratory studies were mistaken to conclude that people are less likely to help a victim when others are present.
options.D: Individuals in a crowd are just as willing to help a victim as individuals who believe they are alone with that victim.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the original bystander experiments is best described as

options.A: respectful of the mechanisms they uncovered but critical of the sweeping lesson popularly drawn from them.
options.B: undecided, since the passage weighs older laboratory work against newer field studies without reaching a view.
options.C: admiring without reservation, since their findings confirmed the newspaper account that inspired them.
options.D: dismissive, treating them as an elaborate scientific dressing for an exaggerated newspaper story.

questions.question: The advice in the last sentence of the passage serves mainly to

options.A: demonstrate that crowds become helpful once the people in them have been taught about the bystander effect.
options.B: suggest that victims, rather than bystanders, are chiefly responsible when help fails to arrive in an emergency.
options.C: show that the research offers practical guidance drawn from the mechanisms it found, not from the sweeping popular claim.
options.D: concede that the popular version of the bystander effect is broadly accurate after all, despite the doubts raised earlier.

questions.question: According to the passage, some participants in the minimal group experiments

options.A: preferred divisions that widened the difference between the two groups even when another division would have given their own group more.
options.B: met the other members of their category before the task and divided the money according to friendships they had formed.
options.C: gave more to the other group when they believed that members of their own group were watching their choices.
options.D: refused to give any money at all to members of the other group once they learned which group they belonged to.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the reciprocity account described in paragraph 3?

options.A: Participants assigned to groups by an openly random coin toss showed favouritism as readily as those grouped by a dot-counting task.
options.B: Participants were reluctant to impose penalties on the other group even when they were free to impose any penalty they liked.
options.C: Participants favoured their own group just as strongly when assured that nobody would ever learn how they had allocated.
options.D: Participants favoured their own group more strongly when the allocation involved large sums of money than when it involved small sums.

questions.question: The final paragraph functions primarily to

options.A: dismiss the minimal group paradigm as irrelevant to the study of how real groups behave in the world outside the laboratory.
options.B: withdraw the hopeful conclusion of paragraph 4 by conceding that real divisions are too deep to be redrawn by any mechanism.
options.C: argue that intergroup conflict is caused by competition over land, jobs and power rather than by any sense of shared identity.
options.D: set a limit on what the experiments can explain, separating the origins of group loyalty from the causes of bitter conflict.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Favouritism towards an arbitrary group is the same tendency that, when intensified, produces conflicts between nations and religions.
options.B: That arbitrary categories take hold so easily gives grounds for hope as well as for concern about relations between groups.
options.C: Because the experiments found favouritism rather than hostility, prejudice between real groups is largely a matter of rational reciprocity.
options.D: Since a label can be conjured from a coin toss, the categories people adopt have little real effect on how they treat others.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the statement 'what is wrong is its range' means that

options.A: the feeling is excessively intense, so that it overwhelms the person who experiences it and clouds judgement.
options.B: the feeling lasts too long, so that sympathy for a past wrong continues to shape behaviour years later.
options.C: the feeling is real, but the selective set of people it reaches and excludes is what makes it harmful.
options.D: the feeling is not truly felt, but is a pretence adopted in order to justify punishing members of a group.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author considers compassion better suited than empathy to guiding help for strangers partly because compassion

options.A: is entirely free of the preference for the near and the similar that distorts every other form of moral concern.
options.B: does not require sharing a stranger's feelings, and so is not confined to people one can vividly imagine.
options.C: is a purely rational commitment to principle that involves no feeling of any kind towards the person helped.
options.D: is felt more intensely than empathy, and therefore moves people to act more quickly when they encounter suffering.

questions.question: The passage attributes each of the following tendencies to empathy EXCEPT a tendency to

options.A: weaken as the person who is suffering becomes more familiar to the one who feels it.
options.B: favour the present over the future when people weigh whose needs to attend to.
options.C: be turned from sympathy for one wronged person into demands to punish a whole group.
options.D: respond more strongly to a single identifiable victim than to large numbers suffering in the same way.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's central claim about empathy?

options.A: Doctors who feel strong empathy for their patients form closer relationships with them and are trusted more by the patients they treat.
options.B: Appeals that describe one named victim in detail raise more money for a cause than appeals that report the total number of victims.
options.C: People who help strangers out of a sense of fairness report feeling less emotional exhaustion than those who help out of shared distress.
options.D: The most intensely empathic people turn out also to give the most generously and impartially to distant populations they will never see.

questions.question: According to the passage, gossip is important to indirect reciprocity because it

options.A: carries news of a person's conduct to people who were not present and never witnessed it.
options.B: discourages people from cheating by making them fear immediate punishment from those who watched them.
options.C: allows relatives and neighbours to coordinate the return of favours that they owe to one another.
options.D: replaces the need to judge other people's motives with a simple record of who helped whom.

questions.question: Paragraph 3 implies that if observers counted every refusal to help as bad conduct, then

options.A: cooperation would become more stable, because people would have stronger reasons to help everyone they met.
options.B: observers would need to keep track of people's motives and of whom they had refused to help, and why.
options.C: cheats would gain from the rule, since anyone who refused to help them would be marked down for doing so.
options.D: people would stop gossiping about one another, since there would be nothing distinctive left to report.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the author treats the reply about habits formed in a world where anonymity was rare as

options.A: an implausible excuse, invented after the fact, which defenders of the account should drop altogether.
options.B: a plausible defence that nonetheless changes the type of explanation from calculation to disposition.
options.C: evidence that the laboratory studies using pictures of eyes were poorly designed and should be repeated.
options.D: a decisive answer that fully restores the claim that reputation explains all cooperation among strangers.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the conclusion the passage reaches?

options.A: Indirect reciprocity cannot work in large societies, because observers cannot judge whether refusing to help a cheat is wrong.
options.B: Reputation fully explains cooperation among strangers once the spread of gossip and the careful judging of motives are taken into account.
options.C: Cooperation among strangers is better explained by dispositions formed in small societies than by any concern for reputation.
options.D: Concern about being talked about is a major support of cooperation among strangers, though it cannot explain all generosity and needs accurate talk.

questions.question: It follows from the argument of paragraph 3 that a person who hears a correction and keeps the false belief with unchanged confidence

options.A: shows that the larger studies described in paragraph 2 were mistaken about how people respond to corrections.
options.B: demonstrates that people are perfectly unresponsive to evidence whenever a belief is tied to their loyalties.
options.C: offers no support for the view that correcting a false belief is likely to do more harm than good.
options.D: is an example of the backfire effect, since the correction has failed to weaken the belief at all.

questions.question: A town council wants to correct a widely believed false rumour that its water supply has been contaminated. Which approach best reflects the passage's recommendations?

options.A: Repeat the correction over several weeks and explain what actually caused the reports, rather than simply denying the rumour.
options.B: Address the correction only to residents who already doubt the rumour, since firm believers will simply grow more convinced.
options.C: Issue one authoritative denial from the council and treat the matter as settled once the statement has been published.
