options.D: Avoid mentioning the rumour at all, since drawing attention to it is likely to make residents believe it more firmly.

questions.question: The final paragraph contributes to the passage chiefly by

options.A: conceding that the backfire effect is real after all, since the mistaken finding has resisted every attempt to correct it.
options.B: turning the passage's distinction on the history of the finding itself, suggesting that its correction meets resistance but not reversal.
options.C: summarising the evidence of paragraph 2 that factual corrections reliably move people towards the accurate view.
options.D: introducing new evidence that the original backfire studies were deliberately exaggerated by the researchers who conducted them.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that the backfire idea 'confused resistance with reversal'?

options.A: Later studies of corrections recruited a wider range of participants and covered more topics than the early studies of backfire did.
options.B: The effects of corrections typically faded within a few weeks, so that many people returned to the false beliefs they had abandoned.
options.C: Participants who resisted a correction often described the source of the correction as hostile to their political loyalties.
options.D: Several early reports of backfire counted as a backfire any case in which participants' beliefs simply failed to move towards the correction.

questions.question: On the cultural-learning account described in paragraph 2, deference to prestigious people is

options.A: an inheritance shared with other primates that predates the human reliance on cultural learning.
options.B: extracted by skilled people who threaten to withhold their knowledge from anyone who refuses it.
options.C: a payment that learners make in return for being allowed close to those with skill.
options.D: a sign that learners have already mastered the skills of the person they defer to and wish to show it.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'overspill' refers to

options.A: learners copying traits of an admired person that have nothing to do with the skill for which the person is admired.
options.B: the surplus of deference that a prestigious person receives over and above what his real skill would justify.
options.C: the spread of a skilled person's methods to more learners than he could ever teach directly in person.
options.D: the conversion of a prestigious person's following into allies and resources that can be used to coerce.

questions.question: The passage suggests that indiscriminate imitation is less costly in a small community chiefly because

options.A: learners in small communities can always tell which of a successful person's habits are responsible for the success.
options.B: the habits that accompany a person's skill there are more likely to be connected with it for good reasons.
options.C: prestigious people in small communities are seldom able to convert their following into the power to coerce.
options.D: people in small communities defer to skilled individuals far less than people living in large societies do.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates the complication the author describes in paragraph 4?

options.A: A factory manager who threatens to dismiss workers is obeyed promptly, although the workers neither admire him nor try to learn from him.
options.B: A famous athlete's opinions on diet and politics are widely adopted by fans who know nothing of his views on either subject beyond his fame.
options.C: A young musician copies her teacher's practice routine and posture and becomes noticeably better at playing her instrument as a result.
options.D: A scholar admired for her research uses the loyalty of her many students to block the appointment of critics, while her admirers see only her brilliance.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: accept that status can rest on fear or on freely given deference, while showing that prestige has hazards of its own and mixes with dominance.
options.B: argue that modern institutions, by rewarding prestige rather than force, have largely solved the problem of how status is distributed.
options.C: show that the distinction between dominance and prestige breaks down in practice and should therefore be abandoned by students of status.
options.D: defend the cultural-learning explanation of prestige against the objection that prestige is merely dominance in a more respectable disguise.

questions.question: According to the passage, one of the practices that helped a literature look more robust than it was involved

options.A: running studies so large that trivial effects appeared to be meaningful and worth publishing.
options.B: fabricating data for the most celebrated studies in order to make their findings more dramatic.
options.C: trying several reasonable analyses of the data and reporting the one that produced a result.
options.D: translating experimental materials poorly when studies were carried out in different countries.

questions.question: The reference in paragraph 3 to recognising a related word more easily serves to

options.A: show that the behavioural priming studies of paragraph 1 were in fact correct, since both kinds of priming rest on the same mechanism.
options.B: support the defenders' reply that priming effects vary across cultures, generations and sets of experimental materials.
options.C: illustrate the kind of surprising result that, according to paragraph 2, is most likely to be false and also most celebrated.
options.D: narrow the scope of the doubt by separating a well-established kind of priming from the contested claim about social behaviour.

questions.question: Which of the following reasoning patterns is most similar to the one the author criticises at the end of paragraph 4?

options.A: A forecaster claims only that his method works for one coastal region and is consistently accurate within that region.
options.B: A forecaster explains each failed prediction, after the event, by pointing to local conditions that he had never said would matter.
options.C: A forecaster revises his model after a failure and states in advance which conditions the revised model is meant to cover.
options.D: A forecaster publicises the predictions that came true and quietly leaves out the many that did not when describing his record.

questions.question: The author regards the framing of the debate as a trial as unhelpful chiefly because it

options.A: wrongly accuses researchers whose work was entirely sound and whose results were later confirmed by larger studies.
options.B: points attention at individual dishonesty when the deeper problem lay in practices that were widely accepted as normal.
options.C: implies that the people who carried out the failed replications were themselves acting dishonestly or out of malice.
options.D: delays the methodological reforms that the field needed by turning a technical debate into a personal quarrel.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the reforms described in the final paragraph is best described as

options.A: guarded approval, made conditional on finding ways of reducing the costs in time and money that the reforms impose.
options.B: reluctant acceptance, tempered by regret that the field will no longer produce the striking results that once made it famous.
options.C: unqualified enthusiasm, on the grounds that the reforms will improve the field without costing it anything of real value.
options.D: firm endorsement, with an open acknowledgement that they make research slower, costlier and less dazzling.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain why people who have been blind from birth continue to gesture while they are speaking.
options.B: urge schools to drop rules that require pupils to keep their hands still during lessons.
options.C: argue that gesture serves the speaker's own thinking as well as the listener's understanding.
options.D: show that gesture contributes more to successful communication than the spoken words it accompanies.

questions.question: The examples of telephone conversations and of speakers who have been blind from birth are used in paragraph 2 to

options.A: show that people keep gesturing in situations where their gestures cannot inform anyone.
options.B: show that gesturing is learnt by watching others, since people copy movements that they have seen.
options.C: suggest that listeners understand speakers better when they are able to see the speaker's hands.
options.D: prove that gesture plays no part in helping a listener to follow what a speaker is saying.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'The more economical conclusion' refers to a conclusion that

options.A: accounts for the observations without needing any strained extra assumptions.
options.B: costs researchers less time and money to test than the listener-only explanation does.
options.C: saves the speaker effort by reducing the number of movements needed to communicate.
options.D: can be stated in fewer words than the explanation it is replacing.

questions.question: Based on the passage, a child whose hands show one strategy for a sum while her words describe a different one is best understood as someone who

options.A: already understands the correct method fully but lacks the vocabulary needed to put it into words.
options.B: has revealed that her spoken reasoning is unreliable, so that her gestures ought to be trusted over her words.
options.C: may be nearer to grasping a new method than her spoken explanation on its own would reveal.
options.D: is using her hands mainly to help the teacher follow a strategy that she finds hard to describe.

questions.question: According to the passage, the octopus's intelligence is said to have been 'assembled independently' because

options.A: octopuses learn their skills alone, without any parents or companions to teach them how to hunt.
options.B: each of its arms developed its own nervous system separately during the octopus's own evolutionary history.
options.C: the octopus has a far larger share of its neurons in its central brain than vertebrates have in theirs.
options.D: its lineage split from ours before either had developed anything like a complex brain.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards describing the octopus as 'an animal with nine brains' is best described as

options.A: dismissive of the anatomy behind it, since the author doubts that octopus arms do much on their own.
options.B: critical, since the description inflates a real anatomical fact into a claim the facts do not support.
options.C: neutral, since the author reports the description without saying whether it is accurate or misleading.
options.D: approving, since the description captures in vivid terms what the observations of the arms have shown.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the octopus's way of distributing control is best explained by

options.A: the small size of the octopus's central brain, which leaves it unable to issue commands to its arms.
options.B: the very long period during which the octopus lineage has evolved apart from vertebrates.
options.C: the advantage to an animal that often loses arms of having limbs that can go on acting on their own.
options.D: the difficulty, for any single centre, of controlling flexible and boneless limbs that can bend at any point.

questions.question: Which of the following arrangements most closely resembles the organisation of the octopus as the author describes it?

options.A: A building firm whose director sets the goals of a project while each specialist crew decides for itself how to do its own part of the work.
options.B: A street market with no authority of any kind, in which whatever order exists arises entirely from many separate traders.
options.C: A loose federation of towns, each pursuing its own aims and cooperating with the others only when doing so happens to suit it.
options.D: An army in which a general issues detailed orders for every movement and each unit carries out those orders exactly as given.

questions.question: According to the passage, what must an animal grasp in order to pass the mirror test?

options.A: That a mirror is a flat surface which reverses left and right in the image it reflects.
options.B: That the figure in the mirror is not another animal but corresponds to its own body.
options.C: That the mark on its forehead was placed there by the researchers who are running the test.
options.D: That its past and its future belong to one continuing individual with a history of its own.

questions.question: The comparison with a person asked a question in an unfamiliar language (paragraph 3) is meant to show that

options.A: self-recognition depends on language, so that animals without language cannot recognise themselves in mirrors.
options.B: researchers have been careless in choosing marks and mirrors that suit the senses of the species they study.
options.C: a test that does not suit the subject's way of engaging with the world can produce failure that reveals little.
options.D: animals that fail the mirror test would pass if the test were explained to them in a form they could understand.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument about what failure on the mirror test shows?

options.A: Animals that pass the mirror test also tend to live in large and complex social groups.
options.B: Some animals that pass the mirror test go on to use mirrors to inspect parts of their bodies that they cannot otherwise see.
options.C: Several species of monkey that fail the mirror test perform well on other tests of memory and problem solving.
options.D: Dogs that ignore their reflection sniff a sample of their own scent far longer when it has been altered with an added odour than when it is left unchanged.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the author's view of the mirror test EXCEPT:

options.A: A species whose members do not groom may fail the test without lacking the capacity it is meant to detect.
options.B: Animals that pass the test probably have some representation of their own bodies as objects among others.
options.C: Animals that pass the test can be credited, on that evidence, with thinking of themselves as having a past and a future.
options.D: The test remains worth running, provided its results are not allowed to settle on their own which animals are self-aware.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the critics' view that brain metaphors are 'fashions' is best described as

options.A: partial agreement, accepting that no metaphor was the whole truth while denying that they were merely fashionable.
options.B: firm rejection, holding that the computer metaphor, unlike earlier ones, describes the brain literally and exactly.
options.C: complete agreement, accepting that the computer image will soon look as quaint and empty as the hydraulic one.
options.D: indifference, treating the question of whether the metaphors are fashions as unimportant to understanding the brain.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the main contribution of the computer metaphor as the idea that

options.A: the brain can be divided into hardware and software, with programs that run independently of the structures doing the work.
options.B: what matters about neural signals is the information they carry and how it is transformed, not the material that carries them.
options.C: signals must travel from the senses to the centre and back again to the muscles along definite routes.
options.D: memories are held in fixed locations in the brain, where each record remains unaltered until it is retrieved.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the critics in paragraph 2?

options.A: Researchers who used the switchboard image also held many beliefs about the brain that later turned out to be false.
options.B: The ideas credited to each metaphor were already established by direct study of nerves before that metaphor came into use.
options.C: Some present-day researchers prefer to describe the brain using images drawn from biology rather than from machines.
options.D: The hydraulic picture of the nerves was far more widely accepted among scholars than the switchboard picture ever was.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Machine metaphors for the brain have each made something real thinkable, and the risk is in mistaking them for literal descriptions.
options.B: The computer is the most accurate metaphor for the brain yet devised, because it is the most complex machine so far built.
options.C: Brain metaphors drawn from machines are passing fashions, and brain science would progress faster if it gave them up.
options.D: Memory is better described as reconstruction than as storage, contrary to what the computer image of the brain suggests.

questions.question: According to the evolutionary explanation described in the passage, perception seems easy to us because

options.A: children practise it constantly in their earliest years, long before they begin any formal schooling.
options.B: it requires very little computation compared with abstract tasks such as algebra and chess.
options.C: the processes that carry it out operate almost entirely outside conscious awareness.
options.D: it is performed by a small and specialised part of the brain that works without needing effort.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as a mistake?

options.A: Holding that the skills of seeing, grasping and moving were refined over a very long period of animal evolution.
options.B: Recognising that machines now identify images and speech far better than early researchers expected.
options.C: Doubting that skill at chess and formal logic is the best measure of how intelligent a creature is.
options.D: Concluding that a skill must demand a great deal of computation simply because people perform it without any effort.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the account of the paradox given in paragraph 2?

options.A: Upgrading the parts of a machine so that it completes in seconds a calculation that once took hours.
options.B: Judging the size of an iceberg from the part above the water, and so overlooking the far larger mass beneath it.
options.C: Finding a subject hard at school because it was taught badly, and later finding it easy under a better teacher.
options.D: Believing that a familiar walk is shorter than an unfamiliar one of equal length, simply because it is familiar.

questions.question: Given the passage as a whole, the author's answer to whether the 'paradox' 'deserves the name' is best captured by which of the following?

options.A: It is a genuine contradiction in the science of machines, and recent progress in machine perception has now largely resolved it.
options.B: It is misnamed, because machines have in fact always found perceiving and moving easier than reasoning.
options.C: It deserves the name, since the evolutionary account cannot explain why some effortless skills are also easy for machines.
options.D: The finding is surprising only on the assumption that the effort a task costs humans measures how much intelligence it requires.

questions.question: The sentence 'If a language were a prison, its inmates would not so regularly be found outside the walls' functions in paragraph 1 to

options.A: introduce the weaker form of the view that the passage goes on to examine in paragraph 2.
options.B: suggest that translation between languages, however carefully attempted, is never fully possible.
options.C: sum up, in a single image, the objections that count against the strong form of the view.
options.D: concede that the strong view contains a real, if limited, truth about how language confines its speakers.

questions.question: The finding described in paragraph 3 matters to the author's argument chiefly because it suggests that

options.A: the colour advantage reflects words being drawn on during the task, not a lasting change in how colours are seen.
options.B: speakers with only one basic word for blue tell blues apart by relying on spatial memory rather than on words.
options.C: the advantage reported in paragraph 2 was an artefact of careless experimental design and should be disregarded.
options.D: the verbal and visual systems draw on one shared store of memory, so that occupying either one weakens the other.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the interpretation the author offers in paragraph 4?

options.A: A larger study finds that lifelong speakers with two words for blue keep the boundary advantage even while their verbal system is fully occupied by another task.
options.B: Languages differ in how many basic words they have for shapes and textures as well as for colours.
options.C: The boundary advantage for speakers with two words for blue is larger when the two colours are shown side by side than when they are shown one after the other.
options.D: Speakers of a language with one basic word for blue quickly learn to tell lighter and darker blues apart when rewarded for doing so.

questions.question: The passage suggests that defenders and critics of linguistic relativity alike

options.A: accept that the strong form of the view, though discredited, is still defended by many researchers.
options.B: agree that the effects of colour words on perception are too small to be worth studying further.
options.C: recognise that ordinary thought is often partly carried out in words even where it seems wordless.
options.D: judge the importance of language by whether it leaves a lasting mark on how speakers perceive.

questions.question: According to the passage, Morgan's canon was first proposed as a response to

options.A: a growing belief among scientists that animals were mere machines that lacked any mental faculties at all.
options.B: disputes over whether chimpanzees and humans rely on similar mechanisms when they behave in similar ways.
options.C: reports of animal intelligence in which observers read their own feelings into what animals did.
options.D: experiments on animals that had been designed so poorly that they could not rule out simpler explanations.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that, when two closely related species behave alike in similar circumstances, the author regards an explanation in terms of shared mechanisms as

options.A: certainly correct, since close kinship guarantees that similar behaviour arises from similar mechanisms.
options.B: possibly the more parsimonious account, contrary to what the rigid reading of the canon implies.
options.C: a kind of anthropomorphism that the canon was rightly designed to prevent scientists from adopting.
options.D: impossible to test, since the mechanisms behind behaviour can never be observed directly in either species.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude towards Morgan's canon?

options.A: Critical of Morgan for having meant his rule as a ban on crediting any animal with a higher faculty.
options.B: Hostile, since the author holds that it set the study of animal minds back by encouraging excessive caution.
options.C: Approving of the presumption it later became, while regretting that it began as a reaction against anecdote.
options.D: Appreciative of what it achieved as a corrective, but critical of the fixed presumption it later hardened into.

questions.question: The author criticises the presumption in favour of the lowest explanation on each of the following grounds EXCEPT that it

options.A: can require separate explanations for similar behaviour in closely related species, rather than fewer.
options.B: relies on experiments that are unable, in principle, to tell lean explanations apart from rich ones.
options.C: equates a lower explanation with a simpler one, and a simpler explanation with a more probable one.
options.D: guards against crediting animals with capacities they lack while ignoring the error of denying capacities they have.

questions.question: A researcher wants to know whether crows that hide food take account of which other birds have watched them. Which approach best reflects the 'symmetrical standard' the author recommends?

options.A: State both an association account and an account in which crows track what others have seen, and design trials in which the two predict different behaviour.
options.B: Design an experiment to test the association account first, and accept the richer account only if the association account clearly fails.
options.C: Collect many careful reports from experienced bird-watchers, and accept whichever account the largest number of reports supports.
options.D: Accept the account in which crows track what others have seen, since crows are widely regarded as unusually intelligent birds.

questions.question: The example of early thermometers in paragraph 4 is used to

options.A: suggest that the study of consciousness is still at the stage that the study of heat was centuries ago.
options.B: argue that no-report methods should replace reports entirely in the study of conscious experience.
options.C: show that a circle of mutual checking among imperfect measures need not be a vicious one.
options.D: show that bodily sensations are a more trustworthy guide to temperature than thermometers are.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the masking experiments described in paragraph 3, holding the physical stimulus constant matters because it

options.A: shows that subjects' reports of what they have seen are accurate and can be accepted without checking.
options.B: rules out differences in the image itself as the cause of differences in brain activity between kinds of trial.
options.C: removes any influence that the act of reporting might have on the brain activity that is recorded.
options.D: ensures that the subject has actually seen the image on every trial, whatever her report says.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a subject's sincere report that she saw nothing on a particular trial

options.A: is less reliable than the involuntary eye movements that are used to track which image is being experienced.
options.B: should be set aside, since reports are shaped too strongly by expectation and the wish to please to count as data.
options.C: settles that she had no experience of the image on that trial, since no one else is better placed to know.
options.D: is evidence about her experience that could, in principle, turn out to be mistaken.

questions.question: Which of the following most closely parallels the reasoning the author uses to answer the critics in paragraph 4?

options.A: A witness's account of an accident is accepted in full because the witness is sincere and had a clear view of what happened.
options.B: A measuring tape is thrown away for good once it is found to stretch slightly whenever the weather is hot.
options.C: Two independent methods for dating ancient timber, each with known errors, come to be trusted more once they agree across many samples, and each is then used to refine the other.
options.D: A new thermometer is trusted because it was made in the same workshop as an older thermometer that has always been reliable.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Reports are fallible evidence that can be calibrated, so doubts about them do not rule out a science of consciousness, whatever its final reach.
options.B: Sincere reports may misdescribe detail, but they remain the final authority on what a subject actually experiences.
options.C: Because reports so often misdescribe experience, consciousness research should rely on no-report methods instead of on reports.
options.D: A science of consciousness will explain why experience exists once its methods of measurement have been calibrated against one another.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that secure tenure matters more to the residents of informal settlements than drains, water supply or paved lanes.
options.B: argue that improving informal settlements where they stand generally serves residents better than relocating them, while noting where this approach falls short.
options.C: argue that informal settlements, having been built by their own residents, should be left as they are rather than altered by public authorities.
options.D: explain why planners in the last century preferred to build replacement housing on cheap land at the edge of the city.

questions.question: According to the passage, the relocation blocks were often half empty within a few years because

options.A: the land chosen for the estates was prone to flooding and landslides during the heavy rains of the monsoon.
options.B: the new blocks lacked the drains and secure walls that the residents had been promised before they agreed to move.
options.C: the residents were ungrateful and did not understand which kind of housing would serve their interests best.
options.D: moving to them cut households off from the work, schools and markets that had made their earlier location valuable.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the statement that the empty blocks were 'not a puzzle but a verdict' means that the empty blocks were

options.A: a judgement on relocation that residents delivered by moving out, once the costs of distance are understood.
options.B: a court ruling that later stopped the authorities from clearing further settlements across the city.
options.C: a mystery that planners could not explain, even after they had studied the residents' reasons closely.
options.D: an official finding that the new housing had been badly designed and poorly built by the authorities.

questions.question: The author would most likely describe a programme that paves the lanes and lays sewers in a settlement but gives residents no protection against eviction as

options.A: a romantic attempt to keep the settlement exactly as it was, against the wishes of most of its residents.
options.B: a successful upgrade, because residents stay where they are and the networks that sustain them are preserved.
options.C: an incomplete improvement, because residents would remain unwilling to invest in houses they might still lose.
options.D: worse than relocation, because improving such a settlement amounts to investing in a future disaster.

questions.question: According to the passage, density differs from crowding in that

options.A: density is a ratio of people or dwellings to land, while crowding concerns too many people for the room they have.
options.B: density is found mainly in large cities, while crowding is a problem that arises chiefly in villages.
options.C: density damages the health of residents, while crowding is merely uncomfortable for those who experience it.
options.D: density refers to how many people share a room, while crowding refers to how many live on a hectare.

questions.question: The comparison of two districts with the same number of residents per hectare (paragraph 2) serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that maps showing population per hectare are usually drawn from inaccurate or outdated figures.
options.B: show that areas equal in density can differ sharply in how crowded daily life within them is.
options.C: prove that tall apartment buildings are always better places to live than low houses on narrow lanes.
options.D: illustrate the method by which nineteenth-century reformers tried to spread the urban population out.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the nineteenth-century reformers mentioned in paragraph 3

options.A: deliberately exaggerated the dangers of density in order to win public support for large building programmes.
options.B: succeeded in lowering death rates in industrial cities chiefly by persuading residents to move to less dense districts.
options.C: were mistaken in thinking that anything about conditions in the industrial cities needed to be changed at all.
options.D: rightly sensed that the industrial cities were unhealthy but located the cause in density rather than in rooms and sanitation.

questions.question: A city has a district in which several families typically share one room. Which approach would the author most likely recommend?

options.A: Capping the number of residents per hectare and moving those above the limit to new settlements on the edge of the city.
options.B: Replacing every low house in the district with high towers, because building upward removes crowding wherever it is tried.
options.C: Increasing the floor space available to each household and supplying water and drains, without necessarily reducing residents per hectare.
options.D: Leaving the district as it is, since residents' sense of being crowded counts for less than the measured density of the land.

questions.question: The passage implies that, before walkability indices became common, walking was widely regarded in planning as

options.A: a fallback way of getting about for people who had no option of driving.
options.B: the most important consideration in the design of new residential districts.
options.C: a form of exercise that estate agents promoted in order to sell homes in the suburbs.
options.D: a leisure pursuit with little bearing on how people reached shops and schools.

questions.question: Each of the following is a claim the author makes about walkability indices EXCEPT that they

options.A: rest on an assumption that the main purpose of walking is to reach some destination or other.
options.B: can be raised by a city without making the experience of walking in it any better than before.
options.C: tend to overstate the number of shops, schools and stops that lie within a short walk of a typical home.
options.D: have helped to bring walking into the calculations that planners use when they lay out districts.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that two districts with identical scores can offer entirely different experiences of walking?

options.A: Many residents of districts with high index scores continue to own cars and drive for most of their journeys.
options.B: Homes in districts with high index scores tend to sell for more than similar homes in districts with low scores.
options.C: Narrow pavements beside fast traffic are found in about as many high-scoring districts as low-scoring ones.
options.D: Across a large sample of districts, residents' ratings of how pleasant their streets are to walk along closely match the districts' index scores.

questions.question: On the author's view, a city that wished to improve walking in a district, and not merely its walkability score, should begin by

options.A: abandoning composite indices and relying instead on residents' own descriptions of what their streets are like.
options.B: studying the routes residents actually use between their homes and nearby destinations, and the conditions they meet along them.
options.C: raising the share of homes that lie near public transport, since reaching transport is what walking is chiefly for.
options.D: permitting more shops, clinics and services to open within a short radius of the homes already in the district.

questions.question: According to the passage, developers come to provide plazas, arcades and gardens open to the public because

options.A: the city pays them for the ground at a price well above what it would fetch on the open market.
options.B: building codes in most large cities require every new tower to include some open space at its base.
options.C: they are allowed to build larger or taller than the rules would otherwise permit in return.
options.D: open spaces attract tenants and shoppers, and so add to the rents that the developer can later charge.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, private managers tend to withdraw the permissions listed in paragraph 3 chiefly because

options.A: those permissions bring the owner a little risk and no income, rather than because owners dislike the public.
options.B: planning law in most cities forbids protest and leafleting on land that remains in private ownership.
options.C: few people who use such plazas actually wish to stay in them, meet others there or hand out leaflets.
options.D: owners regard the people who would linger or protest in their plazas with open hostility and contempt.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the practice of trading extra floor area for open space is best described as

options.A: weary indifference, because ownership settles very little and the resulting spaces will be much the same either way.
options.B: qualified approval: the exchange is sound in principle but worthless unless the city secures and enforces permissions.
options.C: warm enthusiasm, because the city obtains open space without spending any public money and owners keep it well maintained.
options.D: outright rejection, because a space in private ownership can never become genuinely public whatever rules are attached to it.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that the important question is who writes a space's rules and to whom the writers must answer?

options.A: A study in one city found that its privately owned plazas were, on average, smaller, darker and harder to find from the street than its publicly owned squares.
options.B: Surveys in one city found that visitors consistently rated its privately owned plazas as cleaner, quieter and safer than publicly owned squares of a similar size and age.
options.C: Over a period of several decades, developers in one city were granted progressively larger floor-area bonuses for each plaza, arcade or garden that they provided.
options.D: In one city, private plazas whose rules of use the municipality set and published were as open to loiterers and leafleters as its best squares; plazas with owner-written rules were not.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain how districts designed around the car leave the young, the old and the poor unable to reach shops on foot.
options.B: defend the suburb as a better form of settlement than the dense centre of a large city, in which families are denied space.
options.C: show that the residents of suburban streets lead far more varied lives than novelists and critics have claimed.
options.D: argue that criticism of the suburb should address its remediable design faults instead of condemning what its residents want.

questions.question: The author treats the uniformity of the language used against the suburb (paragraph 1) as

options.A: evidence that many critics had studied suburbs closely and independently reached the same conclusions.
options.B: a sign that suburban residents themselves had come to accept the critics' description of their lives.
options.C: grounds for doubting that the indictment does justice to what suburban life is actually like.
options.D: proof that suburban streets really are as monotonous as the critics' descriptions make them out to be.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 2 in the passage?

options.A: It concedes part of the critics' case but casts those faults as products of design, preparing the later contrast between design and desire.
options.B: It dismisses the critics' practical objections to the suburb before the author turns to answer their cultural objections.
options.C: It raises a fresh objection to the suburb that the critics described in paragraph 1 had failed to notice or discuss.
options.D: It sets out the strongest evidence for the author's thesis that the suburb is a better place to raise children than the city.

questions.question: Which of the following proposals for an existing suburb would the author most likely regard as answering the objections accepted in paragraph 2, in the way the passage recommends?

options.A: Halting all further suburban building in the district, because development of this kind consumes land and fuel at a great rate.
options.B: Allowing a grocer and a clinic on a few corner plots, and making the main road safe for children to cross.
options.C: Replacing detached houses with blocks of flats, so that families learn to prefer shared space over private gardens.
options.D: Requiring new houses to have varied facades and materials, so that the streets no longer look monotonous to visitors.

questions.question: The author implies that the count of departures described in paragraph 1, if carried out carefully, would

options.A: be impossible to carry out in practice, because households that leave a district cannot be traced afterwards.
options.B: measure what it set out to measure, but would miss a kind of harm suffered by residents who stay.
options.C: show that long-standing residents of gentrifying districts leave much faster than residents of districts that have not changed.
options.D: prove that complaints about gentrification amount to little more than nostalgia for a vanished streetscape.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the 'loss of standing' that the author distinguishes from 'a loss of scenery' refers to

options.A: a fall in the market value of the resident's home as the neighbourhood around it changes and its prices rise.
options.B: the disappearance of familiar shopfronts, benches and buildings that once gave the street its particular look.
options.C: the resident's being compelled, sooner or later, to leave the district in which she has lived for many years.
options.D: the decline of the resident's accepted place in her street: her ease in using it and her claim to belong there.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the distinction the author draws in paragraph 4?

options.A: Planners report that judging which relations a place sustains is a good deal harder and slower than counting the households that leave it.
options.B: Newcomers to gentrifying districts frequently form close ties with one another through the new shops, schools and associations that open there.
options.C: Residents of many affluent districts that resist new housing object chiefly that newcomers would erode the informal ties and local voice they have built up over decades.
options.D: Later and more careful counts showed that departures from gentrifying districts were in fact somewhat higher than the earlier counts had suggested.

questions.question: The passage supports each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: A resident who stays in a gentrifying district loses more of her neighbourhood than one who is forced to leave it.
options.B: A count of departures, however careful, cannot register the losses of residents who remain in a changing district.
options.C: Judging character by the relations a place sustains demands more of planners than counting those who leave.
options.D: The same appeal to a neighbourhood's character can serve both to describe a genuine loss and to justify exclusion.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, circular migration, when viewed on its own terms rather than through the one-way story, appears as

options.A: a way of spreading a household's risk across two places, so that a setback in one is softened by the other.
options.B: a choice made chiefly because wages in the city are so much higher than anything the village can offer.
options.C: a temporary stage in a longer journey, which comes to an end once the migrants' children have been absorbed into city life.
options.D: a means by which migrants avoid paying the school fees that the city charges to families who settle there.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the remark that for some migrants circularity is 'less a strategy than a sentence' means that for them it is

options.A: a legal penalty imposed by the city's courts on workers whose residence there is irregular or unregistered.
options.B: a condition forced on them by the city's failure to offer a place, not a course they would choose.
options.C: a brief phase that will soon end as they save enough money to buy land and settle in their village.
options.D: a carefully planned way of spreading risk between a job in the city and a farm in the village.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the persistence of circular migrants' village ties

options.A: will gradually disappear once the migrants' children have grown up speaking the idiom of the city.
options.B: shows that circular migrants have no wish to become part of the cities in which they work for months or years.
options.C: is partly a result of their exclusion from the city, and so cannot fairly be taken as proof that they do not belong there.
options.D: was the original reason why city governments decided to exclude them from housing, schools and the electoral roll.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the one-way story of urbanisation is best described as

options.A: dismissive, since the author regards it as a myth that never described the experience of any real migrants.
options.B: neutral, since the author presents it only as one account among others and passes no judgement on its influence.
options.C: approving, since the author treats it as the proper goal against which circular migration ought to be measured.
options.D: critical of its use as a yardstick for all migration, while granting that it fits many families' history.

questions.question: The recommendations in paragraph 5 are suited to the difficulty raised in paragraph 4 chiefly because they

options.A: would help both migrants forced to circulate and those who choose to, without the city having to tell the two groups apart.
options.B: would end circular migration altogether by removing the hostility of cities that is its underlying cause.
options.C: would persuade migrants who prefer a life in two places to settle permanently in the city instead.
options.D: would identify which migrants wish to settle, so that each group could be offered a programme designed for it.

questions.question: The example of the tenant on a twelve-month lease in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: argue that strict limits on rent increases are the most effective single measure for improving the lives of tenants.
options.B: suggest that tenants ought to be allowed to knock down walls and alter the structure of the houses they rent.
options.C: show that a short, revocable and restrictive tenancy, not renting as such, keeps a person from making a home.
options.D: show that renters, whatever the terms of their tenancy, invest less of themselves in their rooms than owners do.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard the owner described at the end of paragraph 3, whose mortgage consumes most of his income, as

options.A: a person who has 'failed to arrive' at home because of the debts he took on in order to buy his house.
options.B: someone who holds title yet may lack the security on which making a home depends.
options.C: proof that owning a house is generally a worse arrangement than renting one on secure and long-term terms.
options.D: an exception that confirms the rule that ownership always supplies both of the conditions a home requires.

questions.question: The argument of paragraph 5 depends on the assumption that

options.A: renters as a group take less interest in local schools than owners do, whatever the length and security of their tenancies.
options.B: the attachment residents feel to a neighbourhood depends mainly on the physical design of its streets and public spaces.
options.C: most households that rent would prefer to own their homes if the price of buying one were to fall far enough.
options.D: people are less willing to invest effort in places and relationships they expect soon to be separated from.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?

options.A: What people value in a home is above all security rather than control, so tenancy reform should give every tenant a lease without any end date.
options.B: Renting has become the usual tenure in cities, and tenancy law has failed to keep pace with the growing number of households that rent.
options.C: Ownership confers no real advantage over a secure tenancy, so public support for buyers should be ended and redirected entirely to tenants.
options.D: Home is made through practices that need control and security, which ownership usually but not necessarily supplies, so policy should not treat ownership as the only route to home.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the policies mentioned in paragraph 1 can 'present themselves' as the extension of home rather than as choices among ways of housing people because

options.A: once home is defined as ownership, promoting ownership seems to need no defence against alternatives.
options.B: tenants who bought the public housing they had rented reported feeling far more at home there after the purchase.
options.C: their designers knew that renters could never make real homes and therefore saw no alternative to promoting ownership.
options.D: subsidised mortgages and the sale of public housing have in fact extended home to nearly all of those who lacked it.

questions.question: According to the passage, in a teknonymous system the new name that a parent receives chiefly announces that

options.A: the parent has acquired property that will later pass to the child whose name now appears in the title.
options.B: the parent has reached the age at which the community grants full rights to take part in its decisions.
options.C: the parent's place among their kin has shifted, not that the parent has become a different individual.
options.D: the parent's earlier personal name has been formally prohibited and may no longer be spoken by anyone.

questions.question: The comparison with calling a judge by a childhood nickname in court (paragraph 3) suggests that addressing a parent by the old personal name would be

options.A: a mark of special intimacy that only the parent's closest relatives are entitled to claim.
options.B: a lapse of manners rather than a breach of any rule, since the old name is out of place but not banned.
options.C: acceptable in formal settings such as courts but quite inappropriate in ordinary daily conversation.
options.D: a serious offence that the elders of the community would be expected to punish severely.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, the statement that the personal name has been 'outranked' means that it has been

options.A: displaced in everyday use by a title that carries greater social weight.
options.B: forgotten entirely by the community soon after the birth of the first child.
options.C: replaced in law through an official ceremony of renaming the parent.
options.D: judged inferior in moral worth to the personal names of the parent's children.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Fixed personal names in the West are really a concealed form of teknonymy, since surnames identify people through their descendants.
options.B: Teknonymy is unjust to childless adults and should be judged a less humane way of naming people than the system of fixed names.
options.C: Naming parents through their children expresses a view of persons as made by their place among kin, differing from fixed naming in emphasis.
options.D: Teknonymy shows chiefly that the societies practising it value their children more highly than societies that use fixed names do.

questions.question: According to the passage, the opportunity-cost method values an hour of household work by

options.A: the wage that would have to be paid to someone hired to carry out the same tasks.
options.B: the price of the nearest service that can be bought, such as a meal eaten in a restaurant.
options.C: the number of hours recorded for that task in a national survey of how people use their time.
options.D: what the person doing the work could have earned in paid employment in that hour.

questions.question: The example of an hour of childcare by a surgeon (paragraph 2) serves to

options.A: argue that the opportunity-cost method is in general more accurate than the replacement-cost method.
options.B: show that the two methods can disagree about the value of particular work, not merely about totals.
options.C: suggest that highly paid professionals tend to spend rather less time on childcare than most other parents do.
options.D: illustrate why early statisticians found household work too difficult to observe and record.

questions.question: The author's remark that recording household care at zero 'is also a valuation' (paragraph 3) implies that

options.A: the replacement-cost method ought to replace the zero convention in the national accounts of every country.
options.B: national accounts are generally so inaccurate that they should no longer be used to guide policy.
options.C: leaving such care out of the accounts is itself a contestable choice and not a refusal to choose.
options.D: the critics are right that every possible way of valuing household work is equally arbitrary.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the reason the author gives in paragraph 4 for treating a figure for unpaid care as a floor rather than a measure?

options.A: Elderly people cared for by both paid workers and their own children often value the children's care for reasons unrelated to the tasks.
options.B: Families that pay for help with cleaning tend to report spending more of their own time on looking after children.
options.C: Hired carers are generally able to carry out most household and nursing tasks as efficiently as members of the family can.
options.D: Wages paid to professional care workers have risen faster in recent years than wages in most other occupations.

questions.question: According to the passage, in some societies the bridewealth goods must be returned if a marriage ends before any children are born because

options.A: the groom's family is entitled to be repaid for the expenses it incurred in arranging the wedding.
options.B: what the goods secure is the attachment of the couple's future children to the husband's lineage.
options.C: the bride's father is obliged to give back whatever profit he gained when his daughter married.
options.D: colonial administrators insisted on such refunds as a way of discouraging couples from divorcing.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author treats the chain in which the same cattle pass from family to family (paragraph 2) as evidence that

options.A: families in such societies cared more about their sons' marriages than about their daughters' marriages.
options.B: households joined by such chains usually knew one another well and met often to settle obligations.
options.C: the goods given as bridewealth had little or no economic value for the families who received them.
options.D: bridewealth sets up lasting connections among groups, which is the reverse of what a sale does.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards critics who see a market in cash-based bridewealth (paragraph 4) is best described as

options.A: wholehearted agreement, since their judgement is extended to bridewealth in every setting.
options.B: qualified acceptance: their judgement is granted for such cases without the older verdict being revived.
options.C: studied neutrality, because the author declines to say whether their judgement has any merit.
options.D: dismissive, because they are seen as repeating the early travellers' error in a modern form.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as a way in which bridewealth in its older form differs from a market purchase EXCEPT that

options.A: the transfer opened several continuing relationships instead of closing a single one.
options.B: the goods were shared out among many of the bride's relatives instead of being kept by one recipient.
options.C: the bride herself could take back the goods for her own use if her husband's family mistreated her.
options.D: the bride's kin kept an interest in how the marriage went and some reason to step in when it went badly.

questions.question: The reference to saints painted 'with golden discs around their heads' (paragraph 2) serves to

options.A: prove that medieval parents thought of their children as holy beings rather than as ordinary people.
options.B: illustrate how artistic styles changed between the medieval centuries and the early modern centuries that followed.
options.C: suggest that medieval artists cared far more about religious subjects than about painting children at all.
options.D: show that medieval images followed conventions and so are not plain records of how children were seen.

questions.question: The passage as a whole is primarily concerned with

options.A: rescuing a defensible core from an influential thesis much of whose evidence has been overturned.
options.B: showing that medieval parents loved and grieved for their children just as much as parents do today.
options.C: explaining why historians should stop using paintings as evidence about the past for any purpose.
options.D: defending the claim that no notion of childhood existed in Europe before the early modern period.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that the critics of the original thesis

options.A: were wrong to treat letters and court records as reliable evidence of feeling within families.
options.B: showed that schools divided into classes by age were common throughout medieval Europe.
options.C: failed to find any convincing evidence that medieval parents mourned their dead children.
options.D: settled one question while leaving open the one on which the thesis is still illuminating.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that childhood 'as a segregated, age-graded stage, organised by institutions, is far more recent' (paragraph 3)?

options.A: Records from many medieval towns show most ordinary children attending age-sorted schools and barred by local rule from adult work until their teens.
options.B: Medieval sermons in many regions often urged parents to treat very young children with tenderness, patience and a particular kind of care.
options.C: Early modern painters increasingly showed children with body proportions, faces and clothing that were quite unlike those of the adults around them.
options.D: Many early modern families continued for generations to send young children to work beside adults in the fields for long hours.

questions.question: According to the passage, the old-age dependency ratio is calculated by

options.A: dividing the number of people drawing pensions by the number of people actually in paid employment.
options.B: counting how many older people in a population depend for their daily needs on unpaid care from relatives.
options.C: dividing the number of people above a set age by the number in the conventional working-age band.
options.D: comparing the years that a population can still expect to live with the years it has already lived.

questions.question: The mention of grandparents who look after small children (paragraph 2) is meant to suggest that the ratio

options.A: wrongly assumes that parents who depend on grandparents for childcare are less productive at their jobs.
options.B: treats as pure dependants some people whose work makes it possible for others to earn.
options.C: overlooks the fact that most grandparents would prefer to stay in paid work than to look after children.
options.D: ignores the many families in which working grandparents reduce the need for public spending on pensions.

questions.question: A planning ministry that fully accepted the author's argument would be most likely to forecast its future obligations to older citizens by

options.A: projecting actual rates of paid and unpaid work at each age and the number likely to need intensive care in very late life.
options.B: dropping all projections of spending on health care for older people, since ageing has turned out to be largely costless.
options.C: continuing to rely on the ratio as it is now defined but adding a generous margin to its forecasts to allow for error.
options.D: moving the threshold of old age from sixty-five to seventy and otherwise keeping the familiar ratio exactly as it stands.

questions.question: In the sentence 'The objection is not to concern but to calibration' (paragraph 4), 'calibration' refers to

options.A: how pension payments are adjusted each year to keep pace with prices and the general cost of living.
options.B: how accurately the size of the problem and the point where it bites are gauged.
options.C: how soon governments should begin to respond to the rising number of older citizens in the population.
options.D: how the responsibility for caring for the old is divided between public services and private households.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, under the older vocabulary, a tie between two children nursed by the same woman would have been classed as

options.A: real, because it carries the same bar on marriage that a tie of birth carries.
options.B: biological, because nursing involves the sharing of a bodily substance.
options.C: fictive, because it does not rest on birth or descent.
options.D: metaphorical, because it is modelled on the bond between brothers and sisters.

questions.question: The third paragraph functions chiefly to

options.A: withdraw the earlier claim that the label 'fictive' misdescribes many non-Western forms of kinship.
options.B: argue that new reproductive technologies have now made biological kinship an obsolete idea in the West.
options.C: introduce evidence that biology is the single most important idiom of relatedness in every society.
options.D: limit the scope of the argument and show that its point applies within Western kinship too.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as a way in which, in some societies, people may become kin EXCEPT

options.A: inheriting a share of the same land from a common ancestor.
options.B: eating food that has been grown on the same land.
options.C: making their home together in the same house.
options.D: being nursed as infants by the same woman.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates the author's claim that kinship is 'something people do as well as something they are born into'?

options.A: A woman tracing her ancestry learns from a genetic test that she has a number of cousins living on another continent whom she has never met.
options.B: A girl orphaned in childhood is placed by a court with an uncle she has never met, chosen because he is her nearest living relative by birth.
options.C: A family insists that a long-serving household servant, though deeply loved by all of them, can never be counted as kin because she shares no blood.
options.D: A man raised from infancy by his stepfather comes to regard him, and not the father he never met, as the parent whose funeral rites he must perform.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain why marketers, journalists and employers have come to depend so heavily on labels for each new generation.
options.B: argue that calendar-based generation labels misplace the causes of difference, while granting a narrower, event-anchored notion of generation.
options.C: show that differences in age and period matter less for explaining how people behave than differences of class and region do.
options.D: demonstrate that genuine differences between generations can never be detected in survey data, whatever methods researchers choose to use.

questions.question: A survey carried out in a single year finds that people then in their twenties change jobs more often than people then in their fifties. On the reasoning of paragraph 2, the survey

options.A: would separate age from cohort effects if it were simply repeated with a much larger and more representative sample.
options.B: has shown that the difference is a period effect, since every person surveyed was observed in the same year.
options.C: cannot by itself show whether the difference reflects age or a lasting imprint left on each group by its birth cohort.
options.D: has established that the difference is an age effect, because paragraph 2 says that young people change jobs more often.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's objection to generational boundaries in paragraph 3?

options.A: People who came of age during a major war have been found to show lasting differences in their attitudes to saving and spending money.
options.B: Attitudes shift sharply among people born within a year or two of the usual dividing line between two named generations but change little within each span.
options.C: People born within any one fifteen-year span differ widely in their incomes and outlooks according to their class, region and schooling.
options.D: Different sources that use generational labels routinely disagree by four or five years about where each generation begins and ends.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the idea that people who come of age during a war or a depression may carry its mark for life is best described as

options.A: respectful but restrictive, accepting it as real provided it is not stretched into a character shared by a whole cohort.
options.B: indifferent, mentioning it only so that it can be set aside as irrelevant to the argument against the labels.
options.C: enthusiastic, presenting it as proof that the calendar-based generational labels are broadly accurate after all.
options.D: dismissive, treating it as a piece of marketing that has merely been dressed up in the language of social science.

questions.question: With which of the following statements would the author be LEAST likely to agree?

options.A: Attributing young adults' insecure work to their temperament makes the problem seem less open to a remedy through policy.
options.B: A lasting difference between cohorts is more credible as generational when it can be traced to a specific event in their early years.
options.C: A difference between two cohorts observed at the same age in different decades must be a cohort effect, with no further assumption needed.
options.D: Some members of a cohort may be marked by a formative event far more deeply than others who were born in the same year.

questions.question: According to the passage, a joint household often divides when

options.A: the parents decide to divide the household's property among their daughters.
options.B: the eldest son marries and brings his new wife into his parents' home.
options.C: one of the sons migrates for work to a city hundreds of kilometres away.
options.D: the father dies and his sons set up separate hearths of their own.

questions.question: The population described in paragraph 2, in which every family follows the cycle exactly, is introduced in order to show that

options.A: nuclear households are more stable over time than joint households and therefore make up the larger share of any count.
options.B: a count made on one day can find mostly nuclear households even where joint living is a near-universal stage of life.
options.C: most families in South Asia do in fact follow the developmental cycle exactly as the paragraph describes it.
options.D: census officials have deliberately undercounted joint households in order to lend support to the story of decline.

questions.question: As used in the last sentence of paragraph 4, 'the jointness that matters most to its members' refers to

options.A: the shared obligations and joint decisions that bind relatives even when they live apart.
options.B: the condition of several married couples sharing one roof, one kitchen and one purse.
options.C: the legal co-ownership of ancestral property by a group of brothers and their sons.
options.D: the authority that the eldest man in a family exercises over all its other members.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 2?

options.A: Many families living in nuclear households regularly send money to parents who remain in their home village.
options.B: In some regions brothers commonly divide their parents' household before their father's death rather than after it.
options.C: Studies following the same families for several decades find that most of their members never lived in a household with more than one married couple.
options.D: A count taken on a single day in one region finds that most of its households consist only of parents and their unmarried children.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: The joint family is essentially unchanged, since migrants remain bound by their families' expectations wherever they live.
options.B: The contests over authority within joint households show that the story of decline was right after all, if for the wrong reasons.
options.C: Industrialisation in South Asia has had no effect of any kind on the ways in which households are formed and divided.
options.D: Whether the joint family is declining depends partly on whether it is defined by co-residence or by shared obligation.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: defending superstition as a hidden form of practical wisdom that modern societies have been wrong to dismiss.
options.B: arguing that education will in time remove superstition by filling the gaps in people's knowledge of causes.
options.C: explaining superstition as a response to uncontrollable stakes and proposing that it be judged by what it displaces.
options.D: proving that skilled professionals are more superstitious than other people because their work involves greater danger.

questions.question: According to the passage, the fishing communities mentioned in paragraph 2

options.A: gave up their rites for open-sea voyages once they had acquired enough skill to make those voyages reliable.
options.B: regarded lagoon fishing as more dangerous than open-sea fishing, even though the lagoon reliably yielded a catch.
options.C: used protective magic in the lagoon and on the open sea alike, since their beliefs about the world did not change.
options.D: used no protective magic in the sheltered lagoon but surrounded open-sea voyages with elaborate rites.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that the tennis player's routine is valuable to her chiefly because it

options.A: gives her a fixed action at the point where further deliberation could only unsettle her play.
options.B: allows her to skip some of the training she would otherwise need to complete before a match.
options.C: improves the physical accuracy of her serve through repeated rehearsal of the same muscular movement.
options.D: persuades her that she can influence the result of the point through forces beyond ordinary physics.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as a superstition that has crossed the line described in paragraph 4?

options.A: A pilot touches the nose of the aircraft before each flight, after all the required safety checks are complete.
options.B: A farmer leaves a dry field unirrigated because he trusts a rite performed at sowing to bring enough rain.
options.C: A student who has prepared thoroughly for every examination wears the same small pendant into each of them.
options.D: An actor recites the same short phrase in the wings before every opening night, whatever role she is playing.

questions.question: According to the passage, the main work of the fixed days of traditional mourning was to

options.A: ensure that widows stayed away from celebrations for as long as the family remained in mourning.
options.B: settle in advance how relatives, neighbours and the bereaved household should conduct themselves after a death.
options.C: measure how long sorrow normally lasts, so that the bereaved would know when their grief ought to end.
options.D: give community elders a means of supervising how each family spent its money after a death.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, 'the labour of inventing their own conduct' refers to

options.A: the strain of displaying more sorrow in public than one actually feels in private.
options.B: the task of devising new ceremonies that later generations of the community can follow.
options.C: the effort of working out, unaided, how to behave and what to do while newly bereaved.
options.D: the physical work of arranging the funeral and preparing the gatherings that follow it.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that, where shared mourning scripts have weakened,

options.A: people who want to support the bereaved are often held back by not knowing what is expected of them.
options.B: the bereaved now grieve for a shorter time, because no outward schedule keeps their sorrow going.
options.C: grief has become more authentic and more personal, even if it has also become somewhat lonelier.
options.D: communities have usually replaced the old customs with newer rules that are just as rigid.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards traditional mourning customs is best described as

options.A: detached neutrality, setting out the case on each side without ever coming to a view of its own.
options.B: firm disapproval, on the ground that the customs forced private feeling to follow a public schedule.
options.C: nostalgic admiration, joined to a hope that the older rules will one day be restored in full.
options.D: qualified appreciation of their coordinating role, together with criticism of the coercion some of them involved.

questions.question: The list of features at the end of paragraph 1 (seclusion, shaved heads, identical garments and so on) serves mainly to

options.A: show why the transitional phase of such rites has drawn more attention than the other two.
options.B: establish that every rite of passage, in every culture, uses exactly the same set of practices.
options.C: suggest that rites of passage are often cruel to novices and ought to be reformed for that reason.
options.D: contrast the transitional phase with the more elaborate ceremonies that mark incorporation.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that removing the markers by which novices were ranked

options.A: is an unintended side effect of seclusion that the organisers of the rite neither foresee nor value.
options.B: permanently erases the differences of rank between the families from which the novices come.
options.C: helps to create bonds among novices that are not organised by the standing or wealth of their families.
options.D: makes novices less willing to accept instruction from elders who come from humbler families.

questions.question: The passage attributes each of the following to the traditional liminal phase EXCEPT

options.A: firm limits on its duration and on the novices' conduct, set by the community's elders.
options.B: a temporary removal of the markers by which novices had previously been ranked.
options.C: a heightened readiness to learn among people deprived of their usual footing.
options.D: an open-ended freedom in which novices themselves decided when their transition was complete.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's conclusion about what made liminality productive?

options.A: Many young people who drift between education and employment say that they feel disoriented, lack companions and cannot tell when, if ever, their transition will be over.
options.B: Young people passing through open-ended, unmarked transitions are found to form lasting ties and take on new roles just as well as novices in bounded rites do.
options.C: In some societies the period of seclusion during initiation lasted several years rather than a few weeks.
options.D: Elders in some traditional societies extended the seclusion of novices who had broken the rules of the rite.

questions.question: According to the passage, what has happened in many places since modern transport made distant shrines easy to reach?

options.A: Pilgrimage has dwindled, because the effort that once gave the journey its meaning has disappeared.
options.B: The authorities at many shrines now require pilgrims to cover the whole route to them on foot.
options.C: Pilgrims have come to value the sight of the shrine far more than any hardship they might meet on the road leading to it.
options.D: Pilgrims have chosen to bring back some of the effort, for instance by walking the last part of the way.

questions.question: The contrast between blisters on a hiking holiday and blisters on the way to a sacred place (paragraph 2) implies that

options.A: hardships on pilgrimage routes are usually more severe than those met with on ordinary walking holidays.
options.B: pilgrims value suffering for its own sake, wherever and for whatever purpose it is undergone.
options.C: the same bodily hardship can carry different meanings depending on the goal towards which it is directed.
options.D: hikers come to regard their discomfort as an offering once they reach the end of a long trail.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: The effort of the road and the fixed destination give each other their significance in pilgrimage, so neither can be understood on its own.
options.B: The chief value of pilgrimage lies in the inner change produced by long days of walking, whatever the destination happens to be.
options.C: Modern transport has emptied pilgrimage of its meaning, which can be recovered only by walking the whole of the route.
options.D: People who walk old pilgrim routes for reasons they would not call religious are deceived about the value of what they find.

questions.question: The author would most likely say of someone who walks an old pilgrim route with no fixed destination in mind that

options.A: his experience must be illusory, because a change in a person that is not religious cannot be a real one.
options.B: the walk may change him genuinely, though it lacks the gravity that a fixed and unchangeable destination helps to give a journey.
options.C: he is having the pilgrim's experience in a secular form, since the walking itself is where the value lies.
options.D: he would have the pilgrim's experience if he happened to end his walk at a famous shrine along the route.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'a sudden demand for definition' refers to

options.A: the wish of each community to agree with the others on a single name and story for the saint.
options.B: an insistence by some outside authority that the site be formally assigned to one tradition.
options.C: a gradual build-up of disagreement between the different communities who visit the site.
options.D: a request by visitors that the custodians explain the meaning of the rites performed at the site.
