questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 2 in the passage?

options.A: It supplies the observations of how sharing actually works on which the author's rejection of both stories rests.
options.B: It describes how shared shrines decline once the communities start to disagree about the identity of the saint.
options.C: It gives evidence for the harmony story, which the author then accepts subject to the qualifications in paragraph 4.
options.D: It explains how custodians from one community gradually come to take control of sites that were once shared.

questions.question: Which of the following arrangements most closely resembles the kind of sharing the author describes?

options.A: Two clubs share a hall only after long meetings in which they agree on a common purpose for their activities.
options.B: Two clubs take turns in a hall after a court has ruled on which of them is its legal owner and on what terms.
options.C: Two clubs meet in the same hall on different evenings, each calling it by its own name, and the caretaker never asks which club owns it.
options.D: Two clubs merge into a single society with a common constitution so that they can make joint use of one hall.

questions.question: The author's description of ambiguity as 'a social achievement in its own right' (paragraph 4) suggests that

options.A: the communities using shared shrines have, over many generations, quietly agreed among themselves to adopt one common interpretation of the saint and his story.
options.B: leaving ultimate questions unsettled is more valuable than agreement about them in every area of social life.
options.C: shared shrines have survived only where outside authorities protected their ambiguity through law and regulation.
options.D: the vagueness at shared shrines is actively sustained, for instance by custodians not asking about belief, and is not simply a lack of clarity.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: demonstrate that religion has been confined to private life in most societies that have modernised.
options.B: show that the secularisation thesis was right after all, once the evidence of its critics is properly understood.
options.C: explain why religious movements revived in the late twentieth century in societies that were growing wealthier.
options.D: argue that the secularisation debate went astray by treating several independent claims as a single thesis.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a society in which religious attendance is high but courts and hospitals operate free of clerical control as

options.A: consistent with the differentiation strand of the thesis while failing to fit the decline strand.
options.B: an unusual and unstable combination that the pressures of modernisation will sooner or later break apart.
options.C: proof that privatisation has taken place in that society even though decline has plainly not.
options.D: evidence that the secularisation thesis has now been refuted in every one of its forms.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the religious resurgence 'tends to presuppose' differentiation?

options.A: Some religious movements commission surveys and use the language of rights more skilfully than many secular campaigning groups.
options.B: Membership of religious organisations fell steadily in several wealthy countries over the same decades in which the resurgence occurred elsewhere.
options.C: In several countries resurgent movements won influence mainly by restoring clerical authority over courts and schools, not by competing within independent institutions.
options.D: Religious movements that lobby legislatures and contest elections tend to attract more members than those that stay out of politics.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards those former defenders of the thesis who 'said as much' (paragraph 1) is best described as

options.A: approving, since the author agrees that the evidence of religious resurgence refuted the secularisation thesis as a whole.
options.B: critical of their recantation for sharing the confusion behind their earlier confidence, without endorsing their original prediction.
options.C: dismissive, since the author regards every question about secularisation as one that no evidence could ever settle.
options.D: sympathetic, since the author believes that their original prediction was correct and that they abandoned it too readily.

questions.question: According to the passage, the fact that rulers have both funded and banned festivals of inversion

options.A: shows that rulers regarded these festivals as harmless entertainment with no political significance.
options.B: has been cited by supporters of each of the two dominant explanations as evidence for their view.
options.C: proves that the festivals tended to turn into riots wherever the authorities allowed them to continue for long enough.
options.D: indicates that such festivals were supported mainly by the elite and opposed mainly by ordinary people.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that a historian asking why a particular carnival became an uprising should look first at

options.A: any changes in the masks, songs and other forms that the festival used in that particular year.
options.B: whether the festival belonged by its nature to the safety valve type or to the subversive type.
options.C: the economic and political conditions surrounding the festival in the year that it turned violent.
options.D: how much money the authorities had spent on funding and staging the festival in earlier decades.

questions.question: Paragraph 4 functions in the passage mainly to

options.A: introduce the account of inversion as a lesson in hierarchy that the final paragraph goes on to develop.
options.B: provide evidence that festivals of inversion generally increased the grievances of those who took part in them.
options.C: defend the second explanation by showing that the first cannot account for carnivals that turned into riots.
options.D: attack one of the two explanations on a ground distinct from the objection raised against both in paragraph 3.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's criticism of the safety valve theory in paragraph 4?

options.A: Town records show that formal complaints against local officials rose rather than fell in the weeks after festivals mocking those officials.
options.B: Town records show that rulers who funded festivals of mockery seldom faced open rebellion during the years that followed.
options.C: Collections of songs that mocked local officials during festivals were later printed and read as a form of popular literature.
options.D: Some festivals of mockery were banned after riots in which participants had used their masks to hide their identities.

questions.question: Which of the following best reconciles the account in paragraph 5 with the claim in paragraph 3 that inversion 'does not carry its own political charge'?

options.A: Because inversion always teaches the existing order by displaying it, it reliably conserves that order, whatever the circumstances in which it occurs.
options.B: Because inversion displays the hierarchy in a way that can be read as confirming or exposing it, the surrounding situation must decide which reading prevails.
options.C: Because inversion requires the active cooperation of the authorities being mocked, its effects depend on how willingly those authorities take part in it.
options.D: Because inversion shows rank to be a convention, it always weakens hierarchy in the long run, even when a festival passes off without any trouble.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'only nominally attached' most nearly means

options.A: committed to the group for a short trial period before full membership.
options.B: attached to the group through a name inherited from one's family.
options.C: belonging to the group in name while lacking any real commitment to it.
options.D: connected to the group informally, without ever having formally joined it.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, on the signalling account, a group that lowers its demands may lose members because

options.A: the members who remain must take on a larger share of the cost of the rituals that are left.
options.B: outsiders conclude from the change that the group has quietly abandoned its central doctrines.
options.C: long-standing members resent losing practices that they had come to enjoy for their own sake.
options.D: belonging becomes less valuable once uncommitted people can enter more easily and draw on its benefits.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as a limitation of the signalling account EXCEPT

options.A: its inability to explain why groups that relax their demands sometimes lose members.
options.B: its silence on why communities insist on the exact form of a rite.
options.C: its neglect of how a demanding practice can create the commitment it shows.
options.D: its difficulty with demanding practices imposed on very young children.

questions.question: Which of the following best illustrates the 'third gap' described in paragraph 4?

options.A: A club refuses a generous donation from a new member offered as a substitute for the arduous initiation that it normally requires of everyone who joins.
options.B: Parents enrol their newborn in a demanding religious order partly to show their neighbours how devout the household is.
options.C: A volunteer who joined a relief group half-heartedly finds, after months of exhausting night shifts, that she is now deeply loyal to it.
options.D: A village extends credit only to those who have completed a long and difficult fast, judging them to be trustworthy.

questions.question: The claim in paragraph 4 that 'cost does not only reveal commitment but helps to manufacture it' depends on the assumption that

options.A: people who take on demanding practices do so chiefly in order to impress observers with their devotion.
options.B: what people report about being changed by demanding practices is broadly accurate rather than a later rationalisation.
options.C: practices imposed on children produce a stronger commitment than practices that adults choose for themselves.
options.D: observers are generally unable to tell genuinely committed members apart from those who are free riding.

questions.question: The image of a crowd at a parade in which 'everyone stands on tiptoe' (paragraph 2) serves to

options.A: suggest that graduates are worn out by the number of years they have spent studying.
options.B: show that employers have quietly agreed among themselves to keep raising the qualifications they demand from applicants.
options.C: demonstrate that a degree gives an individual employer no useful information about applicants.
options.D: illustrate how choices that make sense for each employer combine into an outcome that helps nobody.

questions.question: According to the passage, when few people held degrees, an employer who asked for one

options.A: was picking out a small group who tended, on average, to be more persistent and better connected.
options.B: was asking for a master's degree in order to separate the strongest applicants from ordinary graduates.
options.C: was ensuring that new staff had already been thoroughly trained in the particular tasks that the job would require.
options.D: was deliberately excluding applicants whose families could not afford fees, since that was the intended purpose.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Governments should prohibit employers from asking applicants for degrees unless the job needs specialist knowledge.
options.B: Most jobs now advertised for graduates involve exactly the same tasks that they involved fifty years ago, despite the new paperwork.
options.C: A rise in the education a job demands does not by itself show that the job has become harder.
options.D: The main value of a university education lies in the signal of persistence it sends to employers.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the 'more economical account' given in paragraph 2?

options.A: In a firm that began requiring degrees for clerks, graduates did the job's tasks markedly better, and the gap was traced to their coursework.
options.B: Employers who dropped their degree requirements found that screening applicants by other means took them longer and cost them considerably more.
options.C: The proportion of school leavers going on to university kept rising in the years after the requirement became common.
options.D: In a firm that began requiring degrees for its clerks, the new recruits came mostly from families able to pay for several years of study.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the remark that 'a block that was the same for everyone could be sold to' most nearly means that

options.A: leisure became so expensive that most working families could no longer afford to enjoy the free time they had won.
options.B: employers could buy back their workers' Saturdays by offering them extra pay for working at the weekend.
options.C: workers were now free to sell their weekend hours to whichever employer offered them the best terms.
options.D: free time falling at the same hours for everyone became a market that businesses could plan to serve.

questions.question: According to the passage, what did employers gain from the compromise that produced the weekend?

options.A: Influence over how workers spent their Sundays, since leisure was now organised and supplied by employers themselves.
options.B: Workers who could be relied upon to arrive, in a fit state, at the start of the week.
options.C: Lower wage bills, since workers accepted reduced pay in return for having all of Saturday free.
options.D: A longer total working week overall, since Saturday afternoons were exchanged for extra hours on the other weekdays.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the weekend is best described as

options.A: grateful, crediting factory owners with the generosity that first gave workers a Saturday free of labour.
options.B: appreciative of what it won for workers, while noting how it reshaped the nature of leisure.
options.C: nostalgic, regarding the irregular rhythm of pre-factory work as a freer and healthier way of living.
options.D: dismissive, treating the weekend as a defeat for workers that was presented to them as a victory.

questions.question: Which of the following situations most closely parallels the change described in paragraphs 2 and 3?

options.A: Workers in a factory strike for higher wages and win a large raise, though their daily hours of work stay exactly as they were.
options.B: A town council turns a disused railway yard into a public park so that residents have somewhere to spend their free afternoons.
options.C: A company abolishes its fixed holiday calendar and allows staff to take leave whenever they choose, provided that their work is done on time.
options.D: Musicians who rested whenever bookings dried up join an orchestra with a fixed August holiday, and travel firms begin selling August trips to its players.

questions.question: The back staircases and basement bells mentioned in paragraph 1 serve primarily as

options.A: proof that servants in large houses were treated more harshly than those employed in small households.
options.B: illustrations of the technical improvements that made large households cheaper and easier to run in that period.
options.C: examples of how a house was laid out so that the work of servants went unseen.
options.D: evidence that nineteenth-century families valued privacy from one another as much as privacy from their servants.

questions.question: The author describes app designers' talk of 'removing friction' (paragraph 3) as revealing because the phrase

options.A: treats as a nuisance what is often simply the customer's meeting with the person doing the work.
options.B: shows that app designers have consciously modelled their services on the households of the nineteenth century.
options.C: suggests that technical faults in apps are now the main obstacle standing between customers and good service.
options.D: admits that delivery and cleaning apps make the work of couriers and cleaners physically harder than it used to be.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: A wish to keep social inferiors out of sight does not fully explain why servants were made invisible.
options.B: Comfort that seems to require no effort can depend on a great deal of labour deliberately kept from view.
options.C: The modern means of receiving service without seeing the worker reach many more people than the older means did.
options.D: Couriers and cleaners today work under essentially the same conditions as Victorian servants, though under a different name.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Victorian families hid their servants out of snobbery, and apps have now made that same snobbery affordable for the middle classes.
options.B: The disappearance of large-scale domestic service shows that the social hierarchy it once supported has also come to an end.
options.C: Hiding the labour behind comfort once helped a class seem exempt from necessity, and the wish behind that concealment outlives the old form of service.
options.D: Modern delivery and cleaning work amounts to a revival of domestic servitude, and its workers ought to be recognised openly as servants.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, the 'ownership' of emotion at work refers to

options.A: who sets the terms on which a worker's feelings are displayed, and for whose benefit.
options.B: the legal rights that a worker holds over the recordings her employer makes of her calls.
options.C: whether the worker genuinely feels the warmth or calm that she shows to the people she serves.
options.D: how much emotion a particular job demands in comparison with the emotional demands of other jobs.

questions.question: On the author's account, the builder in paragraph 1 who keeps his temper with clients would most likely count as

options.A: no emotional labourer, because the feelings of manual workers play no real part in how well they do their jobs.
options.B: no emotional labourer in the strict sense, provided nobody else scripts or monitors how his courtesy is displayed.
options.C: an emotional labourer, because every job that requires the management of feeling falls within the concept.
options.D: an emotional labourer, because he would lose business and income if he failed to manage his feelings with clients.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the author's suggestion in paragraph 3 about where the cost of emotional labour lies?

options.A: In one chain of shops, staff whose greetings were scripted and scored were more exhausted than staff serving the same customers as they saw fit.
options.B: Surgeons report higher levels of stress at work than call-centre agents do, especially during long and difficult operations.
options.C: Workers whose jobs involve dealing with members of the public all day report more exhaustion than people who work largely on their own.
options.D: Customers rate scripted greetings as noticeably less sincere than greetings that shop staff are free to phrase however they like.

questions.question: The author's reply to the critics in paragraph 2 implies that

options.A: they are right that the concept is too broad, and that the remedy is to restrict it to occupations whose main task is serving customers.
options.B: they are right about how the term is often used, but wrong to infer that the concept itself picks out nothing distinctive.
options.C: their examples of the surgeon and the lawyer reveal that professionals perform more emotional labour than call-centre agents.
options.D: they have shown that the concept should be dropped and replaced with a narrower term that names only scripted forms of feeling.

questions.question: According to the passage, the older 'simple map' of taste held that

options.A: educated people enjoyed both high and popular culture, though they tended to enjoy the two in quite different settings.
options.B: elites marked themselves out mainly by how much they spent on concerts, exhibitions and other cultural events.
options.C: taste was largely a matter of individual preference, with only a loose and unreliable connection to social class.
options.D: a person's social standing could be read from where their preferences fell on a ladder from refined to popular culture.

questions.question: The author's discussion of the 'knowing, curatorial attitude' (paragraph 3) suggests that

options.A: omnivores secretly dislike the popular forms they claim to enjoy and consume them only in order to appear open-minded.
options.B: the manner in which something is liked matters more than breadth of taste in every form of social distinction.
options.C: two people may enjoy the same popular film while their way of enjoying it marks quite different social positions.
options.D: popular culture is transformed into high culture once educated audiences begin to adopt it and write about it.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely treat as an instance of the shifted boundary described in paragraph 4?

options.A: A graduate who boasts of enjoying every kind of music but finds one genre, loved chiefly by her town's least schooled residents, beneath notice.
options.B: A music critic who dismisses all popular music as worthless and attends only concerts of classical and early music.
options.C: A student who listens to a very wide range of music, from folk to jazz, because her friends keep introducing her to new things.
options.D: A retired factory worker who listens only to the songs he grew up with and has never felt any wish to attend an opera.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the final paragraph in the passage?

options.A: It introduces evidence showing that the omnivore pattern found in surveys is confined to a small number of wealthy countries and does not hold elsewhere.
options.B: It shows that the old snobbery of paragraph 1 has returned among the highly educated in exactly its earlier form.
options.C: It adds a further reason to doubt that hierarchy has ended, grants that real change has occurred, and then restates that distinction persists in a new form.
options.D: It withdraws the doubts raised in paragraph 3 by conceding that the loosening of cultural hierarchy is genuine after all.

questions.question: The example of persistent unhappiness in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that psychiatrists have been steadily losing ground to clergy and social workers in the treatment of unhappiness.
options.B: demonstrate that licensing has failed to protect the public from practitioners who are not properly qualified to help.
options.C: illustrate that some human problems are too complex for any single profession to treat adequately on its own.
options.D: show that the profession to which a problem belongs is decided by rivalry among professions rather than by the problem itself.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the two accounts in paragraph 1 as

options.A: incompatible with each other, so that anyone who accepts one of them is bound to reject the other entirely.
options.B: each capturing a real effect of licensing, while sharing an assumption that prevents either from explaining professional change.
options.C: correct when taken together, since in combination they give a complete account of how professions rise and fall.
options.D: equally mistaken, since licensing in fact neither protects clients from charlatans nor raises the fees that professionals charge.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about how knowledge matters in contests over problems (paragraph 3)?

options.A: Practitioners in a profession that lost a problem to a rival were later found to have been entirely competent at treating it.
options.B: After one profession won control of a problem, licensing rules were rewritten so as to bar its rivals from treating that problem.
options.C: Across many contests over newly recognised problems, the winner was usually the group with the best record of treating them, whatever theories its rivals offered.
options.D: A profession with an abstract theory took over a problem that its rivals had long treated, and later lost it again when that theory fell from favour.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: The state's part in professional life is confined to certifying the competence of individual practitioners through licences.
options.B: A body of practitioners could become more skilled over a decade and still end it with a narrower field of work.
options.C: The size of a profession at a given moment is a reliable measure of how well it serves the clients who rely on it.
options.D: A profession armed with abstract theory will always defeat a rival whose knowledge is purely practical in a contest over a problem.

questions.question: According to the passage, conspicuous display has lost much of its power to separate the advantaged from others because

options.A: rising taxes on imported luxury goods have made open displays of wealth far more costly than they were.
options.B: the wealthiest households now keep most of their wealth in savings rather than in goods of any kind.
options.C: satirists and moralists have made the owners of showy goods into figures of public ridicule.
options.D: cheaper production has put passable versions of once-rare goods within reach of most people.

questions.question: The contrast between a diamond and a childhood in good schools (paragraph 3) implies that

options.A: advantages built into a person are passed on more securely than those held as saleable property.
options.B: diamonds are a poor financial investment compared with spending on a child's education, which yields a higher return.
options.C: parents who spend money on jewellery tend to care less about their children's futures than parents who pay for schooling.
options.D: the benefits of a good education can be gained just as readily in adult life as in childhood, given enough money.

questions.question: The reference to gold-plated taps in paragraph 3 serves to

options.A: suggest that inconspicuous consumption is simply conspicuous consumption carried on in more refined and tasteful forms.
options.B: concede that the turn away from showy spending is, in some respects, a genuinely welcome change.
options.C: illustrate the sort of quiet, hard-to-copy goods on which affluent households now prefer to spend their money.
options.D: argue that wealthy households ought to be discouraged by public policy from spending on luxuries of every kind.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that inconspicuous goods reproduce advantage more effectively than conspicuous ones?

options.A: Most affluent parents who pay for private tuition say that they do so out of concern for their children's learning and not out of any wish for status.
options.B: Households that spend on organic food and exercise classes report better health than households of similar income that do not.
options.C: Imitations of luxury handbags, cars and watches have continued to become cheaper and more widely available to ordinary households.
options.D: Children of wealthy families that spent heavily on schooling ended up no better placed as adults than children of equally wealthy families that spent on luxuries.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards inconspicuous consumption is best described as

options.A: critical of its social effects, while declining to impugn the motives of those who practise it.
options.B: approving, regarding it chiefly as a welcome advance in good taste over the vulgar display of earlier generations of the rich.
options.C: scornful, regarding it as a form of hypocrisy that disguises a hunger for status as healthy and responsible living.
options.D: neutral, describing a change in the spending of the rich without passing any judgement on what that change brings about.

questions.question: The image of the escalator in paragraph 2 conveys that

options.A: a society can carry people downwards just as easily as it carries them upwards, depending on economic conditions.
options.B: people born near the bottom rise faster than those born near the top whenever the economy is growing quickly.
options.C: living standards can rise for everyone together while people's ranking relative to one another stays fixed.
options.D: moving up in society is automatic and calls for no effort or ability on the part of the individuals concerned.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that people who conclude, when growth slows, that society has become less fair

options.A: have generally lived through a genuine fall in relative mobility that the usual measures have failed to detect.
options.B: are mistaken in believing that they are doing no better than their parents did at the same stage of life.
options.C: are reacting chiefly to a rise in downward mobility among the children of comfortable and well-placed families.
options.D: may be rightly sensing a real loss but wrongly attributing it to a decline in openness.

questions.question: Which of the following would be a case of relative mobility rising while absolute mobility falls, in the passage's sense?

options.A: In a booming economy where most children outearn their parents, the order of families in the income ranking remains exactly what it was before.
options.B: In a booming economy where nearly all children outearn their parents, the income ranking is substantially reshuffled from one generation to the next.
options.C: In a stagnant economy where few children outearn their parents, children of poor families increasingly overtake children of rich families in the income ranking.
options.D: In a stagnant economy where few children outearn their parents, children remain in much the same place in the income ranking as their parents held.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Relative mobility is the only true measure of whether a society is open, while absolute mobility merely reflects how fast its economy is growing.
options.B: Since absolute and relative mobility answer different questions and can diverge, running them together leads people to misread slowdowns and to ignore what fairness costs.
options.C: Social mobility has not stalled as its critics claim; it has simply become much harder to measure than it was in earlier generations.
options.D: Comfortable families use private tuition and housing choices to block relative mobility, and governments should act to prevent them from doing so.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a government promising to raise relative mobility while ensuring that no family moves down the ranking

options.A: is promising something that cannot be delivered when positions are ranked, whatever the rate of economic growth.
options.B: is making essentially the same promise as a government that pledges to raise the living standards of each new generation.
options.C: could keep its promise provided that the economy grew fast enough to raise the incomes of every family at once.
options.D: could keep its promise by abolishing private tuition and other devices that comfortable families use to defend their position.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that collectors value the objects they gather for their beauty and rarity rather than for the places they fill in a set, whoever happens to have designed that set.
options.B: trace how private collections of timetables, matchboxes and editions gradually developed into the public museums of today, and to praise the collectors who began them.
options.C: show that collecting is a compulsion created by manufacturers, who profit by persuading buyers to complete sets that they never wanted until the empty spaces were shown to them.
options.D: distinguish collecting in which the collector defines the series from collecting in which a seller does, and to show that the latter's harm lies in removing that power.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a collector would pay far more than an outsider for a particular stamp chiefly because

options.A: the collector has run out of space and must buy only the most valuable items.
options.B: the stamp fills a gap in a series that the collector is close to completing.
options.C: the stamp is an object of unusual beauty that only a trained eye can fully appreciate.
options.D: collectors usually know more than outsiders about how rare such stamps have become.

questions.question: By saying that 'The empty album is the real product' (paragraph 2), the author means that

options.A: the stickers themselves are of such poor quality that only the album has any lasting value.
options.B: the albums are sold at a higher profit than the stickers that are later bought to fill them.
options.C: what the seller really offers is the outline of an unfinished whole, which makes each later purchase feel necessary.
options.D: buyers prefer to keep their albums empty because an unfilled album is worth more to other collectors.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates what the author calls the danger of the commercial version of collecting?

options.A: A woman who has long gathered old bus tickets from her town starts judging her collection against a numbered checklist that a company now sells with reproduction tickets.
options.B: A man who collects matchboxes from closed hotels becomes so absorbed in the hunt that he spends most weekends searching second-hand shops for the few he still lacks.
options.C: A collector of a minor poet's editions decides that pamphlet reprints do not count as part of her set and so stops looking for them.
options.D: A child buys a single plastic figure from a cereal box because she likes its colour, and never shows any interest in finding the remaining eleven.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is curious about many buyers of retro goods?

options.A: They are mostly older people trying to recover the products of their own youth.
options.B: They are too young to remember the original products that the goods imitate.
options.C: They tend to prefer the reissued versions to the originals once they compare the two.
options.D: They usually know that the advertising behind such goods presents a false golden age.

questions.question: The examples of the record player with a phone socket and the camera that 'adds the scratches digitally' (paragraph 3) serve to

options.A: illustrate that retro design keeps the look of the past while removing the inconveniences that defined it.
options.B: prove that young buyers are deceived into thinking that the reissued goods are genuine antiques.
options.C: show that modern retro products are more fragile and costly than the originals that they copy.
options.D: suggest that the makers of retro goods are trying hard to preserve the technology of earlier decades.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the buyers of retro goods is best described as

options.A: wholly indifferent, since the author describes the retro market without expressing any view about those who buy from it.
options.B: openly contemptuous, since the author regards them as gullible victims of advertisers who have invented a golden age.
options.C: warmly admiring, since the author presents their taste as a wise and successful rejection of disposable modern goods.
options.D: clear-sighted but not contemptuous: the author declines to scorn them while insisting on naming what they actually buy.

questions.question: The author's view of the explanation that buyers of retro goods are 'being fooled' (paragraph 2) is that it

options.A: applies to the buyers of drinks and cameras but not to buyers of record players, who know the originals well.
options.B: is entirely correct, since advertisers have invented a golden age that young buyers cannot check against memory.
options.C: contains some truth but wrongly assumes that buyers want an accurate past rather than an answer to a present mood.
options.D: has no basis at all, since advertisers make no claims about the past when they sell retro goods to the young.

questions.question: Paragraph 1 suggests that when reviewers call a dish authentic, their judgement depends chiefly on

options.A: the modest and unfamiliar setting in which the dish is served rather than the dish itself.
options.B: how much the critic has paid for the meal compared with similar restaurants.
options.C: whether the cook has been trained in the region from which the cuisine comes.
options.D: how closely the recipe matches the way the dish is cooked in its region of origin.

questions.question: The hypothetical family restaurant in paragraph 2 functions in the argument mainly to

options.A: demonstrate that immigrant cooks change their recipes chiefly because they are pressured by reviewers who demand authenticity.
options.B: show that migration itself produces a distinct cuisine, which sets up the author's objection to the purists' idea of decline.
options.C: illustrate the kind of loss that occurs when cooks strip a cuisine of everything difficult so that it is recognised only by name.
options.D: provide evidence that restaurants which adapt to local tastes are commercially more successful than those that refuse to adapt.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the second menu is only 'one stage of a continuous adaptation'?

options.A: Many cooks who run such restaurants say they would like to cook more ambitious dishes than their customers will accept, and would do so if the rent allowed it.
options.B: Diners from the home community order mostly from the second menu, while other customers rarely know that it exists or how to ask for it.
options.C: Reviewers praise restaurants with second menus more highly than restaurants that offer only a single menu to all diners, whatever the cooking on either menu is like.
options.D: The dishes on such second menus are found to be prepared with imported ingredients and unchanged methods, and to match versions cooked in the home region.

questions.question: Which of the following tests for judging a restaurant would the author most likely endorse?

options.A: Whether its adaptations were chosen by the cooks rather than prompted by complaints from customers.
options.B: Whether it has entirely resisted the commercial pressures that lead cooks to simplify a cuisine.
options.C: Whether those cooking its food have the latitude to make the dishes they themselves consider good.
options.D: Whether its dishes are prepared in the way they are still prepared in the region of origin.

questions.question: According to the trickle-down account described in the passage, those at the top abandon a style when

options.A: designers begin borrowing it from the clothing of a street subculture.
options.B: cheap copies of it begin to reach shops within a few weeks of its appearance.
options.C: it has spread so widely that it no longer sets them apart from others.
options.D: the people just below them stop copying it and turn to something new.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relation between paragraph 2 and paragraph 3?

options.A: Paragraph 2 raises an objection about the direction of influence; paragraph 3 replies that direction was never the theory's central claim.
options.B: Paragraph 2 refutes the theory's account of motive; paragraph 3 concedes the refutation but rescues the theory's account of direction.
options.C: Paragraph 2 presents the author's own view of fashion; paragraph 3 reports a rival view that the author goes on to reject in paragraph 4.
options.D: Paragraph 2 offers evidence for the old theory; paragraph 3 qualifies it by adding that styles sometimes move upwards from the street.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, the movement of styles from subcultures to luxury houses

options.A: refutes the old theory entirely, since the theory depended on fashion always moving from the top downwards.
options.B: shows that the wish to stand apart no longer plays any part in how the wealthy choose what to wear.
options.C: benefits the members of subcultures, who gain prestige when their clothing appears in expensive shops.
options.D: fits the motive that the old theory identified, even though it contradicts the direction that theory described.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's account of what has changed, as given in paragraph 4?

options.A: Copies sold in inexpensive shops are usually made of poorer materials and fall apart far sooner than the garments they imitate.
options.B: Even where cheap copies appear within weeks, the people most eager for status rely more than before on being seen in the newest visible styles.
options.C: Small releases that sell out in minutes are often bought by resellers who have no interest in fashion and want only to profit.
options.D: Members of street subcultures often abandon a style soon after a luxury house has adopted it and begun to sell it at high prices.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the phrase 'a local flavour in a global grammar' suggests that

options.A: the chain's local dishes are so heavily modified that they no longer taste like anything eaten locally.
options.B: local cooks have learned to describe their traditional dishes in the vocabulary of international cuisine.
options.C: a locally adapted dish is delivered through a structure that is itself global and carries its own assumptions.
options.D: global chains succeed only when they combine local ingredients with recipes perfected in the home country.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Debates centred on a chain's menu miss that its format is what travels, while the meanings customers give it are made locally.
options.B: A chain's willingness to adapt its menu is the clearest sign of how far it respects the identity of the country it enters.
options.C: Local customers decide what global chains mean in their countries, so worries about cultural influence are largely misplaced.
options.D: Global chains erase local food cultures less through their menus than through a format that imposes foreign assumptions on customers.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as the strongest sign of a global chain's cultural influence on a country?

options.A: The chain adds several new regional dishes to its menu each year in response to suggestions made by its local customers and staff.
options.B: The chain's outlets in the country sell more of its standard home burger than of the dishes it has created for the local market, year after year.
options.C: Families in the country choose the chain's restaurants for birthdays and linger there long after they have finished eating.
options.D: Local family eateries begin taking orders at a counter, posting fixed prices and standardising their kitchens, while still serving their old dishes.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as part of the format that a global chain exports EXCEPT

options.A: a promise that a given meal will taste the same from one month to the next.
options.B: a set of new dishes devised specially to suit the tastes of the local market.
options.C: a counter at which customers place their orders without being served by a waiter.
options.D: a fixed price for each item that is displayed to customers before they order.

questions.question: According to the passage, households that live close to scarcity keep spare parts, old jars and oversized coats because

options.A: they wish to display their thrift to neighbours who might otherwise think them wasteful.
options.B: they cannot be sure of being able to buy such things again when they need them.
options.C: they reject the fashion for owning less as one more passing style of the wealthy.
options.D: they have more space at home than wealthier households living in crowded cities.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the point made in paragraph 2 about discarding objects freely?

options.A: A family living far from any market keeps old tins, spare buttons and broken tools in case they are someday needed.
options.B: A student keeps few books in her room because the rules of her hostel forbid students to own large amounts of property.
options.C: A wealthy collector displays rare porcelain in glass cabinets so that visitors can see how much he has spent.
options.D: A traveller sets out on long trips with only a small bag, confident that anything forgotten can simply be bought on arrival.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author be most likely to accept?

options.A: A person who owns very little purely for the sake of calm may still, without intending it, be signalling financial security to others.
options.B: A person who owns very little purely for the sake of calm sends no social signal, since signals depend on what a person intends.
options.C: A person who owns very little for the sake of calm is probably deceiving herself, since the true motive of minimalism is to impress.
options.D: A person who owns very little can practise minimalism only if she is wealthy, so the poor can never adopt such a way of life.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the movement for owning less is best described as

options.A: approving of it as a sound ethical response to consumerism, though aware that a few practise it for show.
options.B: contemptuous of its followers, whom the author regards as status-seekers disguising their wealth as virtue.
options.C: doubtful of its claim to be a social critique, while accepting that many who practise it do so sincerely.
options.D: dismissive of it as a passing style that will soon give way to some newer fashion in consumption.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?

options.A: Brand communities are an illusion created by advertisers, who borrow the language of tribes to make ordinary customers feel they belong.
options.B: Brand communities involve real solidarity, but because they gather around symbols a firm owns, the tribal comparison is only partly apt.
options.C: Brand communities are true tribes in every important respect, and firms that fail to see this lose the loyalty of their best customers.
options.D: Firms ought to give the members of their brand communities legal rights over the designs and emblems that the members care about.

questions.question: According to the passage, how do the most loyal customers often respond when a company moves production to another country?

options.A: As enthusiasts who quietly accept the change because the product remains largely the same.
options.B: As disappointed consumers who decide to transfer their loyalty to the brand of a rival firm.
options.C: As owners who take legal action to stop the company from altering the products they bought.
options.D: As members who feel that something of theirs has been taken from them without their agreement.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as a respect in which brand communities resemble tribes EXCEPT

options.A: the difficulty of leaving the group once one has joined it.
options.B: a shared body of lore that newcomers are expected to learn.
options.C: a habit of defining the group partly against outsiders.
options.D: the policing of boundaries between real and false members.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim in paragraph 4 that the solidarity of brand communities is real?

options.A: Members of a computer brand's online forums spend considerably more each year on the brand's products than its other customers do, and buy new models sooner.
options.B: Owners of one brand of motorcycle are found to speak more unfavourably of a rival brand than the owners of that rival speak of theirs.
options.C: An owners' club for a long-discontinued car still meets, shares spare parts and helps members with repairs, decades after its maker stopped all promotion.
options.D: Attendance at events organised and paid for by a motorcycle maker rises sharply in the years when the firm spends heavily on advertising.

questions.question: The author's remark that the anger after an unpopular redesign reveals 'the limits of an ownership they had felt but never possessed' (paragraph 4) implies that

options.A: members' legal rights over the brand had been violated when the firm altered its design.
options.B: members' moral sense of owning the brand had outrun any power they actually held over it.
options.C: members had cared mainly about the product and not about one another all along.
options.D: the community had never been more than an illusion, which the redesign finally exposed.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the description of staged back regions as 'another front, built in the shape of a back' means that they are

options.A: presentations prepared for visitors that are designed to look like unstaged private life.
options.B: private spaces that hosts rebuild in a new style after visitors have finished their tours.
options.C: genuinely private spaces that visitors mistakenly believe were arranged for their benefit.
options.D: public monuments that are decorated so as to resemble the houses of ordinary villagers.

questions.question: The theatre audience mentioned at the end of paragraph 3 is used to suggest that

options.A: hosts who stage back regions for visitors should be regarded as artists and paid accordingly.
options.B: tourists enjoy staged performances more than they enjoy experiences that are genuinely unstaged.
options.C: knowing an experience has been arranged need not mean that one has been deceived by it.
options.D: tourists who believe they have found the real thing are no more foolish than people at a play.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about tourists in paragraph 3?

options.A: Some tourists say that they prefer an openly staged performance in a hotel courtyard to a visit to a village household, since the performance asks less of them.
options.B: Many families who run homestays say privately that they resent having to keep their own lives confined to a few back rooms during the months when guests arrive.
options.C: Homestays usually cost visitors considerably more than hotel rooms of a similar standard in the same town or village, even though they offer fewer comforts.
options.D: Most guests at homestays, on learning that the household had been prepared for their visit, say they feel cheated and would not have paid had they known.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Since most tourists knowingly accept staged back regions, such tourism raises no serious ethical question that needs to be answered.
options.B: The ethical question raised by staged back regions concerns less the deception of tourists than the shrinking private lives of their hosts.
options.C: Critics are right that the search for unstaged life leads tourists only into more expensive staging, so visitors should stop seeking back regions.
options.D: Tourism inevitably destroys the authentic culture of the communities it reaches, replacing their ways of life with performances.

questions.question: Which of the following practices would best fit the author's view of what a tourism that 'respected its hosts' would do?

options.A: A village expands its range of homestays and kitchen tours so that more households can share in the income from visitors.
options.B: A regional tourism office prints leaflets explaining to visitors that homestays and craft demonstrations are arranged for their benefit.
options.C: A tour company guarantees in writing that every household its customers visit is unprepared and shown exactly as it is lived in.
options.D: A village keeps certain festivals and quarters closed to visitors, although tourists would readily pay to attend or enter them.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a neighbour who returns a dish of sweets on the same evening she received one

options.A: treats the gift as repayment of a favour that she had done for the giver earlier.
options.B: shows that she values the friendship even more highly than the original giver does.
options.C: signals a wish to end the exchange rather than to keep a relationship going.
options.D: lacks the means to prepare a return of a different value at a later date.

questions.question: The author mentions anonymous donations in paragraph 3 in order to

options.A: suggest that the gifts usually called free earn that name by deliberately blocking a tie from forming.
options.B: illustrate how patrons use gifts that can never be repaid to bind those who receive them.
options.C: show that the most generous gifts in modern societies are those whose givers choose to stay unknown to the receiver.
options.D: recommend that anonymous giving be replaced by gifts matched to what the receiver can return.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about what sustains the bond between neighbours who exchange gifts?

options.A: In one town, people say they feel mildly uneasy whenever they remain in a neighbour's debt for more than a few weeks at a time.
options.B: Households that exchange gifts often with their neighbours are more likely to help those same neighbours in an emergency.
options.C: In a village where gifts are always returned at once and in exactly equal value, friendships between neighbours prove as close and lasting as anywhere.
options.D: Among several farming communities, gifts sent by clients to their patrons are seldom returned in any form whatsoever.

questions.question: Suppose a wealthy household regularly sends a much poorer neighbour gifts far larger than the neighbour could ever return. On the author's argument, the main problem with this practice is that

options.A: it keeps the poorer neighbour always somewhat in the household's debt, an imbalance that harms the bond in itself.
options.B: the gifts close the account between the two households before a friendship can develop.
options.C: any gift given in the expectation of a return is tainted and falls short of real generosity.
options.D: it leaves the neighbour under an obligation he has no way of discharging, so that his thanks become reliance.

questions.question: According to the passage, barter tends to be found

options.A: where the parties lack the trust needed to leave a debt outstanding.
options.B: mainly in the earliest stage of a society's economic history, before credit develops.
options.C: chiefly in small villages where neighbours settle their debts at harvest time.
options.D: in societies that have not yet found a commodity that everyone will accept.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'running accounts' refers to

options.A: written ledgers kept by villagers to record the exact value of every item exchanged.
options.B: ongoing obligations between neighbours that are repaid loosely and over time, if at all.
options.C: arrangements in which every exchange between two neighbours is completed on the spot.
options.D: debts that are measured in coins and must be repaid by a fixed date each year.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the defence of the textbook story in paragraph 4 is best described as

options.A: treating it as irrelevant, since thought experiments have no place in the study of money.
options.B: dismissing it as a deliberate attempt by economists to mislead their students.
options.C: accepting it fully and so withdrawing the historical objection raised earlier.
options.D: granting it partial force while denying that it makes the story harmless.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the double coincidence of wants is a serious obstacle mainly for

options.A: parties who need each exchange to be settled at the moment it takes place.
options.B: communities that already use money to keep a record of mutual obligations.
options.C: villagers who prefer to repay what they owe in labour rather than in goods.
options.D: neighbours whose harvests happen to fail in the same year as each other.

questions.question: The rituals listed in paragraph 2, such as the offering of water and the exchange of names, are presented as

options.A: customs so varied that no general account of hospitality can be given.
options.B: stages by which an uncertain stranger is turned into a guest with a defined position.
options.C: ways in which guests repaid their hosts for the food, water and shelter they received on arrival.
options.D: evidence that strangers were usually welcomed without any suspicion at all.

questions.question: The passage implies that the customary limit on the length of a guest's stay

options.A: reflects the small amount of food that most households could afford to share.
options.B: shows that traditional hospitality was less sincere than its admirers have claimed.
options.C: helps keep intact the host's authority, on which the welcome itself depends.
options.D: exists mainly to prevent guests from being adopted into the host's kin group.

questions.question: The passage associates each of the following with the acceptance of hospitality EXCEPT that

options.A: the guest who shares the host's food implicitly undertakes not to harm the household.
options.B: the host becomes responsible for protecting the guest against harm from third parties.
options.C: the guest may stay indefinitely on the same terms on which he was first received.
options.D: the guest submits, for a time, to an order of rules that the host administers.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Customary limits on a guest's stay show that hospitality was designed to protect the household, not the guest.
options.B: The host's authority over the guest is not a flaw in hospitality but what allows strangers to be received at all.
options.C: The ideal of unconditional hospitality is incoherent, so suspicion towards outsiders is fully justified.
options.D: Hospitality is better understood as a method of neutralising dangerous strangers than as an act of generosity towards those who are in need.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as a way in which village commons have been regulated EXCEPT

options.A: imposing fines on offenders that increase each time the offence is repeated.
options.B: limiting a household's animals to the number it can feed through the winter.
options.C: moving grazing between sections of the hill in a fixed order of rotation.
options.D: auctioning the right to graze each season to whichever household bids the most.

questions.question: According to the passage, what distinguishes a commons from 'open access'?

options.A: A commons belongs to a community that can make and enforce rules for its use.
options.B: A commons is owned by the state, while open access land is held privately.
options.C: A commons is always smaller and so easier to watch than an open access resource.
options.D: Open access resources are used only by outsiders who ignore the village's customs.

questions.question: Which of the following developments would the author regard as most likely to lead to the collapse of a well-run village forest commons?

options.A: Households agree to change the order in which sections of the forest are used after a dry year.
options.B: A new road lets timber traders from distant towns enter a forest whose rules bind only villagers.
options.C: The village raises the grain it pays its watchman after a dispute over the forest boundary.
options.D: A village with a stable population raises the fines it charges for repeated offences.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard a government scheme that replaces a village's grazing rules with uniform national regulations as

options.A: a risk to the commons if the villagers neither understand the new rules nor accept them as legitimate.
options.B: an unwelcome change, but one that cannot affect whether the commons survives, since that depends on human nature.
options.C: a fair remedy for the inequality of village arrangements that give larger shares to households holding more land.
options.D: a safeguard the commons needs, since local rules cannot restrain households once the resource rises in value.

questions.question: According to the passage, which kind of content in oral tradition is often transmitted with unusual fidelity?

options.A: The middle generations of a genealogy, since they serve no present interest of the community.
options.B: Accounts of who led an ancient migration, which communities have reason to remember exactly.
options.C: Fixed forms such as formulaic songs and ritual phrases, even when their meaning has been lost.
options.D: Stories that explain why one lineage holds the best land in the settlement.

questions.question: The author's remark in paragraph 3 about 'details that serve no present interest' serves mainly to

options.A: argue that oral traditions are more reliable as sources than the written chronicles of the same period and region.
options.B: concede that most of the content of an oral tradition was invented to serve present interests.
options.C: explain why formulaic songs are handed down more faithfully than ordinary narrative.
options.D: show how knowing what a tradition is for lets a historian judge which of its parts to trust.

questions.question: The author's disagreement with the sceptics described in paragraph 1 is best characterised as a disagreement about

options.A: whether the founders named in genealogies were real persons or later inventions.
options.B: whether oral traditions change at all as they are handed down from one generation to the next.
options.C: whether the changes oral traditions undergo are of a kind that a historian can partly correct for.
options.D: whether societies without writing developed precise techniques for memorising long texts.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's case against the sceptic's manuscript analogy?

options.A: A tradition recorded at intervals over a century changed in ways that bore no relation to shifts in the community's alliances or landholding.
options.B: A tradition was found by excavation to be right about the route of an ancient migration but wrong about the leader it named.
options.C: Chronicles kept by a monastery were found to have been altered over time to support the land claims of the monks who copied them.
options.D: Singers in one community preserved ritual phrases word for word for many generations although none of them understood the words.

questions.question: The reference in paragraph 3 to knowledge about medicinal plants or fishing grounds being used by outsiders serves to illustrate

options.A: why communities have usually refused to share what they know with outside researchers.
options.B: how often local beliefs about medicine turn out to be mistaken once they are tested.
options.C: the claim that local knowledge must be translated into a form that evaluators can handle.
options.D: how validation can move control over knowledge away from the people who held it.

questions.question: The passage suggests that if one of the signs a farmer uses, tested on its own, predicted rainfall poorly, this result would

options.A: indicate that the sign ought to be dropped from the set she relies on in future.
options.B: fail to show that her overall judgement about when to sow is unreliable.
options.C: show that she had been taught a mistaken sign by older members of her community.
options.D: prove that knowledge of the weather held by farmers cannot be put into words at all.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the practice of validating local knowledge is best described as

options.A: qualified approval: it improves on dismissal but rests on questionable assumptions.
options.B: outright hostility, since validation is nothing more than a disguised form of theft.
options.C: detached neutrality, describing the practice without passing any judgement on it.
options.D: unreserved enthusiasm for the respect it shows towards long-neglected expertise.

questions.question: Which of the following arrangements would best fit the approach the author recommends in the final paragraph?

options.A: Biologists test every claim that fishers make about spawning sites and publish only the claims that tagging data confirm, naming the fishers as their sources.
options.B: Fishers' knowledge is recorded in their own words and kept away from scientists, so that outsiders cannot misuse it.
options.C: Fishers are trained in tagging methods so that they can validate their own claims before offering them to scientists.
options.D: Fishers and biologists jointly choose which spawning sites to study, and the biologists' stock estimates are also checked against what fishers see on the water.

questions.question: Which of the following does the passage present as an instance of earmarking that gives a household member a sphere of decision of her own?

options.A: Coins meant for the temple being kept apart from other money in a tin.
options.B: A woman spending her earnings from tailoring on her children's schooling.
options.C: A grandmother's gift to a newborn being placed in an untouched savings account.
options.D: A windfall being spent on a celebration that a salary would never fund.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the statement that money 'renders them comparable' means that money

options.A: removes from goods any record of who made them or where they came from.
options.B: requires strangers to disclose the histories of the goods they exchange.
options.C: lets goods with different origins be measured on a single common scale.
options.D: makes all goods equally valuable regardless of how useful they are.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's interpretation of the tailor's spending?

options.A: Women who earn money from tailoring spend more on their children's schooling than women who earn no money of their own.
options.B: Shopkeepers in the town accept the tailor's rupees on exactly the same terms as the rupees earned by her husband.
options.C: Women whose earnings are pooled with their husbands' say they have less influence over household spending than women who keep their earnings apart.
options.D: Households that earmark their money pay more interest over a year than households that pool all of their income together.

questions.question: In responding to the objection raised in paragraph 4, the author

options.A: concedes that earmarking reflects only feelings and so leaves money's fungibility untouched.
options.B: argues that the market is itself a distortion of the money that people use at home.
options.C: denies that money is fungible even in impersonal trade between people who are strangers.
options.D: accepts its point about market exchange but argues that fungibility holds only in particular settings.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Money behaves as one interchangeable medium only where people agree to ignore where sums came from; elsewhere they mark it deliberately.
options.B: Because money carries social meanings, the economic principle of fungibility is simply false and ought to be abandoned by economists.
options.C: Mental accounting is not an error at all, because keeping money in separate categories costs households nothing.
options.D: Households earmark their money chiefly because cognitive shortcuts are easier than ranking all their needs together.

questions.question: According to the passage, in the bidding versions of a rotating association

options.A: the pot is awarded to whichever member has contributed the most over the whole cycle.
options.B: a member who wants the pot urgently takes a smaller sum, and the others share the difference.
options.C: the order in which members receive the pot is fixed by drawing lots at the first meeting.
options.D: members compete to receive the pot as late as possible in order to earn the most interest.

questions.question: The argument of paragraph 4 implies that the association's two characteristic features, its protection of savings and its vulnerability to default, are linked because

options.A: dense ties among members reduce the size of the discounts that desperate members accept in the bidding versions.
options.B: members who refuse loans to their cousins lose the trust of the other members of the group.
options.C: early recipients default most often when relatives make claims on the pot they have received.
options.D: the ties that make a refusal to kin acceptable are the same ties that keep early recipients paying.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the explanation that associations supply discipline is best described as

options.A: accepting it as partly right while holding that it misplaces the chief difficulty.
options.B: regarding it as relevant only to the bidding versions of the association.
options.C: endorsing it as a complete solution to the puzzle raised in paragraph 2.
options.D: rejecting it entirely as a view that members themselves dismiss as mistaken.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the function the author attributes to rotating associations?

options.A: A man often asked for loans by his friends keeps his savings in a bank account that none of his friends knows about.
options.B: A trader borrows from a moneylender at a high rate of interest because no bank in his town will lend to him at all.
options.C: A shopkeeper tells relatives seeking loans that her cash is pledged to her suppliers' cooperative, a commitment they accept she cannot break.
options.D: A student joins a study group because she knows she will not work regularly unless others expect her to attend.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's account of why people join rotating associations?

options.A: Some members who receive the pot early later stop contributing and leave the town without repaying the others.
options.B: Members whose relatives and neighbours make no claims on their money join as often, and pay as reliably, as members facing many such claims.
options.C: Associations formed among recent migrants to a city collapse more often than those in villages where members have lived side by side for several decades.
options.D: Members of bidding associations sometimes accept very large discounts when they need money urgently for an emergency.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: defend first come first served as the fairest principle for allocating any scarce public service among people who are strangers.
options.B: explain how some nations have produced more patient citizens than others through long traditions of waiting in line.
options.C: show that numbered tickets and railings are the most effective means available to offices for reducing conflict among customers.
options.D: argue that orderly queuing among strangers is better explained by how visible the rule is than by any national character.

questions.question: According to the passage, people waiting at the doors of a bus often jostle because

options.A: waiting for a bus feels more urgent to them than waiting at a ticket counter does.
options.B: no official is present at the bus doors to punish those who push ahead.
options.C: no one can tell with confidence who arrived first, so there is no clear order to defend.
options.D: people in a crowd become more selfish than they are when standing in a line.

questions.question: The example of a hospital that treats patients 'strictly in order of arrival' serves mainly to

options.A: show that informal norms collapse wherever people are unable to see a line forming in front of them.
options.B: concede that allocating a service by order of arrival can be orderly and yet unjust where needs differ.
options.C: suggest that hospitals are generally less well organised than the ticket offices described in paragraph 3.
options.D: illustrate how numbered tickets can be adapted for use in settings where urgency matters to those waiting.

questions.question: A popular food stall finds that customers push and argue at its counter at busy times. Which of the following measures would the author's account most clearly predict to reduce the problem?

options.A: Marking a single line on the ground leading to the counter, so that each newcomer's place is plain to everyone.
options.B: Inviting customers who believe they have waited longest to call out when the counter becomes free.
options.C: Asking each customer to state how urgently they need food so that the neediest can be served first.
options.D: Posting a notice at the counter reminding customers that patience is a civic virtue they should show to others.

questions.question: The remark that the retired teacher 'has lost not her wages, which she never had, but her say' implies that

options.A: part of what volunteers value is control over how and with whom they contribute, which managerial roles can take away.
options.B: volunteers who leave reorganised clubs are mainly those who had hoped that the new arrangements would bring them some form of payment.
options.C: retired teachers are especially ill suited to working under coordinators because they are used to running their own classrooms.
options.D: the reading club ceased to be of any benefit to the children once it was turned into a programme with targets.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the professionalisation of volunteering is best described as

options.A: detached neutrality: reporting what supporters and critics claim without offering any judgement of the author's own.
options.B: outright hostility: treating any form of training or rules for volunteers as a betrayal of what voluntary life stands for.
options.C: qualified scepticism: accepting it for demanding tasks but doubting it as a general model for voluntary bodies.
options.D: warm approval: welcoming it as clear evidence that voluntary bodies have at last matured into reliable organisations.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the third paragraph in the passage?

options.A: It offers evidence that professionalised organisations deliver their services less reliably than informal groups of volunteers do.
options.B: It answers the objection that rules are needed for demanding tasks such as rescue work on a mountain or work with children.
options.C: It explains why funders prefer to support organisations that can report the hours their volunteers have given.
options.D: It identifies a second cost, beyond individual volunteers' loss of say, that falls on the practice of collective self-government.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's suggestion that managerial practices lead some long-standing volunteers to drift away?

options.A: Some volunteers who left professionalised organisations later joined informal groups such as allotment societies and reading clubs.
options.B: Among comparable groups, long-serving volunteers left at the same rate whether or not their group had adopted role descriptions and supervisors.
options.C: Organisations that adopted role descriptions and supervisors reported more volunteer hours to their funders than they had before.
options.D: Many newly recruited volunteers say that clear role descriptions made them more willing to join an organisation in the first place.

questions.question: According to the passage, the tests on which early placement into streams is based measure

options.A: children's ability alone, although teachers later tend to misread what the results of those tests mean.
options.B: a mixture of ability and other factors, such as a child's maturity and the help she has had at home.
options.C: chiefly the quality of the teaching that each child has received in the school before the tests.
options.D: a child's real talent more accurately at the age of seven than it could be measured at fifteen.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the meaning of 'The door is open, but the corridor behind it grows longer every term' as used in paragraph 3?

options.A: The number of pupils moving up from the lower streams rises steadily as the school year goes on and they improve.
options.B: Schools deliberately add new requirements each term in order to keep pupils in the streams first assigned to them.
options.C: Pupils in the lower streams gradually lose their motivation and so stop trying to win a place in a higher group.
options.D: Movement between streams is formally permitted but becomes harder in practice as the groups' coverage drifts further apart.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the later examination results of pupils in different streams

options.A: are determined mainly by the age at which pupils first entered school rather than by what they were taught.
options.B: prove that pupils who were placed in lower streams had equal ability to the others at the outset.
options.C: cannot be taken as straightforward confirmation that the original placements were accurate.
options.D: show that the original placement tests detected no real differences at all between the pupils who sat them.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that streams partly produce the gaps they are said to detect?

options.A: Pupils with almost identical placement scores, assigned to adjacent streams only because a cut-off fell between them, differed markedly in attainment a few years later.
options.B: Pupils in the upper streams report enjoying school more, on average, than pupils who have been placed in the lower streams.
options.C: Teachers of classes with widely mixed attainment report that planning their lessons is far more demanding than teaching a single stream.
options.D: Pupils who were placed in lower streams at the age of seven also tended, on average, to obtain noticeably lower scores in their examinations at fifteen.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the usual explanation of why benefits go unclaimed

options.A: rests on accurate information about how many eligible people have never heard that the benefit exists.
options.B: is correct for most of those entitled but fails to account for a small group of the seriously ill.
