options.C: overlooks the demands that the process of claiming itself places on the people entitled to the benefit.
options.D: was devised by governments in order to justify reductions in the money spent on welfare programmes.

questions.question: The hypothetical government in paragraph 3 that 'wished to spend less on a programme but did not wish to say so' serves to

options.A: show that governments routinely add documents to application forms as a deliberate way of cutting spending on welfare.
options.B: argue that all requirements to renew a claim should be abolished because they serve no legitimate purpose at all.
options.C: demonstrate that laws on welfare are usually drafted with far more care than the forms used to administer them.
options.D: illustrate how changes in procedure can narrow a programme's reach while its rules of entitlement remain unchanged.

questions.question: Which of the following reforms would best accord with the 'sound design' described in the final paragraph?

options.A: Hiring more officials to examine completed forms so that a greater share of fraudulent claims is detected each year.
options.B: Letting officials confirm eligibility from records already held by other public offices instead of asking applicants to collect them.
options.C: Requiring claimants to renew their claims more often so that any change in their circumstances is detected sooner.
options.D: Removing every check on eligibility so that anyone who applies for the benefit receives it without delay or question.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: Burdens on claimants are introduced chiefly by governments that want to cut spending without public debate.
options.B: The costs of verification fall partly on applicants, and these are often left out of the reckoning.
options.C: A requirement that is a minor nuisance for one applicant may be decisive for another applicant.
options.D: A fall in the number of people receiving a benefit need not reflect any change in the rules that define who is entitled to it.

questions.question: In the example of the family that moves to a city, the people from its home district

options.A: find the family a permanent home in a neighbourhood where many different communities live.
options.B: refuse their help unless the family agrees to marry and to trade only within the group.
options.C: discourage the family from forming any friendships with neighbours from a different background.
options.D: help the family to secure a room, a loan and practical knowledge of offices and employers.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements about bridging ties?

options.A: They can be created reliably by public policies that weaken networks within communities.
options.B: They are formed mainly by people who do not belong to any close group of their own.
options.C: They are often formed through contacts that bonding ties first make available to a person.
options.D: They are less valuable than bonding ties, which deserve the civic esteem that writers usually give to bridging.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the statement that 'the closeness that was a resource becomes a closure' means that

options.A: the dense ties that once supported a group's members come to restrict what those members may choose to do.
options.B: the group's material resources are used up because too many dependent newcomers have relied on them.
options.C: the community stops offering help to its members and gradually dissolves as more and more of them leave.
options.D: outsiders become unable to learn what the community believes because its members refuse to speak to them.

questions.question: Judging by the criterion in the final paragraph, which of the following close groups would the author regard most favourably?

options.A: A community whose ties have loosened over the years, which leaves members free to make contacts elsewhere but gives newcomers little help.
options.B: A tightly knit association of traders from one region that helps newcomers open shops and encourages them to take partners from outside it.
options.C: A close neighbourhood community whose members help one another generously but expect their children to marry within it.
options.D: A group of families whose members have deliberately cut back their ties to one another in order to fit in better with the wider city.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, players' tolerance of refereeing errors before video review depended partly on

options.A: the lower stakes of professional matches in the years before cameras were introduced into the game.
options.B: rules that allowed teams to appeal against a decision once the match in which it was made had ended.
options.C: the expectation that, over a season, mistakes would not consistently favour or harm any one side.
options.D: players' belief that officials on the field were usually more accurate than replays would later turn out to be.

questions.question: The contrast in paragraph 3 between whether 'a challenge was reckless' and whether 'a toe was ahead of a defender's shoulder' serves to

options.A: illustrate the claim that officials on the field judge fouls less competently than the officials who watch replays.
options.B: argue that video review ought to be restricted to questions that can be settled as matters of measurable fact.
options.C: show that offside decisions are easier for officials to get right than decisions about how reckless a challenge was.
options.D: distinguish a question openly treated as judgement from one presented as fact that in truth rests on concealed choices.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: The disputes that review provokes show that replays are less accurate than the eyes of a trained referee.
options.B: A replay system can remove real injustices and still weaken officiating if it is used to settle marginal calls.
options.C: Review would provoke no new disputes if the lines drawn on screens were made more precise than they are now.
options.D: Since finality matters more than accuracy in sport, cameras used for review do more harm to games than good.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation of why disputes over decisions now seem less settled?

options.A: In competitions that use review only for clear and obvious errors, supporters argue over decisions just as long as in those that review marginal calls.
options.B: Before video review was introduced, supporters often claimed that referees were biased against the team they followed.
options.C: Referees who work with video review report feeling less confident when making decisions during play on the field.
options.D: Supporters of teams that lose a match tend to argue about refereeing decisions for longer, and far more bitterly, than supporters of the teams that win.

questions.question: According to the passage, the tendency of answers about quite different institutions to rise and fall together suggests that

options.A: the various institutions have tended to improve or to decline in their performance at the same times.
options.B: survey responses largely reflect a general disposition rather than considered judgements about particular bodies.
options.C: people trust the courts and the press for exactly the same reasons as each other.
options.D: respondents are much better informed about some public institutions than they are about others.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'well-calibrated trust' refers to trust that

options.A: stays at a moderate level, avoiding both complete confidence and complete suspicion of an institution.
options.B: is based on direct personal dealings with an institution rather than on its reputation alone.
options.C: rises or falls according to how reliable the institution in which it is placed actually is.
options.D: remains steady over the years regardless of how an institution's record happens to change.

questions.question: The example of people who distrust the courts yet 'continue to sign contracts that only courts can enforce' is used to suggest that

options.A: survey answers may be a weaker guide to trust, understood as reliance, than what people actually do.
options.B: people who express distrust of institutions while continuing to use them are being hypocritical.
options.C: trust in the courts is, in general, considerably higher than trust in the health service.
options.D: contracts would be signed far less often than they now are if the courts were trusted more.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the explanation that a particular fall in measured trust records 'an improvement in the public's knowledge' of the institutions concerned?

options.A: The fall in measured trust coincided with the publication of several well-documented reports of misconduct within the police.
options.B: People who had dealt with the courts directly reported higher trust in them than people who knew the courts only by their reputation among friends and neighbours.
options.C: Information about the failures of these institutions became far more widely available during the period in which measured trust fell.
options.D: The fall was steepest among people who had seen no reports of the institutions' failures, while trust held steady among those who followed such reports closely.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: A fall in measured trust in institutions is usually a sign that citizens have become better informed about them.
options.B: A sharp rise in measured trust in a police force would not, by itself, be a reason for satisfaction.
options.C: Public policy should aim to raise citizens' trust in institutions to the highest level that they are willing to accept.
options.D: Because survey answers about trust are unreliable, a decline in measured trust has no practical consequences.

questions.question: According to the passage, in the professionally managed organisations a member is typically

options.A: a person whose views on the organisation's policy are regularly sought and acted upon through surveys.
options.B: a person who gives time at the central office, working alongside the organisation's professional staff.
options.C: a person chosen by a local branch to represent it at the meetings of a regional or national body.
options.D: a person whose membership consists in having contributed money rather than in taking part in meetings.

questions.question: The author's reading of the evidence implies that the remedies mentioned at the end of paragraph 1 are

options.A: unnecessary, since people already gather in online groups and networks that serve the same civic purposes.
options.B: suitable for older citizens but not for younger people who grew up absorbed in private amusements.
options.C: misdirected, since they target individuals' willingness to join when the change lay largely in what organisations offered.
options.D: sound in their aim but too gentle, since only shaming would be strong enough to bring people back to meetings.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of the final paragraph?

options.A: It grants the faults of the older associations and the strengths of newer forms while restating what has been lost.
options.B: It abandons the earlier contrast and concludes that the old and the new organisations are of equal value.
options.C: It argues that excluding women and others was the main reason why the old federations went into decline.
options.D: It proposes that online groups be reorganised so that they can replace the federations of local branches.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: The fall in civic membership owes more to how organisations were rebuilt than to individual withdrawal, and it has cost citizens practice in governing themselves.
options.B: The decline of membership associations reflects organisations' choices about cheaper ways of raising money rather than any change in what ordinary people want.
options.C: Civic life has collapsed because people now prefer private amusements to the meetings and offices that earlier generations valued.
options.D: Professionally managed organisations are less legitimate than federations because they change laws without consulting their members.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as a step towards repairing the loss the passage describes?

options.A: A national charity doubles its number of supporters by advertising widely and begins to consult them through more frequent and detailed surveys.
options.B: A national charity gives local groups of its supporters budgets to manage and lets them elect delegates who vote on its policy.
options.C: An online forum lets supporters of a cause exchange views freely and at length, without officers, budgets or binding votes.
options.D: A public campaign urges every citizen to join at least one association in their town and to attend its meetings.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain how colonial clerks deliberately falsified reports in order to conceal the real causes of unrest from their superiors.
options.B: argue that the historians who read against the grain have mostly projected their own sympathies onto the people they study.
options.C: show that colonial archives are so distorted by official categories that historians should set them aside in favour of oral and material sources.
options.D: defend a way of reading official records while insisting that it has a boundary which honest historians must acknowledge.

questions.question: The statement 'Fear, in such documents, is a kind of evidence' (paragraph 2) suggests that

options.A: the anxious repetition of an official denial can show that the thing denied mattered to those involved.
options.B: officials' fears about rumours were usually justified, since most rumours in colonial districts later proved to be true.
options.C: the people who spread rumours did so mainly in order to frighten the officials who governed them.
options.D: historians should rely on emotional language in documents rather than on figures such as revenue collected or owed.

questions.question: Which one of the following best captures the meaning of 'Reading against the grain still reads the grain' as used in paragraph 3?

options.A: A critical reading of official records must begin with an uncritical reading, so that the historian first understands what the officials meant.
options.B: Historians who claim to read against the grain usually end up accepting the administration's categories without noticing that they have done so.
options.C: However critically the records are read, the method can only work with the people and events that those records happened to capture.
options.D: Records produced by the state are the only reliable source available for the lives of ordinary people under colonial rule.

questions.question: A historian studying a colonial district finds that its records say almost nothing about the farm work done by women. Which response would the author of the passage most likely endorse?

options.A: Generalising about all the district's women from the few court cases in which women appear as defendants or as petitioners.
options.B: Stating plainly that the records are silent, and turning to evidence such as surviving tools, field layouts and remembered work songs.
options.C: Treating the silence itself as proof that officials deliberately suppressed women's resistance, and reconstructing that resistance from it.
options.D: Concluding that because the district's records rarely mention it, women's farm work was probably a minor part of the local economy.

questions.question: According to the passage, what a public statue records most precisely is

options.A: a choice, made by certain people at a certain time, to honour its subject in that place.
options.B: the settled judgement of an entire community about the moral worth of the person it depicts.
options.C: the events that its subject took part in, as they were understood when those events occurred.
options.D: the main achievements of its subject, set down in a form that passers-by can easily read.

questions.question: The discussion of the explanatory plaque in paragraph 4 serves mainly to

options.A: show that plaques are the best available means of preserving a statue's value as historical evidence.
options.B: challenge the assumption that keeping a statue and adding text beside it is a choice free of anyone's judgement.
options.C: illustrate how committees in the past used inscriptions to assert the standing of a group or cause.
options.D: argue that statues of figures held in disrepute should always be removed rather than explained.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the claim that removing a statue 'erases history' as

options.A: correct only for statues raised soon after the events they depict, since later statues have no value as evidence of anything.
options.B: beside the point, because statues contain no evidence of any kind and their removal therefore costs a society nothing at all.
options.C: mistaken about what is lost, since removal ends an act of honour and some evidence of past values, not knowledge of the subject.
options.D: broadly correct, because a statue is the main means by which most ordinary citizens come to learn about the leading figures of their nation's past.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the views expressed in the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: The wording of an explanatory plaque reflects the judgement of whoever was given the task of writing it.
options.B: A statue raised long after its subject died may reveal more about its builders' concerns than about its subject.
options.C: A generation may legitimately decide to stop honouring a figure whom an earlier generation, with purposes of its own, chose to honour.
options.D: A statue moved from a public square into a museum gallery goes on honouring its subject much as it did before.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the critics mentioned at the start of paragraph 2 is best described as

options.A: studied neutrality: reporting their charge without indicating whether it is persuasive.
options.B: dismissive disagreement: treating their charge of anachronism as a basic misunderstanding of how history is actually written.
options.C: unreserved support: endorsing both their charge and the claim that national history is simply invented.
options.D: qualified agreement: accepting their central charge while rejecting one conclusion some of them draw from it.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the 'coherence' of a national history of the kind it criticises is achieved chiefly by

options.A: omitting or condemning those parts of the past that pointed towards other political outcomes.
options.B: relying on poets and chroniclers who were themselves committed to the idea of a unified nation.
options.C: describing how rival political projects were peacefully absorbed into the nation once it was formed.
options.D: tracing real continuities of language, worship and trade over many centuries of the region's history.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that older continuities shaped which communities later found it easy to imagine themselves as one?

options.A: Some medieval rulers spoke several languages and held lands in regions that now belong to two or three different modern countries.
options.B: National histories in many countries trace the nation back to a legendary founder whose actual existence cannot be confirmed from any surviving written or archaeological source.
options.C: Studies of several regions found that national feeling formed just as readily within borders that cut across older zones of shared language, worship and trade.
options.D: Many modern states, once formed, required a single standard language in their schools and steadily suppressed regional dialects in all official business.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the structure of the passage?

options.A: A criticism of national history is stated, the criticism is rejected as anachronistic, examples of its errors are given, and national history is defended.
options.B: A way of writing history is described, a criticism of it is accepted but limited, the harm of the error is traced, and an alternative proposed.
options.C: Two rival accounts of the origins of nations are compared, evidence for each is weighed, and the author concludes that both are partly mistaken.
options.D: A historical example is narrated in detail, a general principle is drawn from it, and the principle is applied to the teaching of history in schools.

questions.question: According to the passage, a mistake made independently by many witnesses differs from an individual slip of memory in that it

options.A: becomes a feature of shared understanding that needs to be explained rather than merely corrected.
options.B: can be corrected more easily, because the written records usually show where the witnesses went wrong.
options.C: is less likely to be an error at all, since agreement among witnesses usually indicates that they are right.
options.D: reveals the date of the event more reliably than an official document written at the time could do.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, the phrase 'a social fact' most nearly means

options.A: an event that is confirmed by both oral testimony and official written records.
options.B: a falsehood that a community spreads deliberately in order to mislead outsiders.
options.C: something true of the community's shared outlook, as distinct from a single person's lapse.
options.D: a statistic about how often older people make errors when recalling dates.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that, in the mining-town case, the records showing when the strike and the flood occurred

options.A: are of little further use to the historian once the residents' interviews have been recorded and analysed.
options.B: are needed to establish that the residents' dating is mistaken before that mistake can be interpreted.
options.C: should be doubted, since so many residents interviewed separately agreed on a different account of the dates.
options.D: show how the residents felt about the mine's owners during the years between the two events.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: In mining towns, residents tend to merge separate disasters because they blame the owners of the mines for both.
options.B: Oral testimony is more trustworthy than written records, because documents generally leave out the meanings that people gave to events.
options.C: Older people's memories of local events are usually inaccurate, so oral history should be confined to questions of meaning.
options.D: Shared mistakes in oral testimony can reveal how a community understood its past, once documents have shown them to be mistakes.

questions.question: The example of the harvest failure and the revolt in paragraph 1 serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate the kind of speculative question that the author agrees has no place in serious history.
options.B: demonstrate that economic hardship is the most common cause of popular revolts in history.
options.C: show that an ordinary causal claim already contains a counterfactual within it.
options.D: suggest that historians usually overstate the importance of single events such as failed harvests.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a book that traces how the whole of the following century would have unfolded had one particular battle gone the other way as

options.A: of little historical value, because the consequences it describes lie far beyond the horizon over which they could be judged.
options.B: legitimate history, since it does openly what every historian making a causal claim does implicitly.
options.C: valuable, provided the battle's outcome was something that people at the time actually contemplated as possible.
options.D: useful mainly for showing that the actual outcome of the battle was inevitable from the start.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's position on how counterfactuals can defeat claims of inevitability?

options.A: Many causal explanations offered by historians rest on assumptions about the behaviour of societies that the historians never state explicitly.
options.B: Historians who use explicit counterfactuals have frequently disagreed with one another about what would actually have followed from an altered decision or battle.
options.C: Politicians often describe outcomes as inevitable mainly in order to discourage people from questioning decisions that have already been taken.
options.D: Options seriously debated at the time have often proved, on fuller evidence, to have been out of reach given the forces at work.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, for the author, the main advantage of an explicit counterfactual over an ordinary causal explanation is that it

options.A: allows the historian to establish with some confidence what would have followed from a different decision.
options.B: brings into the open the assumptions about how events connect that the causal explanation leaves tacit.
options.C: depends on fewer untested assumptions about which social pressures are strong and which choices are free.
options.D: lets the historian fill gaps in the evidence by reconstructing events that left no trace in the records.

questions.question: According to the passage, the writers among whom the phrase 'The Middle Ages' took hold regarded the centuries it named as

options.A: a stretch of years grouped together merely for convenience, without any particular judgement implied.
options.B: a time of steady decline that began long before the ancient world had reached its height.
options.C: a gap between the learning of the ancient world and its revival in their own time.
options.D: the period in which universities, cathedrals and towns first laid the ground for later achievement.

questions.question: The passage suggests that calling a period in the history of a region far from Europe 'medieval' is problematic chiefly because it

options.A: wrongly suggests that the region was less advanced than Europe during the same span of years.
options.B: may lead historians to seek a pattern such as decline and rebirth that the region's own evidence does not show.
options.C: implies that the region had no universities, cathedrals or growing towns during the centuries the label covers.
options.D: uses a European word for a period that the region's own historians had already named differently.

questions.question: Which of the following practices would the author most likely regard as following the recommendation in the final paragraph?

options.A: A historian replaces all named periods with numbered centuries, so that no judgement about the character of an age enters the account.
options.B: A historian chooses a period name at the outset of a project and then organises the search for sources around the features the name suggests.
options.C: A historian refuses to group years together at all and narrates events year by year, leaving readers to form their own periods.
options.D: A historian keeps an established name for an era, checks whether its implied features appear in the sources, and drops it where they do not.

questions.question: Each of the following can be inferred from the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: Dividing the past into numbered centuries would avoid the distortions that named periods introduce into historical writing.
options.B: Achievements of the period called the Middle Ages contributed to developments that came after it.
options.C: A name for a period can go on shaping how the period is perceived after the view behind the name has been abandoned.
options.D: Some period names carry a judgement about the worth of the period that was made before the period was closely studied.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Heritage is a legitimate celebratory use of the past, but it becomes objectionable when it passes off its selective story as historical knowledge.
options.B: Heritage falsifies the past for commercial ends, and historians are right to treat it with suspicion and to resist its growing popularity.
options.C: Public money should be moved from heritage attractions back to archives and libraries, which serve the purposes of serious historical study.
options.D: Heritage and history are in the end the same activity, since both make use of the same buildings, objects and stories from the past.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the remark that heritage 'usually offers the past with the smell taken out' most nearly means that heritage

options.A: tends to attract visitors who have no real interest in the physical conditions of earlier times.
options.B: relies on modern materials and methods when it restores old buildings, cottages and other sites.
options.C: presents the past in an agreeable form from which its unpleasant realities have been removed.
options.D: concentrates on the visual appearance of old buildings rather than on how people actually used them.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the historians described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: wholly approving: sharing both their observations about heritage and their conclusion that it is a falsification of the past.
options.B: partly sympathetic: granting that their observations are accurate while holding that they misjudge what heritage is for.
options.C: openly contemptuous: treating their objections as snobbery towards popular pleasures that deserves no serious reply.
options.D: indifferent: reporting their view without indicating whether it is accurate or mistaken in any respect.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that, in the author's view, a heritage display becomes objectionable chiefly when it

options.A: charges visitors for admission and earns most of its income from the sale of replicas and souvenirs.
options.B: draws large numbers of visitors who had shown no interest in the past before they arrived.
options.C: leaves out unpleasant features of the past, such as poor sanitation or the crowded quarters of servants.
options.D: offers its selective celebration as an account of what the past was really like.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's suggestion that heritage can serve history as a doorway?

options.A: Some heritage sites present events in ways that professional historians have shown to be inaccurate or misleadingly incomplete.
options.B: Several historians have said that their interest in the past first began during a childhood visit to a restored house or village.
options.C: Among visitors to heritage sites who later took up serious historical reading, nearly all had already been keen readers of history before they first visited.
options.D: Heritage sites in many countries attract far more visitors each year than public archives, libraries and university history departments combined.

questions.question: According to the passage, what the peace agreements described in paragraph 2 actually established was

options.A: a requirement that citizens put the events of the conflict out of their minds.
options.B: a public record naming those responsible for the worst crimes of the conflict.
options.C: a ban on private remembrance of the dead in homes, kitchens and graveyards.
options.D: a limit on how past wrongs could be used in courts and in political life.

questions.question: The passage implies that those who treat remembrance as an unqualified duty after a conflict

options.A: take for granted that detailed public remembering always helps former enemies to live together.
options.B: generally belong to the side that lost the conflict and wish to see the victors punished.
options.C: would accept a temporary silence if they were shown that it had preserved the peace.
options.D: are mistaken in thinking that the truth about past crimes has any moral importance.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 3 in the argument of the passage?

options.A: It shows that full public reckoning after a conflict has always reopened the war that it was intended to bring to an end.
options.B: It argues that the case for agreed silence turns on timing, being strongest soon after a conflict and weaker a generation on.
options.C: It explains why the victims of a conflict, rather than its perpetrators, bear most of the cost of an agreed public silence.
options.D: It offers historical examples of societies that made peace by agreeing not to prosecute those responsible for the conflict.

questions.question: Thirty years after a civil war ended in an amnesty, the country's institutions are stable and the former combatants are elderly. The grandchildren of victims ask for the sealed records of the war to be opened, and the government refuses, saying that the peace was built on silence. The author would most likely regard the refusal as

options.A: justified, because an agreed silence that has kept the peace for thirty years ought to be preserved for as long as possible.
options.B: hard to justify, since the amnesty was defensible as a provisional arrangement and the conditions that once supported it have largely passed.
options.C: the predictable result of a mistake made at the start, since the records should never have been sealed in the first place.
options.D: acceptable only if opening the records were certain to lead to the prosecution of every surviving perpetrator of the war.

questions.question: The author's claim that the worst outcome is 'a silence that becomes permanent by default' implies that

options.A: whether a silence is acceptable depends partly on its remaining a deliberate and revisable choice rather than an unexamined habit.
options.B: a permanent silence is a worse outcome for a society than the renewed conflict that might follow a full public reckoning.
options.C: any silence is acceptable, however long it lasts, provided that every party to the conflict agreed to it at the outset.
options.D: the passing of the generation that fought a conflict automatically brings to an end any justification for continued silence.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that unplanned uses of colonial railways by ordinary people show that the benefits of empire outweighed its costs.
options.B: demonstrate that, taken as a whole, colonial railways did more harm than good to the societies through which their lines happened to run.
options.C: explain why colonial governments chose railway routes that served export trade and military control rather than local need.
options.D: show that weighing empire as a ledger misleads, since imposed works are not gifts and the question of who decided is left out.

questions.question: According to the passage, the ledger debate 'can continue indefinitely' because

options.A: defenders and critics of empire agree about the facts but hold sharply different moral principles about foreign rule.
options.B: most of the benefits of colonial railways appeared only after the colonial period had come to an end.
options.C: each side chooses what to count, and neither can say what a fair price for a railway would be.
options.D: the records needed to total the two columns were largely lost or destroyed when the colonial governments finally withdrew.

questions.question: The distinction between 'being affected by something' and 'being given it' (paragraph 2) implies that

options.A: colonial railways had no real effect on the daily lives of the people who lived and worked along the routes they followed.
options.B: railways built by colonial governments were of poorer quality than those an independent society would have built.
options.C: colonised societies are owed compensation equal to the full cost of every railway built during colonial rule.
options.D: a railway's effects on a colonised population do not by themselves show that the railway was a benefit conferred on it.

questions.question: The examples of passengers visiting shrines and attending political meetings (paragraph 3) serve mainly to

options.A: show that the colonial authorities used the railways mainly to prevent political meetings from taking place.
options.B: grant that local people put the railways to real use while showing that such use cannot be credited to the builders.
options.C: prove that colonial railways were designed chiefly with the comfort and needs of passengers in mind rather than freight.
options.D: confirm that the ledger records the benefits of empire correctly as long as unintended uses are added to its first column.

questions.question: In the final paragraph, the author calls the census 'closer to a mould'. This most nearly means that the census was

options.A: an invention that brought into being communities which had never existed before the enumerators arrived.
options.B: a faithful copy that reproduced the existing social order exactly as it was, without altering it in any way.
options.C: an instrument that gave a fixed shape to social distinctions which already existed but had been fluid.
options.D: a slow source of decay that gradually weakened the older identities until they disappeared from social life.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, the double answers that the census treated 'as an error to be corrected' (paragraph 2) often

options.A: reflected the way many people had ordinarily understood their own belonging, rather than a mistake on their part.
options.B: showed that the older vocabularies of lineage, occupation and locality had already fallen out of use.
options.C: resulted from enumerators who lacked the training needed to record complicated answers accurately.
options.D: indicated that respondents were deliberately concealing their true identity from officials they distrusted.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's interpretation of the petitions submitted in census years?

options.A: Many of the petitions were drafted by a small number of educated members of each group, acting on behalf of the rest of their community.
options.B: Some groups petitioned to be listed under names that had appeared in texts written long before colonial rule.
options.C: Petitions to change a recorded category were as frequent where categories had no bearing on recruitment, land or representation as where they did.
options.D: Census officials rejected most of the petitions that asked for a higher place in the order of precedence.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the view that colonial censuses did not so much count the peoples of the empire 'as invent them' is best described as

options.A: detached neutrality, reporting the thesis and the objections to it without taking a position of the author's own.
options.B: firm opposition, on the ground that the distinctions the census recorded were already present in the societies counted.
options.C: wholehearted endorsement, since the author agrees that the categories were creations of the administrative imagination.
options.D: qualified appreciation: crediting it with a useful corrective while holding that its strong form misplaces what was new.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following distinguished indentured workers from slaves?

options.A: They were free to leave the estate whenever the work was not as they had been promised.
options.B: They could not be sold, and their status was not passed on to their children.
options.C: They were paid wages equal to those earned by free workers in the same colonies.
options.D: They were protected by the colonial courts from criminal penalties for absence from work.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that the author regards the enforcement of indenture contracts by the courts as

options.A: evidence that coercion operated through the contract itself rather than in spite of it.
options.B: the main reason that most indentured workers chose to return home when their terms had ended.
options.C: a departure from the contracts, which on paper had guaranteed workers the freedom to leave when they wished.
options.D: a safeguard that, though imperfect, limited the power that planters could exercise over their workers.

questions.question: Which of the following present-day arrangements would the author regard as most clearly raising the question posed at the end of the passage?

options.A: A volunteer who works unpaid for a charity on weekends without having signed any written agreement at all.
options.B: A farm worker whose employer lent the recruitment fee and who may not change jobs until the loan, deducted from wages, is repaid.
options.C: A freelance designer who loses a client after missing a deadline that was set out in the signed contract.
options.D: A worker who is paid less than the contract promised but remains free to resign and look for other work at any time.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the structure of the argument in the passage?

options.A: It concedes that a system amounted to slavery and then argues that its contractual form made it less harsh than slavery.
options.B: It defends one of two opposing classifications of a system against objections and then applies it to present-day migration.
options.C: It narrates the history of a labour system from its origins to its abolition and then assesses its economic consequences.
options.D: It sets aside two opposed ways of classifying a system, identifies a feature both overlook, and draws a wider lesson from it.

questions.question: According to the passage, one reason several multilingual states have kept the colonial language is that

options.A: its native speakers formed a clear majority in most of the newly independent states.
options.B: it is the language most widely spoken among the rural majority of the population.
options.C: doing so spares the state from declaring one community's speech superior to another's.
options.D: international bodies required its use as a condition of recognising the new state.

questions.question: The statement 'equal foreignness is not equal access' (paragraph 3) means that

options.A: although the colonial language is native to almost no group, some citizens are far better placed to use it than others.
options.B: because the colonial language is foreign to everyone, every citizen finds it equally difficult to learn, to speak and to use well.
options.C: languages from outside a region are generally harder to learn than the languages spoken within it.
options.D: access to schooling in the colonial language was restricted by law to a small and wealthy class.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Policies that use several languages at different levels of government remove the inequalities that one official language creates.
options.B: Retaining the colonial language is the fairest option open to a multilingual state, since it disadvantages every group equally.
options.C: Debates about official languages after independence have been driven mainly by nostalgia for the colonial past or by national pride.
options.D: A rural citizen who natively speaks the chosen indigenous official language may gain more from that policy than from keeping the colonial language.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: The colonial language should be kept in multilingual states because it is the only option that treats all language communities alike.
options.B: Language policy after empire has been shaped chiefly by the need to communicate with the wider world rather than with citizens.
options.C: Choosing an official language after independence is chiefly about how advantage is shared among citizens, not authenticity against convenience.
options.D: Newly independent states ought to replace the colonial language with indigenous languages as quickly as is practical, whatever the cost.

questions.question: According to the passage, the straight-line borders on the map of Africa

options.A: follow rivers, watersheds or the limits of existing states wherever the terrain made this at all possible.
options.B: are found mostly in deserts and thinly populated regions, where they divided relatively few people.
options.C: were drawn at the Berlin conference by diplomats who settled each boundary with a ruler on the map.
options.D: have caused most of the wars fought between African states in the decades since independence was gained.

questions.question: The reference to the borders of Europe in paragraph 3 serves to

options.A: show that the charge of artificiality, if accepted, would equally condemn borders not usually blamed for chronic conflict.
options.B: suggest that African states should redraw their inherited borders by the methods used in European peace conferences.
options.C: argue that the borders of Europe were drawn with far more care for local wishes than any colonial boundary was.
options.D: explain why the Organisation of African Unity chose to accept the boundaries that its member states had inherited.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the decision of post-independence leaders to accept the boundaries they inherited as

options.A: evidence that the colonial borders in fact closely matched the boundaries of the states that existed before conquest.
options.B: a condition imposed on the new states by the former colonial powers before they agreed to grant independence.
options.C: a mistake that locked the new states into the conflicts that their artificial borders were bound to produce.
options.D: a considered judgement about the risks of redrawing, not a sign that they thought the borders were well drawn.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim about where the more serious colonial legacy lay?

options.A: Many European borders were also settled at peace conferences that made no attempt to consult the people living near them.
options.B: Most of the straight-line borders on the continent run through desert regions that had very few permanent inhabitants at the time.
options.C: Among former colonies, later instability tracks how extractive the colonial administration was far more closely than how straight or divisive the borders were.
options.D: Several boundaries fixed by survey commissions cut pastoral communities off from the grazing grounds they had always used in the dry season.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, under indirect rule, a ruler who had a genuine traditional claim to his office

options.A: became less constrained by those beneath him than he had been before colonial rule began.
options.B: kept exactly the position he had held before, since the policy preserved the existing institutions.
options.C: lost most of his authority to the warrant chiefs whom colonial officials appointed in his place.
options.D: was required to share his power with councils of elders, age-grades and religious associations.

questions.question: According to the passage, the written codes of customary law did all of the following EXCEPT

options.A: reflect the interests of the senior men who described the custom to colonial officers.
options.B: allow local communities to revise the rules themselves as their circumstances changed.
options.C: record as fixed a number of rules that had previously been flexible and open to dispute.
options.D: tend to favour men over women in matters such as marriage, land and inheritance.

questions.question: The author's disagreement with the architects of indirect rule is best captured by the claim that the policy

options.A: did not preserve existing authority but produced a new kind that answered to the colonial state rather than the governed.
options.B: was adopted mainly because it cost less than direct administration, not out of any real respect for local institutions.
options.C: should have been abandoned in favour of direct rule so that colonised peoples could adopt European institutions sooner.
options.D: replaced tradition with customs that colonial officials invented and imposed on subjects who had no part in shaping them.

questions.question: The final paragraph functions primarily to

options.A: introduce a fresh example of colonial invention, drawn this time from the record of post-colonial governments.
options.B: summarise the case that the defenders of indirect rule made for the policy before the author goes on to reject it.
options.C: reverse the argument of the earlier paragraphs by showing that tradition was in fact preserved by indirect rule.
options.D: qualify the preceding account by acknowledging the agency of local elders, then state the author's overall conclusion.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, which of the following would have counted as appropriating land under the view of property described there?

options.A: Moving across a region with the changing seasons.
options.B: Enclosing a field and ploughing it for crops.
options.C: Burning grassland at intervals to renew its growth.
options.D: Hunting over the same territory for many generations.

questions.question: The remark that the settlers' error was 'not a failure to see but a theory of what was worth seeing' (paragraph 2) implies that

options.A: the land practices of the original inhabitants were in fact less productive than European agriculture.
options.B: the settlers were unaware of the methods by which the original inhabitants managed and used the land.
options.C: the doctrine could not be overturned merely by establishing that the land had been inhabited.
options.D: the settlers knowingly told a lie in order to justify taking land they knew belonged to others.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the 1992 repudiation of terra nullius and the native title regimes that followed is best described as

options.A: dismissive, since the author regards the decision as a symbolic gesture that changed nothing for claimants.
options.B: unreservedly celebratory, since the author treats the decision as the full dismantling of the doctrine.
options.C: indifferent, since the author holds that legal recognition has no bearing on the deeper question of title.
options.D: appreciative of the repudiation's significance but critical of the standard of proof attached to it.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 4?

options.A: Native title courts routinely accept oral evidence of songs, hunting rules and fire practices as full proof of connection without any written record.
options.B: Some native title claims have succeeded where claimants could show long, unbroken written records of their occupation of the land.
options.C: Many claimant communities were forcibly removed from their land by government policy during the twentieth century and were never able to return.
options.D: Courts in most legal systems require evidence before they will recognise any claim to land, whoever the claimant happens to be.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main argument of the passage?

options.A: The doctrine of terra nullius was a fiction that settlers adopted while knowing perfectly well that it was false and self-serving.
options.B: Native title regimes ought to be replaced by forms of restitution that do not require claimants to prove anything at all.
options.C: Rejecting the claim that the land was empty has not removed the doctrine's underlying view of which relationships to land amount to ownership.
options.D: European theories of property, from the early modern period to the present, have consistently undervalued pastoral and nomadic life.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author mentions the nationalisation of a foreign-owned mine (paragraph 3) as an example of

options.A: economic dependence coming to an end at exactly the same moment as the transfer of sovereignty.
options.B: a power that formal independence genuinely conferred, whatever the wisdom of exercising it in a given case.
options.C: one of the ruinous mistakes that showed many new governments were not yet ready for sovereignty.
options.D: a concession that former imperial powers demanded of new states during the bargaining over the transfer of power.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, 'an unbundling' refers to

options.A: the deliberate dismantling by new governments of every institution that they had inherited from colonial rule.
options.B: the transfer of each colonial institution to new owners in a single ceremony on the day of independence.
options.C: the division of a single former empire into a number of separate and fully independent new states.
options.D: the separation, at different speeds and in different places, of relations that imperial power had held together.

questions.question: With which of the following statements would the author most likely agree?

options.A: The continuities that survived independence were for the most part imposed on the new states by their former imperial rulers.
options.B: The neo-colonial critique rightly saw that independence could coexist with dependence, but wrongly concluded that it changed nothing of substance.
options.C: The ceremonial picture is accurate about sovereignty and so remains the most useful framework for historians of decolonisation.
options.D: Because empire was a bundle of relations, the formal moment of independence had little real significance for the new states.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim in paragraph 5 that the governments of independent states must answer for some continuities?

options.A: Several former imperial powers kept military bases in their former colonies under formal agreements signed with the new governments at the time of independence.
options.B: Many members of the new governing elites had been educated in the former metropolis and admired its institutions.
options.C: The institutions that seemed to be kept by choice were in fact kept because foreign loans had been made conditional on keeping them.
options.D: Several newly independent governments wrote entirely new constitutions within a decade of gaining their independence.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Both standard accounts wrongly treat empire as one thing; its strands ended at different times, so the real question is which changed when.
options.B: Decolonisation was largely a ceremony, since the economic substance of imperial rule survived the formal grant of independence almost entirely intact.
options.C: The governments of newly independent states bear most of the responsibility for the persistence of colonial patterns after independence.
options.D: Formal sovereignty, which ended at a stroke, was the only part of imperial rule that independence was ever able to change.

questions.question: The central argument of the passage is that

options.A: the preventive ideal behind modern policing was an illusion, since visible officers do not reliably reduce the crime that gets recorded.
options.B: police forces, founded on the aim of preventing offences through visible patrol, have drifted toward the countable arrest at some cost to that aim.
options.C: the uniformed police replaced watchmen and constables chiefly because they caught offenders far more efficiently than the older arrangements had.
options.D: patrols reduce crime far more than arrests do, so police forces ought to stop measuring the number of arrests altogether.

questions.question: According to the passage, what was new about the reformed police forces of the nineteenth century?

options.A: The claim that a paid, disciplined and constantly visible body of officers could stop offences before they happened.
options.B: Their greater success in recovering stolen goods and returning them to the people from whom they were taken.
options.C: Their practice of judging officers mainly by the number of people detained in the course of each year.
options.D: Their reliance on unpaid residents who served as constables and walked fixed rounds through the parish at night.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a quiet street is a poor measure of what a patrol has achieved because

options.A: officers on patrol tend to avoid quiet streets and spend their time in districts where arrests are more likely.
options.B: residents of quiet streets rarely report offences to the police, so the crime that occurs there goes unrecorded.
options.C: the streets that are quiet are usually those where officers have made many arrests in earlier years.
options.D: the quiet cannot show whether it was produced by the officer's visit or would have occurred without it.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, the word 'legible' most nearly means

options.A: clearly printed or handwritten, so that a report can be read without difficulty.
options.B: lawful, in the sense of being permitted and approved by the public.
options.C: readily recorded, counted and reported to those who oversee the institution.
options.D: of greatest benefit to the residents whom the patrol is meant to protect.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that the requirement to carry passports after the First World War

options.A: outlived the wartime anxieties that had first led governments to impose it.
options.B: was imposed mainly because railways had made travel too fast for frontier officials to manage.
options.C: was withdrawn once fears about spies had passed and was reintroduced only much later.
options.D: was resisted by most travellers, who regarded it as an unjustified intrusion on their liberty.

questions.question: The reference to stateless people in paragraph 3 serves primarily to

options.A: illustrate how documents issued by some states admit their holders to far more countries than those issued by others.
options.B: prove that passports were introduced mainly to protect vulnerable travellers rather than to control their movements.
options.C: suggest that every state ought to issue papers to all who live within its territory, whatever their origin.
options.D: show that the protection a passport confers is substantial, by indicating what a person without one is exposed to.

questions.question: According to the passage, two passports of identical design may differ in

options.A: how much personal information about the holder each records and checks at the frontier.
options.B: how long the issuing state allows each document to remain valid before it must be renewed.
options.C: how readily the countries a traveller visits will admit the person who carries the document.
options.D: whether each entitles its holder to return to the state that issued it in the first place.

questions.question: Each of the following is a claim the passage makes about passports EXCEPT that they

options.A: certify the identity of the bearer and which state answers for the person who holds them.
options.B: were first required in order to speed up travel once railways had made crossing frontiers routine.
options.C: entitle their holders to seek help from the officials of the issuing state when abroad.
options.D: reflect a ranking among states that the individual holder can rarely do anything to alter.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Since frontline officials cannot avoid exercising judgement, reform should aim to expose and guide that judgement rather than to legislate it away.
options.B: Most of the unfairness in public agencies arises because officials are given more cases than they can handle in the time available.
options.C: Frontline officials should be given wide freedom to depart from rules, because they understand applicants' circumstances better than those who write the rules.
options.D: Detailed rules remain the fairest way to treat applicants alike, although officials sometimes apply such rules more rigidly than they should.

questions.question: The example of the clerk and the proof of address in paragraph 2 suggests that

options.A: clerks often misread eligibility rules on purpose in order to turn away applicants whom they happen to dislike.
options.B: rules about proof of address are usually drafted with little regard to how applicants actually live and where they stay.
options.C: applicants who live with relatives are more likely than others to be refused benefits by the clerks they deal with.
options.D: a rule can state what is required while leaving open how much effort an official spends helping an applicant meet it.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates the claim in paragraph 2 that judgement 'retreats into these less visible choices'?

options.A: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, supervisors begin publishing how often each caseworker's applicants are approved and refused.
options.B: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, its caseworkers come to differ chiefly in how quickly they schedule interviews for the different applicants they serve.
options.C: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, its caseworkers openly refuse to use it and carry on assessing applicants exactly as they did before.
options.D: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, fewer applicants are approved, because the new sheet is stricter than the assessments it replaced.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards frontline discretion is best described as

options.A: studied neutrality: the passage sets out competing views of it without favouring either side over the other.
options.B: warm admiration: it lets sympathetic officials rescue the families whom rigid rules would fail.
options.C: realistic acceptance: it is unavoidable and open to abuse, so it should be brought into view.
options.D: deep suspicion: it is chiefly a channel through which prejudice enters public administration.

questions.question: The analysis in paragraph 2 suggests that the soil principle

options.A: was adopted in some places for reasons of state interest that had little to do with openness to newcomers.
options.B: was abandoned by most states once their need for soldiers and taxpayers had declined over time.
options.C: was imposed on immigrant parents against their wishes and was widely resented by the families it affected.
options.D: is in practice more exclusive than the descent principle, despite its reputation for being open.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the soil and descent contrast is a misleading guide to how welcoming a society is?

options.A: Some children who acquire citizenship under the soil principle later renounce it in favour of the nationality held by their parents.
options.B: In several states that follow the soil principle, long-term residents must wait many years and pay high fees before they can naturalise.
options.C: States following the soil principle almost always offer quick, cheap naturalisation, while states following the descent principle almost always make it slow and costly.
options.D: Some states that follow the descent principle require applicants for naturalisation to pass a test of the national language before they are admitted.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 4 in the passage?

options.A: It summarises the historical motives for each principle that were set out earlier in paragraph 2 of the passage.
options.B: It grants a genuine merit of the soil principle while denying that this merit settles how open a society is.
options.C: It shifts the discussion away from nationality law towards the practical hardships of residents without secure status.
options.D: It reverses the earlier argument by admitting that the soil principle is after all the defining mark of an open society.

questions.question: According to the passage, the descent principle has been useful to countries that

options.A: needed to populate large and empty territories and to secure enough soldiers and taxpayers for the state.
options.B: sought to make naturalisation for adult residents quick, cheap and predictable.
options.C: wished to claim the children of newcomers automatically on the ground of their birth.
options.D: have many citizens living abroad and want their children to keep a tie to the homeland.

questions.question: The passage as a whole is best described as

options.A: an account of how particular resource-rich states built competent institutions before their revenue arrived and so avoided its harms.
options.B: an examination of a thesis linking sources of revenue to accountability, which keeps a narrowed form of it after weighing objections.
options.C: a rejection of the claim that the way a state raises its money has any real bearing on how it treats its own citizens.
options.D: a defence of the thesis that resource revenue inevitably makes governments unaccountable, against critics who doubt that it does.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that a government living mainly on resource sales abroad

options.A: is unable to provide subsidies to its citizens, because its income depends on a few foreign contracts.
options.B: must negotiate constantly with its own citizens in order to keep its contracts with foreign buyers.
options.C: can sustain itself without detailed knowledge of who its citizens are or what they earn.
options.D: usually builds a larger administrative apparatus than a government that relies on taxing its people.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most support the claim in paragraph 4 that 'it is the dependence, not the tax form as such, that does the work'?

options.A: Several resource-rich states that had strong institutions before their windfalls arrived went on to manage the revenue with notable openness.
options.B: Two governments equally dependent on their citizens' compliance, one funded by income taxes and the other by sales taxes, differ sharply in how openly they account for spending.
options.C: Citizens of states that tax heavily are more likely than others to tell survey researchers that they follow public affairs closely.
options.D: A ruler funded by customs duties collected at a few ports, needing no cooperation from most citizens, proves as unresponsive as rulers funded by mineral sales.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT

options.A: Raising more revenue from citizens is in itself a dependable way of making a government more accountable to them.
options.B: Taxation obtained by force need not bring the people who pay it any representation in return.
options.C: A government that needs its citizens' compliance has some reason to attend to what they demand.
options.D: The timing of a resource boom relative to the growth of institutions affects what the boom does to a state.

questions.question: The reasoning in paragraph 2 implies that emergencies are commonly prolonged because

options.A: the threats that justify emergencies usually grow more severe the longer the emergency lasts.
options.B: officials fear being blamed for lifting powers too early more than they fear keeping them too long.
options.C: citizens demand that the powers stay in place long after officials would prefer to lift them.
options.D: leaders invent threats in order to dismantle the constitution gradually, one renewal at a time.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as the clearest sign that an emergency regime has failed?

options.A: A government declares an emergency during an epidemic and restricts movement for several months before the powers lapse.
options.B: Emergency powers are renewed three times in succession, each time by a larger majority of the legislature than the time before.
options.C: A constitution contains detailed provisions allowing the executive to rule by decree in time of war or invasion.
options.D: Detention powers first granted for a particular crisis are later moved into an ordinary statute and are no longer debated.

questions.question: The final sentence of paragraph 1 functions in the argument to

options.A: argue that emergency powers should be drafted so broadly that improvisation in a crisis is never necessary.
options.B: introduce the danger of normalisation, which the rest of the passage treats as the main problem with emergency powers.
options.C: explain why including emergency powers in a constitution is defensible despite the risks the passage goes on to describe.
options.D: show that governments in a crisis usually act outside the law even when emergency provisions are in place.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards sunset clauses is best described as

options.A: qualified approval: they help somewhat but leave renewal far too easy to secure.
options.B: strong endorsement: they are the most effective safeguard that a written constitution can provide.
options.C: grudging hostility: they are a distraction that has delayed the adoption of better designs.
options.D: outright rejection: they make abuse of emergency powers more likely than having no time limit at all.

questions.question: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to

options.A: defend a formal understanding of the rule of law as naming a real but limited virtue that should be kept apart from other political goods.
options.B: compare the formal and richer conceptions of the rule of law and conclude that the choice between them is a merely verbal matter.
options.C: show that the formal conception of the rule of law prevents oppressive regimes from enacting and enforcing unjust laws against their subjects.
options.D: argue that the rule of law should be defined to include rights and fair distribution, since formal properties on their own are morally empty.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, the word 'congenial' most nearly means

options.A: familiar to them from long and settled practice.
options.B: warm, friendly and sociable in personal manner.
options.C: legally binding upon them in a time of crisis.
options.D: suited to their aims and convenient to use.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a regime which publishes clear, prospective laws excluding a minority from public office, and enforces them impartially through independent courts,

options.A: is less unjust than it first appears, because formal legality prevents most of the harm that such laws are meant to cause.
options.B: satisfies the formal rule of law while committing a serious wrong that has to be condemned on other grounds.
options.C: shows that formal legality has no value whatever once the content of the law it applies becomes objectionable.
options.D: does not truly satisfy the rule of law at all, since its laws deprive a minority of rights it ought to enjoy.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author's formal conception classify as a failure of the rule of law, as distinct from a failure of justice or of democracy?

options.A: A state holds no national elections, but its laws are general, public, stable and applied by courts independent of the rulers.
options.B: A state whose courts are independent of the government faithfully applies a clearly drafted and stable law restricting public protest.
options.C: A state with generous welfare statutes lets local officials decide case by case, without any published criteria, which applicants will actually be paid.
options.D: A state publishes and impartially enforces a tax code that places the heaviest share of the burden on its poorest citizens.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a reason to value formal legality EXCEPT that it

options.A: tends to get in the way of the methods that governments bent on oppression usually prefer.
options.B: binds the officials who administer the law as well as the citizens who are subject to it.
options.C: allows people to know in advance what will be required of them and to plan their lives accordingly.
options.D: prevents governments from pursuing grave injustice through laws that have been properly enacted and published.

questions.question: Within the author's argument, the example of the sailor in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: illustrate the self-binding defence of entrenchment, which the author then argues is a poor fit for constitutions.
options.B: show that a people, like a single person, can protect itself from its own passions by entrenching its rules.
options.C: explain why amendment rules often require the approval of most regions as well as of the legislature.
options.D: suggest that constitutions should be easier to amend in calm periods than in times of political agitation.

questions.question: The author's objection to the self-binding defence rests chiefly on the point that

options.A: a sailor tied to the mast can usually persuade his crew to release him once the dangerous song begins.
options.B: those whom a constitution binds are not, in any straightforward sense, the people who chose to be bound.
options.C: peoples, unlike individuals, are seldom calm enough to foresee the passions they will feel at a later time.
options.D: entrenchment protects a society against its own impulses less effectively than ordinary legislation does.

questions.question: The defence of entrenchment offered in paragraph 3 depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: That a supermajority requirement will lead most proposals for amendment to win support from more than one faction.
options.B: That the present minorities who block amendments are usually right about the matters basic to their standing.
options.C: That amendment remains achievable in practice, so that whether a change passes is decided by the present balance of support.
options.D: That the framers of most constitutions intended amendment to be easy enough for any broad coalition to achieve.

questions.question: In which of the following cases would the author most likely say that the objection from the 'dead hand' applies with full force?

options.A: An amendment backed by a narrow majority of citizens fails because a large regional minority votes against it.
options.B: A constitution requires two-thirds of the legislature and the approval of most regions for any amendment, and amendments have passed only rarely.
options.C: A constitution's amendment rules were drafted by framers who could not have foreseen the conditions under which citizens now live.
options.D: A provision declared permanently unamendable continues to bind citizens even though nearly all of them now wish to change it.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's stance towards the objection from the dead hand?

options.A: It is confused, because amendment rules never impose the judgement of a constitution's framers on anyone now living.
options.B: It is decisive, and shows that no generation may legitimately place any limits on the political choices of the next.
options.C: It fails as a case against entrenchment in general, though it has real force against constitutions that are effectively impossible to change.
options.D: It is best answered by the self-binding defence, provided that defence is stated with more care than usual.

questions.question: The author's main purpose in the passage is to

options.A: defend elections against the charge that they systematically keep ordinary citizens such as shift workers and pensioners out of public office.
options.B: argue that selection by lot has genuine democratic merits but is better suited to supplementing elected bodies than to replacing them.
options.C: trace how the ancient Greek preference for filling offices by lot came to be abandoned in favour of the elections that modern states now hold.
options.D: show that randomly chosen citizens would legislate more competently than elected politicians and should therefore take their place in most chambers.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the ancient Greek writers mentioned in paragraph 1 regarded election as less democratic than lot because election

options.A: favours people who already stand out from their fellow citizens, whereas lot gives everyone an equal chance.
options.B: allowed wealthy donors and party managers to decide in advance which candidates the citizens would be permitted to choose between.
options.C: required ordinary citizens to judge the competence of candidates on matters of law about which they knew very little.
options.D: made it impossible for those holding office to be removed by the citizens before their term of office had ended.

questions.question: The author mentions that an elected representative who revises a position 'risks being called a turncoat' in order to

options.A: illustrate the problem of accountability that the author says the defenders of lot have never answered.
options.B: concede that selection by lot shares a weakness with election that its defenders usually prefer to overlook.
options.C: explain why members chosen by lot are in a better position to let evidence change their views.
options.D: criticise elected representatives for caring more about appearing consistent than about reaching the right answer.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the competence objection in paragraph 3?

options.A: Panels chosen by lot, unlike legislators, prove unable to judge which of their expert witnesses are reliable, and tend to adopt the view of whoever spoke last.
options.B: Legislators who disappoint their voters are often re-elected anyway, because voters remain loyal to the party under whose name they stand.
options.C: Elected legislators who depend heavily on staff and committees are often captured by those advisers, and end up voting as the advisers recommend.
options.D: Most elected legislators possess specialist knowledge of at least one policy area, usually drawn from the occupation they followed before entering politics.

questions.question: According to the passage, the laws that make voting compulsory typically require citizens to

options.A: pay a small fine each time they vote, which is returned if they can give a good excuse.
options.B: vote for one of the listed candidates, though the ballot itself remains secret from officials.
options.C: serve on a jury and complete the census form as well as attend the polling station on election day.
options.D: turn up to vote, while leaving them free to spoil the ballot paper or leave it blank.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, where voting is voluntary, campaigns tend to stir up anger against opponents mainly because
