options.A: angry voters pay closer attention to policy, and so are more likely to reward a party that offers a well-argued programme.
options.B: getting likely supporters to the polls matters more than winning over the uncommitted, and anger is a cheap way to do it.
options.C: undecided citizens can be won over only by campaigns that frighten them about what the other side would do in office.
options.D: voters who are older and wealthier are, by temperament, more easily made angry or afraid than other citizens.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the claim that compulsory voting 'produces wiser decisions' is best described as

options.A: sceptical, because a duty to attend a polling station does nothing by itself to inform the voter.
options.B: dismissive, because the author believes that most citizens forced to vote simply choose a name at random.
options.C: approving, because the author holds that a larger electorate makes better choices than a small and angry one.
options.D: undecided, because the author thinks the evidence about the quality of compelled votes is still inconclusive.

questions.question: Which of the following obligations is most similar to the kind of duty the author says compulsory voting imposes?

options.A: Members of a housing society must sign a declaration supporting the committee's plans before they are allowed to attend its annual meeting.
options.B: Members of a housing society must attend its annual meeting, but each may vote, abstain or leave the ballot blank on every motion.
options.C: Members of a housing society may attend its annual meeting only if they have first passed a short test on the society's rules.
options.D: Members of a housing society are encouraged to attend its annual meeting, and those who stay away face no penalty of any kind.

questions.question: The examples of the kitchen table and the telephone in paragraph 4 serve mainly to

options.A: suggest that the secret ballot was never as effective in protecting voters as its nineteenth-century supporters had claimed.
options.B: support the old liberal view that a vote seen by others is more likely to be cast for the good of the community.
options.C: show that newer ways of voting can recreate the exposure to pressure that secrecy was meant to remove.
options.D: argue that voting at home and voting with a telephone in the booth should both be prohibited in order to protect the ballot.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the statement that secrecy makes a certain kind of corruption 'unenforceable' means that

options.A: voters who accept bribes are legally obliged to vote as they promised, though in practice few do.
options.B: corruption of every kind becomes impossible to prosecute once voters can no longer be observed.
options.C: officials can no longer enforce the laws against intimidation, because voters will not report it.
options.D: a corrupt bargain over a vote cannot be checked, so neither side can rely on it.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the nineteenth-century liberals who opposed the secret ballot

options.A: correctly saw that being watched alters conduct but misjudged whose standards the watching would enforce.
options.B: were insincere when they described the vote as a trust to be exercised on behalf of the community.
options.C: rightly predicted that a secret vote would lead citizens to cast their ballots for more selfish reasons.
options.D: opposed it chiefly because they themselves gained from the ability to pressure the people who voted.

questions.question: By the reasoning of paragraph 3, which of the following arrangements would best preserve the protection that secrecy gives against vote buying?

options.A: Ballots are cast openly, but any voter who reports an attempt to buy a vote is given full legal protection against the person who made it.
options.B: Ballots are marked in private, but each voter is handed a numbered slip, and the marked papers are published with their numbers after the count.
options.C: Voters may decide whether to keep their ballots secret, and those who choose to disclose their vote receive an official receipt recording the choice.
options.D: Voters may photograph their ballots, but any voter may later cast a fresh ballot that silently replaces the earlier one, so no photograph proves the final vote.

questions.question: According to the passage, hostility to elites cannot by itself serve as a definition of populism because

options.A: voters who distrust elites are often moved by real grievances that deserve a hearing.
options.B: many movements hostile to elites have promised to cut public spending rather than increase it.
options.C: criticising those in power is a normal activity of opposition in every democracy.
options.D: elites in most democracies have themselves adopted the language of their populist critics.

questions.question: The final paragraph of the passage serves primarily to

options.A: argue that populist movements are justified in their methods because the complaints of their supporters are real ones.
options.B: warn that a sound definition of populism can be misused to brush aside the complaints on which populist movements draw.
options.C: show that populism is, after all, merely a label for any style of politics the speaker happens to dislike.
options.D: withdraw the definition defended in the preceding paragraphs on the ground that it is unfair to the ordinary voters who support populists.

questions.question: The passage implies that an analyst who treats every supporter of a populist movement as a victim of manipulation would be

options.A: showing that the definition based on a moral monopoly is too narrow to explain why populism attracts support.
options.B: acting reasonably, since the complaints that draw voters to populist movements are seldom ones that institutions could address.
options.C: applying the anti-pluralist definition correctly, even if without much sympathy for the voters concerned.
options.D: reproducing, in another form, the refusal to grant opponents the standing of citizens who disagree for reasons.

questions.question: Which of the following movements would most clearly count as populist on the definition the author defends?

options.A: A movement that accuses the established parties of ignoring rural districts and asks the voters of those districts to judge it at the next election.
options.B: A movement that promises the largest programme of public spending in the country's history and draws its support mainly from the poorest voters.
options.C: A movement with cautious economic policies that calls its rivals' voters traitors to the nation and blames any election it loses on fraud.
options.D: A movement that campaigns fiercely against the influence of large banks on government and accepts the result whenever it loses an election.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: For all their faults, parties do work democracy needs, so their failings call for improving them rather than bypassing them.
options.B: Parties deserve far more admiration than they receive, since the functions they perform show that they are fundamentally virtuous.
options.C: Open primaries, though meant to democratise parties, usually produce candidates with intense followings rather than broad appeal.
options.D: Parties have become so self-serving that reformers are right to replace them with independent candidates and direct votes on policy.

questions.question: According to the passage, a legislature made up entirely of independents would be a problem for voters because it

options.A: would be unable to assemble the conflicting interests of millions of people into any kind of legislation.
options.B: would leave them without any collective body that they could reward or punish at the next election.
options.C: would be dominated by wealthy individuals who had paid for the campaigns of most of its members.
options.D: would contain members who had been screened too strictly by organisations remote from local life.

questions.question: When the author says that defenders of party government have 'mistaken the indispensability of parties for their innocence', the point is that these defenders

options.A: have confused the innocent intentions of party founders with the conduct of the parties they built.
options.B: have wrongly believed that democracy could function perfectly well without any parties at all.
options.C: have assumed that because parties are necessary to democracy, they must also be free of blame.
options.D: have argued that parties are guilty of misconduct only when they face no serious competition.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim in paragraph 3 about candidates chosen in open primaries?

options.A: Where parties adopted open primaries, turnout in those contests was high among committed party activists and very low among everyone else.
options.B: Where parties adopted open primaries, the candidates who won were generally those whom uncommitted voters rated most highly in polls.
options.C: Party membership has fallen as steeply in countries that never adopted open primaries as in countries that adopted them early.
options.D: Candidates chosen in open primaries tend to spend more money on their campaigns than candidates chosen by party committees.

questions.question: According to the passage, disruption is close to the centre of democratic protest because

options.A: the public has always come to regard the causes of disruptive protesters as just once their methods are forgotten.
options.B: protesters who cause no disruption are usually breaking the law, while those who cause disruption usually are not.
options.C: governments in most democracies treat every inconvenience caused by protesters as an emergency requiring a response.
options.D: groups lacking money, office or press access have few other ways of bringing an issue to public notice.

questions.question: The remark that 'A march that nobody notices, held where nobody has to walk around it, is hardly a protest' suggests that the author believes

options.A: imposing some cost on others is part of what lets a protest function as a public claim.
options.B: complaints about inconvenience caused by protests are unfair and should be ignored by those who govern.
options.C: protests should be held in the busiest places available, whatever inconvenience this causes to the public.
options.D: most protests fail because their organisers choose places where they will not be noticed by anyone.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: Disruption is legitimate whenever the cause it serves is later judged by most people to have been just.
options.B: Governments should avoid treating every inconvenience caused by protesters as if it were an emergency.
options.C: A protest may legitimately impose costs on people who bear no responsibility for the grievance concerned.
options.D: Protesters ought to weigh the harm that their methods cause against the importance of their message.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most clearly regard as disruption that 'seeks to impose an outcome'?

options.A: Protesters occupy a public square for a weekend, holding speeches and handing out leaflets to passers-by.
options.B: Protesters chain shut the doors of a council chamber so that a scheduled vote cannot be held.
options.C: Protesters march through the city centre during the evening rush hour, delaying traffic for most of the evening.
options.D: Protesters stand silently outside a council chamber with banners while councillors arrive for a scheduled vote.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Local newspapers were the most trustworthy watchdogs that democracies have ever had, and their closure has left local government without any honest observers at all.
options.B: The closure of local papers matters mainly because communities lose the obituaries, sports results and notices that bound their members together.
options.C: The chief democratic loss when local papers close is routine scrutiny of local government, which must now be sustained by other means despite the papers' own failings.
options.D: The internet has replaced local newspapers as a source of information about councils, though it spreads rumours more quickly than facts.

questions.question: The comparison with a speed camera in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: show that most of what local reporters wrote led to fines or penalties for the officials they wrote about.
options.B: suggest that local reporters, like speed cameras, were resented by the officials whose meetings they attended.
options.C: argue that local governments should be watched by automatic recording devices rather than by journalists.
options.D: illustrate that the value of monitoring lies mainly in the misconduct it deters rather than in what it exposes.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards a neighbourhood online forum as

options.A: quick to circulate claims about local government but poorly placed to scrutinise it in a sustained way.
options.B: a dangerous source of misinformation that local governments would be justified in regulating closely.
options.C: an adequate substitute for a local reporter wherever its members are willing to attend council meetings.
options.D: more useful than a national outlet, because it reports on local government before the damage is done.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the local newspapers of the past is best described as

options.A: nostalgic, since the author regards their disappearance as the loss of a better and more honest era of journalism.
options.B: appreciative of the observation they performed while critical of their deference to local power.
options.C: indifferent, since the author thinks any institution could have performed their work equally well or better.
options.D: contemptuous, since the author believes that their timidity with advertisers made their coverage worthless.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim about how monitoring works in paragraph 2?

options.A: Officials in towns with a local paper said that they seldom read the paper's reports of their own meetings.
options.B: In their final decade, the papers that eventually closed had published very few investigative reports about their councils.
options.C: In towns whose papers closed, residents said they now read more news about their council online than they had before.
options.D: In towns whose papers closed, the cost of public contracts rose steadily over the next few years, although no new scandals were reported there.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 1, 'rational ignorance' refers to

options.A: the tendency of voters to draw illogical conclusions from the political information that they already happen to possess.
options.B: ignorance that voters conceal by offering reasonable-sounding justifications for choices they made without any real thought.
options.C: a lack of knowledge that comes from sensibly weighing the cost of learning against a vote's tiny chance of mattering.
options.D: knowledge that governments deliberately withhold from voters in order to avoid the scrutiny that an informed public would bring.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard the claim that a voter equipped with cues 'can vote much as she would if she were fully informed' as

options.A: true only under conditions, such as stable and distinct parties, that a democracy cannot assume will hold.
options.B: broadly true, because party labels, prices and endorsements together give voters a reliable picture of every government.
options.C: false, because voters are in general incapable of using simple cues such as party labels in a sensible way.
options.D: beside the point, because the author holds that what matters is who would set and mark a test of voters' knowledge.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply in paragraph 4 to those who would weight votes by knowledge?

options.A: Voters who score highly on tests of political knowledge often disagree sharply with one another about which policies are best.
options.B: Political parties in many democracies have grown more fragmented over recent decades, making their labels less informative to voters.
options.C: Even in settings where cues are highly reliable, voters' choices still differ markedly from the choices they would make if fully informed.
options.D: Tests of political knowledge have proved very difficult to design without favouring the education of some social groups over others.

questions.question: The reference to voters who punish an incumbent 'for a drought' serves to

options.A: support the critics' view that the franchise should be weighted towards citizens who know more about policy.
options.B: show how a reasonable-seeming cue can hold governments responsible for things they do not control.
options.C: suggest that governments are generally less competent than voters believe, but are rarely punished for it.
options.D: show that voters who rely on how things are going reason worse than those who follow the endorsements of trusted organisations.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the author's overall position?

options.A: Since shortcuts are too unreliable to depend on, democracies should do much more to make every citizen properly informed about policy.
options.B: Since voters' ignorance is rational, it poses no real threat to the quality of democratic decisions and requires no remedy.
options.C: Since uninformed voters can easily be misled, the critics of democracy are right to give greater weight to the votes of informed citizens.
options.D: Since voters' competence depends partly on institutions, democracies should make the cues voters rely on more reliable instead of restricting who may vote.

questions.question: The author's main purpose in the passage is to

options.A: explain why small states usually prefer forming alliances with one another to relying on the protection of a great power.
options.B: show that neutral states have nearly always stayed out of wars, provided that they kept armies strong enough to deter invasion.
options.C: recast neutrality, which critics treat as moral evasion, as a costly strategy by which small states try to keep out of wars.
options.D: defend neutral states against the charge of profiteering by showing that very few of them have gained from wars nearby.

questions.question: According to the passage, a neutral state must arm itself

options.A: against all of its neighbours at once, since it must be ready to resist whichever of them crosses its frontier first.
options.B: only so far as is needed to reassure its neighbours that its forces pose no threat to any of them.
options.C: against the strongest of its neighbours, since that power is the one most likely to want its territory as a road or a base.
options.D: together with other neutral states, so that their combined forces make the occupation of any one of them expensive.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the author describes a neutral that cannot defend its borders as 'simply unclaimed'. The word suggests that such a state is

options.A: free of any formal alliance with a larger power, which is exactly the condition that a policy of neutrality aims to secure.
options.B: thinly settled and of little economic value, so that its larger neighbours have no particular reason to want it.
options.C: not recognised as a sovereign state by the great powers of its region and so lacking any standing under international law.
options.D: outside any effective protection, its own or anyone else's, and therefore open to seizure by whichever power moves first.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a neutral state's conduct in peacetime matters chiefly because

options.A: treaties of friendship signed in peacetime would legally bind a neutral to support its partner once a war broke out.
options.B: foreign governments read minor gestures as clues to its wartime loyalties, and its security rests on their believing it impartial.
options.C: critics of neutrality judge a state mainly by its peacetime record rather than by what it does once fighting begins.
options.D: a neutral that behaves impartially in peacetime can count on the great powers to respect its borders in any later war.

questions.question: Paragraph 2 functions in the passage chiefly to

options.A: offer cases that the popular lesson cannot explain and to propose different factors that decide whether a settlement lasts.
options.B: prove that severe settlements are, as a rule, more durable than lenient ones and should therefore be preferred by victors.
options.C: describe in detail how the terms of the settlement after the First World War came to be evaded one by one.
options.D: explain why victorious powers find it comforting to believe that a generous peace is both noble and prudent.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that a lenient settlement is likely to fail when

options.A: the defeated state resents being offered trade, membership of institutions and the eventual lifting of restrictions.
options.B: the defeated state takes the mildness of its terms as a sign that its defeat was not decisive.
options.C: the victors later conclude that their terms were too generous and try to impose harsher ones in their place.
options.D: the defeated state is too weak after the war to make use of the generous terms it has been offered.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's account of what makes a peace settlement last?

options.A: A harsh settlement that the exhausted victors stopped enforcing was overturned by the defeated state within a decade of being signed.
options.B: A lenient settlement lasted for several decades after the victors made it clear that they had won decisively and would defend its terms.
options.C: Historians continue to disagree about whether the settlement that followed the First World War was in fact unusually harsh.
options.D: A settlement that matched the balance of strength and was firmly upheld by united victors still collapsed within a few years because its harshness was resented.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the lesson described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: dismissive of it, since the author holds that magnanimity toward a defeated enemy is imprudent whatever the circumstances.
options.B: detached from it, since the author reports the lesson and the evidence about it without reaching any judgement of their own.
options.C: sceptical of it as too simple, while granting that generosity toward the defeated, properly timed, has real value.
options.D: approving of it, since the author agrees that a generous peace reliably turns former enemies into dependable partners.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a sanctioned government can blame foreigners for shortages with some success partly because

options.A: its citizens generally trust their own rulers far more than they trust the governments of foreign powers.
options.B: the foreign governments imposing sanctions seldom explain in public why they have chosen to impose them.
options.C: the shortages really are caused in part by measures that foreign governments have chosen to impose.
options.D: the educated groups who might dispute the claim have already taken control of the country's press.

questions.question: According to the passage, each of the following can help a sanctioned regime keep or tighten its hold on power EXCEPT

options.A: its control over who receives imported medicine, fuel and spare parts once these goods have become scarce.
options.B: its ability to present shortages as the deliberate work of hostile foreign governments rather than its own doing.
options.C: the departure or impoverishment of the educated and commercially minded groups best placed to demand change.
options.D: the targeting of named officials' assets, which provokes ordinary citizens to rally in sympathy behind those officials.

questions.question: Which of the following most closely parallels the kind of measure the author criticises at the end of paragraph 4?

options.A: A lender freezes a borrower's accounts without ever saying what payment would release them, and the struggling borrower stops negotiating altogether.
options.B: A landlord raises the rent for every tenant until one noisy tenant moves out, announcing that rents will fall again as soon as that tenant has left.
options.C: A club bars one member who broke its rules from its premises but still admits that member's family, sparing them while punishing the offender.
options.D: A lender freezes a borrower's accounts and states exactly what sum must be repaid to release them, and the borrower soon pays it.

questions.question: The author's remark that targeting 'reduces the moral cost of sanctions more reliably than it increases their effect' implies that

options.A: governments have largely abandoned broad sanctions because their moral cost became too high to defend in public.
options.B: the surer benefit of targeted sanctions is that they spare ordinary people, not that they bring a dependable gain in pressure on policy.
options.C: targeted sanctions usually fail because officials cannot be identified precisely enough to be named in them.
options.D: targeted sanctions are, on the whole, less effective than broad sanctions at persuading a regime under pressure to change the policies it pursues.

questions.question: According to paragraph 3, how strongly the stability-instability paradox operates depends on

options.A: how confident each side is that a limited clash can be prevented from escalating.
options.B: whether the rival states fight through proxies or commit their own regular forces to a clash.
options.C: whether small wars were already common in the region before nuclear weapons appeared there.
options.D: how many nuclear weapons each side possesses in comparison with the arsenal of its rival.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the statement that stability at the top 'loosens the rungs near the bottom' most nearly means that

options.A: the lowest levels of military force become too expensive for states to keep up once nuclear arms exist.
options.B: the restraints that once discouraged minor acts of aggression grow weaker as fear of the largest war recedes.
options.C: minor clashes become more likely than before to climb rapidly into a general war between the two powers.
options.D: the weakest states in the system lose their capacity to resist the demands made on them by stronger states.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the reasoning set out in paragraph 2?

options.A: Two rival states fought several border wars against each other in the decades before either of them acquired nuclear weapons.
options.B: Several non-nuclear states bordering a nuclear power reduced the size of their armies in the years after it acquired its arsenal.
options.C: After two rivals acquired secure nuclear arsenals, raids across their border grew more frequent, with officials on both sides expecting the raids to stay contained.
options.D: Soon after two rival states acquired nuclear weapons, a minor border incident between them led within hours to a nuclear alert on both sides.

questions.question: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.A: Small wars in the nuclear age are caused mainly by the confidence that mutual deterrence gives to the leaders of rival nuclear-armed states.
options.B: The author regards nuclear deterrence as a failure, since it has not succeeded in removing organised violence between rival states.
options.C: The paradox shows that the largest powers have in fact become more willing to fight each other directly once both are armed.
options.D: Where leaders doubt that clashes can be contained, deterrence is likely to weaken restraint on low-level aggression less than where they are confident of control.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: The laws of war should be revised so that soldiers who fight for an aggressor can be prosecuted for the killing of those who defend against them.
options.B: The critics of the laws of war are mistaken, since a soldier acting on lawful orders cannot fairly be compared with a robber acting on his own.
options.C: Because nearly every belligerent believes its cause just, the morality of a war cannot be judged, and its soldiers bear no moral responsibility for it.
options.D: Although soldiers fighting for an aggressor may lack a real moral right to kill, the laws of war are wise to treat combatants on both sides alike.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a soldier who knowingly fights in a plainly aggressive war, while observing every rule of conduct, as

options.A: free of legal blame under the convention, but not for that reason morally innocent of the killing that he does.
options.B: morally blameless for as long as he obeyed his orders, since orders transfer responsibility to the government that issued them.
options.C: guilty of a crime under the laws of war, since those laws ought in principle to follow the justice of the cause.
options.D: free of both legal and moral blame, since the convention exists precisely to relieve soldiers of judging the cause they serve.

questions.question: The example of the robber and the guard in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: suggest that soldiers who kill on the orders of their government are more to blame than criminals who act alone.
options.B: demonstrate that the laws of war were originally modelled on the ordinary domestic law governing self-defence.
options.C: show, through an everyday case outside war, that an unjust attacker gains no right to kill those who resist him.
options.D: illustrate the author's own view that soldiers of an aggressor commit crimes under the laws of war when they kill defenders.

questions.question: The author's argument in paragraph 3 for treating combatants alike depends most on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Most wars are fought between sides whose causes are, on a fair reckoning, roughly equal in their justice.
options.B: No authority exists whose ruling on which side has the just cause would be accepted by the belligerents while the fighting continues.
options.C: The moral truth about killing in war is too uncertain for anyone, philosophers included, to determine.
options.D: Soldiers who believe their own cause to be just fight with greater restraint than soldiers who privately doubt the justice of their war.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, under a balance of power, a state is most likely to join a coalition against another state when

options.A: the international organisation to which it belongs has formally condemned the other state.
options.B: the other state is a close trading partner whose goodwill it needs in some other region.
options.C: the other state's growing strength threatens to let it dominate the states around it.
options.D: the other state has attacked a small neighbour without any justification that others accept.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward collective security is best described as

options.A: indifferent, since the author treats the choice between it and the balance of power as of little practical consequence.
options.B: respectful of the legitimacy its principle can confer, but doubtful that states will bear the costs it asks of them.
options.C: contemptuous, since the author regards its principle as a cynical cover for the interests of the great powers.
options.D: enthusiastic, since the author holds that its impartiality makes it superior to the balance of power in every respect.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how the passage is organised?

options.A: A historical failure is described, its cause is traced to a single mistaken leader, and a remedy is proposed for future reformers.
options.B: Two principles are compared, the first is shown to be morally superior, and the second is recommended as the more practical guide.
options.C: One principle is defended against its critics, its failures in practice are explained away, and it is recommended without reservation.
options.D: Two principles are introduced, the weakness of each is examined in turn, and the author argues that orders which last combine them.

questions.question: Which of the following situations would the author most likely regard as an instance of the combination described in paragraph 4?

options.A: States already uneasy at a neighbour's military growth unite against it once it seizes a border province, citing a shared rule against conquest to win wider support.
options.B: Two great powers agree to divide a weak buffer state between them so that neither gains an advantage, and the arrangement keeps the peace between them for a generation.
options.C: A group of states pledges to defend any member that is attacked and honours the pledge even against a small aggressor that could never threaten any of them.
options.D: A worldwide body votes by a large majority to condemn the invasion of a remote island and calls on its members to resist, but no member sends any forces.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: arguing that recasting sovereignty as a responsibility shifts, rather than settles, the question of who decides on intervention, leaving a choice between risks.
options.B: defending the traditional doctrine of non-interference against those who would permit outside powers to intervene to stop atrocities.
options.C: proposing that no use of force across a border be permitted until a broad body of states has authorised it under common rules.
options.D: showing that interventions to stop mass killing have generally been pretexts used by powerful states to pursue their strategic interests.

questions.question: According to the passage, the traditional rule of non-interference was justified on the ground that

options.A: governments could on the whole be trusted to treat their own populations decently without supervision from outside.
options.B: it protected small states from being dominated by an international organisation acting in the name of all members.
options.C: it made every state responsible for protecting its own people, so that no outside protection was needed.
options.D: allowing any state to enter another whenever it disliked how it was governed would lead to constant intervention by the strong.

questions.question: The author's remark that the old doctrine gave 'a clear answer to the question of who may enter: nobody' suggests that the author

options.A: believes that powerful states in fact obeyed the old doctrine without exception for as long as it prevailed.
options.B: sees value in the old doctrine's refusal of discretion as a safeguard, even while rejecting the answer it gave.
options.C: considers the old doctrine preferable, on balance, to the new formula and would like to see it restored in full.
options.D: regards clarity as the most important quality that any rule governing intervention could possibly possess.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT

options.A: A requirement of proper authorisation can itself contribute to inaction while a population is being killed.
options.B: The places where interventions have occurred are roughly what one would expect of a rule leaving the decision to interested parties.
options.C: The responsibility formula is valuable chiefly because it ends the conflict between sovereignty and the demand to stop atrocities.
options.D: Whether an intervention is legitimate depends partly on how the decision was reached and not only on what was happening.

questions.question: In the final sentence, 'a change of vocabulary' refers to

options.A: the insistence that an intervention be called legitimate only when a broad body of states has approved it.
options.B: the habit of replacing the word 'intervention' with milder terms that conceal the use of armed force.
options.C: the shift from describing sovereignty as a wall to describing it as a shield behind which murderers can hide.
options.D: the redescription of sovereignty as a responsibility that a state can forfeit rather than a right it holds unconditionally.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a state fearing entrapment would be most worried that

options.A: its adversary might decide that the alliance's commitment is hollow and choose to test it.
options.B: its partner might fail to come to its aid if the state itself were attacked by a third power.
options.C: its partner, sure of being supported, might start a dispute that the state would then be obliged to join.
options.D: its partner might begin looking for other friends and arming itself in ways that alarm its neighbours.

questions.question: The example of the island partner in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate how a protecting power can leave a guarantee deliberately unclear in order to restrain both its partner and its adversary.
options.B: show that great powers often fail to think through how far their guarantees extend until a crisis forces the question.
options.C: demonstrate that ambiguous guarantees usually lead adversaries to test them, sometimes with disastrous results.
options.D: provide evidence from a particular historical case that a policy of ambiguity has in fact preserved the peace.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the dilemma described in paragraph 2?

options.A: An employer who keeps the terms of a bonus vague so that staff keep working hard without counting on any fixed reward.
options.B: A parent's promise to pay all of a grown child's debts reassures but invites borrowing; withholding it curbs borrowing but leaves the child feeling deserted.
options.C: A shopkeeper who offers a generous guarantee on every item she stocks sells more goods but must then pay to repair the ones that break.
options.D: A teacher who sets a very difficult examination finds that the strongest students in the class rise to it while the weakest ones simply give up.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, deliberate ambiguity in an alliance commitment is most likely to succeed when

options.A: the commitment is made steadily firmer and more public in the years after the alliance is formed.
options.B: the partner is confident that its patron will support it whatever conduct it chooses to adopt.
options.C: the protecting power judges accurately how both its partner and its adversary will read the uncertainty.
options.D: the adversary concludes from the vague wording that the commitment is unlikely ever to be honoured.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim in paragraph 3 that ambiguity gives the partner 'reason to be careful'?

options.A: Ambiguous guarantees are frequently attacked in the protecting power's own press as a sign of weakness or indecision.
options.B: Partners with vague guarantees generally act as boldly as those with firm ones, assuming that their patrons could never let them fall.
options.C: Protecting powers that gave firm guarantees often found that their partners began taking greater risks than before.
options.D: Adversaries facing vague guarantees have on several occasions decided to test them, only to find that the guarantees were honoured in full.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that the great fairs were never important as markets for goods, since most of their business was carried on in promises to pay rather than in coin.
options.B: describe the kinds of commercial news, such as distant prices and harvest failures, that merchants exchanged when they met each year.
options.C: explain how permanent shops in growing towns gradually took away the retail trade on which the great periodic fairs had always depended.
options.D: argue that the great fairs mattered chiefly as fixed meetings for settling credit and sharing news, functions that the view of them as large markets overlooks.

questions.question: According to the passage, relatively little coin had to change hands when merchants settled their accounts at a fair because

options.A: what one merchant owed another could be cancelled against debts owed among other merchants present.
options.B: most merchants preferred to pay one another in goods such as cloth and livestock rather than in money.
options.C: banks that kept accounts all year round had already settled most debts before the fair opened.
options.D: the merchants who attended were generally too poor to carry significant quantities of coin with them.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the statement that a fair 'was a calendar as much as a place' most nearly means that

options.A: the fair was held in a different town each year, so that merchants had to follow a calendar to find it.
options.B: the fair was important chiefly as a holiday that broke the routine of the working year for ordinary townspeople.
options.C: much of its value lay in fixing recurring dates by which debts fell due and to which traders were expected to return.
options.D: merchants used the fair mainly to learn the dates of harvests and religious festivals in distant regions.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation of why the great fairs declined?

options.A: Merchants in several regions kept settling their year's accounts at the fairs for decades after banks and regular posts were established there.
options.B: In several regions permanent shops had taken over most of the retail trade in cloth before the fairs themselves began to decline.
options.C: In several regions merchants who attended the fairs were sometimes ruined by false rumours about the solvency of trading houses.
options.D: In several regions the great fairs continued for centuries as the main places where farmers bought and sold livestock.

questions.question: According to the passage, in records of pre-industrial working households the word 'family' often referred to

options.A: the head of the household together with the wider community to which he was answerable.
options.B: the parents and children of a household, as distinct from the servants who worked for them.
options.C: the wider kin group of a village, including relatives who lived in separate dwellings nearby.
options.D: the whole group living and working under the household head, servants and apprentices included.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 3 in the passage?

options.A: It argues that the working household was a better arrangement than the modern family, since its hierarchy gave everyone a definite place.
options.B: It heads off a nostalgic reading of the argument by noting the working household's harshness and limited reach, while keeping the claim that it differed in kind.
options.C: It introduces the shift of production into mills and offices that the final paragraph goes on to treat as a decline of the family.
options.D: It abandons the earlier claim that home and work were once combined, conceding that most people in fact worked for wages outside the home.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a feature of the pre-industrial working household EXCEPT that

options.A: people who were not related by blood lived and ate under the same roof and authority.
options.B: the place of production, such as a loom or a dairy, stood within the dwelling itself.
options.C: its members understood it chiefly as a private refuge governed by affection rather than by discipline.
options.D: its head was held answerable to the community for the conduct of those in his charge.

questions.question: The author would most likely respond to the claim that families today care less for one another than families did three centuries ago by saying that the claim

options.A: mistakes a narrowing of the tasks households perform for a weakening of the affection within them.
options.B: is broadly correct, because the household lost its economic role when production moved into mills and offices.
options.C: is mistaken, because affection within families has grown steadily stronger since the household lost its working role.
options.D: is supported by the harsh discipline of the old working household, which made affection a secondary concern.

questions.question: According to the passage, before the railways, differences between the local times of neighbouring towns went largely unnoticed because

options.A: most towns took their time from the same distant observatory, so that their clocks seldom disagreed by much.
options.B: travel between towns was too slow for a discrepancy of a few minutes to have any practical effect.
options.C: church authorities in each town insisted that the local hour be kept and discouraged comparison with other places.
options.D: few people owned clocks, so the hour of noon was a matter of rough guesswork in every town alike.

questions.question: The comparison with 'agreeing on a common gauge for the rails' in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: illustrate the author's own view that the change to standard time was, at bottom, a technical matter with technical consequences.
options.B: show that the railway companies regarded standard time and a common gauge as equally urgent problems requiring government action.
options.C: suggest that standard time, like a common rail gauge, was imposed on towns by distant astronomers who never consulted local opinion.
options.D: characterise the standard account as treating the new time as a neutral technical fix, a view the author goes on to call incomplete.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the townspeople who resisted railway time is best described as

options.A: sympathetic reappraisal: they are credited with a real insight, though their preference for local time is not endorsed.
options.B: detached neutrality: their objections are recorded without any judgement about whether they understood the change.
options.C: wholehearted endorsement: they are presented as having been right that standard time did more harm than good.
options.D: affectionate condescension: their resistance is presented as a charming but finally foolish attachment to old habits.

questions.question: Which of the following situations most closely parallels the change that paragraph 2 describes?

options.A: A town that has kept its own weights for centuries decides to keep them alongside the new national weights, using each for different purposes.
options.B: A group of market towns, confused by each using its own weights, agrees on a common weight so that traders moving between them stop being cheated.
options.C: A village replaces its old sundial with a more accurate mechanical clock that is still set each day by observing the sun overhead.
options.D: A village whose fields were measured in paces that anyone could walk out adopts a unit defined by a distant bureau and checked only against that bureau's instruments.

questions.question: According to the passage, one reason why voicing a text was a useful aid to early readers was that

options.A: silent reading was regarded as discourteous in households and monasteries where others were present.
options.B: texts were often written with no spaces separating one word from the next.
options.C: most readers had learned their letters by reciting them aloud to a teacher in a group.
options.D: books were so expensive that a single copy had to be shared among many listeners at once.

questions.question: The point made in paragraph 2 about the ancient writer's surprise implies that

options.A: silent reading must have been the usual practice among learned readers of the time, despite the writer's reaction.
options.B: the anecdote is unreliable as evidence, since the writer probably exaggerated his surprise for effect.
options.C: an observer's astonishment at a practice reveals what was customary around him, not what people could do.
options.D: the man the writer observed had invented a technique of reading that others later learned from him.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Reading aloud survived well into the age of print, which shows that the move to private reading never really took place at all.
options.B: Silent reading was not a late invention; what changed was the setting of reading, from shared to private, and that shift still mattered for how readers held their thoughts.
options.C: Silent reading was a late discovery that transformed the inner life of the West, as an ancient anecdote of surprise clearly shows.
options.D: Because silent reading was always possible, the history of reading has no real bearing on how people came to think of the self.

questions.question: The last two sentences of the passage suggest that the author believes private reading

options.A: produced a private self whose influence on later habits of thought cannot now be traced or assessed.
options.B: had no real effect on how people thought of themselves, whatever historians have claimed.
options.C: was the decisive development that brought the modern sense of a private self into being.
options.D: contributed to people's sense of owning their thoughts without being the sole or sufficient cause of it.

questions.question: The passage suggests that in older towns a smell was most likely to provoke sustained complaint when it

options.A: was linked in residents' minds with a particular trade or with neighbours they disliked.
options.B: was believed by physicians to carry disease, since every bad smell was then treated as a medical danger.
options.C: was stronger than the ordinary smells of household refuse and animal dung that residents lived beside.
options.D: came from the drains and sewers that reformers had recently built to carry waste away from the streets.

questions.question: The sentence 'The theory was wrong, but it was productive' (paragraph 3) functions in the argument to

options.A: concede that the reformers' achievements were largely illusory, since they acted on a mistaken account of illness.
options.B: argue that reformers understood the true causes of disease but used the language of smell to persuade the public.
options.C: introduce the point that a false belief about disease nonetheless drove reforms that really did improve health.
options.D: suggest that the germ theory which replaced the older view was itself productive only because it was wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the claim that 'What made a smell intolerable depended less on its strength than on what it was thought to mean'?

options.A: Records from one town show residents raising no objection to a strong stench from their own stables while petitioning against a fainter smell from a newly arrived dyeworks.
options.B: Records from one town show that complaints about smell rose sharply in summer, when heat made every source of odour noticeably stronger.
options.C: Records from one town show that covered sewers built by reformers sharply reduced both the smell of its streets and its rate of disease.
options.D: Records from one town show that its residents complained about smell far more often than the residents of a neighbouring town did.

questions.question: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred about the social meanings of smell, as the passage presents them?

options.A: They faded as cities grew cleaner, because fewer residual smells remained to be attached to particular groups of people.
options.B: They did not begin with the germ theory, but they grew more prominent once smell no longer carried medical weight.
options.C: They were an invention of the period after the germ theory, having had no counterpart in the complaints of older towns.
options.D: They were a lingering form of the foul-air theory, and they disappeared once the germ theory had fully replaced it.

questions.question: According to the passage, one reason why goods from the far end of the chain were so costly was that

options.A: the producers who wove the silk demanded very high prices from the first merchants who bought it.
options.B: bandits and wars so often closed the route that most caravans were lost before arriving.
options.C: a margin was added each time the goods changed hands on their way along the chain.
options.D: the merchants who carried them had to make the entire long and dangerous journey in person.

questions.question: The passage implies that buyers at one end of the chain held fanciful beliefs about the origins of their luxuries mainly because

options.A: the goods passed so quickly from one end of Asia to the other that no information could keep pace with them.
options.B: traders deliberately invented stories about distant origins so that they could charge higher prices for their goods.
options.C: the long-distance travellers who did reach the source left accounts that were exaggerated and widely misread.
options.D: no trader they dealt with had travelled beyond his own stretch of the route to see where the goods began.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a consequence of the relay structure of the trade EXCEPT

options.A: the wealth of cities at the junctions where neighbouring trading circuits met one another.
options.B: the lasting fame of a few pilgrims and envoys whose journeys spanned the entire distance.
options.C: the poor transmission of knowledge about the sources of goods from one end to the other.
options.D: the ability of goods to find alternative routes when war or banditry closed one segment.

questions.question: The contrast between seeing 'a road' and seeing 'a web' at the end of the passage serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that both pictures of the trade are equally valid, each being the natural result of the kind of sources a historian happens to prefer.
options.B: dismiss the written accounts of pilgrims and envoys as unreliable, since their authors misunderstood the routes they themselves had travelled.
options.C: argue that the exceptional travellers mattered more than ordinary traders to the trade, because only they ever saw the whole route from end to end.
options.D: trace the misleading picture of the trade to a reliance on memorable exceptional journeys, and to affirm that routine exchange explains how it worked.

questions.question: Which of the following does the passage mention as a way in which some cities reduced the burden that quarantine placed on households?

options.A: Feeding shut-up households at public expense and compensating them for goods that had been destroyed.
options.B: Allowing households that reported a case promptly to leave the city before the doors were sealed.
options.C: Excusing households that reported a case from having their bedding and clothing burned.
options.D: Rewarding neighbours who informed on a household that had concealed a death from the inspectors.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Modern health authorities should provide generous relief to quarantined households, since history shows that coercion fails to contain disease.
options.B: Harsh punishment of concealment drove plague underground, and this is why the measures taken by early modern cities usually failed.
options.C: Plague measures relied on people reporting illness, so their success depended on how far authorities reduced what reporting cost.
options.D: Plague measures in early modern cities were essentially coercive, and their apparent humanity has been exaggerated by historians of public health.

questions.question: In the final sentence, the phrase 'make knowing bearable' most nearly refers to

options.A: limiting what authorities try to find out about households, so that people are not burdened by intrusive questioning.
options.B: lowering the price that people who reveal illness must pay, so that the information the authority needs reaches it.
options.C: helping officials to cope with the distress of learning how widely an epidemic had already spread through the city.
options.D: teaching the public enough about how disease spreads that the facts of an epidemic no longer seem frightening to them.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the argument of paragraph 4?

options.A: Where penalties for concealment were sharply raised, early reports of cases increased, and no later rise in hidden deaths came to light.
options.B: Cities that imposed severe penalties for concealment usually provided relief to shut-up households at the same time.
options.C: Guards posted outside shut-up households were frequently bribed to let members of the household leave at night.
options.D: Cities that punished concealment most severely also recorded some of the highest plague mortality of any cities in their region during the same period.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the evidence about relief discussed in paragraph 3 as

options.A: conclusive proof that public relief lowered plague mortality in the cities that were able to afford it.
options.B: too unreliable to support any conclusion at all, since it comes mainly from the complaints of officials.
options.C: suggestive about relief's effect on whether families concealed illness, but insufficient to show its effect on the death toll.
options.D: evidence that relief was generous enough to remove the costs of reporting for most of the households affected.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 4 in the passage?

options.A: It returns to the history of liberation described in paragraph 1, which the author now accepts, after all, as the correct and complete account.
options.B: It offers evidence that the crowds who broke lamps in paragraph 3 were acting against the interests of most townspeople.
options.C: It withdraws the claim of paragraph 3 that street lighting extended policing, conceding that safety was the sponsors' only real aim.
options.D: It keeps the critique of paragraph 3 from becoming a new one-sided story, showing that lighting also widened access to the night.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, the phrase 'a separate jurisdiction' most nearly means

options.A: a legal code written specifically for offences committed after dark, with harsher penalties than by day.
options.B: a zone of complete freedom in which no rules of any kind applied to those who were out after dark.
options.C: a period in which daytime authority held only loosely and different customs and people governed the street.
options.D: a district of the town placed under the control of the night watch rather than of the ordinary magistrates.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how the author interprets the crowds who broke street lamps?

options.A: As probably sensing, even if they could not say so, that the lamps carried an authority they had grounds to oppose.
options.B: As vandals whose actions have been wrongly dignified by historians eager to find political resistance.
options.C: As giving clear proof that most townspeople opposed street lighting from the moment it was installed.
options.D: As defending the freedom that thieves and other night dwellers had enjoyed before the lamps were put up.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to what the author says, in paragraph 5, that lighting did to the night?

options.A: A town holds a festival one night a year at which ordinary rules are suspended and people may behave as they never would by day.
options.B: A public library extends its opening hours into the evening so that its regular readers can stay and read for longer after work.
options.C: A council installs cameras in an empty square that nobody had used at night, so that the area can be monitored by the police.
options.D: A beach once used at dawn only by fishermen, under their own customs, becomes a public promenade with council rules, drawing families but ending the fishermen's ways.

questions.question: The final sentence of the passage implies that the usual histories of light have gone wrong chiefly because they

options.A: neglect to measure how far lighting actually lengthened the hours that people spent working, travelling and shopping.
options.B: see the street through one kind of user's eyes, missing that a single change brought gain to some and loss to others.
options.C: count lighting as a gain when, properly understood, its effects on everyday life were very largely a loss for townspeople.
options.D: depend on the testimony of the officials who installed the lamps, and so repeat those officials' claims about safety without ever questioning them.

questions.question: According to the passage, the decoy effect is weakest when

options.A: the menu contains more than three options, so that no single comparison stands out.
options.B: buyers already know from experience what they want, or when the decoy is obviously inferior.
options.C: the products on the menu are expensive, so that customers take more care over every comparison they make.
options.D: the product on sale is cheap and bought on impulse, like the popcorn sold in a cinema.

questions.question: The 'regular who knows exactly how much popcorn she can eat' (paragraph 3) is mentioned in order to

options.A: show that a buyer whose preference is already settled gives the decoy little to work on.
options.B: prove that the standard economic account of choice is correct for most customers after all.
options.C: suggest that frequent cinema-goers resent being steered and therefore buy the smallest size available.
options.D: illustrate the claim that people lean on the easy comparison and let it settle the hard one.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, on the standard account described in paragraph 2, adding the medium tub to the menu should

options.A: reduce total sales, since customers faced with more options take longer and buy less.
options.B: raise sales of the medium tub among customers who could not decide between the other two sizes.
options.C: make the large tub look like a bargain to customers who had previously preferred the small one.
options.D: leave unchanged the proportion of customers who prefer the large tub to the small one.

questions.question: The passage is mainly concerned with

options.A: showing that ordinary customers are easily fooled by marketers and should distrust every menu they see.
options.B: explaining how cinemas and software firms can raise their revenue by adding options that nobody buys.
options.C: using the decoy effect to argue that how options are arranged helps shape what people choose.
options.D: defending the standard economic account of choice against evidence drawn from experiments on pricing.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the statement that the winning firm 'has been selected for its error' means that the firm

options.A: will be excluded from future auctions once the seller discovers that it has overpaid.
options.B: was chosen by the seller because its survey team had a reputation for careless work.
options.C: made a deliberate error in bidding above its own estimate in order to defeat its rivals.
options.D: won the tract mainly because its survey happened to overstate what the tract was worth.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's account of why the winner's curse is learned away only slowly?

options.A: Experienced bidders in many auction markets are observed to bid somewhat below their own estimates.
options.B: In most such auctions the losing bidders are told, soon afterwards, how much the tract actually yielded.
options.C: Firms that repeatedly overpay for tracts eventually run short of money and stop taking part in auctions.
options.D: The yield of a single tract often differs from its expected value because of geological chance.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of the final paragraph in relation to the rest of the passage?

options.A: It draws on the earlier analysis to locate a remedy in the auction's information structure, without ranking formats outright.
options.B: It abandons the claim of paragraph 2 that bidders should shade, in favour of the claim that only design matters.
options.C: It shows that sealed-bid auctions should be replaced by open bidding wherever the value of a prize is uncertain.
options.D: It introduces a second cause of the curse, the signalling between rivals, which the earlier paragraphs overlooked.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that the winner's curse, as the author describes it, would be LEAST likely to arise when

options.A: bids are submitted in sealed envelopes and opened only at the end.
options.B: each bidder's survey is honest and, taken on its own terms, unbiased.
options.C: every bidder relies on one shared survey instead of commissioning its own.
options.D: a very large number of firms compete for the same tract of seabed.

questions.question: According to the passage, for goods whose qualities can be inspected before purchase, advertising

options.A: is more likely than other advertising to manipulate buyers by associating products with glamour.
options.B: informs buyers directly, so that no signalling explanation of it is required.
options.C: works mainly as a signal that the maker is wagering on a long stream of repeat purchases from satisfied customers.
options.D: is largely wasted, since buyers can examine the goods for themselves before paying for them.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a firm that knows its cheap, frequently bought product is mediocre

options.A: would always advertise exactly as heavily as a firm with a good product, so that the expense revealed nothing.
options.B: could not afford to advertise at all, since it expects most of those who try its product never to return.
options.C: would gain less from a lavish campaign than a rival whose product is good.
options.D: would do better to sell its product as something that customers buy only once in a lifetime.

questions.question: The signalling argument, as limited in paragraph 3, would most clearly explain which of the following?

options.A: An expensive, almost wordless campaign launching a new toothpaste, a cheap item that households buy every few weeks.
options.B: A costly campaign by a firm that installs home swimming pools, something most households buy at most once.
options.C: A furniture maker's printed catalogue that lists the dimensions and the price of every table in its range.
options.D: A railway company's advertisement announcing the fares and the timetable for a newly opened route.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as a limit on, or qualification of, the signalling account EXCEPT:

options.A: it does not settle whether advertising also manipulates the people who see it.
options.B: it applies most clearly to goods judged only after use and bought repeatedly.
options.C: a firm's heavy spending may reflect vanity or miscalculation rather than confidence.
options.D: ordinary consumers do not consciously reason about the economics of repeat purchase.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a nudge that stops working as soon as its purpose is explained as

options.A: evidence, though not proof, that it depended on people not understanding what they were doing.
options.B: no different in principle from one that survives, since every presentation of options influences choice.
options.C: conclusive proof that the institution using it has acted manipulatively and must abandon it.
options.D: a sign that disclosure is itself distracting and so should not be expected of institutions.

questions.question: The author's claim that the argument from inevitability 'answers a weaker objection than the one that matters' assumes that

options.A: the critics who deny that any arrangement of options is inevitable are more numerous than the careful critics.
options.B: most of the nudges now used by public bodies would fail if their purposes were explained.
options.C: an influence's being unavoidable does not show that every way of exercising it is equally acceptable.
options.D: people who are paying attention are almost never affected by the way in which their options are presented.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the defenders of nudging is best described as

options.A: suspicious: they are suggested to be hiding their real motives from the people whose choices they steer.
options.B: deferential: their reply to critics is taken to have answered the charge that nudging is manipulative.
options.C: dismissive: their reply to critics is treated as confused and as missing the obvious unavailability of any neutral menu.
options.D: partly sympathetic: their central argument is accepted, but not as settling the issue that matters most.

questions.question: Which of the following practices would most clearly pass the test proposed in paragraph 3?

options.A: A government form redesigned so that the most common answer appears first, its designers never having asked what would happen if the reason were stated.
options.B: A clinic's texted appointment reminders that keep cutting missed visits after patients are told they are sent for that reason.
options.C: A bank's default savings option, explained in the fine print of a long contract, whose take-up is unchanged though almost no customers read that section.
options.D: A website's pre-ticked box for marketing emails, whose sign-ups fall sharply once a notice explains that the box was ticked to raise them.

questions.question: According to the passage, competition does little to hold down the price that users pay for free services because

options.A: the firms that provide such services face no rivals offering a similar product to the same users.
options.B: users generally prefer the services that absorb the largest share of their day.
options.C: users cannot readily tell how much of their time a service takes, or whether a rival would take less.
options.D: advertisers rather than users decide how much attention each service collects.

questions.question: When the passage says that 'the user is less a customer than a supplier of the commodity being traded' (paragraph 2), it means that the user

options.A: provides the attention that the service gathers and sells on to its advertisers.
options.B: is paid by the service, in the form of free features, for recommending its advertisers' products.
options.C: matters more to advertisers than to the firm that actually provides the service.
options.D: writes the articles, messages and videos that the service later sells to other users.

questions.question: The author would most likely describe a free application designed to absorb as much of its users' time as possible as

options.A: a reason for governments to prohibit services that are offered to their users at no charge.
options.B: a predictable response to a market in which the price paid in attention cannot be seen.
options.C: likely to lose many of its users to rival applications that take up less of their time each day.
options.D: evidence that people who use such free services are dupes who fail to understand the bargain they have struck with the provider.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the case for the remedy proposed in the final paragraph?

options.A: Advertisers pay providers more for the attention of users who spend long hours on a single service.
options.B: Most users say in surveys that they enjoy free services and would not want to pay money to use them.
options.C: Users shown regular reports of their screen time usually stop reading them within a few weeks.
options.D: Users given weekly reports of their time on each application shifted towards those that served the same purpose in less time.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that unravelling harms employers chiefly because

options.A: candidates who receive early offers usually refuse them in the hope that better ones will follow.
options.B: it obliges candidates to conceal their real preferences and to rank a likely employer first.
options.C: competition for the strongest candidates pushes up the salaries that employers have to offer.
options.D: very early offers must be made on scant evidence of how able the candidates are.

questions.question: The final sentence of paragraph 3 ('Such clearinghouses show ... freedom alone creates') serves to

options.A: generalise from the remedy to a claim about what markets can be, against the view that they only arise of their own accord.
options.B: summarise the three failures of matching markets described in the preceding paragraph and explain which one is most serious.
options.C: concede that clearinghouses restrict the freedom of applicants and employers and so carry a cost the designer must weigh.
options.D: establish that markets in which people trade freely will fail unless a clearinghouse is constructed for them.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as a limit on what clearinghouses can achieve EXCEPT that

options.A: no procedure gives both sides full reason for honesty while always producing stable outcomes.
options.B: the choice of procedure involves judging whose interests most deserve to be protected.
options.C: they cannot produce assignments in which no unmatched applicant and employer would both prefer each other.
options.D: they depend on enough applicants and employers choosing to take part in them.

questions.question: Which of the following is the clearest instance of the strategic misrepresentation described in paragraph 2?

options.A: A law firm, keen to secure the strongest graduates, makes its offers in their first year of study rather than their last.
options.B: In a ranked-list scheme for course places, a student puts a less popular course first, fearing that naming her favourite would lose her the safer place.
options.C: A graduate accepts the only offer she holds because it must be answered within hours, and later learns of a better one.
options.D: A prestigious hospital declines to join the clearinghouse and fills its posts by recruiting the doctors it wants privately.

questions.question: According to the passage, the theory that located value in the costs of production had difficulty explaining

options.A: why a good as essential to life as water should nevertheless be so cheap in most places.
options.B: goods whose prices bear little relation to the effort that went into obtaining or making them.
options.C: why the same bucket of water is worth far more to a traveller in a desert than in a town.
options.D: why resources such as clean air are treated as having no value until they become scarce.

questions.question: The statement that the marginal account 'moved value from things to situations' (paragraph 3) means that it

options.A: shifted attention from the labour needed to produce a good to the situations in which that labour is performed.
options.B: showed that the value of a good depends mainly on the place where it happens to be produced and sold.
options.C: replaced the study of individual goods with the study of whole markets, in which many buyers and sellers meet together.
options.D: made value depend on a person's circumstances, such as how much of a good she already has, not on fixed qualities of the good.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about a resource that is cheap today because it is plentiful?

options.A: It will remain cheap because the price of a resource reflects the labour needed to collect it.
options.B: It should be withdrawn from markets so that prices cannot mislead the public about its importance.
options.C: Its present price may be a poor guide to what it would be worth if it were to become scarce.
options.D: Its low price shows that the resource contributes little to the welfare of the society that uses it.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the marginal account of value is best described as

options.A: appreciative of how it resolved the puzzle, while insisting on the limits of what it can tell us.
options.B: regretful, since it is blamed for encouraging the public habit of treating cheap resources as worthless.
options.C: uncritical, since it is taken to show that market prices are a reliable ranking of what matters to a society.
options.D: sceptical, since it is presented as no real advance on the cost theory that it replaced in the later nineteenth century.

questions.question: In the light of the passage as a whole, the eighteenth-century conclusion that exchange value 'must therefore have some source other than usefulness' is best regarded as

options.A: correct, because the later theory confirmed that the labour needed to produce a good is what fixes its price in exchange.
options.B: mistaken, because price does reflect usefulness, but that of one more unit rather than of the good as a whole.
options.C: mistaken, because water turns out to be worth more in exchange than diamonds once its total supply is taken into account.
options.D: correct, because the later theory showed that price reflects scarcity, which is quite separate from how useful a good is.

questions.question: According to the standard interpretation described in paragraph 2, owners ask more for the mug than non-owners will pay because

options.A: owners come to regard the mug as stock to be sold, and so set a price as a dealer would.
options.B: the owners, though chosen at random, turn out to care more for mugs than the non-owners do.
options.C: parting with the mug counts as a loss, which weighs more than the equal gain of acquiring it.
options.D: owners suspect that the experimenter knows the true value of the mug and fear underpricing it.

questions.question: The reference to investors who are reluctant 'to sell shares that have fallen in value' (paragraph 2) serves to

options.A: show that the endowment effect is found mainly among people who invest in shares rather than in ordinary goods.
options.B: suggest that professional traders, who deal routinely in what they hold, are as prone to the effect as anyone else.
options.C: support the rival interpretation that the gap in prices is an artefact of how experiments are conducted.
options.D: illustrate how far beyond the laboratory the loss-aversion account appears to reach.

questions.question: The author's reading in paragraph 4 implies that a person who bought a mug at a market stall intending to resell it the next day would most likely

options.A: show a smaller gap between the prices at which she would sell and buy such a mug than a person given one to use.
options.B: value it as highly as someone who had been given the mug to use and had kept it for some time.
