options.C: ask far more for it than a buyer would pay, since owning the mug would make it seem more valuable to her.
options.D: show a larger gap than participants in the mug experiments, because she paid money for her mug instead of receiving it free.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the rival interpretation presented in paragraph 3?

options.A: Investors who hold shares that have fallen in value turn out to sell them as readily as shares that have risen in value.
options.B: Participants who are given mugs report liking them somewhat more after they have been given them than before.
options.C: Many first-time participants say afterwards that they found the instructions for stating a selling price hard to follow.
options.D: The gap stays as large as ever among participants who have practised the procedure and know that misstating their values cannot help them.

questions.question: On the author's reading in paragraphs 4 and 5, which of the following would be expected to show the LARGEST gap between the price asked to sell an item and the price offered to buy an identical one?

options.A: A student who bought a bicycle on a resale platform last week, planning to sell it on again for a profit.
options.B: A family asked to sell a bicycle given to them an hour ago, still unpacked, which they have not yet decided whether to keep.
options.C: A family asked to sell a bicycle given to them months ago, which their child has ridden every day since.
options.D: A bicycle shop owner asked to sell one of the identical bicycles displayed in the showroom.

questions.question: The author's main purpose in the passage is to

options.A: establish that poverty and inequality are, in practice, the same thing, so that measuring one measures the other.
options.B: defend relative poverty lines against the charge that they only measure inequality, while showing why they need an absolute companion.
options.C: argue that absolute poverty lines mislead governments because they ignore what it costs to take part in the ordinary life of a society.
options.D: show that relative poverty lines are superior to absolute ones and should replace them in official statistics.

questions.question: According to the passage, what can happen to a relative poverty count when median income falls in a recession?

options.A: A household whose income is unchanged may stop being counted as poor though it is no better off.
options.B: The count rises sharply, because the poorest households are the first to lose their jobs in a slump.
options.C: The count can no longer be calculated reliably, because the median becomes unstable during a recession.
options.D: The line stays fixed at an earlier standard, so the count simply follows changes in real purchasing power.

questions.question: The examples in paragraph 2 of school clothes, a returned dinner invitation and a telephone suggest that the author regards poverty as

options.A: essentially a shortage of the food and shelter that a person needs in order to stay alive and healthy.
options.B: a condition that disappears once a country passes a fixed level of national income per head.
options.C: a matter of spending choices that poor families could make differently if they planned more carefully.
options.D: an inability to take part in the ordinary life of one's society, judged by that society's own standards.

questions.question: Which one of the following best captures the meaning of 'moving threshold of participation' as used in paragraph 2?

options.A: A poverty line that governments revise downward whenever median income falls during a recession or a slump.
options.B: The income at which households begin to vote, join associations and take part in the civic life of their community.
options.C: The level of resources needed to live as others in one's society do, a level that rises as the society grows richer.
options.D: The share of a society's members who can afford goods, such as refrigerators, that were once luxuries.

questions.question: The references to pensioners and tax refunds in paragraph 1 serve mainly to

options.A: show that the fear of misuse is applied selectively to the poor rather than to everyone who receives public money.
options.B: demonstrate that almost all public spending is already unconditional, so that conditions are rare in practice.
options.C: argue that cash transfers to the poor should be paid through the same offices that administer pensions.
options.D: suggest that pensions and tax refunds are themselves frequently wasted, so that the poor are no worse than others.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author considers transfers in kind inferior to cash chiefly because they

options.A: are designed by officials who are, as a rule, indifferent to what poor households actually need.
options.B: apply one assumption about need to households whose most pressing needs differ from one another.
options.C: cost more to deliver than cash in remote places, where transport and storage of goods are expensive.
options.D: are usually resold by recipients at a loss, so that much of their value disappears before it is used.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the general presumption that poor people will misuse cash is best described as

options.A: contemptuous, dismissing anyone who holds the presumption as acting in bad faith towards the poor.
options.B: neutral, presenting it as one reasonable position among several without taking a side on the question.
options.C: sceptical, treating it as a suspicion that the evidence has largely failed to bear out.
options.D: approving, since the presumption protects public money from being wasted on drink and gambling.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the reasoning in paragraph 2 for preferring cash to transfers in kind?

options.A: In a few remote villages, cash transfers raised local prices because traders could not bring in more goods quickly.
options.B: Some households in cash programmes spent part of the money on livestock or tools rather than on food for the family.
options.C: Pensioners in richer countries spend a larger share of their income on alcohol than recipients of cash transfers do.
options.D: In several programmes, nearly all households spent their cash on the same few items that a standard bundle in kind would have supplied.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the modest average effects found by careful evaluations of microcredit

options.A: prove that small loans to the poor are worthless and that the money would be better spent in other ways.
options.B: say more about a mistaken assumption regarding borrowers' aims than about whether the loans were of any use.
options.C: were caused mainly by competition among lenders, which drove many households into taking one loan to repay another.
options.D: show that poor borrowers were never as creditworthy as the early lenders and their repayment figures claimed.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as a use to which borrowers put their loans EXCEPT

options.A: paying for travel to a city to look for work.
options.B: meeting a bill from a hospital stay.
options.C: paying the costs of a family wedding.
options.D: putting a new roof on before the rains.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's view that microcredit is best understood as a financial service?

options.A: Borrowers who had run established businesses before their first loan saw clearly larger gains in profit than other borrowers did.
options.B: In districts where several lenders competed, a large share of households held more than one loan at the same time.
options.C: Within five years of their first loan, most borrowers in one region had doubled their household incomes.
options.D: Borrowers asked what losing access to loans would mean most often said they would struggle to meet sudden large expenses.

questions.question: According to the passage, why do many poor people run tiny enterprises?

options.A: Running a stall allows them to fit paid work around school fees, weddings and other expenses that fall due together.
options.B: Steady wage work is not available to them, and many would accept such work if they could.
options.C: Microlenders require a business plan before they will lend, so borrowers start businesses in order to qualify for loans.
options.D: They are frustrated entrepreneurs who have been held back only by their lack of access to capital.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Inequality in developing countries can be expected to fall only after episodes of war and inflation destroy concentrated wealth.
options.B: The inverted U is mathematically mistaken, since moving workers between two sectors cannot change the overall level of inequality.
options.C: The inverted U records some historical episodes rather than a law, and gives governments no reason to expect inequality to correct itself.
options.D: Recent rises in inequality in rich countries are passing disturbances that further economic growth will in time reverse.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that the author regards the historical declines in inequality as

options.A: having involved more than the shift of workers between sectors, since the fall usually came together with other changes.
options.B: having been caused chiefly by the destruction of concentrated wealth in wars and periods of high inflation.
options.C: having been produced by measures that governments adopted deliberately in order to reduce inequality.
options.D: evidence that the inverted U never actually described the experience of any economy at all.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most clearly regard as an instance of the 'damage' described in paragraph 3?

options.A: A finance ministry turns down a plan to expand rural schooling, arguing that the inequality brought by industrial growth will correct itself.
options.B: A statistics office revises its estimates of national inequality after discovering errors in the household survey data.
options.C: A government expands public schooling in the hope of narrowing a growing gap between urban and rural incomes.
options.D: An economist assembles data from many countries and shows that inequality sometimes rises again after a long decline.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 2 in the passage?

options.A: It introduces the inverted-U hypothesis and explains how the idea came to be proposed in the first place.
options.B: It offers an alternative reading of the curve as a record of particular structural shifts and political choices.
options.C: It grants that the mechanism is arithmetically sound and then argues that real economies have not reliably followed it.
options.D: It describes the consequences for policy of treating the hypothesis as a law of economic development.

questions.question: The passage implies that a programme allowing firms to register online would mainly benefit

options.A: the poorest informal workers, whose earnings are too low to meet the obligations that formality brings.
options.B: owners of established informal businesses who have weighed the costs of registering and decided against it.
options.C: government agencies that hope to collect more in fines from firms that are found to be evading taxes.
options.D: formal-sector employers who are looking for cheaper suppliers among the many unregistered firms nearby.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the description of informality as 'a waiting room' implies that informal workers

options.A: have chosen a refuge in which they can avoid the taxes and regulations that formal firms must bear.
options.B: are learning, while they wait, the skills that formal employers will later demand of them.
options.C: are passing through a stage that every economy must go through on its way to becoming industrial.
options.D: occupy their position only until a better opening, in this case formal work, becomes available.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the error that paragraph 2 attributes to both camps?

options.A: One survey of renters interviews young professionals and calls renting a lifestyle choice; another interviews families refused mortgages and calls renters shut out.
options.B: Two surveys of the same group of renters reach opposite conclusions because one asks about preferences and the other asks about income.
options.C: A survey calls renting a lifestyle choice, but a later check of its own figures shows that most of the renters it studied had in fact been refused mortgages.
options.D: A city that cuts registration fees for landlords finds that the number of officially registered rental homes rises in the following year.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the two camps described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: approving of both camps, regarding their disagreement as a useful division of labour among researchers.
options.B: indifferent, because the author regards the informal economy as a collection of unrelated cases.
options.C: sympathetic to the exclusion camp and dismissive of the choice camp as a cover for the evasion of taxes.
options.D: even-handed but critical, granting each a real basis while faulting both for treating a part as the whole.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that an earmarked grant is least likely to be diverted to other uses when

options.A: the donor attaches a plaque and a public ceremony to the project so that its role is widely seen.
options.B: the recipient government had already set aside its own revenue to pay for the same project.
options.C: most of the recipient's spending is locked into commitments that cannot easily be cut or moved.
options.D: the recipient government has sound priorities and is free to move money to where it is most needed.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, studies comparing donors' allocations with recipients' overall spending have often found that aid labelled for a sector

options.A: raised spending in that sector by more than the amount given, because it attracted matching funds from governments.
options.B: raised spending in that sector, though usually by less than the full amount of the aid.
options.C: was mostly lost to corruption before it could be spent in any sector of the recipient's budget.
options.D: had no measurable effect at all on spending in the sector for which it was labelled.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim that donors 'are funding governments, not projects'?

options.A: A government that received a grant for roads reduced its own road budget by almost exactly the amount of the grant.
options.B: Recipient governments seldom publish detailed accounts showing how their own revenue is divided among sectors.
options.C: Donor-funded vaccination teams reached regions left out of the health ministry's own plans, while the ministry's spending elsewhere was unchanged.
options.D: Donors that earmark their grants report greater satisfaction with the results than donors who give general budget support.

questions.question: The hypothetical clinic in paragraph 1 functions chiefly to

options.A: show that clinics paid for by donors are seldom actually built by the governments that receive the money.
options.B: illustrate how money given for one purpose can end up financing something quite different.
options.C: argue that recipient governments tend to divert aid money into military spending rather than social services.
options.D: demonstrate that fungibility is harmful whatever the priorities of the government that receives the aid.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the effects of geography described in paragraph 3 as

options.A: illusions created by comparing countries whose histories and political systems were quite different.
options.B: minor in comparison with institutional effects, which explain most of the differences between countries.
options.C: the only effects of geography that statistical exercises are able to measure with any reliability.
options.D: real constraints on prosperity that better laws and government cannot simply remove.

questions.question: The example of the two halves of a peninsula in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: show that large differences in prosperity can open up between places that do not differ in geography.
options.B: support the geographers' view that places with a shared climate and soils will tend to share outcomes.
options.C: illustrate how colonisers chose institutions according to the disease environment they met on arrival.
options.D: show that political division of a country makes both of its resulting halves poorer than they would have been.

questions.question: The author's claim that the reversal story is 'a story about geography working through institutions' implies that

options.A: the regions that were prosperous five centuries ago owed their early prosperity to good institutions rather than to geography.
options.B: statistical estimates of the effect of geography on income are too large, because they wrongly include effects of institutions.
options.C: evidence the institutional camp cites against geography is partly evidence of geography's indirect influence.
options.D: institutions have no influence on prosperity apart from what the underlying geography of a region has given them.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 4?

options.A: Public health campaigns have greatly reduced the burden of malaria in a number of tropical regions over recent decades.
options.B: Colonial records show that the choice between settling and extracting followed home-country policy, without regard to local disease or soils.
options.C: Several landlocked countries have reached high incomes despite the extra cost of moving their goods to distant markets.
options.D: Statistical studies that include both geography and institutions find that institutions account for more of the variation in income.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as a way in which geography may affect a country's prosperity EXCEPT

options.A: by favouring crops suited to large estates worked with coerced labour, and so shaping institutions.
options.B: by raising the cost of moving the goods a country produces to the markets where they are sold.
options.C: by imposing a burden of disease that reduces the health of a country's workers.
options.D: by fixing the prices that the country's minerals and crops will fetch on world markets.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: defend judging development by freedoms against the charge of arbitrary weighting, while warning against collapsing it into one index.
options.B: show that income per head is a worthless statistic that development agencies should stop reporting altogether.
options.C: propose a definite list of capabilities, with weights attached, that would improve on existing composite indices.
options.D: explain why market prices are the fairest available way of weighing very different goods against one another.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the 'old' difficulty mentioned at the end of paragraph 4 is that

options.A: critics of the capability approach have long disagreed among themselves about which capabilities belong on the list.
options.B: the poor are frequently unable to afford staple goods that a market economy treats as being of low value.
options.C: figures for income per head cannot be meaningfully compared across different countries or across decades.
options.D: any summary measure of well-being must weight unlike things, and so embodies value judgments whether or not it states them.

questions.question: Which of the following findings would best illustrate the central point of paragraph 2?

options.A: A district whose average income doubled over a decade saw adult literacy rise in roughly the same proportion.
options.B: Within a single district, households with higher incomes are on average better nourished than households with lower incomes.
options.C: Two districts with equal average incomes differ widely in girls' completion of secondary school, because only one has a school within walking distance.
options.D: Ranking districts by a composite index of capabilities places them in a different order from ranking them by income.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the objection set out in paragraph 3 is best described as

options.A: persuaded, concluding that freedoms cannot be measured and that income must remain the standard.
options.B: respectful but unpersuaded, treating it as a real question that tells against income measures as well.
options.C: indifferent, because the author holds that questions of measurement do not matter to judging development.
options.D: dismissive, regarding it as a misunderstanding raised in bad faith by the defenders of income measures.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a reason why the same income may yield different freedoms to different people EXCEPT

options.A: the use of market prices to weight goods when incomes are added up into a national figure.
options.B: a custom that prevents women from travelling alone, whatever the income of their household.
options.C: a bodily condition, such as pregnancy, that raises what a person needs to reach the same level of nourishment.
options.D: a climate that obliges some households to spend on heating what others can spend as they please.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that explaining firms as savings on market costs, though sound about their boundaries, overlooks the competence that firms themselves create.
options.B: reject the view that firms exist to economise on the costs of finding suppliers, bargaining with them and enforcing contracts.
options.C: explain the method by which a firm decides which activities it should perform itself and which it should buy from outside suppliers.
options.D: show that coordination by command inside firms is generally more efficient than coordination by prices in open markets.

questions.question: According to the passage, the bargaining view correctly predicts that firms tend to

options.A: draw up longer and more detailed contracts for tasks whose requirements cannot be fully stated before the work begins.
options.B: buy routine tasks that recur daily from outside suppliers, since frequent purchases allow the buyer to compare terms more easily.
options.C: perform for themselves the activities peculiar to their own operations, where an indispensable supplier could exploit them.
options.D: keep expanding once internal organisation becomes cheaper than contracting, until no outside purchases remain in their accounts.

questions.question: When the author says that what the bargaining view leaves out 'is suggested by its own vocabulary', the implication is that

options.A: the technical terms of the bargaining view are too abstract for the managers who must decide whether to make or buy a component.
options.B: describing the firm only by the costs it avoids presents it as at best equal to a costless market, which hides what firms add.
options.C: the bargaining view uses the word 'cost' in different senses in different parts of its argument and so contradicts itself.
options.D: economists who use the bargaining view have deliberately excluded evidence about informal knowledge because it cannot be measured.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely offer as an example of 'the most valuable thing a firm possesses'?

options.A: A long-term contract with a parts supplier that spares a firm the expense of renegotiating terms every few months.
options.B: A brilliant engineer whose personal expertise is so well known that rival companies regularly offer her a higher salary.
options.C: A detailed operating manual that records every procedure of a workshop so that a new hire can follow it from the first day.
options.D: A surgical team whose members, after years together, anticipate one another's moves in ways that equally qualified strangers could not.

questions.question: According to the passage, quarrels among third-generation owners arise mainly because

options.A: outsiders hired to manage the firm tend to side with those owners who want to reinvest rather than distribute the profits.
options.B: owners with different ties to the firm want different things from it, and those who wish to leave may find no agreed buyout price.
options.C: the grandchildren of the founder have grown up in comfort and are therefore unwilling to work as hard as their parents did.
options.D: the founder usually leaves the largest share of the firm to the child who has worked longest in the business.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the folk wisdom described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: approving, since the author's examples of quarrelling cousins and absent heirs confirm what the saying predicts.
options.B: neutral, since the author reports the saying and the alternative account without indicating which is more convincing.
options.C: doubtful of the explanation it gives while allowing that it is not wholly false.
options.D: contemptuous, since the author regards it as a story with no basis whatsoever in how family firms actually behave.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that a founder who wishes to improve the chances of a good succession should

options.A: make sure that the next chief executive is chosen from among the relatives who already work in the business.
options.B: stay at the head of the firm for as long as possible, so that the heirs gain experience under his direct guidance.
options.C: divide the ownership equally among the heirs, so that none of them feels unfairly treated when a successor is named.
options.D: settle the matter of who will lead the firm well before illness or conflict forces the question.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation of why family firms decline?

options.A: Firms whose shares passed to a single heir in each generation declined as often as firms whose shares were spread among many relatives.
options.B: Family firms that adopted written rules for selling shares within the family reported fewer disputes among owners than those that did not.
options.C: In many family firms, the grandchildren of the founder have spent a large part of their inheritance on personal consumption.
options.D: Some long-lived family firms are run by family members who were chosen only after competing openly with outside candidates for the post.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the incumbent's 'careful attention to its best customers' contributed to its decline because

options.A: those customers demanded lower prices, which reduced the incumbent's margins until it could no longer compete with the newcomer.
options.B: the incumbent spent so heavily on serving them that it had no money left over with which to improve its existing products.
options.C: those customers judged the new technology by standards it did not yet meet, so their advice steered investment away from it.
options.D: those customers were secretly switching to the new technology while telling the incumbent that they had no interest in it.

questions.question: In the argument of the passage, paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: introduce a new example of an incumbent that survived a shift in technology by setting up a separate unit.
options.B: concede that the complacency explanation offered in paragraph 1 is correct in most of the cases that matter.
options.C: argue that incumbents should invest in every cheap technology because any one of them might eventually displace the existing product.
options.D: raise an objection to the account and turn it into further support for the author's conclusion.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as a reason the incumbent passes over the new technology EXCEPT that

options.A: its engineers lack the technical skills needed to work with the newer and simpler design.
options.B: the market for the new technology is too small to matter to a company of its scale.
options.C: its existing customers, when asked about the new technology, say that they do not want it.
options.D: the profit margins it could earn from selling the new technology look thin when examined.

questions.question: The author's recommendation in paragraph 4 depends most on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: A separate unit can reliably predict which of the many cheap new technologies will eventually improve enough to serve the mainstream market of the parent.
options.B: A large firm's criteria for funding projects reflect its size and costs, so a smaller unit with its own measures can value what the parent dismisses.
options.C: Parent companies usually leave their separate units free of interference, supply them generously with funds and allow them to set their own prices.
options.D: Managers placed in charge of a separate unit are generally more alert to emerging technologies and to new customers than the managers of the parent company.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: showing that the effect of chief executives on results is commonly overstated, and that the overstatement is costly.
options.B: explaining why business journalists prefer stories about individual leaders to accounts of markets and industries.
options.C: proving that chief executives have no measurable effect on the performance of the companies they are appointed to run.
options.D: recommending that company boards stop appointing outsiders as chief executives and promote only from within.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the statement 'The error lies in degree, not in kind' means that the mistake consists in

options.A: blaming leaders for small declines in results while crediting them for large recoveries.
options.B: misjudging the kinds of decision that leaders make, rather than how often they make them.
options.C: attributing a firm's results to the wrong kind of leader, rather than to the right one.
options.D: exaggerating how much leaders matter, rather than in believing that they matter at all.

questions.question: The remark that 'the second firm has no story to tell' (paragraph 3) suggests that

options.A: unremarkable managers who have run a firm for many years usually achieve better results than celebrated leaders brought in from outside.
options.B: the comparisons that would reveal how much success owes to circumstances are seldom made, because unremarkable success draws little attention.
options.C: the second firm actually performed worse than the first, which is why its results were not reported in the business press.
options.D: journalists deliberately ignore firms with ordinary managers in order to protect the reputations of the celebrated leaders they admire.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most similar to the error the passage describes?

options.A: A scientist who makes an important discovery insists on sharing the credit with the laboratory team that performed the experiments.
options.B: A company promotes an employee who has outperformed colleagues doing the same work in the same conditions over many years.
options.C: A new head teacher is praised for rising examination results that stem from teaching reforms her predecessor introduced years earlier.
options.D: A town council blames unusually heavy rainfall for floods that were in fact caused by its own failure to clear the drains.

questions.question: According to the passage, defenders of forced ranking argue that it corrects which tendency?

options.A: Managers, out of kindness or to avoid awkward conversations, rate nearly everyone above average, so the ratings convey nothing.
options.B: Teams tend to hide the weak performance of individual members by presenting all of their results as joint work.
options.C: Managers rate their own friends more generously than other staff, so that ratings come to reflect loyalty rather than performance.
options.D: Employees overestimate their own performance and resent any rating below outstanding, which makes appraisals difficult to hold.

questions.question: The passage implies that, under a permanent system of forced ranking, a team made up entirely of strong performers would most likely

options.A: become more cooperative than other teams, because its members would know that each of them was equally capable.
options.B: be recognised as exceptional and therefore exempted by senior managers from the requirement to rank its members.
options.C: find it harder to keep and attract able people, since some of its good members must still be rated poorly.
options.D: improve further, because competition among able colleagues for the top ratings would push each of them to work harder.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that forced ranking discourages cooperation?

options.A: Teams that shared ideas freely produced better results than teams that did not, whether or not their firms used forced ranking.
options.B: Where forced ranking is used, the rank of each employee depends chiefly on colleagues' accounts of how much that person helped them.
options.C: Managers in firms that use forced ranking report that appraisal meetings have become more uncomfortable than they were before.
options.D: Employees who left their firms after receiving a poor rating under forced ranking usually found comparable jobs within a few months.

questions.question: The way the author treats the case made by defenders of forced ranking in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: ironic, suggesting that the defenders do not really believe the argument they put forward and have other motives for it.
options.B: dismissive, presenting the case only in order to show that it rests on a misunderstanding of what ratings are for.
options.C: approving, since the author ends by agreeing that managers should be obliged to say what they already know about their staff.
options.D: fair-minded, presenting the case as reasonable before examining what it takes for granted.

questions.question: The example of the chemical plant in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: demonstrate that the safety limits written into plant manuals are usually set lower than they need to be.
options.B: show that engineers at hazardous plants often disregard written procedures because they care more about cost than about safety.
options.C: provide an instance of the kind of individual culprit whom inquiries into disasters rightly hold responsible.
options.D: illustrate how a working standard can shift through decisions that are each sensible, without anyone choosing to change it.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the outsider's question in paragraph 3 'sounds naive' to those inside the plant because

options.A: the outsider lacks the technical training needed to understand how the pressure vessel actually works.
options.B: running above the limit has become so habitual that insiders no longer perceive it as a departure from the rules.
options.C: insiders know that the plant has been running above its limit only for a few nights and see no cause for alarm.
options.D: the written limit in the manual has been officially revised and the outsider has consulted an old copy.

questions.question: In the final sentence of the passage, the phrase 'drift answers to no one' most nearly means that

options.A: a gradual change in practice cannot be reversed once it has continued for long enough within an organisation.
options.B: informal departures from procedure are never reported to the senior managers who are formally in charge.
options.C: a change that accumulates without ever being decided leaves no one accountable for having made it.
options.D: staff who allow standards to slip usually refuse to explain their actions when an inquiry questions them.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: The deviations most likely to end in disaster are those large enough to attract attention at the moment they are made.
options.B: The fact that a risky choice caused no harm is not, by itself, good evidence that the risk was small.
options.C: Some departures from written procedures improve the way an organisation works and are worth keeping.
options.D: An inquiry that names a person at fault may be accurate about the facts and still mistaken about the cause.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Organisations should always keep as much spare capacity as they can afford, because neither shocks nor useful experiments can be predicted in advance.
options.B: The savings claimed by efficiency programmes are largely illusory, because the costs they remove reappear later in other parts of the organisation.
options.C: Most of the slack found in large organisations shelters inefficiency and protects the privileges of the departments that hold it.
options.D: Much spare capacity serves real if irregular purposes, so slack should be held deliberately and judged by its use rather than cut wholesale as waste.

questions.question: According to the passage, a supply chain that holds no spare stock

options.A: works smoothly in most weeks but is overwhelmed whenever demand rises above its usual average.
options.B: recovers from the failure of a supplier more quickly, because it has less unsold inventory to clear.
options.C: is cheaper to run on ordinary days but stops altogether when a single supplier fails.
options.D: costs more to run than one with reserves, because it must place smaller orders far more often.

questions.question: The author's statement that the critics of slack 'are answering a question that is badly posed' implies that

options.A: the critics of slack are chiefly motivated by a wish to reduce the influence of departments that compete with their own within the firm.
options.B: slack cannot sensibly be assessed as a single amount, since reserves serving a purpose and reserves sheltering comfort call for opposite treatment.
options.C: the critics are mistaken in believing that any part of an organisation's spare resources could reasonably be described as waste.
options.D: the amount of slack in an organisation cannot be measured at all, so organisations should stop trying to keep account of their spare resources.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the claim made in paragraph 3?

options.A: In several firms, the most profitable products began as projects staff pursued with time or money not assigned to any plan.
options.B: Engineers who are given unscheduled afternoons report that they enjoy their work more than colleagues whose time is fully allocated.
options.C: Most of the informal experiments that engineers carry out in their free time are abandoned within a few months without any result.
options.D: Firms that eliminated their spare inventory reported large savings in the first year, with no rise in costs in the years that followed.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the author says that 'To judge slack by ordinary days is to judge an umbrella by the weather on days when it did not rain.' The comparison suggests that

options.A: efficiency audits should not consider the cost of reserves at all, since a reserve's cost has no bearing on whether it is kept.
options.B: the worth of a reserve held against rare events cannot be seen by looking only at periods in which no such event occurs.
options.C: the main value of slack lies in protecting against shocks rather than in leaving room for the experiments that produce change.
options.D: reserves are worth holding only by organisations whose operations face disruptions that are frequent and can be predicted in advance.

questions.question: According to the passage, the records of failed firms are seldom examined because

options.A: their former managers are unwilling to discuss their mistakes with authors who intend to publish the findings.
options.B: the practices of failed firms were so different from those of successful ones that comparison seemed pointless.
options.C: readers of business books are interested only in success and would not buy accounts of companies that failed.
options.D: such firms leave little documentation and attract neither researchers nor opportunities for interviews.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 4 in the passage?

options.A: It withdraws the objection made in paragraph 2, conceding that comparison with less successful firms fully solves the problem of selection.
options.B: It introduces the author's own preferred method of studying business success, which replaces the study of winners with the study of failures.
options.C: It grants that a proposed remedy improves the method, then shows that it leaves one objection standing and fails to address another.
options.D: It offers evidence that the companies praised in such books were in fact poorly run, which their later difficulties made clear.

questions.question: In saying that the explanation for the later stumbles 'can be given whatever happens', the author implies that

options.A: the explanation cannot be tested, because the abandonment of the principles is inferred from the very failure it is meant to explain.
options.B: the companies in fact kept the principles that had made them great, so the explanation offered for their decline is simply false.
options.C: matched comparisons with less successful firms would confirm that the companies that stumbled had abandoned their founding principles.
options.D: the principles identified by such books were sound but were applied by the companies in markets for which they were unsuitable.

questions.question: Each of the following is a criticism that the passage makes of the method described in paragraph 1 EXCEPT that

options.A: its account of why admired firms later decline is framed so that no outcome could count against it.
options.B: it cannot tell whether the practices it praises were also common among firms that failed.
options.C: it rests on too few companies for any of its conclusions to reach statistical significance.
options.D: its descriptions of a firm's practices may be coloured by what observers already know of its results.

questions.question: Which of the following studies would avoid the first difficulty described in the passage while remaining open to the second?

options.A: A study of the ten most profitable firms in an industry, rating each firm's culture from staff surveys conducted years before its results were known.
options.B: A study of the firms that survived longest in an industry, rating each firm's culture from interviews with managers held after the firm had become well known.
options.C: A study of every firm founded in one industry in a given decade, rating each firm's culture from staff surveys conducted every year from its founding.
options.D: A study of every firm founded in one industry in a given decade, survivors and failures alike, rating cultures from interviews held after each fate was known.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that schemes such as early retirement and caps on weekly hours fail because firms refuse to hire young workers.
options.B: reject the idea that work is a fixed quantity while granting that technological change still harms particular workers.
options.C: defend the fears of displaced workers as a sound reason for slowing the spread of new technology across an economy.
options.D: show that labour-saving machines create more jobs than they destroy within the very trades into which they are introduced.

questions.question: According to the passage, job losses are more visible than job gains because

options.A: losses tend to arrive as single identifiable events, while gains are spread thinly over many trades and places.
options.B: newspapers prefer stories about closures and deliberately ignore the slower growth of new industries elsewhere.
options.C: the new jobs usually pay less than the old ones, so workers who take them rarely describe them as gains.
options.D: the new jobs appear only a generation later, by which time the closures they replaced have been forgotten.

questions.question: Which of the following arguments rests on the same mistaken premise that the passage criticises?

options.A: A town should not assume that the jobs created by a new factory will go to the people whose old jobs it replaced.
options.B: A town should expect a cheaper bus service to draw extra riders, some of whom will spend their savings in local shops.
options.C: A town should plan for retraining to take years, because laid-off workers rarely have the skills that new employers want.
options.D: A town should refuse a permit for a second cinema, since its filmgoers would merely be split between two halls and no new jobs could result.

questions.question: The author refers to 'a fifty-year-old weaver whose skills no longer have a buyer' most likely in order to suggest that

options.A: technological change reduces the total amount of work available in an economy once a transition is complete.
options.B: caps on weekly hours would protect older workers better than schemes that push them into early retirement.
options.C: an argument about the total amount of work can be correct and still say nothing to the people who lose out.
options.D: the lump of labour premise turns out to be correct whenever older workers are the ones who are displaced.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'the employment bundle' refers to

options.A: the group of workers who share one employer and a fixed schedule, as clerks in an office traditionally did.
options.B: the set of protections and obligations that come together with the legal status of being an employee.
options.C: the package of fares, routes and passengers that a platform assigns to each driver who logs into its app.
options.D: the combined earnings that a single worker collects from the several apps for which she drives in a week.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the two dominant responses described in paragraph 2 as

options.A: each accurate about a feature of platform work that the other response neglects.
options.B: unequal in merit, the case for treating platform workers as employees being clearly the stronger one.
options.C: irreconcilable, since the platform's control over work and the worker's flexibility cannot both be protected.
options.D: equally mistaken, since neither gives an accurate description of the way platform work is organised.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that some protections 'depend on nothing that a flexible schedule makes impossible'?

options.A: Paid holidays calculated over a working year proved very hard to arrange for drivers who worked for three different apps.
options.B: A minimum rate for time worked could be enforced only if platforms fixed in advance the hours a worker counts as available, ending free log-ins.
options.C: Firms that were offered a menu of separable protections lobbied, in several places, for the cheapest selection on the menu.
options.D: Many platform workers say they would prefer employee status if it could be combined with the freedom to choose their own hours.

questions.question: The final paragraph of the passage primarily serves to

options.A: report that firms have already moved many employees into a new category created to accommodate the platforms.
options.B: withdraw the proposal to unbundle protections and recommend a third legal category of worker in its place.
options.C: summarise the two dominant responses to platform work and show that the courts have already chosen between them.
options.D: acknowledge the risks of the author's proposal while explaining why it remains preferable to the binary.

questions.question: According to the passage, the pay of the musicians must rise over time because

options.A: the cost of running concert halls has increased faster than the general level of prices.
options.B: audiences now expect a higher standard of performance than listeners did a century ago.
options.C: they would otherwise move to other occupations, where wages have risen along with productivity.
options.D: innovations have allowed musicians to perform the same quartet more quickly than before.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the comparison of a class of sixty pupils with a class of thirty is used to

options.A: show that raising output per worker in such services can change the service rather than supply it more cheaply.
options.B: illustrate that productivity in teaching has grown about as fast as productivity in manufacturing.
options.C: suggest that many schools waste money by employing more teachers than their pupils actually need.
options.D: argue that schools ought to keep their classes small, however much it costs the public budget to do so.

questions.question: Suppose a public hospital's costs have risen much faster than prices in general for several decades. The author would most likely say that this fact

options.A: shows that society can no longer afford hospital care at its present relative price and must ration it.
options.B: fits the pattern of the cost disease but does not by itself show that none of the increase is waste.
options.C: must be explained by the cost disease, because health care consists largely of a person's time and attention.
options.D: shows that the hospital's administrative layers must have multiplied, since the cost disease cannot account for it.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a limit on the argument or on its consolation EXCEPT that

options.A: public budgets that depend on unpopular taxes may cut services well before the arithmetic of affordability requires it.
options.B: the higher relative price of care weighs most on people whose incomes have not shared in the general gain.
options.C: manufacturing productivity may one day stop growing, which would remove the cause of the cost disease.
options.D: rising relative costs in a service may partly reflect administrative growth that the cost disease does not excuse.

questions.question: The passage is mainly concerned with

options.A: arguing that the common debate about remote work overlooks how it affects the way juniors learn their jobs.
options.B: showing that experienced professionals produce less at home than they did when they worked in the office.
options.C: explaining why video calls are a less efficient way to settle routine matters than face-to-face meetings.
options.D: arguing that firms should require junior staff to return to the office for most of their working week.

questions.question: According to the passage, remote arrangements tend to remove the learning described in paragraph 2 because

options.A: most accounting problems are too complicated to be explained clearly in an email or video call.
options.B: juniors at home tend to spend the hours they save on commuting on matters unrelated to work.
options.C: senior staff working from home are generally unwilling to answer questions from their juniors.
options.D: that learning relies on unplanned exposure, while contact in remote work is mostly scheduled.

questions.question: The passage implies that the partners of the hypothetical firm in paragraph 2

options.A: had trained their juniors mainly through formal courses before the firm sent everyone home.
options.B: found that the firm's billable work fell sharply in the years that followed the first year at home.
options.C: judged the move by a measure that could not register what their newest recruits were losing.
options.D: knew that their juniors were learning less but decided that the loss did not matter to the firm.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that the cost of remote work is 'real but delayed'?

options.A: Billable work at firms that sent everyone home rose slightly during the first year after the change was made.
options.B: Juniors placed among seniors who kept their office doors shut learned little more than juniors working at home.
options.C: Experienced accountants report that working from home has made them more satisfied with their jobs than before.
options.D: Staff who joined remote firms as recruits took longer, years afterwards, to be trusted with difficult client work than earlier cohorts had.

questions.question: According to the passage, early researchers in artificial intelligence assumed that

options.A: perception and movement would be the hardest faculties to build, having taken longest to evolve.
options.B: the tasks people find easy would also be the easy ones for a machine to master.
options.C: a machine able to play respectable chess would still be far from being able to fold laundry.
options.D: the difficulty of any task could be measured by the amount of computation it requires.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the word 'cheap' in 'the cheap ones to mechanise' most nearly means

options.A: requiring relatively little effort or computation to reproduce in a machine.
options.B: quickly and easily acquired by human beings during childhood.
options.C: poorly paid when people perform them in the labour market.
options.D: of little real value to the people who happen to possess them.

questions.question: On the reasoning of paragraph 3, which of the following jobs would be hardest for a machine to take over?

options.A: Restoring antique chairs, each built differently and damaged in its own way, for private collectors.
options.B: Checking insurance claims against a written list of the conditions under which payment is due.
options.C: Allocating hospital shifts to nurses according to a fixed set of rules about rest and seniority.
options.D: Computing the interest owed on thousands of loans using a formula set by the lending bank.

questions.question: Which of the following conclusions would the author most likely regard as NOT warranted by the argument of the passage?

options.A: Ranking jobs as basic or advanced by how hard they seem to people may mislead forecasts of automation.
options.B: The present line between what machines can and cannot do may move as learning methods improve.
options.C: Since care work resists automation, care workers can expect higher pay as machines take over clerical tasks.
options.D: Some clerical jobs may well be automated before cleaning jobs are, contrary to many familiar forecasts.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the textbook view of unions described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: studied neutrality, setting it beside the voice view without preferring one account to the other.
options.B: acceptance of it as an account of one real effect, joined to rejection of it as a full account.
options.C: outright dismissal of it as an ideological error with no basis in the way labour markets work.
options.D: broad agreement with it, together with a complaint that it understates the inefficiency unions cause.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in a firm whose management treats the grievance procedure as an adversary to be outmanoeuvred, the union is likely to

options.A: lead more workers to quit than would quit a comparable firm in which no union had been organised.
options.B: make the firm more productive than its non-union rivals, though by less than under cooperative managers.
options.C: stop bargaining over wages, since its energy is absorbed by disputes conducted through the grievance procedure.
options.D: impose a higher wage bill while yielding little of the information that might have offset it.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most undermine the reasoning of paragraph 2?

options.A: Some managers in unionised firms regard the grievance procedure as a nuisance to be kept to a minimum.
options.B: In firms without unions, workers who complain about safety or supervision are no more likely than silent colleagues to be dismissed or passed over.
options.C: Unionised firms pay noticeably higher wages than otherwise similar firms in which there is no union.
options.D: Workers who leave a firm often take with them skills that their employer finds slow and costly to replace.

questions.question: The sentence beginning 'None of this establishes that unions are good for firms' in the final paragraph serves to

options.A: confine the conclusion to a claim about how unions should be judged rather than a verdict on their worth.
options.B: concede that the textbook view of unions as cartels is, after all, a complete and accurate account of them.
options.C: introduce new evidence that unions, on balance, reduce the productivity of the firms in which they organise.
options.D: withdraw the earlier argument that collective voice can make a unionised firm more productive than its rivals.

questions.question: The central claim of the passage is that working hours stopped falling mainly because

options.A: people came to value income above leisure once competition for status made relative position matter most.
options.B: governments stopped legislating shorter weeks after the middle of the century, leaving the matter to employers.
options.C: the structure of jobs, rather than workers' free choices, has decided how productivity gains are divided.
options.D: forecasts made early in the twentieth century relied on mistaken estimates of how quickly productivity would grow.

questions.question: According to the passage, a firm may prefer fewer people working longer hours to more people working shorter hours because

options.A: workers on short hours tend to leave sooner, so that the firm must keep replacing them at great expense.
options.B: professionals demand long hours as a signal of commitment, and firms must satisfy them to retain talent.
options.C: employees who work longer hours are more productive in each hour than those who work fewer hours.
options.D: some costs of employing a worker, such as recruitment and training, arise per person rather than per hour.

questions.question: The example of the lawyer in paragraph 3 is used chiefly to

options.A: suggest that part-time work no longer exists in any of the professions in which long hours are common.
options.B: demonstrate that the long hours worked in professions such as law raise the quality of the work produced.
options.C: illustrate that a trade of income for time that a worker wants may be unavailable or heavily penalised.
options.D: show that professionals, when offered a genuine choice, prefer a higher salary to a shorter working week.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that 'the hours we observe tell us what jobs offer, not what workers want'?

options.A: Where workers gained a legal right to cut their hours at proportionally lower pay, with no effect on promotion, very few used it.
options.B: Many lower-paid workers reported that they could not obtain as many hours as they wished to work each week.
options.C: Surveys found that most professionals working very long hours said they would prefer to work somewhat less.
options.D: The fixed costs that firms bear for each worker they hire, especially for benefits and training, rose over several decades.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard a national average of weekly hours that has held steady for some decades as

options.A: evidence that workers' preferences about how much to work have stopped changing over that period.
options.B: compatible with longer weeks for some groups of workers and too few hours for others.
options.C: a sign that the old prediction of a much shorter week will come true once productivity rises further.
options.D: proof that the institutional account is mistaken, since the structure of jobs changed during those decades.

questions.question: Paragraph 1 functions in the passage chiefly to

options.A: argue that producing more graduates would reverse the shrinking of employment in the middle of the wage scale.
options.B: state the author's own account of how technology has affected the distribution of pay over time.
options.C: introduce the task-based view that the rest of the passage goes on to defend without any reservation.
options.D: present an earlier explanation whose prediction is contradicted by the pattern reported in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The objection raised in paragraph 3 implies that a forecast that a task is safe from automation because it is non-routine

options.A: proves that reading medical images was always a routine task, since it is now discussed as a candidate for automation.
options.B: is reliable for tasks that demand judgement, since such tasks can never be fully specified in advance.
options.C: fails because the task view cannot explain why employment grew at the bottom of the wage distribution.
options.D: may rest on little more than the fact that the task has not yet been automated.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates the point made in paragraph 4?

options.A: After computers spread through offices, the wages of graduates rose faster than the wages of workers without degrees.
options.B: A task long described as requiring judgement is automated and is then reclassified by analysts as having been routine.
options.C: Two insurers buy identical claims software; one cuts its claims clerks, while the other, whose tax rules favour keeping staff, trains them to settle complex claims.
options.D: A typing pool is closed once word-processing programs become cheap enough to install on every employee's desk.

questions.question: Paragraph 4 presents each of the following as affecting which tasks firms automate EXCEPT

options.A: how many years of schooling the workers in a task have typically completed.
options.B: what machines cost compared with the cost of employing people to do the same work.
options.C: how the tax system treats spending on equipment compared with spending on wages.
options.D: whether managers see their workers as a cost to cut or as a capacity to develop.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: The task view should be abandoned in favour of an account that explains wages through institutions alone.
options.B: Changing how equipment is taxed could alter how far the middle of the wage scale shrinks, though not every task is equally easy to mechanise.
options.C: Polarisation is a result of choices made by firms rather than an effect of technology on the jobs available.
options.D: Because the idea of a routine task is partly circular, no useful prediction about automation can be made.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain how the gold standard came to be adopted by trading nations and why it was eventually replaced by paper money.
options.B: argue that because governments cannot be trusted with money, its supply should be fixed by a rule that no authority can alter.
options.C: challenge the belief that a gold-backed currency protected people, while granting the concern for trustworthy money behind it.
options.D: show that the depression of the 1930s was caused mainly by countries that refused to abandon the gold standard in time.

questions.question: According to the passage, under a metallic standard the quantity of money was governed by

options.A: how quickly metal was mined and how it moved between countries, factors largely unrelated to what trade needed.
options.B: the demands of savers, who exchanged notes for gold whenever they feared that prices were about to rise.
options.C: the volume of trade, since merchants brought metal to the mint whenever commerce expanded and more coins were required.
options.D: the decisions of governments about how much paper money their reserves of metal would allow them to issue.

questions.question: The example of the farmer who borrowed against next year's harvest is used in the passage to

options.A: show that farmers were more careless borrowers than merchants and therefore suffered most under the gold standard.
options.B: illustrate how falling prices raise the real burden of a debt that is fixed in money terms.
options.C: suggest that harvests under the gold standard were smaller, which was why the farmer could not repay his loan.
options.D: prove that creditors deliberately kept the supply of gold scarce in order to profit from the borrowers who owed them.

questions.question: The final sentence of the passage, about a rule that no one made, implies that

options.A: gold was a poor standard mainly because its value had been decided arbitrarily by officials long ago and never revised since then.
options.B: any rule for managing money becomes harmful once it is applied by people rather than determined by nature itself.
options.C: supporters of the gold standard have been dishonest in claiming that their preferred system was never designed by anyone.
options.D: the impersonality that makes gold seem trustworthy is also what makes it unable to respond to changing conditions.

questions.question: According to the passage, an insurer facing adverse selection raises its price because

options.A: medical examinations and questionnaires have made it more expensive to administer each policy it sells.
options.B: compulsory membership has forced it to accept risky customers whom it would otherwise have refused.
options.C: the customers most likely to claim are staying in the pool while safer customers leave it.
options.D: buyers have been concealing their past claims and medical conditions in order to obtain cheaper cover.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the phrase 'no insurance in any useful sense' indicates that

options.A: insurers who examine applicants are breaking the law that requires them to offer every person the same premium.
options.B: a premium matching one's own expected cost leaves nothing of the bad luck shared with other people.
options.C: the person with the costly condition would be refused cover outright by every insurer on the market.
options.D: the policy offered would exclude the costly condition and so pay nothing at all if treatment were ever needed.

questions.question: Which of the following situations most closely shows the process the passage calls unravelling?

options.A: A voluntary repair plan for old cars loses its owners of well-kept cars after each price rise, until only owners of failing cars stay enrolled.
options.B: A repair plan for old cars becomes cheaper after the law requires every owner to join, because careful drivers now share the cost with careless ones.
options.C: A repair plan for old cars collapses after many owners claim for faults they caused on purpose, once they learn the inspectors cannot detect it.
options.D: A repair plan for old cars inspects each vehicle and charges owners according to its condition, so owners of failing cars pay nearly the cost of repair.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards pricing insurance according to each person's risk is best described as

options.A: firmly opposed: it destroys the pooling on which insurance depends and should be replaced everywhere by compulsory membership.
options.B: detached and neutral: the author describes how the method works but declines to say when, if ever, it would be fair.
options.C: broadly approving: it is the technically correct remedy for adverse selection and should be left to the judgement of actuaries.
options.D: conditionally accepting: fair for risks people take on by choice, but troubling for risks imposed by birth or chance.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 1 that the sound bank fails because

options.A: its loans turn out to be less prudent than its managers had believed when they first approved them.
options.B: its depositors behave irrationally, withdrawing money out of fear when they have no reason to do so.
options.C: depositors acting sensibly on a rumour bring about the very trouble that the rumour had wrongly alleged.
options.D: the state has not guaranteed its deposits, and so its managers are free to take excessive risks with them.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, deposit insurance is said to look 'almost like a free lunch' because

options.A: insured depositors receive the protection of their savings without paying any premium for it at all.
options.B: a guarantee that is believed removes the motive to run, so the promised payment rarely has to be made.
options.C: the guarantee costs nothing in the short run, though it encourages reckless lending that is paid for later.
options.D: the cost of insuring deposits is borne by the banks themselves rather than by depositors or by taxpayers.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's reply to the objection in paragraph 4?

options.A: Surveys of insured depositors find that very few of them have ever read their bank's accounts or asked how it lends the money they deposit.
options.B: In several countries the limit on deposit cover has been raised more than once, usually after a crisis had already begun rather than before it.
options.C: Runs on banks without deposit insurance have often begun from rumours that later proved false, and sound banks closed as a result of them.
options.D: Before guarantees existed, depositors steadily moved money away from banks with weaker loan books, well before any panic, and these banks then lent more cautiously.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a proposal to guarantee every deposit in full, with no upper limit, as

options.A: unwise, because it would remove the incentive of large creditors who are among the few equipped to scrutinise banks.
options.B: acceptable, provided depositors were also required to study the loan books of their banks before opening accounts.
options.C: sensible, because if partial cover stops runs, full cover would stop them even more completely at no extra cost.
options.D: pointless, because depositors had already stopped paying attention to their banks once partial insurance was introduced.

questions.question: According to paragraph 1, the analogy between inflation and taxation is exact in that

options.A: in both cases the burden falls most heavily on the poorest households, who hold their wealth in cash.
options.B: in both cases a collector must visit the people who are being taxed and record what each of them owes.
options.C: in both cases resources pass from the public to the authority that collects or issues the money.
options.D: in both cases the measure must be approved by a law before any money can be taken from the public.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 3 in the passage?

options.A: It explains the historical shift from coin clipping to money creation that made the inflation tax possible in modern economies.
options.B: It sets limits on the inflation-tax idea by noting cases in which inflation involves neither intention nor much gain.
options.C: It rejects the inflation-tax idea altogether by showing that inflation is caused by harvests and fuel prices rather than by governments.
options.D: It strengthens the critics' case in paragraph 2 by showing that the burden of inflation falls on savers who hold interest-bearing deposits.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a reason critics consider the inflation tax worse than ordinary taxation EXCEPT that it

options.A: is collected mainly from people with large incomes, who are able to move their wealth abroad.
options.B: benefits debtors, including the state, whose obligations lose real value as prices rise.
options.C: falls heavily on households that keep their savings in cash or live on incomes fixed in money terms.
options.D: does not have to be proposed, debated and voted upon in the way a tax on incomes does.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely accept?

options.A: Since modern deposits pay interest, the idea of an inflation tax is a historical relic best confined to the age of coin clipping.
options.B: Any inflation that reduces the real value of government debt should be described as a tax, whatever its original cause may have been.
options.C: Mild inflation that arrives through the price of imports is a hidden tax imposed by foreign governments on domestic savers.
options.D: Whether a period of inflation deserves to be called a tax depends on examining who gained from it, not only on how much prices rose.

questions.question: According to the reasoning in paragraph 1, a pre-election loosening of money fails to raise output because

options.A: the higher inflation that follows reduces output by more than the loosening had raised it in the first place.
options.B: appointed officials at the central bank refuse to carry out the loosening that the government has ordered.
options.C: voters punish governments that loosen money, so the government reverses the policy soon after the election.
options.D: people expect the loosening and raise wages and prices beforehand, which cancels its effect on output.

questions.question: Which of the following arrangements is most closely analogous to the settlement the author describes in paragraph 3?

options.A: A city council sets a target for reducing road deaths and then chooses each new speed limit itself, consulting the safety agency only for advice.
options.B: A city council sets a target for reducing road deaths, and a safety agency decides how to meet it and must explain any shortfall publicly.
options.C: A city council asks a safety agency to cut road deaths, ease congestion and raise parking revenue, leaving the agency to balance the three goals.
options.D: A city council lets a safety agency decide both how far road deaths should be reduced and how that reduction should be achieved.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Delegating only the means of monetary policy can reconcile credibility with democracy, though the reconciliation weakens as mandates widen.
options.B: Central banks should be made fully independent, since elected governments cannot be trusted to resist loosening money before elections.
options.C: Central banks have lost public trust because they have been given too many goals, such as climate risk and the direction of credit.
options.D: Decisions about interest rates are political and should therefore be returned to elected governments, who can be removed by voters.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: A central bank with a single inflation target faces stronger electoral temptation than a government does before an election.
options.B: Once the legislature fixes an inflation target, the democratic objection to central bank independence ceases to apply in any form.
options.C: A central bank told to support employment as well as stable prices has a weaker case against elected oversight than one with only a price target.
options.D: Asking a central bank to pursue financial stability shows that its officials are cleverer than elected politicians in economic matters.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with arguing that

options.A: the usual moral view of debt is one-sided, since lenders who are paid to bear risk share responsibility for loans that fail.
options.B: bankruptcy laws that grant honest debtors a fresh start benefit creditors more than strict enforcement of debts would.
options.C: borrowers who default should not be blamed, since default is merely a risk that the lender was paid in advance to accept.
options.D: moral language has no proper place in discussions of debt, which ought to be treated as purely a matter of contracts and prices.

questions.question: According to the passage, one reason bankruptcy law in many countries favours a fresh start for honest debtors is that

options.A: debtors who receive a fresh start are more likely than others to borrow again and so increase the profits of lenders.
options.B: courts find it too costly to enforce debts that have remained unpaid for a long time against debtors with few assets.
options.C: lenders who made the original loans were usually aware that their borrowers would be unable to repay them.
options.D: a person weighed down by unpayable debts is of little productive use to anyone, including the creditors.

questions.question: The author's claim that lenders 'collect the premium for risk while disowning the risk itself' (paragraph 2) implies that

options.A: lenders are legally entitled to the premium, but borrowers are never morally obliged to repay the sums they have borrowed.
options.B: lenders who condemn every default are trying to keep the reward for bearing a risk without accepting what that risk entails.
options.C: lenders ought to return the interest they have collected from any borrower who later turns out to be unable to repay.
options.D: lenders charge interest rates that are higher than the actual chance of default can justify, and so profit unfairly.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim in paragraph 3 about the practical effects of a strong moral framing of debt?

options.A: In regions where default carries heavy social stigma, borrowers on average take out smaller loans and repay them in fewer instalments.
options.B: In regions with generous bankruptcy laws, the rate of default is higher than in regions where debts are enforced strictly against debtors.
options.C: In regions where default carries heavy social stigma, lenders check borrowers' incomes less thoroughly, and struggling borrowers seek renegotiation later.
options.D: In regions where default carries heavy social stigma, many people say in surveys that repaying a debt is a matter of personal honour.

questions.question: The example of firms built around a new technology (paragraph 2) serves mainly to

options.A: establish that the size of the eventual fall in prices is the most reliable sign that a market was in a bubble.
options.B: show that investors in new technologies are especially prone to collective madness and so tend to pay too much.
options.C: argue that most firms built around new technologies fail, so investors should avoid such shares until a winner emerges.
options.D: show how a steep later fall in prices can be compatible with the original prices having been a reasonable wager.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, 'passers-on' refers to buyers who

options.A: pass on information about an asset's true value to other investors, so helping prices reflect its actual merits.
options.B: hold an asset only in the expectation of selling it to someone who will pay a higher price for it.
options.C: pass on their losses to the lenders who financed their purchases when prices fall sharply after a boom.
