options.D: sell an asset quickly once they realise that the price they paid for it was based on a mistaken wager.

questions.question: Which of the following purchases would the author regard as speculative in the narrow sense defined in paragraph 3?

options.A: A dealer buys a painting she thinks dull and would never hang, at a record price, because she expects a collector to bid more next season.
options.B: A farmer pays far more than his neighbours think wise for a vineyard, believing that its future harvests will more than repay him.
options.C: An investor borrows heavily to buy shares in a young firm that she believes will dominate its industry and earn profits that justify the price.
options.D: A family buys a house near the top of a boom, paying a price that falls by half over the following three years.

questions.question: The author's objection to proposals that regulators deflate bubbles as they form depends on the assumption that

options.A: most buyers in a rising market are believers in the asset's merits rather than buyers who hope to pass it on.
options.B: raising interest rates or restricting purchases would have no effect at all on the prices of assets in a rising market.
options.C: regulators have no timely way, apart from watching prices, to learn the motives for which buyers are paying them.
options.D: bubbles cause less damage to an economy than the measures that regulators would use in trying to prevent them.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: A market may contain both buyers who rely on an asset's merits and buyers who rely on finding a later buyer, at the same price.
options.B: Measures to deflate a bubble as it forms would, if applied, mostly spare the investments that rested on sound judgements of value.
options.C: Limiting how much buyers may borrow can reduce the harm a collapse does without anyone first judging whether prices are justified.
options.D: Some warnings that a bubble was forming were followed by long periods in which the prices concerned continued to rise.

questions.question: According to the passage, when a bank approves a loan it

options.A: credits the borrower's account with a new deposit that did not exist before the loan was made.
options.B: first obtains from the central bank enough extra reserves to match the full amount of the loan.
options.C: hands the borrower notes drawn from the deposits that savers have accumulated in its vaults over time.
options.D: transfers the amount of the loan from the account of a saver who has agreed to lend to that borrower.

questions.question: The comparison between lending against existing houses and lending to firms that build new things (paragraph 5) is used to

options.A: support the textbook claim that banks are intermediaries that place existing savings with the most efficient borrowers.
options.B: show that lending against houses expands the supply of money less than lending to firms, which creates more deposits.
options.C: illustrate that lending booms which enlarge the money supply alike may differ greatly in what the new money does.
options.D: argue that banks should be prohibited from lending against existing houses so that more new money flows to productive firms.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that, on the author's account,

options.A: banks are not constrained by anything at all, since they can create whatever deposits their borrowers happen to request.
options.B: a single bank can lend without limit, since any deposits it loses to other banks are bound to return to it.
options.C: the central bank can determine the total amount of bank lending by deciding how many reserves to supply to banks.
options.D: the total of deposits across all banks can rise even though no saver has brought any new money to any bank.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the textbook account of banking is best described as

options.A: critical of its picture of the system as a whole, while granting that it describes the funding problem of one bank fairly.
options.B: approving of it as a simplification that is accurate for the system, though misleading about how a single bank operates.
options.C: dismissive of it as a mistake with no basis, since even individual banks never need deposits or reserves to fund their lending.
options.D: neutral towards it, presenting it alongside the alternative without saying which is the better account of modern banking.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument in paragraph 4?

options.A: A bank that expanded its lending faster than its rivals found that many of the new deposits it created moved to other banks.
options.B: In several periods when reserves were made abundant, lending stayed flat because borrowers were reluctant to take on new debts.
options.C: In several periods when reserves were made abundant while borrowers were cautious and banks feared losses, lending still rose in near proportion to reserves.
options.D: Banks that held more capital relative to their loans tended to lend more freely than banks with thin capital during a slowdown.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: advise poorer countries to specialise in the industries where their workers are least productive in absolute terms.
options.B: correct a popular misreading of comparative advantage, while granting objections that leave its logic of opportunity cost intact.
options.C: show that the critics of open trade have misunderstood the costs of moving workers from contracting industries into expanding ones.
options.D: demonstrate that open trade benefits every worker in every country, so that the objections raised by its critics can be safely set aside.

questions.question: According to the passage, the pattern of trade between countries is determined by

options.A: which country can produce a particular good using the fewest workers and machines.
options.B: which country's government offers temporary support to its new industries at the right moment.
options.C: which country's firms are most competitive against foreign rivals in a given industry.
options.D: which country forgoes the least of other goods when it produces a particular good.

questions.question: The example of the lawyer and the secretary implies that

options.A: secretaries generally type faster than the professionals who employ them in their offices.
options.B: someone who is better at a task may still gain by leaving it to someone worse at it.
options.C: a professional should usually learn the routine tasks of her office in order to keep her costs down.
options.D: specialisation tends to reward the more skilled of two parties at the expense of the less skilled one.

questions.question: Which of the following promises would the author regard as incoherent rather than merely difficult to keep?

options.A: Our programme will give this country a comparative advantage in every sector, from farming to software.
options.B: Our programme will help workers in shrinking industries move quickly into the industries that are expanding.
options.C: Our programme will raise output per worker in every sector of the economy, from farming to software.
options.D: Our programme will support promising new industries until their skills catch up with those of foreign rivals.

questions.question: The reference to 'an observer counting shipments' in paragraph 2 suggests that such an observer would

options.A: conclude that the zone had failed because its firms import most of the components that they assemble there.
options.B: underestimate the wages that the zone's firms pay to workers commuting in from outside.
options.C: mistake rising exports from a zone for evidence that it had changed the economy around it.
options.D: notice at once that domestic suppliers were being excluded from the zone's business.

questions.question: The description of a zone as 'less an enclave than a laboratory' in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that zones should favour research-intensive industries over the routine assembly work they usually attract.
options.B: concede that isolating a zone from the rest of the economy is politically necessary.
options.C: explain why generous tax holidays decide which zones succeed and which fail.
options.D: present a zone's purpose as testing arrangements that are meant eventually to operate beyond it.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about what distinguishes the zones that have mattered?

options.A: Several zones offering generous tax holidays attracted large numbers of foreign firms during their first ten years of operation.
options.B: Across many zones, larger tax concessions predict larger gains for firms outside, while the share of inputs bought locally predicts nothing.
options.C: Workers trained inside zones went on to earn higher wages than workers of similar age who had never been employed in one.
options.D: Some zones whose rules were later extended across their countries had begun as enclaves that bought very little from local suppliers.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: A zone that has remained an efficient island for decades points to a reform that has failed to advance.
options.B: A zone can raise a country's exports markedly while leaving most of the economy outside it largely unchanged.
options.C: A zone's isolation from the surrounding economy is a design flaw that reformers should avoid from the very start.
options.D: The wages a zone pays may rest on work that firms would readily move elsewhere if costs were to rise.

questions.question: According to the passage, attention in trade disputes turned to technical standards because

options.A: new trade agreements had required countries to bring their standards into line.
options.B: domestic producers had stopped asking their governments for tariff protection.
options.C: a series of safety scandals had led countries to tighten their product rules.
options.D: tariffs, the more visible kind of obstacle, had come down over several decades.

questions.question: Applying the reasoning of the passage as a whole, the author would most likely say that the wooden-barrel rule in paragraph 2

options.A: imposes a cost on foreign producers that buys no added safety, so its burden is unnecessary to its purpose.
options.B: would become acceptable if foreign dairies were given enough time to switch over to wooden barrels.
options.C: is legitimate because it expresses the country's own judgement about what level of risk is acceptable.
options.D: is protectionist because the officials who wrote it intended from the start to keep foreign cheese out of the domestic market.

questions.question: As used in the last sentence of the passage, 'fit' refers to

options.A: how closely the burden a standard imposes matches what its stated purpose actually requires.
options.B: how closely a standard conforms to the standards adopted by a country's trading partners.
options.C: whether the officials who drafted a standard acted in good faith towards foreign producers.
options.D: how well a standard suits the methods that domestic producers have traditionally followed.

questions.question: The test the author proposes in paragraph 4 depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: That standards written in terms of outcomes impose no costs at all on foreign producers who wish to sell in the market.
options.B: That it is often possible to tell whether another method would achieve the outcome a rule's prescribed method aims at.
options.C: That countries ought eventually to converge on a single shared level of acceptable risk for each kind of product.
options.D: That governments seldom prescribe methods in their standards except when they wish to shelter domestic producers.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes what paragraph 2 does?

options.A: It explains why managers came to see stocks of parts held in warehouses as a form of waste.
options.B: It argues that lean chains harmed firms in poorer countries by shutting them out of richer markets.
options.C: It grants the benefits of lean global chains before showing how they can fail under unusual conditions.
options.D: It recommends that firms bring production home so that a disruption abroad cannot halt their lines.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard a chain that buys a critical part from two suppliers in widely separated regions as

options.A: more exposed than a chain relying on one nearby plant, since deliveries over long distances are less dependable.
options.B: just as exposed as a chain relying on one nearby plant, since each supplier is itself a possible point of failure.
options.C: safe from disruption only if it also keeps no stocks of the part in its own warehouses.
options.D: less exposed to a single disruption than a chain that relies on one plant close to its assembly line.

questions.question: The passage supports each of the following claims about lean supply chains EXCEPT:

options.A: They often held very little stock at any of the stages through which a product passed.
options.B: They allowed some firms in poorer countries to reach markets that would otherwise have been closed to them.
options.C: They were adopted chiefly because managers took no account whatever of the chance of a disruption.
options.D: They passed part of their savings on to consumers in the form of lower prices.

questions.question: Which of the following policies most directly addresses the problem identified in the final paragraph?

options.A: Requiring makers of essential medicines to keep minimum reserve stocks, with part of the cost met from public funds.
options.B: Taxing imported components heavily so that parts made by domestic suppliers become cheaper to buy by comparison.
options.C: Paying firms to move their factories back into the country, however many suppliers those factories end up using.
options.D: Encouraging managers to apply just-in-time methods more strictly so that their supply chains carry even less stock.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Since compensation programmes have repeatedly failed, governments should shield the industries that face the strongest competition from imports.
options.B: Open trade's claim to benefit everyone requires compensation actually paid, through support for displaced workers whatever caused their job loss.
options.C: Open trade reduces a country's welfare, because the losses suffered by displaced workers are larger than the gains spread across households.
options.D: Economists are mistaken in believing that the total gains from open trade exceed the total losses that it imposes on particular towns.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, under the programmes described in paragraph 3, a worker whose plant closed because of both foreign competition and new machinery would probably have

options.A: qualified without difficulty, since foreign competition was at least one cause of the closure.
options.B: received more help than a worker whose job was lost to imports alone, since two causes were involved.
options.C: been retrained for an occupation that was growing, since the programmes were linked to hiring employers.
options.D: found it hard to qualify for help, since the loss could not be clearly traced to imports.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the economists' 'standard reply' in paragraph 2 is best described as

options.A: amused indifference to it as an academic exercise with no bearing on what governments actually do.
options.B: warm endorsement of it as a complete answer to those who complain about the effects of imports.
options.C: acceptance of its arithmetic, joined to criticism of its use as though it settled the question.
options.D: outright rejection of its reasoning as a mistake that has misled policy about the effects of trade.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's recommendation in paragraph 4?

options.A: Where help was open to all displaced workers whatever the cause, more applied and found work than where it was limited to job losses blamed on imports.
options.B: Residents of towns where a large plant closed tend to express much stronger hostility to imports than residents of towns where none closed.
options.C: Training courses tied to employers who were hiring cost noticeably more per worker than the classroom courses offered under earlier programmes.
options.D: Most economists continue to agree that the total gains from lowering barriers to imports are larger than the total losses those barriers prevent.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the value that 'merely passed through' the assembling country is value that

options.A: was added to the shipment by customs officers when they recorded its value at the border.
options.B: was produced in other countries and only embodied in the product during its final assembly.
options.C: was shipped across the assembling country's territory without being used in any of its products.
options.D: was lost in the course of transport between the various countries that took part in the chain.

questions.question: According to the reasoning in paragraph 3, recounting trade on a value-added basis would most likely

options.A: raise the recorded exports of assembling countries to their final markets, since hidden components would be counted.
options.B: confirm that the bilateral balances that attract political attention had been reported accurately all along.
options.C: sharply worsen an assembling country's balance with the rest of the world, since its exports would be revalued.
options.D: leave an assembling country's balance with the world roughly unchanged while altering its balances with particular partners.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the distortion that the passage attributes to gross trade statistics?

options.A: In a group project, every student receives the same mark regardless of how much each contributed to the final report.
options.B: A shop sells imported goods at a price below what it paid for them, so its sales figures overstate how profitable it is.
options.C: A company's accountant mistakenly records the same sale twice, so that the firm's annual revenue appears larger than it really was.
options.D: In a group project, the student who hands in the final report is credited with all of the work, though most was done by others.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: Countries that supply the costliest components may appear in bilateral figures as having sold nothing to the final market.
options.B: Value-added figures ought to replace gross figures for all official uses once the tables behind them are compiled more often.
options.C: A tariff aimed at the partner with the largest recorded deficit may fall mostly on workers who contributed a modest share of the value.
options.D: The tables used to calculate value added are compiled only now and then and are partly filled in with estimates.

questions.question: According to the passage, a new firm that must compete with established foreign rivals at once may fail because

options.A: it may not survive long enough to acquire the experience that would make it efficient.
options.B: its government will be unable to bear the political cost of withdrawing protection from it.
options.C: the workers it trains will leave for competitors before it can benefit from their skills.
options.D: its foreign rivals will deliberately sell below cost in order to drive it out of the market.

questions.question: The phrase 'growing larger without growing up' in paragraph 3 implies that a sheltered firm

options.A: is likely to shrink steadily once its owners realise that the protection will be extended.
options.B: expands so quickly that its managers have no time to learn the skills that it requires.
options.C: can expand its output and workforce while never reaching the efficiency needed to compete unaided.
options.D: learns more slowly than smaller rivals, since large firms are by nature harder to manage.

questions.question: Paragraph 2 contributes to the passage chiefly by

options.A: explaining how protection builds a body of owners, workers and officials who resist its removal.
options.B: offering historical evidence that countries which protected their industries went on to industrialise successfully.
options.C: adding a reason why the market alone will supply too little learning, which strengthens the case set out before it.
options.D: raising an objection to the infant-industry argument that the author then answers in the paragraph that follows.

questions.question: The author's claim that export performance is 'especially revealing' rests on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: That exporting firms are generally given larger subsidies than firms that sell only at home.
options.B: That success in a foreign market is hard to achieve without actually becoming competitive.
options.C: That foreign markets are always easier to enter than the home market was before protection.
options.D: That protected firms usually prefer selling abroad to selling in their sheltered home market.

questions.question: Suppose a country's car industry, sheltered by tariffs for twenty years, became a strong exporter only after a fiscal crisis forced the government to cut those tariffs sharply. The author would most likely regard this case as

options.A: consistent with the view that removing shelter, not prolonging it, supplies the pressure on firms to improve.
options.B: an example of how conditions fixed in advance can make the end of protection credible to firms.
options.C: proof that the infant-industry argument is unsound in principle and should be given up altogether.
options.D: evidence that twenty years of protection was the learning period this particular industry needed.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the statement that 'it does not yet exist' refers to

options.A: the industries that the government has already chosen to support with public funds.
options.B: the roads and the workforce habits that a new export activity would need in order to succeed.
options.C: the profits that investors expect to earn once a new industry has been established in the region.
options.D: knowledge of what a region could produce profitably, which can be gained only by trying.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that because so many state-backed ventures have failed, industrial policy ought to be abandoned by governments.
options.B: describe the practices, such as public criteria and fixed review dates, that keep officials from being captured by firms.
options.C: challenge the picture behind a familiar objection to industrial policy and relocate its main risk to the difficulty of withdrawing support.
options.D: show that government officials are better placed than private investors to identify the industries that will flourish.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the advantage of private investors over officials, as asserted in paragraph 1, as

options.A: illusory in every setting, since officials and investors know equally little about all kinds of markets.
options.B: greatest in activities an economy has never tried, since there investors bear their own losses most directly.
options.C: decisive, so that the state should support only the industries in which investors have already shown interest.
options.D: real when the possible options are already known, but of limited use when what an economy can produce has yet to be discovered.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude towards industrial policy as it emerges by the end of the passage?

options.A: Qualified support that defends its rationale while admitting a risk that cannot be wholly removed.
options.B: Enthusiastic advocacy that treats the objections of its critics as resting on a simple error.
options.C: Detached neutrality that declines to side with either the advocates or the critics of such policy.
options.D: Reluctant rejection on the ground that closeness between officials and firms leads to capture.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 3?

options.A: Officials frequently lack detailed information about local conditions that the firms operating there already possess.
options.B: Later entrants to new export activities usually must repeat nearly all of the pioneer's costly trials, since its lessons cannot be copied.
options.C: Pioneers whose ventures failed had, on average, less access to bank credit than pioneers whose ventures went on to succeed.
options.D: A large share of the ventures that governments have backed in the past failed at considerable cost to public funds.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: contending that who pays whom matters more than efficiency when the law settles a dispute over pollution.
options.B: arguing that because the harm done by pollution is reciprocal, the law should stop treating those who pollute as wrongdoers.
options.C: demonstrating that bargaining between polluters and their neighbours reaches an efficient result whichever party holds the legal right.
options.D: showing that an argument often cited against regulating pollution in fact helps identify where regulation is needed.

questions.question: The passage gives each of the following as a reason why the residents of a large city could not bargain with those who pollute its air EXCEPT that

options.A: every resident has an incentive to let others do the negotiating and the paying.
options.B: residents would disagree among themselves about how much cleaner air is worth to each of them.
options.C: it is hard to establish how much of the harm each polluter has caused.
options.D: each resident bears only a small part of the total harm done by the pollution.

questions.question: When the author says that a certain reading 'takes the conditional for the claim' (paragraph 2), the point is that this reading

options.A: assumes that property rights can always be defined clearly, when in practice they are usually disputed.
options.B: confuses the efficient outcome of a bargain with the fair outcome that the parties ought to reach.
options.C: treats a result that holds only under a stated condition as though it held in general.
options.D: relies on what the parties claim they would accept instead of on what they actually agree to pay.

questions.question: The closing sentence, 'Those who live downwind are not', implies that

options.A: people exposed to pollution care how the legal right is assigned, even when the physical outcome would be unchanged.
options.B: households near a polluting factory rarely understand how the efficient outcome of a bargain is reached.
options.C: an efficient outcome is reached only when the households, not the factory, hold the right to clean air.
options.D: residents downwind of a factory will refuse to pay for a filter however cheaply it could be fitted.

questions.question: According to the passage, the rebound from an efficiency gain tends to be small when

options.A: the efficiency gain applies to an input that whole industries use in production.
options.B: people already consume nearly as much of the service as they want, whatever its price.
options.C: the money saved is spent on other goods and services instead of on more energy.
options.D: households are able to measure their savings precisely and can plan their spending around them.

questions.question: The example of the family that takes a holiday flight (paragraph 3) serves to

options.A: illustrate how money saved on energy can lead to more energy use through spending on something else.
options.B: show that the rebound from efficiency gains in transport is usually larger than the original saving.
options.C: explain why the mechanism behind the rebound is now disputed by economists who study energy.
options.D: suggest that families who save money on fuel ought to spend it on goods that need less energy.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the two camps described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: sympathetic to those who doubt efficiency, since the author concludes that it achieves little on its own.
options.B: supportive of those who favour efficiency, while regretting that the rebound has been overstated.
options.C: dismissive of both, because the author regards the rebound as too uncertain to be worth discussing.
options.D: critical of both, for treating as settled a question whose answer varies with the case.

questions.question: Which of the following policies would best match the recommendation in the final paragraph?

options.A: A city pays for insulating older homes and cuts the tax on heating fuel so that poorer households can afford to keep warm.
options.B: A city raises the tax on heating fuel steeply and ends all of its support for insulation and efficient boilers.
options.C: A city pays for insulating older homes and, over the same years, raises the tax on the fuels used to heat them.
options.D: A city bans the sale of inefficient boilers and leaves the price of heating fuel to be set entirely by the market.

questions.question: According to the passage, if cutting emissions turns out to be harder than expected, a carbon tax will

options.A: lead the government to lower the rate so that firms are not burdened by unexpected costs.
options.B: keep the price per tonne where it was set while emissions end up higher than planned.
options.C: hold emissions at the planned level while firms pay more for each tonne they continue to emit.
options.D: cause the price of emitting a tonne of carbon to rise, perhaps steeply, until firms cut back.

questions.question: Suppose a river pollutant does little harm at low concentrations but kills most of the river's fish once its concentration in any single season passes a known level. By the reasoning of paragraph 2, the better instrument for controlling it would be

options.A: a limit on the total quantity discharged, since keeping below the threshold matters more than a predictable cost.
options.B: either instrument equally well, since a regulator who chose the right level could reach the same outcome by both.
options.C: a fixed charge per unit discharged, since the harm depends on what accumulates over decades and not on any one season.
options.D: a limit on discharges paired with a ceiling on the permit price, since that keeps costs predictable if cutting proves hard.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 3 in the passage?

options.A: It shows that free allocation of permits to industries makes trading schemes unfair and therefore politically unpopular.
options.B: It extends the argument of paragraph 2 by showing how uncertainty over costs affects voters as well as firms.
options.C: It supplies the author's own reasons for preferring a cap to a tax, after the economic case has been weighed.
options.D: It presents an objection from supporters of trading that the economic case for a tax overlooks political feasibility.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Now that hybrids exist, uncertainty about the cost of abatement no longer makes any difference to carbon policy.
options.B: Because they state their goal openly, trading schemes are easier to defend and should be chosen over taxes.
options.C: A tax and a trading scheme that each set a low price on a narrow range of emissions would both do little.
options.D: The long debate between supporters of taxes and of caps was at bottom nothing more than a quarrel about labels.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the example of the road approved through a forest is used to show that

options.A: roads should not be built through forests unless the time saved by drivers is very large.
options.B: the cost of replacing a forest with embankments and pumps is a reasonable guide to its value.
options.C: planning authorities generally overstate the value of time saved by drivers in order to justify new roads.
options.D: declining to put a figure on nature can amount to valuing it at nothing.

questions.question: In saying that very large totals for the value of nature's services 'should therefore be read as rhetoric rather than as accounts' (paragraph 3), the author means that such totals

options.A: are usually calculated dishonestly by people who wish to exaggerate the importance of conservation.
options.B: may draw attention to nature's importance but cannot be treated as meaningful measurements of value.
options.C: should be replaced by totals built up from many small valuations, such as one orchard's bees multiplied out.
options.D: are accurate in principle but too large for governments to use when drawing up their budgets.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the defenders' claim in paragraph 2 that making the value of nature explicit 'protects it from being treated as free'?

options.A: Where explicit valuations are used, low estimates of a habitat's worth have often been cited to approve projects that would otherwise be refused.
options.B: Values in money calculated for the pollinators of the whole world turn out to be impossible to interpret in any useful way.
options.C: Estimates of what it would cost to replace a wetland with embankments and pumps differ considerably from one town to another, even within a single region.
options.D: Surveys find that many people regard it as distasteful to attach money values to forests, rivers and wild animals.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard an explicit money value for a forest as most useful when the decision concerns

options.A: how much all the forests of a large country contribute to the economy that depends on them.
options.B: whether to allow a loss of forest so large that it could not be reversed for generations.
options.C: whether to clear a small part of a forest that will otherwise remain largely intact.
options.D: whether forests ought to be treated as things that can be bought and sold like other property.

questions.question: According to the passage, a gas boom makes life harder for a country's exporting manufacturers because

options.A: a stronger currency prices their goods out of foreign markets while the booming sectors push up the wages they must pay.
options.B: the government taxes manufacturing more heavily in order to fund the expansion of the gas sector and its services.
options.C: cheaper imports of raw materials allow foreign rivals to set up competing factories inside the country.
options.D: their most skilled engineers and managers are recruited to run the government's new fund invested abroad.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the view reported in paragraph 2 against the author's objection to it?

options.A: Funds invested abroad have slowed the rise of the currency in several countries that export large amounts of gas.
options.B: Countries with fertile land have tended, over long periods, to export more food than they import from abroad.
options.C: Workers who moved from factories into the gas sector during booms have usually earned more than they did before they moved.
options.D: Countries whose factories closed during commodity booms have usually rebuilt comparable export industries within a few years of prices falling.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards a resource boom as most damaging when

options.A: manufacturers fail to raise their productivity as fast as the wages they pay to workers in their factories.
options.B: a country decides to extract and sell its gas at all, instead of leaving the reserves untouched for later generations.
options.C: the windfall is spent at home so quickly that it drives up the currency and wages until other exporters disappear.
options.D: the national currency rises in value, whatever the government does with the revenue from the new exports.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the concern the author raises in paragraph 3?

options.A: A city builds a costly stadium for a single sporting event and then finds that the stadium stands empty for most of the year.
options.B: A town lets its orchestra disband while a cheap rival holds its audience, and when interest returns finds its trained players and teachers gone for good.
options.C: A firm pays out an unusually profitable year's earnings as bonuses to its staff and later finds that it cannot meet its debts once its profits return to normal.
options.D: A farmer switches from wheat to rice when rice prices rise and switches back when they fall, losing little each time he changes crops.

questions.question: The example of the household that sells its furniture (paragraph 2) is used to

options.A: show that national accounts already deduct the wear on machines and buildings when they calculate net product.
options.B: argue that welfare cannot be measured at all, since households commonly misunderstand their own finances.
options.C: show by analogy why counting the proceeds of running down an asset as income gives a misleading picture.
options.D: suggest that national governments, like households, should avoid selling any of their natural assets at all.

questions.question: By the reasoning of paragraph 3, which of the following would add to GDP while leaving people no better off than they were before the damage occurred?

options.A: Families in a city whose air has worsened buy air purifiers so that the air in their homes is as clean as it used to be.
options.B: A hospital builds a new wing that allows it to treat far more patients each year than it was ever able to treat before.
options.C: A factory installs equipment that cuts its discharges into a river to well below the level they were at when it opened.
options.D: A government replants with trees a stretch of land that had been bare and unproductive for as long as anyone can remember.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards those critics who urge that GDP be abandoned is best described as one of

options.A: agreement, since the author has shown in two paragraphs that GDP misrepresents what happens to the environment.
options.B: indifference, as the author thinks that whether GDP is kept or dropped matters little beside the problem of valuation.
options.C: contempt, because the author holds that only those who misunderstand national accounts could make such a demand.
options.D: disagreement, on the ground that GDP still serves well the purposes for which it was built.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author be most likely to accept?

options.A: Corrections for depletion should be built into GDP itself, so that a single headline figure reflects natural capital.
options.B: An account of changes in natural assets is worth publishing even if its estimates of depletion rest on uncertain assumptions.
options.C: The depletion of a fishery could be valued exactly once the rate at which its stock regenerates is known.
options.D: A country whose GDP is rising while its natural assets are falling must be growing poorer as a result.

questions.question: According to the passage, advocates of degrowth explain part of the apparent separation of output from emissions in rich economies as the result of

options.A: costs of clean power falling much faster than forecasters had predicted only a generation ago.
options.B: electricity being generated from cleaner sources and heavy industry giving way to services at home.
options.C: recessions that struck services harder than heavy industry and so reduced output faster than emissions.
options.D: polluting production having been moved to other countries instead of being avoided altogether.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the claim that much of the separation of output from emissions is 'merely relative' means that

options.A: each unit of output has become cleaner, but output has grown enough to keep total emissions from falling.
options.B: the separation can be seen only when emissions are measured relative to imports instead of to output.
options.C: emissions have fallen in some rich countries only in relation to the higher emissions of poorer ones.
options.D: emissions and output have separated in absolute terms, though rather less in some sectors of the economy than in others.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Because the cost of clean power has fallen so fast, emissions in rich countries will now decline quickly enough.
options.B: Proof that a rich country's emissions fell while its output rose would not by itself show that green growth is an adequate response.
options.C: Once the carbon embodied in imports is counted, no rich country has reduced its emissions while its output grew.
options.D: Those who favour degrowth are mistaken in wanting a different kind of society from the one that now exists.

questions.question: The two hypothetical economies in paragraph 3, one growing while its emissions fall and one shrinking while its emissions rise, serve mainly to

options.A: show that policy should aim to shift output from heavy industry towards services such as teaching, nursing and repairing.
options.B: show that green growth is correct to hold that output and emissions can move apart in rich economies.
options.C: show that the size of GDP is only loosely tied to environmental harm, so making it the target in either direction is a mistake.
options.D: show that recessions do more environmental damage than periods of growth, which counts against the case for degrowth.

questions.question: It follows from the stance proposed in paragraph 4 that an advocate of degrowth who accepted it

options.A: would have to give up any wish for a different kind of society once the environmental limits were being met.
options.B: could still argue for a smaller economy, but not on the ground that the environment requires it once the limits are being met.
options.C: would treat any fall in output within the limits as a failure of policy that ought to be corrected.
options.D: would have to agree that output must keep rising, since growth within the limits would then be the aim of policy.

questions.question: According to the passage, the drawback of assigning default carbon values to imports by product and by country is that such values

options.A: are set so high that most imports from poorer countries are excluded from the importing country's market altogether.
options.B: allow exporters to claim rebates that are larger than the carbon price they actually paid at home.
options.C: penalise clean producers located in dirty countries while rewarding dirty producers located in clean ones.
options.D: can be observed directly only by the government of the country where the goods were made.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Leakage has been greatly overstated, so a country can price carbon alone without any measures at its border to protect its industry.
options.B: A border charge on carbon is the obvious answer to leakage, since it puts domestic and foreign producers on equal terms and removes any reason to relocate.
options.C: Border charges on carbon are protection dressed in green and will provoke retaliation, so countries should avoid introducing them.
options.D: A border charge on carbon is hard to administer and may meet a smaller threat than feared, yet if well designed it could draw other countries into pricing carbon.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim in paragraph 3 that the problem of leakage has been overstated?

options.A: When one region's carbon price rose to a high level, its heavy industries moved a large share of their output to regions with no such price.
options.B: Managers of industrial firms report that access to markets is the main consideration when they decide where to build a plant.
options.C: Several heavy industries in countries with carbon prices have received free allowances that shield them from most of the cost.
options.D: Across most industries, differences in wages between countries turn out to be far larger than differences in the cost of carbon.

questions.question: The exporting country's reasoning described in paragraph 4, which lets a border charge work as 'a lever', depends on the charge being one that

options.A: lets the importing country keep all of its revenue, so that it can be spent on reducing emissions at home.
options.B: applies only to trading partners whose own carbon prices are already as high as the importing country's price.
options.C: is set high enough to stop most imports from countries that have not yet introduced a price on carbon.
options.D: is reduced or waived for goods whose makers have already paid a carbon price in their own country.

questions.question: The phrase 'not unreasonably' in the final sentence indicates that the author

options.A: believes that poorer exporting countries would be right to retaliate against every carbon charge at the border.
options.B: would think the charge of protectionism justified against a border charge lacking the design features just listed.
options.C: considers the critics unreasonable in their accusation but understands why they feel aggrieved by it.
options.D: regards the charge of protectionism as valid against any border adjustment, however carefully it is designed and presented.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that average differences between human populations are environmental rather than genetic.
options.B: correct a widespread habit of treating heritability as a measure of how unchangeable a trait is.
options.C: explain how breeders use heritability to predict how quickly a herd will respond to selection.
options.D: show that heritability estimates are too unreliable to be of use to breeders or to researchers.

questions.question: According to the passage, if every child in a group received exactly the same diet, schooling and care, the heritability of most traits would rise because

options.A: the environmental differences among the children would have been removed, leaving mainly genetic ones.
options.B: identical upbringing would allow the children's genes to exert a stronger influence on development.
options.C: children raised in identical conditions come to resemble their parents more closely in every trait.
options.D: measurements taken in uniform settings are more precise than measurements taken in varied ones.

questions.question: The example of finger number in paragraph 2 is used to show that

options.A: accidents are the main source of variation in most human physical traits.
options.B: developmental programmes are more dependable than environmental influences on the body.
options.C: a trait built by a genetic programme can still show low heritability.
options.D: heritability rises whenever the environments of a group are made more uniform.

questions.question: A study finds that within each of two towns, differences in children's reading scores are highly heritable, and that the average score in one town is well above that in the other. Which conclusion is most consistent with the passage?

options.A: Reading scores in the lower town cannot be raised much by improving its schools or its libraries.
options.B: The gap between the towns must be largely genetic, since heritability is high within each town.
options.C: The study must be mistaken, since a trait cannot be heritable within towns that differ on average.
options.D: The gap between the towns could be produced entirely by differences between their schools or homes.

questions.question: According to the passage, a signal that any animal can produce

options.A: is preferred by females because it costs its bearer very little to display.
options.B: soon stops telling the receiver anything about the animal that sends it.
options.C: is the kind most often found among antelope when they spot a predator.
options.D: is eventually replaced by an ornament that females come to find more beautiful.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, 'the embarrassment' that the reply 'turns ... into the explanation' refers to

options.A: the burden that an extravagant ornament places on the animal that carries it.
options.B: Darwin's failure to propose any explanation at all for why such ornaments exist.
options.C: the awkwardness of the courtship display that the peacock performs before females.
options.D: the difficulty that females face in judging which of many males is healthiest.

questions.question: The remark that 'a signal equally costly for all would sort no one' (paragraph 4) implies that

options.A: the more expensive a display is in absolute terms, the more reliably it identifies the fittest males.
options.B: most of the ornaments seen in nature cost every member of a species roughly the same amount.
options.C: females are unable to tell males apart once every male in a population has an ornament.
options.D: a display reveals quality only if weaker animals find it harder to bear than stronger ones do.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the costly-signal explanation is best described as

options.A: neutral, setting out the explanation without indicating any judgement of its merits.
options.B: sceptical, regarding it as an ingenious proposal that has gathered little real support.
options.C: appreciative of what it explains while insistent that it does not explain everything.
options.D: unreserved, treating it as a complete account of why ornaments evolve in animals.

questions.question: The comparison with the fragility of a glass in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that camouflaged moths are, in practice, as easily destroyed as glassware on a shelf.
options.B: show that fitness, like fragility, can be established only after the organism has died or survived.
options.C: argue that chance matters more than inherited traits in deciding which organisms survive.
options.D: show that fitness can be a real property of an organism even when outcomes fail to display it.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the existence of drift as

options.A: evidence that fitness and the actual record of reproduction are not the same thing.
options.B: the main reason why biologists usually measure fitness by counting offspring.
options.C: a difficulty that the propensity view of fitness cannot yet satisfactorily explain.
options.D: a sign that natural selection does not operate at all in small populations.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the complaint that natural selection is a tautology?

options.A: Some predictions made by applying the theory of natural selection to particular populations have turned out to be false.
options.B: For most traits, the only available way to tell which variant raises expected reproduction is to see which variant has in fact left more offspring.
options.C: In some populations, the variants that ecological analysis rates fittest sometimes leave fewer offspring than other variants do.
options.D: Field biologists studying wild populations usually estimate the fitness of a variant by counting the offspring it leaves.

questions.question: The passage supports each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: Loose writing about fitness can blur the difference between measuring it and defining it.
options.B: Whether a variant is fitter can, at least in some cases, be established without counting its offspring.
options.C: Predictions derived from natural selection have so far been confirmed whenever they were tested.
options.D: In small populations, organisms that are less fit can leave more offspring than fitter ones.

questions.question: Which of the following does the passage cite as evidence against the argument based on the peculiar inheritance of ants, bees and wasps?

options.A: A worker that never reproduces cannot pass on the traits that make it a good worker.
options.B: Males in ants, bees and wasps develop from eggs that have not been fertilised.
options.C: Termites, which lack that pattern of inheritance, have also evolved sterile castes.
options.D: Workers in social insect colonies typically raise relatives rather than unrelated young.

questions.question: In describing sterility as 'an extreme point on a continuum of helping' (paragraph 2), the author implies that

options.A: sterility in insects evolved earlier than the milder forms of helping seen among relatives.
options.B: helping relatives is common only in those insect species whose workers are sterile.
options.C: workers lose the ability to reproduce as a consequence of the effort spent raising siblings.
options.D: sterile workers differ from other helpful relatives in how far they help, not in the kind of explanation they need.

questions.question: Paragraph 3 functions in the passage mainly to

options.A: present an appealing refinement of the kinship argument and then show why it proved inadequate.
options.B: show that biologists have since abandoned the general kinship argument set out in paragraph 2.
options.C: explain why Darwin's proposal that selection acts on the family was eventually rejected.
options.D: supply the decisive evidence that ecological conditions, not kinship, explain sterile castes.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Kinship plays only a minor part in explaining why workers in insect colonies forgo reproduction.
options.B: Two insect species with similar relatedness among nestmates might differ in whether sterile castes evolve, because of differences in their surroundings.
options.C: Sterile castes are unlikely to evolve in any species whose nestmates are only modestly related to one another.
options.D: Where a queen mates with several males, the colony cannot sustain a caste of sterile workers.

questions.question: According to the passage, a change to one of a toolkit gene's switches can be less disruptive than a change to the gene itself because

options.A: switches are shared by almost all animals, whereas toolkit genes differ from lineage to lineage.
options.B: a change to the gene would alter where its protein is made but not the shape of the protein.
options.C: changes to switches arise far more often than changes to the toolkit genes that they regulate.
options.D: a switch can alter a single structure while leaving the others in which the gene acts untouched.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, 'a shared plan' most nearly means

options.A: an inherited timetable fixing the order in which each organ appears during growth.
options.B: a common design for the structures that the developmental genes bring into being.
options.C: an intention that guides evolution towards a fixed and predetermined final form.
options.D: a common set of genes that decide where the head, limbs and segments of a body form.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as an example of 'the opposite error' described in paragraph 4?

options.A: Concluding that the hearts of two distant animals must be built alike because the same gene starts heart formation in both.
options.B: Concluding that the eyes of insects and vertebrates were assembled separately, since their structures differ.
options.C: Concluding that much change in animal form has come from altered switches rather than from new proteins.
options.D: Concluding that a fly and a mouse share no developmental genes because their bodies look so different.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the organisation of the passage?

options.A: A discovery about eyes is described, its practical uses in medicine are listed, and objections to it are dismissed.
options.B: Two rival theories of animal form are set out, the evidence for each is weighed, and one is finally preferred.
options.C: An expectation is overturned by a discovery, whose lesson is then accepted in part and guarded against overextension.
options.D: A puzzle about form is posed, several proposed solutions are rejected in turn, and the question is left open.

questions.question: According to the passage, during ordinary stretches of geological time the species more likely to vanish are those that

options.A: belong to groups that have long lived in the shadow of their competitors.
options.B: depend on a narrow range of foods, occupy small areas or breed slowly.
options.C: are large-bodied and unable to wait out a period of scarcity in a dormant state.
options.D: had flourished for a very long time under conditions that were stable.

questions.question: The author calls the traits that aided survival at the end of the Cretaceous 'accidents' (paragraph 2) because they

options.A: show that survival in a mass extinction was decided by pure chance rather than by traits.
options.B: appeared suddenly in the surviving animals in the years just after the asteroid struck.
options.C: had not arisen as adaptations to the kind of crisis in which they turned out to be decisive.
options.D: gave no real advantage during the crisis to the animals that happened to possess them.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim about the mammals in paragraph 3?

options.A: Large mammals with specialised diets also died out at the end of the Cretaceous, while small mammals with varied diets survived.
options.B: Some mammals of the late Cretaceous had larger brains in proportion to their bodies than dinosaurs of a similar size.
options.C: After the crisis, mammals diversified rapidly into many of the ways of life that the dinosaurs had once occupied.
options.D: Several groups of dinosaurs had already been declining in number of species for some time before the asteroid struck.

questions.question: The author would be LEAST likely to accept which of the following?

options.A: Explaining which groups exist today requires knowing both how well they were adapted and what catastrophes occurred.
options.B: The diversification of groups that survive a mass extinction proceeds through ordinary natural selection.
options.C: The extinction of a lineage need not show that it was poorly suited to the conditions it normally faced.
options.D: Because the traits that mattered in mass extinctions were accidents, the survivors of those events were not selected at all.

questions.question: According to the passage, the discovery that strengthened the replicator-first case was that RNA

options.A: is the molecule in which the cell stores most of its instructions for building proteins.
options.B: can copy itself with high accuracy in water without the help of any protein at all.
options.C: forms readily from simple ingredients and a source of energy near hot springs on the sea floor.
options.D: can speed up chemical reactions as well as carry information.

questions.question: In arguing that 'something like inheritance exists before any gene' (paragraph 3), metabolism-first theorists are responding chiefly to

options.A: the discovery that the cell's protein-building machinery is made largely of RNA.
options.B: the claim that a network without heredity has no means of building up improvements.
options.C: the claim that the building blocks of RNA are difficult to make without enzymes.
options.D: the proposal that life began on mineral surfaces near hot springs on the sea floor.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the phrase 'in a chemical vacuum' refers to

options.A: the absence of any earlier chemistry to supply materials and energy.
options.B: a stage of history in which no selection among competing molecules had yet begun.
options.C: a setting without the RNA molecules on which all later living things came to rely.
options.D: a region of space entirely empty of matter, where no molecules could exist.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Replicator and metabolism theorists often address different questions, which is why each wins easy points against the other's weakest claim.
options.B: Because replicators could not have assembled themselves unaided, the metabolism-first account of life's origin is the more plausible one.
options.C: Accounts giving priority to replication or to self-sustaining chemistry are better read as describing successive stages than as rivals.
options.D: Because the earliest stages of life left almost no record, the question of which came first should be set aside as unanswerable.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the 'easy points' mentioned in paragraph 4 are won by

options.A: attacking claims that a staged account combining both views would not need to make.
options.B: raising questions about the earliest stages of life that can now never be answered.
options.C: the metabolism camp alone, through its criticisms of the chemistry of the RNA world.
options.D: showing that the central thesis of the opposing camp is mistaken about life's origin.

questions.question: The image of the ball in paragraph 2 implies that

options.A: the outcomes of evolution are fixed in advance by the physical shape of the environment.
options.B: the history of a lineage is of no use in understanding what that lineage became.
options.C: an end point reached by a route no one could repeat may still have been very likely to be reached.
options.D: contingency enthusiasts are wrong to claim that many forms appeared only once.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the two schools is best described as

options.A: partisan, favouring the convergence school and treating the contingency school's case as anecdote.
options.B: even-handed, crediting each with a real insight while faulting how it treats evidence.
options.C: dismissive, regarding the entire debate between them as confused and not worth pursuing.
options.D: deferential, accepting the claims of each school and declining to judge between them.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the reconciliation proposed in paragraph 3?

options.A: Intelligence that is capable of language and the making of tools has arisen in only one lineage of animals so far.
options.B: Far more forms of life have appeared once in the history of life and never recurred than have appeared repeatedly.
options.C: A replay of evolution would probably not produce birds as the main flying animals, nor backboned animals as the main swimmers.
options.D: Most supposed independent origins of eyes, wings and streamlined bodies turn out to descend from one shared ancestral form.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 4 that the author regards the repeated evolution of eyes and wings as

options.A: good evidence that intelligence like ours was most probably a fluke of one lineage's history.
options.B: good evidence that intelligence like ours is a likely outcome of any rerun of evolution.
options.C: irrelevant to any question about what a replay of evolution would be likely to produce.
options.D: insufficient grounds for expecting a replay of evolution to produce a creature like us.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most analogous to the reconciliation of the two schools in paragraph 3?

options.A: A town rebuilt after a flood would almost surely again have bakeries and schools, though chance would decide who ran them.
options.B: A river fed by the same snowmelt every spring rises on the same day each year and always reaches exactly the same height.
options.C: A chess game replayed from the same opening position follows a different course every time and ends in a different result.
options.D: Two engineers working apart design nearly identical bridges because both have copied the same famous earlier bridge.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: criticise public figures who take part in planting ceremonies mainly in order to be photographed doing something popular.
options.B: argue that forest recovery should be judged by the lasting forest it produces rather than by the number of saplings that are planted.
options.C: argue that tree planting campaigns should be replaced everywhere by the protection of land, so that forests can regenerate naturally without any planting.
options.D: explain the practical techniques by which nurseries and planters can raise the survival rate of the saplings they put into the ground.

questions.question: According to the passage, one reason natural regeneration is undervalued is that

options.A: it succeeds only on grasslands, which many people wrongly assume were once covered by forest.
options.B: it usually costs more than planting because the protected land has to be guarded against grazing, fire and clearing.
options.C: for several years after protection begins, the land looks like scrub and does not resemble visible progress.
options.D: the species that arrive by themselves are often poorly suited to the soil and climate of the site where they settle.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the statement 'The objection is not to the spade but to the scoreboard' means that the author

options.A: objects to competition between rival campaigns that try to outdo each other in the number of trees they plant.
options.B: objects to manual planting by volunteers and prefers that saplings be put in by trained professionals.
options.C: accepts the counting of saplings planted, provided that the trees are put in during the correct season.
options.D: objects to the way the success of forest campaigns is measured, not to the act of planting trees itself.

questions.question: Which of the following programmes would the author of the passage most likely regard as best designed?

options.A: One that waters and tends every sapling through its first dry months, so that the number of trees reported as planted is accurate rather than inflated.
options.B: One that refuses to plant anywhere, including on badly degraded soils, and instead fences every site and waits for a forest to return on its own.
options.C: One that fences off land near surviving seed trees, plants only on degraded plots with no seed source, and reports how much forest still stands after fifteen years.
options.D: One that plants a wide mix of native species instead of a single fast-growing tree, and reports the total number of saplings put into the ground each season.

questions.question: According to the passage, protecting a large predator can benefit less appealing species because

options.A: the large area that such a predator needs, once protected, also shelters many other species living in it.
options.B: donors who first give money for the predator are later persuaded to give money for the less appealing species too.
options.C: breeding programmes and tracking collars for the predator also yield information about the other species.
options.D: the predator keeps down the animals that would otherwise eat or crowd out the less appealing species.

questions.question: The list 'a single cave, a spring, a patch of chalk grassland, the gravel bed of one river' in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate the kinds of places in which donors most often refuse to pay for conservation work of any kind.
options.B: give examples of habitats whose threatened species would gain nothing from the protection of a charismatic animal.
options.C: suggest that conservation money should be moved away from tiger reserves towards caves, springs and rivers.
options.D: show that small habitats are generally richer in species than the forests and grasslands that large predators need.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the use of flagship species in conservation is best described as

options.A: detached neutrality: the passage sets out the critics' complaint and its defence without deciding between them.
options.B: strong enthusiasm: by protecting whole landscapes they answer the critics' complaint about neglected species.
options.C: qualified approval: they are a useful means of raising attention and money but an incomplete guide to priorities.
options.D: firm disapproval: they let the tastes of donors distort priorities and should therefore be dropped from conservation appeals altogether.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that a donation made in the name of a famous animal does most to answer the critics' complaint when it is

options.A: given by donors who are already aware that small and drab species are more threatened than famous ones.
options.B: spent on breeding programmes that increase the number of the famous animal itself living within its protected reserves.
options.C: raised in an appeal that features a beetle or mussel alongside the famous animal in its pictures.
options.D: spent on protecting the habitat that the animal shares with many other species, rather than on the animal alone.

questions.question: According to the passage, compensation schemes fall short in practice partly because they

options.A: are run by conservation charities that do not understand the cost of farming close to the forest edge.
options.B: pay only for the market value of damaged crops and leave out losses such as sleep, schooling and constant fear.
options.C: pay farmers more than their crops were worth, which removes any reason for them to guard their fields at night.
options.D: reach only those farmers who have retaliated against elephants and so reward hostility rather than tolerance.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the claim that such a scheme 'does not shift the burden; it documents it' means that the scheme

options.A: records that farmers have suffered a loss while leaving most of that loss with the farmers who suffered it.
options.B: produces useful records of elephant movements that can later be used to plan deterrents for affected villages.
options.C: requires so much paperwork that farmers spend more on completing forms than they ever receive in payment.
options.D: transfers the cost of elephant damage from the farmers to the state, but only after a long and frustrating administrative delay.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that hostility to elephants should not be read as ignorance?

options.A: Villages that received prompt and full compensation reported far less retaliation than villages where payments were slow and partial.
options.B: In affected villages, farmers who retaliated against elephants could describe the animals' role in spreading the seeds of forest trees as accurately as farmers who never retaliated.
options.C: Farmers who had lost nothing to elephants were as likely to retaliate as those with heavy losses, and retaliation fell sharply after lessons on the animals' role.
options.D: Tolerance of elephants differed widely between neighbouring communities that had suffered similar losses, reflecting differences in tradition.

questions.question: The author's remark that deterrents push 'elephants onto the next village's fields' suggests that

options.A: neighbouring villages ought to coordinate their deterrents so that elephants are steered back into the forest.
options.B: a remedy that lowers one village's losses may only pass them to neighbours, leaving the wider question of who pays unresolved.
options.C: the costs of a recovered elephant population are in fact spread evenly across the villages that border the forest.
options.D: beehive fences and chilli repellents seldom reduce losses at all, since elephants soon learn to ignore them and return to the same fields.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, the frequent low-intensity fires of many dry forests

options.A: cleared away the material on the forest floor while leaving most of the older, thick-barked trees unharmed.
options.B: were started deliberately by forest agencies to reduce the fuel that had built up under years of suppression.
options.C: killed off the older trees so that young trees and undergrowth could grow in the light that was let in.
options.D: climbed into the crowns of the trees but burned out before they could spread to neighbouring stands.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as contributing to catastrophic fires EXCEPT

options.A: the spread of houses and settlements into land that is covered by woods and forest.
options.B: long spells of drought and heat in the seasons when the most destructive fires break out.
options.C: the build-up of undergrowth and fallen branches in dry forests after decades of fire suppression.
options.D: the planting of fast-growing, thin-barked trees in place of the older species of dry forests.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a sharp rise in burning in a wet forest where fire had historically been rare as

options.A: evidence that the rise must have been caused by housing spreading into the wooded land around it.
options.B: further proof that suppressing fires is always a mistake, since fuel must have built up there as well.
options.C: a welcome correction, because fires in every forest clear the undergrowth and protect the older trees.
options.D: a genuine danger to that forest, not a sign that fire is returning to its natural place there.

questions.question: The asymmetry described in the last paragraph implies that

options.A: the public blames managers equally for escaped planned burns and for wildfires caused by accumulated fuel.
options.B: a manager may keep suppressing fires even when aware that doing so raises the risk of catastrophic fire later.
options.C: planned burns are in fact more dangerous to towns than wildfires that grow from decades of accumulated fuel.
options.D: managers continue suppressing fires mainly because they have not yet understood how fuel builds up on the floor of dry forests.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Because exclusion carries certain costs and often only assumed benefits, removing residents from protected land should be justified in each case rather than treated as the default.
options.B: Because romantic images of forest dwellers are as misleading as images of wilderness, conservation should rely on neither residents nor parks to protect species.
options.C: Because national parks were founded on a false picture of untouched nature, the model should be abandoned and replaced by community management everywhere.
options.D: Because local residents shaped many admired landscapes over centuries, they should never be removed from land that is set aside for conservation.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, removing residents from landscapes that had long been shaped by them

options.A: allowed grasslands to stay open because grazing animals could now move freely without being herded.
options.B: was generally carried out with fair compensation for the homes, graves and sacred places that were lost.
options.C: started an unplanned change in which some of the qualities that made the places worth protecting declined.
options.D: returned the land to the original state that visitors had admired before the residents first arrived.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 3 in the passage?

options.A: It offers new evidence that most forest communities now hunt and clear land at rates that the land can no longer sustain.
options.B: It explains why the founders of national parks believed that nature was most fully itself where people were absent.
options.C: It abandons the critique of fortress conservation and argues that strict exclusion is usually the more effective form of protection.
options.D: It guards the critique of fortress conservation against an opposite oversimplification before the author states a conclusion.

questions.question: In which of the following cases would the reasoning of the passage most clearly support excluding people from an area?

options.A: A cliff used by a seabird that deserts its nests at slight disturbance, where counts show breeding fails whenever people enter, and which no community has ever used.
options.B: A river valley whose fishing families have lived there for centuries, where a recent survey found fish numbers stable and a proposal to remove them cites the general belief that wildlife does better alone.
options.C: A grassland that herders have grazed and burned for centuries, which visitors admire as wilderness and would prefer to see without any settlements.
options.D: A forest from which a village has gathered fruit and firewood for generations, where officials hold that the rare birds living there are probably disturbed by people.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the description of keystone status as 'a property of a relationship in a particular setting' means that

options.A: a species keeps its keystone role wherever it lives, once that role has been demonstrated in one setting.
options.B: whether a species has outsized influence depends on the community and conditions in which it lives.
options.C: a keystone species is one that forms close partnerships with a small number of other species.
options.D: keystone species are found only in particular kinds of habitat, such as rocky shores, and not elsewhere.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard the unqualified statement that 'a certain predator is a keystone species' as

options.A: adequate, provided that the predator's effect has been carefully measured in at least one community.
options.B: false, because the passage shows that no species really has an influence larger than its abundance suggests.
options.C: incomplete, since it leaves out the particular system in which the predator's influence was found.
options.D: harmful, because naming keystone species always draws money away from the diffuse interactions in a community.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the argument of paragraph 3?

options.A: On one coast, removing a single predator led to the collapse of a mussel bed, but on another coast removing the same predator had little effect.
options.B: In a meadow, removing any single species of grazing insect changed little, but removing several of them together altered the plant community sharply.
options.C: In a lake, removing a single fish species that was rare but fed on grazing animals caused a large growth of algae within a few seasons.
options.D: Conservation funding in one region rose sharply after a campaign that described a single bird as the keystone of its forests.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the keystone concept is best described as

options.A: indifferent, regarding the question of whether it is accurate as less important than whether it raises funds.
options.B: dismissive, regarding it as a misleading metaphor that ecology would be better off discarding entirely.
