options.C: appreciative of its value as a memorable idea but wary of its being taken as a general model of communities.
options.D: admiring, regarding it as an accurate account of how most ecological communities are actually held together.

questions.question: The contrast between a plant that crosses a mountain range by itself and one that crosses in a shipment of grain (paragraph 1) serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate that species carried by people usually spread faster and farther than those moving by natural means.
options.B: suggest that plants arriving in shipments of grain should be protected in the same way as native plants are protected.
options.C: show that species which spread on their own as the climate warms are less harmful than those carried by trade.
options.D: show that the label of invader turns on how a species travelled rather than on anything about the species or what it does.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the author's main disagreement with the ecologists described in paragraph 2 concerns

options.A: whether the effects of an introduced species can be known at the time when a decision about it has to be taken.
options.B: whether the origin of a species is in itself a form of harm to the ecosystem into which it has been introduced.
options.C: whether introduced species are, as a rule, more likely than native species to damage the communities they enter.
options.D: whether many eradication campaigns have been carried out without first asking if the targeted species was causing damage.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's case for a presumption against newly arrived species?

options.A: Species introduced long ago, whose effects have been studied for decades, turned out on close examination to be mostly harmless where they had settled.
options.B: Introduced species that eventually caused serious harm could almost always still be removed cheaply once that harm became evident, even decades after they arrived.
options.C: Several species now described as native were themselves carried by people long before the date that is usually used to define native status.
options.D: Forecasts of how newly arrived species would behave proved much less accurate than forecasts for long-established species living in the same region.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, the case for treating an introduced species with suspicion

options.A: rests on evidence that introduced species are generally more damaging to native wildlife than native species are.
options.B: applies with equal force to a species established for a century, since the species' origin has not changed at all.
options.C: is justified only once the species has begun to spread rapidly, since harm before that point cannot be shown.
options.D: weakens as the species' effects in its new home become observable, so that in time those effects should carry the decision.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, campaigns to remove introduced species can themselves cause harm by

options.A: spreading the seeds of introduced plants into new areas as the plants are cut down and carried away.
options.B: killing the pollinators that had learned to feed on native flowers growing among the introduced plants.
options.C: taking away cover that native animals had come to rely on, as well as through chemicals and disturbed ground.
options.D: encouraging the deliberate import of replacement species to fill the spaces left behind by those removed.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: By declining to name an end state, rewilding does not remove human choice but moves it to the start of the process, which its advocates should admit.
options.B: Because a rewilding project without a target can never be shown to have failed, restoration towards a recorded earlier state remains the more accountable method.
options.C: Since every reference state is chosen and climate change puts old states out of reach, conservation should restore natural processes and leave the outcome entirely to nature.
options.D: Holding rewilding projects to account for the processes they restore, rather than for their outcomes, fully answers the charge that the method cannot fail.

questions.question: The example of cattle and ponies at different densities (paragraph 4) implies that

options.A: grazing animals should be released at low density on large areas so that closed woodland is able to return.
options.B: what a rewilding project will produce can often be foreseen from choices made at its start, even though no end state was named.
options.C: the number of grazing animals matters less to the result of a project than whether its rivers are allowed to flood.
options.D: measuring processes is of little real use, because the numbers of grazing animals roaming large areas cannot be counted reliably.

questions.question: Which of the following projects best matches what paragraph 4 describes as holding a project to account for its processes rather than its outcome?

options.A: One that promises to let a river overflow its banks in wet years and reports each year whether it did, without saying which habitats should result.
options.B: One that promises to recreate the marsh shown on a map from a chosen century and reports each year how closely the site now matches that map.
options.C: One that makes no commitments of any kind and describes whatever landscape appears on the site as the result that nature has chosen.
options.D: One that promises to raise visitor numbers and reports each year how many people came and how much money they gave to the project.

questions.question: The passage presents each of the following as a reason given by advocates of rewilding for refusing a fixed target EXCEPT that

options.A: holding a landscape to an old picture would call for ever more mowing, planting, culling and weeding.
options.B: selecting one past condition of a site as its true form gives one moment of its history priority over all the others.
options.C: under a changing climate the conditions that once sustained a historical community may no longer exist at all.
options.D: a fixed target would make it harder to win support from funders and neighbours who prefer projects without set goals.

questions.question: The objection in paragraph 3 that a project with no target 'cannot fail' depends on the assumption that

options.A: a project should be judged by how closely its result comes to resemble the condition of the site at an earlier date.
options.B: the people who live beside a rewilding project ought to be the ones who decide what the landscape should become.
options.C: a project or claim deserves to be taken seriously only if some possible outcome would count against it.
options.D: unwelcome results such as scrub swallowing a valued meadow show that most rewilding projects end in failure.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that seismology deserves credit for long-term probabilities that guide construction, rather than blame for failing to predict individual earthquakes.
options.B: criticise engineers for designing hospitals and schools without making use of the probabilities that seismologists already publish.
options.C: explain why the conditions deep in the crust that decide the size of an earthquake can never be measured by any instrument.
options.D: show that the search for warning signs before earthquakes has been a waste of effort and ought now to be given up.

questions.question: According to the passage, a prediction differs from a forecast in that a prediction

options.A: is issued by seismologists to the public, whereas a forecast is prepared by engineers for use in drafting building codes.
options.B: names a place, a magnitude and a short time window, while a forecast gives a probability over a longer period.
options.C: relies on instruments placed in fault zones, whereas a forecast is built only from historical records of earlier earthquakes.
options.D: concerns large and destructive earthquakes only, whereas a forecast also covers the small tremors that people barely feel.

questions.question: The passage suggests that nobody experiences a city's absorbed long-term hazard 'as a warning' because

options.A: the probabilities on which building codes rest usually turn out to be wrong about which buildings will fail.
options.B: it is written in technical language that only the engineers who design hospitals are able to understand.
options.C: it arrives years before any earthquake and asks for spending rather than a decision to leave.
options.D: officials keep the probabilities from residents for fear that publishing them would cause needless panic.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the objection that a probability is too vague to act on?

options.A: Engineers in several countries already decide how much to reinforce schools by consulting thirty-year probabilities of strong shaking.
options.B: Many residents of earthquake-prone cities ignore official orders to leave their homes, even when a strong earthquake later follows.
options.C: A newly proposed warning sign appears to have preceded several recent earthquakes in widely separated parts of the world.
options.D: In most earthquake-prone regions, buildings are demolished or replaced within a few years of construction, long before a thirty-year hazard is likely to occur.

questions.question: The example of the phone application in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: show that the models used by phone applications are cruder than the ones that forecasting centres run many times.
options.B: show how a single summary symbol throws away the information about uncertainty that running many forecasts provides.
options.C: prove that weather forecasts presented to the public turn out to be wrong about rainfall more often than not.
options.D: support the view that forecasts ought to be issued to the public only by meteorologists trained in reading ensembles.

questions.question: The author implies that judging a forecast by whether it rained on the day is

options.A: a reasonable test for forecasts made more than two weeks ahead but an unfair one for forecasts of the next few days.
options.B: a test that forecasters would like the public to apply more strictly to every forecast they publish.
options.C: a poor test of a forecast that expressed uncertainty, since such a forecast allowed for more than one outcome.
options.D: the very method that forecasting centres use to check whether the spread of an ensemble can be trusted.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward ensemble forecasting is best described as

options.A: detached: describing how ensembles are run and what they show while declining to judge whether the approach is a good one.
options.B: wholly enthusiastic: convinced that running many forecasts has removed the uncertainty that chaos once seemed to impose.
options.C: suspicious: inclined to treat the method as an elaborate way of disguising the failure of weather prediction.
options.D: appreciative but qualified: impressed that a limit became a method, yet alert to what the method cannot reveal.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best illustrates the specific weakness described in paragraph 4?

options.A: Every run of an ensemble forecasts a dry week for a valley because the shared model mishandles air rising over nearby hills, and heavy rain falls there.
options.B: The runs of an ensemble fan out widely after a few days, and forecasters announce that several quite different outcomes are still possible.
options.C: A single forecast run from a slightly inaccurate measurement of today's winds drifts further from reality with each passing day.
options.D: A phone application shows a sun for Saturday although about half of the ensemble's runs had forecast showers for that day.

questions.question: According to the passage, the air in an ice core's bubbles is younger than the surrounding ice because

options.A: the weight of later snowfall forces newer air downward into deeper ice that had already been sealed.
options.B: fresh air seeps into the ice through cracks that open when a core is drilled and lifted to the surface.
options.C: the top layer of snow stays porous for a long time, letting surface air mix downward until the bubbles seal.
options.D: summer melting each year reworks the ice and traps air from later seasons in layers of older snow.

questions.question: The passage implies that dating the air in an ice core involves a particular difficulty, namely that

options.A: the air and the ice at any one site are usually exactly the same age, leaving no gap that could be measured.
options.B: the volcanic traces used to align records are absent from cores drilled in Greenland and found only in Antarctica.
options.C: the proportions of heavier and lighter water in the ice change after drilling, so the record has to be corrected.
options.D: the model used to date the air needs values of temperature and snowfall that the core itself is meant to supply.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of the final paragraph?

options.A: It concedes that critics of climate science are right to treat interpreted evidence as less reliable than raw data.
options.B: It extends what ice cores show into a general claim about how evidence should be judged, including in public debate.
options.C: It summarises the technical steps by which researchers align the records drawn from ice cores at opposite ends of the planet.
options.D: It introduces a different kind of climate record that, unlike ice cores, avoids the need for interpretation altogether.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the way, according to the passage, ice cores earn their authority?

options.A: A historian accepts the date of a flood because a farmer's diary, a tax ledger and a church register, kept for unrelated reasons, all agree on it.
options.B: A historian accepts the date of a flood because five chronicles record the same date, each copied from one older chronicle.
options.C: A historian accepts the date of a flood because the manuscript recording it has survived for centuries without being altered.
options.D: A historian accepts the date of a flood because the only account of it was written by a witness who watched the water rise.

questions.question: According to the passage, coastal defences become harder to give up over time because

options.A: residents grow attached to the wall itself as a landmark, and so resist any plan that would remove it from view.
options.B: each raising of a wall encourages more building behind it, so abandoning the wall would mean abandoning more property.
options.C: each raising of a wall makes it stronger, so engineers become more confident that it will hold against future storms.
options.D: the cost of each new round of wall-building falls as the town's builders gain experience with the same structure.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, the phrase 'commitments that grow' most nearly means

options.A: structures whose physical size must keep increasing because the materials they are built from weaken with age.
options.B: formal promises by governments to keep building walls whatever the cost to the towns that live behind them.
options.C: agreements among neighbouring towns to share the rising expense of protecting one stretch of shared coastline.
options.D: obligations that enlarge themselves, because each defence draws investment that later demands still more defence.

questions.question: The author would regard each of the following as consistent with planned retreat as the passage describes it EXCEPT

options.A: requiring every household in the most exposed areas to move inland by a fixed date set by the national government.
options.B: offering to purchase homes in threatened areas at the point when their owners decide of their own accord to sell.
options.C: refusing permits for new houses in the most exposed areas while allowing existing homes to remain occupied for now.
options.D: rebuilding an ageing clinic on higher ground inland at the time when it would have had to be replaced anyway.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the usual framing of the choice, as one between defending a town and giving it up, as

options.A: accurate, because retreat from the shore is in every case an admission that the town has been given up for lost.
options.B: misleading, because defending a coastline is never worth its cost once the sea has begun to rise noticeably.
options.C: misleading, because it hides the likelihood that retreat will come anyway, only on far worse terms.
options.D: accurate for poor coastal places, which cannot afford walls and therefore have no option except abandonment.

questions.question: By saying that behind the announcement lies 'not an event but a decision' (paragraph 1), the author means that

options.A: forecasters decide each year, after the season ends, whether the monsoon as a whole should be called normal or poor.
options.B: the date is moved from year to year to suit public hopes and the headlines that a delay is likely to produce.
options.C: the onset date results from forecasters applying chosen criteria to a gradual change, not from observing one sharp moment.
options.D: officials use the announcement to decide on behalf of farmers the day on which sowing should begin across the country.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 2 in the passage?

options.A: It reports that onsets have come steadily earlier over many decades, as consistent records now make plain.
options.B: It argues that the criteria for onset should be revised each year so that they keep pace with the latest observations.
options.C: It presents the main objection to the declared date, namely that farmers are misled into sowing too early.
options.D: It forestalls the reading that a conventional date must be baseless, by showing what consistent criteria achieve.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the farmers whose seedlings withered (paragraph 3) were misled chiefly because they

options.A: were never told that the long-term average onset date had moved later than the one they remembered from earlier years.
options.B: took a threshold crossed somewhere on the coast as information about the moisture in their own fields.
options.C: followed local measures of soil moisture that had been recorded in a different district from the one they farmed.
options.D: relied on forecasters who had declared the onset before its criteria had in fact been satisfied along the coast.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the recommendation the author makes in paragraph 4?

options.A: Where sowing advice followed local soil moisture, crop losses after stalled rains were clearly lower than where it followed the declared onset.
options.B: Farmers far from the coast often begin sowing several days before the onset is declared, prompted by early showers nearby.
options.C: Onset dates worked out with one consistent definition show no clear trend toward earlier or later arrival over the past century.
options.D: Rainfall along the southern coast in the week of onset closely tracks how much rain the rest of the country receives that season.

questions.question: According to the passage, a hazard differs from a disaster in that a hazard

options.A: is a physical event of some size, which becomes a disaster only on meeting people and structures unable to withstand it.
options.B: is an event that scientists can forecast in advance, whereas a disaster is one that arrives without any warning at all.
options.C: is caused by human activity such as building on deltas, whereas a disaster has wholly natural causes such as storms.
options.D: affects only empty coastlines and open country, whereas a disaster is confined to cities with many unreinforced houses.

questions.question: The author suggests that describing a disaster's outcome as natural tends to

options.A: lead the people harmed to blame themselves for having chosen to live in places exposed to known hazards.
options.B: encourage scientists to study how often hazards of a given size recur instead of examining the societies they strike.
options.C: push governments to enforce building standards more strictly in cities that have already suffered heavy losses.
options.D: move public effort away from prevention beforehand and toward sympathy once the damage is done.

questions.question: Paragraph 3 functions in the passage chiefly to

options.A: shift attention from earthquakes and cyclones to eruptions and great waves as the most dangerous hazards for coastal cities.
options.B: qualify a position the author largely accepts, by identifying the ways in which it claims too much.
options.C: provide further support for the slogan by showing that even very large eruptions cause losses shaped by society.
options.D: reject the slogan outright as a false and harmful belief that researchers would do better to abandon entirely.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely accept?

options.A: Studying how societies come to be exposed matters more than knowing how often hazards of a given size tend to recur.
options.B: When a hazard is large enough to overwhelm well-prepared places, the losses it causes are purely the work of nature.
options.C: Even when a hazard is too large for any society to withstand fully, the extent of the loss still owes something to earlier choices.
options.D: Every death in a disaster could in principle have been prevented by better decisions taken before the hazard struck.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with arguing that

options.A: the middle of the twentieth century is the most defensible position for the boundary, since its markers are the sharpest the record offers.
options.B: geologists insist on physical reference points for boundaries because the time scale must let strata on different continents be matched.
options.C: the idea of the Anthropocene is a slogan used by commentators, and it will gain scientific standing only once a boundary is formally ratified.
options.D: the criteria for a formal geological boundary sit poorly with the history of human influence, which does not need such a boundary to be taken seriously.

questions.question: According to the passage, the later candidate dates for the boundary are favoured partly because

options.A: the evidence for them is preserved in ice, which records change more accurately than rock does.
options.B: the traces that mark them were laid down within a few years across almost the whole planet.
options.C: they rest on records of carbon and nitrogen that are less disputed than the evidence for early farming.
options.D: they coincide with the period in which human influence on the Earth first became noticeable.

questions.question: As used in the final sentence of the passage, 'diachronous' most nearly means

options.A: taking place at different times in different places rather than at one moment everywhere.
options.B: so gradual that no change at all can be detected within the span of a single human lifetime.
options.C: caused by two separate forces, one human and one natural, acting together on the Earth.
options.D: recorded in two kinds of archive, layers of sediment on land and layers of ice at the poles.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely accept?

options.A: Because human influence began with farming, the spread of farming is the correct place to fix the boundary.
options.B: Formal ratification of a boundary would add nothing of value to the work of researchers who study human impact.
options.C: A boundary chosen because it serves the purpose of correlating rocks can still misrepresent the history of the change it is taken to mark.
options.D: The traces left by nuclear weapons tests are weaker evidence of human impact than the records of cleared forests.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 3?

options.A: Fallout from nuclear weapons tests has been detected in lake sediments and glacial ice on every continent, including the most remote.
options.B: Human effects on forests, soils and animal populations were negligible until the twentieth century and then appeared almost simultaneously across the globe.
options.C: Large-scale clearing of forests began in some regions several thousand years before it reached others, and in some places it never took hold.
options.D: Commentators outside geology frequently use the term Anthropocene loosely, without reference to any particular boundary or measurement.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the twentieth-century resistance to the flood and impact hypotheses arose mainly because

options.A: the evidence offered for each hypothesis was too thin to justify any firm conclusion at that time.
options.B: the rule of preferring known causes forbade geologists from ever accepting an unobserved cause.
options.C: the hypotheses required the laws of nature to have worked differently in the past from the way they work now.
options.D: the proposals resembled a style of explanation that geologists had long since learned to distrust.

questions.question: Paragraph 4 serves chiefly to

options.A: guard against an overcorrection that paragraph 3 might invite, by showing that the demand for known causes was reasonable and helped the later catastrophes win acceptance.
options.B: add further examples of sudden events whose acceptance was delayed because they sounded like the catastrophism of the past.
options.C: withdraw the criticism made in paragraph 3, by showing that twentieth-century geologists were right to doubt the flood and impact hypotheses.
options.D: show that the early catastrophist accounts were largely correct and had simply been rejected before the necessary evidence was available.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT

options.A: the assumption that the laws of nature have not changed is close to a precondition of reconstructing the Earth's past.
options.B: the rates at which the Earth has changed have varied widely, from long slow stretches to rare episodes of great violence.
options.C: the preference for explaining the record by known causes was the root of the twentieth-century error and has since been given up.
options.D: the hypothesis of a large impact gained acceptance by meeting, rather than escaping, the standard of evidence that had been applied to it.

questions.question: Which of the following most closely parallels the error described in the last sentence of paragraph 3?

options.A: Doctors taught to consider common illnesses before rare ones come to dismiss a rare illness even when test results clearly point to it.
options.B: A hospital requires a second opinion before major surgery, and the rule sometimes delays treatment for patients whose need is urgent.
options.C: Doctors who suspect a rare illness withhold the diagnosis until a confirming test is found, and the diagnosis is then accepted by colleagues.
options.D: Doctors taught to rule out rare illnesses first order expensive tests for every patient, including those with obvious common complaints.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the founders of uniformitarianism is best described as

options.A: admiring without reservation: endorsing the familiar account in which patient observation defeated speculation.
options.B: regretful: holding that their victory set geology back by locking it into a belief it took over a century to escape.
options.C: respectful but discriminating: crediting their rules of method while treating their claim about steady rates as a hypothesis that partly failed.
options.D: dismissive: regarding their doctrine as a speculation that replaced one unsupported story about the Earth with another.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: arguing that ordinary observations are in general more informative about the cosmos than the results of specialised instruments.
options.B: showing how an everyday fact, the darkness of the night sky, counts decisively against one long-favoured picture of the universe.
options.C: tracing how astronomers used clouds of interstellar dust to defend the idea of an infinite universe against an awkward observation.
options.D: proving that the universe had a beginning by showing that every rival explanation of the dark night sky has failed under scrutiny.

questions.question: According to the passage, interstellar dust cannot resolve the puzzle of the dark sky because

options.A: the dust between the stars is spread far too thinly to absorb any significant share of the light of distant stars.
options.B: clouds of dust would hide nearby stars as well as distant ones, making the sky far darker than it is actually observed to be.
options.C: dust absorbs only some wavelengths of starlight, so that the remaining wavelengths still reach the earth unhindered.
options.D: over an unlimited time the dust would be heated by the light it absorbs until it shone as brightly itself.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the proposal to arrange stars in 'clusters within clusters' was regarded with suspicion mainly because it

options.A: was contradicted by observations showing that stars are in fact spread evenly through space.
options.B: seemed to have been devised only to dispose of the puzzle, with no other reason to believe it.
options.C: required the universe to have a finite age, an assumption that the astronomers of the period regarded as unacceptable.
options.D: conflicted with the dust explanation, which most astronomers of the time preferred to accept.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the reasoning set out in paragraph 1?

options.A: In a large but walled garden, a visitor can see open sky between the trees because the planting stops at the wall some distance away.
options.B: In a city at night, the lamps of distant buildings look fainter than nearby ones, so that the skyline appears brightest close at hand.
options.C: A lamp seen through thick fog grows dimmer the farther the observer walks from it, until at last it cannot be seen at all.
options.D: In a forest that extends without limit in every direction, a walker anywhere would find that every line of sight ends, sooner or later, at a tree trunk.

questions.question: According to the passage, differences in local time between towns became a problem when

options.A: the market, the place of worship and the field in a single town began to keep different times.
options.B: astronomers found that solar noon falls at different moments in different seasons of the year.
options.C: people and goods began moving between towns quickly enough for a difference of minutes to matter.
options.D: governments began to require one uniform time for keeping official records and collecting taxes.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward standard time is best described as

options.A: appreciative of its benefits but critical of the claim that it corrected an earlier error.
options.B: hostile, regarding it as a needless break with the natural rhythm of daylight in each town.
options.C: indifferent, treating the choice between local and standard time as having no real practical consequence.
options.D: enthusiastic, celebrating it as the triumph of common sense over a long period of local confusion.

questions.question: The mention of 'single tracks' in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that railway accidents were caused chiefly by poor engineering rather than by timekeeping.
options.B: illustrate how governments compelled reluctant railway companies to adopt a single standard time.
options.C: explain why railways in regions that kept local time were built more slowly than those elsewhere.
options.D: show that mismatched local times created a real danger on the railways, not merely an inconvenience.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: A way of setting clocks should be judged by how well it suits the needs of those who keep it, not by its closeness to a true time.
options.B: Solar time is the true time, and standard time is merely a convenient approximation that the railways adopted for their own purposes.
options.C: Standard time corrected errors in local timekeeping that small towns had failed to notice because they traded mainly with themselves.
options.D: Once the railways had spread, the position of the sun ceased to have any importance for daily life.

questions.question: According to the passage, the value assigned to the constant in the new definition of the kilogram was chosen

options.A: by a calculation that made no reference to any earlier measurement of the mass of physical objects.
options.B: to correct for the mass that the cylinder near Paris was believed to have lost over the decades.
options.C: so that the new kilogram would agree with the old one as closely as instruments could tell.
options.D: to match the average mass of the official copies, which were thought more reliable than the cylinder.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the phrase 'a peculiar kind of blindness' refers to

options.A: the general public's ignorance of the fact that all the world's measurements of mass led back to one cylinder.
options.B: the impossibility, in principle, of detecting any change in a standard that served as its own definition.
options.C: the failure of the officials in charge to notice that the official copies were drifting away from the cylinder.
options.D: the inability of most laboratories in the world to realise the kilogram directly from a constant of nature.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the drift between the cylinder and its official copies?

options.A: It proved that the copies had gained mass over the decades while the cylinder itself stayed unchanged.
options.B: It showed that something had changed, without making it possible to establish what.
options.C: It was the reason the constant was given a value slightly different from the one that matched the cylinder.
options.D: It was too slight to have any bearing on scientific measurement, which is why the redefinition changed little.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's final claim about what the redefinition achieved?

options.A: Ordinary users of balances and scales noticed no change at all in their measurements when the new definition came into force.
options.B: Most of the world's weighing instruments are still calibrated against physical masses rather than against direct realisations of the unit.
options.C: The constant was assigned a value chosen to reproduce the old kilogram, so the new unit simply inherits the size of the cylinder.
options.D: Each of the few laboratories that can realise the kilogram uses a unique design whose results no other laboratory is able to reproduce or check.

questions.question: The analysis of steam engines mentioned in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: show that a result reached within the caloric framework could outlast the framework itself.
options.B: prove that caloric gave a correct account of heat at least in so far as engines were concerned.
options.C: illustrate how close study of engines eventually exposed the caloric theory as mistaken.
options.D: explain why heat moves from hot bodies to cold ones in the way that water runs downhill.

questions.question: The author's view of the defenders of caloric who answered the cannon-boring objection is that they

options.A: were right to dismiss the observations of cannon boring as the product of careless experimental work.
options.B: were being stubborn in refusing to accept evidence that plainly and decisively refuted their theory.
options.C: acted reasonably in retaining a productive theory while no rival yet explained as much.
options.D: produced replies that were uniformly ingenious and that fully disposed of the objection for decades.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the cannon-boring observations troubled the caloric theory chiefly because

options.A: they demonstrated that heat has a measurable weight, whereas caloric was supposed to be weightless.
options.B: a fluid that is merely conserved and released should not be available in a supply without limit.
options.C: they showed that heat could pass from colder bodies into hotter ones when metal was being bored.
options.D: they were carried out by investigators who had already rejected caloric in favour of another theory.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the author's account of the caloric theory?

options.A: An old map drawn on a mistaken belief about the shape of the land records routes between towns accurately, and later mapmakers keep the routes while redrawing the outline.
options.B: An old map is mistaken in places, but mapmakers keep using it unchanged for generations only out of loyalty to the person who drew it.
options.C: An old map records accurate routes but a mistaken outline of the land, and later mapmakers throw it away entirely because the outline is wrong.
options.D: An old map is accurate in every detail but is replaced because a newer method of printing makes it cheaper to draw a fresh one.

questions.question: According to the passage, the pulsating stars can serve as measures of distance because

options.A: their shift against the background as the earth travels around the sun can be converted into a distance.
options.B: they shine so brilliantly when they explode that they can be seen across much of the universe.
options.C: their light, unlike that of ordinary stars, is not dimmed by the dust lying between the stars.
options.D: the timing of their cycle of brightening and fading reveals how bright they truly are.

questions.question: By saying that the chain image is apt 'but only half of it' (paragraph 3), the author means that

options.A: the image fits the lower rungs of the ladder well but fails for the upper rungs that rely on exploding stars.
options.B: only about half of the rungs rest on the rungs beneath them, while the others are measured independently.
options.C: the rungs do depend on one another, but that dependence also lets them test one another, as links cannot.
options.D: the ladder is far stronger than its weakest rung, because errors made at the bottom are never carried upward.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the discovery that two kinds of pulsating star had been taken for one

options.A: showed that the ladder as a whole is too unreliable to be used in measuring how fast the universe expands.
options.B: was made by geometry alone, without any appeal to the other methods by which astronomers measure distance.
options.C: is an instance of an error common to every rung, of the kind that comparisons between methods could not catch.
options.D: came about because distances found by different rungs for the same objects failed to agree.

questions.question: The claim in paragraph 3 that interdependence is 'the means by which they are caught' depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Methods that can be applied to the same objects nearly always give answers that agree within their stated uncertainties.
options.B: At least some of the errors that affect one method of finding distances do not also affect another method used on the same objects.
options.C: The geometric measurements of the nearest stars are free from any error that could be carried up the ladder.
options.D: The expansion rate inferred from the early universe is more trustworthy than the rate found with the ladder.

questions.question: The passage is chiefly concerned with

options.A: arguing that conservation laws are better understood as consequences of symmetries, a shift that alters how they explain rather than proving them.
options.B: demonstrating that the conservation of energy is a truth of logic, which no observation of nature could ever overturn.
options.C: recounting how a mathematician's theorem persuaded physicists who had long doubted the conservation laws to accept them.
options.D: explaining how the expansion of the universe has forced physicists to give up the conservation of energy altogether.

questions.question: The passage pairs each of the following features of the laws of nature with the quantity it implies is conserved EXCEPT

options.A: laws that ignore which way a system is facing, with the conservation of angular momentum.
options.B: laws that are the same here as in the next room, with the conservation of momentum.
options.C: laws that stay the same however fast a system is moving, with the conservation of energy.
options.D: laws that are the same today as they were yesterday, with the conservation of energy.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, convincing evidence that the laws of physics had changed slightly over time would

options.A: count as evidence against the strict conservation of energy, since evidence about the symmetry is in effect evidence about conservation.
options.B: leave the conservation of energy untouched, since the theorem establishes conservation as a matter of logic alone.
options.C: show that the theorem itself had been mathematically mistaken when it linked the symmetries of laws with quantities that are conserved.
options.D: cast doubt on the conservation of momentum while leaving the conservation of energy secure.

questions.question: The discussion of the expanding universe in paragraph 4 functions mainly to

options.A: concede that the theorem breaks down on the largest scales and therefore holds only for systems of modest size.
options.B: report evidence that the conservation of energy has been observed to fail throughout the expanding universe.
options.C: illustrate the 'scandal' that has led physicists to doubt the conservation laws they once treated as bedrock.
options.D: show that treating conservation as resting on symmetry pays off, by telling us where a conservation law should lose its hold.

questions.question: The observation in paragraph 2 that the boundary 'can be drawn anywhere convenient without altering the predicted statistics' serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that measuring devices, unlike the particles they record, do not obey the smooth equation of the theory.
options.B: show that the measurement problem has in effect been solved, since the location of the boundary makes no difference.
options.C: explain why a gap in the theory's foundations makes so little difference to how the theory is used.
options.D: support the claim that rival interpretations differ in their predictions only for sufficiently large systems.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the process, described in paragraph 3, in which a system's entanglement with its surroundings suppresses the signs of superposition?

options.A: It is the means by which the theories that modify the smooth equation produce their spontaneous tendency to collapse.
options.B: It deals with one part of what the measurement problem asks but, on most accounts, leaves the occurrence of a particular outcome unexplained.
options.C: It makes the textbook rule unnecessary, because it shows why an apparatus records one result rather than a superposition.
options.D: It is dismissed by most physicists as irrelevant, since superpositions of large objects are in fact readily observed.

questions.question: The author regards the view that the dispute over interpretations is 'metaphysics' as

options.A: correct about the theories that modify the equation but mistaken about those that leave the equation untouched.
options.B: a sound conclusion, given that the rival pictures agree with one another in every experiment ever performed.
options.C: a dishonest evasion by physicists who privately believe the theory to be false but prefer not to admit it.
options.D: a natural reaction that wrongly treats one incomplete interpretation as if it were a neutral standard.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim in paragraph 4 that the rival pictures are not 'strictly equivalent'?

options.A: Most working physicists compute reaction rates successfully without committing themselves to any interpretation.
options.B: The theories that modify the equation can always be adjusted so that their departures fall below anything experiment could detect.
options.C: The smooth equation has been confirmed to great precision in experiments on single particles and small molecules.
options.D: Experiments of increasing delicacy, carried out on ever larger systems, have so far found no departures from standard behaviour at all.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Physicists ought to settle which interpretation is correct before they rely on the predictions that the theory makes.
options.B: The measurement problem would vanish if experiments confirmed that all the rival pictures make identical predictions.
options.C: The chief defect the author finds in the textbook rule would be removed if the theory stated precisely what counts as a measurement.
options.D: The interpretations that leave the equation untouched are to be preferred, because they alone avoid an undefined notion of measurement.

questions.question: The comparison with the swimming pool in paragraph 2 is used to illustrate

options.A: how conclusions drawn from a sample selected by the conditions of observation can mislead.
options.B: the claim that the constants of nature fall within narrow ranges that permit observers to exist.
options.C: why living things are more likely to arise on some planets than on others in the same system.
options.D: how the ambitious form of anthropic reasoning accounts for the fine tuning of physical constants.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the lottery example that, in the author's view, the existence of observers would explain nothing about the constants if

options.A: ours were the only universe there is, with its constants fixed once and for all.
options.B: the other regions of a large ensemble turned out to be unobservable to us in principle.
options.C: a great many universes existed whose constants differed from ours, most of them hostile to life.
options.D: the constants permitted observers to exist only within some very narrow range of values.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT

options.A: Selection effects belong to sound reasoning in the empirical sciences, and neglecting them leads to error.
options.B: Some claims that the constants of nature are set with extreme precision have not held up under examination.
options.C: Anthropic reasoning is unscientific, since the many universes it relies on can never be observed.
options.D: The modest form of anthropic reasoning is a correct and useful warning about a bias in what we observe.

questions.question: The statement at the end of paragraph 4 that 'Anthropic reasoning cannot certify its own premise' means that

options.A: the cosmological theories that imply many regions were devised only in order to rescue anthropic reasoning.
options.B: the varied ensemble on which the ambitious explanation depends needs support from evidence other than the fact that we exist.
options.C: anthropic reasoning is circular and therefore can never form any part of a good scientific explanation of the constants of nature.
options.D: the modest principle cannot be shown to be true, because its truth would depend on the existence of observers.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Anthropic reasoning explains fine tuning wherever many regions exist, and current cosmological theories have now shown that such regions exist.
options.B: The apparent fine tuning of the constants is largely an illusion, produced by selection effects that physicists have so far failed to take into account.
options.C: The modest form of anthropic reasoning is an empty truism, while the ambitious form is speculation that has no place in science.
options.D: Reasoning from our existence rightly corrects for bias, but it explains fine tuning only given a varied ensemble that it cannot itself establish.

questions.question: The central concern of the passage is that

options.A: officials who run prevention programmes deserve far more public trust than they now receive, since their claims about averted outbreaks are accurate.
options.B: the benefits of preventive measures are hard to perceive, which erodes support for them unless their record can be checked.
options.C: governments spend too much on hospitals and should move that money to food inspection, where it would buy more health.
options.D: vaccines against rare diseases have become more dangerous than the diseases themselves, which explains why many parents now hesitate.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, the doubting parent's calculation is 'not foolish' because

options.A: health officials have exaggerated the dangers of diphtheria in order to protect their budgets.
options.B: the parent has personally watched a child struggle to breathe and so understands the risk at first hand.
options.C: the disease really has become uncommon in the parent's daily life, so its danger seems remote.
options.D: the side effects of the vaccine are in fact more serious than the disease would have been for the child.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a food inspection service is especially easy to cut because

options.A: the harm done by weakening it appears slowly and thinly and is usually blamed on something else.
options.B: it usually costs considerably more to run than treating the illnesses that contaminated food would otherwise cause.
options.C: the public has come to believe that contaminated food no longer poses any real danger in modern shops.
options.D: its officials have often been caught exaggerating the number of outbreaks it has prevented.

questions.question: Which of the following actions best fits the response to invisibility that the author recommends in the final paragraph?

options.A: A health department launches a campaign in which senior doctors explain why the public should trust their expertise on vaccination.
options.B: A health department stops publishing any estimates of illnesses averted, since such estimates concern events that never happened and can be inflated.
options.C: A health department shifts much of its budget from prevention to treatment so that its spending produces results people can see.
options.D: A health department reports outbreaks averted alongside comparisons with similar districts that lacked the measure and an account of its side effects.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is most striking about the historical references to waking in the night?

options.A: They attribute the waking interval to the spread of cheap artificial light in the evenings.
options.B: They treat the waking interval as a normal part of the night, not as a cause for complaint.
options.C: They come mainly from medical advice written for people who could not manage to sleep through the whole night.
options.D: They describe in close detail the prayers and conversations with which people filled the interval.

questions.question: The author mentions that people used the night-time interval 'to pray, tend the fire, talk quietly, or simply lie in the dark and think' in order to

options.A: show that the interval was filled with everyday activities, consistent with its being treated as ordinary.
options.B: prove that the waking interval was caused by household duties such as keeping the fire alight.
options.C: argue that people in pre-industrial Europe spent their nights more usefully than people do today.
options.D: suggest that waking in the night was a religious custom observed mainly by devout households.

questions.question: The reasoning in paragraph 3 implies that a person who regularly wakes for an hour in the night would probably sleep better if he or she

options.A: got up and kept busy until feeling tired again, because lying awake in the dark is what makes the waking last longer.
options.B: went to bed much earlier and avoided artificial light altogether, so as to restore the pre-industrial pattern of two sleeps.
options.C: sought medical treatment for insomnia at once, since any waking during the night is a disorder that needs correcting.
options.D: regarded the waking as an unremarkable part of the night rather than as a sign that something had gone wrong.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the idea that segmented sleep is the natural human pattern is best described as

options.A: approving, since the idea provides a welcome corrective to the modern insistence on eight unbroken hours.
options.B: indifferent, since the author regards historical evidence about sleep as having no bearing on medicine.
options.C: sceptical, since the historical evidence shows sleep taking several forms rather than one original form.
options.D: hostile, since the author believes that consolidated sleep is the biologically correct pattern for adults.

questions.question: In context, the words 'It is both' at the start of paragraph 2 assert that the improvement seen in a placebo group is

options.A: genuine, and also worth investigating in its own right.
options.B: unreal, though it remains of some interest to researchers.
options.C: a measure of the drug and of the context at the same time.
options.D: produced partly by deception and partly by honest explanation.

questions.question: The passage implies that the open-label trials are important chiefly because they

options.A: prove that inert pills can relieve the symptoms of an infection even when patients know they are inert.
options.B: establish that the novelty of taking part in an unusual study is the real source of placebo responses.
options.C: cast doubt on the belief that using placebo effects on purpose requires misleading patients.
options.D: show that symptoms reported by patients themselves are too unreliable to be used in clinical trials.

questions.question: The final sentence of the passage serves mainly to

options.A: recommend that doctors use inert pills more often in order to replace the time lost from shorter consultations.
options.B: draw a practical consequence from the argument that the context of care has effects of its own.
options.C: concede that the evidence for placebo responses is too weak to have any bearing on medical practice.
options.D: show that clinical trials have systematically overstated the effects of the drugs they test.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the suggestion in paragraph 3 that 'the ritual may matter more than the belief that the pill is active'?

options.A: Improvements among patients openly given inert pills persisted for several months, well after the novelty of the study had worn off.
options.B: Patients openly given inert pills reported less pain and nausea but showed no change in laboratory measures of their underlying disease.
options.C: Patients given longer and more attentive consultations improved more than those given brief ones, whether or not they also received any pill at all.
options.D: Patients openly given inert pills improved no more than patients given identical consultations without pills, while patients told the pills were active improved markedly.

questions.question: According to the passage, responsible use of a new antibiotic harms the finances of the company that makes it because

options.A: responsible use allows bacteria to develop resistance to the new drug more quickly than careless use would.
options.B: health systems refuse to pay more for a new antibiotic than they already pay for older and cheaper ones.
options.C: regulators prevent companies from promoting reserve antibiotics to doctors during the life of the patent.
options.D: it recovers its costs by selling in quantity while its patent lasts, and responsible use keeps sales low.

questions.question: Which of the following arrangements is closest in principle to the payment scheme described in paragraph 3?

options.A: A city pays a builder a single fixed price to construct a flood wall, after which the builder has no further role.
options.B: A publisher pays an author a royalty on every copy of the author's book that is sold, for as long as it stays in print.
options.C: A hospital pays a supplier a yearly fee to keep a standby generator ready for it, whether or not the power ever fails.
options.D: A pharmacy receives a fee from the health system for each prescription that it fills during the year.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the forms of misuse listed in paragraph 1 as

options.A: genuine causes of resistance that have nonetheless drawn attention away from a separate economic problem.
options.B: the main reason that large pharmaceutical firms have stopped developing new antibiotics.
options.C: exaggerated worries that distract attention from what is in fact the true and only cause of antibiotic resistance.
options.D: problems that the payment schemes in paragraph 3 would largely solve once they were adopted.

questions.question: The argument in paragraph 2 that responsible use makes a new antibiotic 'a commercial disaster' depends most on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Older and cheaper antibiotics will soon stop working against most common infections, leaving doctors with no alternative to the new drug.
options.B: The price per course of a reserve antibiotic cannot be set high enough to recover its costs from a few patients.
options.C: Medicines for chronic conditions cost more to develop than new antibiotics do, which gives their makers stronger incentives.
options.D: A genuinely new antibiotic will usually prove less effective against common infections than the older and cheaper drugs it backs up.

questions.question: According to the passage, the ecological vocabulary accounts for the intestinal infection that can follow a broad course of antibiotics by pointing out that

options.A: the drug directly strengthens the harmful species that it fails to kill in the gut.
options.B: the drug clears away resident species that had been keeping a harmful one under control.
options.C: the harmful species is carried into the gut along with the antibiotic during treatment.
options.D: the immune system is weakened by the drug and can no longer repel invading microbes.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the war metaphor is best described as

options.A: nostalgic, since the author wishes that medicine would return to the clarity of its older language.
options.B: neutral, since the author declines to judge whether the war picture or the ecological picture explains more.
options.C: dismissive, since the author treats it as a piece of decoration that held back medical research for decades.
options.D: appreciative of what it achieved, while holding that it misdescribes most of the body's microbes.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author objects to products that promise to 'rebalance' the gut chiefly because

options.A: their promises are too vague to be tested, so no evidence could show that they fail.
options.B: ecologists have shown that no community of microbes in the gut can ever remain stable for long.
options.C: they rely on the language of war while presenting themselves as products based on ecology.
options.D: they contain species of bacteria that are known to harm the gut when taken in large amounts.

questions.question: Which of the following uses of the ecological picture would the author most clearly endorse?

options.A: A textbook that swaps its talk of invading germs for talk of an unbalanced gut while leaving its explanations otherwise unchanged.
options.B: A clinic that advises patients to restore their gut to its natural original community through a carefully planned diet.
options.C: A study that predicts how quickly particular gut species return after antibiotic treatment and then tests the prediction against measurements.
options.D: A public campaign that urges people to refuse antibiotics because the bacteria in their bodies are partners rather than enemies.

questions.question: The example of pain felt in amputated limbs (paragraph 2) is used to

options.A: suggest that surgical amputation is a common cause of pain that lasts for many years.
options.B: show that the brain suppresses pain during moments of danger or intense concentration.
options.C: present a case in which pain occurs although no tissue remains that could be damaged.
options.D: illustrate the claim that pain normally fades once the injured tissue has healed.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, calling pain a 'verdict' rather than a 'reading' suggests that pain is

options.A: a final judgement that, once reached, cannot be revised however circumstances change.
options.B: a faithful report that passes on the exact extent of the damage done to the tissues.
options.C: a penalty that the body imposes on itself whenever some part of it has been injured.
options.D: a conclusion that the brain reaches by weighing several kinds of information together.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that, for a patient whose pain has continued long after an injury has healed,

options.A: a scan that shows no damaged structure does not show that the pain is imaginary.
options.B: operating on whatever abnormality a scan reveals is the most promising route to relief.
options.C: the original injury was probably far more severe than any of the doctors had realised.
options.D: the pain is best treated by persuading the patient that it has no real basis in the body.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Long-lasting pain is caused by damage too small for present scans to detect, so better imaging is the most urgent need.
options.B: Pain is better seen as the brain's judgement about threat than as a measure of injury, which bears on treating pain that outlasts healing.
options.C: The gauge picture of pain is mistaken even for everyday injuries, which is why burns and scratches are so poorly understood.
options.D: Pain that continues after healing is largely imaginary, and patients should be helped to understand that it can be safely ignored.

questions.question: In the hypothetical case of the woman described in paragraph 2, detection by scan at sixty-three

options.A: adds five years to her life by allowing treatment to begin before symptoms appear.
options.B: fails her because the tumour is found too late in its course to be treated successfully.
options.C: shows that her tumour must have belonged to the slow-growing kind that repeated tests tend to catch.
options.D: lengthens the survival recorded after her diagnosis without postponing her death.

questions.question: When the author says that the comparison in paragraph 1 is 'rigged' (paragraph 2), the point is that

options.A: comparisons of survival are worthless for judging any medical treatment, whether or not it involves screening.
options.B: the way it is made favours screening whether or not screening saves lives, though nobody intends this.
options.C: researchers have deliberately arranged survival figures so as to make screening programmes look successful.
options.D: patients whose cancers are found by screening receive better treatment than patients who come with symptoms.

questions.question: The observation that 'every overdiagnosed patient experiences the treatment as a rescue' (paragraph 3) contributes to the argument chiefly by

options.A: explaining why the harm of overdiagnosis tends to build support for screening rather than doubts about it.
options.B: showing that overdiagnosed patients are simply wrong to believe that they were ever found to have cancer.
options.C: suggesting that patients ought to be told at diagnosis whenever their tumour is of the harmless kind.
options.D: revealing that screening programmes recruit their former patients as advocates in order to protect their funding.

questions.question: Which of the following findings would the author regard as the strongest evidence that a particular screening programme is beneficial?

options.A: Patients whose cancers were found by the programme survived, on average, twice as long after diagnosis as patients found through symptoms.
options.B: People who chose to attend the programme were less likely to die of the disease than people in the same area who chose not to attend.
options.C: When comparable populations were assigned at random to be screened or not, fewer people in the screened population died of the disease.
options.D: After the programme began, far more cancers were diagnosed each year than before, and a much larger share of them were at an early stage.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the passage's account of overdiagnosis EXCEPT:

options.A: It can lead people to undergo surgery or radiation that they did not in fact need.
options.B: It improves a screening programme's survival figures without preventing any deaths.
options.C: It cannot be recognised in any individual patient at the time the patient is treated.
options.D: It occurs when a pathologist mistakes harmless cells for cancerous ones under the microscope.

questions.question: According to the passage, a doctor's personal experience is a weak guide to who benefits from a treatment because it

options.A: cannot be written down or shared with colleagues and so cannot be checked by anyone.
options.B: rests on few patients, has no comparison group and is shaped by memorable cases.
options.C: is biased in particular towards remembering those patients whom the treatment harmed.
options.D: covers too few patients with any one condition for a doctor to form an impression at all.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: explaining why analysis of subgroups is the most reliable way to identify which patients benefit from treatment.
options.B: defending the clinical judgement of experienced doctors against the growing authority of randomised trials.
options.C: showing how evidence from trials about groups should, and should not, guide decisions about individual patients.
options.D: arguing that trials within single patients should replace large randomised trials for most medical conditions.

questions.question: The discussion of the stroke drug in paragraph 2 implies that promising a patient that the drug will cut his own risk by three points is unjustified because

options.A: the trial result fits patterns of benefit under which that patient's own risk would not fall by three points.
options.B: no individual patient's risk can be changed by a drug whose effects are known only as averages.
options.C: the drug actually harms more patients than it helps, a fact that the favourable average conceals.
options.D: the true average benefit of the drug is probably smaller than the three points the trial estimated.

questions.question: Which of the following doctors is reasoning in the way the author would most clearly endorse?

options.A: One who withholds the drug from a patient because three earlier patients of hers who took it suffered outcomes she vividly remembers.
options.B: One who departs from the trial-based default for a patient whose genetic variant is known to block the drug's mechanism, an effect confirmed in a later trial.
options.C: One who prescribes the drug to an elderly woman because, among many subgroups in the original trial, women over eighty benefited most.
options.D: One who prescribes the drug and assures the patient that his own risk of a stroke will now fall by exactly three points.

questions.question: The reference to trials within a single patient in the final paragraph serves mainly to

options.A: propose a design that should take the place of large trials for chronic conditions whose symptoms are stable.
options.B: show that the average from a large trial is of no value whenever a patient's symptoms come and go quickly.
options.C: indicate what a genuinely individual conclusion would demand, by contrast with a mere claim that a patient is different.
options.D: concede that, for chronic illnesses at least, a doctor's intuition about an individual patient is a reliable guide.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: trace how the word 'computer' came to name a machine instead of the occupation that it originally described.
options.B: claim that electronic machines added little to calculation apart from a gain in speed over the offices they displaced.
options.C: show that human computing offices produced more reliable results than the first electronic machines that replaced them.
options.D: argue that electronic computers took over a way of organising calculation that human computing offices had already developed.

questions.question: According to the passage, how were errors caught in the human computing offices?

options.A: The same column was worked out by two people separately, and any mismatch sent it back to be redone.
options.B: Results were compared against published tables of positions and tides that earlier offices had already computed.
options.C: The planner who designed the procedure checked every finished sheet against their own understanding of the problem.
options.D: Workers were trained to understand the purpose of each step so that they would notice when a result looked wrong.

questions.question: The opening sentence of the final paragraph ('None of this is to say that the machines merely did faster what people had done slowly') serves mainly to

options.A: summarise the evidence that the designers of electronic machines borrowed techniques from the offices.
options.B: concede that the computing offices were in fact slower and less accurate than is usually assumed.
options.C: head off an overstatement that the passage's stress on continuity might otherwise invite.
options.D: introduce a new thesis that replaces the claim of continuity made in the preceding paragraphs.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that, in the computing offices, a worker's not understanding why a step was there was

options.A: an intended feature of the method, since the procedure was meant to yield correct results without that understanding.
options.B: a temporary arrangement that the offices dropped once their workers had grown familiar with the problems.
options.C: a weakness that planners put up with only because workers with mathematical training were too scarce to hire.
options.D: the main source of the errors that the practice of computing each column twice was intended to catch.

questions.question: The example of the two songs in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: illustrate the fragmentation of a shared public into sealed niches tuned to individual listeners.
options.B: suggest that the second song was neglected because early listeners judged it to be the weaker work.
options.C: prove that listeners cannot tell apart songs of equal appeal without guidance from an algorithm.
options.D: show how an accidental early advantage can grow into a large gap when ranking rewards prior engagement.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the 'early hope' mentioned in paragraph 3 has been undermined chiefly because

options.A: digital platforms have, in practice, offered far fewer obscure works than their early promoters had claimed.
options.B: making a vast catalogue available does little for obscure work if ranking keeps people from encountering it.
options.C: personalised systems confine each user to a narrow niche that obscure work is unable to reach.
options.D: users, left to themselves, prefer familiar and popular works to obscure ones that might suit them better.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that an automated ranking is 'partly manufacturing' what people want?

options.A: Bestseller lists in the decades before online platforms also showed a few large successes and a great many neglected works.
options.B: When the same new songs were ranked separately for several groups of listeners, different songs became hits in each group, depending on early chance.
options.C: Most users of streaming services now listen to a narrower range of genres than they did before such services became common.
options.D: Listeners who rely on recommendation engines report that they enjoy the suggested songs more than songs that were picked for them at random.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author's view of the 'remedy' mentioned in the final paragraph?

options.A: It would aim chiefly at showing users fewer of the items that match the tastes they have already displayed.
options.B: It would remove popularity from rankings entirely, since amplifying success is a harm peculiar to algorithms.
options.C: It would be achieved once automated rankings were made as slow to respond as the choices of booksellers.
options.D: It would ask whether apparent popularity shows real preference or just the prominence an item had earlier.

questions.question: According to the passage, a person who submits a sample to a genetic testing service

options.A: gives up legal ownership of the sample and of any information that may later be drawn from it.
options.B: reveals information only about themselves, provided that they have read the privacy notice first.
options.C: may disclose facts about relatives, some of whom may not even know that the test was taken.
options.D: can protect their relatives fully by refusing permission for the results to be used in research.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the statement that 'consent cannot carry the load it has been given' means that

options.A: consent has been relied on to provide more protection than individual choices are able to supply.
options.B: consent has turned out to be worthless and ought to be dropped in favour of rules on inference.
options.C: consent forms have grown too long and too complicated for most people to read with any care.
options.D: people are now asked for consent so often that they agree to requests without considering them.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the condition the author has in mind when comparing privacy to 'clean air or quiet streets'?

options.A: A tenant who refuses to sign an unfair lease is turned away, and so ends up with no flat on that street at all.
options.B: A shopper who reads the terms carefully before signing is later charged a fee that the terms had deliberately concealed.
options.C: A gardener who fences her own plot keeps out the deer that go on damaging the unfenced plots beside it.
options.D: A household that stops burning wood in its stove still breathes smoky air, because most of the town keeps burning wood.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument in paragraph 3?

options.A: Deceiving people about how their information will be used remains a serious wrong even when the data involved is collective.
options.B: Traits inferred about non-sharers from others' data prove so unreliable that they seldom reveal what a refuser meant to hide.
options.C: Many people who upload their contact lists do not realise that they are disclosing information about other people.
options.D: Systems that infer traits from shared data become steadily more accurate as more people choose to disclose those traits.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that failures blamed on operators often stem from how automation shapes their role, and to suggest design responses.
options.B: show that operators of automated systems are usually careless and need stricter supervision and training.
options.C: argue that automated systems are more dangerous than manual ones and should be introduced only where unavoidable.
options.D: explain why official accident reports are required to name a single cause for every failure they describe.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, why do people supervising a highly reliable machine tend to monitor it poorly?

options.A: They trust the machine so completely that they decide there is no longer any need to watch it closely.
options.B: They have been given less training than the operators who used to do the work by hand.
options.C: Attention drifts when nothing happens for long stretches, and a reliable machine makes such stretches longer.
options.D: The displays they watch are usually too complicated to be read quickly when an emergency arises.

questions.question: The passage suggests that an improvement in how well an automated system works under ordinary conditions could

options.A: make supervisors more attentive, since a dependable machine frees them to concentrate on what remains.
options.B: remove the need for human supervisors, since rare emergencies would then be handled entirely by the machine itself.
options.C: leave its overseers worse equipped for unusual crises, so that their lapses come as more of a shock.
options.D: make emergencies so infrequent that the skill of the people supervising the system would hardly matter.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the label 'human error' is best described as

options.A: approving, since it correctly points to the operator as the part of the system most in need of reform.
options.B: indifferent, treating it as a harmless habit of official reports that has no real effect on what happens.
options.C: dismissive, on the ground that operators are never really responsible for what goes wrong in such systems.
options.D: sceptical of it as an explanation of failure, while granting that it is accurate in a narrow sense.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as part of the material reality behind the cloud EXCEPT

options.A: satellites that relay stored data between continents when undersea links fail.
options.B: water drawn from local supplies to keep buildings full of servers cool.
options.C: sites chosen because they offer cheap power or favourable taxes.
options.D: cables laid along railway lines as well as across sea floors.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the final paragraph in the argument?

options.A: It brings forward fresh evidence about the environmental costs of data centres to reinforce the claims of paragraph 2.
options.B: It answers a defence of the metaphor by separating what users need from what those who govern the infrastructure need.
options.C: It concedes that hiding complexity is what good computing does and therefore withdraws the earlier criticism of the metaphor.
options.D: It argues that ordinary users ought to learn where their data is physically stored before they make use of online services.
