questions.question: The author's remark that a cloud 'is diffuse, which suggests resilience' implies that

options.A: users are unable to tell where their files travel between one of their devices and another.
options.B: storing old files indefinitely uses up so much energy that the system will eventually be unable to cope.
options.C: the image invites a belief that services are widely spread, when they may hinge on a few points of failure.
options.D: data centres are often built on unstable ground, which makes them liable to sudden and widespread failure across a region.

questions.question: Which of the following situations most closely parallels the author's reply to the defenders of the metaphor?

options.A: A map that leaves out minor roads misleads every traveller, since it gives a false picture of the ground to anyone who uses it.
options.B: A driver who knows nothing about engines is a worse driver than one who understands how the car works under the bonnet.
options.C: A city that buries its power lines for the sake of appearance pays more to repair them, since faults become harder to find.
options.D: Using a tap without a thought for reservoirs is a convenience, but a water board that planned as if water came from taps would plan badly.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that both sides in the debate wrongly treat understanding as all-or-nothing, and to propose mapping separate abilities instead.
options.B: show that fluent machines lack the grounding in perception and action without which there can be no genuine understanding.
options.C: argue that no question about machine understanding can be answered until the nature of inner experience has been settled.
options.D: defend the view that behaviour indistinguishable from that of a competent person is sufficient evidence of genuine understanding.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, saying that a system 'really understands' is said to flatten 'this profile into a verdict'. This means that the claim

options.A: exaggerates what the system can do by ignoring the failures that it shows on trivial variations.
options.B: reduces an uneven pattern of strengths and weaknesses across abilities to a single yes or no judgement.
options.C: replaces a careful technical description of the system with an emotional reaction to its fluency.
options.D: simplifies the technical vocabulary of research so that readers without special training can follow it.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the argument of paragraphs 2 and 3?

options.A: The abilities by which we judge understanding always come together, each present to exactly the degree the others are.
options.B: Some machines that converse fluently fail at trivial variations of problems that they otherwise solve quickly and with ease.
options.C: Many people who exercise a practical skill expertly are unable to explain the principles on which it rests.
options.D: Philosophers continue to disagree about whether an inner experience of meaning could ever be detected from behaviour.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the question of whether understanding involves an inner experience of meaning as

options.A: decisive, so that practical decisions about such systems ought to wait until the question has been resolved.
options.B: perhaps a real question, but not one peculiar to machines or one on which most practical decisions turn.
options.C: a question that arises only for machines, because only their inner workings are closed to inspection.
options.D: meaningless, since nothing that cannot be inspected from outside could ever be the subject of a sensible question at all.

questions.question: According to the passage, the criteria of fairness described in paragraph 1 cannot all be met together when

options.A: the lender relies on more than one measure of creditworthiness when it decides whether to approve a loan.
options.B: the difference in default rates between the groups is itself the result of earlier unfair treatment.
options.C: the groups differ in how often their members actually default and the predictions are less than perfect.
options.D: the scoring system has been poorly engineered or built from too small a body of past lending records.

questions.question: The reference to the conflict between honesty and kindness in paragraph 3 serves to

options.A: suggest that fairness, like kindness, ought to give way whenever it comes into conflict with truthfulness.
options.B: illustrate that everyday moral notions are too vague to offer any guidance to those who design algorithms.
options.C: show that the builders of scoring systems ought to be guided by their personal virtues rather than by arithmetic.
options.D: support the claim that a conflict between two demands does not show that either demand is empty.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the decision about which fairness criterion should give way

options.A: cannot be made on any principled basis, because the competing criteria have been shown to be incompatible.
options.B: would rest partly on how heavily each kind of mistaken decision falls on those who must bear it.
options.C: should favour whichever criterion produces the smallest total number of errors across both groups combined.
options.D: should be left to those who build the scoring system, since they understand the arithmetic of prediction best.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the formal analysis of fairness criteria is best described as

options.A: appreciative of its having exposed a hidden trade-off, but wary that the clarity it brings may be wasted.
options.B: dismissive, since it only restates a dilemma that loan officers had always acknowledged openly in their decisions.
options.C: enthusiastic, regarding it as having shown how every reasonable demand of fairness can at last be met together.
options.D: suspicious, holding that its technical vocabulary was deliberately designed to hide choices that belong to discretion.

questions.question: The passage implies that a loan officer who judges applicants by experience, when the groups differ in base rates,

options.A: treats applicants more fairly than an algorithm, since personal discretion allows the special features of each case to count.
options.B: escapes the trade-off, because without an explicit score none of the criteria is ever strictly applied to the decisions.
options.C: sacrifices at least one of the criteria just as a scoring system must, though possibly without knowing which one.
options.D: can satisfy every criterion together, provided that the officer takes enough care over each individual application.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, a file left on an old disk

options.A: survives neglect better than a paper letter, because a digital copy does not decay in the way that paper does.
options.B: can be read a century later by anyone who knows the language in which the file was originally written.
options.C: becomes unreadable within a few years, however carefully the disk itself is stored and looked after over time.
options.D: can be read later only if the disk, a machine able to read it and software able to interpret the file all survive.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?

options.A: The belief that the internet never forgets is a myth, since nearly everything posted online eventually disappears without a trace.
options.B: Whether digital material lasts turns on reasons to copy it, which explains both complaints and makes preservation an institutional task.
options.C: Digital records are far less durable than paper and should be printed out whenever they need to be kept for the long term.
options.D: Libraries and archives should copy everything that appears on the web so that no record of the present is ever lost to historians.

questions.question: The claim that digital persistence 'tracks attention and interest rather than value' implies that

options.A: material may matter a great deal for later understanding and still be among the first things to be lost.
options.B: the value of a piece of material can be judged reliably by counting how often it has been copied.
options.C: material that attracts a lot of attention is generally of little value to anyone who studies it later.
options.D: valuable material is always lost before trivial material, whatever efforts are made to preserve it.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the first paragraph?

options.A: It rejects both of the familiar complaints about digital information as exaggerations that do not survive scrutiny.
options.B: It states the author's thesis that digital information is more durable than paper and then lists evidence for it.
options.C: It sets out two complaints that seem to contradict each other, a tension that the following paragraphs then resolve.
options.D: It describes a puzzle about digital information that the author concedes in the end cannot be fully resolved.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT

options.A: an organisation that preserves material must be willing to keep paying for it after interest in it has faded.
options.B: an archive's decision about what to copy from the web is in effect also a decision about what to let vanish.
options.C: the ease of copying is what allows some digital material to outlast the efforts made to delete it.
options.D: print archives never had to choose what to keep, since the volume of print was small enough to preserve in full.

questions.question: The central claim of the passage is that

options.A: publishing papers before they are reviewed is better than any arrangement that relies on the private judgement of specialists.
options.B: anonymous review becomes hard to defend chiefly when secret reports also decide whether a paper is published at all.
options.C: junior researchers need the protection of anonymity, since senior figures in their fields often control decisions about their promotion.
options.D: anonymous review should be abolished outright, because referees routinely use their concealment to suppress the work of their rivals.

questions.question: According to the passage, the usual defence of anonymity in peer review is that it

options.A: ensures that a manuscript is judged by its arguments rather than by the reputation of whoever wrote it.
options.B: spares referees the labour of explaining their recommendations to authors and readers in public.
options.C: lets less powerful researchers criticise the work of influential authors without having to fear for their own careers.
options.D: prevents editors from choosing referees who have close personal ties to the authors of a manuscript.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 1, 'candour to flow upward' refers to

options.A: honest criticism travelling from junior researchers toward the people who hold power over them.
options.B: junior researchers gaining promotion more quickly once they have refereed for prominent journals.
options.C: the quality of published research rising steadily as referees become more experienced over time.
options.D: frank opinions passing from journal editors to the specialists whom they invite to assess papers.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would regard the anonymity of referees as largely harmless in a system where

options.A: referees remain unnamed and their reports, seen only by the editor, settle whether a paper appears in print.
options.B: referees remain unnamed but are chosen only from researchers who are in the early years of their careers.
options.C: editors keep the names of referees secret even from one another, so that no outside pressure can be applied to them.
options.D: every paper is published, with the unsigned referee reports printed beside it and the authors free to reply.

questions.question: According to the passage, a published literature from which failed studies are missing leads its readers to

options.A: treat the positive studies they read as if those studies had been conducted with unusually large samples.
options.B: overestimate both how frequently the effect being studied occurs and how strong it tends to be when it does.
options.C: doubt the positive findings they read, because they suspect that many failed studies have been quietly hidden from them.
options.D: assume that journals reject every study that fails to find a difference between the groups it compares.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a researcher who obtains a null result often leaves it unwritten mainly because

options.A: she fears that publishing it would contradict the published findings of senior colleagues in her field.
options.B: editors have made it clear in advance that they will not consider studies that find no effect.
options.C: she herself often cannot tell what the absence of the expected effect actually means.
options.D: she is too occupied with newer projects to spend time on work that has already failed.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the argument of paragraph 4?

options.A: In fields where sample sizes and procedures must be declared before data are collected, researchers submit a far larger share of their null results.
options.B: Researchers whose null results came from carefully designed studies report that journals still often refuse to publish such results.
options.C: Most researchers say they would write up their null results if doing so counted toward their promotion and toward their chances of winning grants.
options.D: Null results that have appeared in print are cited much less often than positive results on the same research questions.

questions.question: Each of the following is mentioned in the passage as something a null result might reflect EXCEPT

options.A: too few cases having been studied for a real effect to show up.
options.B: a person running the study having misunderstood its procedure.
options.C: a material used in the experiment having been impure.
options.D: a hypothesis framed too loosely for any experiment to count against it.

questions.question: The example of the two similar warblers in paragraph 1 serves to

options.A: illustrate the kind of error that critics expected untrained volunteers to make when recording what they saw.
options.B: show that bird song is a more dependable guide to identifying species than a bird's appearance.
options.C: explain why well-run projects began asking volunteers to photograph what they had observed.
options.D: prove that volunteer records of birds have turned out to be less accurate than records of flowers.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that a bird which 'seems to be thriving in the suburbs'

options.A: is probably being confused by volunteers with a rarer species that looks very similar to it.
options.B: may appear common there partly because the suburbs are where many observers happen to be.
options.C: is recorded accurately because suburban volunteers tend to be more skilled than rural ones.
options.D: has been driven out of farmland and into gardens by the spread of industrial estates.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the early objection that amateurs would make mistakes is best described as

options.A: fully supportive, since the author believes misidentification remains the chief threat to such projects.
options.B: dismissive, since the author holds that volunteers make no more errors than trained specialists do.
options.C: sympathetic to why it was raised, while holding that another weakness of volunteer data matters more.
options.D: puzzled, since the author cannot understand why scientists ever doubted the abilities of volunteers.

questions.question: Which of the following projects would best address the concern raised in paragraphs 3 and 4?

options.A: A bird survey in which specialists examine each unusual record before it is added to the shared database.
options.B: A flower survey that invites as many people as possible to send in photographs from wherever they choose to walk.
options.C: A butterfly survey that trains its volunteers for several weeks so that they can identify every species they meet.
options.D: A frog survey in which each volunteer visits an allocated pond on set evenings, wherever that pond happens to lie.

questions.question: The description of the public as 'a vessel with a hole in it' (paragraph 1) suggests that the deficit model

options.A: regarded scientists as having failed to notice what the public already knew about many scientific matters.
options.B: regarded ordinary people as unable to retain scientific facts however often these were explained to them.
options.C: regarded the press as distorting expert opinion on its way from the laboratory to ordinary readers.
options.D: regarded ordinary people as defined only by an absence of knowledge that experts were expected to fill.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Engineers and public officials ought to be held legally responsible whenever the assurances they give to the communities near their projects prove wrong.
options.B: Well-informed people are generally more likely than poorly informed people to reject the considered consensus of scientific experts.
options.C: Public resistance to expert conclusions often reflects judgements about trust and risk, so supplying facts is at best a partial remedy.
options.D: Scientific explanations rarely change anyone's mind, so communicators should give up explaining and concentrate on negotiating with their audiences.

questions.question: The example of the village and the dam in paragraph 3 is used to

options.A: illustrate the claim in paragraph 2 that people who read widely become more certain as they learn more.
options.B: show that scepticism can rest on considerations of trust and fairness that a technical briefing leaves out.
options.C: show that villagers often understand engineering better than the officials who are sent to reassure them.
options.D: suggest that the dam is in fact unsafe and that the assurance given by the engineers is mistaken.

questions.question: The author's claim that communication which starts from the audience's concerns 'will at least explain the right thing' implies that

options.A: a briefing under the deficit model can be accurate and still address a question other than the one troubling its audience.
options.B: communicators should explain only those matters about which the members of an audience have asked them directly and in advance.
options.C: an audience will come to accept a scientific conclusion once its fears and its experiences have been properly listened to.
options.D: explanations given under the deficit model usually contained factual errors that, once discovered, did lasting damage to public trust.

questions.question: According to the passage, the geologist judges her work successful when

options.A: her hypothesis survives a controlled experiment that has been designed in order to refute it.
options.B: she can find natural cases that differ from one another in just the one respect she wishes to compare.
options.C: her account of past events hangs together and explains the scattered evidence she has found.
options.D: the instruments she has built for the purpose can be made to work reliably in the field and laboratory.

questions.question: The author's remark that a single recipe may become 'so general that it no longer guides anyone' suggests that

options.A: the textbook sequence has been revised so many times that it has become too complicated to be followed.
options.B: every science would be better served by a recipe written specifically for its own distinctive subject matter.
options.C: researchers in most fields disregard general instructions and rely instead on intuition and luck when they work.
options.D: a description broad enough to fit every science would be too vague to tell any researcher what to do next.

questions.question: The author objects to the textbook account of the scientific method on all of the following grounds EXCEPT that it

options.A: gives too much weight to criticism by colleagues as a way of testing scientific claims.
options.B: overlooks the considerable effort of getting instruments and procedures to function in the first place.
options.C: fails to prepare people for long periods in which results conflict and experts disagree with one another.
options.D: implies that sciences which are unable to run experiments are of lower standing than those that can.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about what the sciences have in common?

options.A: Students who were taught the norms of criticism and revision did no better on tests of experimental procedure than students who had memorised the steps.
options.B: In one long-established and productive science, central claims are customarily shielded from colleagues' attacks and are not expected to be revised in the light of evidence.
options.C: Geologists, unlike chemists, seldom run controlled experiments in a laboratory and rely mainly on traces left by events in the distant past.
options.D: Some eminent scientists who were shown to be wrong took many years to accept the evidence against their views, and a few never accepted it.

questions.question: The passage suggests that readers who give priority to papers by well-known authors are

options.A: responding sensibly to the impossibility of reading everything that is published in their field.
options.B: unaware that the unknown co-authors of such papers usually did most of the work that the papers report.
options.C: behaving unfairly and ought to be trained to ignore the names that are attached to the research they read.
options.D: motivated mainly by admiration for eminent figures rather than by any practical consideration of their own.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the view that the Matthew effect is 'a problem of fairness' is best described as

options.A: treating it with open contempt as a complaint voiced only by those who have themselves been denied credit.
options.B: rejecting it entirely, on the ground that credit in science is in fact distributed according to merit.
options.C: accepting it as accurate as far as it goes, while holding that it misses the more serious harm.
options.D: endorsing it fully, since the author regards the effect chiefly as an injustice done to unknown researchers.

questions.question: Which of the following measures is most in keeping with the remedy the author proposes?

options.A: A university that awards prizes to junior co-authors whose contributions to celebrated papers went unrecognised.
options.B: A journal that prints every paper without the names of its authors, so that readers cannot be swayed by reputation.
options.C: A professional society that publishes a yearly ranking of the most frequently cited researchers in each field.
options.D: A funding agency that assesses a share of the applications it receives with the applicants' names and records removed.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, the most serious consequence of the Matthew effect is that

options.A: unknown researchers leave science altogether because they receive too little credit for the work they have done.
options.B: a field may commit its resources to some ideas and neglect others for reasons that have little to do with their merit.
options.C: well-known researchers gradually come to believe that their own ideas are better than those of their colleagues.
options.D: readers stop judging papers for themselves and simply accept whatever a famous author happens to have written.

questions.question: According to the passage, panels judging research proposals are reasonably good at

options.A: separating proposals that are scientifically sound from those that are not, at the threshold of quality.
options.B: ranking the strongest proposals in the order of their likely scientific value to the field.
options.C: recognising when their own preferences have influenced a decision about where the funding line falls.
options.D: predicting which of the riskier projects before them will eventually produce the largest payoff.

questions.question: The author mentions the efficiency argument for lotteries in paragraph 2 primarily in order to

options.A: concede that lotteries are cheaper but argue that their savings in cost outweigh the loss of careful judgement.
options.B: show that funding agencies adopted lotteries mainly in order to reduce the workload of their panels.
options.C: grant it but set it aside as a weak justification before presenting what the author considers the stronger one.
options.D: refute the common view that ranking proposals costs panels a great deal of time and careful effort.

questions.question: The sentence 'Hidden chance is not neutral chance' (paragraph 3) implies that

options.A: panels deliberately favour applicants whom they know personally whenever the funding line is close.
options.B: lotteries are themselves biased, because the proposals entered into them are chosen by cautious panels.
options.C: chance plays a smaller part in conventional ranking than defenders of lotteries usually suppose.
options.D: when merit cannot settle a decision, the outcome is shaped by systematic leanings rather than by pure luck.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the objection that lotteries will corrode scientists' motivation?

options.A: Some researchers say they would rather lose a draw than be told that their proposal was ranked just below the funding line.
options.B: Projects ranked just above the funding line have consistently gone on to outperform those ranked just below it.
options.C: Agencies that fund by lottery spend considerably less on assessing proposals than agencies that rank every proposal they receive.
options.D: Members of a panel sometimes disagree about whether a borderline proposal is sound enough to be entered into the draw.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Agencies should publish how close their decisions near the funding line were instead of adopting lotteries at all.
options.B: Where panels cannot reliably separate good proposals, drawing lots is preferable to a ranking that disguises chance as judgement.
options.C: The main advantage of funding by lottery is that it saves both agencies and panels a great deal of time and money.
options.D: Funding by lottery should replace ranking by expert panels, because the judgements of such panels are shaped by bias at every stage.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, 'the promise' that 'is only partly kept' is the idea that

options.A: a competent reader who follows a paper's written methods will be able to obtain the findings it reports.
options.B: researchers will share their materials and equipment with any laboratory that asks to repeat their work.
options.C: scientific knowledge will in time be cleared of the errors made by the people who first produced it.
options.D: a failed replication shows that either the original claim or the replicators' own care must be at fault.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that the groups that succeeded after a visit

options.A: were given secret details that the original laboratory had deliberately kept out of its published papers.
options.B: had discovered errors in the published descriptions, which the original authors then went on to correct.
options.C: may have acquired the decisive skill without identifying which part of the procedure it concerned.
options.D: were more careful and more competent than the groups that had worked only from the published papers.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the account of instrument-building in paragraph 3?

options.A: A baker refuses to reveal one key ingredient, and rivals who copy her bread cannot match its flavour until a former employee discloses what it is.
options.B: Cooks who follow a recipe all succeed at the first attempt, but only those with many years of experience are able to explain why each of its steps matters.
options.C: A recipe is printed with a wrong oven temperature, and the cooks who follow it keep failing until the publisher prints a correction in the next edition.
options.D: Cooks using a baker's detailed recipe keep failing to match her bread until one spends a week in her kitchen, after which he succeeds without knowing what he changed.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Failed replications should generally be blamed on the replicators' lack of skill rather than on any weakness in the original claim.
options.B: Knowledge carried in the skills of practitioners is less reliable than knowledge that has been stated explicitly in published papers.
options.C: A field could report its techniques far more fully than it now does and still find that some of its results are hard to reproduce elsewhere.
options.D: Because tacit skills cannot be written down, efforts to improve the way methods are reported in papers are largely a waste of effort.

questions.question: Each of the following is proposed or endorsed by the author as a way of helping others check published results EXCEPT

options.A: paying for researchers to spend time working in one another's laboratories.
options.B: counting the training of those who attempt a replication as part of what the replication costs.
options.C: including in papers the details that are now omitted to save space or to keep an advantage.
options.D: lengthening methods sections until each of them captures the whole of the technique it describes.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that an unreliable narrator's deepest effect is to make readers question the trust they give to all narration.
options.B: explain the techniques by which novelists plant the clues that let readers reconstruct the true events behind a distorted account.
options.C: condemn novels that hold back a revelation until their final chapters, since such books give their readers no real pleasure.
options.D: show that novels told by unreliable narrators are generally inferior to those told by calm and impersonal third-person narrators.

questions.question: According to the passage, novels that keep a revelation for their final chapters tend to go flat on a second reading because

options.A: the clues planted in the early chapters become obvious once the reader knows where to look for them.
options.B: the one question they raised has been answered, leaving the reader nothing to wonder about.
options.C: their narrators turn out to have been lying, whereas the narrators of better novels merely select and omit.
options.D: readers resent having been misled for so long and are unwilling to trust the narrator a second time.

questions.question: The observation that the clues to a narrator's distortions 'are supplied by the same narrator' (paragraph 2) implies that

options.A: unreliable narrators usually intend their distortions to be noticed by an attentive reader of the novel.
options.B: novelists who employ unreliable narrators ought to include a second, trustworthy voice to settle what happened.
options.C: the reader can confirm the true story by comparing the narrator's account with the account of another character.
options.D: the reader's version of what really happened rests on testimony that the reader has already decided to doubt.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the effect that the author attributes to the best uses of the unreliable narrator?

options.A: A detective who exposes a lying suspect closes the case, confident that the full sequence of events is now known.
options.B: A juror who catches one witness contradicting himself concludes that all the remaining witnesses must therefore be telling the whole truth.
options.C: A juror who catches one witness contradicting himself starts to ask what the apparently consistent witnesses may also have left out.
options.D: A reader who discovers that one memoir contains invented episodes resolves never to trust any memoir again.

questions.question: The example of the woman packing a suitcase (paragraph 2) serves primarily to

options.A: demonstrate that short stories most often take domestic life and the breakdown of marriages as their subject.
options.B: show that a story grows more moving once the backgrounds of its characters have been explained in some detail.
options.C: illustrate how a story makes an unstated history felt through what it chooses to show and leave out.
options.D: suggest that photographs and other personal objects are the most effective details a writer can place in a scene.

questions.question: According to the passage, a novel earns its effects chiefly through

options.A: the very large amount of background information it supplies about the earlier lives of its characters.
options.B: the length of time over which the reader lives alongside its characters and watches them change.
options.C: the pressure of selection, which turns a few chosen details into a kind of meaning.
options.D: the variety of minor characters and subplots that its greater length allows it to sustain.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a critic's praise of a story as 'as rich as a novel' as

options.A: evidence that most critics do not read short stories with any real attention or care.
options.B: an accurate account of what the best short stories manage to achieve within their few pages.
options.C: a sign that publishers have at last begun to value collections of short stories as highly as novels.
options.D: a compliment that measures the story by a standard that belongs to a different form.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about expanding fine stories?

options.A: Readers comparing admired stories with later full-length versions by the same writers mostly found the longer versions stronger, because of the added history.
options.B: Publishers continue to report that collections of short stories sell fewer copies than novels by the same writers.
options.C: Several admired novels are known to have grown out of rough, unfinished short pieces that their authors went on revising, sometimes for many years, before finally publishing them.
options.D: Writers who began with short stories and later turned to novels often say that the shorter form taught them economy.

questions.question: The heroine 'killed by a runaway carriage' (paragraph 2) is mentioned in order to

options.A: prove that tragic endings are in general less honest than the happy endings that serious readers distrust.
options.B: show that an unhappy ending forced on a story from outside is as arbitrary as a contrived happy one.
options.C: suggest that sudden accidental deaths are seldom believable in novels whose stories are set in earlier centuries.
options.D: illustrate the kind of courageous ending that serious readers are right to admire in a novel.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, an ending is said to 'console' when it

options.A: makes up to the reader for the sadness and suffering of the earlier chapters.
options.B: rewards the characters the reader likes and punishes those the reader has come to dislike.
options.C: marks clearly the point beyond which the story will not go on being told.
options.D: leaves the reader reassured about the world that the novel has depicted.

questions.question: The author makes each of the following claims EXCEPT that

options.A: readers ought to prefer novels that end in marriage or reconciliation to novels that end in failure.
options.B: some endings that arrive from outside the story deserve the reader's feeling of having been cheated.
options.C: every story, whatever its tone or subject, has to stop at some point and leave the rest untold.
options.D: an unhappy ending can meet the expectations of some readers as predictably as a happy one can.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the 'suspicious reader' described in paragraph 3?

options.A: Such a reader is right to object to consolation in fiction but mistaken in admiring unhappy endings for their courage.
options.B: Such a reader believes that every serious novel must end in death, separation or failure if it is to count as honest fiction.
options.C: Such a reader treats a dislike of reassurance as if it were an objection to bringing a story to a definite end.
options.D: Such a reader consciously prefers novels that refuse to finish at all, ranking them above both happy and tragic ones.

questions.question: According to the passage, a turn in the ninth line of a sonnet registers as a turn because

options.A: the reader already knows the point in the poem at which a turn is expected.
options.B: readers of sonnets are taught to look for a contradiction of the poem's opening.
options.C: the ninth line is by tradition the longest and most emphatic line of the poem.
options.D: the poet abandons the rhyme scheme at that line so as to mark the change clearly.

questions.question: The author lists 'the fractured chronology' and 'the unnamed narrator' (paragraph 4) in order to

options.A: illustrate the inventions by which literary novels create their own shape instead of inheriting one.
options.B: show that literary fiction also depends on inherited conventions that can be followed mechanically.
options.C: argue that literary fiction has become more formulaic than any of the popular genres it looks down on.
options.D: identify techniques that genre writers have recently borrowed from the literary novel.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the pleasure of the devoted genre reader as

options.A: confined to checking whether a writer has followed every rule of the genre correctly.
options.B: lesser than the pleasure of meeting an unconventional novel for the first time without expectations.
options.C: depending on close knowledge of the conventions against which a particular book can be measured.
options.D: arising chiefly from the comfort of meeting familiar situations and outcomes once again.

questions.question: The claim that a departure from convention in a detective story 'is felt with a precision no unconventional novel can command' depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Readers of unconventional novels generally read with less attention and care than the devoted readers of detective stories.
options.B: Detective stories that break their conventions are more highly valued than detective stories that keep them.
options.C: Most readers of detective stories have read more widely than most readers of literary fiction.
options.D: How sharply a departure is felt depends on how firmly the reader expected the thing departed from.

questions.question: According to the passage, during the pause after the line 'she said she would not leave', the reader takes the woman to be

options.A: forbidden by someone else in the house from leaving until it is safe to go out.
options.B: agreeing to leave the house as soon as the rain outside has finally stopped falling.
options.C: refusing to leave at all, until the next line narrows her refusal to the weather.
options.D: speaking insincerely, so that the reader begins to doubt whether she means what she says.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, line breaks that were 'decoration' are breaks that

options.A: restore some of the rhyme and regular metre that free verse otherwise abandons.
options.B: give a text the look of verse while adding nothing to its meaning or its pace.
options.C: make a poem visually attractive on the page, which the author treats as a legitimate secondary aim.
options.D: enrich a poem's language with ornamental words that make its images more vivid.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author regard as the best evidence that the line breaks in a particular free verse poem are doing real work?

options.A: When the poem is printed as a continuous paragraph, a second sense that one of its lines had carried disappears.
options.B: Readers who are shown the poem set out as prose still recognise it at once and find it just as effective.
options.C: The poet explains in an interview that every break in the poem was chosen with great care over many drafts.
options.D: The lines of the poem are strikingly unequal in length, some a single word long and some running nearly to the margin.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the objection that free verse is 'merely prose with the margins moved' is best described as

options.A: partial agreement: it succeeds against free verse in general, though a few exceptional poems happen to escape it.
options.B: reluctant sympathy: poets have generally failed to answer it, so it remains in effect unanswered by anyone.
options.C: firm rejection: it rests on a misunderstanding and in practice holds against almost none of the poems published today.
options.D: qualified acceptance: it is fair against many poems but cannot become a verdict on the form itself.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Round characters succeed only when a novel first presents them as flat and later reveals their hidden depth.
options.B: Flat characters do work of their own in fiction, so treating roundness as the only mark of achievement misreads many novels.
options.C: Flat characters are more lifelike than round ones, because people in ordinary life are known to us only by their habits.
options.D: The best novels are those that portray a whole society rather than the inner life of a single individual.

questions.question: The man who consults the same almanac after every misfortune (paragraph 3) is introduced in order to

options.A: suggest that superstition was a favourite target of the satirical fiction of earlier periods.
options.B: demonstrate that comic novels seldom contain any round characters at all among their casts.
options.C: show how a character's comic effect can depend on his being unable to act in any other way.
options.D: argue that a novel always gains in seriousness when its comic figures are given moments of inner doubt.

questions.question: The passage suggests that characters such as the aunt and the official in paragraph 2 contribute to a novel chiefly by

options.A: embodying an unyielding social world against which the changing characters can be measured.
options.B: delivering the novelist's moral message more directly than the major characters ever could.
options.C: standing in for the reader, who also experiences the society of the novel from outside it.
options.D: revealing, late in the story, depths that overturn the reader's first impression of them.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 2?

options.A: Novels centred on the inner life of one individual have been studied far more often than novels about societies.
options.B: Several critics who prefer round characters also count novels portraying an entire society among their favourite books.
options.C: In many novels about a society, the unchanging minor figures are also among the funniest characters in the book.
options.D: Readers of novels about whole societies report learning the society's pressures almost entirely through the changing main characters, and barely recall the fixed minor ones.

questions.question: According to the passage, the essay taught in schools and universities

options.A: encourages students to record the abandoned lines of thought by which they reached their conclusions.
options.B: was first designed in order to replace the treatise as the standard form of academic writing.
options.C: opens with a thesis and restates it at the close, after setting out evidence and dealing with objections.
options.D: has no real virtues that could justify the place it now holds in teaching and examination.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the phrase 'a standpoint from nowhere in particular' refers to

options.A: a voice that remains vague about which subject or question it is actually addressing.
options.B: a writer who conceals his own name and publishes his work anonymously or under another name.
options.C: a writer who declines to commit to any definite conclusion about the matter under discussion.
options.D: a voice that presents its claims as if they did not depend on anyone's particular position or experience.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the author's view of the treatise?

options.A: Its manner of presentation can make a conclusion seem more inevitable than the evidence by itself warrants.
options.B: Its impersonal voice is always a form of self-display disguised as a neutral and objective manner.
options.C: It is an inferior kind of writing that schools ought to stop teaching in favour of the provisional essay.
options.D: Its conclusions are, as a rule, less reliable than those reached by writers of the provisional essay.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the claim that the provisional essay leaves the reader 'better placed to disagree'?

options.A: Readers shown an argument that included the writer's abandoned paths were more likely than other readers to accept its final conclusion.
options.B: Readers shown an argument that included an alternative the writer had rejected could state reasoned objections to its conclusion more readily than readers shown the conclusion alone.
options.C: Readers generally report finding essays written in the first person more enjoyable and more personal than essays written in an impersonal voice.
options.D: Students who are trained to write thesis-first essays score higher than other students on tests of clarity and economy in writing.

questions.question: The final paragraph functions chiefly to

options.A: concede that the thesis-first essay is, after all, more useful than the provisional essay the author has praised.
options.B: guard the argument against being taken as a defence of writing that never commits itself to a claim.
options.C: summarise the historical change in how essays are taught that was first described in the second paragraph.
options.D: introduce a fresh objection to the provisional essay which the author admits cannot be satisfactorily answered.

questions.question: According to the passage, recurring characters with distinctive habits of speech helped readers of serial novels by

options.A: making it easier to find their place in the story after a month away from it.
options.B: signalling which of the many characters would turn out to matter by the end of the novel.
options.C: allowing authors to fill the length they were paid for without having to invent any new plots.
options.D: giving readers figures whose opinions and manners resembled those of the readers themselves.

questions.question: The author suggests that the critical view described in paragraph 1 assumes that

options.A: authors who wrote in instalments were on the whole indifferent to the quality of what they produced.
options.B: a chapter that ends in suspense is always a sign of poor craftsmanship in a novel of any kind.
options.C: the serial novel that readers actually have falls short of a better book its author would otherwise have written.
options.D: serial novels were read less carefully by their first readers than they are read by modern critics.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the view that adjusting a novel in response to readers is 'a surrender of artistic control' is best described as

options.A: indifferent, since the author regards the question of control as irrelevant to a novel's merits.
options.B: contemptuous, since the author treats it as a confusion that no serious critic could still hold.
options.C: approving, since the author agrees that serial novelists gave up too much to their audiences.
options.D: even-handed, since the author grants it as one possible reading while offering an alternative that is equally reasonable.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT that

options.A: some cliffhangers in serial novels read badly once the instalments had been collected into a volume.
options.B: the ideal of the unified novel arose because serial publication had made novels too long to plan in advance.
options.C: readers' responses to early instalments could influence the later course of a serial novel.
options.D: a feature that looks like digression in a bound volume may have served a purpose for the novel's first readers.

questions.question: The reference to long television dramas in the final paragraph serves mainly to

options.A: argue that television has now replaced the novel as the principal home of serial storytelling for most audiences.
options.B: suggest that modern critics have become less demanding than those who once apologised for the instalment novel.
options.C: suggest that serial forms can succeed only where audiences are able to discuss each episode before the next one appears.
options.D: point out that qualities once excused in the instalment novel are now admired when they appear in a similar form.

questions.question: According to the passage, lists of untranslatable words tend to undermine their own claim because they

options.A: explain each supposedly untranslatable word clearly in the very language said to have no equivalent for it.
options.B: present foreign words without examples, so that readers never learn how the words are used in daily speech.
options.C: include many words that are invented or exaggerated and that ordinary speakers of the original language never use.
options.D: show that speakers of every language share exactly the same experiences, which makes the special words unnecessary.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, the word 'packages' refers to

options.A: the cultural information that a word conveys about the community that first found an experience worth naming.
options.B: the process by which a translator compresses a long explanation of a word into a brief footnote.
options.C: the way one language bundles into a single word a meaning that another language spreads across several words.
options.D: the attractive manner in which popular articles present foreign words so that they seem more exotic than they are.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 3 in the passage?

options.A: It argues that explanatory footnotes are the most effective means a translator has of restoring what is lost.
options.B: It abandons the argument of paragraph 2 by admitting that some experiences cannot be grasped outside their own language.
options.C: It gives the example of a particular poem whose translation failed because it contained a single untranslatable word.
options.D: It concedes that something is lost in translation, while locating that loss in qualities other than a word's basic sense.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

options.A: A translation may render a word's sense accurately and yet fail to carry over much of what that word does in the original.
options.B: The real difficulties of translation are confined mostly to rare words that name experiences peculiar to one culture.
options.C: Languages with larger vocabularies allow their speakers to perceive a wider range of experiences than other languages do.
options.D: Since every language lacks words for many things, the presence or absence of a word reveals nothing about a community.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: defending film directors against the charge that they borrow the titles of famous books merely to attract an audience.
options.B: explaining why novels narrated by untrustworthy characters can rarely be adapted successfully for the screen.
options.C: arguing that adaptations should be judged by whether they achieve what their source achieved, not by how little they change.
options.D: showing that film is an inferior medium to the novel because it cannot represent what happens inside a character's mind.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following is a difference between novels and films?

options.A: A novel is written for a small circle of devoted readers, whereas a film is made for a large and ready-made audience.
options.B: A novel can linger over or summarise events as it likes, whereas a film moves at a pace the viewer cannot slow.
options.C: A novel must preserve every one of its incidents, whereas a film is free to drop a subplot or merge characters.
options.D: A novel depends on a narrator to tell its story, whereas a film can show events only plainly and from the outside.

questions.question: Which of the following adaptations would the author most likely regard as the most faithful to its source?

options.A: A film of a comic novel that keeps every scene and nearly every line of dialogue but is acted so solemnly that the book's humour disappears.
options.B: A television series that keeps the title and the characters' names of a famous satirical novel but turns its story into a simple romance.
options.C: A film of a novel about a child's confused view of adult quarrels, shot from the adults' side, with added scenes that explain each quarrel.
options.D: A play based on a novel told in letters, which cuts several letters but has each actor speak straight to the audience, so each character's partial view is felt.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the complaint against adaptations that merely borrow a famous title as

options.A: understandable but unfair, since such films often lead viewers to read the book they are based on.
options.B: misguided, because a film is entitled to change whatever it wishes once it has acknowledged its source.
options.C: justified, though for a reason that a checklist of departures from the book does not capture.
options.D: justified, because such adaptations usually depart from the book on more points than other adaptations do.

questions.question: According to the passage, those who favour silence over negative criticism argue that

options.A: critics who write unfavourably about books are usually settling personal scores with their authors.
options.B: the space available for criticism is scarce and should go to books that deserve attention.
options.C: readers stop trusting critics who praise too many of the books that they choose to discuss.
options.D: unfavourable notices damage the sales of small publishers who take risks on unknown writers.

questions.question: The remark that such a reader 'will read the next novel more alertly' (paragraph 2) suggests that

options.A: a reasoned negative argument can be of use even to a reader whom it fails to persuade.
options.B: the chief value of criticism lies in helping readers choose more wisely which novel to read next.
options.C: readers ought to be suspicious of any novel that they find themselves admiring on a first reading.
options.D: readers who disagree with a careful critic will usually come round to that critic's view in time.

questions.question: According to the author, the argument for silence rests on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Criticism exists solely to help readers decide which books are worth their time.
options.B: Most of the books published each year are of poor quality and deserve no attention.
options.C: A poor book that is ignored will sell fewer copies than one that is attacked in print.
options.D: Critics take more pleasure in writing unfavourable notices than favourable ones.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT

options.A: contesting the reputation of a heavily promoted book can be one of the most useful acts of criticism.
options.B: the case for keeping silent about a weak book is strongest when few people are likely to read it.
options.C: criticism that never says no can inform readers just as well as criticism that sometimes dissents, provided its praise is carefully argued.
options.D: an account of why a book fails also indicates, at least implicitly, what success would have required.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the statement that a canonical work's status is 'less a medal than a position in a network of replies' means that the work

options.A: has been awarded prizes less often than it has been attacked by the readers who came after it.
options.B: has a reputation that rises and falls as each new generation of critics comments upon it.
options.C: is valued chiefly for its own replies to earlier books rather than for any originality of its own.
options.D: matters because so many later works respond to it, not because it has been judged to excel.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about a highly polished novel that later writers never took up?

options.A: It would become canonical once a syllabus committee had placed it on a sufficient number of reading lists.
options.B: On the conversational account it would probably not be canonical, however excellent it is judged to be.
options.C: Defenders of the list model would rank it above many canonical works, and they would be wrong about its quality.
options.D: It must have been neglected because its author belonged to a group that was denied access to publishers.

questions.question: The final paragraph of the passage serves mainly to

options.A: reject the conversational account in favour of the view that the canon simply records the tastes of a narrow group of readers.
options.B: set out a specific programme of reforms to publishing and education that would make future canons fairer than past ones.
options.C: qualify the conversational account by showing that it inherits, in a new location, the exclusions that critics of the canon object to.
options.D: show that the critics of the canon were right all along about the biased judgements of tastemakers and teachers.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the account of canons defended in paragraph 2?

options.A: Reading lists drawn up by syllabus committees have changed considerably over the course of the last century.
options.B: Many works that all parties agree are canonical turn out to have been almost never quoted, imitated, parodied or answered by later writers.
options.C: Several works of great finish that provoked no answer from later writers have stayed popular with ordinary readers for centuries.
options.D: Some of the most firmly canonical works are regarded by most readers as clumsy and tedious for long stretches.

questions.question: According to the passage, the 'usual answer' to why translations age is that

options.A: translators of earlier generations were simply less skilled, and less faithful to their originals, than the translators who are at work today.
options.B: each generation of readers demands a translation that reflects its own concerns and preoccupations.
options.C: the originals are now read mainly by scholars, who are unusually tolerant of difficult and archaic language.
options.D: a translation uses the idiom of its own time, which changes, while the original is read with allowance for its age.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Translations date because each must settle what its original leaves open, and so preserves one period's reading of it.
options.B: Translations date chiefly because the idioms of the language into which they are made keep changing over time.
options.C: The best translations are those that become works of literature in their own right and so stop ageing.
options.D: Great works can never be adequately translated, because no translator is able to preserve their openness.

questions.question: The passage suggests that an old translation which is 'perfectly intelligible' may 'still feel inadequate' because

options.A: it was made from an unreliable copy of the original that later scholarship has corrected.
options.B: its translator misread the original language at important points and introduced errors.
options.C: the decisions it made about undecided passages reflect concerns its present readers no longer share.
options.D: its language, though understandable, sounds too formal and dignified to a modern reader's ear.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the process described in paragraph 3?

options.A: A dictionary is revised every few decades to record the words and senses that have entered the language since its last edition.
options.B: A historian rereads old letters and finds that a phrase she took for sarcasm was, in its own period, an ordinary courtesy.
options.C: A painting darkens as its varnish yellows with age, so that restorers must clean it every so often to recover its original colours.
options.D: Actors staging an old play must decide how each ambiguous line is spoken, so every production shows its own era's reading while the script stays open.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the intentionalist and anti-intentionalist positions is best described as

options.A: firm support for the anti-intentionalist position, tempered by some sympathy for the intentionalist's concern with an author's purpose.
options.B: partial acceptance of each, joined to the claim that both rest on the same mistaken picture of intention.
options.C: impatience with both, on the ground that the question they dispute cannot in principle ever be answered.
options.D: neutral detachment, setting out the strongest form of each position without deciding between them.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would treat a novelist's public statement about what her book means as

options.A: evidence worth weighing, which counts only insofar as it helps to reveal patterns that are present in the work.
options.B: decisive whenever it is sincere, since the intention that matters to criticism is the one the novelist actually held.
options.C: entirely irrelevant, since the meaning of a published work is fixed by the public language in which it is written.
options.D: more reliable than the novel itself, because the novelist has access to choices that the text cannot show.

questions.question: The example of the novel written to celebrate a way of life (paragraph 4) serves mainly to

options.A: establish that novelists are in general unaware of the social costs of the ways of life they choose to depict.
options.B: demonstrate that a writer's private notebooks can expose patterns that the finished work keeps hidden.
options.C: illustrate the anti-intentionalist claim that an author's purpose has no bearing on what a work means.
options.D: show that a work can mean more than its author meant without that reading being a defiance of the work's design.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the author's account of intention EXCEPT

options.A: a work may support a reading that its author, if asked, would have rejected outright.
options.B: recognising a repetition in a poem as deliberate already involves attributing a purpose to the text.
options.C: the intentions that matter to criticism lie hidden behind a text, which can at best report them faithfully.
options.D: an author's diary can sometimes help a critic notice a pattern in the work that had been overlooked.

questions.question: According to the passage, a first reading typically involves

options.A: forming judgements of characters that the book later shows to be mistaken.
options.B: recognising which of the passages one most admires are in fact the weakest.
options.C: dwelling on descriptions in order to anticipate how the story will end.
options.D: noticing images that return later in the book with an altered meaning.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the statement that knowing the outcome 'does not empty these details; it fills them' means that

options.A: rereaders tend to supply from their own imagination whatever an author has left unsaid in a scene.
options.B: such details gain significance once a reader can see what they were preparing for.
options.C: a reader who knows the ending will find such details tedious, though still necessary to the book.
options.D: the suspense of a first reading is replaced on rereading by a complete knowledge of the plot's events.

questions.question: The example of the story of a marriage (paragraph 3) suggests that

options.A: a reader's growing experience can reveal qualities in a book that were present but unseen before.
options.B: young readers are usually right to find stories about ordinary people rather dull.
options.C: novels about marriage are best understood by readers who are themselves married.
options.D: the meaning of a book changes as the culture surrounding it changes over time.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the view that rereading is 'a kind of nostalgia' is best described as

options.A: sympathetic, since the author shares the regret that a first encounter with a book cannot be repeated.
options.B: critical, though willing to grant that a first reading has a real value of its own.
options.C: neutral, since the passage lays out the arguments for both kinds of reading without favouring either.
options.D: dismissive, holding that a first reading offers nothing that a later reading cannot supply better.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as the best evidence that a novel is more than 'a mechanism for producing suspense'?

options.A: Readers who begin it find themselves unable to put it down until they have reached the last page.
options.B: Critics praised it highly on its first appearance, well before its ending had become widely known.
options.C: Readers who already know how it ends report finding more in it on a third reading than on a second.
options.D: Its final twist recasts the earlier chapters so completely that first-time readers are astonished by it.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following is an objection that has been made to distant reading?

options.A: The charts that such studies produce are too complex for most literary scholars to interpret.
options.B: Computers are not yet able to process anything close to the full output of a century of novels.
options.C: Distant reading has been applied mostly to canonical novels and has neglected forgotten ones.
options.D: A frequency count cannot register the irony or dramatic context on which a word's meaning depends.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author values the anomalies mentioned in paragraph 3 chiefly because they

options.A: prove that the canon was assembled by readers whose tastes were narrow and unrepresentative.
options.B: point readers towards particular books that then repay being read closely.
options.C: can be interpreted with confidence without anyone reading the books in which they occur.
options.D: show that machines detect features of style that human readers are incapable of perceiving.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?

options.A: The objections to computational reading are decisive, since counting words can never produce any understanding of literature.
options.B: The literary canon is an unrepresentative sample, and its study should give way to the study of forgotten novels.
options.C: Computational reading should take the place of close reading, since it can study the entire output of a period instead of a sample.
options.D: Computational reading cannot interpret texts by itself, but it can pose questions for close reading and test claims drawn from a biased sample.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim made in paragraph 4 about the independent contribution of distant reading?

options.A: Some canonical novels turn out to cluster with obscure ones on features of style that critics had never before thought to examine.
options.B: Scholars who use computational methods also spend much of their working time reading individual novels closely.
options.C: The novels available in digital form for analysis are mostly the same books that later readers chose to keep in print.
options.D: Many of the patterns reported by computational studies merely confirm what attentive readers had already suspected.

questions.question: The statement that a claim about 'the novel' which describes only the surviving books 'was never a claim about the novel at all' implies that such a claim

options.A: while offered as a history of a form, in fact describes the preferences that decided which books were kept.
options.B: could be made responsibly only by a scholar who had personally read every novel of the period concerned.
options.C: is simply false, because the canonical novels are unlike the rest of the period's output in every respect.
options.D: reveals that the idea of a single literary form called the novel is an illusion produced by the syllabus.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that visitors who read labels before looking at a painting understand it less well than those who do not.
options.B: propose that a label should be judged by whether it sends the visitor back to the work, not by its length.
options.C: argue that museums should replace long wall labels with audio guides and screens that visitors can consult at will.
options.D: defend the purist view that a painting should be encountered without any written explanation beside it.

questions.question: The passage suggests that removing labels altogether would most likely

options.A: encourage most visitors to spend longer with each painting, since they would have nothing else to read.
options.B: make visitors rely more heavily on catalogues, which the author regards as the proper home for all information.
options.C: leave many visitors feeling shut out, so that they pass the work more quickly instead of studying it.
options.D: have little effect on visitors, who already pay more attention to paintings than to the panels beside them.

questions.question: The two sentences about the merchant's portrait in paragraph 3 are used to

options.A: contrast a statement that can be taken in without looking with one that sends the reader to the canvas.
options.B: suggest that labels about portraits should avoid biographical facts about the people who commissioned them.
options.C: show that the merchant's marriage is more important to the meaning of the portrait than the objects he holds.
options.D: prove that painters of merchants used lighting to signal which of the sitter's possessions mattered most.

questions.question: Which of the following labels for a painting of a busy kitchen would the author most likely approve for the gallery wall?

options.A: Critics have long agreed that this is the most accomplished of the painter's works and a turning point in his career.
options.B: The crowded kitchen expresses the painter's lifelong anxiety about poverty, which haunted him after his father's business failed.
options.C: The painting passed through the hands of four private collectors in three countries before the museum acquired it in a recent sale.
options.D: Figures by the window are in quick, broken strokes, those in shadow smooth; which group does your eye reach first?

questions.question: According to the author's reasoning, public disputes over removing old statues become bitter chiefly because

options.A: the statues offer no built-in occasion for reconsideration, so disagreement is held back until it bursts out all at once.
options.B: bronze and stone are expensive materials, and removing works made of them wastes the money a town once spent.
options.C: the statues are usually so unfamiliar to passers-by that few people are able to say why they were put up.
options.D: later generations change their opinions too quickly to respect the judgements of the people who raised the statues.

questions.question: The author accepts permanence as appropriate for which kind of public work?

options.A: A mural that residents have grown fond of during the years it has been on display.
options.B: A statue of a civic leader whose reputation has stayed secure for several generations.
options.C: A sculpture commissioned for a central square that is visited by large numbers of tourists.
options.D: A memorial to the dead of a disaster, since its purpose is to resist forgetting.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, the phrase 'an occasion rather than a verdict' most nearly means that temporary public art

options.A: is judged by experts once the work has been removed, rather than by the people who saw it in place.
options.B: is an event that invites the public to respond and argue, not a settled judgement handed down to be accepted.
options.C: avoids taking any position at all, rather than making a claim that some members of the public might dispute.
options.D: is held for special celebrations only, rather than being on view to the public throughout the year.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that a city expecting its public art to change would face no crisis over what stands in its squares?

options.A: Several temporary sculptures have provoked angry letters to newspapers and heated public meetings while they were on display.
options.B: Visitors to war memorials often say that the permanence of the stone is what makes the place feel solemn to them.
options.C: A city with a rotating plinth for decades still endured years of bitter petitions over removing a nearby statue.
options.D: Most of the works shown on rotating plinths are forgotten by the public within a year or two of being removed.

questions.question: Which point in favour of the cleaners does the author accept?

options.A: Varnish yellows with age, so preferring the darkened colours can mean preferring an accident to the painter's choice.
options.B: Cleaned paintings are in every respect identical to the pictures as they looked when they left the studio.
options.C: Cleaners have never removed the final glazes that painters used to soften their effects.
options.D: Admirers of the darkened pictures are moved by sentiment and have no real reason for their preference.

questions.question: The author implies that a freshly cleaned painting

options.A: will usually be darker and less harmonious than it was before its old varnish was removed.
options.B: is in most cases a closer approximation to the original than the same painting before cleaning.
options.C: should be covered again with a varnish so that its appearance matches what earlier viewers loved.
options.D: may present colour relationships the painter never saw, because faded and unfaded parts now appear together.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the cleaners is best described as

options.A: enthusiastic agreement: he believes they have recovered what the painters intended and should say so with confidence.
options.B: outright hostility: he regards them as zealots whose work has destroyed much of what earlier painters achieved.
options.C: qualified support: he accepts their practice and results but rejects the strength of their central claim.
options.D: detached neutrality: he reports both parties' views without indicating which arguments he finds more persuasive.

questions.question: The argument in paragraph 3 that cleaning cannot return a painting to its original state relies on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: The varnish on old paintings was not applied by the painters themselves as part of the finished work.
options.B: Removing varnish does not also undo the fading and browning that the pigments themselves have undergone.
options.C: Viewers who knew the painting before cleaning were mistaken about the colours the painter had chosen.
options.D: The darkened state of a painting before cleaning was closer to its original appearance than the cleaned state.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Viewers should learn to check images for doctored pixels, because unaltered photographs are always accurate about the events they record.
options.B: Concern with doctored images neglects the commoner danger of selective framing, so a photograph's worth as evidence rests on its context.
options.C: Photographers who choose where to stand and when to press the shutter are mainly responsible for the dishonest stories told with images.
options.D: Software that can alter photographs invisibly has made every image unreliable, so photographs should no longer count as evidence.

questions.question: The example of the photograph of a crowded square in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: show that an image with nothing added or removed can still leave the event unclear.
options.B: illustrate how software can be used to add figures to a crowd without leaving a visible trace.
options.C: argue that photographs of demonstrations are less reliable than photographs of other public events.
options.D: suggest that most demonstrations are smaller than the photographs published of them make them appear.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a viewer who has confirmed that an image has not been digitally altered

options.A: should go on to assume that the image was staged, since honest photographs are more misleading than forged ones.
options.B: has wasted effort, because doctored images are now so rare that checking them is no longer worth doing.
options.C: has done all that can reasonably be asked, since an unaltered image cannot be used to support a false account.
options.D: has settled one real question but has learnt little about whether the story built on the image is true.

questions.question: Which of the following best exemplifies the 'false sense of security' described in paragraph 3?

options.A: A reader who learns that one picture in a newspaper was retouched decides to distrust every photograph that the paper prints afterwards.
options.B: A photographer who arrived too late restages a scene with volunteers and publishes it with a caption calling it a reconstruction.
options.C: An editor, told that a photograph of empty shelves is unaltered, runs it as proof of a citywide shortage without asking where it was taken.
options.D: A court admits a photograph after an expert confirms it is unaltered and the photographer testifies to exactly when and where she took it.

questions.question: According to the passage, a newly accepted attribution can raise a painting's price sharply because

options.A: the painting becomes scarcer once it is known to be by a celebrated artist who produced very few works.
options.B: museums begin competing to acquire the painting so that they can display it to large numbers of visitors.
options.C: buyers pay partly for the name on a work, which can change while the picture stays the same.
