options.D: experts who examine the painting again find qualities in its brushwork that earlier owners had failed to notice.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that two paintings of equal artistic merit

options.A: would reach equal prices at auction, since informed buyers pool their judgements of quality.
options.B: would eventually fetch similar prices once critics had studied both of them for long enough.
options.C: could not be compared at all, because artistic merit has no connection with what buyers pay.
options.D: might fetch very different prices if one were by a far more famous artist than the other.

questions.question: The comparison with a credit rating in paragraph 3 is used to

options.A: illustrate how one thing can track another at second hand while remaining a different kind of thing.
options.B: warn that the art market, like the market for company debt, is liable to sudden collapses in value.
options.C: suggest that auction prices are as carefully calculated by experts as the ratings given to companies.
options.D: argue that buying paintings is a sounder investment than lending money to companies with good ratings.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented in the passage as an effect of treating prices as verdicts EXCEPT:

options.A: people gathering in front of the most expensive work in a gallery while neighbouring works go unvisited.
options.B: galleries raising the asking prices of other works whose style resembles that of the record-breaking canvas.
options.C: artists early in their careers taking note of what kinds of work the market rewards.
options.D: museums becoming reluctant to put certain works on display or send them to other institutions.

questions.question: The remark that 'a theory that can detect a difference only once it has been told where to look is not much of a theory' serves to

options.A: cast doubt on the second explanation by pointing out that the supposed visible flaws are noticed only after exposure.
options.B: introduce the author's own account, which holds that forgeries can always be distinguished by close study.
options.C: reject the first explanation by showing that critics who praised the forgery were not motivated by snobbery.
options.D: support the second explanation by showing that trained eyes can find the deadness of a forgery once they are alerted.

questions.question: In objecting that the snobbery explanation 'proves too much', the author implies that a satisfactory account of the reaction to forgery must

options.A: show that snobbery and the wish to resell play no part in the fall in a forgery's price.
options.B: allow that someone could mind the difference for reasons other than prestige or resale.
options.C: establish that the pleasure visitors took in the forgery was not genuine pleasure but a kind of mistake.
options.D: explain why historians are better placed than collectors to judge whether a painting is a forgery.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the author's own account of why the exposure of a forgery changes our appreciation?

options.A: Students who build an exact model of a famous building as an exercise are praised by teachers for the skill of their copy.
options.B: A copy of a novel loses most of its value to collectors when it turns out to be a later printing, though its text is identical.
options.C: A chess game admired as brilliant play in an unforeseen position is found to have been copied move for move from an older game.
options.D: A wine praised in a blind tasting is revealed to be a cheap one, after which the same tasters begin to describe it as thin.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the view that 'what matters in a painting is what can be seen in it' is best described as

options.A: endorsing it reluctantly, since the reaction to forgery cannot be explained without some appeal to visible features.
options.B: dismissing it as a form of snobbery that values the label over the evidence of the eye.
options.C: accepting it for ordinary visitors while holding that experts must also weigh facts about a painting's making.
options.D: rejecting it as a full account, while admitting his alternative makes value rest partly on unseen facts.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: arguing that older portraits are artistically superior to modern ones because they honestly record a sitter's social position.
options.B: explaining how photography destroyed the market for painted portraits in the nineteenth century and after.
options.C: describing the symbols, such as dogs and columns, that court painters used to signal their sitters' virtues.
options.D: showing that the demand for psychological insight in portraits is a historical development, not a timeless standard for the genre.

questions.question: According to paragraph 3, likeness mattered in older commissioned portraits chiefly because

options.A: the purpose of such portraits was to reveal the sitter's private character to later generations.
options.B: the face had to be recognisable enough for the role shown to be attached to the right person.
options.C: patrons insisted that painters should show exactly how the sitter looked, without any flattery at all.
options.D: painters were judged mainly by their skill in capturing the particular features of each sitter's face.

questions.question: When the author says such a portrait 'was closer to a document than to a confession' (paragraph 2), the point is that it

options.A: was a truthful account of the sitter, while psychological portraits are works of imaginative fiction.
options.B: was valued mainly as a legal record that could be used to prove a family's ownership of land.
options.C: recorded the sitter's public standing in a readable form instead of disclosing his inner life.
options.D: was painted from written descriptions of the sitter rather than from the sitter in person.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the arrival of photography affected portrait painting by

options.A: taking over the trade in cheap likenesses, so that painters turned to offering what a camera seemed unable to give.
options.B: bringing to an end the tradition of painting sitters with symbols of office, such as chains and columns.
options.C: making painted portraits more truthful, because painters could now correct their work against photographs.
options.D: introducing the belief that a person's truth lies within, which painters then tried to express in their portraits.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: The similarity among many older portraits reflects an intention of the patrons rather than a lack of skill.
options.B: A painter working within the conventions of a court portrait could still let something of the sitter's character appear.
options.C: Older portrait painters were largely indifferent to whether the people they painted could be recognised.
options.D: A portrait made today for a company boardroom may serve much the same purpose as a portrait made for a royal court.

questions.question: Which of the following does the author mention as a merit of slow looking?

options.A: It gives visitors who seem to need it permission to remain with a single work.
options.B: It replaces the reading of labels, which visitors often do in place of looking.
options.C: It trains beginners to ask where the light in a painting comes from.
options.D: It guarantees that whoever stays long enough will discover something new in the picture.

questions.question: The statement 'Time is a condition of seeing, not a cause of it' (paragraph 2) most nearly means that

options.A: seeing a painting well takes no time at all once the viewer has the right questions in mind.
options.B: seeing requires time but time does not by itself produce seeing, since something else must turn it into perception.
options.C: the conditions in a gallery, such as crowding and noise, affect seeing more than the time spent there.
options.D: people who spend more time in front of a picture always see less than those who spend less time.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that a beginner who sits before a painting for an hour is likely to

options.A: look less carefully than an expert, since beginners give up their attention sooner than trained viewers.
options.B: discover the features that experts miss, since he has no expectations that tell him where not to look.
options.C: see as much as an expert does in a few seconds, provided that he keeps looking attentively.
options.D: dwell on whatever is most conspicuous or familiar, since no question is directing where he looks.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim in paragraph 4 about the risk carried by expertise?

options.A: Experts told in advance to search for an anomaly in a painting found it much faster than untrained viewers did.
options.B: Experts identified the school of an unfamiliar painting far more quickly and accurately than untrained viewers did.
options.C: Untrained viewers who looked at a painting for fifteen minutes listed more details than those who looked for two minutes.
options.D: Shown a painting with an odd detail clashing with its school, experts noticed the detail less often than untrained viewers did.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the passage as a whole?

options.A: A defence of expertise against slow looking, concluding that guided questions should replace the habit of long and unstructured contemplation.
options.B: A criticism of museums for allowing visitors to glance at pictures briefly and spend most of their time reading the labels instead.
options.C: An assessment of a museum practice that grants its value, disputes the reasoning behind it, and recommends combining it with what expertise supplies.
options.D: An argument that slow looking matters chiefly because it lets trained viewers set aside the expectations that their knowledge creates.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: challenge a popular picture of improvisation by arguing that its freedom rests on conventions the performer has fully absorbed.
options.B: argue that improvisers are best understood as skilled recombiners of phrases that they have memorised during long training.
options.C: show that improvisation in Indian classical music is more tightly governed by rules than improvisation in jazz.
options.D: recommend that teachers of improvisation stop encouraging students to imitate and instead train them to recall the rules.

questions.question: According to the passage, a student of improvisation who is told simply to be free is likely to

options.A: imitate the phrases of established players more closely than a student given strict exercises.
options.B: produce something without shape or rely on a few habits acquired by chance.
options.C: discover a personal style sooner, though at the cost of breaking with the tradition.
options.D: learn the rules of the tradition more slowly, but understand them more deeply in the end.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author regards the years of imitation in an improviser's training as

options.A: an inefficient custom that persists mainly because teachers in both traditions were trained in the same way.
options.B: the main source of what listeners value most in a great improvised performance.
options.C: a stage that suppresses creativity, which the student must later unlearn in order to improvise freely.
options.D: the way the conventions of a tradition become second nature, which later makes confident variation possible.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the author's account of what makes a great improvised moment?

options.A: A poet who has written strict sonnets for decades breaks the expected rhyme in the final line, and readers feel the break as deliberate and apt.
options.B: A beginner who has never studied verse writes a poem with no metre or rhyme, and some readers find its roughness refreshing and honest.
options.C: A poet with an exceptional memory for other people's verse assembles a new poem entirely from lines borrowed from famous earlier poems.
options.D: A translator who looks up every word in a dictionary produces a version that is accurate in each line but stiff when read aloud as a whole.

questions.question: According to the passage, many companies that hold detailed records of their repertoire

options.A: use notation to correct the drift that has crept in through generations of teaching.
options.B: regard the notated record as the authoritative version of a dance when teachers disagree.
options.C: still revive works through direct teaching and use the written record to support memory.
options.D: have abandoned studio teaching now that film and video can capture complete performances.

questions.question: The author would most likely expect a revival staged by dancers who learned a role only from a film of one performance to

options.A: fail chiefly because film cannot show the position of each part of the body over time.
options.B: risk copying one performer's personal habits and errors as though they were part of the choreography.
options.C: convey the weight and timing of each movement more faithfully than a revival taught in the studio, since film records every detail.
options.D: be closer to the choreographer's original intentions, since the film is free of the drift that teaching introduces.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the transmission of dance from dancer to dancer is best described as

options.A: nostalgic, regretting that newer tools such as film and notation are steadily replacing it in most companies.
options.B: ambivalent, finding its losses roughly equal to its gains and declining to prefer it to documentation.
options.C: defensive, insisting that the method causes no real change to the dances handed down by it.
options.D: appreciative, while openly admitting that the method gradually alters the works it preserves.

questions.question: In the first paragraph, the suggestion that the remedy for dance's fragility is 'simply better documentation' functions as

options.A: the thesis that the author defends throughout the remaining paragraphs.
options.B: a natural conclusion that the rest of the passage goes on to qualify.
options.C: a historical claim about how choreographers once preserved their work.
options.D: an objection to the view that dance has the most fragile relation to its past.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a wrong note matters more on a recording than in a concert because

options.A: on a recording it is heard every time the performance is replayed, instead of passing once and being forgotten.
options.B: listeners at home concentrate harder than audiences in a hall, who are distracted by their surroundings.
options.C: recording equipment exaggerates small errors that the acoustics of a concert hall would soften.
options.D: performers who record are expected to be more skilled than those who play only in concerts.

questions.question: The 'curious inversion' mentioned in paragraph 3 refers to the fact that

options.A: performers who once took risks in the concert hall now take them only in the recording studio.
options.B: editing, once used to remove errors from recordings, is now used to add effects that cannot be produced live.
options.C: a recording, intended to copy a performance, now serves many listeners as the model that live performances are judged against.
options.D: listeners who once went to concerts to hear new works now go mainly to hear works they already know.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim that some performers have responded to recordings by playing more cautiously in concerts?

options.A: Many listeners now say that they prefer recordings to concerts because recordings are free of the slips that so often occur in live performance.
options.B: A few celebrated performers refused to make recordings at all because they disliked the conditions of the studio.
options.C: Recordings have allowed students of music to compare dozens of interpretations of the same work in a single afternoon.
options.D: Broadcasts of live concerts from before and after edited recordings became common show that the same kinds of performers took risks just as often.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the effects of recording on musical life is best described as

options.A: a qualified appreciation that values what recording made possible while rejecting the view that it left performing and listening unchanged.
options.B: a guarded scepticism that doubts recording has widened access to music as much as is often claimed, though it accepts its value for comparison.
options.C: a neutral detachment that describes the effects of recording on performers and listeners without judging whether any of them is desirable.
options.D: a regretful nostalgia that concedes the conveniences of recording but holds that musical life has on balance declined since concerts lost their place.

questions.question: The reference to a carved mask in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: support the second view that sadness is enjoyable when it arrives without a real loss behind it.
options.B: illustrate the first view's claim that listeners recognise sadness in music without themselves feeling it.
options.C: show that visual art expresses sadness less powerfully than music, which can move listeners to tears.
options.D: express the author's own position that the pleasure of sad music lies in skill rather than feeling.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the pleasure a listener takes in a lament depends chiefly on

options.A: the listener's recognition of the composer's skill in depicting sorrow without being affected by it.
options.B: the listener's confidence that the sorrow has no real cause and will have no consequences afterwards.
options.C: the way the music leads a real sorrow through an ordered course from beginning to resolution.
options.D: the intensity of the sorrow the music arouses, so that the most moving laments are the most enjoyed.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation of why some grieving people cannot bear sad music?

options.A: Listeners who are not grieving often report being moved to tears by laments, and not merely noticing that the music is sad.
options.B: Some listeners enjoy sad music most when they hear it in a concert hall among strangers rather than alone at home.
options.C: Grieving listeners who avoid sad music for a time usually return to it once their own grief has become less raw.
options.D: Grieving listeners find sad music that wanders without clear form or resolution just as unbearable as laments that move to a settled close.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: The frame view correctly predicts that people in grief will find sad music harder to bear than before.
options.B: On the frame view, the sadness of music can be savoured because no loss causes it and no consequences follow.
options.C: A lament may return to a phrase heard earlier in the piece before it finally comes to rest.
options.D: The view that listeners only recognise sadness can explain why sad music does not spoil a listener's day.

questions.question: According to the passage, one result of performing older music on period instruments was that

options.A: audiences came to prefer small ensembles to large orchestras for music of every period.
options.B: textures that had seemed heavy under large modern orchestras came to sound transparent.
options.C: composers' written complaints about their instruments were finally resolved by better reconstructions.
options.D: dissonances that later audiences had stopped noticing began to startle listeners once again.

questions.question: The argument of paragraph 2 implies that a perfect reconstruction of the instruments and tempi of an early work would still

options.A: sound less transparent to modern ears than a performance by a large modern orchestra.
options.B: be impossible to achieve, because the treatises written in the period are too vague to guide performers.
options.C: fail to reproduce the original listeners' experience, because later music has shaped how modern audiences hear it.
options.D: contradict the composer's intentions, since composers disliked the instruments of their own time.

questions.question: Which of the following arguments makes the same error that paragraph 3 identifies?

options.A: A playwright's audiences knew stories that modern audiences do not, so modern productions cannot recreate the effect the plays first had.
options.B: A playwright's early productions were praised by critics, so modern productions that copy them will be equally admired today.
options.C: A playwright whose plays were first staged in small rooms lit by candles must have wanted them staged that way, so modern productions should do the same.
options.D: A playwright left detailed notes on how certain scenes should be staged, so directors who follow those notes are closer to the writer's stated wishes.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Because authenticity is unreachable, performers should set historical research aside entirely and judge each interpretation solely by whether it succeeds as music.
options.B: Authentic performance of early music is possible only if modern audiences are first taught to hear it as its original listeners did.
options.C: Period-instrument performances, however vivid and revealing, are on the whole less faithful to what composers intended than careful performances on modern instruments.
options.D: Period-instrument performances are valuable for the musical possibilities their research uncovered, not for any success in reproducing how the music first sounded.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a singer who replaced the name of a town in a ballad with one her listeners knew was

options.A: following an ordinary practice of fitting the song to the audience in front of her.
options.B: damaging the song in the way the collectors feared, though for an understandable reason.
options.C: departing from the custom of her tradition, which required songs to be sung as they were learned.
options.D: making an error that later singers corrected when they learned the song from printed texts.

questions.question: The reference to the editing of ancient manuscripts in paragraph 2 serves mainly to

options.A: provide evidence that the collectors were trained as classical scholars before they turned to rural music.
options.B: trace the collectors' method to a field where it suited its object, and so show why it misfitted songs.
options.C: show that folk songs, like classical texts, descend from single originals that careful editing can recover.
options.D: suggest that the editing of manuscripts is as flawed a method as the collectors' reconstruction of songs.

questions.question: In the final sentence, the word 'noise' refers to

options.A: differences between versions, which the collectors' theory treated as interference obscuring an original song.
options.B: the names of individual singers, which the collectors considered irrelevant to the songs themselves.
options.C: the sound of rural performances, which the collectors found rough compared with concert singing.
options.D: the many songs the collectors judged too corrupt to record and therefore left out of their notebooks.

questions.question: Which of the following records of a folk song would the author most likely judge the most valuable?

options.A: A single printed text carefully assembled from the best verses of several singers, with notes explaining each editorial choice.
options.B: The oldest written version of the song that survives, found in a manuscript that predates every known rural performance.
options.C: A sound recording, made with modern equipment, of the version that most singers in the region now agree is the standard and correct one.
options.D: Handwritten transcriptions of the song from six singers in different villages, each kept separate and noted with the singer's name and the occasion.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following does a score specify with the greatest precision?

options.A: The exact speed at which a lively movement should be taken.
options.B: The pitches of the notes and the order in which they come.
options.C: How loud a passage should be in a given performance space.
options.D: How long a performer should linger at the high point of a phrase.

questions.question: The example of a performer who takes a slow movement at double speed is used to

options.A: support the claim that a performer who alters the notes has made a mistake whatever the result sounds like.
options.B: illustrate how imprecise tempo markings allow performances of one piece to differ widely in character.
options.C: show that the view that the work is the performance cannot account for judgements musicians routinely make.
options.D: suggest that informed listeners disagree too often about tempo for any standard of performance to exist.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a performer who plays every note exactly as written but ignores the conventions by which the style is ordinarily read has

options.A: been faithful to the work, since a performance is good to the degree that it delivers what the notation contains.
options.B: created a new work, because a work changes whenever the practice used to read its score changes.
options.C: been accurate to the marks on the page without being faithful to the work they belong to.
options.D: exercised a performer's right to complete the score in whatever way she judges best.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument against the view that the work simply is the performance?

options.A: Performers and critics often disagree about the best tempo for particular movements, and both sides defend their choices at length in print.
options.B: When informed listeners independently judge performances of the same piece, their verdicts on which are wrong-headed agree no more than chance would predict.
options.C: Some modern scores specify loudness and tempo far more exactly than older scores, using numbers rather than words.
options.D: Some performers have deliberately ignored the conventions of a style and later persuaded many listeners that their readings were justified.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: propose that a work is its score as read within a shared practice, after showing two simpler views fail.
options.B: argue that because performing practices keep changing, musical works can have no stable identity from one generation to the next.
options.C: defend the traditional view that the score is the work against critics who would grant performers unlimited interpretive freedom.
options.D: show that musical notation is too imprecise to guide performers and should be made far more exact.

questions.question: According to the passage, the length of the pause that comic actors leave before a line varies between performances because

options.A: directors change the timing of each scene during a run to keep the actors alert.
options.B: comedies are drilled less precisely than other plays and leave actors more freedom.
options.C: actors in large houses cannot see the audience and must guess when to continue.
options.D: the laughter at the previous line differs from one night to the next.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, a silence that tells the performers 'they have the room' indicates that

options.A: the performers have more physical space to move about than in a smaller theatre.
options.B: the audience has stopped responding and the actors may now ignore it.
options.C: the audience's attention is fully held by what is happening on stage.
options.D: the auditorium is full and the production has sold every seat in the house.

questions.question: The comparison with a lecture delivered in person (paragraph 1) is meant to show that

options.A: lectures, like plays, lose much of their value when they are recorded for a screen.
options.B: being physically present does not by itself make an event more valuable.
options.C: theatre is valuable chiefly because it teaches its audiences, as a lecture does.
options.D: audiences respond to lecturers in the same way that they respond to actors.

questions.question: Which of the following productions would the author regard as making the fullest use of what the stage offers and the screen does not?

options.A: A play in a mid-sized theatre whose cast is rehearsed to let the pacing of scenes follow the audience's reactions each night.
options.B: A play staged in a tiny room with spectators an arm's length from the actors, who are directed never to vary the timing of any line.
options.C: A play performed with such precision that critics who attend on different nights report seeing an identical performance.
options.D: A play that projects close-ups of the actors' faces onto large screens so that every spectator can see the smallest expression.

questions.question: The author would be LEAST likely to agree with which of the following?

options.A: The quality of an audience's silence can affect how long performers sustain a moment.
options.B: The familiar appeal to presence, though weak as usually stated, points the way towards a stronger defence of theatre.
options.C: Film possesses expressive means of its own, such as the close-up, that the stage does not share.
options.D: Every live production is responsive to its audience to some degree, even when spectators do not notice it.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with arguing that

options.A: a mistake that many people repeat with one object usually signals poor design rather than personal carelessness.
options.B: every error that people make with everyday objects is the fault of the designers who made those objects.
options.C: written signs and printed warnings are useless and should be removed from doors, appliances and public buildings.
options.D: designers ought to test every new product on hurried first-time users before it is allowed to reach the market.

questions.question: According to the passage, when the hardware on a door and the sign above it give conflicting messages, people tend to

options.A: stop and read the sign with care before deciding whether they should push the door or pull it.
options.B: wait until someone else uses the door so that they can copy whatever that person does first.
options.C: act on what the shape of the hardware suggests, since form is read faster than printed words.
options.D: push the door whatever its fittings, since pushing is the most natural movement for someone in a hurry.

questions.question: At a railway station, many passengers keep inserting their tickets upside down into the entry gates. Which response would the author most clearly favour?

options.A: Placing staff beside each gate to remind passengers, politely but firmly, how to hold their tickets.
options.B: Fining passengers who jam the gates, so that they learn to take more care with their tickets next time.
options.C: Printing a large red arrow on every ticket showing passengers which way up it should be inserted.
options.D: Reshaping the slot and ticket so that a ticket can enter the gate only the right way up.

questions.question: The hospital example in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: show that hospital staff are, as a rule, more careless than the people working in most other occupations.
options.B: contrast what follows from treating a mistake as a personal failing with treating it as a design problem.
options.C: illustrate the claim that look-alike containers are the most common cause of serious errors in hospitals.
options.D: prove that disciplining an employee never does anything at all to reduce the number of mistakes made at work.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the admirers' account of vernacular building is best described as

options.A: dismissive, since the author regards their claims about the climatic benefits of traditional building forms as simply mistaken.
options.B: indifferent, since the author treats vernacular building as a subject of purely historical interest today.
options.C: appreciative of what it gets right, but critical of the idealised picture of the past that it presents.
options.D: wholly approving, since the author endorses their call for modern builders to copy traditional forms directly in their own work.

questions.question: According to the passage, village builders used earth for their walls chiefly because

options.A: it was found close at hand and cost nothing to bring to the building site.
options.B: the hot climate made thick earth walls the only kind that could keep their rooms cool.
options.C: it was the walling material that took the least labour to keep in good repair from year to year.
options.D: they had compared it with the other available materials and judged it to be the best of them.

questions.question: The remark that the failures 'left nothing for us to photograph' (paragraph 2) suggests that

options.A: most of the vernacular buildings ever put up have since collapsed or been abandoned by their communities.
options.B: a judgement of traditional building drawn only from surviving examples is likely to overstate how well it worked.
options.C: early photographers of the countryside chose to record only the most handsome and best built village houses they found.
options.D: traditional communities deliberately destroyed their failed buildings in order to hide their mistakes from later generations.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as having genuinely learned from vernacular building?

options.A: A builder who uses thick earth walls on every project in every region, on the ground that earth is the traditional material.
options.B: A developer who reproduces the domed earth roofs of a desert village on a housing estate in a cold and rainy northern city.
options.C: An engineer who abandons all traditional materials and relies on mechanical cooling, since village forms were shaped by poverty.
options.D: An architect in a humid coastal town who records how a trial house behaves through a monsoon and revises the next design.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the phrase 'an undifferentiated cliff' refers to

options.A: a wall whose stone has weathered so unevenly over the years that it now resembles a natural rock face.
options.B: a facade so heavily carved and moulded that the eye can no longer pick out its individual parts.
options.C: a tall wall offering no visible divisions by which someone passing could judge how big it is.
options.D: a building constructed on the edge of a steep slope, so that it seems to rise directly from the rock.

questions.question: The author implies that the progressive architects described in paragraph 1

options.A: recognised as genuine uses only those functions that would show up in a structural calculation.
options.B: produced no buildings of lasting value, since their designs ignored what people on the street needed.
options.C: eventually gave up their position once the shortcomings of plain buildings became widely known.
options.D: were motivated above all by a wish to lower building costs and only later found moral reasons for their view.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claims about blank walls in paragraph 3?

options.A: Much of the ornament on older commercial buildings was copied from pattern books with no thought for its purpose.
options.B: Strangers asked to find the entrances of plain modern buildings do so as quickly as visitors to richly ornamented ones.
options.C: Several plain modern buildings are widely admired by the public for the clarity and simplicity of their design.
options.D: Ornamented buildings turn out to cost considerably more to build and to maintain than plain buildings of a similar size.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the position the passage argues for?

options.A: Ornament and structural honesty are incompatible, so every architect must decide which of the two a building will sacrifice.
options.B: Traditional ornament should now be revived everywhere, because plain modern buildings have proved to be dishonest about their structure and their purposes.
options.C: The critics of ornament were right in principle but wrong to apply their principle to the commercial building of their own day.
options.D: Ornament should be judged by what it does for people at street level, a test that some ornamented and some plain buildings fail.

questions.question: According to the passage, in earlier periods irregularity in a crafted object was generally regarded as

options.A: a decorative effect that weavers and potters added at the end to make each piece distinctive.
options.B: a welcome trace of the material's character that a master would leave deliberately in place.
options.C: a sign of inexperience or haste, which skilled makers took pride in removing from their work.
options.D: the proof that a person rather than a machine had made the object, which buyers valued most of all.

questions.question: The phrase 'a premium paid for a story' (paragraph 2) implies that, if irregularity is what buyers value,

options.A: the extra price buys a belief about how an object was made, not a quality visible in it.
options.B: buyers knowingly pay more for objects whose irregularities they understand to be produced by machines.
options.C: the prices of handmade goods are set mainly by advertising rather than by the cost of the materials used.
options.D: handmade goods are usually sold together with invented accounts of the lives of the people who made them.

questions.question: Each of the following is supported by the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: An ordinary buyer is generally unable to distinguish simulated irregularity from that of a hand-thrown piece.
options.B: A weaver may adjust the work in progress in response to changes in the moisture of the surrounding air.
options.C: Some goods that are sold as handmade are produced without any attention to the particular piece being made.
options.D: Machines are in principle incapable of responding to the particular qualities of the material they work on.

questions.question: By the test proposed in the final paragraph, which of the following would most clearly count as craft?

options.A: A factory press that stamps a different random dent into every metal bowl so that no two bowls are ever identical.
options.B: A bread machine that measures the moisture of each batch of flour and changes its kneading time to suit that batch.
options.C: A hand-knitted scarf made by repeating a fixed chart row after row, without any notice taken when the yarn thickens.
options.D: A workshop in which each worker performs one hand motion all day on identical parts that have been cut in advance.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 1, 'strangely inert' describes manuals that

options.A: are rarely read, because they sit unopened in libraries long after their publication.
options.B: fail to make their readers competent even though what they record is accurate.
options.C: are written in such dry and technical prose that ordinary readers lose interest in them.
options.D: contain so many errors of measurement that following them leads readers astray.

questions.question: The example of metal that 'turns the colour of straw' (paragraph 2) is used to show that

options.A: a spoken or written instruction can rely on the very perception that it is meant to pass on.
options.B: manuals would succeed if their authors replaced comparisons with precise measurements of temperature.
options.C: colour is a less dependable guide to the heat of iron than the sound or feel of the work.
options.D: smiths historically chose vague comparisons on purpose, so as to keep their methods secret from outsiders.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the master's repeated 'now' and 'not yet' were valuable chiefly because they

options.A: reminded the apprentice of rules that he had already learned from older written sources on the craft.
options.B: kept the apprentice obedient and dependent on the master during the long years of his training.
options.C: joined words to what the apprentice was perceiving at that instant, gradually training where he looked.
options.D: supplied a fixed technical vocabulary that could later be collected and published in manuals.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's argument?

options.A: Some tasks, such as baking a cake from a printed recipe, can be learned almost entirely from written instructions.
options.B: Many apprentices in earlier centuries left their masters before finishing their training because they were badly treated and poorly fed.
options.C: Experienced joiners who read a good manual improved their technique noticeably over the following months of ordinary work.
options.D: Novices who studied only a detailed manual for a year matched, in masters' judgement, apprentices trained for that year.

questions.question: According to the passage, those who favour conserving a building's layers want new work to be distinguishable from old work so that

options.A: visitors can see the building as it was meant to be seen by its very first builders.
options.B: the cost of each repair can be estimated separately from the value of the surviving parts.
options.C: later additions such as staircases and windows can be removed easily whenever they are no longer wanted.
options.D: nobody later takes a modern reconstruction for part of the building's original fabric.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a conservator who leaves a hurried partition in place over an important painted ceiling has

options.A: made a judgement about which part of the building's past matters, though it may look like simple restraint.
options.B: acted correctly, since a conservator's first duty is to keep every layer that happens to have survived.
options.C: behaved exactly as a restorer would, by imposing a modern idea of the past upon the building.
options.D: avoided interpreting the building at all, leaving the question of its meaning to later generations.

questions.question: The sentence 'Keeping everything is also an interpretation' (paragraph 3) functions to

options.A: give a practical example of a layer that ought to be removed in order to reveal something older.
options.B: extend the author's qualification by showing that even refusing to remove anything involves a judgement.
options.C: withdraw the author's earlier preference for conservation and move the argument towards restoration instead.
options.D: introduce a criticism of restoration that the defenders of conservation had not previously considered.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Restoration is preferable whenever reliable evidence of a building's original state survives, and conservation is preferable otherwise.
options.B: Neither approach can be preferred to the other, since each of them is equally an interpretation of a building's past.
options.C: Both approaches interpret the past, but conservation is preferable because it leaves its interpretations open to later correction.
options.D: Conservation is preferable to restoration because, unlike restoration, it preserves buildings without imposing any interpretation on their history.

questions.question: According to the passage, people who appear in the typical photographs of a new building are there mainly to

options.A: make the empty rooms look warmer and more welcoming than they would otherwise appear.
options.B: hide the defects in finishes and furnishings that had not yet been completed on the day.
options.C: indicate the size of the spaces rather than to show how the building is actually used.
options.D: show prospective occupants what it will feel like to live or work in the building.

questions.question: The contrast between white render and brick at the end of paragraph 3 suggests that

options.A: photographers deliberately light brick buildings so that they look duller than they really are on opening day.
options.B: brick should be preferred to white render in all new buildings, whatever their purpose or setting.
options.C: occupants are usually happier in buildings faced with brick than in those finished with white render.
options.D: how a material looks when new can mislead about its long-term merits, which opening-day images cannot reveal.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 4 in the passage?

options.A: It grants the factual claims of the photograph's defenders while arguing that they leave the author's real objection untouched.
options.B: It argues that critics should judge only those buildings that they have visited and experienced in person over time.
options.C: It admits that the author's criticism of photography has been overstated and partly withdraws the charge made in paragraph 3.
options.D: It shows that architectural drawings were a more honest medium than photographs for judging the merits of buildings.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that architects have come to 'design for the photograph'?

options.A: Buildings that win major architectural awards are photographed far more often, and more widely published, than ordinary buildings.
options.B: Over several decades, award-winning designs show ever more dramatic visual features alongside steadily less attention to acoustics and weathering.
options.C: Many prominent architects say in interviews that they dislike the way photographers present their completed buildings.
options.D: Occupants of celebrated buildings report problems with heat and leaks at about the same rate as occupants of ordinary buildings.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: showing how judging buildings through opening-day images skews both criticism and design toward what one frame can show.
options.B: contrasting the honesty of architects' hand drawings with the distortions that were later introduced by the camera.
options.C: exposing the ways in which architectural photographers misrepresent buildings so that their clients' work becomes easier to sell.
options.D: arguing that critics ought to visit buildings in person instead of relying on published photographs of them.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'slack' most nearly means

options.A: carelessness in construction that leaves a building unfinished or poorly fitted for its purpose.
options.B: a period of low demand during which an old building stands empty before it is converted.
options.C: spare capacity in a building's dimensions and structure beyond what its first use demanded.
options.D: the freedom given to occupants to move partitions and walls to wherever they please.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, an old mill and a flexible-plan office differ chiefly in that

options.A: the mill fitted its original use exactly, whereas the flexible-plan office failed to fit any particular use at all.
options.B: the mill is built of more durable materials, which is the main reason it has outlasted the flexible-plan office.
options.C: the mill's builders anticipated the uses it would later be put to, whereas the office's designers did not foresee change.
options.D: the mill adapts because it is generously and simply built, whereas the office relied on mechanisms its users seldom worked.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to what the author calls loose fit?

options.A: A jacket with zip-off sleeves and detachable panels for every season, which most of its owners never trouble to change.
options.B: A suit cut with generous seam allowances, so that tailors in later years can let it out or take it in as its wearer changes.
options.C: A coat made in a single standard size that hangs badly on every customer and offers no margin at all for alteration.
options.D: A suit tailored precisely to its wearer's measurements for a wedding day and much admired for the perfection of its fit.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation of why old warehouses and mills proved so adaptable?

options.A: Warehouses with low ceilings and irregular columns proved as easy to convert as those with generous ceilings and regular grids.
options.B: Most warehouses and mills were built without the slightest expectation that people would one day live or work in them.
options.C: Flexible-plan offices built in recent decades have been demolished far more often than old warehouses in the same districts.
options.D: Some warehouses converted into flats were later returned to storage when the demand for housing in their district fell.

questions.question: The author's attitude to precision in architectural design is best described as

options.A: enthusiastic endorsement, since precision is the profession's distinctive strength and its main source of pride.
options.B: qualified scepticism: precision suits uses that are fixed and exacting but burdens most ordinary buildings.
options.C: outright rejection, on the ground that a precise fit makes every kind of building brittle once its use changes.
options.D: indifference, since the author regards the closeness of fit as irrelevant to how well a building adapts.

questions.question: According to the passage, a lack of craft cannot be what makes an object kitsch because

options.A: judgements of craft vary so widely between viewers that they cannot ground any definition.
options.B: clumsy work usually provokes stronger feelings in its viewers than skilful work does.
options.C: most kitsch objects are produced by trained artists rather than by amateurs or children.
options.D: skilfully made objects can be kitsch, while much clumsy work is not.

questions.question: The reference to a serious painting that shows grief 'in a particular face' (paragraph 2) serves mainly to

options.A: illustrate the technical skill that the makers of kitsch characteristically lack.
options.B: suggest that portraits are a more truthful form of art than scenes of soldiers and kittens.
options.C: show that a work can move us deeply while still demanding close attention.
options.D: demonstrate that serious art, unlike kitsch, almost never moves its viewers to tears.

questions.question: The passage suggests that kitsch 'tends to flatter' its viewers because it

options.A: is made by people who copy the tastes of wealthy buyers in order to sell their work.
options.B: deals with sentimental subjects, which are by their nature more pleasing than serious ones.
options.C: portrays its viewers as more refined and better educated than they really are.
options.D: calls up feelings viewers already hold and approve of, making their pleasure a kind of self-approval.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as an instance of the danger described in the final paragraph?

options.A: A national memorial service that leaves its audience proud and tearful but tells them nothing about the events it commemorates.
options.B: A gifted painter who sells many technically polished sunsets to tourists visiting a lakeside town.
options.C: An elderly widow who treasures a cheap mass-produced figurine on her shelf because it reminds her of her late husband.
options.D: A news report on a distant famine that sets out detailed causes and interviews several aid workers.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.A: explaining why children, unlike adults, enjoy hearing the same story told many times over.
options.B: questioning the belief that knowing a story's outcome destroys its value, while granting that something real is lost.
options.C: arguing that stories built around a single surprise are inferior to stories that reward rereading.
options.D: defending the etiquette against spoilers as the necessary protection of what gives every story its value for an audience.

questions.question: The bedtime story and the tragedies drawn from well-known legends (paragraph 2) are offered as

options.A: illustrations of how the customs of storytelling have changed over the centuries.
options.B: examples of stories built around a single reversal that cannot be enjoyed twice.
options.C: evidence that people seek out and enjoy stories whose outcomes they already know.
options.D: support for the view that suspense depends entirely on uncertainty about the final scene.

questions.question: In paragraph 1, the comparison with 'a lottery ticket that has already been scratched' conveys the idea that

options.A: stories, like lotteries, reward only a lucky few among those who take part in them.
options.B: revealing a story's ending is a theft that ought to be punished like any other.
options.C: the author regards watching films as a form of gambling with one's time and money.
options.D: a story, on the theory described, is worthless once its outcome is known.

questions.question: The author would most likely say that a reader rereading a mystery novel whose solution she remembers

options.A: can still take pleasure in its telling, though not in the shock of first discovering the solution.
options.B: will feel no suspense of any kind, since suspense is no more than uncertainty about outcome.
options.C: will enjoy it more than on a first reading, because the plot no longer distracts her attention.
options.D: gains nothing from the experience, since a mystery depends entirely on the reader's ignorance.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, confessing to a guilty pleasure works as 'a kind of insurance' because

options.A: it guarantees that the listener will forgive the speaker for her lapse of taste.
options.B: the speaker is safe whether her listener shares the enthusiasm or scorns it.
options.C: it allows the speaker to abandon her stated opinion later without any embarrassment.
options.D: it obliges the listener to confess an embarrassing enthusiasm of his own in return.

questions.question: Paragraph 3 suggests that the author suspects the ranking which the phrase depends on

options.A: has been carefully examined by critics over many years and found to be broadly sound in most of its judgements.
options.B: places every predictable work below every unpredictable one, whatever audience it attracts.
options.C: is shaped partly by the social standing of the audiences associated with works, not only by the works themselves.
options.D: is imposed on the rest of the public by teenagers and provincial and domestic audiences.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the phrase 'guilty pleasure' is best described as

options.A: approving, because the author sees it as a healthy awareness of the limits of one's taste.
options.B: amused and tolerant, since the author regards it as a harmless habit of polite talk.
options.C: openly contemptuous of the people who use it, whom the author treats as snobs.
options.D: sceptical of its apparent modesty, while allowing that some pleasures do deserve genuine unease.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim in paragraph 3 that the phrase 'tends to preserve the hierarchy it seems to question'?

options.A: Habitually confessing a pleasure as guilty is found, over time, to make people rate that work as highly as the approved ones.
options.B: The works that are most often called guilty pleasures turn out in fact to be associated mainly with audiences of very little cultural prestige.
options.C: Many people who use the phrase do so without any conscious wish to display their own good taste to others.
options.D: Some enjoyments, such as laughing at another person's humiliation, really do deserve to make us uneasy.

questions.question: According to the passage, an explained joke usually fails to produce a laugh because

options.A: analysis damages the fragile, almost mystical quality on which all humour depends.
options.B: the listener is denied the chance to discover the second meaning for himself.
options.C: most listeners resent being told something that they were perfectly able to work out.
options.D: the explanation offered is usually far less clever than the joke it tries to rescue.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 3 in the argument of the passage?

options.A: It concedes that the study of comedy is self-defeating but defends that study on other grounds.
options.B: It offers a second explanation of why explained jokes fail, independent of the one in paragraph 2.
options.C: It turns the account of why explained jokes fail into grounds for thinking humour can be analysed.
options.D: It introduces circumstances in which explaining a joke at the moment of telling can be helpful.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: A listener may laugh at a joke after being told what an unfamiliar allusion in it refers to.
options.B: Being told the answer to a riddle tends to take away the satisfaction of solving it.
options.C: A joke that has once been closely examined can never again amuse anyone who has studied it.
options.D: Analysing a comic routine afterwards can deepen one's understanding of a laugh already enjoyed.

questions.question: Which of the following situations best corresponds to the kind of explanation the author defends in paragraph 4?

options.A: A teacher, seeing a student stuck on a puzzle, shows her the complete solution at once so that she can check her own working.
options.B: A critic writes a long essay explaining why a famous comedy succeeded with its first audiences.
options.C: A comedian whose punchline draws no laugh repeats it more slowly and more loudly a second time.
options.D: A guide tells visitors a street's former name, and a moment later they see for themselves why a mural there is ironic.

questions.question: According to the passage, the camera and the viewpoint sign resemble the tinted mirrors of earlier travellers in that they

options.A: alter the colours of a landscape so that it looks more dramatic than it is.
options.B: select and frame a view so that the land is seen as a picture.
options.C: were devised by painters in order to teach travellers the rules of composition.
options.D: encourage travellers to spend long periods studying a single carefully chosen view.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a marsh or a stretch of flat scrub is especially vulnerable because

options.A: its failure to compose into a pleasing view makes it easier to regard as empty land.
options.B: it supports far less plant and animal life than dramatic landscapes such as gorges do.
options.C: roads with viewpoints are seldom built near it, so that few travellers ever see it at all.
options.D: landscape painters have always refused to depict it, and so it has no place in the tradition.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, the phrase 'under this regime' refers to

options.A: the official rules that decide where along mountain roads the viewpoints are built.
options.B: a way of valuing land according to how well it can be composed as a picture.
options.C: the strict conventions that landscape painters once imposed on one another's work.
options.D: the historical period in which travellers carried tinted mirrors and framing devices.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the link the author draws in paragraph 3 between habits of looking and the fate of particular places?

options.A: Campaigns to protect wetlands tend to win more public support when they display striking photographs of the wildlife there.
options.B: Most travellers who stop at signposted viewpoints spend only a few minutes there before driving on to the next.
options.C: Many marshes and stretches of scrub support a greater variety of species than the gorges that visitors stop to admire.
options.D: Officials who decide whether to drain or build on land give no weight at all to whether people find it beautiful.

questions.question: According to the passage, the features that people find cute

options.A: were first devised by advertisers in order to sell stickers, toys and other goods.
options.B: differ widely from one culture to another, as most other matters of taste do.
options.C: are those of the very young, such as a large head and big eyes.
options.D: appeal to us only when they belong to creatures that genuinely need care.

questions.question: The example of 'a cartoon kettle with eyes' (paragraph 2) is used to

options.A: show that the care-securing explanation leaves unexplained our response to things that need no care.
options.B: illustrate how advertisers use cuteness to make products and organisations seem harmless.
options.C: suggest that people feel the response to cuteness most strongly towards household objects.
options.D: prove that the explanation proposed by students of animal behaviour is simply false.

questions.question: The remark that the cute object is 'an image of something that will never answer back' (paragraph 3) implies that

options.A: cuteness appeals partly through the sense of power it gives the viewer over its object.
options.B: real children, unlike cute objects, are seldom found appealing by the adults around them.
options.C: cute objects are usually designed without mouths so that they appear to be silent.
options.D: the response to cuteness is, at bottom, a mechanism that secures care for the young.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Cuteness is a manipulative commercial style, and delight in it should be resisted as a kind of moral failing.
options.B: The response to cuteness is a biological mechanism that evolved to secure care for the very young.
options.C: Cuteness, though a trivial quality, is the one on which people across cultures most readily agree.
options.D: Cuteness is a powerful, ambivalent aesthetic whose capacity to disarm judgement makes it worth serious attention.

questions.question: According to the passage, a disagreement about the taste of coriander differs from a disagreement about a novel in that

options.A: it is a judgement about the quality of a thing rather than a report of a reaction.
options.B: neither party to it believes that the other has missed something about what is being tasted.
options.C: it is far more likely to end with one of the two parties tiring and giving up.
options.D: it can be settled by appeal to a fact, as a dispute about boiling water can.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the statement that 'some disagreements reach a floor' means that

options.A: aesthetic argument can in the end yield proof of the kind that the relativist demands of it.
options.B: some disputes about a work become so heated that the parties refuse to continue them, though both still have reasons to give.
options.C: some disputes persist even when both parties agree about every feature of a work, because they value different qualities.
options.D: most disputes about taste end only after the parties have exhausted every reason they have.

questions.question: The author refers to people who remember someone who 'showed them something they had not been able to see' (paragraph 3) in order to suggest that such experiences are

options.A: cases of being persuaded into a new preference by a more forceful or confident personality.
options.B: proof that there are facts about books that are wholly independent of readers' reactions.
options.C: rare exceptions that leave the general truth of the relativist's reply largely intact.
options.D: evidence that aesthetic disputes can succeed even though they cannot end in proof.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the relativist in paragraph 3?

options.A: Two careful readers who agree on every feature of a poem may still disagree about whether it is good.
options.B: Disputes about the boiling point of water have sometimes been prolonged for years by errors in measurement.
options.C: When people report having been shown a quality in a work, their new view usually matches that of whoever argued most confidently.
options.D: Many people invoke the maxim about taste mainly in order to avoid an argument that might otherwise become unpleasant for both of them.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the final paragraph?

options.A: It turns the maxim's claim to humility against it, arguing that it withholds the seriousness that respect requires.
options.B: It restates the distinction between preference and judgement from paragraph 2 without adding anything to it.
options.C: It introduces a new argument that aesthetic disputes can, after all, be settled by some form of proof.
options.D: It concedes that the maxim, though confused, is in the end justified by the courtesy it makes possible.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 2 in the passage?

options.A: It explains why indignation was a natural and understandable response from authors to a new practice.
options.B: It weakens the authors' position by showing that exclusive ownership of characters is a fairly recent idea.
options.C: It proves that the laws which made authorship a form of property were mistaken from the beginning.
options.D: It shows that fan writing is superior to modern authorship, since it continues a far older practice.

questions.question: On the passage's reasoning, which of the following would give an author the strongest grounds for complaint?

options.A: A poet retells an ancient legend that she too once retold, adding new episodes and a different ending.
options.B: A reader writes and circulates a story in which two of her minor characters fall in love on holiday.
options.C: A reader alters several chapters of the author's novel and circulates them, under the author's name, as the original text.
options.D: A fan community holds long debates over which events in her series ought to count as canon.

questions.question: The author says that the fans' champions 'claim too much' (paragraph 3) chiefly because they

options.A: keep the assumption that stories can be owned and merely change who the owner is.
options.B: underestimate how much an author loses when readers imagine new episodes for her characters.
options.C: deny that an author may object to having her text copied and sold under another person's name.
options.D: ignore the historical evidence that retelling was once the ordinary way in which stories lived.

questions.question: The irony described in paragraph 4 lends most support to which of the following ideas?

options.A: Fan writing is in the end a kind of trespass, just as the indignant authors first claimed it was.
options.B: Authors ought to adopt the rules that fan communities have developed about what counts as canon.
options.C: Fan communities are, taken as a whole, more hostile to newcomers than authors have ever been to readers.
options.D: The urge to guard a story's boundaries comes from attachment to the story, not only from an author's interests.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author's position on the quarrel described in paragraph 1?

options.A: The fans have the better claim, since they keep a story's world alive and continue a much older tradition.
options.B: Each side errs, since a particular telling may rightly be protected while an imagined world was never truly ownable.
options.C: The authors are right to object, since laws long ago made authorship a form of property in their characters.
options.D: The quarrel cannot be resolved, because some retellings wound authors in ways that no distinction can capture.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: trace how naming laws grew out of earlier state measures for schooling and vaccinating the young.
options.B: argue that states should abolish every legal restriction on the names that parents may give their children, however unusual those names are.
options.C: show that strict naming rules really guard a stock of names, not children, and need defending as cultural policy.
options.D: defend approved lists of names as a legitimate means of protecting a nation's linguistic heritage.

questions.question: According to the passage, a rule that names may use only the letters of the national alphabet can

options.A: prevent parents from registering brand names and strings of numbers as the names of their children.
options.B: single out a child of immigrant parents by imposing a corrected spelling of a family name.
options.C: make it difficult for teachers and officials to pronounce the names of children from other countries.
options.D: protect immigrant children from mockery by giving them names that classmates find familiar and easy to read.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of paragraph 2 in the passage?

options.A: It argues that names matter more to the people who hear them than to the person who bears them.
options.B: It reports the view of the rules' defenders, which the author goes on to reject in every particular.
options.C: It supplies the main evidence for the author's claim that naming rules are really a form of cultural policy.
options.D: It grants that the protective argument justifies some refusals before the author shows that most rules go beyond them.

questions.question: Which of the following naming policies would the author of the passage most likely find acceptable?

options.A: Any name may be registered unless a registrar finds that it would expose the child to serious ridicule, with a right of appeal.
options.B: A name not found on the approved list may be registered once the parents pay a fee and wait a year for approval.
options.C: Names from other traditions are welcome, provided they are respelt to follow the national alphabet and pronunciation.
options.D: Parents may register any name at all, including brand names and numbers, because the choice belongs entirely to them.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, the phrase 'earns its keep' most nearly means

options.A: has been observed by educated writers for long enough to count as traditional.
options.B: is followed by enough speakers that breaking it causes genuine confusion.
options.C: offers readers enough real benefit to justify the effort of observing it.
options.D: can be traced back to a principle of logic or to the grammar of Latin.

questions.question: The example of the speaker who avoids a construction in a job application is used to

options.A: show that speakers are inconsistent in their usage and therefore need clear prescriptive rules to guide them.
options.B: demonstrate that the rule against the avoided construction is grounded in logic rather than in convention.
options.C: suggest that the way people speak at home is a more authentic guide to the language than formal writing.
options.D: show that judgements of correctness are real features of a community's linguistic life that a description must include.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

options.A: Linguists have been mistaken in pointing out the recent and dubious origins of many usage rules.
options.B: A usage rule with no basis in logic may still bind writers wherever readers expect it to be followed.
options.C: A convention that tests whether a writer was taught it is, for that reason, a convention that earns its keep.
options.D: A usage rule that cannot be justified by logic or by Latin ought to be abandoned by careful writers.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that rules of usage are not 'mere prejudice' but social facts a description must include?

options.A: Readers who claim to judge writers by a rule, when tested blind, neither notice breaches of it nor rate the writers lower.
options.B: Speakers who carefully observe usage rules in formal letters often ignore the same rules in conversation with friends.
options.C: The rule against ending a sentence with a preposition was first proposed by a grammar writer modelling English on Latin.
options.D: Many of the most admired writers in English have broken the rule against splitting an infinitive, and have done so for several centuries.

questions.question: According to the passage, recordings of bilingual conversation suggest that switches between languages tend to occur

options.A: at the end of a sentence, so that each sentence stays within a single language.
options.B: where the speaker lacks a word in the language with which the sentence began.
options.C: where the grammatical structures of the two languages can be joined without clashing.
options.D: mainly when a speaker is tired or distracted and pays less attention to grammar.

questions.question: The remark that 'the translation would lose the grandmother' (paragraph 3) implies that

options.A: the language in which words were first spoken can be part of what the speaker means to convey.
options.B: older members of bilingual families usually speak only one of the two languages used in the household.
options.C: proverbs cannot be translated accurately from one language into another without changing their sense.
options.D: the speaker has forgotten how to express the proverb in the language of the rest of the conversation.

questions.question: Which of the following involves an error most similar to the one the author identifies in the final paragraph?

options.A: Judging a chess player only by her results in fast games, while ignoring her long and strong record in slow, classical games.
options.B: Praising a novelist for freely mixing genres even when readers report that the resulting books are hard to follow.
options.C: Requiring a surgeon to use only the instruments approved for a particular operation, although she is equally skilled with several others.
options.D: Grading a musician trained in two traditions only on how strictly she keeps them apart, and treating her blending of the two as poor training.

questions.question: The passage mentions each of the following as a reason a bilingual speaker might switch languages EXCEPT

options.A: to include one listener in a conversation or exclude another.
options.B: to show respect to a listener who is older than the speaker.
options.C: to indicate that a remark is not meant to be taken seriously.
options.D: to fill a gap where a word was learnt in only one language.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.A: A word's original sense settles nothing about what it means now, though word histories keep other kinds of value.
options.B: Etymology is a worthless pursuit, since the history of a word tells us nothing about the language.
options.C: Words that have drifted far from their original senses should be restored to those senses by careful writers.
options.D: Shifts in meaning are always harmless, because speakers continue to understand one another whatever happens.

questions.question: The critic in paragraph 2 who 'insists on the Roman sense' of the word 'decimate' is mentioned in order to

options.A: show that the Roman sense of 'decimate' is the only correct one and should be preserved by writers.
options.B: show that those who appeal to origins apply their principle only to the words they happen to choose.
options.C: illustrate how a word can lose a fine distinction when it comes to be used loosely by speakers.
options.D: explain why most words have histories that run back past the languages in which they are used.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the appeal to origins 'cannot be applied consistently'?

options.A: A number of common words have kept their earliest recorded senses with little change for many centuries.
options.B: Historians doubt that the Roman punishment from which 'decimate' takes its name was often carried out in practice.
options.C: Most current dictionaries list 'destroy most of' as a standard sense of 'decimate' alongside the older sense.
options.D: Those who insist on the Roman sense of 'decimate' also reliably use every other word in the earliest sense on record.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author accept as a legitimate reason for resisting a new, looser use of a word?

options.A: The looser use breaks the link between the word and the older word from which it is derived.
options.B: The looser use would have puzzled the writers who first used the word several centuries ago.
options.C: The looser use makes it harder to express a distinction that readers still find useful.
options.D: The looser use departs from the sense that the word had when it first entered the language.

questions.question: The comparison with 'a photographed forest' in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: suggest that recordings of endangered languages are often of poor quality and of little later use.
options.B: illustrate the difference between a record of a living practice and the practice itself.
options.C: argue that conserving forests is a more urgent task than documenting endangered languages.
options.D: show that revived languages are always artificial copies of the languages that were lost.

questions.question: The passage suggests that, when resources are short, support for transmission tends to lose out to documentation because

options.A: doctors and teachers, who decide how such funds are spent, advise families against the home language.
options.B: communities whose languages are endangered usually prefer to have their speech recorded and archived.
options.C: its results are hard for the bodies paying for it to measure and present as achievements.
options.D: it has been shown to be less effective than documentation at keeping endangered languages alive.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards projects that document endangered languages is best described as

options.A: enthusiastic, since the author sees such projects as the surest way to keep a language alive.
options.B: dismissive, since the author regards such projects as a waste of resources needed elsewhere.
options.C: neutral, since the author describes what such projects do without passing any judgement on them.
options.D: appreciative of their worth but critical of how they are commonly understood and ranked.

questions.question: The claim that a policy spending most of its effort on documentation 'has quietly accepted defeat' depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Where fluent speakers remain, effort put into transmission could make it more likely that children go on acquiring the language.
