options.B: Documentation and the support of transmission cannot both be paid for within a single language programme.
options.C: Communities that later try to revive their languages rarely make any real use of the material held in archives.
options.D: Recordings kept in archives eventually deteriorate, so that documentation alone cannot preserve evidence of a language for long.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that the rapid birth of new sign languages proves the capacity for grammar is built into each human mind.
options.B: explain why the first signers in a new community never fully master the language that they themselves created.
options.C: contend that sign languages are conventions agreed among their users rather than products of the mind.
options.D: argue that new sign languages show grammar to depend on both learners' biases and transmission within a community.

questions.question: The author treats the solitary home signer as significant chiefly because she

options.A: reveals that the brains of deaf children differ in ways that make full grammar harder to acquire.
options.B: demonstrates that a family's unwillingness to learn signs is what keeps home signs from becoming languages.
options.C: lacks just the condition, a community of users across generations, that the new sign languages had.
options.D: shows that a deaf child cannot develop any structured system of communication without being taught.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's account of how a new sign language reaches full grammatical form?

options.A: In a new signing community, the adults who created the system used it as regularly as the children who later learned it from them.
options.B: Home signers who later join an established signing community quickly adopt the grammar used by the other signers there.
options.C: Children in a new signing community regularised the system more when they had more older signers to learn from.
options.D: In villages where hereditary deafness is common, many hearing residents also learn to sign with their deaf neighbours.

questions.question: Which of the following is most analogous to the process described in paragraph 3?

options.A: A committee of musicians agreeing on a standard pitch for tuning, which every orchestra in the country then adopts by rule.
options.B: A folk tune, sung a little differently by each singer, settling into a fixed form as each generation of learners sings it more uniformly than they heard it.
options.C: A solitary musician refining a melody over the course of a long life until, in old age, she judges it finally complete.
options.D: A composer writing out a complete symphony in a single sitting, working from a structure she had carried in her head for years.

questions.question: According to the passage, what marks a dead metaphor off from a living one?

options.A: A dead metaphor no longer shapes the way speakers reason about the subject.
options.B: A dead metaphor comes from an older stage of the language than a living one.
options.C: A dead metaphor cannot be extended into new expressions that listeners readily understand.
options.D: A dead metaphor is used far less often in ordinary speech than a living one.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Ordinary metaphors are alive as patterns of expression, but whether they shape thought beyond speech needs other evidence.
options.B: Ordinary metaphors are fossils whose origins say nothing about what their users think or mean today.
options.C: Ordinary metaphors are the surface of deep conceptual mappings that determine how speakers reason about the world.
options.D: Ordinary metaphors can never be shown to influence thought, because every piece of relevant evidence is linguistic.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: Studies of how people solve problems are beside the point, since the debate is at bottom a question about language.
options.B: The mapping view should be abandoned, because most of the expressions it relies on turn out to be frozen idioms.
options.C: Because the metaphors of time are productive, they must influence the way speakers remember past events.
options.D: Finding that speakers readily coin new warlike phrases about argument would not show they argue more combatively as a result.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would supply the kind of evidence the author says is needed to support the mapping view's stronger claims?

options.A: Asked to invent new expressions about time, speakers produced spatial ones far more often than any other kind.
options.B: In a wordless task, people set pictures of earlier events in the direction that their language's time expressions assign to the past.
options.C: Asked about their own speech, most speakers said they did not picture space when talking about deadlines.
options.D: A large survey found that spatial expressions for time outnumber all other kinds in every language examined.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the author's claim that many everyday metaphors are 'alive' means that they

options.A: occur in ordinary speech more often than the dead metaphors that speakers no longer notice.
options.B: are still felt by speakers as figurative, so that their origin is present to mind whenever used.
options.C: can serve speakers as patterns for forming and understanding new expressions, whatever their effect on reasoning.
options.D: govern how speakers reason about argument and time even when they are not speaking at all.

questions.question: The passage gives each of the following as a reason why mutual intelligibility fails as a test for separating languages from dialects EXCEPT that

options.A: speakers often pretend not to understand a variety they dislike.
options.B: neighbours along a chain may understand each other when the ends cannot.
options.C: how well people understand depends on topic and speed of speech.
options.D: one group may understand another better than it is understood.

questions.question: The example of the traveller passing from village to village in paragraph 2 serves to

options.A: show that people living in villages understand neighbouring varieties better than city dwellers do.
options.B: show that intelligibility gives no principled point at which to divide a continuous chain of varieties.
options.C: suggest that the borders of states were first drawn to follow the boundaries between languages.
options.D: prove that every variety along such a chain must be treated as a separate language in its own right.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that a variety now commonly called a dialect

options.A: is usually harder for outsiders to understand than a variety that is commonly called a language.
options.B: has a less fully developed grammar than the standard variety from which it is distinguished.
options.C: will in most cases die out within a few generations unless its speakers succeed in having it recognised as a separate language.
options.D: could come to be called a language by gaining a written standard and a place in schooling, its grammar unchanged.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the writers who conclude that the distinction is 'empty' is best described as

options.A: uncertain, since the author thinks that the question of whether the distinction is real cannot yet be settled.
options.B: dismissive of both their starting point and their conclusion, which the author thinks rest on bad evidence.
options.C: in full agreement, since the author also regards the distinction as politics dressed up as science.
options.D: accepting the observation they start from while firmly rejecting the conclusion they draw from it.

questions.question: A campaign argues that a regional variety deserves recognition as a language because linguists have measured large differences between its grammar and that of the standard. The author would most likely respond that the campaign

options.A: rests its case on the wrong ground, since recognition turns on a society's arrangements rather than on measured features of speech.
options.B: is illegitimate, since the line between a language and a dialect is in the end nothing more than politics.
options.C: should first establish whether speakers of the standard can understand the variety without any difficulty.
options.D: is well founded, since measured grammatical distance is the most objective basis there is for applying the label.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Typing should replace handwriting in early schooling, since writing is mainly a way of getting words from the mind onto a surface.
options.B: Joined handwriting should again be made compulsory in schools because it preserves an elegant tradition that a keyboard culture is losing.
options.C: Handwriting deserves a place in schooling because writing by hand supports learning in ways that an argument from speed and efficiency overlooks.
options.D: Students who take notes by hand always understand lectures better than students with laptops, so laptops should be kept out of classrooms.

questions.question: According to the passage, students who take notes by hand are forced to compress what they hear because

options.A: forming each letter by hand fixes its shape in memory and leaves little attention for the lecture itself.
options.B: they cannot write quickly enough to record a lecture word for word, so they must select and rephrase.
options.C: their teachers deduct marks for notes that are untidy or that do not follow a single joined style.
options.D: lectures are usually designed with summaries that students are expected to rewrite in their own words.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the phrase 'a delivery system' describes handwriting understood as

options.A: a set of rules for joined script that schools impose on their pupils.
options.B: a method of teaching young children the shapes and directions of letters.
options.C: a way of sending written messages to people who live far away from the writer.
options.D: nothing more than a means of moving words from the mind onto a page.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

options.A: Research has firmly established that writing letters by hand is how children first learn to recognise them.
options.B: A practice can be valuable partly because of the very slowness that makes it look outdated.
options.C: Typing lessons should be postponed until children have fully mastered a neat and consistent joined hand.
options.D: The old emphasis on elegant script did real harm to children's learning and explains why many of them read poorly.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that, before it became the dominant form, the codex was regarded as

options.A: a modest format suited to practical, everyday writing rather than to works of literary standing.
options.B: an expensive luxury that only wealthy communities could afford to adopt for their sacred texts.
options.C: the preferred format for prestigious literature, which was too long to fit on a single roll.
options.D: a format that every community took up at the same moment once its savings became clear.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the economic explanation of the codex's success is best described as

options.A: endorsing it as the best account of literary adoption while thinking it irrelevant to everyday documents.
options.B: treating it as the most convincing account of why early Christian communities adopted the codex first.
options.C: accepting the facts it relies on while denying that they account for the pattern and pace of the change.
options.D: rejecting it outright on the grounds that the codex did not in fact use writing material more economically.

questions.question: The examples of a legal compilation, a book of scripture cited in argument and a technical manual (paragraph 3) serve mainly to

options.A: show that lawyers, clergy and engineers were the first groups to adopt the codex before it spread to other readers.
options.B: identify works that readers consult at chosen points rather than read through, and which therefore suited the codex.
options.C: prove that a scroll was physically unable to hold the long texts that such specialised works usually required.
options.D: illustrate the prestigious literature that, according to the passage, remained on the roll for generations.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument against a purely economic explanation in paragraph 2?

options.A: The codex spread to literature fastest where papyrus was dearest, and almost as soon as its savings were understood.
options.B: Because of their wide margins, early codices saved much less writing material than historians have usually supposed.
options.C: Some early Christian communities that favoured the codex continued to keep a few of their texts on rolls.
options.D: Page numbers and indexes did not become common in codices until many centuries after the codex had become dominant.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, in the large historical dictionaries a definition was written

options.A: before volunteer readers were sent out to find quotations that would confirm the editors' chosen meaning.
options.B: by the volunteer readers themselves, who copied out each quotation together with its source and date.
options.C: only once the quotations gathered for a word had been sorted by the senses they seemed to show.
options.D: only for those senses of a word that the editors judged to be correct and respectable usage.

questions.question: In saying that the printed quotations are 'not decoration but the grounds on which it rests' (paragraph 2), the author means that the quotations

options.A: matter more than the definitions themselves, which careful readers can safely ignore.
options.B: guarantee that each definition is correct and will not need to be revised in the future.
options.C: were included chiefly to display the range of the editors' literary reading to the dictionary's users.
options.D: are the evidence that a definition summarises and against which it can be tested.

questions.question: The author would most likely regard a dictionary's label 'nonstandard' as

options.A: a purely factual report that follows mechanically from the quotations gathered for the word.
options.B: proof that the dictionary has abandoned its evidential method and turned itself into a court.
options.C: a reliable sign that careful writers ought to avoid the word in serious work.
options.D: a judgment by the dictionary's makers, even though it is presented as a plain description of usage.

questions.question: Which of the following has an authority most like the one the author attributes to a good dictionary in paragraph 4?

options.A: A respected elder whose rulings on proper manners are followed because of his long standing in the community.
options.B: A coastal survey trusted because its measurements are recorded, can be rechecked and are redrawn when the shoreline shifts.
options.C: A referee whose decision on a disputed goal stands as final, whatever later replays of the match may show.
options.D: A photograph that records a street scene exactly as it was, without any choice made by the photographer.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: argue that weaker reading on screens stems largely from trained habits, while granting that paper keeps some genuine advantages.
options.B: show that screens are destroying the capacity of a generation raised on phones to follow long arguments.
options.C: recommend that schools return to printed books because paper gives readers a better sense of place in a text.
options.D: demonstrate that the medium of reading makes no difference to comprehension once habits are corrected.

questions.question: According to paragraph 4, which advantage does paper offer that a scrolling screen supplies only weakly?

options.A: A greater willingness among readers to slow down and summarise what they have read.
options.B: Faster reading of long and demanding texts when the reader is working against the clock.
options.C: Physical cues of position and length that help some readers recall where an idea appeared.
options.D: Freedom from the headlines, messages and feeds that interrupt reading on a device.

questions.question: A habitual phone reader is asked to read a long essay on a tablet and then write a summary of it. Based on the passage, the author would most likely expect this reader's comprehension to be

options.A: closer to what the same reader would manage on paper than if no summary had been asked for.
options.B: no better than with no summary at all, because the screen itself is what damages understanding.
options.C: markedly better than the same reader would achieve when reading the essay on paper.
options.D: unchanged, since the passage says that only extra time, not a change of task, narrows the gap.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the explanation offered in paragraph 2?

options.A: Readers of printed books were better than screen readers at remembering on which page an idea had appeared.
options.B: Adults who had seldom used screens before showed the same comprehension gap on tablets as habitual screen readers did.
options.C: Readers given extra time to finish a long text on a screen understood noticeably more of it than readers who were hurried.
options.D: Most of the material that people read on their phones each day consists of short headlines, messages and search results.

questions.question: The comparison of a good edit to 'good stage lighting' in paragraph 2 is used to suggest that

options.A: editors make weak passages look more impressive than they really are to the reader.
options.B: editing is a theatrical skill that most authors lack and must therefore hire from others.
options.C: editors are chiefly responsible for the visual design and layout of the printed page.
options.D: editorial work is successful when readers of the finished book are not aware of it.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the exceptions mentioned in paragraph 3?

options.A: They have become more frequent as publishing has grown more commercial and more dependent on editors.
options.B: They show that the solitary author is usually a fraud whose books are largely written by others.
options.C: Their unsettling effect reveals an ordinary expectation that the author, not the editor, is a book's main maker.
options.D: They arise when editors who want their contribution celebrated insist on rewriting large parts of an author's manuscript.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward the view that editors are 'secret co-authors' is best described as

options.A: strict neutrality, since the author reports the view without passing any judgment on it.
options.B: understanding why it appeals but rejecting it as an overstatement of a real point.
options.C: wholehearted agreement, since the finished text is rarely the text that the author first submitted.
options.D: contemptuous dismissal, on the ground that editors' contributions to a book are in fact trivial.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Authors are best understood as directors of an editorial process rather than as the source of their books' material and voice.
options.B: Editors deserve the same credit as authors, because the finished book is seldom the manuscript that was first submitted.
options.C: Publishers should print editors' names on covers so that readers stop skipping the acknowledgements page.
options.D: Treating authorship as one person's undivided possession hides the graded collaboration through which most books are made.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that a modern scholar who wants to know exactly what a hand-press edition printed on a particular page should

options.A: consult any one surviving copy, since every copy of an edition was printed from the same type.
options.B: prefer a manuscript copy of the work, since manuscripts were more dependable than early printed books.
options.C: compare several surviving copies of that edition, since they may not agree on that page.
options.D: rely on a later reprint of the edition, since reprints corrected the errors of the original printing.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the statement that 'the same commonplace is now being run in reverse' means that

options.A: the belief that technology alone decides textual stability now yields a forecast of instability for digital texts.
options.B: digital texts are being converted back into print so that they will become stable once again.
options.C: the history of printing is now being read backwards, starting from the digital present.
options.D: historians are now arguing that the printing press made texts less stable than hand copying had ever done.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the claim in paragraph 3 that fixity was a social achievement the technology 'made possible but did not by itself deliver'?

options.A: Hand-press printers in fact seldom stopped the press to correct errors, so most copies of an edition were identical.
options.B: Some medieval copyists produced manuscripts so accurate that later scholars could find very few errors in them.
options.C: When powered presses replaced hand presses, variation between copies of one edition largely vanished even before any rights over copies were enforced.
options.D: Where presses were common but rights over copies and collation were absent, printed texts of one work kept varying for generations.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: show that digital texts are inherently unstable, unlike printed books, which became fixed as soon as the press was invented.
options.B: refute the thesis that printed books were more dependable than manuscripts, and argue that digital texts are equally unreliable.
options.C: qualify a common thesis about print by crediting institutions as well as the press with fixity, and extend the lesson to digital texts.
options.D: describe in detail the methods by which printers in the hand-press period corrected errors while their sheets were still being printed.

questions.question: The author suggests that the uneven division of the religion class in the scheme described in paragraph 2 is best explained by

options.A: the collections and assumptions of the libraries that were familiar to the person who devised the scheme.
options.B: the technical limits of decimal notation, which could not divide a single class into more than a few parts.
options.C: a deliberate effort by its maker to push the world's other religious traditions to the margins of libraries.
options.D: the near absence, anywhere in the nineteenth century, of published books about religions other than Christianity.

questions.question: The hypothetical study of household labour in paragraph 3 serves mainly to

options.A: show that schemes allot too little shelf space to subjects that their makers did not consider central.
options.B: illustrate how a scheme, by deciding a book's neighbours, frames the way browsing readers meet its argument.
options.C: suggest that authors, rather than librarians, should decide where their books are placed on the shelves.
options.D: argue that studies of household labour belong among works on economics rather than among works on the family.

questions.question: The passage offers each of the following as a reason not to replace classification with keyword search EXCEPT that

options.A: without some order, readers could find only what they already knew to ask for.
options.B: search systems rank their results, and ranking involves choices just as shelving does.
options.C: a collection without any arrangement would be unusable rather than neutral.
options.D: keyword search cannot cope with subjects that older schemes had crammed into long, unwieldy numbers.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: A classification scheme revised often enough could eventually achieve complete neutrality about knowledge.
options.B: Giving a book several subject headings partly offsets its being able to stand in only one place.
options.C: Local fixes to an inherited scheme are the best way for a library in a diverse city to correct its biases.
options.D: Keyword search, unlike shelving, allows readers to meet books without any viewpoint being imposed on them.

questions.question: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the point about adjacency made in paragraph 3?

options.A: A museum shows one painting among devotional works, then among portraits, and visitors see it as worship in one room and a likeness in the other.
options.B: A curator labels a painting with the wrong date, and the error is corrected decades later after visiting scholars point it out to the museum.
options.C: A museum has wall space for only a fraction of its paintings, so works from traditions its founders neglected stay in storage while others are displayed.
options.D: A visitor uses the museum's search terminal to locate a painting she already knows by name and goes straight to it without looking at anything else.

questions.question: According to the passage, the characters of Chinese are

options.A: signs that stand only for syllables, which places them one rung below the alphabet.
options.B: for the most part pictures of the things they name, much as the ladder described them.
options.C: in large part compounds in which one component indicates meaning and another loosely indicates sound.
options.D: an early and incomplete stage in a development that leads naturally toward the alphabet.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, to 'mistake a family tree for a law of nature' is to

options.A: confuse the biological ancestry of peoples with the history of the scripts that those peoples happen to use.
options.B: regard scripts that are historically related to one another as if they had developed quite independently.
options.C: assume that scripts change by a process of natural selection in which the fittest systems survive.
options.D: treat the particular line of descent of some scripts as a sequence through which every writing system must pass.

questions.question: The discussion of the Korean script in paragraph 4 implies that

options.A: judging one script better than another can be defensible when the judgment is tied to particular users and ends.
options.B: the ladder was right to rank phonetic scripts above others, since the Korean designers reached the same view.
options.C: scripts that were deliberately designed are in general better than scripts that developed gradually over centuries.
options.D: once the costs of learning are taken into account, every script turns out to be equally suited to every language.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim in paragraph 5 about what literacy rates chiefly depend on?

options.A: Several societies using alphabets but lacking widespread schooling have had low adult literacy for long periods.
options.B: With schooling, reading matter and rewards for reading held equal, societies using regularly spelled alphabets had far higher adult literacy.
options.C: Children learning an alphabet with regular spelling begin decoding unfamiliar words earlier than children learning a script that represents meaning.
options.D: Learners of English must memorise many irregularly spelled words almost as wholes before they can read fluently.

questions.question: The passage supports each of the following claims EXCEPT that

options.A: how economical an alphabet is depends partly on how closely its spelling follows pronunciation.
options.B: the ladder's ordering of scripts carried an implicit judgment about the peoples who used them.
options.C: the mixed system used for Japanese is easier for beginners to learn than an alphabet with regular spelling.
options.D: rejecting the ladder is compatible with holding that some scripts suit certain purposes better than others.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Journalism should stop treating novelty as a test of newsworthiness and should report events in proportion to how often they occur.
options.B: Readers misjudge risks mainly because they follow too little news, and wider and more regular reading would correct their sense of how often events occur.
options.C: The news misleads chiefly because of how news is defined, and the fault is better corrected by adding context than by seeking cheerful stories.
options.D: Editors favour bad news because it attracts paying readers, and this commercial taste is the main reason that audiences overrate rare and dramatic dangers.

questions.question: According to the passage, gradual improvements tend to go unreported because

options.A: editors deliberately hold them back, believing that cheerful stories sell far fewer copies than alarming stories about decline.
options.B: they are spread thinly over time, so that no single day offers an event the definition of news can register.
options.C: readers distrust any outlet that reports good news, so publications avoid such stories in order to protect their credibility.
options.D: they are usually too technical to explain clearly in the limited space that an ordinary news story can allow them.

questions.question: The author's observation that improvements are 'gradual and diffuse' while deteriorations are 'often abrupt' implies that

options.A: abrupt deteriorations matter less than gradual improvements and should therefore receive less space in the news.
options.B: most news reports about social trends contain errors of fact that systematically exaggerate how far things have declined.
options.C: societies are in fact improving in most respects, whatever impression their news happens to give them.
options.D: a society's news can mislead it about the direction of change even when each individual report is accurate.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 4, 'report the denominator alongside the numerator' most nearly means

options.A: present an event together with the wider count of cases against which its frequency can be judged
options.B: divide the space available evenly between rare events and the common events that seldom make headlines
options.C: balance each day's alarming stories with an equal number of cheerful stories about the same subjects
options.D: publish the statistics behind a story in place of the narrative account of what actually happened on the day

questions.question: According to the passage, one advantage of funding news through subscriptions is that a publication

options.A: becomes answerable to its own readers and has less reason to chase brief online clicks.
options.B: can make sure that its best reporting reaches readers who could not otherwise afford it.
options.C: can target its advertising at particular audiences far more precisely than printed newspapers could.
options.D: can lower the price that readers pay for careful reporting and so share it more widely.

questions.question: The passage implies that readers who do not pay for subscriptions

options.A: are mostly people who prefer opinion to reporting and would not read careful journalism if it were free.
options.B: are likely to depend more on cheaply produced material such as opinion, rumour and aggregation.
options.C: are largely protected from misinformation by the better-informed subscribers who live around them.
options.D: tend to stop following public affairs altogether once careful reporting is placed behind a wall.

questions.question: Which of the following is most similar to the author's reason, in paragraph 3, for treating news differently from most products?

options.A: A restaurant meal, which costs more at a better restaurant but satisfies the diner's hunger whichever one is chosen.
options.B: A gym membership, whose benefits go to the member alone and in proportion to how often the member actually attends.
options.C: A luxury watch, whose value to its owner is quite unaffected by whether anyone else in the town owns one or not.
options.D: Fire safety in a block of flats, where a household that takes every precaution is still endangered if its neighbours take none.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the shift to subscription funding is best described as one of

options.A: enthusiastic endorsement, treating it as the solution to the problems that the advertising era left behind.
options.B: nostalgic regret, wishing that the advertising arrangement it replaced could somehow be brought back again.
options.C: qualified approval, valuing the independence it brings while insisting that the exclusion it causes be reduced.
options.D: resigned pessimism, doubting whether any measure could do much to reduce the exclusion it creates.

questions.question: The example of the council's road proposal in paragraph 1 serves mainly to

options.A: suggest that disputes in local politics turn on questions of fact rather than of values.
options.B: illustrate a kind of dispute in which giving the competing cases equal space is appropriate.
options.C: show that local reporters tend to favour the views of residents over those of officials.
options.D: demonstrate how the habit of balance misleads readers about the true weight of opinion.

questions.question: The passage suggests that in a report giving equal time to one scientist from each camp, the misleading element lies chiefly in

options.A: the statements of the dissenting scientist, who misrepresents the evidence in order to seem credible.
options.B: the reporter's decision to quote any dissenting scientist at all on a question that is largely settled.
options.C: the reader's unreasonable belief that a newspaper would never stage a contest between unequal parties.
options.D: the arrangement of the report, which implies a parity between the two camps that does not exist.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's reply to the first point of the objection in paragraph 3?

options.A: In many fields there is no reliable way to tell how researchers' views are distributed, since such opinion is seldom surveyed.
options.B: Several majorities in the history of science later abandoned their views after new and unexpected evidence came to light.
options.C: Many journalists who report on science have no formal training in any of the fields that they cover.
options.D: Readers say that they trust reports quoting two scientists more than reports quoting only a single scientist.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT:

options.A: If a minority scientific view later prevails, the way the question is reported ought to change.
options.B: Giving rival positions comparable space is appropriate when the dispute concerns values or interests.
options.C: Where researchers disagree, reporters should present the majority view in a field as the settled answer.
options.D: A report can be entirely fair to each person it quotes and yet leave its readers with a false picture.

questions.question: According to the passage, the click on a headline measures

options.A: how much better informed a reader has become after finishing the article that the headline introduced.
options.B: the importance that editors attach to a story compared with the other stories on the page.
options.C: how many of the readers who opened a story were disappointed by what they found in it.
options.D: how strongly a headline draws a reader at the moment of deciding which article to open.

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that coverage of foreign elections tends to shrink mainly because

options.A: resources follow a measure that cannot register the value such coverage has for readers.
options.B: readers have shown through their choices over many years that they no longer want to read it.
options.C: editors have concluded after deliberation that such subjects are no longer worth the effort of reporting.
options.D: such stories cost far more to produce than the lighter stories that tend to perform well on screens.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Audience figures have damaged journalism, and newsrooms would serve the public better by returning to editorial instinct.
options.B: Audience figures record genuine choices but are misused when newsrooms treat them as a verdict on value.
options.C: Headline testing misleads readers by promising stories that the articles behind the headlines fail to deliver.
options.D: Refined measures such as return visits and subscriptions can at last settle what a public needs to know.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation in paragraph 3 of why some subjects thin out?

options.A: Stories about committee hearings draw fewer clicks than stories about celebrities, although their readers stay with them longer.
options.B: Headline testing has raised the total number of readers that most news websites attract each month, sometimes by a wide margin.
options.C: In newsrooms that never adopted live audience figures, coverage of the same subjects declined over the same years at the same pace.
options.D: Some editors privately regret the shrinking space given to foreign elections but feel unable to do anything to reverse the trend.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 1, the phrase 'the story cannot be stood up' indicates that

options.A: the reporters cannot gather enough evidence to justify publishing the story they had suspected was there.
options.B: the person at the centre of the story has refused every request from the reporters to be interviewed about it.
options.C: the story has grown far too long to fit into the limited space that the publication has made available for it.
options.D: a rival publication has already reported the same story before the team could finish its own work.

questions.question: The author's remark that 'a quiet year may be evidence of its success' suggests that

options.A: a lack of published exposures proves that the deterrent effect of investigative reporting is working as it should.
options.B: a lack of published exposures indicates that the publication has failed to fund enough investigations to be effective.
options.C: a lack of published exposures shows that officials have learned to conceal their wrongdoing more skilfully than they once did.
options.D: a lack of published exposures need not mean the reporting was idle, since it may have prevented wrongdoing.

questions.question: Paragraph 2 contributes to the argument of the passage chiefly by

options.A: establishing that most investigations fail to produce a story that a publication is able to print.
options.B: explaining why the market tends to supply less investigative work than a society would want.
options.C: demonstrating that readers place little value on the results that investigative reporting produces for them.
options.D: showing that rival publications act unfairly when they repeat findings that another paper paid to uncover.

questions.question: Which of the following policies most closely reflects the reasoning of the final paragraph?

options.A: A city publishes every inspection report online so that diners can compare kitchens and choose the cleanest restaurants for themselves.
options.B: A city awards a public prize each year to the inspector whose findings led to the most dramatic and widely reported restaurant closure.
options.C: A city keeps a small team of inspectors visiting restaurants unannounced all year round, instead of a large campaign every few years.
options.D: A city trains its food inspectors so thoroughly that their findings against restaurants are almost never overturned when owners appeal against them.

questions.question: The passage implies that a reader who, after seeing the correction, still blames the stored chemicals for the warehouse fire

options.A: probably never saw the correction at all, since notices of this kind are seldom noticed or read by anyone.
options.B: may well accept that the correction is true while having no other account to put in place of the old one.
options.C: has rejected the correction because it was printed too late and too far away from the original report it was meant to correct.
options.D: trusts the original report more than the correction simply because the original report happened to be published first.

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the explanation offered in paragraph 2?

options.A: Readers who saw the correction on the same page as the original report remembered it better than readers who saw it elsewhere.
options.B: Readers recalled retracted claims more often when the original report had been repeated by several different outlets before the retraction.
options.C: Readers whose correction named another cause of the fire later cited the discarded cause far less often than readers whose correction named none.
options.D: Readers who refused to accept the correction were mostly those who already distrusted the particular newspaper that had printed it.

questions.question: The author would endorse each of the following practices EXCEPT

options.A: stating in a correction what the investigators now think likely, even when the true cause is not yet certain.
options.B: holding back a causal explanation of an event until the facts on which it depends are better established.
options.C: explaining, when no alternative cause is yet known, why the original claim was made and why it seemed plausible.
options.D: wording a correction so that it avoids restating the false claim, to keep that claim from growing more familiar.

questions.question: A paper wrongly reported that a train was delayed by a signal failure, and the real cause is still unknown. Which correction would the author regard as most likely to work?

options.A: One saying the cause is still being investigated and explaining that a signal switched off for repairs had been mistaken for a fault.
options.B: One that avoids any mention of signals and says simply that an earlier report about the delay contained an error.
options.C: One printed prominently on the front page the following morning, stating only that the earlier report of a signal failure was wrong.
options.D: One issued within the hour, saying that the signal report was wrong and apologising for the haste with which it had been published.

questions.question: The comparison with a laboratory in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: argue that scientists, unlike reporters, are free of the personal ambitions that would otherwise distort their judgement.
options.B: illustrate how the labour of verification usually remains invisible to the people who go on to read the results.
options.C: show that trust can rest on how work is arranged rather than on the character of the people doing it.
options.D: suggest that newsrooms should adopt the full experimental methods of the natural sciences in their daily reporting work.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, on the author's account, a story that quotes two officials making incompatible claims and checks neither

options.A: is preferable to a story in which the reporter states, on the evidence, which of the two officials is right.
options.B: meets the standard of objectivity as its early champions understood it, though not as its critics understand it.
options.C: fails mainly because the reporter allowed strong personal opinions to shape the way the story was framed.
options.D: displays the outward signs of objectivity while lacking the practice that those signs were supposed to indicate.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Objectivity was always an impossible pose, and journalists should replace it by stating their own commitments openly to readers.
options.B: Objectivity as a checkable method rather than personal neutrality remains worth defending, though much criticism fairly targets a debased form of it.
options.C: Objectivity declined because reporters abandoned the flat tone and balanced quotation that had once made their fairness visible to readers.
options.D: Objectivity is valuable because a disciplined method of verification allows newsrooms to become impartial in choosing their stories.

questions.question: The statement in paragraph 5 that the concession 'limits the claim rather than defeating it' implies that

options.A: the defence of objectivity survives once it is confined to making reports answerable and no longer promises impartiality.
options.B: the critics of objectivity were right after all to say that it cannot be defended against the charge of bias.
options.C: the concession is too slight to affect the argument for objectivity in any way that a reader would need to notice.
options.D: the bias shown in choosing stories can in time be brought under the same discipline of verification as reporting.

questions.question: Which of the following practices best fits objectivity as the passage says its early champions understood it?

options.A: A reporter refuses to state any conclusion and gives each side of a dispute exactly the same number of paragraphs.
options.B: A reporter declines to cover any subject on which she holds strong opinions, so as to keep her own work neutral.
options.C: A reporter known for strong views publishes an investigation listing the documents and named sources behind each of its claims.
options.D: A reporter begins every story by declaring her political commitments, so that readers can make allowance for them.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'a common silence' refers to

options.A: the shared absence from public discussion of matters that the gatekeepers chose not to raise.
options.B: the reluctance of mass audiences to criticise the broadcasters whose bulletins they listened to every evening.
options.C: the quiet that settled over public life once the coffeehouses and reading societies had finally closed.
options.D: an agreement freely reached among citizens to avoid raising the topics that most divided them from one another.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the lament described in paragraph 1 is best described as

options.A: wholly supportive, endorsing both its account of the shared past and its proposal to restore that past.
options.B: dismissive, treating its concern about lost common ground as a misunderstanding that has no real basis at all.
options.C: detached, describing the lament and its critics without committing to a view of its own on the question.
options.D: sympathetic to the worry it expresses but critical of the history it assumes and of the remedies it suggests.

questions.question: The passage implies that the breadth of broadcast-era audiences

options.A: made public discussion more inclusive than the coffeehouse gatherings in every respect that mattered for democracy.
options.B: came at the cost of narrowing who could take part in public discussion as speakers rather than listeners.
options.C: resulted from the efforts of editors and producers to widen the range of views considered respectable.
options.D: was achieved by excluding from the audience those who lacked the leisure and literacy to take part.

questions.question: Each of the following is consistent with the author's argument EXCEPT:

options.A: Groups that read quite different publications may still resolve their factual disputes with one another if they accept the same rules of evidence.
options.B: The decline of the mass audience is to be regretted mainly because it ended the experience of a nation attending to the same events.
options.C: An attempt to restore a few dominant news outlets could also bring back the exclusions that once accompanied their authority.
options.D: A shared body of reported facts, even one assembled selectively, made it easier for political opponents to argue usefully about policy.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the fragmentation of audiences matters less than the fragmentation of standards?

options.A: In the broadcast era many citizens distrusted the bulletins they watched yet still accepted the facts those bulletins reported.
options.B: Several plural democracies contain many small publics that settle their disputes through courts and statistical offices trusted by all.
options.C: The coffeehouse debates of early modern Europe were in fact far less exclusive than their modern critics have usually supposed.
options.D: Groups that rarely encounter one another's news gradually stop accepting the same rules of evidence, so separate audiences breed separate standards.

questions.question: The author's main point about the cycle of replacement terms is that it

options.A: shows that renaming alone cannot change attitudes, though each new term briefly allows more courteous speech.
options.B: reflects a dishonest habit through which speakers flatter themselves while only appearing to spare their listeners.
options.C: can be halted altogether once schools and officials agree to adopt one carefully chosen set of terms.
options.D: proves that renaming is futile and that reformers should give up trying to replace words that have become offensive.

questions.question: According to the usual explanation described in the passage, replacement terms lose their neutrality because

options.A: the reformers who choose replacement terms misjudge how ordinary speakers will actually use them.
options.B: each new term is usually borrowed from an older vocabulary that already carried traces of contempt.
options.C: attitudes towards the thing a word names pass, while they last, to any word that reliably refers to it.
options.D: speakers soon grow tired of any word that is introduced through official forms and school teaching.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 2, 'displacement activity' refers to

options.A: an action that gives a sense of having dealt with a problem while leaving its cause untouched.
options.B: a process through which the meaning of one word is gradually transferred to another.
options.C: a deliberate effort to push a disliked word out of polite speech and into the slang of everyday talk.
options.D: an activity that shifts the work of reform from public officials onto ordinary speakers.

questions.question: It can be inferred that the author would expect a replacement term to keep its neutrality longest in a society where

options.A: the term has been chosen by a body of experts rather than by reformers.
options.B: what the term names has largely ceased to be treated as something shameful.
options.C: the new term is gentler and more delicate than any of the terms before it.
options.D: officials use the term consistently on forms and in their public documents.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following is one of the efforts required to follow an argument one disagrees with?

options.A: Taking written notes so that each of the speaker's points can be checked against the evidence later.
options.B: Asking the speaker to slow down so that the separate parts of the argument can be connected.
options.C: Holding back from preparing a reply while the speaker is still partway through a sentence.
options.D: Agreeing provisionally with the speaker until the whole of the argument has been stated.

questions.question: The reference to 'a meeting in which three people answer a point that nobody made' (paragraph 2) serves to

options.A: support the objection that a culture of listening lets persistent speakers exhaust others.
options.B: show that meetings are an unsuitable setting for arguments between people who disagree.
options.C: suggest that public meetings should be made smaller so that every participant can be heard.
options.D: illustrate what follows when the effortful work of listening is carried out poorly.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the suggestion made in paragraph 4?

options.A: Most people who had been trained in debating at school said they rarely used those skills in their later working lives.
options.B: Committees required to restate one another's points before replying reached decisions in fewer total hours than similar committees without the rule.
options.C: Committees that allowed every member unlimited time to speak took far longer to reach decisions than committees with strict time limits.
options.D: Members of committees required to restate one another's points before replying said they found the meetings more pleasant than before.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the objection discussed in paragraph 3 is best described as

options.A: complete dismissal of it as a misunderstanding of how deliberation in meetings actually proceeds.
options.B: reluctant agreement that it shows that teaching people to listen would do more harm to public argument than good.
options.C: partial acceptance of the concern it raises combined with rejection of its view of what listening is for.
options.D: neutral reporting of it without any indication of whether the author finds it persuasive.

questions.question: The contrast between the villager and the commuter in paragraph 2 is used to

options.A: argue that online platforms ought to be designed to resemble small villages rather than trains.
options.B: illustrate that being anonymous has no effect at all on how people speak to strangers.
options.C: show that people who live in villages are by nature more courteous than people who live in cities.
options.D: suggest that the prospect of meeting people again restrains behaviour more than being identifiable does.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the passage that a pseudonymous account would be most likely to be used with restraint if

options.A: it had been used in the same community long enough to carry a reputation its owner valued.
options.B: it was used mainly to post on large platforms that reach a broad and constantly changing audience.
options.C: its owner's legal name could be discovered by the platform whenever a complaint was made about it.
options.D: its owner had been required to verify an identity with the platform before choosing the pseudonym.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraphs 2 and 3?

options.A: Legal action against online abusers proved easier to bring on platforms that required every user to verify an identity.
options.B: Many employees who had reported misconduct online said they would not have done so if made to use their own names.
options.C: On one forum, users who kept the same pseudonym for years proved as abusive as users whose accounts were created and abandoned within a week.
options.D: On large platforms, users posting under their real names proved slightly less abusive than anonymous users posting on the same platforms.

questions.question: The author would agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT

options.A: The civility of an online space depends chiefly on whether its members could be identified by outsiders.
options.B: Real-name rules might curb some of the most severe abuse while imposing burdens on speakers who need cover.
options.C: Being unidentifiable does make some people more willing to say harsh things to others.
options.D: Courtesy between strangers who do not expect to meet again cannot be taken for granted.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, 'a tacit rule about what kind of thing goes in the slot' refers to

options.A: the original caption, which every later version of the meme must repeat.
options.B: a written guideline issued by the platform on which the meme first appeared.
options.C: an agreement among sharers to keep the meme's message the same in each version.
options.D: an unstated shared sense of which contents suit a particular template.

questions.question: It can be inferred that, in the author's view, a person who shares a version of a political meme

options.A: is usually trying to ridicule the view that the original version of the meme expressed.
options.B: may be showing skill with a familiar form rather than declaring support for the view its caption expresses.
options.C: has in effect cast a small vote that analysts can reliably count as a sign of agreement with the meme's sentiment.
options.D: is generally unaware that earlier versions of the same template carried quite different messages.

questions.question: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the spread of the cat photograph as the passage describes it?

options.A: A rumour changes a little with every retelling until its original source can no longer be traced at all.
options.B: A melody becomes the basis of hundreds of new songs whose lyrics are unrelated to each other and often contradictory.
options.C: A news photograph is shared widely because it records an important event that many people wish to remember.
options.D: A campaign slogan is repeated, word for word, by thousands of supporters who all agree with what it says.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how paragraph 4 relates to paragraph 3?

options.C: followed strict conventions that told every reader exactly when a writer intended to be ironic.

options.D: the person receiving the message usually hides whatever offence it has happened to cause.

options.C: offer evidence that governments elected on detailed platforms handle crises worse than those elected on slogans.
options.D: show that the critics' preferred alternative involves a pretence of its own, so that detail is no simple cure for vagueness.

options.A: It is the generality of a slogan that makes it the feature of political language most deserving of criticism.
options.B: Holding a government strictly to a detailed platform may reward an unwillingness to adapt to events.
options.C: A slogan can serve a coalition well even though it asserts little that a voter could check.

questions.question: The passage as a whole is primarily concerned with

options.A: proposing that platforms rank posts according to what users say, on reflection, that they value most.

options.C: arguing that engagement ranking neither invents outrage nor simply mirrors it, but amplifies and reshapes it.

options.B: ranking systems ought to treat a brief pause as much weaker evidence of interest than a written reply.
options.C: people who linger over provocative posts are usually unaware that they are doing so at the time.

questions.question: The sentence 'A mirror that trains the face in front of it is not a mirror' (paragraph 4) implies that

options.A: the anger found in feeds is produced by ranking systems rather than by the people who write the posts.
options.B: those who write for online feeds are cynical in adjusting their tone to whatever the system rewards.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of paragraph 4?

options.A: Readers of online feeds were found to spend more time on angry posts than on calm posts of a similar length and subject.
options.B: Writers shown detailed figures on each post's performance kept the same tone over time as writers shown no figures.
options.C: Many users, when asked, said that they would prefer feeds containing fewer provocative posts than they now see.
options.D: Some writers who had adjusted their tone to what the feed rewarded said that they disliked having to write in that way.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the objections to ranking by reflective preference (paragraph 5) is best described as

options.B: regarding them as technical difficulties that better measurement will soon be able to overcome.
options.C: treating them as decisive reasons for continuing to rank feeds by momentary reaction.

A promise binds us partly because it lets another person plan around what we will do. That is why a promise cannot simply be cancelled when keeping it becomes inconvenient: the inconvenience was foreseeable, and the other person relied on us precisely so that our later moods would not matter. Yet it does not follow that every promise binds in every circumstance. If I promise to meet a friend for lunch and on the way I find a stranger injured on the road, no sensible friend would think I had wronged them by stopping. What releases me is not my changed preference but a change the promise was never meant to cover, one that both of us, had we thought of it, would have agreed to exclude. The force of a promise, then, is real but bounded by what it was understood to be about.

Two pictures of moral worth pull in different directions. On one, the person who is honest only by overcoming a strong temptation to lie deserves more credit than the person to whom lying never occurs, since the first has had to do something and the second has merely been lucky in temperament. On the other, the person who must struggle reveals that part of them still wants the wrong thing, while the person for whom honesty is second nature shows what a good character actually looks like. Each picture captures something. The struggler's effort is admirable as an achievement, but we would not wish our friends to remain strugglers for ever; we hope that effort will eventually turn into ease. Effort, on this view, is the honourable path to virtue rather than its finest form.

Moral philosophers often test principles against imagined cases: a runaway trolley, a surgeon with five dying patients, a drowning child beside an expensive suit. The method is defended on the ground that stripping away messy detail isolates the feature that matters. But the stripping is not neutral. A real surgeon could never be certain that the transplant would succeed, that no one would find out, or that the healthy visitor had no one depending on him; our reluctance to approve the killing may be a sound response to exactly these uncertainties, which the case asks us to set aside but which our intuitions were formed to track. When an intuition about an idealised case conflicts with a principle, it is therefore unclear which has been refuted. This does not make imagined cases useless, since they can still show that a principle has implications its defenders had not noticed; it makes them weaker as evidence against principles than they are usually taken to be.

It is sometimes objected that an institution cannot meaningfully apologise for wrongs committed before any of its present members were born, since none of them did anything wrong. The objection assumes that an apology is mainly a confession of personal guilt. But an apology also does something else: it states publicly that what happened was a wrong, not a misfortune or a regrettable necessity, and it commits the speaker to a relationship in which that wrong is not repeated or excused. A university, a company or a city persists across generations precisely as the bearer of such commitments; it signs contracts that outlive its staff and honours debts its founders incurred. If it can inherit obligations of this kind, it can also inherit the duty to acknowledge what was done in its name. What it cannot do is make its present members feel personal guilt, and an apology that demands such feeling misunderstands its own purpose.

Nostalgia was once treated as a kind of illness, a homesickness that weakened soldiers and emigrants. A more recent view sees it as doing useful work. People tend to become nostalgic when they feel lonely, uncertain or adrift, and the memories they return to are usually of moments shared with others: a family meal, a school trip, a celebration. Recalling such moments reminds a person that they have been valued and connected, and that sense of continuity can steady them in an unsettled present. Nostalgia is not always benign; it can harden into a refusal to accept change, or into a fantasy of a past that never was. But in its ordinary form it seems less a flight from the present than a way of drawing on the past to cope with it.

When a decision turns out badly, observers tend to judge it as having been a poor decision, even when they are told exactly what the decision-maker knew at the time. A doctor whose reasonable choice of treatment is followed by a rare complication is rated as less competent than one who made the same choice and was lucky. This tendency to grade decisions by their outcomes is often described simply as an error, and in many settings it is one. Yet it is not wholly irrational. In daily life we rarely know what someone knew, and outcomes are often the only evidence we have of their judgement; a rule of thumb that trusts outcomes is a sensible response to that ignorance. The difficulty is that we go on applying the rule even when the facts that would make it unnecessary are placed in front of us.

Ask people why they chose one pair of socks over another, why they liked a job candidate, why they moved house, and they will readily give reasons. It is tempting to treat these reasons as reports, read off from some inner record of what actually moved them. There is good ground for doubt. People's explanations often match what an outsider would guess, given the culture's ordinary theories of why people act, more closely than they match whatever in fact influenced the choice; and when an influence was something they did not notice, such as the position of an item on a shelf, they seldom mention it. It does not follow that people know nothing of their own minds. They are usually right about what they feel and what they are attending to. What is shaky is their access to the causes of their choices, which they seem to infer much as anyone else would, while experiencing the inference as direct knowledge.

Procrastination is usually treated as a failure of time management, and the usual remedies follow from that diagnosis: calendars, lists, deadlines broken into smaller pieces. These help some people, but they often fail the chronic procrastinator, who typically knows perfectly well how much time remains and what needs to be done. A better account starts from feeling rather than scheduling. The task that is put off is usually one that provokes some discomfort, whether boredom, self-doubt or fear of being judged, and delay offers immediate relief from that discomfort at the cost of greater trouble later. Seen this way, the procrastinator is not miscalculating time but managing a mood, badly. Planning tools are not useless, but they work best when they also make the task feel less threatening, for instance by turning a vague, daunting assignment into a first step small enough to begin without dread.

It is often said that public libraries have lost their purpose now that so much information can be found online. The argument mistakes what libraries do. Lending books was always only part of their role; they are also among the few indoor public places where a person may stay for hours without buying anything, where a student without a quiet room at home can study, an elderly reader can find company, and a job seeker can use a computer and ask for help. These functions have not moved online, and for people with little money or space they may matter more than ever. Libraries certainly need to change what they offer, but the case for keeping them does not rest on books alone.

Jokes are notoriously the hardest thing to translate, and the reason is not simply that they rely on puns. Even a joke with no wordplay depends on what its audience already knows and expects: which professions are thought pompous, which towns are thought backward, which subjects are too serious to mention lightly. The joke works by briefly upsetting these expectations, and a listener who does not share them sees nothing upset. A translator can explain the background, but an explained joke has lost the speed on which its effect depends. The more faithful strategy is often to replace the joke with a different one that does similar work for the new audience, accepting that fidelity to the effect may require infidelity to the words.

Two attitudes have long divided those who care for old buildings. One holds that a ruined church or fort should be restored to the state its builders intended, replacing lost towers and repainting faded walls, so that visitors see the work as it was meant to be seen. The other holds that such restoration is a kind of forgery: the building's age, its damage and its later alterations are part of its history, and the honest course is to stop further decay while leaving the marks of time visible. The second attitude has largely prevailed among conservation specialists, and with reason, since reconstruction often rests on guesswork about what the original looked like. Yet it is not costless. Collectors who travelled villages writing down folk songs are usually praised for saving a heritage that would otherwise have vanished. The praise is deserved, but it hides a paradox. A song in oral circulation has no single correct version: each singer alters the words, the tune and the length to suit the occasion, and this variation is not corruption but the way the tradition lives. Once a collector prints one version, often the one sung by the most cooperative informant on a particular afternoon, that version tends to become the standard, taught in schools and performed at festivals, while the others come to seem like mistakes. The act of preservation thus fixes what was fluid. None of this means collectors should have stayed at home; without them most of these songs would be lost entirely. It means that a printed collection should be read as a snapshot of a moving practice, not as the authentic original from which variants departed.

Historians value memoirs for their vividness but treat them with caution, and the reasons are not mainly about honesty. A memoir is usually written long after the events, when the author knows how things turned out, and memory tends to reshape the past to fit that knowledge: doubts are forgotten, lucky guesses become foresight, and decisions made in confusion acquire a clear purpose. Memoirists also write for an audience and often to defend a reputation. None of this makes memoirs worthless. They record impressions, motives and atmosphere that official papers omit, and read alongside letters and documents from the time, they can be revealing. The caution is about using them alone as a record of what happened and why.

Counterfactual history, the study of what might have happened had some event gone differently, is often dismissed as a parlour game for historians with too much time. The dismissal overlooks that every causal claim in history is already a counterfactual. To say that a drought caused a rebellion is to say that without the drought the rebellion would not have occurred, or would have come later or smaller; a historian who refuses to think about alternatives cannot weigh causes at all. The real objection is to counterfactuals that stray far from the moment in question, imagining chains of consequences decades long, where every step multiplies uncertainty. Asking what was genuinely possible for the people involved, given what they knew and could do, is not fantasy but part of explaining why events took the course they did.

We tend to think of a map as a picture of what is already there, accurate or inaccurate according to how faithfully it copies the land. Many maps in history did more than copy. When a state surveyed a frontier region and drew a line across it, the line often did not record a boundary that people on the ground recognised; it created one, which taxes, passports and armies would later enforce. Historians have learned to read archives not only for what they say but for what they leave out. An archive is the residue of an administration's interests: it keeps tax rolls, court cases and correspondence among officials, and so it records people mainly when they paid, offended or petitioned. Whole areas of life, such as household work, friendship and private belief, appear only when they collided with authority. It has become common to conclude that the archive simply silences the powerless. That conclusion goes too far. The same court records that reduce a person to a defendant often preserve, in the words of witnesses, details of daily life recorded nowhere else, and a petition written to flatter an official can still reveal what its writer wanted. The archive is biased in what it selects, but read against its grain it yields more about ordinary lives than its makers ever intended.

A price of zero is not just a very low price. People respond to free offers far more strongly than a small drop in price would predict: a product reduced from a small sum to nothing attracts many more takers than one reduced by the same amount to a slightly smaller sum. This is why many online services charge nothing and earn their revenue from advertising or data instead. The user does pay, in attention and in information about themselves, but these costs are spread out and hard to count, and so they do not trigger the caution that a visible price, however small, would.

Open-plan offices were promoted on the promise that removing walls would bring colleagues together and multiply the chance conversations from which ideas emerge. When companies have tracked what actually happens after such a move, the picture has often been the reverse: people conscious of being overheard send more messages and speak less face to face, wearing headphones to create the privacy that walls once gave. Teams whose work requires constant quick coordination, such as a newsroom or a trading floor, may genuinely benefit. The lesson is that physical closeness does not by itself produce interaction; whether it does depends on what the work requires and on whether people feel free to talk without being observed.

National income accounts leave out the cooking, cleaning and care done unpaid within households, and the omission is often called a simple bias that a better statistic would correct. The criticism is right that something valuable goes unmeasured, and that this can distort judgements: when a family starts paying for childcare it once provided itself, measured output rises though little more care may be given. But the remedy is less simple than it sounds. To add household work to the accounts one must price it, and every method of pricing an hour of unpaid care, whether at what a hired carer would earn or at what the carer could have earned elsewhere, imposes a market valuation on activity whose meaning to those who do it is often precisely that it is not done for money. The omission is a real flaw, but the obvious fix may trade one distortion for another.

Two strategies compete for the limited money available to protect plant diversity. Seed banks store frozen samples of thousands of species in secure vaults, offering insurance against extinction at modest cost. Conservation in the wild protects plants where they grow, along with the insects, fungi and soils they depend on. The seed bank's great advantage is security, but its samples are frozen in time: a population kept in a vault stops adapting to changing climate and pests, and some species have seeds that cannot survive drying and freezing at all. Wild populations go on evolving, but they are exposed to every threat the vault avoids. Neither strategy can substitute for the other. The vault is best understood as a backup for living populations, not a replacement for them.

Naturalists have long divided into those who tend to lump similar organisms into one broad species and those who split them into many narrow ones. The dispute is often presented as a quarrel of temperaments, as if one side were simply careless and the other fussy. In fact it reflects something real about living things. Populations diverge gradually, and at any moment some pairs are clearly distinct, some clearly the same, and many lie in between, interbreeding a little or differing in a few traits. For these intermediate cases no fact of nature settles whether there are one species or two; the answer depends on which criterion one adopts. This does not make classification arbitrary, since the clear cases are clear. But it means that some disputes about species are disagreements about definitions rather than about the organisms.

Projects that recruit volunteers to count birds, record flowering dates or photograph insects are often dismissed by professional researchers on the grounds that amateurs make mistakes. The objection is true and largely beside the point. Individual records from volunteers are indeed less reliable than those of trained surveyors, but the errors tend to be random rather than systematic, and random errors shrink in importance as the number of observations grows. Advocates of rewilding sometimes speak as though removing fences and reintroducing a few large animals will return a landscape to the condition it was in before human interference. The promise is appealing but confused. There is no single earlier condition to return to: the landscapes in question have changed continuously for thousands of years, with shifts in climate, in the species present and in the ways people used them. Choosing a baseline is therefore a decision about which past to prefer, not a discovery of the true one. This does not make rewilding pointless. Letting natural processes such as flooding, grazing and decay operate with less management can produce richer and more resilient ecosystems. But the honest case for it is about the processes it allows, not about a lost original it claims to restore.

An offset that pays to plant a forest is often treated as cancelling an equivalent quantity of emissions from a flight or a factory. The equivalence is only arithmetical. Carbon released from burning fossil fuel stays in the atmosphere for centuries, while carbon stored in trees is held only as long as the trees survive fire, disease, drought and the decisions of future landowners. The two quantities are measured in the same tonnes, yet one is a near-permanent addition and the other a reversible loan. None of this means that planting forests is worthless; a stored tonne buys time, and time has value. It means that an offset should be counted as a delay whose worth depends on how securely the storage can be guaranteed, rather than as an erasure that lets the original emission be forgotten.
