Software engineers speak of technical debt: the future cost created when code is written quickly rather than well. The metaphor is apt in one respect, since like a loan a shortcut lets a team deliver something sooner in exchange for paying more later, and taking it on can be a sensible choice. But it misleads in another. A financial debt has a known balance and a schedule of payments, so a borrower can decide whether it is worth it. The cost of hasty code is rarely visible; it shows up as features that take longer than expected and failures nobody can easily trace, and it grows in ways no one has agreed to. Teams therefore tend to take on far more of it than they would if the bill arrived in writing.

Engineers often speak of legacy systems as if they were merely old, but what makes a legacy difficult is not its age but the number of things that have come to depend on it. A file format, a connector or a programming interface that was widely adopted becomes a promise to everyone who built on it, and each new version must keep that promise or break their work. This is why designs that almost everyone agrees are clumsy survive for decades: the cost of changing them would be borne not by the designer but by thousands of users who would all have to adapt at once. The awkwardness of a long-lived standard is therefore less a sign of poor judgement than a record of its success; only what was widely adopted acquires enough dependants to become impossible to fix.

It is often said that the banners asking website visitors to accept or refuse tracking have handed people control over their personal data. The claim assumes that a choice offered is a choice made. In practice, a visitor who wants to read an article is asked, at the worst possible moment, to weigh consequences that are invisible and distant against an obstacle that is immediate and irritating. Many banners make acceptance a single click while refusal requires several screens of toggles. Unsurprisingly, most people click whatever makes the banner disappear. A mechanism built in this way records the visitor's impatience rather than the visitor's preference, and it lends the appearance of consent to an outcome largely decided by the design of the box.

Making a machine more efficient seems an obvious way to reduce the energy it consumes, but economists have long noted an awkward complication. When a service becomes cheaper to run, people tend to use more of it: a more economical car makes longer journeys affordable, and cheaper lighting invites more of it. Some of the expected saving is therefore taken back in additional use. It does not follow, as enthusiasts of the idea sometimes conclude, that efficiency is futile. Whether the rebound swallows a small or a large part of the saving depends on how much more of the service people actually want once its price falls, and for many household uses that appetite is limited; nobody keeps the fridge door open because the fridge is economical. The finding is a reason to estimate savings honestly, not a reason to abandon the pursuit of them.

Much of the software that businesses rely on is maintained by a handful of volunteers, sometimes by a single person working in spare hours. Companies that would never run a factory on an unpaid supplier routinely build products on such code and treat it as a free natural resource, like air. The comparison flatters them. Air does not need anyone to fix it; code does, and the work of fixing security flaws, answering bug reports and keeping up with changes elsewhere does not get easier as more people use a project. It gets harder. Popularity, which looks like a sign of health, can thus be precisely what exhausts the few people who keep a project alive. A firm that depends on such work and contributes nothing to it is not enjoying a free good but drawing down a stock that someone else is paying to replenish.

Readers who complain that a novel simply stops often assume that an ending exists to settle what the story has raised: who is guilty, who marries whom, whether the journey succeeds. Some endings do that, and do it well. But an ending can also be judged by whether it completes the shape of the book's attention. A novel that has spent three hundred pages showing how hard it is to know another person would contradict itself if its last chapter revealed everything; the unresolved close is then not a failure of nerve but the argument carried through. Openness is not a virtue in itself, and a writer who withholds an answer merely to seem profound has evaded rather than completed the work. The question is not whether an ending is closed but whether it is faithful to what the novel has been about.

A familiar view holds that strict poetic forms, with their fixed line counts and rhyme schemes, are cages that a free imagination must escape. Poets who have worked in such forms often describe the opposite experience. The need to find a rhyme or to fit a thought into a fixed number of syllables pushes them away from the first phrase that comes to mind, which is usually the most worn, and towards words and connections they would not otherwise have found. The constraint works less as a wall than as a prompt. This does not make every sonnet good; a form can be filled mechanically. But the assumption that freedom from rules is the natural condition of creativity mistakes the absence of resistance for the presence of invention.

One school of critics holds that a poem means what its author intended, and that interpretation is the patient reconstruction of that intention from the text and its circumstances. Another holds that once a work is published its meaning belongs to its readers, so that the author's own account is just one reading among many. Each position captures something the other cannot. The first explains why we can be wrong about a poem, as we are when we take an ironic line for a sincere one; the second explains why a work can say more than its author knew, as when a later age sees in an old novel a pattern its writer never noticed. What neither can do alone is account for both experiences, of being corrected by the text and of being surprised by it, and a defensible view of interpretation will have to make room for both.

Why do people who insist they cannot sing keep turning up, week after week, to rehearse with amateur choirs? Part of the answer lies in what choral singing asks of them. Unlike a solo performance, it does not demand that any one voice be remarkable; it demands that each voice listen to the others and adjust, breathing and entering together. Members describe the result less as a musical achievement than as a feeling of belonging that few other activities supply so directly. The music matters, but for many singers it is the occasion for the coordination, and the coordination is what they come back for.

Campaigns to purify a language usually begin from the fear that borrowed words are a kind of erosion, each foreign term a small loss of the native stock. The fear misdescribes how languages grow. A borrowed word rarely displaces an existing one outright; more often it settles beside it and the two divide the territory, one taking a formal shade and the other an everyday one, so that the language ends up able to say more rather than less. Borrowing is also old: most languages that purists wish to protect were themselves assembled from earlier contacts. None of this means that every borrowing is welcome or that speakers cannot reasonably prefer a native coinage. It means that the decision is one of taste, not a defence against decay.

Comparisons of online discussions are often said to show that comment threads in which participants use their real names contain fewer insults than anonymous ones, and the point is regularly offered in support of ending anonymity. The inference moves too fast. Sites that require real names tend to differ from anonymous ones in other ways as well: they are often smaller, more closely moderated and frequented by people who already know one another, any of which could explain the gentler tone. Even where the effect is genuine, it is bought at a price that the comparison does not measure, since the people most likely to fall silent when they must identify themselves include those with the most to fear from speaking, such as an employee criticising an employer. Less abuse in the threads that remain is not the same as better discussion overall.

Giving each side of a dispute equal time looks like the essence of fair reporting, and on questions where informed opinion is genuinely divided it is. But when nearly all of those who have studied a matter agree and a small minority dissents, presenting the two positions as evenly matched misinforms the audience about the very thing it most needs to know: where the weight of evidence lies. The audience leaves believing that experts are split when they are not. Fairness to persons, letting each view be heard, has been confused with fairness to the evidence, which requires that views be presented in proportion to their support. A report can include a dissenting voice and still be accurate, provided it does not pretend that the dissent is as strong as the consensus.

Proposals to make English spelling match pronunciation have a strong case on one side and a stubborn obstacle on the other. In favour, a regular system would spare children years of memorising exceptions and would make reading easier to learn. Against it stands not mere habit but the sheer amount already written: every reform would make the existing stock of books, signs and records look strange to the next generation, and the more successful the reform, the more foreign the past would become. The case for reform rests on the convenience of future learners; the case against rests on continuity with what has been written and the variety of present speech.

Memory researchers have repeatedly found that trying to recall material, for example by answering questions on it, fixes it in memory better than reading it again for the same amount of time. Students tend to resist the finding because rereading feels productive: the text grows familiar, and familiarity feels like knowing. Recall, by contrast, is effortful and exposes gaps, which feels like failure. The finding has limits that its enthusiasts sometimes forget. Testing oneself helps most when the material has first been understood; quizzing a student on ideas that were never properly explained simply rehearses confusion. Recall is a way of strengthening learning, not a substitute for the teaching that makes something worth recalling.

Arguments over whether schools should group pupils by ability usually proceed as if the choice were between two outcomes: grouping helps able pupils and harms the rest, or mixing helps the rest at some cost to the able. Both sides assume that the group itself does the work. Yet much of what happens to a pupil placed in a lower group depends on what the school then does with that group: whether it is given the most experienced teachers or the least, a demanding curriculum or a diluted one, and whether pupils can move up when they improve. A lower set taught ambitiously and kept open differs more from a lower set treated as a holding pen than either does from a mixed class. Asking whether grouping works is therefore a less useful question than asking what it is used to do.

Sleep researchers broadly agree that during adolescence the body clock shifts later, so that teenagers who are sent to bed early often lie awake and then struggle to wake for an early start. This has led to calls for secondary schools to begin later in the morning, in the expectation that pupils will then sleep longer. The expectation is reasonable but less simple than it looks. A later start helps only if bedtimes do not drift later in step, and the gain can be eroded by evening screens or by family and transport timetables that a school cannot alter. The biological finding is sound; what it shows is that early starts work against teenagers, not that moving the bell alone will give them the sleep they lack.

Detailed marking rubrics are usually defended as a protection for students: they make expectations explicit, reduce the influence of a marker's mood and allow two examiners to reach the same grade. These are real gains, especially for routine tasks. The trouble begins when the same apparatus is applied to work whose value lies in doing something unexpected. A rubric can list only the qualities its authors anticipated, and a student who learns to satisfy each line, an introduction here, three examples there, is rewarded for matching the template rather than for thinking. An essay that takes an original route may score worse than a dutiful one because its strengths fall between the boxes. Consistency is worth having, but a scheme that is perfectly consistent about the wrong things is not fair; it is reliably unfair.

It is often observed that students who take notes by hand remember a lecture better than classmates who typed nearly every word. The explanation is not that pens are magical but that they are slow. Unable to keep up with the speaker, the student writing by hand must decide what matters, compress it and put it in their own words, and this selecting and rephrasing is itself a form of learning. The advantage, then, belongs to the mental work rather than to the instrument, and a typist who deliberately summarises instead of transcribing can recover much of it.

Online symptom checkers are usually compared with doctors, and by that standard they look poor: they miss diagnoses a clinician would catch and raise alarming possibilities a clinician would dismiss. But for most people the realistic alternative to a symptom checker is not a consultation; it is a search engine, a relative's opinion or simply waiting. Against those alternatives, a tool that asks structured questions and advises when to seek care may do better, even if it diagnoses worse than a doctor. The relevant question is not whether such tools match professionals but whether they improve the decisions people would otherwise make, and in particular whether they send the right people to a clinic and reassure the right people to stay at home.

A round daily target of steps has become, for many people, the definition of an active day, and falling short of it can feel like failure. The number is better treated as a convenient goal than as a threshold. Nothing happens to the body at the moment the counter reaches it; the benefits of walking appear to rise gradually with activity, and an inactive person who adds a modest amount of walking gains something real even if the target remains far off. Treating the figure as a pass mark can discourage exactly the people who stand to gain most, by making their improvement look like a shortfall. A target is useful as an encouragement and harmful only when it is mistaken for a line between health and its absence.

Why do warnings that once alarmed people come to be ignored? The usual answer is that people grow careless, but the process is more reasonable than that. A warning that appears everywhere, on products that are mostly harmless as well as on ones that are genuinely dangerous, teaches its readers that it carries little information. Each false alarm lowers the value of the next, and a sensible person learns to discount the signal. The fault then lies less with the reader than with the issuers, who, wishing to cover every conceivable risk, spend the credibility that a warning needs in order to work. A label that warned about fewer things would protect people better, because they would have reason to believe it.

When most of a community is vaccinated against a contagious disease, the few who are not are protected too, because the infection struggles to find a path to them. This makes refusal look costless to the refuser, and some ethicists describe the unvaccinated as free riders on the efforts of others. The label is apt for some and unjust to others. It fits a person who could safely be vaccinated and declines because others have made the risk small, since that person's safety is borrowed from neighbours who accepted the minor burden. It does not fit an infant too young for the vaccine or a patient whose treatment rules it out; for them, the protection of the crowd is not a free ride but the only protection available, and it is precisely the reason the rest of us have to keep it intact.

When a bypass takes through traffic away from a small town, shopkeepers on the old main road often predict ruin, and in the first months after it opens some of them do lose trade from passing motorists. Yet the longer story is frequently different. Freed from heavy lorries, the main street grows quieter and safer to walk along, and the visitors who now stop do so because they mean to, staying longer than the drivers who once paused for fuel. Businesses that served passing traffic, such as filling stations and roadside cafes, tend to suffer most, while those that depend on people lingering may gain. Whether a town is helped or harmed thus depends on which kind of trade it lived on, and the early losses are a poor guide to the eventual result.

Residents who move into walled housing estates with guarded gates usually describe their decision as a private one: they want safety for their families and are willing to pay for it. Taken one by one, such decisions are understandable. Their sum is something none of the residents chose. City master plans often treat informal settlements as blank spaces awaiting proper development, marking them for clearance or for replacement by orderly blocks of housing. Settlements that grew without permission frequently contain dense networks of their own: workshops next to homes, credit circles, arrangements for sharing water and minding children, all of them fitted to the needs of people with little money and long working days. Two drivers take the same corner too fast after the same glass of wine; one reaches home, the other strikes a cyclist who appears suddenly from a side lane. Most people blame the second driver far more, even though the two drivers made identical choices and differ only in what happened next, which neither controlled. If we applied that principle strictly, we would have to say the drivers are equally culpable, and that our sharper condemnation of the second is a kind of error. After learning the outcome of an event, people find it remarkably hard to recover how uncertain it looked beforehand. Lavish weddings are often criticised as a simple failure of prudence: families spend their savings, or borrow, for a single day that leaves nothing behind. The criticism misreads what the money buys. In many communities a wedding is the occasion on which a family displays its standing to a wide network of relatives, neighbours and future in-laws, and that standing affects the marriages its other children can make, the help it can call on and the credit it is offered. It has become routine to dismiss the history of great individuals as naive, on the ground that leaders merely ride forces (economic, demographic, technological) that would have produced much the same results without them. The correction was needed, but it has been pushed too far. Structural forces set the range of what is possible; they rarely settle which possibility is realised. At moments of crisis, when institutions are weak and outcomes hang on a few decisions, the character and judgement of particular people can tip events one way or another, and the effects can last for generations. The sensible position is not to return to heroic biography but to ask, case by case, how wide the range left open by circumstance actually was, since that width determines how much any individual could matter.

A standard textbook argument holds that raising the minimum wage must reduce employment, since employers buy less of anything that becomes more expensive. Comparisons of neighbouring areas where the wage floor rose in one and not the other have often found smaller job losses than that argument predicts, and sometimes none at all. One explanation is that where few employers compete for workers, wages were held below what a competitive market would pay, so a modest floor can raise pay without cutting jobs. But this evidence concerns modest increases in places where the floor was low relative to local wages. It says little about large rises, or about poorer regions where a single national floor sits close to the typical wage, and treating it as proof that minimum wages never cost jobs stretches it beyond what it shows.

Port cities have long been more open to strangers than inland towns of similar size, and the usual explanation credits the sea with broadening minds. The cause is more practical. A port lives by trade with people it cannot choose, and its merchants, dock workers and officials learn that a ship's crew from a distant coast must be housed, fed, paid and understood if business is to continue. When trade declines or shifts to other harbours, the practical reason for accommodating outsiders weakens, and port cities have sometimes turned as suspicious of strangers as any inland town.

It is sometimes said that a politician who lies to the public or bargains with a ruthless faction to prevent a greater harm has simply done the right thing, and that once the calculation favours the act, no moral residue remains. This tidy view misdescribes the situation. The act may be justified, all things considered, and still involve doing something wrong: deceiving people who were owed the truth, or lending strength to people who deserved none. A leader who felt nothing after such a choice would be more worrying than one who felt the weight of it, because that weight is how a person registers that a real claim was overridden rather than dissolved. Justification answers whether one should act; it does not erase what the act cost those it wronged.

Early laboratory work on helplessness suggested a simple lesson: animals exposed to shocks they could not escape learned that nothing they did mattered, and later failed to escape even when escape became easy. The idea spread quickly into accounts of human depression and of children who stop trying at school. Later research reversed the emphasis. Passivity in the face of prolonged stress, it now appears, is the default response, and what is learned is the opposite: that one's actions can make a difference. Experiences of control teach organisms to override the default. The practical implication shifts accordingly. Rather than looking only for the damage done by uncontrollable events, one should ask whether a person has had enough experiences of mastery to learn that effort pays.

Diners often praise a restaurant for serving the authentic version of a dish, meaning the one that matches how it is made in its place of origin. The standard is harder to apply than it sounds. Most celebrated dishes have changed repeatedly, absorbing ingredients that arrived through trade or conquest, and cooks in the same region disagree about the correct recipe. What is called authentic is usually one moment in that history, often the version a visitor first encountered, fixed and treated as the original. This does not make every claim of authenticity empty. A cook who learned a tradition from the inside and respects its logic is doing something different from one who merely borrows a name; but the difference lies in that understanding, not in matching a single correct recipe.

A familiar account of why great empires fall points to overextension: they conquer more territory than they can defend or administer, and the cost of holding distant frontiers drains the centre. The account is attractive because it turns decline into a lesson about limits. Its weakness is that it is applied after the fact. Empires that collapsed are described as having overreached, while others that held equally vast and costly territories for centuries are not, and the difference is rarely explained by size alone. What seems to matter more is whether the centre could keep the loyalty of provincial elites and raise revenue without provoking revolt, capacities that some large empires possessed and some small ones lacked.

Almost every company now publishes a mission statement, and most of them sound alike: commitments to customers, integrity, innovation and people. Because the words cost nothing and exclude nothing, they tell an outsider very little about how the firm will behave. We defer to experts on bridges and medicines without hesitation, yet many people feel that deferring to someone else on a moral question (adopting a view on the ethics of eating meat simply because a thoughtful philosopher holds it) would be a failing. Fashion moves in cycles because it serves two opposed wishes at once: to resemble the people one admires and to stand apart from the people one does not. A style adopted by a small, admired group spreads as others imitate it; but the more widely it spreads, the less it distinguishes anyone, and the group that began it abandons it for something new. The style then lingers among late adopters until it seems dated, and it becomes available for revival only once it has been forgotten long enough to look fresh. The engine of change is therefore social rather than aesthetic: styles are dropped not because they stop being attractive but because they stop being distinctive.

It seems natural to expect revolutions where misery is deepest, yet they have often broken out in societies that were growing richer and whose rulers had begun to reform. Two responses are common when a celebrated figure from the past is found to have held views now regarded as abhorrent. One insists that such people be judged by the standards of their own time, since no one can be expected to see beyond the moral horizon of their age. Imagine a sealed jar of coins auctioned to a room of thirty people, each of whom guesses its contents by eye. Their guesses will fall on both sides of the real sum, and taken together they may average out remarkably well. Yet the person who takes the jar home is the one who guessed highest, and so, even if every guesser is sensible and the crowd as a whole is accurate, the buyer has very probably paid more than the jar holds. Victory in such a contest is itself evidence of having guessed too high. Better guessing cannot cure this, since no guess is free of error; what helps is to offer less than one's own guess, and to hold back further when the room is larger, because a bigger crowd throws up a more extreme top guess.

It became common, after a run of supply disruptions, to say that lean manufacturing had been exposed as a mistake: firms that held almost no inventory had saved money in calm years and paid for it many times over when deliveries stopped. The charge contains a truth but misplaces it. Holding little stock was never the whole of the method; its purpose was to make problems visible quickly so that they could be fixed, and the firms that practised it most seriously also cultivated close, long relationships with a few suppliers and knew in detail where their parts came from. What failed in many cases was a cheaper imitation: low inventory adopted as a cost target, combined with suppliers chosen solely on price and scattered across distant regions that nobody had mapped. The lesson, then, is less that buffers are always wise than that thin buffers are safe only where the knowledge and relationships the method assumed are actually present.

But treating gardening as a solution to reef decline mistakes a holding action for a cure, since only reducing the warming itself addresses the cause.

It is tempting to describe the history of science as a sequence of ideas, each tested by instruments built to check it. Often the order runs the other way. A new instrument, made for some modest practical purpose, reveals phenomena that no existing theory anticipated, and theory then scrambles to absorb them; the instrument, in effect, sets the agenda. This does not make theories mere reflections of the tools available, for a device shows nothing until someone has ideas about what its readings mean, and the same image has been read differently by observers holding different views. But it does suggest that the questions a science finds pressing at any moment depend heavily on what it has lately become able to see, and that some questions remain unasked not because they are unimportant but because nothing yet exists to make them answerable.

It is natural to conclude that city life has bred a new temperament, and in some populations there may be genuine inherited change. But at least two other explanations fit the same observation. Each would produce bold urban animals, and only careful study, such as raising young from both settings under identical conditions, can tell them apart.

When software ships with a setting already chosen, most users never change it, and this is often described as laziness. A more charitable reading is available. A default carries an implicit message that this is what the makers, who presumably understand the product, consider suitable, and many users reasonably treat it as advice. That reading, however, cuts both ways. If defaults function as recommendations, then the people who set them bear something like the responsibility of an adviser, and a default chosen because it serves the maker's interest in data or revenue, rather than the user's, is not a neutral starting point but a misleading recommendation. The defence of inert users thus becomes a charge against designers.

A writer revising a manuscript on paper keeps, if anything, a few dated drafts, and the reasons behind each change are lost unless recorded separately. Software teams that use version control keep something quite different: every change, however small, is stored with its author, its time and a short note explaining it, so that any earlier state of the work can be recovered and the history of a single line traced. Because nothing is irretrievably lost, programmers can experiment boldly, abandoning a failed approach without fear; and because each change is explained, a newcomer can learn why the code is as it is rather than only what it does.

Critics of ghostwriting say that a memoir written by someone other than its named author deceives readers, who believe they are reading the subject's own words. The charge assumes a convention that many readers do not share. Few people who buy the autobiography of a famous athlete suppose that the athlete sat alone composing sentences; what they expect is that the story, the opinions and the memories are genuinely the athlete's, and that he or she has approved the result. Measured against that expectation, a ghostwritten memoir deceives only when the content is invented or the subject has not endorsed it. Where readers do expect sole authorship, as with a novel or a scholarly article, concealed ghostwriting remains a real deception.

Audiences sometimes wonder what a conductor does, since the players have the notes in front of them and could, it seems, keep together by listening to one another. In a small ensemble they often do. But in an orchestra of eighty or more, spread across a wide stage, sound takes a noticeable time to travel, and players at the back may hear their colleagues at the front slightly late; following the ear alone would make the orchestra drag. The conductor's beat gives everyone a visual signal that arrives at once. Most of the conductor's work, however, happens earlier, in rehearsal, where decisions about balance, tempo and phrasing are made and agreed, so that the gestures in performance mainly remind players of what has already been settled.

Two habits divide painters of abstract pictures. Some call their works 'Untitled' or give them only numbers, on the ground that a title would tell viewers what to see and so narrow a picture meant to be met on its own terms. Others give evocative titles, a word or phrase that suggests a mood or a landscape. The first habit protects the viewer's freedom but can leave the uncertain viewer with nothing to hold on to; the second offers a way in but risks fixing one reading so firmly that others become hard to notice. Neither is simply correct, and the choice reveals less about the picture than about how much guidance the painter believes a viewer wants.

When a forecast announces a seventy per cent chance of rain, many listeners are unsure what has been promised. Some suppose it will rain over seventy per cent of the area, others that it will rain for seventy per cent of the day. The intended meaning is different: on days when conditions resemble today's, rain falls at the given place on about seven days in ten. The confusion arises because the number answers a question listeners did not know had been asked, namely 'out of what?', and forecasters seldom say. A forecast can be perfectly accurate in its own terms and still mislead an audience that supplies the wrong reference class.

Corporate jargon is usually mocked as empty: phrases about 'leveraging synergies' and 'circling back' are taken to show that those who use them have nothing to say. The mockery misses what the vocabulary does. Much of it serves to soften or blur, so that a decision to close a department can be announced as a 'realignment' without anyone having to state plainly that people will lose their jobs. Such language is not empty but evasive, and evasion has uses for the speaker. This makes it more troubling than the critics allow, not less: an empty phrase merely wastes time, whereas an evasive one shifts the burden of understanding onto listeners, who must work out for themselves what is being done to them.

Newspaper obituaries have long followed a convention of discretion: the dead are praised for their achievements, while their failings are passed over or hinted at in phrases that knowing readers decode. The convention is defended as kindness to grieving families, and kindness is a real consideration. But an obituary is also the first draft of a public record, often consulted later by people who never knew the subject. When it omits the serious harm a powerful person did, it does not merely spare feelings; it misinforms everyone who relies on it afterwards. Discretion is defensible for private failings that harmed no one beyond the household, far less so for public conduct that harmed many.

Teachers are now widely advised to praise children for effort rather than for cleverness, on the reasoning that a child told she is clever may avoid hard tasks for fear of disproving it, while one praised for trying learns that ability grows with work. What seems to matter is less the word used than whether praise connects what the child did to what resulted, so that the child learns which kinds of effort work.

Schools that pair older pupils with younger ones for tutoring usually set out to help the younger children, and they often do. A recurring observation, however, is that the tutors gain as much or more: having to explain an idea to someone who does not yet grasp it forces the tutor to organise what he or she half knows, to notice gaps and to find examples. Schools sort children by year of birth so routinely that the practice seems like a law of nature rather than an administrative convenience. Yet grouping by age assumes that children born within the same twelve months are ready for the same material at the same moment, an assumption that every experienced teacher knows to be false. In classrooms that deliberately mix ages, the older children consolidate what they know by explaining it, and the younger ones see, in the work of those just ahead of them, what the next step looks like. None of this makes mixed-age teaching easy: it demands careful planning and a teacher able to manage several levels at once, and without these it can fail badly. But that difficulty is a reason to prepare teachers for the task, not a reason to treat the age-graded class as the only sensible arrangement.

Comparisons of test scores taken at the end of one school year and the start of the next have often suggested that children lose ground over the long holiday, and that children from poorer homes lose more. The finding has been used to argue that much of the gap between richer and poorer pupils opens not in school but outside it. Later work has complicated the picture. Some of the apparent loss depends on which tests are used and how their scores are scaled, and some estimates shrink considerably when the same children are measured in a different way. What survives scrutiny is more modest: holiday loss is real for some children, but it is smaller and less consistent than first reported, so it cannot by itself account for the gap, even if the long break remains a time when unequal home resources count for more than usual.

A familiar remedy for textbooks that students find hard is to rewrite them in shorter sentences with commoner words, guided by formulas that score a text by the length of its words and sentences. The formulas do measure something, but what makes a passage hard to understand is often not its vocabulary so much as the gaps it leaves for the reader to fill. Cutting one long sentence into three short ones frequently removes the very words, such as because, although and therefore, that told the reader how the ideas were related; the result scores as easier and is harder to follow. None of this means that dense prose is a virtue or that difficult words never obstruct learning. It means that a readability score measures surface features, and a text revised to improve its score can lose the connective tissue on which comprehension depends.

It is widely believed that a teacher's expectations can shape how well pupils perform: tell a teacher that certain children are about to blossom, and they will. There is evidence that expectations matter, since teachers who expect more of a pupil may give that pupil more attention, more time to answer questions and more demanding work. It seems obvious that an operation cannot work by suggestion: the knife either repairs the tissue or it does not. For this reason, many surgical procedures entered routine use on the strength of surgeons' observations that their patients felt better afterwards. But patients who undergo surgery also receive attention, hope and a period of rest, and their symptoms often fluctuate and improve on their own. When some procedures have been tested against sham operations, in which patients are anaesthetised and given an incision but the key step is omitted, the improvement in the two groups has turned out to be similar. Such trials raise real ethical questions, since the sham group bears risk without the prospect of direct benefit. Yet without them, it is hard to know whether an operation helps because of what the surgeon does or because of everything that surrounds it.

Much of what is believed about diet and health rests on asking people what they eat. The objection usually raised against such surveys is that people forget, and forgetting, being random, merely adds noise. The deeper difficulty is that the errors are not random. People tend to under-report foods they regard as unhealthy and over-report those they think virtuous, and the size of the distortion varies with body weight, with education and with how much a person cares about appearing healthy. Since those same characteristics are themselves linked to health, the error can manufacture associations or hide real ones, rather than simply blurring them. This does not make dietary surveys useless; for some questions they are the only practical source. But it means that a large sample, which cures random error, offers no protection against this kind.

Studies that follow people over many years have found that those who report feeling lonely or socially isolated tend to die earlier than those who do not, and the association has led some to describe loneliness as a threat to public health. The finding is consistent and worth taking seriously. It is not, however, a simple demonstration that loneliness causes illness. People who are already unwell may withdraw from others, and poverty or disability can produce both isolation and poor health. Researchers try to adjust for such factors, but the most that can be said with confidence is that loneliness and early death travel together, and that loneliness may contribute to it.

Hospitals that check whether staff clean their hands by sending observers onto the wards routinely record high rates of compliance. The rates are less impressive than they look. Staff who notice an observer wash more often while the observer is present, so the audit measures behaviour under observation, which is precisely the condition that does not hold for most of a working day. Where observed rates have been compared with counts from electronic dispensers or with unannounced checks, the observed rates have often turned out considerably higher. The point is not that staff are dishonest, nor that audits are pointless, since being watched does improve hand hygiene for a time. It is that a measure which changes the behaviour it measures cannot tell us how people behave when no one is looking.

Two ideas of the residential street compete in suburban planning. The grid connects every street to several others, so drivers and walkers can take many routes and no single road carries the whole load. The cul-de-sac layout, with its looping roads and dead ends, keeps through traffic out, and residents of the closed streets often value the quiet and the safety of children playing outside. The difficulty is that the quiet is bought with distance: a shop a few hundred metres away as the crow flies may be more than a kilometre away by road, so residents drive for trips they might have walked, and the few roads that connect the loops carry heavy traffic. Each layout serves something real; the cul-de-sac simply moves its costs out of sight of those who enjoy its benefits.

When rain falls on a field or a forest, much of the water soaks into the soil, and what runs off reaches the streams slowly. When the same rain falls on roofs, roads and car parks, almost none of it soaks in; it is gathered by gutters and drains and delivered to the river within minutes. A city can therefore flood after a storm that would have caused no trouble before the land was built on, not because more rain falls but because the rain reaches the river all at once. Wider drains can carry more water away, but they also speed its journey, which is why some cities now try to slow runoff with green roofs, permeable paving and ponds.

In places where many people cycle, the risk of injury for each cyclist tends to be lower than in places where few do. This pattern is often read as proof that drivers become more careful when cyclists are common, so that simply encouraging more cycling will make it safer. The pattern is real, but the causal story may run partly the other way. Cities that have built protected lanes and calmed their traffic attract more cyclists precisely because cycling there is already safer, and more cautious people take up cycling only when it feels safe. Driver adaptation may contribute as well; nobody needs to deny it. What the pattern does not support is the hope that numbers alone, without the infrastructure that draws them, will deliver safety.

Faster roads and railways are usually justified by the time they will save commuters. Yet in many cities and over long periods, the average time people spend travelling to work each day has stayed surprisingly stable. The explanation is that people treat travel time, not distance, as the quantity to be budgeted. When a new motorway cuts the journey, many households eventually move further out, to larger and cheaper homes, until the commute is roughly as long as it was before. The investment is not wasted: people gain space and a wider choice of jobs and housing. But its benefit arrives as a larger city rather than as the shorter commute that was promised.

Most people feel that they would be obliged to help a stranger in danger in front of them, yet feel no comparable obligation to help a stranger in equal danger on another continent. Some philosophers conclude that this feeling is simply a bias: distance, they argue, cannot by itself make a moral difference, so our duties to the distant are as strong as our duties to the near. The argument is powerful, but it moves too quickly. Distance usually travels with other features that may matter, such as whether one is uniquely placed to help, whether one's help will actually arrive, and whether many others could help equally well. To show that the feeling is mere bias, one must show that it survives when these features are held constant, and that is harder than the argument assumes.

When a crime is discovered decades after it was committed, it is sometimes said that punishing the offender now punishes a different person: the frail old man in the dock shares a name with the young man who did the deed, but little else. The objection has force where punishment is meant to reform, for a person who has long since changed has nothing left to reform. It has less force where punishment is meant to answer the wrong itself, to affirm that the victim mattered and that the act was not acceptable. For that purpose what matters is not whether the offender has changed but whether he is the one responsible, and a change of character, however real, does not transfer responsibility to someone else. Time may therefore weaken some reasons for punishment while leaving others intact.

Many people believe there is a moral difference between telling a lie and saying something true that is designed to mislead. Asked whether he has been drinking, the driver who answers 'I had a glass of water an hour ago' has not lied, though he hopes the listener will draw a false conclusion. One defence of the distinction is that the misleader leaves the listener a share of the responsibility, since the false belief comes from the listener's own inference. But the listener drew that inference precisely because the speaker counted on it. Whatever difference remains seems to lie less in the harm done to the listener than in what the speaker permits himself: a rule against outright falsehood that he keeps even while evading its purpose.

Arranging choices so that people are steered towards better outcomes, by setting a sensible default for pension saving or putting fruit at eye level in a canteen, is often defended on the ground that no option is forbidden and anyone can choose otherwise. A specialist asked to introduce a field to newcomers frequently leaves them more confused than before, and ill will rarely has anything to do with it. Understanding, once gained, erases the memory of what it was like to lack it. So the specialist jumps over steps that now feel self-evident, reaches for terms that have become automatic and misjudges how much time a novice needs to keep up. The mastery that earns someone the right to teach thus hides from that person the view of the subject a newcomer has. The best teachers get round this not by knowing less but by repeatedly testing what their audience has in fact understood.

In a familiar kind of experiment, people given a simple object such as a mug ask for considerably more to part with it than others, not given one, will pay to acquire it. The gap has been taken as evidence that owning a thing makes us value it more, simply because it is ours. The finding has proved robust in many settings, but its size depends on circumstances. It tends to shrink among experienced traders, who regard goods as stock to be sold, and it is larger for items people expect to keep and use than for those they hold only for exchange. People tend to overestimate how many others share their opinions, habits and preferences. Part of the reason is that we spend most of our time with people like ourselves, so the sample of views we meet is not representative of the wider population. Ask people how well they understand how a zip, a flush toilet or a bicycle works, and most will rate their understanding highly. Ask them then to explain, step by step, how the device actually works, and many find they cannot; when asked to rate their understanding again, they mark it down. For years it was widely accepted that self-control draws on a limited resource, so that resisting one temptation leaves a person less able to resist the next. The idea was supported by many small experiments and fitted the everyday experience of feeling worn out after a demanding day. When the effect was retested in large studies run to a common plan across many laboratories, it proved much smaller than the earlier work had suggested, and in some cases indistinguishable from zero. It would be too quick to conclude that people never tire of exercising self-control. What the episode shows is that a stack of small studies, each published because it found an effect, can make a weak or absent phenomenon look established, and that agreement with everyday experience is no substitute for a test designed in advance.

Languages that oblige speakers to choose between a familiar and a respectful form of 'you' are sometimes thought more hierarchical than those, like modern English, that use a single form for everyone. The comparison is misleading. Speakers of English mark distance and rank in other ways: through first names or titles, through how directly they make requests, through who may start a conversation and who may end it. If anything, the explicit pronoun makes the rules of respect easier to see and therefore easier to learn.

Gossip has a poor reputation: it is condemned as idle, malicious and a waste of time. A more sympathetic view, now common among those who study small communities, holds that gossip performs a social function, spreading knowledge of who can be trusted and deterring cheats who fear for their reputations. This view is a useful corrective, but it can slide into a defence of gossip as such. The same mechanism that deters the cheat also punishes the nonconformist, the newcomer and anyone whose private life departs from local expectation, and it does so without a hearing. To say that gossip enforces norms is to say nothing yet about whether the norms deserve enforcing, or whether those it targets had any chance to answer.

Critics of everyday courtesy often complain that phrases such as 'how are you' or 'thank you so much' are empty, since the speaker rarely wants a medical report and is seldom overwhelmed with gratitude. The complaint assumes that words are sincere only when they report an inner state. But many polite formulas are not reports at all; they are moves in a shared routine, closer to a handshake than to a confession. Their meaning lies in being offered and returned, and their omission is noticed precisely because nobody expects them to carry personal feeling. To call them insincere is therefore to judge them by a standard they never claimed to meet. This does not mean that every courteous word is innocent: a formula can be used to hold someone at a distance or to cover contempt. Yet that misuse is possible only because the routine itself has a recognised social meaning.

It is tempting to think of the rules of a game as fences around an activity that exists without them, but moving a bishop diagonally is not a restriction on some freer way of moving a carved piece; outside the rules there is no bishop to move. Rules in this sense constitute a game rather than regulate it. From this some infer that whatever the rules permit is fair, and that a player who finds a loophole has simply played well. The inference is too quick. Rules are written to make a particular contest possible, and a move that satisfies their letter while dissolving that contest, such as a team deliberately losing to secure an easier opponent later, keeps the form of the game while emptying it. Still, the spirit of a game is no free-floating ideal that referees may invoke at will; it can only be read from the contest the rules were built to create, which is why the usual remedy for such an exploit is a better-drafted rule rather than an appeal to conscience.

Travellers who move between cultures with different attitudes to time often conclude that one kind of society is disciplined and the other careless. The comparison misleads. Where meetings start exactly on the hour, time is treated as a resource divided among commitments, and lateness signals that one has taken someone else's share. Where arrival times are loose, the priority is usually the relationship in hand: leaving a conversation abruptly to keep the next appointment would be the real discourtesy. Neither is without costs, since clock-bound societies can turn every encounter into a transaction while relationship-bound ones can leave outsiders and the less well connected waiting indefinitely. What looks like the presence or absence of discipline is a difference in what discipline is for.

Decimal systems of measurement are often presented as a triumph of reason over custom: once a simple, coherent set of units was available, the argument runs, the tangle of local measures was bound to give way. The history is less tidy. Traditional units were not merely clumsy; many were tied to things people actually did, a day's ploughing or a load a person could carry, and they let communities check trade by familiar standards. Where the new units spread, they often succeeded less through their logic than through the backing of states that needed uniform measures for taxation, armies and national markets, and they met long resistance where that backing was weak. None of this makes the decimal system less convenient; it suggests that its convenience was not, by itself, what made it prevail.

They were less a test of administrative skill, which could be learned in office, than a means of producing officials who shared a common learning and owed their position to the state rather than to birth, a valuable asset for rulers wary of entrenched aristocracies. To recognise this function, however, is not to accept the systems as meritocracies in a modern sense. Years of unpaid preparation lay beyond most families, so the examinations widened access to office without opening it to all, and the 'merit' they measured was the merit they themselves defined.

Before the telegraph, an ambassador posted far from home often waited weeks for instructions, and in the meantime had to decide for himself how to answer a foreign court. Of the writing produced in the ancient world, only a fraction survives, and it is natural to suppose that what remains is the best of it, the works later readers judged worth preserving. There is some truth in this: texts that nobody valued were seldom recopied, and a text not recopied every few generations was likely to perish with its material. But value to later copyists is not the same as quality. Works survived when they suited the needs of schools and religious communities, when they were short enough to copy cheaply, or when they had been gathered into anthologies that travelled together; a brilliant treatise in an unfashionable field could vanish while a mediocre school text was copied hundreds of times. The surviving corpus is a record of what later centuries used, and our sense of what the ancients thought best is partly an inheritance of those uses.

Selling more seats than a flight holds looks, at first, like a plain breach of faith, since some passengers who paid will be turned away. Yet the practice rests on a reasonable prediction: on most routes a fairly steady share of ticket holders does not turn up, and a carrier that held every seat for them would fly emptier planes and, in the long run, charge everyone more. The real question is not whether to overbook but how to treat those who are bumped. A system that asks for volunteers and pays them enough to give up their seats turns an occasional surplus of passengers into a voluntary exchange; one that removes people at random, with little compensation, makes them bear a cost that the whole system creates.

Textbooks have long used the lighthouse as the model of a good that markets cannot supply: once the light shines, every passing ship benefits, and no owner can make a captain pay for a beam he cannot be stopped from seeing. The example is weaker than it looks. Ships do not merely pass lights; they enter ports, and a charge levied on vessels docking nearby can fund a light without anyone being excluded from its beam. Yet the rescue of the market is also partial. Such a charge works only because some authority, a port or a government that grants the right to collect it, can compel payment at the quay, so the arrangement shows less that private provision succeeds without the state than that the line between private and public provision is drawn in the details of who may collect what.

The idea of a keystone species, one whose removal brings an ecosystem's arch tumbling down, has been enormously useful in persuading people that a single unremarkable creature can matter far beyond its numbers. But the image smuggles in assumptions. An arch has one keystone, fixed by its geometry; in living systems the importance of a species often depends on circumstances, so that a predator that holds a community together in one bay may be of little consequence in the next, or may matter only in dry years. Treating keystone status as a permanent property of a species can lead conservation to concentrate on a few celebrated animals while overlooking the conditions that made them important. The metaphor is worth keeping, as long as it is read as describing a role that a species plays in a place, not an identity it carries everywhere.

When mountain glaciers shrink, the rivers they feed do not at first run dry; they often swell. Melting ice releases water that has been stored for centuries, so communities downstream may enjoy unusually generous summer flows just as the glaciers are disappearing. The abundance is borrowed. Planners in dry regions have often judged land by its average rainfall, asking whether a district receives enough water in a typical year to support crops or herds. The question sounds sensible but can mislead badly. In arid places the average is a statistical fiction that few actual years resemble: runs of meagre seasons are broken by an occasional deluge, and the mean sits between them, describing no year that anyone lives through. Herders who move their animals in search of rain and keep flexible claims to distant pasture are responding to this variability, not ignoring good practice, while schemes that settle them on plots sized for an average year can fail in the first drought. Averages are not useless, since over long periods they still say something about a region's water; but where variation is the dominant fact, a plan built on the mean is a plan for a climate that does not exist.

When an inferior technical standard becomes universal, it is common to blame the stubbornness of users who will not switch to something better. The explanation misplaces the problem. A standard is valuable largely because others use it: a plug fits more sockets, a file format opens on more machines, a keyboard layout matches the one in the office. A user who switches alone bears the costs of incompatibility while gaining little, so each person's reluctance is reasonable even if everyone would be better off moving together. This does not mean that a dominant standard is always inferior, a claim that is often made and harder to prove; it means only that its dominance is no evidence of its merit.

Early machine translation was easy to distrust: its sentences were stiff and ungrammatical, and readers could see at once where it had gone wrong. Newer systems produce smooth, natural prose, and this real improvement brings a new and less obvious difficulty. When a translation reads fluently, readers tend to assume it is accurate, yet a fluent sentence can still drop a negation, confuse two names or soften a warning. The very polish that makes the output pleasant to read also hides its mistakes, so errors that once announced themselves now pass unnoticed.

The complaint has force, but it assumes that a photograph's value lies in being kept and contemplated. Many of today's pictures do a different job. When factories first replaced steam engines with electric motors, the gains in productivity were for a long time disappointing, and some observers concluded that the new power source had been oversold. The disappointment had a simpler cause. Early adopters typically installed one large motor in place of the old engine and kept the rest of the plant unchanged: the same system of shafts and belts, the same buildings arranged around a central drive. Electricity's real advantage, that small motors could be placed wherever work was done, could be exploited only when factories were redesigned around it, and that required new buildings, new layouts and managers who had learned to think in a new way. The lesson is not that every new technology will eventually pay off once organisations catch up, but that its early returns are a poor guide to what it can do when they do.

Each generation seems to need its own translations of the great works, and this is sometimes taken as proof that earlier translators failed. Yet a translation ages in a way the original does not. The original belongs to its language at a fixed moment and is read with the allowances we make for the past; a translation is written in the reader's language and is judged as contemporary prose, so its period idioms, once invisible, eventually begin to sound quaint or stiff. A new version therefore need not correct its predecessor. It may simply restore the effect of a text that, in its own time, did not sound old. That is not to say that every retranslation is an improvement; some merely trade one set of mannerisms for another.

The classic detective story asks the reader to accept an unusual bargain: every clue the detective uses must be shown on the page before the solution, so that a sufficiently attentive reader could, in principle, reach it first. The convention turns the novel into a contest between writer and reader, and much of the genre's pleasure comes from losing that contest fairly. But fairness has a price. A writer who must lay out every clue while still surprising the reader is tempted to reduce people to suspects and conversations to evidence, and many such books are remembered for their solutions rather than their characters. The finest examples avoid this by hiding clues inside character itself, so that understanding a person and solving the crime become the same act.

'A child could have painted that' is the oldest complaint against abstract art, and defenders usually reply that the painter could also draw a perfect likeness and chose not to. The reply concedes too much. It accepts the critic's assumption that a picture is valuable in proportion to the difficulty of making it, and merely insists that the difficulty lies elsewhere, in the years of training behind the apparent simplicity. But much of what matters in such work is not difficulty at all; it is the decision about what to leave out, the sense of when a canvas is finished, the placing of a single shape so that it holds a whole surface. A child might produce something similar by accident, as a monkey at a keyboard might type a line of verse, without the result being the same kind of achievement. The complaint is answered not by proving the painter skilful but by showing that skill was never the right measure.

Performing old music on the instruments of its own time has revealed a good deal. Gut strings, valveless horns and lighter keyboards produce textures that modern instruments smooth over, and many listeners have found that familiar works sound clearer and livelier when played this way. Yet the movement's claim to 'authenticity' needs care. We can rebuild the instruments, but not the ears of the original audiences, for whom these sounds were ordinary rather than novel, and much about how the music was actually played is not recorded anywhere. Period performance gives us a valuable new way to hear old music, not the old way restored.

Publishers often keep the translator's name off the cover of a translated novel, on the theory that readers want to feel they are meeting the author directly and that a second name reminds them of an intermediary. The reasoning is understandable, but it rests on a fiction. Every sentence the reader of a translation encounters was chosen by the translator: the rhythm, the register, the jokes that land or fall flat. To hide that person is not to remove the intermediary but to conceal one who is doing a great deal of the work, and the concealment has costs. Readers who do not know a book is translated cannot judge whether an awkward phrase belongs to the author or to the rendering, and translators whose names are buried find it harder to build the reputations that would let them command better fees and better projects. Naming the translator does not spoil the illusion of direct contact so much as make the reader's trust an informed one.

Abridged editions of classic novels are often defended as a gentle doorway: a twelve-year-old who would abandon an eight-hundred-page original might finish a hundred-page version and come back for the real thing later. The trouble is that what abridgement removes is rarely random. Editors cut digressions, descriptions and the slow passages in which characters think, because these are what make a book long, but they are also what make it the particular book it is. What survives is the plot, and plot is the part of a classic that a film or a summary could deliver just as well. A young reader who finishes such a version may therefore conclude that they have read the book, and that it was merely a story, and see no reason to return. The doorway can easily become a wall.

Recorded laughter on television comedies is often mocked as a crude instruction to the audience, a machine telling viewers when something is funny. Yet its persistence for decades suggests it answers a real need. Laughter is overwhelmingly a social behaviour: people laugh far more readily in company than alone, and they often laugh less at a joke than at the shared recognition that a joke has been made. A viewer watching a comedy alone at home is deprived of that company, and the track supplies a substitute, a sense of sitting among others who are enjoying the same thing. This explains why the track feels most intrusive to viewers who are themselves watching in a group, since they already have the company it imitates.

Critics of sampling in popular music often argue that a producer who builds a track from fragments of other people's recordings is not composing at all but merely assembling, and that the result borrows its value from the originals. The argument assumes that originality lies in producing sounds no one has produced before. On that test, however, very little music of any period would pass: composers have always worked with inherited scales, forms, rhythms and even melodies, and much admired music is openly built on borrowed tunes. What distinguishes a composer is not the novelty of the materials but what is done with them, the choices of selection, placement and transformation that make a familiar element mean something new. This does not settle whether any particular sampled track is good, or whether the original performers deserve payment; those are separate questions. It shows only that sampling cannot be dismissed as uncreative merely because its raw materials already exist.

Style manuals routinely tell writers to avoid the passive voice, and the advice has hardened into a rule that many writers apply without thinking. The case against the passive is real but narrow. A passive sentence can hide the agent ('mistakes were made'), and a long run of passives can make prose feel inert. But the passive also does work that nothing else does as neatly. It lets a writer keep the topic of a paragraph in the subject position, so that a passage about a disease can go on talking about the disease ('it is spread by mosquitoes') rather than lurching to whatever happens to cause it. It lets scientists foreground a procedure rather than the person who carried it out, when the person is irrelevant. The useful question is never whether a sentence is passive but whether the reader needs to know who acted, and what the sentence should be about.

A news photograph is often treated as the most neutral element of a report: the words may spin, but the camera simply records. Yet every published photograph has been cropped, and cropping is a choice about what the event was. A picture of a single protester shouting at a line of police tells one story; the same frame widened to show a quiet crowd of hundreds behind him tells another, and the wider frame may show that the shouting man was alone. Nothing in either version is false, and no pixel has been altered. The distortion, if there is one, lies entirely in the boundary. That is why a reader who wants to judge a photograph should ask not only what it shows but what its edges leave out.

Whether listening to an audiobook counts as reading is usually argued as a question of status, with defenders insisting that the story reaches the mind either way and sceptics treating listening as a lesser substitute. Both sides tend to miss what actually differs. For narrative of moderate difficulty, a competent listener appears to follow and remember the story about as well as a reader does, so the sceptic's claim that listening is shallower is hard to sustain as a general rule. The difference lies in control. A reader sets the pace, slows down at a difficult sentence, glances back to check who said what, and lets the eye run ahead; a listener receives the text at the narrator's speed and must make an effort to go back. For a thriller this hardly matters. For a dense argument, where comprehension depends on rereading, it may matter a great deal. The useful question is therefore not whether listening is reading, but what kind of text is being taken in.

Teachers and parents have long worried that the abbreviations of text messaging, the dropped vowels and phonetic shortcuts, would corrode children's spelling. Suppose a school compares its pupils and finds that the heaviest users of such abbreviations are, if anything, slightly better spellers than the rest. It would be tempting to conclude that texting improves spelling, but the finding cannot carry that weight. To abbreviate a word playfully a child must usually know how it is spelled in full, so skill with abbreviations may simply be a sign of a comfort with language that the better spellers already had. What the finding does undermine is the fear itself: if abbreviating were steadily eroding spelling, the heaviest abbreviators should be doing worse, not better. A correlation that cannot prove benefit can still be evidence against harm.

Textbook writers often add vivid asides to dry material: an anecdote about a scientist's eccentricities in a chapter on electricity, a dramatic photograph of lightning beside a diagram of charge. The intention is to hold interest, and readers do report finding such pages more enjoyable. Yet experiments on learning from text have repeatedly suggested that interesting but irrelevant details can reduce how much of the central explanation students remember and can apply, apparently by drawing attention and memory towards themselves. This does not mean that interest is the enemy of learning. Details that are vivid and also carry the core idea, such as an example that shows the principle at work, do not seem to carry the same cost. The lesson is that engagement should be built from the material that is to be learned, not borrowed from material beside it.

Open-book examinations are sometimes dismissed as easy, on the assumption that a student who may consult notes need not have learned anything. Anyone who has sat one knows otherwise. Because the facts are available, the examiner cannot reward their mere recall and must instead ask questions that require using them: applying a principle to an unfamiliar case, weighing two sources, building an argument under time pressure. A student who has not understood the material gains little from the book on the desk, since there is no time to learn a subject in the middle of the paper; such students tend to spend the hour leafing anxiously through pages. Open-book examinations do not lower the bar; they move it from remembering to thinking.

Debates over whether schools should still teach joined-up handwriting are usually framed as a contest between tradition and efficiency: cursive is a heritage skill, keyboards are what adults actually use. The framing obscures the fact that the two sides are often talking about different things. The case for teaching some handwriting is fairly strong, since forming letters by hand appears to help young children learn to recognise them, and much early schoolwork is still done with a pencil. But that case is about handwriting in general, not about the particular joined style, and an argument for one is easily mistaken for an argument for the other. The case for cursive specifically rests on weaker grounds: claims that it is faster, or that it builds discipline, are rarely as well supported as their advocates assume. University league tables are defended as a service to applicants, who would otherwise have to choose among institutions they know little about. The defence has some force, but it overlooks what a single ranked list does. Each table combines many measures, such as research output, staff numbers per student and graduate salaries, into one score, and the weights given to each are a choice made by the compiler, not a fact about universities. Different weights would produce a different order. An applicant who wants small classes and an applicant who wants a strong research culture are served by different universities, yet both are handed the same list as if it settled which is best. A table that published its components and let readers set the weights would serve applicants better than one that pretends a single verdict exists.

For a long time, people who hurt their backs were told to lie down and stay down until the pain passed. Current guidance for ordinary, short-lived low back pain has largely reversed this advice: staying as active as the pain allows tends to bring a quicker recovery than prolonged rest, which can stiffen muscles and make a return to normal life harder. This does not mean that a patient should ignore pain or push through heavy work, and a day or two of reduced activity in the worst phase may be sensible. Nor does the advice apply to back pain caused by serious injury or disease, which needs proper assessment. The change is narrower than a slogan like 'keep moving' suggests, but within its range it is clear.

Many health systems now let patients see their test results online as soon as they are ready, often before a doctor has looked at them. Supporters see this as an overdue recognition that the information belongs to the patient; critics point out that a patient may meet an alarming number, or a technical phrase like 'cannot exclude malignancy', alone at midnight with no one to explain it. Both are right about something. Early access removes delays and the paternalism of having a doctor decide what a patient may know, and many patients prefer it even when the news is bad. But a result is not the same as its meaning, and a raw value read without context can frighten patients needlessly or reassure them falsely. The choice is less between access and protection than about whether interpretation arrives with the data or only later.

Hospital wards are full of monitors that sound an alarm whenever a patient's heart rate, oxygen level or blood pressure crosses a threshold. Each alarm is set cautiously, on the reasonable principle that a missed emergency is worse than a false alert. Yet the sum of these cautious settings can make patients less safe. When most alarms turn out to be harmless, triggered by a patient shifting in bed or a sensor slipping, staff learn, quite rationally, to treat them as background noise, to respond slowly or to silence them. The rare alarm that signals a real crisis then arrives in an environment trained to ignore it. The problem is not careless staff but a system in which each device is designed in isolation, as though it were the only voice in the room.

Because a rare disease affects few people, a drug that treats it promises a small market, and companies left to market incentives alone have little reason to develop one. Governments in many countries have therefore offered inducements, such as extended periods of exclusive sale, to make such drugs worth developing. The policy has produced treatments for conditions that once had none, and that achievement is real. But an incentive defined by the number of patients can be met in ways its designers did not intend. A common disease can sometimes be divided into narrowly defined subtypes, each rare enough to qualify, and a drug that later proves useful for many conditions may keep the protections it earned for one. The result can be high prices on drugs whose markets are not small at all. The remedy is not to abandon the incentives but to tie them more closely to the problem they were meant to solve.

Many cities require every new building to provide a minimum number of parking spaces, a rule meant to stop drivers from overwhelming the surrounding streets. The intention is sensible, but the rule carries costs that are easy to overlook because they are hidden in other prices. Parking takes land and money, so the requirement raises the cost of every flat and shop that is built, whether or not its occupants own a car; residents who do not drive in effect subsidise those who do. And by guaranteeing that driving will always be convenient, the rule encourages more of it, partly creating the demand it was meant to accommodate. None of this means a city should have no parking. It means that the amount should be decided by those who build and use it, rather than fixed by a rule that assumes everyone will drive.

When a declining industrial city commissions a spectacular museum from a famous architect, the hope is that the building will draw visitors, investment and a new image, as a few celebrated examples seem to show. The trouble is that the examples are remembered precisely because they are exceptional. For every city whose flagship became a destination, others built expensive buildings that drew crowds for a season and then struggled to fill their galleries or pay their running costs. The successes, moreover, rarely depended on the building alone: they tended to come where the city was already investing in transport, housing and its existing cultural life, so that the museum crowned a wider change rather than causing it. A spectacular building is not useless. But treated as a shortcut to regeneration rather than as one part of it, it is more likely to become a monument to the hope than an instrument of its fulfilment.

But much of what people value in such places was never a matter of facades alone.
