Pedestrian footbridges over busy roads are built to keep walkers safe, yet many stand almost unused while people dodge traffic at street level beneath them. This is less a sign of recklessness than of a design that ignores how walking works. A footbridge typically asks a pedestrian to climb a long flight of stairs or a ramp, cross, and descend again, adding minutes and considerable effort to a crossing that would take seconds at street level. For the elderly, people with heavy bags and parents with prams, the climb can be a real obstacle. Pedestrians weigh effort against risk, as drivers do, and when the safe route is much harder than the dangerous one, many will take the risk.

Impartial moral theories hold that everyone's interests count equally, and they seem to imply that I should be no more concerned with my friend's welfare than with a stranger's. Critics reply that a person who really thought this way would be incapable of friendship, since to be someone's friend just is to give their good special weight. The critics are right that friendship involves partiality, but the impartialist need not concede that partiality is therefore unjustified. One can argue impartially that a world in which people form close attachments and favour those they love is better for everyone than a world of detached benefactors, and so endorse partiality at the level of the practice while denying that each act of favouritism must be weighed against strangers' claims. The cost of this reply is that the friend's special claim is defended, in the end, by appeal to the general good, which some will feel misdescribes why we help our friends.

It is often said that a gift made anonymously is morally superior to one made publicly, since the anonymous donor cannot be seeking praise and so must be acting from pure generosity. The reasoning confuses evidence with value. Anonymity can be good evidence that a donor is not after recognition, but a public donor is not thereby shown to be after it, and even a donor who enjoys the praise may give for reasons that are mostly good. More importantly, the recipients are fed and housed just the same either way, and a well-publicised gift may persuade others to give, multiplying its effect. There may be cases where anonymity matters, as when publicity would humiliate the person helped. But as a general ranking, the preference for anonymous giving judges a gift by what it reveals about the giver rather than by what it does.

Moral rules such as 'do not lie' or 'keep your promises' are often attacked by pointing to exceptions: surely one may lie to save a life, or break a trivial promise to help someone in danger. If a rule has exceptions, the argument runs, it was never really a rule, and we should simply weigh consequences case by case. But the existence of exceptions shows less than this suggests. A rule can be a strong presumption, one that sets the burden of argument and holds unless something weighty overrides it, and such presumptions are valuable precisely because case-by-case weighing is slow, prone to self-serving bias and impossible for others to rely on. Someone who keeps promises only when calculation favours it is not a person others can plan around. The exceptions show that rules are not absolute; they do not show that rules are dispensable.

Consent is usually treated as transforming what would otherwise be wrong into something permissible: the surgeon's knife, the borrowed car, the signed contract. But the transforming power of consent depends on the conditions under which it is given. A worker who accepts dangerous conditions because the alternative is destitution has agreed, in a sense, and it would be odd to say his signature means nothing. Yet when one party can set the terms and the other can only take them or starve, the agreement shows mainly that the worker preferred this bargain to disaster, not that the terms were fair. To treat such consent as settling the matter is to let the stronger party borrow the moral authority of a free choice that was barely available. Consent remains important; it simply cannot do all the justifying work on its own.

Professionals such as doctors and counsellors are bound to keep what their clients tell them confidential, and the duty is sometimes criticised as protecting secrets at others' expense. The criticism misunderstands its purpose. People disclose embarrassing symptoms, private fears and past mistakes only when they trust that the information will go no further, and without such disclosure the professional cannot help them, or help protect others from them. This is also why the duty is not absolute: where keeping a secret would expose someone to serious and imminent harm, the reason for the duty, which was to make help possible, no longer supports silence.

A popular answer to the question of what makes someone the same person over time is memory: I am the person who did the things I can remember doing. The view has real appeal, since it explains why amnesia seems to threaten the self in a way that losing a limb does not. But it struggles with ordinary forgetting. I remember nothing of being two years old, yet I do not think the toddler in the old photographs was someone else. Defenders reply that a chain of overlapping memories, each linking to the one before, is enough. That repair helps, but it quietly concedes the original point: it is not remembering that makes me the same person, but something continuous of which remembering is only one part.

It is often said that there is no disputing about taste, and in one sense this is right: no argument will make someone enjoy a dish they find bitter. Yet people argue about taste constantly, and not pointlessly. When a friend explains what to listen for in a piece of music, or why a film's slow opening earns its later payoff, she is not trying to overrule my pleasure by decree. She is directing my attention to features I may have missed, so that my next response is better informed. Such arguments cannot compel agreement, but they can change what there is to respond to. Taste is not beyond reason; it is simply reached by reasons of a different kind, ones that work by showing rather than by proving.

Critics of paternalism usually frame the issue as a contest between welfare and freedom: the state may make you better off, but only by overriding your choices. This framing concedes too much to the paternalist and too little to the person. It assumes that we already know what is good for someone independently of what they would choose, so that the only question is whether to impose it. In many cases we do not. Whether a risky career, a strict diet or a dangerous hobby serves a person's welfare depends partly on the plans and commitments that give their life its shape, and these are often visible only in their choices. Respecting someone's decisions is therefore not merely a price paid for liberty; it is frequently our best evidence of what their welfare actually is.

Moral relativism is often defended as the natural ally of tolerance: if no culture's values are truer than another's, no one has grounds to impose their own. The alliance is less secure than it looks. If all values are merely local, then tolerance itself is just one local value among others, with no more claim on a culture that rejects it than the custom of eating with chopsticks has on a culture that uses forks. The relativist who tells an intolerant society that it ought to be tolerant is appealing to exactly the kind of cross-cultural standard that relativism denies. Tolerance, it seems, needs at least one value that holds everywhere; it cannot rest on the claim that none does.

Experienced firefighters, chess players and nurses often make good decisions in seconds without being able to say why. It is tempting to conclude that intuition is a general gift that grows with years in any job. But intuition is learned pattern recognition, and it can only be learned where there are patterns to recognise and where mistakes are quickly revealed. A chess position either loses or it does not, and the player soon finds out. A long-range political forecaster or a stock picker works in a world that is noisy and slow to give feedback, and years of experience there can produce confidence without producing skill.

When someone collapses on a crowded street, each passer-by is less likely to help than a person who comes upon the same victim alone. This is often read as evidence that crowds make people callous, but the mechanism looks less like indifference than like confusion. In a crowd, everyone checks everyone else's face for cues, and since each person is trying to look calm, the crowd as a whole seems to signal that nothing is wrong. Responsibility is also spread thinly: if many people could act, no one feels that the duty is specifically theirs. Where a single onlooker is singled out, say by being pointed at and asked to call for help, the effect largely disappears.

Children who can wait for a larger treat rather than take a smaller one at once have long been held up as models of self-control, and their patience has been linked to later success. Yet waiting is rational only if the promised reward is likely to arrive. A child whose adults have reliably kept their word has good reason to wait; a child whose promises have often been broken has equally good reason to take what is on the table. In versions of the test where an adult first breaks a small promise to the child, waiting times tend to fall. None of this shows that self-control is unimportant. It does suggest that a measure taken to reveal a trait of character may also be recording what the child has learned about the world.

A popular idea holds that willpower is like a fuel tank: every decision drains it, so that by evening we are too depleted to resist temptation. The image is vivid, but the evidence for a simple reservoir has proved weaker than its fame suggests, and attempts to repeat some of the best-known experiments have produced smaller effects or none. Some studies suggest instead that expectations matter. People who believe that effort exhausts them tend to flag after demanding tasks, while those who see effort as energising flag less. Tiredness after a long day is real, but how much it governs our choices may depend partly on the story we tell ourselves about it.

Small talk is usually dismissed as the emptiest form of conversation: remarks about the weather or the traffic that convey nothing anyone did not already know. But to judge it by its information content is to mistake its purpose. When strangers exchange a few safe sentences, they are testing whether the other is friendly, cooperative and willing to follow shared rules, at almost no risk to either. The very predictability of the topics is what makes this possible, since a remark nobody could disagree with leaves room only for tone. Small talk is not a failed attempt at real conversation; it is often the means by which strangers decide whether to attempt one.

Many people feel they know a television presenter or a radio host whom they have never met. Psychologists call these one-sided bonds parasocial relationships, and they were once treated as a sign of loneliness or confusion. Later research has painted a less alarming picture. Proposals to let workers choose their own days off, instead of observing fixed public holidays, sound like pure gains in freedom: each person rests when it suits them, and shops and offices need never close. What the proposal overlooks is that the value of a day off depends partly on who else has it. A free Tuesday spent alone while friends and family are at work is a different good from a holiday on which everyone is free together. Fixed holidays solve a coordination problem that individual choice cannot, by guaranteeing that leisure overlaps. Flexibility has real merits for people whose lives do not fit the common calendar, but it should be weighed against what is lost when shared time disappears.

An old wristwatch that no longer keeps time can be worth almost nothing on the market and still be the last thing a family would sell. Its value lies not in the object's properties, which a replica could match exactly, but in its history: it was on a grandfather's wrist, it was handed over at a particular moment. The same feature, however, makes them a burden when the history they carry is one the inheritors would rather forget.

Federal systems are often praised as laboratories: because each state or province can try its own policy, the country can watch what works and copy it. The metaphor flatters the arrangement. A laboratory controls its conditions, but states differ in wealth, population and history, so a policy that succeeds in one may fail elsewhere for reasons that have nothing to do with its design. Nor do governments behave like disinterested scientists; a successful reform is as likely to be ignored for partisan reasons as copied for its results. Decentralisation does allow variety, and variety can teach. But the lessons are harder to read, and less often heeded, than the laboratory image implies.

Surveys of land are often presented as neutral exercises in measurement, but when colonial administrations mapped farmland, they were rarely just recording what was there. To tax land, a state needs to know who is responsible for each plot, and so surveyors assigned single owners to fields that had been held under layered arrangements: a cultivator, a family with rights to part of the harvest, a village with rights to graze after the crop was taken in. Insurance protects people from losses they cannot control, but it can also change how carefully they behave. Someone whose bicycle is fully insured may leave it unlocked for a few minutes longer than they otherwise would, not out of dishonesty but because the cost of a theft has shifted to someone else. Insurers know this, and they rarely offer complete cover. Deductibles, which require the policyholder to bear the first part of any loss, and discounts for fitting locks or alarms keep some of the cost with the insured person, so that they keep an interest in avoiding the loss.

options.B: Complete insurance cover is harmful to society and should be prohibited, since people who are fully protected against loss will take no care at all.
options.C: Bicycle owners who have fully insured their bicycles may leave them unlocked a little longer than owners who would have to bear the cost of a theft.
options.D: Insurance shifts the cost of a loss away from the insured and can make them less careful, so insurers leave part of that cost with policyholders.

In a market for used cars, sellers know far more about their vehicles than buyers do. A buyer who cannot tell a sound car from a faulty one will offer only an average price, and that price is too low for owners of good cars, who are therefore more likely to keep them. As they withdraw, the average quality of the cars on offer falls, and buyers who sense this lower their offers further. The market does not need dishonest sellers to unravel in this way; it needs only an imbalance in what each side knows. Warranties, inspection reports and dealers with reputations to protect matter less as courtesies than as ways of restoring trade that would otherwise shrink.

options.B: When buyers cannot judge quality, average offers drive out sellers of good cars and trade can shrink even without dishonesty; warranties and reputations matter because they correct this imbalance.
options.C: Warranties and inspection reports are offered by sellers mainly as courtesies to reassure nervous buyers, though they do little to change the prices that cars fetch.
options.D: Owners of good used cars tend to keep them, because buyers who cannot tell good cars from bad will pay only an average price for any car offered.

It is sometimes argued that a country which can produce everything more efficiently than its neighbours has nothing to gain from trading with them. The intuition is natural and wrong. What matters for trade is not absolute efficiency but relative cost: what a country gives up to make one good instead of another. Even a country that is better at everything will be much better at some things than at others, and it gains by concentrating on those and buying the rest. The argument does not, however, promise that everyone within each country gains; workers in the industries that shrink may lose, and whether they are compensated is a political question that the logic of trade does not settle.

Inflation is usually described as a tax on everyone, eating away at the value of money, but its effects are far from even. A household that borrowed a fixed sum to buy a house repays the loan in money that is worth less each year, so unexpected inflation quietly transfers wealth from the lender to the borrower. Savers holding cash or fixed-interest bonds lose in the same way that borrowers gain. What matters is not just how fast prices rise but whether the rise was foreseen; lenders who expect inflation can demand higher interest in advance, and the transfer then largely disappears.

options.B: Borrowers always gain from rising prices at the expense of lenders, which is why households carrying large mortgages generally welcome any increase in inflation.
options.C: Inflation does not burden everyone equally: unexpected rises move wealth from lenders and savers to borrowers, whereas inflation that was foreseen can be built into interest rates.
options.D: Inflation works as a tax that falls on everyone alike, because it steadily reduces the value of the money held by households, by lenders and by borrowers.

The departure of doctors and engineers from poorer countries is commonly called a brain drain, as if skill were simply poured out of one economy into another. The picture is incomplete. Emigrants often send money home, and the prospect of working abroad can persuade more young people to train in the first place, some of whom never leave. Those who return may bring capital, contacts and experience. None of this means the loss is imaginary: a rural district that loses its only surgeon is worse off however much is sent home. The question is not whether emigration drains or enriches a country, but which effect prevails in a given place and profession.

options.D: Skilled emigration brings gains such as remittances, extra training and returning talent alongside real losses, so whether it harms a country depends on the particular place and profession.

A common picture of science holds that a single failed prediction refutes a theory. In practice, no theory yields a prediction by itself; every test also relies on assumptions about the instruments, the experimental conditions and other theories taken for granted. When the prediction fails, logic tells us only that something in this bundle is wrong, not which part. Scientists who keep a theory after a failed test and blame an auxiliary assumption are therefore not necessarily being dogmatic; sometimes the faulty instrument really is the culprit. What separates a reasonable rescue from an evasive one is whether the blamed assumption can be checked independently, rather than being invoked only to save the theory.

options.B: Since logic cannot say which assumption a failed prediction refutes, no experiment can ever count against a theory, and every rescue of a theory is equally reasonable.
options.C: A theory is refuted as soon as one of its predictions fails, so scientists who keep it after a failed test are refusing to accept the evidence before them.
options.D: When a prediction fails, scientists should suspect their instruments first, since faulty equipment rather than the theory itself is usually to blame for the failure.

Groundwater is easy to overuse partly because its decline is invisible. A shrinking lake or a dry riverbed is a public sight, but a falling water table shows itself only as wells that must be dug deeper and pumps that must work harder, costs that each farmer meets privately. Each user also knows that the water they leave in the ground may simply be pumped by a neighbour. Under these conditions restraint looks like a sacrifice with no reward, and depletion can continue for years before anyone acknowledges that there is a common problem at all.

options.B: Lakes and rivers are more easily overused than groundwater, because the water in them is visible to everyone and therefore seems to be freely available.
options.C: Groundwater is overused because its decline hides in private costs and because water one user saves may be pumped by others, which makes restraint seem pointless.
options.D: As a water table falls, farmers find that their wells must be dug ever deeper and their pumps must work harder to bring the water to the surface.

Students of animal behaviour have long been warned against anthropomorphism, the error of reading human thoughts and feelings into animals. The warning is sound, but it has a mirror image that receives less attention. A researcher who refuses to credit an animal with any mental state resembling ours, even when the evidence points that way, also makes an error, and it is not obviously the safer one. Species that share much of our evolutionary history are likely to share some of our mental equipment too. The proper aim is not to minimise every resemblance to humans but to let the evidence decide, case by case, which resemblances are real.

options.C: Because many species share much of our evolutionary history, researchers should assume that animals think and feel much as humans do unless it is shown otherwise.
options.D: Denying animals any human-like mental states is a more serious error than anthropomorphism, and it ought to be the main concern of researchers today.

Farm soils can store carbon, and practices such as planting cover crops or ploughing less have been shown in many trials to raise the carbon content of the topsoil. This has made soil an attractive climate solution, since farmers can be paid for carbon they lock away. The finding needs careful handling. Gains are often measured only in the upper layers, and some of the apparent increase may be carbon moved from deeper soil rather than newly captured. Soils also reach a new balance after some years and stop accumulating, and the stored carbon can return to the air if the practices are abandoned. Soil carbon is real, but slower, smaller and less secure than a simple accounting suggests.

When an old dam is taken down, people often expect the river to return at once to the condition it was in before the dam was built. What usually happens is messier. Sediment that piled up behind the wall for decades is released and travels downstream, burying gravel beds and clouding the water for a season or more. Fish that had been blocked may take years to recolonise the upstream reaches, and the plants that first cover the drained reservoir bed are often weeds rather than the species that grew there before. None of this means that removal fails; on many rivers the long-term gains in fish passage and natural flow are substantial. It means that removal starts a process of recovery rather than restoring a finished state, and that the early years can look worse than what came before.

options.B: Sediment released when a dam is removed travels downstream and buries gravel beds, which clouds the water and harms the river for at least a season afterwards.
options.C: Old dams ought to be removed slowly and in stages, so that sediment and weeds do not overwhelm the river and fish can return upstream more quickly.
options.D: Because the first years after removal often look worse than before, taking down old dams usually does more harm to a river and its fish than simply leaving the old walls standing.

Seismologists distinguish between predicting an earthquake and forecasting one, and public discussion often blurs the two. A prediction would name a place, a window of days or weeks and a magnitude, precisely enough to justify evacuating a city. No method has reliably done this, and claims to the contrary have tended to collapse under scrutiny. A forecast is more modest: it estimates the probability of a strong quake in a region over years or decades, using the record of past ruptures and the strain measured on faults. A forecast cannot tell anyone to leave on Tuesday, but it can tell a city how strict its building codes should be and where a hospital ought not to be built. Judged as failed predictions, forecasts look useless; judged as what they are, they are among the most practically valuable things the science produces.

options.C: Better measurement of the strain on faults will soon let seismologists turn their long-range forecasts into precise predictions that justify evacuating whole cities.
options.D: Since seismologists cannot say when an earthquake will strike, their probability estimates are of little practical use and should not be allowed to guide how cities are planned or where they build.

Zoos often justify themselves by pointing to captive breeding: species that have vanished from the wild survive in enclosures and may one day be returned. The argument is not empty; a handful of animals have been reintroduced after being bred in captivity. But the justification works only under conditions that are seldom stated. A captive population must be large and genetically varied enough to avoid inbreeding, the animals must keep the behaviours they need to survive outside, and, most easily forgotten, there must be a wild habitat to return them to. Where the forest has been cleared, or the threat that emptied it persists, breeding preserves a species in something like suspended animation, alive but with nowhere to go. Captive breeding, in other words, is a bridge, and a bridge is valuable only if something is being built on the far side.

Naming a newly described species after a person is an old habit, and some critics now ask whether names honouring patrons, colonial officials or celebrities should be changed. The case for renaming is easy to feel when the honoured figure was cruel. Yet the strongest reason for caution has little to do with the reputations involved. A scientific name is a retrieval key: it links the specimen in a museum drawer to every paper ever written about it. Change the name and that chain is not cut, since the rules keep track of older names, but it is lengthened and made fragile, especially for the many species known only from a single description in an obscure journal. The more promising reform looks forward: choosing descriptive names for new species costs nothing, while renaming old ones carries a real price in scientific record-keeping.

The undo command looks like a minor convenience, but it changes how people use software. When every action can be reversed, users explore: they try an unfamiliar menu, apply a filter just to see what it does, delete a paragraph to judge whether the essay reads better without it. Where actions are permanent, the same users grow cautious, read instructions first and stick to the few operations they already trust. Undo, in other words, lowers the cost of a mistake, and when mistakes are cheap, experimenting becomes rational. Much of what people learn about a program they learn by just such trial and error, so a design that forgives errors also turns out to be one that teaches.

It is common to blame endless feeds on a lack of willpower, as if people who scroll for an hour simply could not stop. This misplaces the problem. Much everyday self-control depends less on resisting temptation moment by moment than on natural stopping points: the end of a chapter, the last page of a newspaper, the credits of an episode. Such boundaries invite a small decision about whether to go on, and many people, offered that decision, stop. A feed that loads new items before the old ones run out removes the boundary and with it the decision. The user never declines to stop; the moment to stop simply never arrives. Designers who wished to respect their users' time would therefore do more by restoring edges than by lecturing anyone about discipline.

options.D: Self-control depends mainly on natural boundaries such as the ends of chapters, which is why people reading printed books rarely lose track of the time.

Firms that replace telephone agents with chatbots often report that customer satisfaction scores barely move, and conclude that customers do not mind. The figure is real, but what it measures deserves a closer look. Satisfaction surveys are usually sent to customers whose conversations ended, and a conversation with a bot ends in two very different ways: the problem is solved, or the customer gives up. Those who give up rarely answer a survey about an exchange they abandoned, and some of them quietly take their business elsewhere. Meanwhile the simple queries that bots handle well, such as tracking a parcel, were never the ones that tested anyone's patience. Steady scores may therefore show only that bots cope with easy cases, while the frustrations of hard cases fall outside what is being counted.

Buyers considering an electric car often worry about range, picturing themselves stranded with a flat battery far from any charger. Yet the typical car spends most days on short trips that use a small fraction of even a modest battery, and owners who charge at home begin each morning with a full one. For many owners the anxiety fades within months, not because the battery has grown but because they have learned how their own driving actually uses it. Range does matter, but less often than the fear of it suggests.

Many nineteenth-century novels first reached readers in instalments, a part at a time over many months, and the form left marks on the books that later readers of the bound volume can miss. Each part needed its own small climax to bring buyers back, so chapters often close on suspense or revelation. Because readers might forget a minor character between instalments, writers gave such figures memorable tags, a phrase or a habit repeated at each appearance. The long gaps also let an author learn how the story was being received, and plots were sometimes adjusted in response. Features that a modern critic might fault as contrived or repetitive were, in their first setting, sensible answers to the conditions of publication.

A familiar complaint about recent fiction is that its villains have become too sympathetic: give every tyrant a sad childhood, the critics say, and evil dissolves into misfortune. The complaint mistakes explanation for excuse. To show how a person came to do terrible things is not to claim that the things were less terrible; it may make them more disturbing, since it removes the comfort of thinking that such acts belong to monsters unlike ourselves. Where the criticism does land is on stories that use the backstory to settle the moral question, inviting the reader to feel that a painful past cancels the harm done. The fault there is not sympathy but a failure of nerve: the writer has explained the villain and then flinched from judging him.

At a symphony concert, a burst of clapping after the opening movement is often answered by hissing from seasoned listeners, who regard unbroken quiet until the final chord as a sacred inheritance. The custom is younger than they suppose. Listeners in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries commonly clapped when a movement ended, and on occasion broke in while the orchestra was still playing. The demand for total quiet hardened only later, once the concert hall began to be approached in a mood of reverence. A case for the pause can still be made: a soft close needs a moment to fade into the room. Yet that case has to stand on its own feet rather than on a claim of antiquity, and it gives no licence for treating first-time listeners with contempt.

Why do ruins draw visitors who would walk past the same building, intact, without a glance? Part of the answer is that a ruin asks the viewer to do some work. The missing roof and broken arches invite the mind to complete them, and an image a person has helped to build feels more vivid than one simply handed over. A ruin also makes time visible: weathered stone and the roots pushing through it show at a glance the centuries that a whole building conceals. This suggests why restorations sometimes disappoint. A restored castle may be more accurate than its broken neighbour, yet it leaves nothing to imagine and hides the very history it was meant to display.

Slang tends to age quickly, and the reason lies in what it is for. A slang word marks its users as insiders: to say it is to show that one belongs to a particular group, often a young one, and knows its current code. That function depends on outsiders not using the word. Once parents, advertisers and newsreaders adopt it, the word stops marking anyone as an insider, and the group that coined it drops it for something fresh. A few slang terms survive this process by losing their flavour entirely and becoming ordinary vocabulary, but most simply fade. The speed of slang's decline is, in this sense, a sign that it worked.

Listeners asked to rate recorded speakers often judge those with certain accents as less competent, even when the words spoken are identical. It is tempting to read this as simple prejudice against particular regions or classes, and partly it is. But some of the effect has a duller source: listeners find an unfamiliar accent harder to process, and the extra effort of understanding is easily misattributed to the speaker, as if a message that was hard to follow had been less clearly thought. This matters because the two explanations call for different remedies. Prejudice must be confronted; mere unfamiliarity tends to shrink with exposure, so that a listener who hears an accent regularly may stop penalising it without ever having examined an attitude.

Defenders of reality television often say that nothing in it is scripted, and in a narrow sense they may be right: the participants choose their own words. But a programme is made in the edit as much as on location. Hundreds of hours of footage are cut to a few, and the choice of which glance to keep, which remark to place after which, and what music to lay underneath can turn an ordinary disagreement into a feud or a tired participant into a villain. No line need be invented for a character to be. The question to ask of such shows is therefore not whether they are scripted but how they are assembled, and that is a question their defenders rarely answer.

Voice notes sit awkwardly between a phone call and a text, and both their appeal and their irritation come from that position. For the sender, a voice note combines the ease of talking with the freedom of a text: there is no need to type, and no need to catch the other person at a convenient moment. For the receiver, the balance often tips the other way. A text can be skimmed in seconds, read during a meeting and searched later for an address; a voice note must be played through at the speaker's pace, in a place where one can listen, and cannot easily be scanned for the one detail that matters. The format, in short, moves effort from the person speaking to the person listening, which explains how the same person can enjoy sending voice notes and dread receiving them.

The quarrel over calculators in primary classrooms is usually staged as a choice between fluency and drudgery: either children grind through long division by hand, or a machine frees them for real mathematics. Both camps miss what hand calculation was quietly teaching. A child who has worked many sums develops a sense of size, so that an answer of four thousand to a problem about the price of a school lunch looks absurd at once. That sense is what catches the mistyped digit, and a calculator, which never doubts itself, cannot supply it. The point is not that the machines should be banned, but that estimation must be taught on purpose once the drills that used to teach it by accident are gone.

Student ratings of teaching are often dismissed as popularity contests, and there is something in the charge: ratings tend to rise when courses are easier and grades kinder, and they can reflect a lecturer's charm as much as what students learn. Yet throwing the ratings out entirely would discard information that no one else possesses. Only students sit through every class; only they know whether the lecturer arrived prepared, returned work on time or answered questions clearly. The sensible course is to ask students about what they observed rather than what they judge. 'Were assignments returned within two weeks?' is a question they can answer reliably; 'Was this a good teacher?' invites them to rate something they are not well placed to assess.

When universities began recording lectures and posting them online, many lecturers feared that their halls would empty, and in some courses attendance did fall. Yet the way students tend to use the recordings is easy to overlook. They seldom sit through a whole lecture a second time; instead they return to the stretch that confused them, pause on a derivation, or replay a definition on the night before an examination. The loss of attendance is real, and a lecture watched alone offers no chance to put up a hand and ask. But the recordings mostly serve as a reference to be consulted rather than a substitute for being there.

It is natural to treat a fever as the illness itself and to bring it down as quickly as possible. Yet fever is in large part a response that the body mounts against infection, and a raised temperature can make conditions harder for some invading organisms while speeding parts of the immune response. This does not mean that fevers should be left alone. Very high temperatures can be dangerous, and in young children, the elderly or people with heart disease the strain of a fever may matter more than any benefit it brings. For most otherwise healthy adults, though, the main reason to take a fever-reducing drug is comfort, and it is worth knowing that one is treating a sign of the fight rather than the enemy.

Asking patients to rate their pain from zero to ten seems a sensible way of bringing a private experience into the clinic, and as a way of following one patient over time it often works: a drop from eight to four after a drug means something. The trouble begins when the numbers are compared across people or treated as targets. One patient's six is another's three, shaped by temperament, culture and past experience of pain, and a ward that aims to bring every score below a set threshold may end up dosing the number rather than the person. The scale is a ruler each patient carries privately; it can measure change in the one who holds it, but it was never calibrated against anyone else's.

Drug trials often measure a surrogate, such as blood pressure or a level in the blood, instead of the outcome patients care about, such as living longer or avoiding a stroke. Clinical guidelines are sometimes resented as cookbook medicine, a set of rules that turns the doctor into a technician. The resentment misunderstands what a good guideline is. It condenses the evidence on how a typical patient with a given condition fares under different treatments, and for that typical patient it will usually beat the unaided judgement of a busy clinician. But no patient is exactly typical. A guideline drawn from trials that excluded the very old, or people with several illnesses at once, says little about the frail patient with four conditions in the consulting room. Following it there is not rigour but a misreading of its scope. The skill that guidelines demand is knowing when a patient falls inside them.

Sentence: To forgive, by contrast, is to accept that the wrong was real and was theirs, and then to give up the resentment one is entitled to feel.

Paragraph: Forgiveness is often confused with excusing, but the two are closer to opposites than to near relations. (1) To excuse someone is to decide that what they did was not really their fault: they were tired, misled or under pressure, and so there is nothing to hold against them. (2) This is why forgiveness can be offered only by someone who has been wronged, and why it can cost her something: the resentment she surrenders was hers by right. An excuse costs nothing of the kind, since it removes the very ground of complaint. (3) It follows that the more readily we excuse, the less there is left for us to forgive. A person who explains away every injury may seem generous, but he has quietly declined to treat others as responsible for what they do. (4)

Sentence: Real projects, by contrast, are seldom spared them: an illness, a late delivery or a resignation befalls almost every one, though no single one could have been foreseen.

Paragraph: People who plan a project routinely underestimate how long it will take, even when they have finished similar projects late many times before. (1) What makes the error puzzling is not its existence but its persistence, since experience ought to correct it. (2) The usual explanation is that planners take an inside view: they picture the particular steps of the task in front of them and add up the time each step seems to need. Such a picture is built out of intentions, and intentions contain no interruptions. (3) The proposed remedy is to take an outside view, setting aside the details of the project and asking how long projects of the same general kind have actually taken. (4) This feels like throwing information away, because it ignores everything the planner knows about her own case. In fact it restores the information that matters most, the record of how such projects usually go wrong, which the inside view had quietly left out.

Sentence: The reason is that a street name is not only an official label but also a piece of shared local knowledge.

Paragraph: When a city renames a street, the new name appears overnight on signs and maps, but it often takes a generation to appear in everyday speech. (1) That knowledge is spread across thousands of small habits: residents give directions by the old name, shopkeepers print it on their cards, and older people use it to locate their memories. (2) An official order can change the label, but it cannot reach what people already know, and so the old name lingers in conversation long after it has vanished from the signs. (3) Newcomers, who never knew the old name, adopt the new one almost at once. For a while the city speaks in two vocabularies, and the change is complete only when those who learned the old name are no longer there to use it. (4)

Sentence: The speed of a message, in other words, mattered less to the history of communication than the question of who was permitted to send one.

Paragraph: Long before electricity carried messages, France in the 1790s began building chains of hilltop towers whose movable arms could be set in many distinct positions, each standing for a letter, word or phrase. An operator watched the neighbouring tower through a telescope, copied its signal and passed it on, so that a message could cross the country far faster than any rider. (1) The system was impressive, but its limits were as instructive as its speed. (2) It worked only in daylight and in clear weather, and every tower needed trained staff who did nothing but watch and repeat. Above all, it was built to serve the state, which saw in rapid communication a means of holding a large territory together. (3) Private citizens were generally not permitted to send messages on it, and the network was never meant to become a public service. (4)

Sentence: A restaurant that raises the price of a single dish must reprint its menus, and a shop must relabel its shelves and explain the change to regular customers.

Paragraph: (1) Economists have long puzzled over why many prices change so rarely, even when the costs behind them move every week. One explanation points to the costs of changing a price itself. (2) Each such cost is small, but if a firm expects the change in its own costs to be temporary, even a small expense can make waiting the sensible choice. (3) The puzzle does not disappear entirely, however, because the sums involved often look far too small to explain the delays observed. A second explanation therefore looks to customers rather than to firms: people may resent frequent price changes and take their business elsewhere. (4) On this account, a stable price is part of what a firm sells.

Sentence: Yet the very openness that lets it live on bare rock leaves it with no defence against whatever else the air contains.

Paragraph: A lichen looks like a single plant, a crust or a leafy fringe on a rock or a branch, but it is in fact a partnership. A fungus provides the structure and holds water, while an alga or a bacterium living inside it makes food from sunlight. (1) Together they can live where neither could survive alone: on bare stone, on desert soil, on the bark of trees in the coldest forests. (2) Because a lichen has no roots and no protective outer skin, it takes in water and nutrients directly from rain and from the air around it. (3) Many species disappear from city centres where sulphur dioxide is common, and some return when the air is cleaned. For this reason, surveys of lichens have long been used as a cheap way of reading the quality of the air in a district. A lichen does not so much measure pollution as record its history, since it grows slowly and responds to years of exposure rather than to a single bad day. (4)

Sentence: Yet if blame should track only what lies within a person's control, this difference is hard to justify, since the child's step was no doing of his.

Paragraph: Two drivers take the same corner too fast on the same wet evening, and both are equally careless. One reaches home without incident; a child steps into the road in front of the other. We blame the second driver far more severely, and so, in all likelihood, does he. (1) One response is to call our reaction an error: the two are equally guilty, and the second is merely unluckier. (2) This keeps the principle of control intact, but at a cost, for it asks us to treat the grief and remorse of the second driver as a kind of confusion. (3) Another response accepts that luck shapes what we are answerable for, and concludes that the principle was never as firm as it seemed. Neither response is comfortable, and the discomfort is itself the discovery: our practice of blame rests on two commitments that do not fit together. (4)

Sentence: The most reliable remedy is to watch beginners attempt the task, since their errors reveal what neither they nor the expert could have put into words.

Paragraph: Experts are often poor at explaining their subject to beginners, and the usual explanation, that they are impatient or careless, misses the deeper difficulty. Once we know something, it becomes very hard to imagine not knowing it. (1) The expert reads a diagram and sees at once what matters; she cannot easily recover the experience of looking at the same lines and seeing nothing in particular. Steps that once cost her effort have become invisible, and so she leaves them out, not from haste but because they no longer seem like steps. (2) The beginner, meanwhile, is unable to say what is missing, since knowing what one does not understand already requires some understanding. (3) The gap therefore persists without either party seeing it clearly. (4)

Sentence: Today, much of that private correspondence has moved to email and messaging services, where it is stored on servers that its writers do not control.

Paragraph: Historians of the last few centuries have relied heavily on private letters. (1) A letter was written for one reader, often in haste, and it preserved opinions and feelings that its writer would never have put into print. (2) Families kept such letters in drawers and attics, and a great many of them eventually found their way into libraries and archives. (3) Messages of this kind are easy to delete, and the accounts that hold them are often closed when their owners die. No one clears out an attic full of messages after a funeral, because there is no attic to clear. (4) Future historians may therefore find that the age which wrote more than any before it has left fewer intimate records behind.

Sentence: Yet the rule could still do some good, because it did not depend on knowing the cause, only on noticing that sickness tended to arrive with people and goods from places already afflicted.

Paragraph: The practice of holding ships and travellers in isolation for a fixed period before they could enter a port took shape in Mediterranean trading cities in the late Middle Ages, in response to repeated outbreaks of plague. (1) Those who devised it had no idea that the disease was carried by microbes; many of them believed it spread through corrupted air. (2) A waiting period long enough for the sick to show their illness could catch infections whatever their mechanism. The episode is sometimes told as a story of luck, as if officials stumbled on a sound practice for the wrong reasons. (3) That reading undervalues what they did, which was to act on a pattern they could observe instead of waiting for a theory they did not have. (4) Public health has often had to work this way, and it still does whenever a new illness spreads faster than its explanation.

Sentence: Yet many employers knowingly pay above that level, and they are not simply being generous.

Paragraph: Standard reasoning suggests that a firm should pay no more than it must, offering the lowest wage at which it can fill its posts. (1) One reason is that a worker who earns more than she could get elsewhere has more to lose if she is dismissed, and so she has reason to work carefully even when no one is watching. (2) A better wage also draws more applicants, letting the firm choose among them, and it reduces the cost of training replacements for those who leave. (3) On this view, a higher wage can pay for itself, since what the firm spends on pay it partly recovers in effort, in selection and in lower turnover. The argument has a limit, however: it works best where effort is hard to monitor and departures are costly, and where output is easily measured, the lowest wage may still be the sensible choice. (4)

Sentence: The protection of a delta, then, may depend less on such walls than on what happens hundreds of kilometres upstream.

Paragraph: A river delta is built from mud and sand that the river carries down from its basin and drops where it meets the sea. As long as this supply continues, the delta can keep pace with the slow sinking of its own soft ground and with the waves that wear its edges away. (1) Large dams interrupt the process at its source. (2) Their reservoirs trap much of the sediment that once travelled downstream, and the water released below them is comparatively clear. Sentence: It does not follow that the criticism is confused, for we can be answerable for things we cannot choose at a stroke.

Paragraph: We often criticise people for what they believe: for trusting a rumour, for clinging to a prejudice, for refusing to accept plain evidence. (1) Such criticism seems to assume that belief is under our control, as an action is. (2) Yet it plainly is not, at least not directly: no one can decide by an effort of will to believe that it is raining while looking at a clear sky. (3) We control what we attend to, which sources we consult, and how long we keep looking before we settle a question. A person who believes a rumour has usually done something earlier: declined to check, preferred a pleasing source, stopped asking once the answer suited him. (4) Criticism of belief is best understood as criticism of these habits of inquiry, which are within our reach even when the belief itself is not. This explains why we excuse a person who was deceived by forged evidence that no reasonable inquiry could have exposed.

Sentence: In the end, it was the timetable, not the sun, that told most people what time it was.

Paragraph: Until the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own time, set by the position of the sun, so that noon in one town fell a few minutes earlier or later than noon in the next. For travellers on foot or on horseback the differences hardly mattered, since no one moved fast enough to notice them. (1) Railways changed this. (2) A timetable that listed departures in a dozen local times was a recipe for missed connections and, on single tracks, for collisions. Railway companies therefore began to run their trains on a single standard time, and the towns along their lines gradually adjusted their clocks to match. (3) Some resisted for a while, fitting the town clock with two minute hands, one for local time and one for the railway's. (4)

Sentence: But this explains only the contributions that some company wants; it does not explain the volunteer who spends her evenings fixing an obscure fault.

Paragraph: Software that anyone may copy, change and share for free poses an obvious puzzle for economics. (1) Thousands of skilled programmers contribute to such projects without being paid by them, and the results compete with products built by firms that charge for theirs. (2) Part of the answer is that many contributors are in fact paid, by employers who depend on the software and find it cheaper to improve a shared tool than to build a private one. (3) For her, the rewards are of a different kind: the pleasure of solving a problem, the respect of peers who can see exactly what she did, and a public record of skill that later employers may value. The last of these rewards is the most economic, and it depends on openness itself, since a contribution hidden inside a firm's private code would be visible to no one outside it. (4) The puzzle is partly dissolved, then, by noticing that open work produces a currency of reputation that closed work cannot.

Sentence: The picture is appealing, and it is not simply invented: substances have been traced moving from one plant to another through fungal threads.

Paragraph: The roots of most land plants are joined to fungi that extend far into the soil, trading water and minerals for sugars that the plant makes in its leaves. (1) Because a single fungus can connect to several plants at once, some writers have described forests as communities in which trees share food and warnings through an underground network. (2) What remains uncertain is how much moves, how often, and whether the movement benefits the receiving plant rather than the fungus that carries it. (3) A fungus is not a public utility; it is an organism with interests of its own, and it may move sugar wherever it gains most from doing so. Describing it as a channel for cooperation between trees may therefore attribute to the trees a purpose that belongs, if to anyone, to the fungus. (4) None of this makes the network less remarkable; it makes the question of who is helping whom more interesting than the popular story allows.

Sentence: Clerks and neighbours added a second name to distinguish one John from another, drawn from a trade, a place, a father or some personal feature.

Paragraph: For much of history, most people in many parts of Europe had a single given name, and a village rarely needed more to tell its members apart. (1) As populations grew and rulers began to tax and count their subjects more carefully, a single name was no longer enough. (3) At first such names could change from one generation to the next, since a baker's son might become a carter. Only gradually did they become fixed and hereditary, passed down whatever the bearer actually did for a living. (4) The surname, in other words, began as a description and ended as a label.

Sentence: A driver whose car is fully insured has a little less reason to park it carefully, and a firm insured against fire has a little less reason to spend money on sprinklers.

Paragraph: Insurance exists to spread the cost of misfortune, but it can also change the behaviour of the people it protects. (1) Economists call changes of this kind moral hazard, though the term implies more wickedness than the problem involves: neither the driver nor the firm has decided to cheat anyone. (2) Insurers respond in ways that are familiar to anyone who has read a policy. They require the insured to bear the first part of any loss, offer lower premiums to those who install alarms, and refuse to pay where carelessness was gross. (3) Each of these devices leaves the insured with some of the risk, which is precisely the point. Full protection would remove the very incentive that keeps losses rare, so a policy that covered everything would soon cost more than anyone would pay. (4)

Sentence: The expansion of space adds a further effect, stretching the light of distant sources until much of it falls outside the range our eyes can see.

Paragraph: Why is the sky dark at night? The question sounds childish, but it troubled astronomers for centuries, because a simple argument seemed to show that the night sky should blaze. If the universe were infinite, unchanging and evenly filled with stars, then every line of sight, extended far enough, would end on the surface of some star. (1) Distant stars appear fainter, but there would be more of them in proportion, and the two effects would cancel exactly. (2) The whole sky would then shine about as brightly as the surface of a typical star. The darkness we see therefore tells us that at least one of the assumptions is false. (3) The modern answer rejects the assumption that the universe is unchanging: it has a finite age, so light from stars beyond a certain distance has not yet had time to reach us. (4)

Paragraph: Seed banks are often described as an insurance policy for agriculture, and the description is a fair one as far as it goes. What a frozen seed cannot do, however, is change. (1) A variety kept in a farmer's field is exposed every season to new pests, shifting rainfall and the farmer's own choices about which plants to save, and it slowly adapts to all of them. Sentence: Such restlessness is not a defect in the method but the very condition it sets out to restore, and recognising this changes what should count as evidence of success.

Paragraph: Conservation has traditionally worked from a picture: a meadow, a heath or a wetland as it looked at some chosen date, to be kept that way by mowing, burning and weeding. Rewilding with large herbivores starts from a different premise. Instead of fixing a picture, it reintroduces grazing animals such as cattle, horses or bison, or their nearest modern stand-ins, and lets their feeding, trampling and wallowing decide what the land becomes. Critics point out that the results cannot be specified in advance, and that a project unable to say what it is aiming at is hard to fund, monitor or defend. (1) The objection is real, but it partly misdescribes the aim. (2) Where a traditional reserve succeeds by holding change at bay, a rewilded one succeeds if change keeps happening: patches opened by grazing, scrub returning where the animals stay away, a mosaic that never quite settles. (3) Monitoring such a site means asking whether those processes are running, not whether a list of target species has been reached. (4) None of this makes rewilding suitable everywhere; a small reserve protecting one rare orchid may need exactly the kind of fixed management that rewilding rejects.

Sentence: But the extra water is borrowed from a store that is not being refilled.

Paragraph: When a mountain glacier begins to shrink, the rivers it feeds do not immediately run low. For years, sometimes decades, they may actually carry more water than before, because the ice is melting faster than snowfall replaces it. Towns and farms downstream can easily read this abundance as a sign that all is well. (1) When the ice has retreated beyond some threshold, less of it remains to melt each summer, and the flows begin to fall year after year. (2) The moment at which flow stops rising and starts declining is sometimes called peak water. (3) Its timing matters greatly for planning, since a valley that has expanded its irrigation during the years of plenty will face the decline with more demand than it ever had. (4) Reservoirs, water-sharing agreements and changes in crops all take years to put in place, which is why the warning has to be heeded while the rivers are still full.

Sentence: A writer about to call a sunset 'bruised' is offered 'beautiful', the commoner word, and accepts it because it is close enough.

Paragraph: Predictive text is usually discussed as a convenience, a way of saving a few keystrokes on a small screen. Its subtler effect is on what gets written at all. A suggestion appears, it is roughly what the writer meant, and accepting it costs less effort than typing the word that was actually in mind. Since the system proposes whatever is most common in the text it learned from, each accepted suggestion pulls the sentence slightly towards the average. (1) No single choice of this kind matters much, but a habit repeated across millions of messages could make written language noticeably more uniform. (2) None of this means the tools should be abandoned; for people who find typing slow or painful, they can make writing possible rather than merely quicker. (3) The point is rather that a convenience which shapes expression deserves to be noticed, and perhaps occasionally refused. (4)

Sentence: Worse than either of these costs, maintainers usually cannot tell which accidents anyone relies on until they remove one and the complaints arrive.

Paragraph: Every widely used piece of software eventually discovers that its users depend not only on what it was designed to do but on what it happens to do. A function that returns results in a particular order, though the documentation never promised any order, will sooner or later be relied upon by someone's program. Fixing such behaviour, or merely changing it for good reasons, then breaks that program, and from the user's side a fix that breaks things is indistinguishable from a bug. (1) Maintainers of mature systems therefore end up preserving accidents alongside intentions, and the line between the two blurs with each release. (2) The cost is not only the effort of carrying old behaviour forward. Each preserved quirk constrains the design of everything built later, so that a system's newest parts are shaped by decisions nobody remembers making. (3) Some projects try to escape this guesswork by announcing in advance which behaviours are guaranteed and declaring the rest open to change, a policy that is honest but only partly effective. Users rarely read such declarations, and a change that breaks enough of them tends to be reversed, whatever the policy said. (4)

Paragraph: The order in which the keys of a typical keyboard are laid out was fixed long before anyone typed on a screen, and few people would claim it was chosen with today's typists in mind. Sentence: What they actually do is find the least effortful way to satisfy the rule.

Paragraph: For years, organisations tried to make passwords safer by making them harder to create. Users were required to mix capitals, digits and symbols, and to change the result every few months. (1) The rules assumed that people would respond by inventing strong, random strings, which is not what people do. (2) Faced with a demand for a capital and a digit, most users capitalise the first letter and add a number at the end; forced to change it, they increase the number by one. Others write the password on a note beside the screen, which defeats the purpose more completely than any weak choice could. (3) Attackers know these habits well and build their guessing tools around them. (4) More recent advice has therefore moved towards long passphrases that are easy to remember, checked against lists of passwords already known to be leaked, and changed only when there is reason to think they have been exposed.

Sentence: A couplet whose second line snaps shut like a trap, for instance, can keep every one of its words in a plain translation and still lose its bite.

Paragraph: Translators of rhymed poetry are usually said to face a simple choice between sound and sense. Keep the rhymes, and the translator must bend the meaning to find English words that chime; keep the meaning, and the poem arrives in prose broken into lines. The framing is convenient, but it assumes that rhyme is ornament laid over a meaning that exists independently of it. (1) In much rhymed verse that assumption fails. A rhyme sets up an expectation at the end of one line and settles it at the end of another, and poets use that rhythm of suspense and resolution to time a joke, sharpen a reversal or make a conclusion feel inevitable. (2) Strip it away, and the words may survive while the timing that gave them their force does not. (3) None of this tells a translator what to do in a particular case; it only means that the choice is between two kinds of meaning, not between meaning and decoration. (4)

Sentence: A servant who insists that his employer was a man of honour may describe, in passing and without comment, the guests who were turned away and the letters that went unanswered.

Paragraph: A narrator who cannot be trusted would seem to be a liability for a story, since the reader depends on the narrator for nearly everything the story contains. (1) Yet a good many celebrated works of fiction are narrated by people who misunderstand themselves, conceal what they have done or simply fail to notice what is happening around them. (2) The device works because a narrator reports more than he or she understands. (3) The reader assembles a picture from these details that the narrator never draws, and the distance between the two pictures becomes the real subject of the book. Such reading demands a kind of double attention, following the voice while quietly checking it against the evidence it supplies. (4) It also depends on trust of a different kind: the reader must believe that the author has planted the evidence deliberately, or the gaps would look like carelessness rather than design.

Sentence: Explaining a trick spoils it, then, not because the secret was precious but because, once the limit is removed, the mind has nothing left to confront.

Paragraph: Stage magic is an odd art, because its audience knows from the start that it is being deceived. No one in the theatre believes that the performer has really sawn a person in half or plucked a thought from a stranger's mind. The pleasure lies elsewhere, in the collision between that certainty and the inability to see how the effect was achieved. (1) This is why magicians guard their methods so jealously, and why exposing a trick is treated within the profession as a kind of theft. Yet the methods, when revealed, are often disappointing in a telling way: a hidden assistant, a duplicate card, a moment of misdirection lasting less than a second. (2) The disappointment shows that the audience was never really interested in the method for its own sake. (3) What it valued was the experience of a mind confronting a limit, of watching closely and still being outwitted. (4)

Sentence: Both reactions are matters of taste, and taste alone cannot settle whether a cleaning was right.

Paragraph: Few decisions in a museum provoke as much argument as the decision to clean an old painting. Over centuries, the varnish that protects a picture yellows and darkens, and grime settles into the surface, until colours that were once bright look brown and muted. Removing these layers can reveal blues and reds that no living viewer has seen. To some visitors the result is a revelation; to others it looks harsh, even garish, beside the mellow image they had grown to love. (1) The deeper dispute is about what the painter intended, since some artists may have added thin tinted layers of their own that a careless cleaning would strip away. (2) Because cleaning cannot be undone, careful restorers proceed slowly, testing small areas first. (3) They stop wherever original paint and later grime become hard to tell apart, preferring to leave a picture slightly dull rather than risk removing the painter's own work. (4)

Sentence: When words flow overwhelmingly in one direction, from the language of a powerful economy or a former ruler into everyone else's, the pattern says something about who holds prestige, and speakers may reasonably resent that.

Paragraph: Campaigns to keep a language free of foreign words usually present borrowing as a kind of contamination. The image suggests a pure original that was whole before outsiders arrived, but few languages have any such original to return to. (1) Most of the vocabulary that purists defend was itself borrowed at some earlier date, and has simply been around long enough to feel native. (2) Borrowed words are also rarely kept intact: they are fitted to the sounds of the language, given its endings and plurals, and often shifted in meaning until their origins are invisible to ordinary speakers. Borrowing on this view is less an invasion than a form of digestion. (3) There is, however, something in the purist's worry that this argument does not dispose of. (4)

Paragraph: A common assumption about sign languages is that they are either elaborate systems of gesture or a way of spelling out the spoken language of the surrounding community with the hands. (2) Many of these rules exploit the possibilities of space. (3) A signer may place a person or object at a point in the space in front of the body and then refer back to it simply by pointing there, much as a speaker uses a pronoun. (4) Such features have no direct equivalent in the spoken language of the same region, which is one reason a sign language cannot be understood simply by knowing that spoken language.

Sentence: Editors who kept such a sense out would simply be left behind, defending meanings that fewer and fewer people recognise.

Paragraph: Modern dictionaries describe themselves as records of how a language is used rather than rulebooks for how it ought to be used. (1) If enough speakers use a word in a new sense, the new sense goes in, whatever earlier editors or schoolteachers might have thought of it. (2) Many readers, however, open a dictionary precisely to be told what is correct, and a record that merely reports usage can seem to have abandoned them. (3) The usage note is the dictionary's answer to this tension. Rather than ruling on a disputed word, it reports that some careful writers avoid it, or that it may strike certain readers as informal, and leaves the decision with the user. (4) Such notes are descriptive in form, since attitudes towards a word are themselves a fact about the language, but in practice they steer readers as firmly as any rule. A writer warned that a usage annoys some readers will usually avoid it, and the warning, repeated across editions, can help keep the disapproval alive.

Sentence: Surprisingly, the reason it works is the very thing that makes it feel inefficient.

Paragraph: Students preparing for an examination tend to study each topic in a single long session, going over the material until it feels secure. (1) Spreading the same hours across several shorter sessions, separated by days, usually produces better recall weeks later. (2) The gaps allow some forgetting, and the effort of retrieving half-forgotten material seems to strengthen the memory more than rereading material that is already fresh. Learners themselves, however, often judge the long session to be more effective. (3) At its end the material feels familiar and easy, and that ease is mistaken for lasting knowledge. (4) Spaced sessions, by contrast, begin each time with the uncomfortable discovery of how much has slipped away. Teachers who want students to space their work therefore have to persuade them to trust a method that feels worse while it is working better.

Sentence: The asymmetry matters because the two parties are not equally able to make up for what they have lost.

Paragraph: Complaints about grade inflation usually focus on employers and admissions officers, who find it harder to tell candidates apart when most of them hold top marks. (1) The complaint has force, but it treats grades chiefly as a sorting device for outsiders. Grades also carry information to the student who receives them, and this function suffers more quietly. (2) When nearly every piece of work earns the same high mark, a student can no longer tell an excellent essay from an adequate one by looking at the grade. The written comments may still make the distinction, but students tend to read the number first and the comments, if at all, afterwards. (3) Outsiders who lose a signal can look for others, such as interviews, tests of their own or samples of work. (4) The student, who needed the signal in order to improve, has fewer places to turn.

Sentence: In one household those resources are plentiful and a parent explains each step; in the next, the sheet is attempted alone after a long day, or not at all.

Paragraph: Homework for young children is often defended as a way of extending learning beyond the school day. The case is stronger for older pupils, who can work independently and whose assignments can build directly on lessons. (1) For children in the first years of school, the benefits are much harder to find, and the costs are easy to overlook. A worksheet sent home to a seven-year-old is rarely completed by the child alone. (2) Its success depends on whether an adult has the time, the patience and the knowledge to help, and those resources are spread very unequally across households. (3) Homework at this age can therefore end up measuring the home rather than the child, and widening the very gaps that schooling is meant to narrow. Reading aloud with a parent is a partial exception, since it asks for time and warmth rather than expertise, and most families can offer some of both. (4)

Sentence: Persuading doctors to accept that risk depends less on warnings about resistance than on arrangements, such as quick tests and clear guidelines, that make restraint safer.

Paragraph: From the point of view of a single doctor facing a single patient, prescribing an antibiotic when in doubt can seem the responsible choice. If the infection turns out to be bacterial, the patient is spared days of illness; if it was viral, the drug does little harm to that patient. (1) The difficulty is that each prescription also gives resistant bacteria an advantage, and the resistance that results does not stay with the patient who received the drug. (2) It spreads through households, hospitals and communities, and eventually reaches people who never took the antibiotic at all. (3) Stewardship programmes ask prescribers to keep these absent people in mind, by testing before treating where possible, choosing narrower drugs and stopping courses when they are no longer needed. This is a hard request, because the benefit of restraint is spread thinly across strangers in the future while its risk falls on the patient in the room. (4)

Sentence: That shift in the starting point would inflate survival figures even if every tumour screening found were a dangerous one, so it is a second distortion, independent of the first.

Paragraph: It seems obvious that finding a cancer early is better than finding it late, and for many cancers it is. Screening programmes, however, find not only the dangerous tumours they are looking for but also small, slow-growing ones that would never have caused symptoms in the person's lifetime. Such tumours cannot usually be told apart from dangerous ones at the moment of diagnosis, so they are treated in the same way, with the same surgery, radiation and anxiety. The patients concerned are counted as cancer survivors, and their good outcomes make the programme look more successful than it is. (1) Even a measure as natural as the share of patients still alive five years after diagnosis can mislead here. (2) Diagnosing a cancer earlier starts the clock earlier, so survival from diagnosis lengthens even if the date of death has not moved at all. (3) The figure that tells us whether a screening programme helps is not how many cancers it finds or how long people live after diagnosis, but whether deaths from the disease fall among those who were screened. (4) By that standard some programmes do well and others less so, which is a reason to evaluate each one rather than to reject screening as such.

Sentence: Far more often, it is the ward itself that works against the habit.

Paragraph: Almost every doctor and nurse knows that cleaning the hands before touching the next patient does more to stop hospital infections than almost any other single habit. Yet observations on busy wards repeatedly find that the step is skipped far more often than staff themselves believe. The gap is rarely a matter of ignorance or indifference. (1) On a crowded shift, a nurse may need to clean her hands dozens of times an hour, and each time the sink or dispenser is a few steps out of the way, the step competes with an alarm, a call or a patient in distress. (2) Campaigns that simply remind staff of the importance of hygiene therefore tend to produce short-lived improvements. (3) More lasting gains have come from changing the setting: placing alcohol rub at every bed and on every trolley, so that the right action is also the easiest one. (4)

Sentence: Two features of a night worker's life keep pulling it the other way.

Paragraph: Working at night would be a simple matter if sleep could be moved as easily as a work schedule. The body, however, keeps its own timetable, governed by an internal clock that is set largely by daylight. (1) A night worker who goes to bed at nine in the morning is trying to sleep at the hour when that clock is pushing hardest towards wakefulness. The sleep that results is usually shorter and lighter than night-time sleep, however dark and quiet the bedroom. One might expect the clock to adjust after a few weeks of steady night work, but it seldom does so fully. (2) Each morning's journey home in bright light nudges it back towards a daytime pattern, and on days off most workers return to sleeping at night to be with family and friends. (3) People do differ in how well they tolerate the arrangement, and some find it far easier than others, but few escape its costs altogether. (4)
