Sentence: The question a health system must eventually face is therefore not whether any single drug is affordable, but how much it is willing to pay, in total, for the progress it asked companies to make.

Paragraph: A medicine for a condition found in only a few thousand patients worldwide faces an awkward arithmetic. Developing and testing it may cost nearly as much as developing a drug for a common condition, but the cost must be recovered from a tiny number of patients. Many countries have therefore offered special incentives for such drugs, including longer periods of market exclusivity and help with the expense of clinical trials. (1) The incentives have worked in the sense that they were intended to: treatments now exist for conditions that companies once had no reason to study. They have also produced prices per patient that can exceed what most families earn in a lifetime, paid in practice by insurers and health systems. (2) Defenders of these prices point out that the total spent on any one rare disease is small, precisely because the patients are few. (3) The answer is accurate but incomplete, since rare diseases are numerous, and their combined cost grows as the incentives succeed in producing more treatments. (4)

Sentence: This indirect shield creates a temptation that any economist would recognise at once: the chance to enjoy a benefit without paying its cost.

Paragraph: Vaccination is unusual among medical choices because its benefits do not stop at the person who actually receives the injection. When enough people in a community are immune, a pathogen struggles to find new hosts, and even those who were never vaccinated are shielded indirectly. (1) A parent who declines a vaccine for a child may reason that, with nearly everyone else immunised, the risk of infection is already tiny. The reasoning is not foolish for any single family, which is precisely what makes it dangerous. (2) If many families reason in the same way, the level of immunity falls below the point at which the shield holds, and outbreaks return. (3) The protection that each free rider counted on then disappears for everyone, including the infants and the sick who could never have been vaccinated in the first place. Public health policy therefore cannot treat vaccination as a wholly private decision, even when it respects the right of individuals to make it. (4)

Sentence: A woman who begins by asking about a persistent cough, for instance, may reach her real worry, a lump she has been afraid to name, only if she is allowed to keep talking.

Paragraph: Medical training has long prized the ability to reach a diagnosis efficiently, and the classic consultation is built around the doctor's questions rather than the patient's story. Efficiency of this kind has obvious virtues in a crowded clinic, where every minute spent with one patient is a minute taken from the next. (1) Yet the habit of steering the conversation early can cost more time than it saves, because the complaint a patient mentions first is not always the one that matters most. (2) Cut off early, such patients leave with a remedy for whatever they happened to mention first, and the problem that really brought them in waits for another visit, or for an emergency. Allowing people to finish their opening account need not take long, and the fear that it will swallow the whole appointment is usually exaggerated. (3) The deeper lesson is that listening is not a courtesy added to diagnosis but one of its instruments, as much a part of the examination as the stethoscope. (4)

Sentence: None of this means that a fever should be left alone in every case.

Paragraph: For much of the modern era, fever has been treated as an enemy, something to be brought down as soon as a thermometer confirmed it. (1) The instinct is understandable, since a high temperature is uncomfortable, frightening in a child and, at its extremes, genuinely dangerous. Yet a rise in body temperature is not simply a malfunction; it is a response the body produces on purpose, at real cost in energy, when it detects infection. (2) Many microbes multiply less efficiently when the body is warmer, and parts of the immune system appear to work faster under the same conditions. (1) But the very inertia that makes the policy effective also makes its moral credentials uncertain. (2) If people remain on the donor register mainly because they never got round to leaving it, their silence is weak evidence of what they actually want. Sentence: There is, however, a less obvious cost that both sides of this debate tend to overlook.

Paragraph: Term limits are usually defended as a safeguard against the slow accumulation of power by a single leader. (1) A ruler who knows that office will end on a fixed date has less reason to pack the courts, intimidate the press or rewrite the rules in their own favour. The argument is persuasive, and in many constitutions the limit has served precisely that purpose. (2) Critics, though, point out that a limit also removes the voters' power to keep a leader with whom they are satisfied. (3) Seen this way, the rule protects democracy by restricting one of its choices, an awkward position for a democratic principle to occupy. (4) A leader who cannot stand again may stop worrying about the next election altogether, so that a final term becomes a period of reduced accountability rather than renewed restraint. Whether the limit restrains power or merely moves the danger into the last years in office depends heavily on the other checks that surround it.

Sentence: Read closely, however, many of them reveal an anxiety less about the poor dressing above their station than about the prosperous spending themselves into ruin.

Paragraph: Sumptuary laws, which in many premodern societies dictated who might wear silk, fur or particular colours, look to modern eyes like snobbery written into statute. (1) Their texts complain repeatedly of fortunes wasted on finery, of households impoverished by competitive display, and of money leaving the realm to pay for foreign luxuries. (2) Seen in this light, the laws were partly an attempt to halt an arms race of appearance, in which each family felt obliged to match the display of its neighbours. (3) That does not make them benign, for they also fixed the visible markers of rank and punished those who tried to blur them. The two motives were probably entangled, since a society that feared ruinous competition also feared the confusion of status that such competition produced. (4) What modern readers see as snobbery and what lawmakers described as prudence may in the end have been a single impulse viewed from two sides.

Sentence: A tenant who voted against his landlord's candidate, or a labourer who defied his employer, could lose his home or his wage soon afterwards.

Paragraph: For much of the history of elections, voting was a public act, in which electors declared their choice aloud or marked a ballot under the eyes of others. (1) Some defenders of open voting held that this was a virtue, since a citizen who voted in public would have to stand behind the choice and answer for it. (2) The argument assumed that the main pressure on a voter came from conscience and the opinion of fellow citizens. In practice, the pressure that counted most often came from those who had power over the voter's livelihood. (3) Secrecy did not make voters braver; it made courage unnecessary, by removing the means through which their choices could be punished. It also made bribery less attractive, since a buyer could no longer check whether the vote he had paid for was actually delivered. (4) The private booth, in other words, served the public purpose of elections by making the individual act invisible.

Sentence: The real question for a city, then, is not whether vendors belong on its pavements but how to make room for them without blocking the way.

(2) A tea stall outside a bus depot or a fruit cart near a hospital meets a need that no formal business has chosen to meet at that spot. Vendors also keep a street watched and occupied after offices close, which can make it feel safer for those walking home late. (3) The means of doing so need not be elaborate: marked zones, fixed hours and modest licence fees have all been tried in different places, and none of them requires treating vendors as trespassers. Sentence: Their apparent clarity, however, conceals two difficulties that treaty makers have repeatedly had to face.

Paragraph: Rivers seem made to be borders: they are visible from far away, difficult to cross and easy to draw on a map. (1) A river that floods can shift its channel by a considerable distance in a single season, leaving a village that stood on one bank suddenly on the other. (2) Even a river that stays in its bed raises a second puzzle, about where exactly within it the line should run. The boundary might follow one bank, the middle of the water or the deepest channel used by boats, and each choice gives a different share of fishing, shipping and islands to each side. (3) Far from settling disputes, a river can multiply them, precisely because it seemed too obvious to need careful definition. (4) Boundaries drawn across dry land, dull as they look on a map, are often easier to keep.

Sentence: Much of it became broad avenues, parks and imposing public buildings, laid out by authorities who now had, for the first time, a large empty belt to design at will.

Paragraph: When the old walls of many European cities came down in the nineteenth century, the change was widely celebrated as a liberation. (1) The walls had lost most of their military value, and they were blamed for crowding, foul air and the high price of land within them. The ground they freed, however, was not simply handed back to the townspeople who had lived in their shadow. (2) The cleared belt proved useful to governments in ways that had little to do with fresh air: wide straight roads were easy to patrol and hard to barricade, and the buildings along them displayed official power. (3) Opening a city, in other words, could also mean opening it to closer supervision. (4) None of this makes the removal of the walls a mistake, since the gains in space and health were real. It does suggest that urban improvements should be asked not only what they remove but whose purposes the cleared space is made to serve.

Sentence: A port whose harbour silts up or whose trade moves to a rival can turn inward within a lifetime, its old tolerance surviving mainly in its street names and recipes.

Paragraph: Port cities have long had a reputation for being more open to outsiders than the inland towns around them. (1) The reason is less a matter of temperament than of trade: a harbour brings strangers every week, and a merchant who refuses to deal with foreigners soon has nobody to deal with. (2) Over generations such cities develop habits that make strangeness ordinary, from markets where several languages are spoken to courts that learn to settle disputes between parties from distant places. Their food, their slang and even their buildings often carry traces of the many shores their ships have touched. (3) This openness, however, is a habit born of usefulness, and it can fade when the usefulness does. (4) Cosmopolitanism of this kind is real, but it is maintained by circumstance rather than guaranteed by character.

Sentence: Yet few people are willing to accept that conclusion, and their reluctance deserves to be taken seriously rather than dismissed as confusion.

Paragraph: It is often said that we owe things to future generations: a habitable climate, fertile soils and institutions that still work. (1) A well-known puzzle complicates this thought, because the particular people who will exist in a century depend on countless choices made now, including choices about how we live. Had we acted differently, different couples would have met at different times, and a different set of people would have been born. (2) It seems to follow that a careless policy cannot harm those future people, since without it they would not have existed at all. (3) One response is that our duty is owed not to particular individuals but to whoever comes after us, much as a builder owes safe stairs to whoever will one day climb them. On that view, harm need not be done to a specific person to be a wrong; it is enough that the world we hand on is worse than one we could easily have left. (4) The puzzle, then, does not dissolve our obligations, though it does change our sense of whom they are owed to.

Sentence: The charge assumes that adults are the best judges of their own interests, and that the state insults them whenever it overrides their choices.

Paragraph: Laws that protect people from themselves, such as rules requiring helmets or restricting certain drugs, are often attacked as paternalism. (1) Yet adults are not always the best judges of their own interests, as anyone who has broken a firm resolution knows. (2) A smoker who wishes to quit, or a gambler who asks to be barred from a casino, is not having autonomy overridden when the law helps keep a commitment already made. (3) Such cases do not settle the matter, because many people covered by protective laws have made no such commitment and would resent the help. For them the law does override a considered choice, and its justification must rest on the size of the harm prevented rather than on any claim to serve their own deeper wishes. (4) The fairest verdict on paternalism is therefore mixed: sometimes it serves autonomy, and sometimes it simply outweighs it.

Sentence: Whether the decision was taken in a clinic, an office or the moments before an accident, then, fairness requires us to see it as it looked before the outcome was known, not as it looks afterwards.

Paragraph: After the result of an event is known, people find it oddly difficult to recall how open the matter seemed while it was still undecided. (1) A business failure, a lost election or a medical complication can seem, in retrospect, to have been plainly foreseeable. We recall the warning signs that pointed towards the outcome and forget the many others that pointed elsewhere. (2) This tendency is harmless in conversation, but it becomes unfair when we use it to judge people who had to decide without knowing the ending. (3) A doctor whose reasonable treatment went wrong, or a manager whose sensible gamble failed, may be blamed for missing what was never clear at the time. Those who investigate accidents face the same temptation, since a chain of causes always looks tidier once it has been traced from the end. (4)

Sentence: This rebuilding matters most in precisely the situations where we rely on witnesses, because it is open to influence from whatever happens after the event.

Paragraph: We tend to think of memory as a recording, so that a confident eyewitness seems to be simply replaying what was seen. (1) Much research on memory points to a different picture, in which each act of remembering partly rebuilds the event from stored fragments. (2) A leading question, a photograph seen in a newspaper or a conversation with another witness can slip details into the reconstruction, which the witness then remembers as part of the original scene. Confidence offers little protection, since a memory that has been rehearsed many times may grow more vivid and more certain as it grows less accurate. (3) None of this means that witnesses are usually wrong, and many recall the central facts of an event perfectly well. (4) It does mean that the way a witness is questioned can shape the testimony later given, and that confidence in court should be weighed with some caution.

Sentence: This hidden slackening is rarely a conscious decision to shirk, and most people who do it would sincerely deny that they had.

Paragraph: When people work together on a shared task, the total effort of the group is often less than the sum of what each member would produce alone. (1) Part of the shortfall is simply a matter of coordination, since people pulling on the same rope rarely pull at exactly the same moment. (2) But a larger part seems to come from a quieter change in motivation. When individual contributions cannot be seen, each member can ease off a little without being noticed, and many do. (3) Appeals to try harder therefore tend to fail, because each member assumes that the appeal is addressed to someone else. What works better is to make contributions visible, or to give each person a part of the task that is recognisably their own. (4) Groups, in short, do not make people lazy so much as they make laziness invisible, and the remedy is to restore visibility.

Sentence: Safety, however, is not the same as delight, and a preference that repetition first builds and then wears out is a mild liking, not real enthusiasm.

Paragraph: People tend to like things more the more often they encounter them, even when they cannot recall having encountered them at all. A tune heard repeatedly in the background, a face glimpsed on a daily commute, an unfamiliar word printed again and again: each tends to grow more agreeable simply by becoming familiar. (1) The effect is often invoked to explain why advertisers repeat the same slogans and why voters warm to candidates whose names they have seen on many posters. (2) On one account, familiarity works as a signal of safety, since something met many times without harm is probably not dangerous. (3) The account also fits a limit the effect seems to have: once a thing has become thoroughly familiar, further repetition adds little and may begin to bore. (4) That is why a slogan can become agreeable without ever becoming loved, and why the things people cherish most tend to offer some surprise each time they return.

Sentence: The change is usually discussed as the loss of a craft, but the more interesting question is what handwriting does for thinking.

Paragraph: Now that so much writing happens on keyboards and screens, a growing number of schools give penmanship only a sliver of the timetable it once had. (1) Writing by hand is slower than typing, and that slowness forces the writer to choose which words are worth recording. (2) A student taking notes on a laptop can transcribe a lecture almost word for word, while a student with a pen must summarise as the lecture goes on. Summarising is a form of understanding, so the slower method may leave more behind in the mind even as it leaves less on the page. (3) None of this argues for abandoning keyboards, which serve many purposes far better than pens ever did. (4) It does suggest that the decision to stop teaching handwriting should be made on evidence about learning, not on the assumption that a faster tool must be a better one.

Sentence: Uniforms, however, do not abolish the signals of wealth so much as move them to places that a dress code does not reach.

Paragraph: A common case for uniforms in schools is that they hide visible differences of wealth among pupils, sparing poorer children the embarrassment of being seen in cheaper clothes. (1) The argument has real force in schools where fashion has become a form of competition, and where the cost of keeping up falls hardest on families who can least afford it. (2) Shoes, bags, phones, haircuts and even the newness of the uniform itself continue to tell pupils who has money and who does not. (3) A uniform may also bring costs of its own, since the prescribed items are sometimes sold only through particular suppliers at prices well above those of ordinary clothing. None of this shows that uniforms are pointless, for many pupils and parents value the sense of belonging they create. (4) It does show that the case for them should rest on belonging and convenience rather than on the promise of hiding inequality, a promise they keep only in part.

Sentence: A household in which both parents work night shifts lacks the first of those conditions, yet it may be close and loving and still almost never sit down to dinner together.

Paragraph: It is often observed that children who regularly eat meals with their families tend to fare better, at school and elsewhere, than children who rarely do. (1) From this a simple prescription is drawn: families should eat together more often, and the benefits will follow. (2) The prescription assumes that the meal itself produces the benefit, when it may merely mark households that already enjoy other advantages. Parents with regular working hours, enough money and a calm home find shared meals easier to arrange, and those same conditions help children in many other ways. (3) Telling families with irregular hours to eat together therefore adds a burden without touching the conditions that actually matter. None of this means that shared meals are worthless, since conversation across a table may well do some good of its own. (4) But the good is likely to be smaller than the bare association suggests, and the advice deserves to be offered with matching modesty.

Sentence: The waves seem to arise instead from a tension that each parent feels privately, with no one setting out to start or end them.

Paragraph: Names for children rise and fall in popularity in waves that look remarkably like fashions in clothing, yet no industry advertises them and no designer sets the trend. (1) Parents usually want a name that sounds fresh without sounding strange, and they judge freshness largely by how rarely they have heard it among the children they know. (2) A name that is rising satisfies both demands at once, which is why more and more parents converge on it. (3) That very convergence destroys its appeal, since a name heard in every playground no longer sounds fresh to the next set of parents. The name then declines, and after two or three generations it begins to sound not dated but quaint, ready to be rediscovered. (4) In this way a trend can rise and fall without anyone directing it, driven only by many private choices that each respond to the choices of others.

Sentence: Preparing for retirement, then, is not only a matter of money but of sparing oneself that slow rebuilding by starting a life beyond the job while the job still lasts.

Paragraph: For many people, work supplies far more than an income: it gives the day a shape, provides a circle of colleagues and answers the question of what one does. (1) Retirement removes all of these at once, which helps to explain why a change that people look forward to for years can leave them unsettled when it finally arrives. (2) Those who adjust most easily are often not simply the ones with the largest savings but the ones who built a life outside their job before they left it. Friendships formed away from the office, a skill pursued for its own sake or a role in a neighbourhood group can all carry over when the job ends. (3) Others find that the freedom they had imagined feels at first more like an absence, and they must slowly build for themselves the structure that work once provided. (4)

Sentence: By inspecting workshops, stamping approved goods and punishing fraud, a guild lent its collective name to each object and so gave strangers a reason to trust it.

Paragraph: Medieval craft guilds are usually remembered as cartels, bodies that fixed prices, limited entry and protected their members from competition. (1) That reputation is not undeserved, but it leaves out a problem the guilds helped to solve. A buyer in a crowded town market had little way of judging whether a bolt of cloth was sound or a silver cup was of the promised purity. (2) Seen this way, the guild's stamp was an early form of the brand, a signal that travelled further than any single maker's reputation could. (3) The difficulty is that the powers needed to police quality were the same powers that could be used to keep newcomers out. An inspection regime that began by rejecting shoddy work could end by rejecting anyone who had not served an apprenticeship under an existing master. (4) The history of the guilds is therefore less a story of good or bad institutions than of a useful tool that was easily turned to private ends.

Sentence: Each year the assembly first decided whether to hold an ostracism at all, and only if it voted to do so did citizens later scratch a name on a piece of broken pottery.

Paragraph: Ostracism in classical Athens is often mentioned as a curiosity, but it was a carefully limited instrument. (1) The man whose name appeared most often had to leave the city for ten years. (2) He was not stripped of his property or his citizenship, and he could return with his standing intact once the period was over. The aim, in other words, was not to punish a crime but to remove a figure who seemed to be gathering too much influence before that influence could harden into tyranny. (3) Because no charge had to be proved, however, the procedure was open to a quieter kind of abuse. A politician with organised supporters could hope to rid himself of a rival simply by persuading enough voters that the rival was dangerous. (4) The very feature that made ostracism gentle, its freedom from the burden of proof, was also what made it easy to turn against inconvenient people.

Sentence: This trade, moreover, went well beyond what travellers strictly needed in order to complete the journey.

Paragraph: Historians of medieval pilgrimage once wrote almost entirely about devotion: the vows, the relics, the hope of healing or forgiveness. (1) More recent work has stressed that the great shrines also sat at the centre of busy networks of buying and selling. (2) Pilgrims needed food, beds, guides, ferries and safe passage, and towns along the main routes grew prosperous by supplying them. (3) Much of it traded on devotion itself: badges, small flasks and other tokens were made and sold near the shrines in large numbers, and churches competed to acquire relics that would draw visitors. (4) It is tempting to conclude from all this that faith was merely the occasion for trade, a pretext that the real business of the roads required. That conclusion reverses the dependence. The innkeepers and badge makers prospered only because travellers believed the journey was worth making, and when belief in a shrine's power faded, its trade usually faded with it. The economy of pilgrimage is better read as a measure of how seriously people took their devotions than as evidence that they did not.

Sentence: A volcano can cause a shortage, in short, but as those two valleys show, whether a shortage becomes a famine is decided largely by the arrangements people have made before it arrives.

Paragraph: A very large volcanic eruption can throw enough fine particles into the upper atmosphere to dim sunlight across much of the globe for a year or more. (1) Summers in the following seasons may turn cold and wet, frosts may arrive out of season, and harvests far from the volcano can fail. It is natural to read the famines that sometimes follow such events as simple consequences of the weather. (2) The historical record suggests a more complicated picture. Regions that suffered similar losses of crops often fared very differently, depending on whether grain could be moved from places that had a surplus, whether stores had been kept and whether authorities acted quickly or hoarded. (3) As a result, the same cold summer could mean hardship in one valley and mass death in the next. (4)

Sentence: Economists call this the sunk cost fallacy, because money that has already been spent cannot be recovered whichever way the decision goes.

Paragraph: When a public project runs far over budget, the most common argument for finishing it is that too much has already been spent to stop. (1) On that view, the only relevant question is whether the benefits still to come exceed the costs still to come. If they do not, every further rupee is wasted, however painful it is to admit that the earlier ones were wasted too. (2) Yet the charge of sunk cost reasoning can be levelled too quickly. (3) Part of what has been spent may have bought something real, such as cleared land, foundations or trained staff, that makes completion cheaper than starting afresh elsewhere. In that case the earlier spending matters, not because it has been spent but because of what it has left behind. (4) The careful test, then, is to ask what the remaining work will cost and yield, counting the past only through its useful remains.

Sentence: Such losses, however, are a fault in the bidders' reasoning rather than in the auction, which punishes only those who forget what their victory tells them.

Paragraph: Imagine a jar of coins auctioned to a room of people, each of whom may study it but none of whom may count what is inside. Their guesses scatter around the true sum, some above it and some below, and their average may be fairly close to it. (1) Yet the person who wins the jar is the one who offered the most, and that is usually the one who guessed highest. (2) Victory, put differently, carries unwelcome information about the prize. A prudent bidder accordingly offers less than her own guess, asking what the jar would be worth on the assumption that her offer turned out to be the highest in the room. (3) The correction is not intuitive, and those who neglect it may find that they consistently pay too much for exactly the things they most wanted to win. (4)

Sentence: The customary explanation is that farmers were bound by habit and suspicious of anything their fathers had not used.

Paragraph: Histories of farming are full of implements that were plainly better than the methods they replaced and yet spread with puzzling slowness. (2) A drill earned its price on large, level fields well cleared of stones, and many farmers worked scattered strips of uneven ground. It also needed draught animals, repairs and some skill in setting it up, none of which came free. (3) For a family whose margin between a fair year and a hungry one was narrow, an untested machine was a gamble whose losses would fall on them alone. (4) What looks in hindsight like stubbornness was often a sound reading of risks that the promoters of the new tool did not have to bear.

Sentence: What matters most, then, is not whether a single hot spell strikes but how long the reef is given to recover before the next one.

Paragraph: (1) A reef that has bleached looks, from a boat, like a field of white bones, and it is natural to assume that the corals beneath have died. Often they have not, at least not yet. (2) Bleaching happens when prolonged heat leads a coral to eject the single-celled algae that live in its tissues and feed it, and the pale colour is simply the skeleton seen through tissue that has lost its tenants. (3) The animal itself is still alive, though it is now going hungry, because those algae supplied most of its food. If the water cools within a few weeks, many corals take in fresh algae from the surrounding sea and gradually regain their colour and their strength. A reef that has lost many of its corals, however, may take many years to rebuild, as new colonies settle and grow. (4)

Sentence: Some advocates have gone further and presented it as a major answer to climate change, on the grounds that farmland covers so much of the earth.

Paragraph: Ploughing turns the soil over, buries weeds and leaves a clean bed for seed, which is why it has been the default on so many farms. (1) It also exposes buried organic matter to air, so that microbes break it down faster and release its carbon as carbon dioxide. (2) Farming without ploughing, in which seed is drilled directly into the stubble of the last crop, has therefore been promoted as a way of keeping carbon in the ground. (3) Measurements have complicated that hope. Untilled fields often hold more carbon near the surface, but some of that gain appears to be offset by less carbon deeper down, where the plough used to carry crop residues. (4) None of this makes the method worthless, since unploughed soil is far less prone to washing and blowing away. It does mean that its value is better argued on the ground of protecting soil than on the ground of storing carbon.

Sentence: Each link in that chain is plausible, and some have support from careful field studies.

Paragraph: The return of wolves to a large park in the American West is often told as a parable about the hidden connections of nature. (1) In the usual telling, the wolves reduced and unsettled the elk, the elk stopped browsing young willows and aspens along the streams, and the recovering trees steadied the banks and brought back birds and beavers. (2) The difficulty is that plausibility is not proof, and the park changed in many ways at once during the same years. Drought, hunting outside the park's boundaries and other predators all affected the elk, and along some streams the loss of beavers had altered the channels so much that willows could not easily return whatever the elk did. (3) Researchers who have studied the same valleys disagree about how much of the change belongs to the wolves. (4) None of this means that predators are unimportant, only that a single dramatic cause is easier to remember than a tangle of modest ones. A parable earns its place when it helps us notice connections; it misleads when it persuades us that the connections have been measured.

Sentence: In many northern forests of North America, however, earthworms are recent arrivals.

Paragraph: Gardeners tend to regard earthworms as unmixed blessings, creatures that loosen the soil and turn dead leaves into rich earth. (1) The glaciers of the last ice age appear to have wiped out any native worms there, and the forests that grew back after the ice retreated developed without them. Their floors came to be covered with a thick, slowly rotting layer of fallen leaves, in which tree seedlings, wildflowers and many small animals found shelter and food. (2) Worms brought in with soil, potted plants and fishing bait can consume that layer within a few years. (3) Where they have done so, the ground is left bare, and the plants and animals that depended on the leaf layer decline. The trees may be affected in time as well, since fewer seedlings survive to replace the old canopy. (4) The creature that the gardener prizes for building soil is, in these forests, a force that takes apart something older.

Sentence: Following, however, is not the same as learning the way.

Paragraph: Satellite navigation has made it hard to get lost in an unfamiliar city. (1) A voice announces each turn shortly before it arrives, and the driver need only follow. (2) People who navigate by spoken instructions tend to form a poorer picture of the area they have passed through than people who have worked out the route for themselves. They may reach the destination without being able to say in which direction it lay or how it related to places they already knew. (3) For most journeys this hardly matters. It matters a good deal when the signal fails, the battery dies or the device sends the driver down a road that has been closed. (4) A traveller who glances at the whole map before setting out, and checks it against the streets now and then, can keep most of the convenience while holding on to some of the old skill.

Sentence: The danger lies elsewhere, in borrowing that nobody writes down.

Paragraph: Programmers speak of technical debt when they take a shortcut that makes software work now but harder to change later. (1) The metaphor is apt in more ways than one. Like a loan, a shortcut gives a team something immediately, perhaps a release in time for an important customer, in exchange for costs that come later. (2) Like a loan, too, it charges interest, since every new feature built on top of the hurried code takes longer to write and is more likely to break. (3) The metaphor also implies, rightly, that debt is not always a mistake. A young company that borrows time to reach the market before its money runs out may be choosing wisely. (4) Teams that record their shortcuts and set aside time to repay them can borrow freely; teams that forget them eventually find that most of their effort goes on interest.

Sentence: For most other purposes, however, energy per kilogram is only one virtue among several, and not always the one that matters most.

Paragraph: Discussions of batteries tend to fix on a single number, the amount of energy that can be stored in each kilogram. For a phone or an electric aircraft, where every gram must be carried, that number is rightly decisive. (1) A battery that stores a great deal of energy but loses much of its capacity after a few hundred charges, for example, is a poor choice for a grid store that will be cycled every day for twenty years. (2) One that can be recharged quickly may matter more to a bus fleet than one that holds a little more. (3) And the chemistries that pack in the most energy are often the hardest to keep from overheating, which counts for a great deal in a building where people sleep. (4) Gains in energy per kilogram are therefore real gains, but they are gains along one axis of a problem that has several.

Sentence: A speaker with no words to draw on would not be more spontaneous, only silent.

(4) The freedom the listener hears is real, but it is the freedom of someone who has mastered a language, not of someone who has escaped from one.

Sentence: Since the closing chapters did not yet exist when the opening ones went on sale, an author could also take account of readers' reactions, giving more room to a favourite character or altering a storyline that had displeased them.

Paragraph: A good deal of Victorian fiction was sold first in parts, a few chapters at a time, so that a single story might hold its public for well over a year. That mode of publication shaped the books in ways that survive in the bound editions we read today. (1) Every part had to finish on something that would carry its buyer through the month until the next, which is why so many chapters break off at a discovery, a threat or a question left hanging. (2) That month's wait also rewarded crowded casts and sharply drawn peculiarities, since a reader had to recognise figures last encountered several weeks earlier. (3) Some critics have regarded these traits as compromises with the market, the sort of thing a writer under no such pressure would have avoided. (4) The verdict is too hasty. Sentence: Yet when a pun fails in this way, the failure is at least plain to see, and in that sense puns are the easy case.

Paragraph: It is often said that jokes are the hardest thing to translate, and puns are the usual example. (1) A pun depends on two meanings sharing one sound, and the chance that another language offers the same coincidence is small. (2) Many jokes contain no wordplay at all and still fail to travel, because they lean on what the audience is assumed to know already: a stereotype about a neighbouring town, the habits of a profession, an advertisement everyone has seen. (3) Translated word for word, such a joke arrives intact and is not funny, and nothing on the page shows why, since the assumption it needed has been left behind. The translator then faces a choice between keeping the words and keeping the laugh. (4) Keeping the laugh usually means replacing the reference with a local one, so that what the new audience enjoys is, strictly speaking, a different joke built on the same frame.

Sentence: They told a reader where to pause and for how long, so that a text could be delivered clearly to listeners.

Paragraph: Many of the marks we now call punctuation began as aids to reading aloud. (1) As silent reading became normal and printed books multiplied, the marks gradually took on a different job. (2) They came to show the structure of sentences, separating clauses and setting off phrases, whether or not a speaker would pause there. (3) The two purposes have never been fully separated, and modern usage carries traces of both. This is why writers still argue about commas, since a comma that marks a breath and a comma that marks a grammatical boundary do not always fall in the same place. (4) Much of the confusion about punctuation comes from treating a mixed inheritance as if it were a single, consistent design.

Sentence: What happens next, when children are born into communities where the pidgin is the main shared language, is one of the more remarkable episodes in the life of languages.

Paragraph: When people who share no common language must trade or work together for long periods, they often improvise a pidgin, a stripped-down tongue assembled from pieces of the languages around them. A pidgin has a small vocabulary, few grammatical endings and a loose word order, and nobody speaks it as a first language. (1) These children do not simply copy the makeshift speech of their parents. (2) Within a generation or two they regularise it, adding consistent markers for tense, settled rules of word order and ways of building complex sentences. The result, called a creole, is a full language in every sense, capable of expressing anything its speakers need. (3) Linguists have long debated whether this rapid growth reveals something innate in the way children acquire language, or simply reflects the pressures of daily use. (4)

Sentence: That traceability matters most where the evidence is hardest for an ordinary reader to reach, as with the unpublished papers kept in archives.

Paragraph: Readers outside the academy often treat footnotes as clutter, the visible residue of a scholar's anxiety to seem thorough. The complaint is understandable, since a page whose lower third is crowded with small print can feel less like an argument than like a legal contract. (1) Yet the footnote performs a function that the main text cannot. It tells the reader exactly where a claim came from, so that anyone with patience and a library card can go and check. (2) A historian who cites a box and folder in such an archive is, in effect, handing her critics the means to test her reading of it. Admittedly, the device can be abused: a thicket of citations can intimidate rather than inform, and some notes point to sources that do not say what they are claimed to say. (3) But the remedy for bad footnotes is better ones, not fewer, because prose that cannot be traced to its sources asks to be trusted rather than examined. (4)

Sentence: Television, by contrast, builds that room for her, finished down to the wallpaper, and builds the same one for every other viewer.

Paragraph: It is usually said that radio drama declined because television could do everything it did and show pictures as well. The argument assumes that the absence of images was a defect, a gap that early broadcasters filled with sound effects only because they had nothing better. (1) Those who wrote for the medium understood it differently. A listener who hears a door creak and footsteps on gravel does not receive a scene; she assembles one, drawing on every door and every path she has known. (2) The room she imagines is therefore more particular to her than any set designer could make it, and more convincing, because she built it herself. (3) This is why certain stories, ghost stories above all, can seem more frightening on the radio than on the screen: the monster that is never shown is shaped by each listener's private fears. None of this means that radio drama was secretly superior, only that its supposed weakness was the very source of its power, and that television replaced it without ever reproducing what it did. (4)

Sentence: The fair conclusion, then, is neither that renaming is futile nor that it works on its own, but that words can only announce a change in feeling that has to happen somewhere else.

Paragraph: Words coined to soften an unpleasant subject tend to have short careers. (1) A term is introduced precisely because the older word has picked up a sting, and for a while the new one sounds neutral, even kind. But the attitudes that gave the old word its sting have not gone anywhere, and they soon attach themselves to the replacement. (2) Within a generation the polite term is being used as a taunt in school playgrounds, and reformers begin searching for another. The cycle can be traced through the vocabulary of illness, disability and poverty, and even through the names for the lavatory, which have turned over again and again. (3) Some observers conclude from this that the effort to find kinder words is pointless, but that does not quite follow, since a new word can at least signal that the speaker means no harm, even if the signal fades. (4)

Sentence: A pupil who has to count on her fingers to find seven times eight, in the middle of a problem about the cost of tiles for a floor, will often have lost track of the problem by the time she has the answer.

Paragraph: Memorising multiplication tables has a poor reputation among educators who want children to understand mathematics rather than recite it. (1) The worry is reasonable, because a child can chant the tables perfectly and still have no idea when multiplication is the right tool. Yet memorised facts and understanding are not rivals, for the mind can attend to only a few things at once, and every fact that must be worked out uses up some of that limited space. (2) A pupil who knows the fact instantly, by contrast, keeps her attention free for the question that matters, which is why the tiles need to be multiplied at all. (3) Fluency, in other words, is not the enemy of thought but one of its conditions. None of this justifies drilling tables before children grasp what multiplication means; the case is for memorising facts that are already understood, not for memorising instead of understanding. (4)

Sentence: For genuine beginners, however, unaided struggle tends to be a poor teacher, because it consumes their attention in searching for a route rather than in noticing why the route works.

Paragraph: A long tradition in teaching holds that people learn to solve problems chiefly by solving them, struggling through difficulties until the method becomes their own. For learners who already know a good deal, that tradition is largely sound. (1) Such learners often reach an answer by trial and error and come away with no clearer idea of the method than they had before. (2) Studying a fully worked solution, step by step, spares them the search and directs their attention to the structure of the solution itself. The advantage does not last, however: as competence grows, the same worked examples become redundant, and learners who are made to study them gain less than those left to tackle problems on their own. (3) The sensible conclusion is not that one method is right, but that the right method depends on where the learner stands. (4)

(2) In practice, a child who must learn to read in an unfamiliar tongue faces two tasks at once: decoding print and making sense of words she does not yet know. This is why the case for teaching in the mother tongue during the first years is not a case against the dominant language but a better route towards it. (4) Parents who want their children taught in the language of opportunity from the first day are not wrong about where opportunity lies; they are mistaken only about the quickest way to reach it.

(3) That popular version, however, went further than the evidence. Sentence: A man with a broken wrist who has waited patiently since early evening may watch a woman who arrived an hour ago with chest pain go straight through to a doctor.

Paragraph: Emergency departments do not treat patients in the order in which they arrive. Instead, a nurse makes a rapid assessment of each newcomer and assigns a priority based on how quickly the patient's condition is likely to worsen without help. The principle can seem unfair to those who wait, since it rewards neither patience nor punctuality. (1) Yet the alternative, a queue in strict order of arrival, would mean that a patient whose life depended on speed might die behind a dozen who could safely have waited. (2) Triage, in other words, does not ignore fairness but rests on a different idea of it, one that weighs the cost of waiting rather than the time already spent. (3) Even so, a department that applies the principle well can still fail its patients by leaving them uninformed, and it is often the silence, rather than the order of treatment, that waiting patients resent. (4)

Paragraph: When hospitals began asking surgical teams to work through a short checklist before each operation, many surgeons were insulted. (2) A pause in which every member of the team introduces themselves and states a concern makes it easier for a junior nurse to point out, minutes later, that something looks wrong. (3) It also explains a less welcome observation: where checklists are introduced as paperwork, ticked by one person in a corner, they tend to achieve very little. Paragraph: Iodine deficiency was once widespread in upland districts and in regions far from the sea, where the soil holds little of the element. (1) Its most visible sign was goitre, a swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck, but its gravest effect was hidden: children born to deficient mothers could suffer lasting harm to their mental development. (2) The remedy turned out to be remarkably simple. (3) Since salt is eaten by almost everybody, in quantities that vary little from day to day, a tiny addition of iodine reaches nearly the whole population with no change of habit required. The cost is small, the taste is unaffected, and no one needs to remember to take a pill. Sentence: Planners have traditionally treated these desire paths as a nuisance to be fenced off or replanted, but a different attitude is possible.

Paragraph: Walk across almost any park and you will find them: narrow strips of bare earth cutting diagonally across the grass, worn by people who preferred a shorter route to the one the designers laid out. (1) Some designers now wait a season or two after a park opens, watch where people actually walk, and only then pave the routes that feet have already chosen. (2) The result is a set of paths that people use, rather than ones they ignore. The approach has its limits, since the shortest route is not always the safest, and a track worn across a fragile meadow may destroy the very thing the park exists to protect. (3) Still, the worn strip of earth is a kind of evidence, recorded without anyone filling in a survey, about how a place is really used. A designer who ignores it is choosing to trust a drawing over the people for whom the drawing was made. (4)

Sentence: The reverse has sometimes been observed as well: when a major road is closed, the expected gridlock on neighbouring streets can fail to appear, as some trips are rerouted, retimed or simply abandoned.

Paragraph: The intuitive response to a congested road is to widen it. For a while the extra lanes do their job, and journeys that once crawled begin to flow. (1) But the faster journey is itself an invitation. People who had avoided the road at peak hours begin to use it, some who had taken the train return to their cars, and new houses are built further out along the route because commuting from them has become bearable. (2) Within a few years the road is often as crowded as it was before, now carrying more vehicles at much the same crawl. (3) Neither observation shows that roads should never be built; together they show that traffic is not a fixed quantity to be accommodated, like water to be piped, but a response to the price of travelling, measured largely in time. (4) Congestion is that price rising, and adding capacity lowers it only until demand has caught up.

Sentence: By the time the air has crossed the crest and begins to descend on the far side, it has shed much of its water, and it grows warmer and drier as it sinks.

Paragraph: Travel inland across certain mountain ranges and the landscape can change within a few hours' drive from dripping forest to dry scrub. The cause lies in what happens to moist air when it meets the mountains. (1) Forced upwards by the slope, the air cools, and because cool air can hold less water vapour than warm air, much of its moisture condenses and falls as rain or snow on the windward side. (2) The lee slopes and the plains beyond, swept by this dry, sinking air, therefore lie in what geographers call a rain shadow, receiving a fraction of the rainfall that soaks the other side. (3) Some of the world's driest regions owe their aridity less to their distance from the sea than to a range of mountains standing between them and the prevailing winds. The point is worth remembering whenever a map is read too simply, as though rainfall were a matter of latitude alone: a single ridge can matter more than hundreds of kilometres. (4)

Sentence: The winding lanes of an old quarter, by contrast, may delight the visitor but tend to resist exactly this kind of gradual reinvention.

Paragraph: Grids of right-angled streets are often written off as unimaginative, the work of surveyors who cared more about parcelling out land quickly than about making beautiful places. There is some truth in the charge, since a grid laid over hills and rivers without regard for them can produce streets that are absurdly steep or that end abruptly at the water. (1) Yet the grid has virtues that its critics tend to overlook. (2) It is easy to find one's way in, because a newcomer who knows two street names can work out how to travel between them. It offers many alternative routes, so that traffic and pedestrians are not all funnelled onto a few main roads. (3) And because its blocks are regular, they can be divided, combined and rebuilt over centuries as uses change, without the whole plan having to be redrawn. (4)

Sentence: Ships built to carry thousands of identical steel boxes needed deep berths and acres of flat ground for stacking, and the cramped quays at the heart of the old city could offer neither.

Paragraph: For most of their history, port cities were organised around the water's edge, where ships were loaded and unloaded by large crews of dock workers. The docks, the warehouses and the streets around them formed a dense, noisy working district, closed to casual visitors but central to the city's life. The shipping container changed that arrangement within a few decades. (1) The new terminals were therefore built downstream or on open land at the edge of the city, and the old docks fell silent. (2) When the abandoned waterfronts were later redeveloped as promenades, museums and apartments, the change was celebrated as a return of the water to the public. (3) There is something to that description, since few residents had ever been able to walk along the old quays. (4) But it is a strange kind of return, in which the waterfront becomes open to everyone at precisely the moment it stops being a place where anyone works.

Sentence: The puzzle becomes sharper, however, if we add one further detail to the story.

Paragraph: Imagine a wooden ship whose planks are replaced one at a time as they rot, until after many years not a single original plank remains. (1) Most people asked about such a case say that it is still the same ship, because the change was gradual and the ship never ceased to sail. (2) That answer appeals to continuity: what makes something the same thing over time is an unbroken history, not the persistence of its material. (3) Suppose that someone has quietly collected every discarded plank and, at the end, reassembles them in their original arrangement. Now there are two ships, and each has a claim: one has the unbroken history, the other has all the original material. (4) Whichever we choose, we seem to give up something our first answer relied upon, which suggests that our ordinary idea of sameness bundles together criteria that usually agree but can come apart.

Sentence: The trouble is that this account cannot easily explain promises on which nobody relies at all, and such promises are not hard to imagine.

Paragraph: A promise is a curious thing: by uttering a few words, I bind myself to a duty that, a moment earlier, was nowhere to be found. (1) One popular explanation is that promising creates expectations in others, who then rely on me and stand to be harmed if I let them down. (2) Suppose I promise a dying friend to look after her garden, and she dies within the hour, before anyone else has learned of my promise. No one now expects anything of me, and no one will be disappointed if the garden runs wild. Yet most people feel that I would still be doing something wrong in breaking my word. (3) If they are right, the obligation must rest on something beyond the harm of dashed expectations, perhaps on the trust that was placed in me at the moment I spoke, which does not lapse merely because the one who gave it can no longer check. (4)

Sentence: But the artificiality is deliberate, in the way that a laboratory is deliberately unlike the world outside it.

Paragraph: Moral philosophers are fond of strange stories: a runaway tram that can be diverted onto a side track, killing one person instead of five, or a surgeon who could save five patients by sacrificing one healthy visitor. Critics complain that such cases are too artificial to teach us anything, since real choices are never so clean. (1) By holding fixed the number of lives at stake and varying only the manner in which they are lost, the cases let us see whether that manner matters to us morally. (2) Many people, when asked, judge the two cases differently, accepting the diversion but recoiling from the surgeon, although each trades one life for five. (3) That difference is a datum which any adequate theory must either explain or explain away. (4) The critics' worry does not disappear, however: a judgement reached about a case stripped of all context may not survive the return of that context, just as a result obtained under controlled conditions may fail in the field.

Sentence: A shopper faced with forty jams may compare them for several minutes, grow weary of weighing small differences, and walk away with none.

Paragraph: It seems obvious that more choice is better: if a shop offers forty kinds of jam instead of six, every customer who would have been happy before can still be happy, and some will find exactly what they wanted. (1) Yet a very wide range of options can sometimes leave people less willing to choose at all, and less satisfied with what they eventually pick. (2) Even those who do buy are more likely to wonder whether one of the thirty-nine they rejected would have been better. (3) The effect is not universal, and it seems weakest when people already know what they want or when the options are clearly arranged. But it is a useful reminder that choice has costs as well as benefits, paid in time, in effort and in the nagging sense of a better option missed. (4)

Sentence: Yet the rule, sound as it is, can be applied too mechanically.

Paragraph: Economists advise that money already spent and unrecoverable should play no part in deciding what to do next. (1) If a concert ticket cannot be refunded, the only question on a stormy evening is whether going will be more enjoyable than staying at home; the price paid is gone either way. (2) People who follow this advice avoid a familiar trap, that of pouring further resources into a failing project simply because so much has already been invested. (3) Past investment sometimes carries information: a firm that has spent heavily on a project may know things about its prospects that an outsider does not. And for individuals, honouring a past commitment can be a way of remaining the kind of person who finishes things, a reputation with value of its own. (4) The error lies not in remembering what has been spent, but in letting the memory substitute for a fresh judgement about what lies ahead.

Sentence: Its features are oddly consistent across activities that otherwise have little in common.

Paragraph: There is a state of mind familiar to musicians, climbers, programmers and anyone who has lost track of time while absorbed in a demanding task. (1) Attention narrows to the task at hand, the sense of self as an anxious observer fades, and effort, though real, no longer feels like a burden. (2) Such absorption seems to arise most readily when the challenge of the task roughly matches the skill of the person performing it. A task that is too easy breeds boredom, while one that is far too hard breeds anxiety, and neither leaves room for complete involvement. (3) This has an encouraging implication for work and study, since it suggests that absorption is less a gift of temperament than a result of how tasks are designed. (4) It also carries a caution: a state that feels so rewarding can be sought in activities, from gambling to endless games, that absorb us without leaving anything of value behind.

Sentence: Relieving every flicker of boredom the moment it appears may therefore remove the very pressure that drives such invention.

Paragraph: Most of us regard boredom as a discomfort to be ended, preferably at once, with whatever entertainment lies within reach. (1) Yet it may have a use. (2) The discomfort of boredom is a signal that our present activity is not engaging us, and like hunger or pain, it pushes us to do something about it. (3) Sometimes what we do is look for a new task; sometimes, with nothing to do, the mind wanders, and wandering minds are often where new ideas and plans take shape. A child left with an empty afternoon may invent a game that no shop could have sold her. (4) This is not an argument for imposing tedium on anyone, only for tolerating a little of it before reaching for a cure.

Sentence: This medical label lingered for a long time, and even after doctors abandoned it the word kept a faint suggestion of weakness and self-indulgence.

Paragraph: Nostalgia was once treated by physicians as a disorder, a homesickness thought to be severe enough to weaken soldiers and sailors serving far from home. (1) Many psychologists now take a different view, describing nostalgia as a mood that does useful work rather than one that simply drags people backwards. When people feel lonely or unsure of themselves, recalling warm episodes from earlier life tends to restore their sense of being connected to others. (2) Such memories also seem to lend a feeling of continuity, a reassurance that the person who lived those moments is the same person now facing the present. (3) None of this means that longing for the past is always healthy, since a mind that lives only in memory may neglect the life in front of it. The point is rather that nostalgia, indulged in moderation, is more often a resource than a symptom. (4)

Sentence: Someone who always lights a cigarette with the first cup of morning tea may find that the craving arrives with the tea itself, before any thought of smoking has formed.

Paragraph: (1) Habits are often described as private achievements of willpower, but much of their strength is borrowed from the settings in which they form. A behaviour repeated in the same place, at the same hour and after the same preceding action gradually comes to be triggered by those cues rather than by a decision. (2) The same dependence on context explains why habits often loosen when people move house, change jobs or go away on a long journey. With the old cues gone, behaviour that once ran automatically has to be chosen again, and for a short period it becomes open to revision. (3) Those who want to drop a habit can therefore treat such transitions as opportunities, while those who want to keep one should expect to rebuild it deliberately. (4)

Sentence: Yet the protection is bought at a price, because the same excuse that softens a failure also empties a success of its meaning.

Paragraph: Procrastination is usually explained as a failure of time management, as though the delayer had simply misjudged how long a task would take. That explanation fits some cases, but it struggles with the person who knows exactly how long the work will take and still postpones it until the last night. (1) For such a person, delay may serve a purpose that has little to do with the clock. (2) If the work is done hastily and turns out badly, the poor result can be blamed on the lack of time rather than on any lack of ability. Delay, in other words, buys an excuse in advance, and the excuse protects a self-image that an honest, unhurried attempt might threaten. (3) A good mark earned in a frantic night proves little about what the delayer could really do, and so the self-image is shielded but never actually confirmed. This is why advice about calendars and planners so often fails such people: it treats a problem of self-protection as if it were a problem of arithmetic. (4)

Sentence: Opening first, then, is a strength only for the well informed; for anyone else it can be a costly way of revealing ignorance to a rival with no reason to correct it.

Paragraph: In many negotiations the first number spoken aloud exerts a pull on everything that follows. Even when both sides know the opening figure is a tactic, later offers tend to cluster around it, moving away from it less than the facts would justify. (1) This has led some advisers to recommend that negotiators should always move first and open boldly. (2) The advice is not wrong, but it rests on an assumption that is easy to overlook: that the person who opens knows roughly what the thing is worth. A seller who badly underestimates the value of an old painting and names a modest price anchors the whole bargaining in the buyer's favour. (3) The buyer, who has done some research, has every reason to accept at once and say nothing. (4)

Sentence: The recipient is expected to accept graciously, to remember the gesture and, sooner or later, to give something of comparable value in return.

Paragraph: A gift looks like the simplest of transactions: one person gives, another receives, and nothing more is owed. (1) In practice, gifts in most societies create obligations that are understood without ever being spoken aloud. A recipient who cannot hope to match it is placed in a debt that may never be repaid, and the generosity begins to feel like a quiet assertion of superiority. (3) For this reason, careful givers often choose presents whose value can comfortably be returned. Far from being a lapse in generosity, such restraint is a way of keeping the relationship one between equals. (4)

Sentence: Linguists tend to distrust such answers, noting that a vowel heard as refined in one country may be heard as rustic in another.

Paragraph: Ask people why one accent sounds educated and another sounds careless, and they will usually point to the sounds themselves: clarity, crispness, a certain precision. (1) If refinement really lived in the sound, it would not change its value at a border. (2) What listeners hear as clarity is better understood as familiarity with the speech of people who already hold status, so that an accent gains prestige by association, much as an address or a school does. (3) None of this makes such judgements harmless. Because they feel like perceptions rather than prejudices, they are seldom examined, and a speaker can be passed over without anyone believing that the accent played any part. (4) The real difficulty is not that people defend accent hierarchies openly but that they rarely notice holding them at all.

Sentence: Yet the same mechanism that disciplines the cheat can also punish the merely unconventional, since gossip does not distinguish between harm and difference.

Paragraph: Gossip has a poor reputation, and most moral traditions warn against speaking about people behind their backs. Some anthropologists, however, have argued that in small communities gossip performs a service that no formal institution could easily replace. (1) Where there are no courts or police close at hand, the knowledge that one's conduct will be discussed is a powerful reason to behave well. (2) A trader who cheats a customer, or a neighbour who shirks the shared work of the harvest, soon finds the story travelling ahead of him. (3) A young woman who refuses a match her family has chosen, or a son who abandons the family trade, may be discussed as harshly as any thief. Gossip, in short, enforces whatever norms a community happens to hold, good or bad, and its value depends on the norms it serves. (4)

Sentence: Once the change was made, the number of letters sent rose steeply, and most of the clerical labour of working out and collecting charges at the door disappeared.

Paragraph: For much of its history, a letter's postage was charged according to the distance it travelled and the number of sheets it contained, and it was often paid by the recipient rather than the sender. The arrangement seemed fair, since carrying a letter across a country plainly cost more than carrying it across a town. Reformers in the nineteenth century argued that this intuition was mistaken. (1) Most of the expense of the post, they claimed, lay not in the journey but in the handling: calculating charges, collecting money at the door and keeping accounts of every item. (2) One cheap charge for every letter, settled beforehand by whoever posted it, would sweep away most of that work at a stroke. (3) Critics of the proposal predicted that the post would be ruined, since each letter would now earn so much less. (4) The lesson reaches beyond the post: a price that tracks one visible cost may conceal a larger cost that the pricing itself creates, and may suppress demand that nobody knew existed.

Sentence: Why would an ambitious owner accept such tight constraints on a business that is legally theirs?

Paragraph: A franchise is an unusual bargain between independence and control. The franchisee owns the shop, hires the staff and bears the risk of failure, yet must follow a manual that dictates everything from the recipe to the colour of the walls. (1) The answer is that the constraints are precisely what is being bought. (2) A traveller in an unfamiliar town trusts a familiar sign because every outlet behind it behaves in the same way, and that trust is worth more than any single owner could build alone. (3) The same uniformity, however, limits what a franchisee can do when local tastes differ from the assumptions written into the manual. An owner who knows that the neighbourhood wants a different menu may be forbidden to offer it, and the independence promised at the outset turns out to be largely financial. (4)

Sentence: What sustains them is neither altruism nor luck but a body of rules that the farmers themselves devised and continue to adjust and enforce.

Paragraph: A common view holds that any resource shared by many users will be overused, because whoever draws a little extra keeps all of the gain while the harm is spread thinly across everyone else. (1) On this reasoning, a canal that waters the fields of an entire village should run dry long before the farmer at the tail end receives a share. Yet many village irrigation systems have run for generations without either private ownership or control by a distant state. (2) The rules are usually precise: turns at the sluice gate are fixed in advance, every household sends labour to clear the channels, and because the fields lie side by side, a farmer who takes water out of turn is likely to be seen by a neighbour. (3) Such systems do not refute the original argument so much as specify when it applies. Overuse becomes likely when users cannot watch one another, cannot keep outsiders away or have no voice in the rules, conditions that are sometimes created, ironically, when a well-meaning authority replaces local arrangements with a uniform code. (4)

Sentence: Such drains are expensive, however, and because their benefits appear only slowly, they are often the first item cut from a tight budget.

Paragraph: Irrigation is usually counted among agriculture's great successes, and rightly so: it has turned dry plains into some of the most productive farmland on earth. Yet all irrigation water, however fresh it looks, carries a small load of dissolved salts. When the water evaporates from the fields or is drawn up by plants, the salts stay behind, accumulating year after year in the upper layers of the soil. (1) Generous watering might seem the obvious remedy, since extra water can wash the salts downwards, beyond the reach of the roots. (2) But where the land drains poorly, the extra water raises the water table instead, and the rising groundwater carries yet more salt towards the surface. (3) Engineers therefore insist that irrigation be paired with drainage, with channels or buried pipes that carry the salty water away from the fields. (4) The result, in more than one region, has been fields once famous for their harvests turning white with salt and being abandoned.

Sentence: Yet the same total can arrive in very different ways: as steady showers spread across four months, or as a late onset, a long dry spell and a few violent downpours at the end.

Paragraph: A seasonal forecast that predicts the total rainfall of a monsoon can be judged correct even when it is of little use to the people who most depend on it. Suppose the forecast says that the season will bring roughly its normal amount of rain, and at the end of the season the gauges confirm exactly that. By the forecaster's measure, the prediction has succeeded. (1) A farmer who sowed on the strength of a 'normal' forecast could lose an entire crop in such a year, even though the season adds up to exactly what was promised. (2) This is why forecasters increasingly try to predict the onset of the rains and the length of dry spells, not merely the seasonal sum. (3) These finer predictions are harder to make and more often wrong, which leaves forecasters with an awkward choice between being reliable about what matters less and unreliable about what matters more. (4)

Sentence: The better the automation, then, the less prepared its supervisor may be for the moment it fails.

(1) In one sense it does: fewer failures mean fewer occasions on which a human must step in. (3) Some designers respond by handing control back to operators from time to time, not because the machine needs help but because the human needs practice. The aim is not to make the system less capable but to keep the person watching it capable as well. (4)

Sentence: Individual letters are drawn with generous open spaces inside them, so that an 'e' does not close up into an 'o' when headlights make the strokes glow and spread.

Paragraph: Road signs are read under conditions that would defeat most printed text: at speed, from a distance, often at night and in rain. Their lettering is therefore designed for legibility rather than elegance. (1) The gaps between neighbouring letters are made wider than in a printed book, for a similar reason. (2) Designers also tend to favour a mix of capital and small letters over capitals alone, since the varied outline of a word in mixed case is thought to help a driver recognise it as a shape before reading every letter. (3) None of these choices is apparent to most drivers, which is as it should be: a sign succeeds when it is read without being noticed. (4)
